explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "so" correctly joins the two independent clauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ice cores drilled from the Antarctic ice sheet contain tiny bubbles of air that were sealed off as layers of old snow were slowly compressed into ice. Because each bubble preserves a sample of the atmosphere from the time it closed, the deepest cores allow scientists to measure carbon dioxide levels from roughly 800,000 years ago. The record from those ancient bubbles and the much younger ones above ______ that carbon dioxide levels today are higher than at any point in that long span.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them; shows
choices.B: them, shows
choices.C: them shows
choices.D: them—shows

explanation.why: The subject of the last sentence is "The record from those ancient bubbles and the much younger ones above them," and its verb is "shows." Even when a subject is long, no punctuation goes between the subject and its verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but it would split the subject from its verb "shows."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb, no matter how long the subject is.
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation separates the long subject from its verb "shows."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A dash can't separate the subject from its verb "shows"; nothing here is being set off.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Built in the thirteenth century at Konark, on the coast of Odisha in eastern India, the Sun Temple was designed to resemble an enormous stone chariot for the sun god Surya, drawn by carved horses. Its twenty-four wheels—each nearly three meters across and covered with images of animals, dancers, and scenes of daily ______ thought by some scholars to have served as sundials, since the shadows cast by their spokes can be used to tell the time of day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: life; are
choices.B: life are
choices.C: life, are
choices.D: life—are

explanation.why: The subject "Its twenty-four wheels" is followed by extra information that describes the wheels and opens with a dash. That information must close with a matching dash before the verb "are thought." The commas inside the list "animals, dancers, and scenes of daily life" belong to the extra information and don't change this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Its twenty-four wheels" from its verb, and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs into the verb "are thought."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject "Its twenty-four wheels" connects to its verb "are thought."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before the twelfth century, the stone walls of large European churches had to be thick and their windows relatively small, because the walls bore the full outward push of the heavy stone vaults overhead. Gothic builders found a way around this ______ shifting much of that push onto flying buttresses, external arches that carried the load down to piers standing away from the building, they were able to open the walls themselves to vast panels of stained glass.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: problem by:
choices.B: problem by
choices.C: problem, by
choices.D: problem: by

explanation.why: "Gothic builders found a way around this problem" is an independent clause, and so is "by shifting much of that push onto flying buttresses ..., they were able to open the walls." The second clause explains what the way around the problem was. A colon can join two independent clauses when the second explains the first.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon can't separate the preposition "by" from its object, "shifting much of that push."
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The commas leave two independent clauses, "Gothic builders found a way" and "they were able to open the walls," joined only by commas; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The colon joins the two independent clauses, and the second clause explains how the builders got around the problem.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Tomasz had promised to be the first seller in the square, so he was up long before dawn, checking the cart against the list his grandmother had dictated. Everything was there: three sacks of rye, ground the night before; a crate of eggs, each wrapped in ______ and the jar of plum preserves that she had insisted, over all his objections, would fetch the best price at the market in town.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: straw,
choices.B: straw
choices.C: straw:
choices.D: straw;

explanation.why: The colon introduces a list of three items, and each item contains its own comma: "three sacks of rye, ground the night before" and "a crate of eggs, each wrapped in straw." When list items contain commas, semicolons separate the items. A semicolon already follows the first item, so one must follow the second as well.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Because the items contain commas, a comma here would not clearly mark where the second item ends; the items must be separated by semicolons, as the first two are.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the second and third items run together, and the eggs seem to be wrapped in straw "and the jar of plum preserves."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon can't separate items in a list, and the sentence already uses a colon to introduce the list.
explanation.D: Correct. The semicolon separates the second item from the third, matching the semicolon after the first item.

items.subject: science
items.passage: An insect rarely more than two centimeters ______ bombardier beetle defends itself with a chemical weapon. When threatened, it squeezes two compounds, hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide, from separate storage sacs into a hardened chamber in its abdomen. There, enzymes trigger a violent reaction that heats the mixture to about the boiling point of water and blasts it out through an opening that the beetle can aim toward an attacker.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: long; the
choices.B: long: the
choices.C: long the
choices.D: long, the

explanation.why: "An insect rarely more than two centimeters long" is an introductory phrase that renames the subject, "the bombardier beetle." An introductory element like this is separated from the main clause by a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "An insect rarely more than two centimeters long" is only a phrase.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "An insect rarely more than two centimeters long" is only a phrase.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a comma, the introductory phrase runs into the subject, and the sentence seems to describe "two centimeters long the bombardier beetle."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma separates the introductory phrase from the main clause "the bombardier beetle defends itself with a chemical weapon."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Fanny Mendelssohn, the older sister of the composer Felix Mendelssohn, was praised by many who heard her as an exceptional pianist, and she wrote more than 450 pieces of music, from short songs to a string quartet and a piano cycle depicting the months of the year. Although several of her early songs were printed under her brother's name and she published only a handful of works under her own before her death in ______ music has been widely performed and recorded since the late twentieth century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.D: 1847, but her

explanation.why: The sentence begins with "Although," so everything up to "her death in 1847" is one long dependent clause. It needs to be joined to the main clause, "her music has been widely performed and recorded," with a comma. The dependent clause already shows the contrast, so no other conjunction is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although several of her early songs ... in 1847" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma correctly links the long introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Although" already links the two parts of the sentence, so adding "but" leaves the sentence with two conjunctions doing one job, and no main clause stands on its own.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In January 1913, Srinivasa Ramanujan, a clerk in Madras with little formal training in advanced mathematics, mailed several pages of theorems to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy. Some of the results were already known, but others were unlike anything Hardy had seen. After studying the pages with his colleague J. E. Littlewood, Hardy had to decide whether their author was a crank or a ______ soon concluded the latter and invited Ramanujan to Cambridge, where the two began one of the most productive partnerships in the history of mathematics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: genius, he
choices.B: genius. He
choices.C: genius he
choices.D: genius? He

explanation.why: "Hardy had to decide whether their author was a crank or a genius" is a statement that reports a question indirectly; it is not itself a question, so it ends with a period. "He soon concluded the latter ..." is a new independent clause, so it must begin a new sentence (or be properly joined).
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join the two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. The period ends the statement containing the indirect question, and "He soon concluded the latter" begins a new sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. An indirect question introduced by "whether" is part of a statement, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Dickinsonia—a flat, oval organism, marked with rib-like segments and sometimes more than a meter long, that lived on the seafloor more than 550 million years ______ long resisted classification: over the decades, paleontologists described it as a lichen, a giant single-celled organism, and a jellyfish-like animal. The debate shifted in 2018, when molecules derived from cholesterol, a compound characteristic of animals, were extracted from exceptionally well-preserved specimens collected in northwestern Russia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ago,
choices.B: ago;
choices.C: ago—
choices.D: ago

explanation.why: The subject "Dickinsonia" is followed by a long description that opens with a dash, and the verb is "resisted." The description contains several commas of its own, but it began with a dash, so it must end with a matching dash before "long resisted classification."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The commas inside the description make a comma tempting, but extra information that opens with a dash can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Dickinsonia" from its verb "resisted," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.C: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the description, so the subject "Dickinsonia" connects to its verb "resisted."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the description is never set off, and "ago long resisted" runs the description into the main verb.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1850s, Chicago sat on ground so flat and so little above the level of Lake Michigan that water pooled in its unpaved streets and diseases such as cholera spread readily. The sewer plan that engineer Ellis Chesbrough proposed in 1855 was the first comprehensive one in the United States. Because the ground was too low for buried pipes to drain into the river by gravity, the plan called for laying the pipes on top of the existing streets and covering them with ______ property owners to raise their buildings, sometimes several stories of brick at a time, to the new street level.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fill. Prompting
choices.B: fill, it prompted
choices.C: fill, prompting
choices.D: fill; prompting

explanation.why: The last sentence's main clause is "the plan called for laying the pipes on top of the existing streets and covering them with fill." What follows describes a result of that plan. A participial phrase beginning with "prompting" can express this result, and it is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period would leave "Prompting property owners to raise their buildings ... to the new street level" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "It prompted property owners to raise their buildings" is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the main clause; this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma attaches the participial phrase "prompting property owners to raise their buildings ..." to the main clause, describing a result of the plan.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "prompting property owners ..." is a phrase with no subject or main verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When a museum in Lyon opened its exhibition of twentieth-century textiles, the curator, Hélène Marchetti, displayed the weavings on open frames rather than behind glass, so that visitors could walk around each piece and study both sides. On the opening night, she defended the decision to a group of skeptical donors who had expected the works to be hung flat against the walls like paintings. "A textile is not a picture of a thing," she told ______ is the thing itself, and you have to be able to see how it was made."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them. It
choices.B: them, "it
choices.C: them "it
choices.D: them. "It

explanation.why: The quotation is interrupted by "she told them," but the two quoted parts are separate sentences: "A textile is not a picture of a thing" and "It is the thing itself, and you have to be able to see how it was made." Because the second part is a new independent clause, a period must follow the speaker tag, and the next quoted sentence begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The period correctly ends the first sentence, but the words "It is the thing itself ..." are still Marchetti's, so they need an opening quotation mark; without it, the closing quotation mark at the end has no partner.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Joining the second complete quoted sentence to the first with a comma creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation after the speaker tag, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the first sentence after the speaker tag, and the capitalized "It" begins the second quoted sentence.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Selin's grandfather, who had sold spices from the same narrow stall in Istanbul's Egyptian Bazaar for half a century and who had, in all that time, never once raised his voice at a ______ merely lifted an eyebrow when the young merchant tried to overcharge him for a new set of brass scales. The merchant faltered, lowered his price, and then, as if on second thought, lowered it again. That single gesture, Selin later realized, had carried more reproach than any lecture could have.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: customer,
choices.B: customer—
choices.C: customer
choices.D: customer;

explanation.why: The subject of the first sentence is "Selin's grandfather," and its verb is "lifted." In between comes a long nonessential element made of two "who" clauses joined by "and." It opens with a comma after "grandfather," so it must close with a comma before "merely lifted"; the commas around "in all that time" sit inside the element and don't close it.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "grandfather," so the subject connects to its verb "merely lifted."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The nonessential element opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the nonessential element is never set off, and "merely lifted" seems to belong to "a customer" rather than to the grandfather.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Selin's grandfather" from its verb "lifted," and neither side would be an independent clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Cepheid variable stars brighten and dim in a regular rhythm, and in 1912 the astronomer Henrietta Swan Leavitt, studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, reported that the brighter stars took longer to complete each cycle. Because all the stars she examined lay at roughly the same distance from Earth, she could conclude that a Cepheid's period is linked to its true ______ astronomers to estimate how far away a Cepheid is by comparing its true brightness with its apparent brightness.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: luminosity, a relationship that allows
choices.B: luminosity; a relationship that allows
choices.C: luminosity a relationship that allows
choices.D: luminosity, this relationship allows

explanation.why: The sentence's last clause, "she could conclude that a Cepheid's period is linked to its true luminosity," is followed by a noun phrase, "a relationship that allows astronomers to estimate ...," that renames and sums up the link just described. Such a summary phrase is not a clause on its own, so it is attached with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma attaches the noun phrase that sums up the period-luminosity link to the end of the sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a relationship that allows astronomers ..." is a noun phrase; its verb "allows" sits inside the "that" clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a comma, the summarizing phrase runs straight into "luminosity," and the sentence seems to say the period is linked to "luminosity a relationship."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "This relationship allows astronomers to estimate ..." is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the clause before; this is a comma splice.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, carved on rocks and pillars across the Indian subcontinent in the third century BCE, became unreadable for centuries after the Brahmi script in which most of them were written fell out of use. Their decipherment in the 1830s drew on several kinds of evidence: coins that gave the same royal names in both Greek and Brahmi; short donor inscriptions from the stupa at ______ of which ended with the same two characters; and painstaking comparisons of letter shapes across hundreds of copied texts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Sanchi; many
choices.B: Sanchi: many
choices.C: Sanchi many
choices.D: Sanchi, many

explanation.why: The colon introduces a list of three items separated by semicolons. The blank falls inside the second item, "short donor inscriptions from the stupa at Sanchi, many of which ended with the same two characters." Within that item, "many of which ..." is a nonessential clause about the inscriptions, so a comma, not a semicolon, sets it off.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The other semicolons make one tempting, but a semicolon here would split the second item in two, leaving "many of which ended with the same two characters" as a separate "item" that names no kind of evidence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon can't be used inside a list item to introduce a relative clause, and the sentence already uses a colon to introduce the list.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A nonessential clause beginning "many of which" must be set off with a comma; without one, the sentence seems to mention "Sanchi many."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma sets off the nonessential clause "many of which ended with the same two characters" inside the second item of the list.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Jørn Utzon's winning design for the Sydney Opera House, chosen in 1957, called for a cluster of soaring white shells, but for years no one could work out how to build them. The curves Utzon had first sketched followed no single geometry that engineers could readily calculate, so each rib would have needed its own costly mold. His solution, reached in 1961 after many rejected schemes, was to derive every ______ different in size and orientation, from the surface of one imaginary sphere, which meant that the ribs could be cast from a small set of standard molds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: shell, however
choices.B: shell; however,
choices.C: shell however
choices.D: shell—however

explanation.why: The phrase "however different in size and orientation" interrupts "to derive every shell ... from the surface of one imaginary sphere." It is nonessential, and it closes with a comma after "orientation," so it must open with a comma after "shell." Here "however" means "no matter how," not "but."
explanation.A: Correct. The comma after "shell" pairs with the comma after "orientation" to set off the interrupting phrase.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but it would cut "to derive every shell" off from the rest of its phrase, and "however different in size and orientation, from the surface ..." is not an independent clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the interrupting phrase is set off on only one side, and the comma after "orientation" is left without a partner.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The interrupting phrase closes with a comma after "orientation," so it can't open with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many reef-building corals reproduce in a single burst each year, releasing bundles of eggs and sperm into the water over just a few nights. The timing is not ______ typically follows the full moon by several days, and within that window, colonies of the same species tend to release their bundles during the same hour or two after sunset, a synchrony that greatly increases the chance that eggs and sperm from different colonies will meet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: random: spawning
choices.B: random, rather, spawning
choices.C: random, which spawning
choices.D: random, spawning

explanation.why: "The timing is not random" is an independent clause, and what follows, "spawning typically follows the full moon by several days, and ... colonies ... tend to release their bundles ...," is also independent and explains why the timing is not random. A colon can join two independent clauses when the second explains the first.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon joins the two independent clauses, and the second one explains what the nonrandom timing looks like.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Rather" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so setting it off with commas still leaves two independent clauses joined only by commas, which is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A "which" clause must have a gap that "which" fills, but "spawning typically follows the full moon" is already complete, so "which" has no role and the sentence is ungrammatical.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join the two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For decades, models of Jupiter's interior assumed that the planet had formed around a small, compact core of rock and ice, which was later buried beneath a deep envelope of hydrogen and helium. Gravity measurements made by NASA's Juno spacecraft, which has orbited Jupiter since ______ that this picture is too simple: the core appears to be large and diffuse, with its heavy elements gradually mixing into the layers above rather than ending at a sharp boundary.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: 2016 suggest
choices.B: 2016, suggest
choices.C: 2016; suggest
choices.D: 2016, suggest,

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "Gravity measurements made by NASA's Juno spacecraft," and its verb is "suggest." The clause "which has orbited Jupiter since 2016" is nonessential and opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before "suggest." No punctuation then goes between "suggest" and its object, the clause beginning "that this picture is too simple."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the nonessential clause is never set off, and "suggest" seems to belong to the "which" clause.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma closes the nonessential clause, and nothing separates "suggest" from the "that" clause it introduces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Gravity measurements" from its verb "suggest," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The first comma is correct, but the second one separates the verb "suggest" from its object, the "that" clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In November 1974, at Hadar in the Afar region of Ethiopia, two researchers searching for fossils spotted a fragment of an arm bone on the slope of a gully. Over the following weeks, their team recovered several hundred pieces of bone representing about 40 percent of a single skeleton, later dated to roughly 3.2 million years ago. The researchers who celebrated the discovery at their camp that ______ the skeleton "Lucy," after the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds," which was playing repeatedly on a tape recorder.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: night; named
choices.B: night—named
choices.C: night, named
choices.D: night named

explanation.why: The subject of the last sentence is "The researchers who celebrated the discovery at their camp that night," and its verb is "named." The "who" clause is essential: it tells which researchers the sentence means, so it is not set off with commas. With no opening comma after "researchers," no punctuation belongs before "named."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb "named," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A dash can't separate the subject from its verb "named"; nothing here opens a pair of dashes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A long subject makes a comma tempting, but a single comma can't separate the subject from its verb "named," and the essential "who" clause needs no commas.
explanation.D: Correct. The essential "who" clause is not set off, so the long subject connects directly to its verb "named."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Carved over several centuries beginning around 600 CE, the Ellora Caves in the western Indian state of Maharashtra are among the most ambitious works of rock-cut architecture in the world. The site includes thirty-four principal caves associated with the Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain ______ was cut directly into a basalt cliff rather than built from separate blocks of stone. The largest, the Kailasa temple, was excavated from the top down, with workers removing an estimated 200,000 metric tons of rock.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: traditions, each of them
choices.B: traditions; each of which
choices.C: traditions, each of which
choices.D: traditions each of which

explanation.why: "The site includes thirty-four principal caves associated with the Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain traditions" is an independent clause. What follows must attach to it without forming a second independent clause. "Each of which was cut directly into a basalt cliff" is a dependent relative clause describing the caves, and it is set off with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Each of them was cut directly into a basalt cliff" is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the first; this is a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "each of which was cut ..." is a dependent relative clause.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma attaches the nonessential relative clause "each of which was cut ..." to the independent clause it describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A nonessential relative clause beginning "each of which" must be set off with a comma; without one, it runs straight into "traditions."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Penhallow regarded the rain for some moments with the air of one who suspects the weather of a personal discourtesy. Her niece, who had long since learned that such silences came before a pronouncement, set down her teacup and waited. "Are we to understand, then, that the bridge is impassable and that we must remain at this inn until the river consents to ______ she asked the landlord, who, having no answer likely to satisfy her, merely bowed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fall?" she
choices.B: fall"? she
choices.C: fall," she
choices.D: fall?," she

explanation.why: Miss Penhallow's words form a direct question ("Are we to understand ..."), so the quotation must end with a question mark. The question mark belongs to the quoted words, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark, and no comma is added before the speaker tag "she asked."
explanation.A: Correct. The question mark ends the quoted question inside the quotation marks, and the speaker tag follows with no comma.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The question is part of the quotation, so the question mark goes inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma before "she asked" is used for a quoted statement, but this quotation is a direct question and must end with a question mark.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When a quotation ends with a question mark, no comma follows it; using both marks is incorrect.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the low-lying wetlands of southern Bangladesh, where fields can remain underwater for months during the monsoon, farmers have for generations grown vegetables on beds that float. Each bed (a raft of water hyacinth and other aquatic plants, piled up to about a meter ______ slowly decomposes as the season goes on, releasing nutrients to the seedlings of okra, gourds, and leafy greens planted in its surface. When the waters recede, the remains of the raft can be spread on fields as fertilizer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: thick)
choices.B: thick,
choices.C: thick),
choices.D: thick

explanation.why: The subject "Each bed" is followed by an explanation in parentheses, and the verb is "decomposes." The parentheses must close after "thick," and because the parenthetical sits between a subject and its verb, no comma should follow the closing parenthesis.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing parenthesis ends the explanation, and the subject "Each bed" connects to its verb "decomposes" with no extra punctuation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The opening parenthesis is never closed, and a comma can't close a parenthetical that opens with a parenthesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The parenthesis is closed correctly, but the comma after it separates the subject "Each bed" from its verb "decomposes."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing parenthesis, the explanation never ends, and "decomposes" seems to belong inside the parentheses.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Under the Mongol Empire of the thirteenth century, official messengers traveled along a network of relay stations known as the yam, which stretched across much of Asia. Stations were spaced a few dozen kilometers apart along the major ______ a messenger carrying an urgent order could exchange an exhausted horse for a rested one and press on with little delay. Relayed in this way, news could cover far more ground in a single day than any one rider and horse could manage alone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: routes; so that
choices.B: routes. So that
choices.C: routes, this meant
choices.D: routes, so that

explanation.why: "Stations were spaced a few dozen kilometers apart along the major routes" is an independent clause. "So that a messenger ... could exchange an exhausted horse for a rested one" is a dependent clause explaining the purpose of that spacing. A dependent clause like this is attached to the independent clause, here with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "so that a messenger ... could exchange ..." is a dependent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period would leave "So that a messenger ... press on with little delay" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "This meant a messenger ... could exchange an exhausted horse" is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the first; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The comma attaches the dependent "so that" clause to the independent clause it explains.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When Filippo Brunelleschi began work on the dome of Florence Cathedral in 1420, the enormous octagonal opening it was meant to cover had remained unroofed for years. The central ______ to vault a span of more than forty meters without the usual wooden framework, since no one could find, or afford, timbers long enough to hold up the masonry while its mortar set. His answer combined two nested shells with bricks laid in a herringbone pattern, which helped lock each new ring of brickwork in place.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: difficulty, was how
choices.B: difficulty was how
choices.C: difficulty was, how
choices.D: difficulty was: how

explanation.why: In "The central difficulty was how to vault a span ...," the subject is "difficulty," the linking verb is "was," and "how to vault a span of more than forty meters" completes the verb. No punctuation goes between a subject and its verb or between a verb and the words that complete it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the subject "The central difficulty" from its verb "was."
explanation.B: Correct. No punctuation separates the subject, the verb "was," and the phrase that completes it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "was" from the phrase "how to vault a span ..." that completes it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "The central difficulty was" is unfinished without the words that complete "was."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea glass begins as ordinary bottles and jars that end up in the ______ years of tumbling against sand and stones wear away the sharp edges and give each piece a soft, frosted surface. Collectors prize the rarest colors, such as red and orange, which come from kinds of glass that were never common in the first place.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ocean over
choices.B: ocean, over
choices.C: ocean. Over
choices.D: ocean and over

explanation.why: "Sea glass begins as ordinary bottles and jars that end up in the ocean" is a complete sentence. "Over years of tumbling against sand and stones" introduces a second complete sentence whose subject is "years" and whose verbs are "wear away" and "give." Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and the second sentence begins with the phrase "Over years of tumbling."
explanation.D: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Rooibos, a reddish herbal tea popular in South Africa and increasingly around the world, is made from the needle-like leaves of a shrub that grows wild in only one place. The dry, sandy slopes of the Cederberg Mountains north of Cape ______ the plant the particular soil and climate it needs, and attempts to farm it elsewhere have largely failed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Town; give
choices.B: Town—give
choices.C: Town, give
choices.D: Town give

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "The dry, sandy slopes of the Cederberg Mountains north of Cape Town," and its verb is "give." No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, even when the subject is long, so nothing goes between "Town" and "give."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A single dash sets off extra information at the end of a sentence; it can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.D: Correct. The long subject "The dry, sandy slopes … north of Cape Town" flows straight into its verb "give" with no punctuation.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The dragon's blood tree, which grows only on the island of Socotra off the coast of ______ has a shape unlike almost any other tree: its branches spread out and up to form a dense, flat-topped crown that looks like an open umbrella. The crown shades the ground beneath it and captures moisture from the fog that drifts over the island.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Yemen;
choices.B: Yemen
choices.C: Yemen—
choices.D: Yemen,

explanation.why: "Which grows only on the island of Socotra off the coast of Yemen" is extra information about the tree. It opens with a comma after "tree," so it must close with a comma too, before the verb "has."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The dragon's blood tree" from its verb "has."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "has."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "tree" and completes the pair around the extra information.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The hurdy-gurdy is a stringed instrument played with a crank rather than a ______ turning the crank spins a wooden wheel coated with rosin, and the wheel rubs against the strings the way a bow would. A small keyboard on the side presses against one string to change its pitch, while other strings sound a steady drone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: bow;
choices.B: bow,
choices.C: bow and
choices.D: bow

explanation.why: "The hurdy-gurdy is a stringed instrument played with a crank rather than a bow" is a complete sentence, and "turning the crank spins a wooden wheel coated with rosin" is another complete sentence. Two closely related independent clauses can be joined with a semicolon.
explanation.A: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Nadia's grandmother had stitched the quilt from the shirts her children had ______ square still smelled faintly of the cedar chest where it had been stored. On winter nights Nadia traced the seams with her finger, trying to guess which faded plaid had belonged to her mother.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: outgrown and every
choices.B: outgrown, every
choices.C: outgrown every
choices.D: outgrown. Every

explanation.why: "Nadia's grandmother had stitched the quilt from the shirts her children had outgrown" is a complete sentence. "Every square still smelled faintly of the cedar chest" is a second complete sentence. Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and "Every square" begins a new sentence.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A bolt of lightning heats the air around it to an astonishing ______ roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius, several times hotter than the surface of the sun. The heated air expands so violently that it sends out a shock wave, which we hear as thunder.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: temperature:
choices.B: temperature;
choices.C: temperature, and
choices.D: temperature

explanation.why: "A bolt of lightning heats the air around it to an astonishing temperature" is a complete sentence. "Roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius" is not a clause but a phrase that states exactly what that temperature is. A colon placed after a complete sentence introduces such an explanation or detail.
explanation.A: Correct. A colon after the complete sentence introduces the phrase that specifies the temperature.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side; "roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius" is only a phrase.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "And" would join "temperature" and "roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius" as if they were two separate things, which makes no sense; the second phrase explains the first.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the phrase "roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius" runs into the sentence with nothing to connect it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The tuft of fine bristles that carries a dandelion seed—a structure that lets most of the air pass straight through ______ creates a stable ring of swirling air just above itself. This ring holds the seed aloft far longer than a solid parachute of the same size would, which helps explain how dandelion seeds travel for kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it
choices.B: it—
choices.C: it,
choices.D: it;

explanation.why: The words between "seed" and "creates" are extra information describing the tuft. That information opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash. The subject "The tuft of fine bristles" then connects to its verb "creates."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "creates."
explanation.B: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject "The tuft" connects to its verb "creates."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a dash, so it can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The tuft of fine bristles" from its verb "creates."

items.subject: science
items.passage: For most of the year, the Atlantic puffin has a dull gray beak. As the breeding season approaches, the outer layers of the beak grow bright orange, yellow, and blue. Researchers who observed puffins through the year ______ the colorful plates are shed again in late summer, leaving a smaller and plainer beak for the winter months.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: concluded that
choices.B: concluded that,
choices.C: concluded, that
choices.D: concluded: that

explanation.why: "Concluded" is the verb of the sentence, and "that the colorful plates are shed again in late summer" is what the researchers concluded—the object of the verb. No punctuation should separate a verb from its object, so nothing goes between "concluded" and "that," or between "that" and the clause it introduces.
explanation.A: Correct. The verb "concluded" flows straight into its object, the clause beginning with "that."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma can't separate "that" from the clause it introduces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "concluded" from the "that" clause that is its object.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon can't separate a verb from its object; it must follow a complete sentence.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the Cappadocia region of central Turkey, volcanic ash hardened long ago into a soft rock that wind and rain have carved into tall cones called fairy ______ rock is easy to cut, so for centuries people hollowed out the cones to make homes, storerooms, and stables with rooms stacked several stories high.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: chimneys and the
choices.B: chimneys. The
choices.C: chimneys, the
choices.D: chimneys the

explanation.why: "In the Cappadocia region … volcanic ash hardened long ago into a soft rock that wind and rain have carved into tall cones called fairy chimneys" is a complete sentence. "The rock is easy to cut, so for centuries people hollowed out the cones" is a second complete sentence. Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.B: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and "The rock" begins a new sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Jianzhi, the Chinese art of paper cutting, dates back more than a thousand years. Artists fold a sheet and cut it with scissors or a knife to produce flowers, animals, and scenes from daily life. The cuttings are traditionally made from red ______ is considered a lucky color, and they are pasted on windows and doors during festivals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: paper, which
choices.B: paper; which
choices.C: paper, it
choices.D: paper. Which

explanation.why: "Which is considered a lucky color" is extra information about the red paper, not a sentence on its own. A "which" clause that adds extra information is attached to the noun it describes with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma attaches the extra "which" clause to "paper," the noun it describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side; "which is considered a lucky color" can't stand alone.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "It is considered a lucky color" is an independent clause, so joining it with a comma alone creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Which is considered a lucky color" can't stand as a sentence on its own; this creates a fragment.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Arif's father ran the tea stall on platform three of the railway station. Every evening Arif stacked the day's coins into neat ______ he carried the full tin to his father at the back of the stall. He was too young to pour the tea himself, but he was proud to be trusted with the money.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: towers then
choices.B: towers, and then
choices.C: towers and then
choices.D: towers, then

explanation.why: "Every evening Arif stacked the day's coins into neat towers" is a complete sentence, and "he carried the full tin to his father" is another. Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as "and." "Then" alone is not a conjunction and can't do that job.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.B: Correct. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "and" joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Then" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma plus "then" joins two independent clauses with only a comma—a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The okapi, a shy forest animal of central Africa, has a dark velvety body and legs marked with bold black-and-white stripes like a zebra's. Why would an animal that hides in dense forest carry such striking ______ think the stripes help young okapis follow their mothers through the dim undergrowth, where the pattern stands out more than the rest of the body does.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: markings, some scientists
choices.B: markings? Some scientists
choices.C: markings. Some scientists
choices.D: markings some scientists

explanation.why: "Why would an animal that hides in dense forest carry such striking markings" is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark. "Some scientists think the stripes help young okapis" is a new sentence that answers it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma can't end a question, and it can't join the question to the independent clause that follows; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. The question mark ends the direct question, and "Some scientists" begins a new sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period correctly separates the two sentences, but the first sentence is a direct question and needs a question mark, not a period.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the question and the sentence that follows run together.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, opened in 1881, climbs almost 2,000 meters from the plains of West Bengal to the hill town of Darjeeling on tracks only 61 centimeters ______ to gain height on slopes too steep to climb directly, its engineers built loops and zigzags into the line. The small trains, affectionately called toy trains, still run today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: apart, which
choices.B: apart;
choices.C: apart,
choices.D: apart

explanation.why: "The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway … climbs almost 2,000 meters … on tracks only 61 centimeters apart" is a complete sentence. "To gain height on slopes too steep to climb directly, its engineers built loops and zigzags into the line" is a second complete sentence. Two closely related independent clauses can be joined with a semicolon.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Which" would turn the second clause into a description of the tracks, but "which to gain height … its engineers built loops" has no place for "which" in the clause and makes no grammatical sense.
explanation.B: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: science
items.passage: The tagua palm of northern South America produces seeds so hard and white that they are known as vegetable ivory. Before plastics became common, factories in Europe and the United States ______ millions of tagua seeds every year into buttons for coats and shirts. Today a few workshops still use the seeds for jewelry and small carvings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: turned;
choices.B: turned
choices.C: turned,
choices.D: turned:

explanation.why: "Turned" is the verb of the sentence, and "millions of tagua seeds" is its object—the thing that was turned into buttons. No punctuation should separate a verb from its object, so nothing goes between "turned" and "millions."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the verb off from its object.
explanation.B: Correct. The verb "turned" flows straight into its object with no punctuation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "turned" from its object "millions of tagua seeds."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete sentence; "factories in Europe and the United States turned" is not complete without its object.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The steel pan of Trinidad and Tobago was first made in the 1930s and 1940s from discarded oil ______ it is now played in concert halls around the world. Makers hammer the bottom of a barrel into a shallow bowl and then shape and tune separate areas of the surface so that each one rings with a different note.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: barrels, but
choices.B: barrels; but
choices.C: barrels,
choices.D: barrels, however

explanation.why: "The steel pan … was first made in the 1930s and 1940s from discarded oil barrels" is a complete sentence, and "it is now played in concert halls around the world" is another. Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as "but," which also signals the contrast between the humble origin and the concert halls.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "but" joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses on its own; it is not used together with "but."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma plus "however" still joins two independent clauses with only a comma—a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Japanese macaques, which live farther north than any other nonhuman ______ have adapted to winters with deep snow. In Jigokudani, a valley in the mountains of central Japan, one troop is famous for soaking in natural hot springs, a habit that researchers first recorded in the 1960s and that the monkeys appear to have passed down through generations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: primate,
choices.B: primate
choices.C: primate;
choices.D: primate, and

explanation.why: "Which live farther north than any other nonhuman primate" is extra information about the macaques. It opens with a comma after "macaques," so it must close with a comma too, before the verb "have adapted."
explanation.A: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "macaques" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "have adapted."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Japanese macaques" from its verb "have adapted."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Once the comma closes the extra information, "and have adapted" is left with nothing to join to; the subject "Japanese macaques" needs "have adapted" as its own verb, not as a second item after "and."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every afternoon Sameer sat beside his grandmother on the worn carpet while she showed him how to pump the bellows of her old harmonium with one hand and press the keys with the other. "Listen to the note before you play the next ______ she told him, "and let your fingers wait for your ears."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: one,"
choices.B: one",
choices.C: one."
choices.D: one"

explanation.why: The grandmother's sentence is interrupted by "she told him" and then continues with "and let your fingers wait for your ears." The first part of a quotation that is interrupted this way ends with a comma, and in American English that comma goes inside the closing quotation marks.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma marks the break before "she told him," and it sits inside the closing quotation marks.
explanation.B: Incorrect. In American English, a comma that ends part of a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks, not outside them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would end the quoted sentence, but the quotation continues with "and let your fingers," which is not a new sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the quoted words run straight into "she told him" with nothing to mark the break.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Although earlier inventors had tried to make a fastener that would close with a single ______ was the Swedish-born engineer Gideon Sundback who, in 1913, designed the row of interlocking metal teeth that made the modern zipper work. The name "zipper" came later, from a company that used the fasteners on rubber boots.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: pull, it
choices.B: pull; it
choices.C: pull it
choices.D: pull. It

explanation.why: "Although earlier inventors had tried to make a fastener that would close with a single pull" is a dependent clause—it begins with "Although" and can't stand alone. The main clause that completes it, "it was the Swedish-born engineer Gideon Sundback who … designed the row of interlocking metal teeth," follows after a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma separates the introductory dependent clause from the main clause that completes the sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, and the "Although" clause can't stand alone.
explanation.C: Incorrect. An introductory dependent clause of this length must be set off from the main clause with a comma.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period after "pull" leaves the "Although" clause standing alone as a fragment.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The electric eel of South America is not a true eel but a kind of knifefish. The thousands of specialized cells stacked along the length of its ______ a small voltage each, like batteries connected in a row, and together they can deliver a shock of several hundred volts to stun prey or drive off a predator.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: body: produce
choices.B: body produce
choices.C: body, produce
choices.D: body; produce

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "The thousands of specialized cells stacked along the length of its body," and its verb is "produce." No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, even when the subject is long, so nothing goes between "body" and "produce."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete sentence; "The thousands of specialized cells stacked along the length of its body" is not one.
explanation.B: Correct. The long subject "The thousands of specialized cells … its body" flows straight into its verb "produce" with no punctuation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The ukulele developed in Hawaii in the 1880s from a small four-stringed guitar brought by immigrants from the Portuguese island of ______ the instrument quickly won the favor of the Hawaiian royal family, which helped it spread across the islands. Its name is often translated as "jumping flea," perhaps because of the way a player's fingers move over the strings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Madeira, and
choices.B: Madeira,
choices.C: Madeira
choices.D: Madeira; and

explanation.why: "The ukulele developed in Hawaii in the 1880s from a small four-stringed guitar brought by immigrants from the Portuguese island of Madeira" is a complete sentence, and "the instrument quickly won the favor of the Hawaiian royal family" is another. Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as "and."
explanation.A: Correct. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "and" joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses on its own; it is not used together with "and."

items.subject: science
items.passage: In a tropical cloud forest, the trees are wrapped in mist for much of the year. Mosses, ferns, and orchids grow thickly on the branches, and they do far more than ______ they comb tiny droplets out of the passing fog, and the water drips to the forest floor. In some cloud forests, this fog drip supplies a large share of the water that reaches the soil.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: decorate, which
choices.B: decorate;
choices.C: decorate
choices.D: decorate,

explanation.why: "Mosses, ferns, and orchids grow thickly on the branches, and they do far more than decorate" is a complete sentence. "They comb tiny droplets out of the passing fog" is a second complete sentence that explains the first. Two closely related independent clauses can be joined with a semicolon.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Which" would attach the second clause to "decorate" as a description, but "which they comb tiny droplets out of the passing fog" has no place for "which" and makes no grammatical sense.
explanation.B: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Lalbagh Fort in Dhaka, Bangladesh, was begun in 1678 by a Mughal prince but was never finished. Visitors today can still see three main ______ a mosque, a tomb, and an audience hall with a bathhouse. Beyond these, much of what the builders planned, including the walls that would have enclosed a far larger complex, was simply abandoned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: structures
choices.B: structures, which
choices.C: structures:
choices.D: structures;

explanation.why: "Visitors today can still see three main structures" is a complete sentence. "A mosque, a tomb, and an audience hall with a bathhouse" is not a clause but a list naming those three structures. A colon placed after a complete sentence introduces such a list.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the list runs into the sentence with nothing to connect it to "three main structures."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Which" introduces a clause with a verb, but "a mosque, a tomb, and an audience hall" is only a list of nouns, so "which" has nothing to attach to.
explanation.C: Correct. A colon after the complete sentence introduces the list of the three structures.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side; the list that follows is not a clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Earth's rotation is not perfectly steady, so a day measured by the sun does not always match a day measured by atomic ______ keep the two in step, timekeepers have occasionally added a leap second to the world's official clocks, most recently at the end of 2016. The practice is now scheduled to end by 2035.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: clocks, to
choices.B: clocks; and to
choices.C: clocks. To
choices.D: clocks to

explanation.why: "Earth's rotation is not perfectly steady, so a day measured by the sun does not always match a day measured by atomic clocks" is a complete sentence. "To keep the two in step" introduces a second complete sentence whose subject is "timekeepers" and whose verb is "have added." Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses on its own; it is not used together with "and."
explanation.C: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and the second sentence begins with the phrase "To keep the two in step."
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For as long as Zara could remember, her grandfather had kept a typewriter repair shop on a side street in ______ a narrow room lined with shelves of spare keys, ribbons, and rollers. Few customers came anymore, but every machine that did arrive left the shop with its letters striking the page as evenly as the day it was made.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Rawalpindi,
choices.B: Rawalpindi. A
choices.C: Rawalpindi;
choices.D: Rawalpindi

explanation.why: "A narrow room lined with shelves of spare keys, ribbons, and rollers" is not a sentence; it is a phrase that renames the shop. Such a phrase is attached to the end of a sentence with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma attaches the phrase that renames the shop to the end of the sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "A narrow room lined with shelves of spare keys, ribbons, and rollers" has no verb and can't stand as a sentence on its own; this creates a fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side; the describing phrase is not a clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the describing phrase runs into "Rawalpindi" with nothing to connect it to the shop.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The roving coral grouper, a reef fish of the Red Sea and the Indian ______ sometimes hunts with a partner of a different species. When prey hides in a crevice too narrow for the grouper to enter, the grouper may swim to a nearby moray eel and shake its head in a signal that researchers have described as an invitation; the eel then follows it to the hiding place and flushes the prey out. Biologists regard this as a rare example of cooperation across species in the wild.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Ocean,
choices.B: Ocean, and
choices.C: Ocean
choices.D: Ocean;

explanation.why: "A reef fish of the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean" is extra information that renames the grouper. It opens with a comma after "grouper," so it must close with a comma too, before the verb "hunts." The semicolon later in the text joins two independent clauses and has no bearing on this boundary.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "grouper" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Once the comma closes the extra information, "and sometimes hunts" is left with nothing to join to; the subject needs "hunts" as its own verb, not as a second item after "and."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "hunts."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The roving coral grouper" from its verb "hunts."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Empress Market, which opened in Karachi in 1889, was named for Queen Victoria and built around a large courtyard where traders sold grain, vegetables, and spices. Its most visible feature is a clock tower some 40 meters ______ a landmark that has stood over the crowded streets of the surrounding district for more than a century. The market is still busy today, and the tower remains one of the best-known sights of the old city.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: high
choices.B: high,
choices.C: high. A
choices.D: high;

explanation.why: "A landmark that has stood over the crowded streets … for more than a century" is not a sentence; it is a phrase that renames the clock tower. Such a phrase is attached to the end of a sentence with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the describing phrase runs into "high" with nothing to connect it to the tower.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the phrase that renames the clock tower to the end of the sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "A landmark that has stood over the crowded streets" contains only a "that" clause and no main verb, so it can't stand as a sentence; this creates a fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side; the describing phrase is not a clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Horton Plains, a high plateau in the central hills of Sri Lanka, is a windswept grassland broken by patches of cloud forest. At its southern edge, the land ends at a cliff known as World's End, where the ground drops away almost 900 meters to the valleys ______ clear mornings, visitors can see the ocean far to the south, but by midmorning fog usually rolls in and hides the view entirely.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: below; and on
choices.B: below, on
choices.C: below. On
choices.D: below on

explanation.why: "At its southern edge, the land ends at a cliff known as World's End, where the ground drops away almost 900 meters to the valleys below" is a complete sentence. "On clear mornings" introduces a second complete sentence whose subject is "visitors" and whose verb is "can see." Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses on its own; it is not used together with "and."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and the second sentence begins with the phrase "On clear mornings."
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, "below on clear mornings" reads as one phrase and the two independent clauses run together.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Foxfire is a faint greenish light given off by certain fungi that grow in rotting wood. The glow comes from a chemical reaction inside the fungus, and people have noticed it for a very long time: Aristotle wrote of glowing wood more than two thousand years ago. Why a fungus would spend energy on light is less clear. A night-flying insect drawn to the glow may land on the ______ then carry its spores away to fresh logs when it leaves, though some researchers suspect that the light is nothing more than a byproduct of the fungus's chemistry.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fungus and
choices.B: fungus; and
choices.C: fungus. And
choices.D: fungus, and

explanation.why: The subject "A night-flying insect" has two verbs: it "may land on the fungus" and "then carry its spores away." When "and" joins two verbs that share one subject, no comma is placed before it, because the words after "and" do not form an independent clause.
explanation.A: Correct. "And" joins the two verbs "may land" and "carry," which share the subject "A night-flying insect," so no punctuation is needed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side; "and then carry its spores away" is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "And then carry its spores away to fresh logs" has no subject and can't stand as a sentence; this creates a fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma before "and" is used when "and" joins two independent clauses; "then carry its spores away" has no subject of its own, so the comma wrongly splits the two verbs.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Teresa owned exactly one thing of value, and she had never once thought of selling it. The ______ her grandfather had carried from Lisbon in a case lined with faded green silk was older than anyone in the family could say, and its varnish had worn to bare wood where generations of chins had rested. When she tuned it on quiet evenings, the sound seemed to fill the small apartment with voices she had never heard.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: violin, which
choices.B: violin that
choices.C: violin, that
choices.D: violin; that

explanation.why: "That her grandfather had carried from Lisbon in a case lined with faded green silk" identifies which violin is meant; it is essential information, so no comma separates it from "violin." The subject "The violin" then meets its verb, "was," with no punctuation in between.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma plus "which" would make the clause extra information, which must then be closed with a second comma before "was"; no such comma exists in the text, so the pair is left open.
explanation.B: Correct. The essential "that" clause attaches directly to "violin," and the subject connects to its verb "was."
explanation.C: Incorrect. An essential clause beginning with "that" is never set off by a comma.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side; "that her grandfather had carried from Lisbon" can't stand alone.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: From 1866 until 1984, Paris delivered urgent messages through a network of pneumatic tubes beneath its streets. A letter sealed in a metal ______ no larger than a rolling pin, was pushed through the pipes by compressed air and could cross the city in under an hour, far faster than any messenger on the crowded boulevards above. At its height the network stretched for more than 400 kilometers, and its capsules carried everything from love letters to stock prices.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: capsule—
choices.B: capsule,
choices.C: capsule
choices.D: capsule;

explanation.why: "No larger than a rolling pin" is extra information describing the capsule. It closes with a comma after "pin," so it must open with a comma too, right after "capsule." The subject "A letter sealed in a metal capsule" then connects to its verb "was pushed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The extra information closes with a comma, so it can't open with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Correct. The opening comma matches the closing comma after "pin" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the extra information is never set off, and the comma after "pin" is left without a partner.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "A letter sealed in a metal capsule" from the rest of its sentence.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 2014, a British company unveiled Vantablack, a coating made of a dense forest of vertically aligned carbon nanotubes, each thousands of times thinner than a human hair. Light that enters the forest bounces between the tubes until nearly all of it is absorbed as ______ the coating swallows about 99.96 percent of the visible light that reaches it. A surface treated with it looks less like a black object than like a hole cut in space, and engineers value the material for lining telescopes, where stray reflections would blur faint images.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: heat; in total,
choices.B: heat in total,
choices.C: heat, in total,
choices.D: heat and in total,

explanation.why: "Light that enters the forest bounces between the tubes until nearly all of it is absorbed as heat" is a complete sentence, and "the coating swallows about 99.96 percent of the visible light that reaches it" is another. "In total" is a transitional phrase, not a conjunction, so the two independent clauses need a semicolon before it.
explanation.A: Correct. A semicolon joins the two closely related independent clauses, and the comma after "in total" sets off the transitional phrase.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; "in total" is not a conjunction, so this is a comma splice.
