explanation.D: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The seeds in the head of a sunflower are arranged in two families of spirals—one curving clockwise and the other ______ and the number of spirals in each family is usually a pair of neighboring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55. The pattern is not a coincidence. Each new seed forms at the center at an angle of about 137.5 degrees from the one before it, and that particular angle packs the seeds more tightly than any other would, leaving no wasted space as the head grows.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: counterclockwise
choices.B: counterclockwise—
choices.C: counterclockwise,
choices.D: counterclockwise;

explanation.why: "One curving clockwise and the other counterclockwise" is extra information explaining the two families of spirals. It opens with a dash after "spirals," so it must close with a dash before the sentence continues with "and the number of spirals."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing mark, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into "and the number of spirals."
explanation.B: Correct. The closing dash matches the opening dash after "spirals" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a dash, so it can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't close a supplement that opened with a dash, and what follows it must be an independent clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Lake Hillier, on an island off the southern coast of Western Australia, is a startling shade of bubble-gum pink. Scientists who have sampled its water point to two likely ______ a salt-loving alga called Dunaliella salina, which produces a red pigment, and bacteria that thrive in extremely salty conditions. Unlike some colored lakes, Lake Hillier keeps its tint when the water is scooped into a bottle, which suggests that the color comes from what is dissolved and living in it rather than from the way light strikes the surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: sources, these are
choices.B: sources;
choices.C: sources:
choices.D: sources

explanation.why: "Scientists who have sampled its water point to two likely sources" is a complete sentence, and what follows is a list naming those two sources. A colon after an independent clause introduces a list or explanation of what came before.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "These are a salt-loving alga … and bacteria" is a second independent clause, and a comma alone can't join two independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but the list that follows is not a clause.
explanation.C: Correct. The colon follows a complete sentence and introduces the list of the two sources.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, "sources" runs straight into the list that names them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The green of the northern lights comes from oxygen atoms about 100 to 150 kilometers up, which give off green light when fast-moving particles from the sun collide with them. Higher still, where the air is far thinner, oxygen atoms are struck less often and have time to release a deep red light ______ is why the rare all-red auroras appear only at the very top of a display. Nitrogen adds the blue and purple fringes sometimes seen along the lower edge.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: instead. Which
choices.B: instead, which
choices.C: instead; which
choices.D: instead which

explanation.why: "Which is why the rare all-red auroras appear only at the very top of a display" is a relative clause that comments on the whole statement before it. Such a clause is not a sentence on its own, so it must be attached to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Which is why …" can't stand alone as a sentence, so the period leaves a fragment.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the "which" clause to the independent clause it explains.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but "which is why …" is not one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A "which" clause that comments on the whole preceding statement must be set off with a comma.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ice cores drilled from the Greenland ice sheet, some of them more than three kilometers ______ hold a record of the atmosphere that stretches back more than 100,000 years. As snow piled up each winter and was pressed into ice, tiny bubbles of air were sealed inside it. By melting a slice of core in a vacuum and measuring the gases that escape, researchers can read the level of carbon dioxide in the air at the time the snow fell, and the visible layers let them count the years, much as rings record the age of a tree.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: long,
choices.B: long;
choices.C: long
choices.D: long—

explanation.why: "Some of them more than three kilometers long" is extra information about the ice cores. It opens with a comma after "sheet," so it must close with a comma before the verb "hold."
explanation.A: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "sheet" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Ice cores" from its verb "hold."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "hold."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Yala National Park, in the dry southeastern corner of Sri Lanka, is thought to have one of the highest densities of leopards anywhere in the world. Visitors who hope to see one have several things on their side, such ______ the park's open scrubland, its many watering holes, and the habit of the Sri Lankan leopard, which has no tigers or lions to compete with, of hunting by day as well as by night. Even so, a sighting is never guaranteed, and guides like to say that the leopard decides when it will be seen.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: as,
choices.B: as
choices.C: as;
choices.D: as:

explanation.why: "Such as" introduces the examples that follow, and the examples complete the phrase. No punctuation should separate "such as" from the items it introduces.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma can't separate "such as" from the examples that complete it.
explanation.B: Correct. "Such as" leads directly into its examples with no punctuation between them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides; the list of examples is not a clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it can't come between "such as" and the examples it introduces.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Tomatoes ripen in response to ethylene, a gas that fruits produce as they mature. Commercial growers often pick tomatoes while they are still green and firm, so that they survive shipping, and then expose them to ethylene in sealed rooms before sending them to stores. A cook can use the same trick at home for free. Because a banana releases ethylene steadily as it ______ a green tomato placed in a paper bag with a banana will turn red within a few days, while one left on an open counter will take considerably longer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ripens.
choices.B: ripens,
choices.C: ripens, and
choices.D: ripens;

explanation.why: "Because a banana releases ethylene steadily as it ripens" is a dependent clause: it begins with "Because," so it can't stand alone. A dependent clause that opens a sentence is followed by a comma and then the main clause, "a green tomato … will turn red."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period leaves "Because a banana releases ethylene steadily as it ripens" standing alone as a fragment.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma separates the introductory dependent clause from the main clause that follows it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "And" joins two equal parts; it can't connect a dependent "Because" clause to the main clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but a clause beginning with "Because" is not one.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The oldest known living tree (a Great Basin bristlecone pine that researchers have nicknamed ______ grows high in the White Mountains of eastern California and has been alive for more than 4,800 years. Bristlecones grow slowly in thin, dry soil near the tree line, and their dense, resin-rich wood resists rot and insects. Even a tree that is mostly dead can keep a thin strip of living bark alive for centuries, which is one reason these twisted, weather-beaten pines outlast nearly every other living thing on Earth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Methuselah
choices.B: Methuselah,
choices.C: Methuselah)
choices.D: Methuselah),

explanation.why: "A Great Basin bristlecone pine that researchers have nicknamed Methuselah" is extra information that opens with a parenthesis after "tree." It must close with a matching parenthesis before the verb "grows."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing parenthesis, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "grows."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a parenthesis, so it can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Correct. The closing parenthesis matches the opening one and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The closing parenthesis is right, but the comma after it separates the subject "The oldest known living tree" from its verb "grows."

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the 1980s, the red kite, a fork-tailed bird of prey, had been reduced in Britain to a few dozen pairs in the hills of central Wales. Beginning in 1989, conservationists released young kites brought from Spain into the Chiltern Hills northwest of ______ worked better than anyone had expected. Within twenty years, hundreds of pairs were nesting in the area, and the birds had spread into neighboring counties. Today a red kite wheeling over a highway is an ordinary sight in parts of England where the species had been absent for more than a century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: London, the plan
choices.B: London, and the plan
choices.C: London the plan
choices.D: London; the plan,

explanation.why: "Conservationists released young kites … northwest of London" is a complete sentence, and "the plan worked better than anyone had expected" is another. Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as "and."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma plus "and" correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The semicolon is fine, but the comma after "plan" wrongly separates the subject "the plan" from its verb "worked."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The corroded lump of bronze that sponge divers pulled from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in ______ to be the remains of a geared device more than 2,000 years old. Working from X-ray scans of its fragments, researchers have shown that its dozens of interlocking bronze gears modeled the movements of the sun and moon, predicted eclipses, and tracked the four-year cycle of the ancient Greek games. Nothing of comparable complexity is known to have been built again for more than a thousand years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: 1901; turned out
choices.B: 1901 turned out
choices.C: 1901, turned out
choices.D: 1901—turned out

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is the long phrase "The corroded lump of bronze that sponge divers pulled from a shipwreck … in 1901," and its verb is "turned out." No punctuation should come between a subject and its verb, however long the subject is.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides; "turned out to be the remains …" is not one.
explanation.B: Correct. The verb "turned out" follows its subject directly, with no punctuation between them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A single dash can't separate a subject from its verb; dashes set off extra information in pairs or introduce an afterthought.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Many people assume that SOS stands for "save our souls" or "save our ship," but the letters were never an abbreviation. When delegates from several countries met in Berlin in 1906 to agree on a single radio distress call, the signal they chose meant nothing at all. Why, then, did they settle on those three ______ answer lies in Morse code. Three dots, three dashes, and three dots form a pattern that is easy to send, easy to recognize through static, and hard to confuse with anything else. The call came into international use in 1908, and the words were attached to it afterward.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: letters, the
choices.B: letters? The
choices.C: letters; the
choices.D: letters. The

explanation.why: "Why, then, did they settle on those three letters" is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark. "The answer lies in Morse code" then begins a new sentence with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses, and the question is left without its question mark.
explanation.B: Correct. The question mark ends the direct question, and a new sentence begins with "The."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't end a direct question; the question needs its own question mark.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before the 1950s, cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece: sacks, barrels, and crates were lifted aboard by crane and stowed by hand, and a vessel could spend more days in port than at sea. Malcolm McLean, a trucking company owner, reasoned that the slow part was not the voyage but the handling. The solution, in his ______ was to pack goods into identical steel boxes that could be lifted straight from a truck onto a ship. In 1956 his first converted tanker carried 58 such boxes from Newark to Houston, and the standardized container it introduced now carries most of the world's manufactured goods.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: view;
choices.B: view,
choices.C: view—
choices.D: view

explanation.why: "In his view" interrupts the sentence "The solution was to pack goods into identical steel boxes." An interrupting phrase is set off by a pair of commas; the first comma is already there after "solution," so a second comma must follow "view."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The solution" from its verb "was."
explanation.B: Correct. The comma after "view" completes the pair of commas that sets off the interrupting phrase.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The interrupting phrase opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The comma after "solution" opens a pair, so a matching comma must close it after "view."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: On December 12, 1901, Guglielmo Marconi sat in a room on Signal Hill in St. John's, Newfoundland, listening through an earpiece to a receiver attached to an antenna held aloft by a kite. He reported hearing three faint clicks, the letter S in Morse code, sent from a transmitter in Cornwall more than 3,000 kilometers ______ physicists at the time insisted that radio waves could not follow the curve of the Earth, so the claim met with doubt as well as excitement. Later experiments proved the principle, and regular transatlantic radio service began within a few years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: away. However many
choices.B: away, however, many
choices.C: away; however, many
choices.D: away however, many

explanation.why: "He reported hearing three faint clicks … more than 3,000 kilometers away" is a complete sentence, and "many physicists at the time insisted that radio waves could not follow the curve of the Earth" is another. "However" is a transitional word, not a conjunction, so the two independent clauses need a semicolon before it and a comma after it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a comma after it, "However" reads as part of "However many physicists," which turns the second sentence into a fragment that never gets to its point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; "however" is not a conjunction, so this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. A semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and commas set off the transitional word "however."
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation after "away," the two independent clauses run together.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries in Europe, barbers did more than cut hair: they also pulled teeth and performed bloodletting, a treatment that doctors of the time believed could cure many ailments. The striped pole outside a barbershop is traditionally said to recall that history. Each part of the design has a meaning: the red stripe stands for ______ the white stripe, for the bandages that were wrapped around a patient's arm; and the pole itself, for the staff a patient gripped to make the veins stand out. Whether or not every detail of the story is true, the sign outlasted the surgery by hundreds of years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: blood, and
choices.B: blood,
choices.C: blood;
choices.D: blood:

explanation.why: The sentence lists three parts of the design, and the second and third items already contain commas ("the white stripe, for the bandages …"). When items in a list contain commas, the items are separated by semicolons, as the semicolon after "arm" shows. The first item, "the red stripe stands for blood," must therefore end with a semicolon too.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "And" belongs only before the last item of a list, and the items here are separated by semicolons, not commas.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The items in this list already contain commas, so another comma would leave the reader unable to tell where one item ends and the next begins.
explanation.C: Correct. The semicolon separates the first item from the second, matching the semicolon already used before "and the pole itself."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon introduces a list; it can't separate one item of a list from the next.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many houses in the Faroe Islands are still topped with a thick layer of living ______ a tradition the islanders inherited from Norse settlers more than a thousand years ago. The roof is built up in layers: wooden boards first, then sheets of birch bark to keep water out, and finally squares of turf laid grass side up. The grass holds the soil together, the soil holds in heat, and the whole layer is heavy enough to stay put in the fierce Atlantic winds. In summer, a turf roof needs mowing like any other lawn.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: turf,
choices.B: turf
choices.C: turf. A tradition
choices.D: turf;

explanation.why: "A tradition the islanders inherited from Norse settlers more than a thousand years ago" is extra information that renames the turf roof; it is not a sentence on its own. An added phrase like this at the end of a sentence is attached with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma attaches the extra information to the sentence it describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a comma, the extra information runs straight into the main clause and is never set off.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "A tradition the islanders inherited …" has no verb of its own, so the period leaves a fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but "a tradition the islanders inherited …" is not one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the Hunza Valley of northern Pakistan, apricots ripen in July, and for a few weeks the flat roofs of the stone houses turn orange with fruit laid out to ______ one of the valley's most important crops. Dried apricots keep through the long winter, when fresh food is scarce, and the kernels inside the pits are cracked and pressed for a sweet oil used in cooking. Older villagers say that a family's wealth was once measured not in money but in apricot trees, and some orchards are still divided among heirs tree by tree.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: dry, the fruit is
choices.B: dry; the fruit being
choices.C: dry. The fruit is
choices.D: dry the fruit is

explanation.why: "In the Hunza Valley … the flat roofs of the stone houses turn orange with fruit laid out to dry" is a complete sentence, and "The fruit is one of the valley's most important crops" is another. A period ends the first sentence, and the second begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but "the fruit being one of the valley's most important crops" has no main verb and is a fragment.
explanation.C: Correct. The period separates the two complete sentences, and "The" begins the new one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Tharu people, who have lived in the Terai lowlands of southern Nepal for ______ traditionally build long houses of mud and reeds that several related families share. The thick walls stay cool in the fierce heat of the plains, and the outer surfaces are often decorated with raised clay figures of birds, elephants, and fish. The Terai floods almost every monsoon, so grain is stored in tall clay bins raised above the floor, and houses are patched or rebuilt each year after the waters go down.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: centuries;
choices.B: centuries
choices.C: centuries—
choices.D: centuries,

explanation.why: "Who have lived in the Terai lowlands of southern Nepal for centuries" is extra information about the Tharu people. It opens with a comma after "people," so it must close with a comma before the verb "build."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The Tharu people" from its verb "build."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "build."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "people" and completes the pair around the extra information.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The airstrip at Lukla, the gateway to the Mount Everest region of Nepal, is often ______ "the most dangerous airport in the world." Its single runway is only about 500 meters long and sits at an altitude of roughly 2,800 meters, where the thin air gives aircraft less lift. The strip tilts steeply uphill to help landing planes slow down, with a sheer drop at the lower end and a mountain wall at the upper one. Once a pilot commits to landing, there is no room to circle around and try again.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: called,
choices.B: called
choices.C: called;
choices.D: called:

explanation.why: The quoted phrase "the most dangerous airport in the world" is built into the sentence as the completion of "is often called"; it is not a separate spoken sentence. A quotation that works as part of the sentence takes no punctuation before it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma introduces a quotation only after a speech verb such as "said"; here the quoted words complete the verb "called" and need no comma.
explanation.B: Correct. The quoted phrase completes the sentence directly, so no punctuation separates it from "called."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides; a quoted phrase is not a clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; "The airstrip … is often called" is not complete without the words that follow.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the old footpaths of Sri Lanka stand small open-sided shelters called ______ were built for travelers and pilgrims who had to cross the island on foot. A typical ambalama is a raised wooden platform under a tiled roof, with no walls, so that breezes pass through and a weary walker can sit, sleep, or share a meal in the shade. Villagers and landowners often paid for them as acts of goodwill, and the finest examples, such as the one at Panavitiya, have wooden pillars carved with dancers, animals, and flowering vines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ambalamas, they
choices.B: ambalamas; which
choices.C: ambalamas. Which
choices.D: ambalamas, which

explanation.why: "Which were built for travelers and pilgrims who had to cross the island on foot" is a relative clause that adds information about the shelters; it is not a sentence on its own. A nonessential "which" clause is attached to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "They were built …" is a second independent clause, and a comma alone can't join two independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but "which were built …" is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Which were built …" can't stand alone as a sentence, so the period leaves a fragment.
explanation.D: Correct. The comma attaches the nonessential "which" clause to the sentence it describes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The familiar shape of the cuckoo clock dates from 1850, when a clockmaking school in the Black Forest town of Furtwangen held a competition for new designs. The winning entry came from Friedrich Eisenlohr, an architect who had designed the small trackside houses for the railway then being built through the Black ______ and it borrowed their shape: a steep roof, a decorative gable, and a little door for the bird. Clocks with carved birds had been made in the region for a century, but Eisenlohr's "railway house" became the pattern that most cuckoo clocks follow to this day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Forest
choices.B: Forest,
choices.C: Forest)
choices.D: Forest—

explanation.why: "An architect who had designed the small trackside houses for the railway then being built through the Black Forest" is extra information about Eisenlohr. It opens with a comma after "Eisenlohr," so it must close with a comma, which also serves as the comma before "and" joining the two independent clauses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off, and "and" joins two independent clauses with no comma before it.
explanation.B: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "Eisenlohr" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.C: Incorrect. There is no opening parenthesis, so a closing parenthesis has nothing to pair with.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the coffeehouses of Vienna around 1900, a single cup of coffee bought the right to a marble-topped table for the whole ______ the cafés as their offices. Newspapers from across Europe hung on wooden holders by the door, waiters brought a glass of water with every order, and nobody was hurried out. Regulars had their mail delivered to a favorite café and met publishers and friends there rather than at home. In 2011, Austria added its coffeehouse culture to the national list of intangible cultural heritage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: day; many writers treated
choices.B: day, many writers treated
choices.C: day many writers treated
choices.D: day; many writers treating

explanation.why: "A single cup of coffee bought the right to a marble-topped table for the whole day" is a complete sentence, and "many writers treated the cafés as their offices" is another. Two closely related independent clauses can be joined with a semicolon.
explanation.A: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but "many writers treating the cafés as their offices" has no main verb and is a fragment.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A popular story ______ that bakers in Vienna invented the croissant in 1683, shaping their dough into a crescent to mock the banner of the Ottoman army that had just failed to capture the city. Food historians find no evidence for the tale. The crescent-shaped kipferl had been baked in Austria for centuries before 1683, and the croissant as the French know it, made of buttery layered dough, appeared only in the 1800s, after an Austrian baker opened a shop in Paris and Parisian bakers began copying his wares.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: holds
choices.B: holds:
choices.C: holds;
choices.D: holds,

explanation.why: "That bakers in Vienna invented the croissant in 1683" is the object of the verb "holds"; it tells what the story holds. No punctuation comes between a verb and the clause that serves as its object.
explanation.A: Correct. The verb "holds" leads directly into its "that" clause with no punctuation between them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; "A popular story holds" is incomplete without its object.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and "A popular story holds" is not complete on its own.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't separate a verb from the "that" clause that is its object.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Scottish Highland bagpipes are filled by the player's ______ the uilleann pipes of Ireland use a small bellows strapped under the right elbow and pumped with the arm. The name comes from uillinn, the Irish word for elbow. Because no breath passes through the bag, the air stays dry and the reeds stay in tune, and the player can sing along or even talk while playing. The uilleann pipes are also quieter and sweeter in tone than Highland pipes, with a range of two full octaves, which suits them to the parlor rather than the parade ground.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: breath, instead,
choices.B: breath instead,
choices.C: breath. Instead;
choices.D: breath; instead,

explanation.why: "Scottish Highland bagpipes are filled by the player's breath" is a complete sentence, and "the uilleann pipes of Ireland use a small bellows …" is another. "Instead" is a transitional word, not a conjunction, so the two independent clauses need a semicolon before it and a comma after it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; "instead" is not a conjunction, so this is a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation after "breath," the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't follow the introductory word "Instead"; a transitional word at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.
explanation.D: Correct. A semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and the comma after "instead" sets off the transitional word.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Sandalwood oil, prized for centuries by perfumers for its warm scent and its ability to hold other fragrances in place, comes largely from the state of Karnataka in southern India. The tree's fragrant heartwood—the dense core that takes decades to ______ is chipped and steam-distilled to draw out the oil. During the First World War, when exports of the wood were cut off and stocks piled up in Mysore, the state government built a factory to turn the surplus into soap. Sandalwood is now so scarce that the trees are protected, and cutting one requires government permission.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: form;
choices.B: form
choices.C: form—
choices.D: form,

explanation.why: "The dense core that takes decades to form" is extra information that explains "heartwood." It opens with a dash after "heartwood," so it must close with a dash before the verb "is chipped."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The tree's fragrant heartwood" from its verb "is chipped."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "is chipped."
explanation.C: Correct. The closing dash matches the opening dash after "heartwood" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a dash, so it can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Swans have glided along the canals of Bruges, in Belgium, for more than five centuries, and the city tells a story to explain why. In 1488, the townspeople rose up against their ruler, Maximilian of Austria, and executed his counselor Pieter Lanchals. Lanchals, whose family name means "long ______ had a swan on his coat of arms. According to the legend, Maximilian punished the city by ordering it to keep swans on its waters forever. Historians doubt that any such order was ever given, but the birds remain, and the city still cares for them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: neck," had
choices.B: neck", had
choices.C: neck;" had
choices.D: neck" had

explanation.why: "Whose family name means 'long neck'" is extra information about Lanchals that opens with a comma after "Lanchals," so a comma must close it before the verb "had." In American English, that comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma closes the extra information and sits inside the closing quotation mark, as American usage requires.
explanation.B: Incorrect. In American English, a comma at the end of quoted words goes inside the closing quotation mark, not after it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Lanchals" from its verb "had," and it is not part of the quoted words.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The comma after "Lanchals" opens a pair, so a matching comma must close the extra information before "had."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The yo-yo is often called one of the oldest toys in the world, and a disk on a string that climbs back up appears on a Greek vase painted around 440 BCE. The modern toy, though, owes its name and its most important feature to the Philippines. Pedro Flores, a Filipino immigrant who started making yo-yos in California in ______ used a string looped loosely around the axle instead of tied to it, so the yo-yo could spin at the end of the string before climbing back up. A businessman named Donald Duncan bought his company within two years, and the trick-friendly design spread around the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.why: "A Filipino immigrant who started making yo-yos in California in 1928" is extra information about Pedro Flores. It opens with a comma after "Flores," so it must close with a comma before the verb "used."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Pedro Flores" from its verb "used."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it can't separate the subject "Pedro Flores" from its verb "used."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "used."
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "Flores" and completes the pair around the extra information.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Tomas had told himself he was coming to the island only to clear out his grandfather's boat ______ by the end of the first week, however, he was rebuilding it. The roof had fallen in, and the old skiff lay beneath a drift of leaves and splintered shingles, its planks gray but sound. Each morning he meant to haul it to the dump, and each morning he found one more reason to wait: a hinge worth saving, a coil of good rope, his grandfather's initials cut into the tiller.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: shed. By
choices.B: shed; which by
choices.C: shed by
choices.D: shed, by

explanation.why: "Tomas had told himself he was coming to the island only to clear out his grandfather's boat shed" is a complete sentence, and "by the end of the first week, however, he was rebuilding it" is another. A period ends the first sentence, and the second begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Correct. The period separates the two complete sentences, and "By" begins the new one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Adding "which" turns the second part into a relative clause that has nothing to refer to and leaves the semicolon without an independent clause after it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The dog had followed the twins home from the bus stop, and by supper it was clear that he was staying. The only question was his name. "He looks like a Biscuit," Mira announced, and the dog, hearing the pleasure in her voice, thumped his tail against the kitchen floor. "We are not calling a dog ______ Anya said, with the firmness of someone who had been the older twin by eleven minutes all her life. By the following week, though, even she was calling him Biscuit, and the dog answered to nothing else.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Biscuit" Anya
choices.B: Biscuit," Anya
choices.C: Biscuit", Anya
choices.D: Biscuit." Anya

explanation.why: Anya's words, "We are not calling a dog Biscuit," are followed by the tag "Anya said," so the quotation ends with a comma, not a period. In American English, that comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, just as in "He looks like a Biscuit," Mira announced earlier in the text.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A quotation followed by a tag such as "Anya said" needs a comma to connect the two.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma ends the quoted words inside the quotation mark and connects them to the tag "Anya said."
explanation.C: Incorrect. In American English, the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, not after it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period ends the sentence, which leaves "Anya said, with the firmness …" cut off from the words she said.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On the last night the cinema was open, Mr. Haddad climbed to the projection booth an hour early, as he had every evening for forty-one years. He had already chosen the film. Mr. Haddad, squinting at a strip of it held up to the ______ could still name the scene from the pattern of its frames, the way a sailor reads weather from the shape of a cloud. Downstairs, a few dozen people settled into the worn seats. When the lights went down, he let the first frames flicker across the screen and allowed himself, for once, to watch.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: light
choices.B: light;
choices.C: light—
choices.D: light,

explanation.why: "Squinting at a strip of it held up to the light" is extra information describing what Mr. Haddad was doing. It opens with a comma after "Haddad," so it must close with a comma before the verb "could still name."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "could still name."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Mr. Haddad" from its verb "could still name."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "Haddad" and completes the pair around the extra information.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: By the time the afternoon wind came up over the rooftops of the old ______ Bilal and his younger brother Saad had already untangled their kite strings three times. Saad wanted to fly the red kite, the one with the long paper tail, and Bilal wanted to fly it too, which was how the tangles had started. In the end they flew it together, Bilal holding the spool and Saad calling out the gusts, and the kite climbed until it was a red fleck above the minarets and the water tanks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: city,
choices.B: city;
choices.C: city:
choices.D: city.

explanation.why: "By the time the afternoon wind came up over the rooftops of the old city" is a long introductory phrase, not a complete sentence; the main clause is "Bilal and his younger brother Saad had already untangled their kite strings." An introductory phrase of this length is followed by a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma separates the long introductory phrase from the main clause that follows.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, but the introductory phrase is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; the introductory phrase is incomplete.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The introductory phrase has no main clause of its own, so the period leaves a fragment.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The common basilisk, a lizard of the rainforests of Central America, is sometimes called the Jesus Christ lizard because of its ability to run across the surface of a pond or stream. When a basilisk is startled by a ______ it drops from its perch and sprints across the water on its hind legs, slapping the surface with long toes fringed with skin. Each slap traps a pocket of air that briefly supports the lizard's weight. Only small, light individuals can keep this up for more than a few meters; heavier adults soon sink and swim the rest of the way.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: predator;
choices.B: predator.
choices.C: predator:
choices.D: predator,

explanation.why: The sentence opens with "When," so "When a basilisk is startled by a predator" is a dependent clause that cannot stand alone. The main clause is "it drops from its perch and sprints across the water." A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "When" clause is dependent.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period would leave "When a basilisk is startled by a predator" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "When" clause is not one.
explanation.D: Correct. A comma links the introductory "When" clause to the main clause that follows it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1806, a Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor shipped a cargo of ice cut from a frozen New England pond to the Caribbean island of Martinique. Most of it melted, and the venture lost money. Tudor kept at it, however, and over the next decades his company and its rivals turned frozen lakes into a major export. Blocks of ice packed in sawdust and stowed in the holds of sailing ______ ports as distant as Calcutta, where ice from Massachusetts sold for less than local supplies and was welcomed by residents enduring the summer heat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ships, reached
choices.B: ships reached
choices.C: ships; reached
choices.D: ships: reached

explanation.why: The subject of the last sentence is the long phrase "Blocks of ice packed in sawdust and stowed in the holds of sailing ships," and its verb is "reached." No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A single comma cannot separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The subject "Blocks of ice … sailing ships" flows straight into its verb "reached" with no punctuation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb, and neither side would be a complete sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "Blocks of ice … sailing ships" has no verb yet.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every evening after the heat broke, Faisal climbed to the roof of his family's house in the old city of Lahore to let the pigeons out. The birds rose in a loose cloud, circled the minarets twice, and came back to him one by one. His favorite—a gray hen with a white collar and a crooked ______ always landed last, as if to make sure he had counted the others first. His mother said the pigeons were a waste of grain. Faisal did not argue, but he noticed that she, too, looked up when the flock passed over the courtyard.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: tail;
choices.B: tail—
choices.C: tail
choices.D: tail,

explanation.why: "A gray hen with a white collar and a crooked tail" is extra information describing "His favorite." It opens with a dash after "favorite," so it must close with a matching dash before the verb "always landed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "His favorite" from its verb "landed," and what comes before it is not an independent clause.
explanation.B: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the description, so the subject "His favorite" connects to its verb "always landed."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "landed."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash cannot close with a comma; the two marks must match.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the southern coast of Sri Lanka, toddy tappers harvest the sap of coconut palms, which is drunk fresh or fermented and distilled into arrack. Rather than climb down and up each tree in turn, a tapper moves from one crown to the next along ropes strung high above the ground. The sap that collects overnight in clay pots tied beneath the cut flower ______ to be gathered before the morning sun warms it, so the work begins in darkness. The job demands balance, a head for heights, and a knowledge of each tree's yield that is usually passed from father to son.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: stalks; has
choices.B: stalks—has
choices.C: stalks has
choices.D: stalks, has

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "The sap that collects overnight in clay pots tied beneath the cut flower stalks," and its verb is "has to be gathered." Everything between "sap" and "stalks" tells which sap is meant, so it is part of the subject, and no punctuation may separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "The sap … flower stalks" has no main verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A single dash here would cut the subject off from its verb; there is no opening dash for it to close.
explanation.C: Correct. The subject "The sap … flower stalks" connects directly to its verb "has" with no punctuation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A single comma cannot separate a subject from its verb; nothing before it opened a pair of commas.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A Noh mask is carved from a single block of cypress and painted in muted tones, and at first glance its expression can seem fixed, even blank. Performers, however, rely on a subtle optical ______ the way shadows gather under the brow when the mask is tilted slightly downward, so that the face appears to grieve, and the way the same features seem to brighten when the mask is lifted toward the light. A skilled actor can thus pass through a whole range of feeling in a single scene without the mask itself changing at all, and audiences often describe the carved face as coming alive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: effect:
choices.B: effect.
choices.C: effect;
choices.D: effect

explanation.why: "Performers, however, rely on a subtle optical effect" is a complete independent clause. What follows, "the way shadows gather … and the way the same features seem to brighten," is a pair of noun phrases, not a clause: they explain what the effect is. A colon after an independent clause is the mark that introduces such an explanation.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon follows the independent clause and introduces the phrases that explain what the optical effect is.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period would leave "The way shadows gather … toward the light" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "the way shadows gather … toward the light" has no main verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, "a subtle optical effect the way shadows gather" runs together and cannot be read clearly.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The bearded vulture, or lammergeier, lives in mountain ranges from the Pyrenees to the Himalayas and feeds almost entirely on bone, a diet unique among birds. Small bones are swallowed whole, and the bird's stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve them within a day or two. Larger bones present a ______ vulture carries them aloft, sometimes to a height of more than a hundred meters, and drops them onto a favored slab of rock, returning again and again until the bone shatters and the marrow inside can be reached. Young birds appear to need several years of practice before they master the technique.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: problem and the
choices.B: problem. The
choices.C: problem the
choices.D: problem, the

explanation.why: "Larger bones present a problem" is a complete sentence, and "the vulture carries them aloft … and drops them onto a favored slab of rock" is another complete sentence. Two independent clauses need a strong boundary between them, such as a period.
explanation.A: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.B: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and the second begins as a new sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The ruins of Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, in northwestern Bangladesh, cover nearly eight hectares and represent one of the largest Buddhist monasteries ever built south of the Himalayas. The complex, which was founded in the late eighth century under the Pala dynasty and remained in use for about four hundred ______ of a square enclosure of some 177 monks' cells arranged around a central shrine that rises in stepped terraces. Thousands of terracotta plaques set into its walls depict animals, dancers, and scenes of daily life, and their varied styles suggest that the artisans came from several different traditions.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: years—consists
choices.B: years consists
choices.C: years; consists
choices.D: years, consists

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "The complex," and its verb is "consists." The clause "which was founded … for about four hundred years" is extra information that opens with a comma after "complex," so it must close with a comma before the verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it cannot close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "consists."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "The complex, which was founded … four hundred years" has no main verb.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "complex," setting off the extra information so the subject connects to "consists."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The orchard had been planted by Nikolai's great-grandfather, and every winter since, someone in the family had gone out with a saw to prune it. This year the task fell to Nikolai, fifteen, who had never cut a living branch. His grandfather, too stiff now to climb a ladder, followed him from tree to tree and ______ a branch growing straight up would bear nothing but leaves, so each cut had to open the crown toward the light. By the third row Nikolai no longer waited to be told. He stood back, studied the shape of each tree, and found that he could already see where the sun would fall.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: explained; that
choices.B: explained that
choices.C: explained, that
choices.D: explained: that

explanation.why: "Explained" is a verb, and the clause "that a branch growing straight up would bear nothing but leaves" is its object: it tells what the grandfather explained. No punctuation should come between a verb and its object.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "that a branch growing straight up would bear nothing but leaves" cannot stand alone.
explanation.B: Correct. The verb "explained" leads directly into its object, the clause beginning with "that."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma cannot separate a verb from the "that" clause that is its object.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "His grandfather … followed him from tree to tree and explained" is left waiting for its object.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Tiger beetles are among the fastest runners in the insect world relative to their size, and some species cover more than a hundred body lengths a second. At that pace the beetle's eyes cannot gather light quickly enough to form a clear image, so the animal is effectively blind while it runs. To catch anything at all, a hunting beetle depends on three ______ short bursts of speed, frequent stops to relocate its prey, and antennae held rigidly forward to detect obstacles it cannot see. High-speed video shows that the pauses last only a fraction of a second, far too brief for the prey to escape.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: tactics:
choices.B: tactics;
choices.C: tactics
choices.D: tactics.

explanation.why: "To catch anything at all, a hunting beetle depends on three tactics" is a complete independent clause, and what follows is a list of the three tactics. A colon after an independent clause is the mark that introduces a list.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon follows the independent clause and introduces the list of three tactics.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "short bursts of speed, frequent stops …, and antennae held rigidly forward" is a list with no main verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, "three tactics short bursts of speed" runs together and cannot be read clearly.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave the list "Short bursts of speed … it cannot see" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Several of the giant stone figures on Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, wear large cylindrical headpieces known as pukao. The figures themselves were carved from volcanic tuff at a quarry on one side of the island, while the pukao, which can weigh more than ten tons each, were cut from red scoria at a separate site and are thought to represent topknots of hair. Visitors have long wondered how the islanders raised these headpieces onto statues as much as ten meters ______ answer favored by recent research is that the pukao were rolled up ramps of rubble built against the front of each figure, then tipped into place.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: tall. The
choices.B: tall, the
choices.C: tall? The
choices.D: tall the

explanation.why: "Visitors have long wondered how the islanders raised these headpieces onto statues as much as ten meters tall" reports a question rather than asking one: it is a statement about what visitors wondered. An indirect question like this ends with a period, not a question mark, and the next sentence then begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Correct. A period ends the indirect question, and "The answer …" begins a new sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join this complete sentence to the next one, "the answer favored by recent research is …"; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A question mark belongs only at the end of a direct question; this sentence is a statement that reports what visitors wondered.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together, and "ten meters tall the answer" cannot be read clearly.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Darwin's bark spider, described from Madagascar in 2010, spins the largest orb webs known. The orb itself can cover nearly three square meters, but what astonished the biologists who first studied it was the anchor ______ suspends the whole structure above a river or lake, sometimes spanning a gap of twenty-five meters from bank to bank. Laboratory tests showed that this silk is tougher than any other spider silk measured, absorbing far more energy before it breaks. The spider appears to release a single strand into the wind and wait for it to snag on the far shore, a strategy that lets it fish for insects flying over the water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: line; that
choices.B: line, that
choices.C: line that
choices.D: line—that

explanation.why: The clause "that suspends the whole structure above a river or lake" tells which anchor line is meant, so it is essential to the sentence's meaning. Essential information is not set off by punctuation, and a clause beginning with "that" is never separated from the noun it describes by a comma, dash, or semicolon.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "that suspends the whole structure …" cannot stand alone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma cannot separate a "that" clause from the noun it describes; a comma marks extra, nonessential information.
explanation.C: Correct. The essential clause "that suspends …" follows "the anchor line" directly, with no punctuation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A dash would set off the clause as extra information, but a "that" clause is essential and cannot be set off this way.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The churches of Ravenna, a city on Italy's Adriatic coast, hold the finest surviving mosaics of the sixth century, a time when the city served as a center of Byzantine power in the West. The craftsmen worked with several kinds of tesserae: cubes of colored glass, whose surfaces were often set at slight angles so that they would catch light from different ______ pieces of marble and limestone, used for faces and hands; and gold tesserae, made by sealing a sheet of gold leaf between two layers of glass. Seen by lamplight, the gold backgrounds seem to shift and glow as the viewer moves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: directions,
choices.B: directions;
choices.C: directions
choices.D: directions:

explanation.why: The colon introduces a list of three kinds of tesserae, and each item contains commas of its own ("cubes of colored glass, whose surfaces …" and "pieces of marble and limestone, used for faces and hands"). When list items contain commas, semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after "hands" shows. The same mark is needed after the first item.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma would blur the boundary between the first item and the second, since the items already contain commas; the semicolon after "hands" shows the separator the list uses.
explanation.B: Correct. A semicolon separates the first item of the list from the second, matching the semicolon before "and gold tesserae."
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the first and second items run together, and "different directions pieces of marble" cannot be read clearly.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon has already introduced the list; a second colon inside it is wrong, and "different directions" is not an independent clause.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Radiating outward from the great houses of Chaco Canyon, in what is now northwestern New ______ a network of roads was laid out by Ancestral Puebloan builders between roughly 850 and 1150 CE. The roads run remarkably straight, climbing over mesas by means of cut stairways rather than bending around them, and some are nine meters wide, far broader than foot traffic would seem to require. Because the builders had no wheeled vehicles or draft animals, archaeologists have suggested that the roads served ceremonial as well as practical purposes, perhaps marking ritual routes between the canyon and outlying communities.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Mexico;
choices.B: Mexico.
choices.C: Mexico
choices.D: Mexico,

explanation.why: "Radiating outward from the great houses of Chaco Canyon, in what is now northwestern New Mexico" is an introductory phrase that describes the subject, "a network of roads." An introductory phrase like this is separated from the main clause by a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the introductory phrase "Radiating outward … New Mexico" has no subject or main verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period would leave "Radiating outward … New Mexico" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a comma, the introductory phrase runs straight into the subject, and "New Mexico a network of roads" cannot be read clearly.
explanation.D: Correct. A comma separates the long introductory phrase from the main clause that begins with "a network of roads."

items.subject: science
items.passage: The argonaut, or paper nautilus, is an octopus that lives in the open ocean rather than on the seafloor. The female secretes a thin, ridged shell from two of her arms and uses it as a brood chamber for her eggs. For centuries the shell was assumed to be a flotation device, yet no one had explained how it ______ 2010 two researchers observing argonauts in the wild found the answer. A female rises to the surface, rocks the shell to trap a bubble of air, and then dives with it; at the right depth the compressed air exactly balances her weight, letting her hover without effort.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: worked and in
choices.B: worked, and in
choices.C: worked, in
choices.D: worked in

explanation.why: "For centuries the shell was assumed to be a flotation device, yet no one had explained how it worked" is a complete sentence, and "in 2010 two researchers observing argonauts in the wild found the answer" is another. Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as "and."
explanation.A: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma plus the conjunction "and" correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together, and "how it worked in 2010" misleadingly reads as one phrase.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The first practical pneumatic tire was patented in 1888 by John Boyd Dunlop, a veterinary surgeon living in Belfast, who wanted to smooth the ride of his young son's tricycle on the city's cobbled streets. Earlier wheels had been rimmed with solid rubber, which absorbed little shock. Dunlop's version was an inflated tube wrapped in materials ______ linen tape and a thin sheet of rubber, which he glued to the wooden rim. Racing cyclists adopted it within a year, and its advantage was so decisive that solid tires soon vanished from bicycles. Dunlop later learned that a Scottish inventor, Robert Thomson, had patented a similar idea decades earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: such as
choices.B: such as:
choices.C: such as,
choices.D: such as;

explanation.why: "Such as" introduces the examples "linen tape and a thin sheet of rubber," which are its object. No punctuation belongs between "such as" and the examples it introduces.
explanation.A: Correct. The phrase "such as" leads directly into its examples with no punctuation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "Dunlop's version was an inflated tube wrapped in materials such as" is left incomplete.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma cannot separate "such as" from the examples it introduces.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "linen tape and a thin sheet of rubber …" cannot stand alone.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The schoolhouse stood where Marisol remembered it, at the end of the lane, though the lane itself had narrowed to a track between hedges. The building, which had been closed for twenty years and sold twice to people who never got around to living in ______ had its bell. She had rung that bell every morning for a decade, pulling the rope with both hands while children came running across the field. Now the rope was gone, but when she pushed the door and stepped inside, the smell of chalk and old wood came to meet her as if no one had ever left.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it; still
choices.B: it, still
choices.C: it—still
choices.D: it still

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "The building," and its verb is "had." The clause "which had been closed … living in it" is extra information that opens with a comma after "building," so it must close with a comma before "still had."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "The building, which had been closed … living in it" has no main verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "building," so the subject connects to its verb "had."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it cannot close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into "still had its bell."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Painters in the Mughal workshops of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries prepared their paper with as much care as their pigments. Sheets were coated with a thin paste, dried, and then burnished with a smooth agate stone until the surface was hard enough to take a line finer than a hair. Colors were ground by hand from minerals and were often costly. The deep blue of a royal robe, for example, came from lapis ______ stone that reached the workshops from mines in the mountains of Badakhshan, in what is now Afghanistan. Brushes for the finest work were said to be made from a few hairs taken from a squirrel's tail.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: lazuli, a
choices.B: lazuli; a
choices.C: lazuli a
choices.D: lazuli. A

explanation.why: "The deep blue of a royal robe, for example, came from lapis lazuli" is a complete sentence. "A stone that reached the workshops from mines in the mountains of Badakhshan" is a noun phrase that renames lapis lazuli, with no main verb of its own ("reached" belongs to the "that" clause). A phrase like this is attached to the noun it renames with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma attaches the renaming phrase "a stone that reached the workshops …" to "lapis lazuli."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a stone that reached the workshops …" has no main verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, "lapis lazuli a stone" runs together and cannot be read clearly.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "A stone that reached the workshops … Afghanistan" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mudskippers are fish of tropical mudflats and mangrove swamps that spend much of the day out of the water, skipping across the mud on their stiff front fins and even climbing the roots of mangrove trees. They manage this because of a set of adaptations unusual in ______ can absorb oxygen through the skin and the lining of the mouth, provided these stay moist, and some species carry a mouthful of water with them to keep their gills wet on land. Their eyes, set high on the head, can be drawn back into fluid-filled sockets to be rewetted.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fish: they
choices.B: fish they
choices.C: fish and they
choices.D: fish, they

explanation.why: "They manage this because of a set of adaptations unusual in fish" is a complete independent clause, and "they can absorb oxygen through the skin …" is another independent clause that explains what those adaptations are. A colon can join two independent clauses when the second explains or spells out the first.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces the clause that explains the adaptations.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The potters of Korea's Goryeo dynasty, which ruled from 918 to 1392, produced a green-glazed stoneware known as celadon that was prized even in China, where the technique had originated. The color came from a small amount of iron in the glaze, which turned a soft jade green only when the kiln was starved of oxygen during firing. Goryeo potters added a technique of their ______ came to be called sanggam, in which designs were incised into the clay, filled with white or black slip, and then covered with the translucent glaze. Cranes and clouds were favorite motifs, and the finest pieces are now treated as national treasures.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: own; which
choices.B: own which
choices.C: own, which
choices.D: own. Which

explanation.why: "Goryeo potters added a technique of their own" is a complete sentence, and "which came to be called sanggam …" adds extra information about that technique. A "which" clause giving extra information is attached to the sentence with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "which came to be called sanggam …" cannot stand alone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a comma, the "which" clause is not set off, and "their own which came to be called" cannot be read clearly.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma attaches the nonessential "which" clause to "a technique of their own."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "Which came to be called sanggam … translucent glaze" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A small jellyfish of the genus Turritopsis has become famous as the "immortal jellyfish," though the name overstates the case. When an adult is injured, starved, or simply aging, it can settle onto a surface and transform its cells back into a polyp, the attached, stalk-like stage from which jellyfish normally bud only once in their lives. Because the polyp then produces new medusae that are genetically identical to the original ______ the animal has in effect returned to its youth. The reversal has been observed repeatedly in laboratory tanks, but most individuals in the sea presumably still fall to predators or disease long before they use this ability.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: adult;
choices.B: adult,
choices.C: adult.
choices.D: adult:

explanation.why: The sentence opens with "Because," so "Because the polyp then produces new medusae that are genetically identical to the original adult" is a dependent clause. The main clause is "the animal has in effect returned to its youth." A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Because" clause is dependent.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma links the introductory "Because" clause to the main clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "Because the polyp … the original adult" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "Because" clause is not one.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Traditional Japanese carpentry is admired for timber frames that stand for centuries without a single metal fastener. Their joints—mortises, tenons, and interlocking notches cut so precisely that they hold without glue or ______ a building to flex during an earthquake and then settle back into place. Because the pieces are shaped to slide together, a damaged beam can be withdrawn and replaced rather than cut out, which is one reason temple buildings are periodically dismantled and reassembled. Apprentices in the craft spend years learning to sharpen and use hand planes before they are trusted to cut a joint on a finished timber.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: nails; allow
choices.B: nails—allow
choices.C: nails, allow
choices.D: nails allow

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "Their joints," and its verb is "allow." Everything from "mortises" to "glue or nails" is extra information describing the joints. It opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash before the verb, even though the description contains commas of its own.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "Their joints—mortises, tenons, and interlocking notches … glue or nails" has no main verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the description, so the subject "Their joints" connects to its verb "allow."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash cannot close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the description is never set off, and "glue or nails allow a building" misleadingly reads as if the nails do the allowing.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Shah Jahan Mosque in Thatta, in Pakistan's Sindh province, was completed in 1647 under the Mughal emperor whose name it bears. Its most striking feature is its tilework: the walls and the ninety-three domes are lined with glazed tiles in blue and white, arranged in patterns that shift as a visitor moves through the arcades. The mosque is also admired for its acoustics, since a prayer spoken at the mihrab can be heard at the far end of the building. It follows the imperial style of the period in most ______ it has no minarets, a feature of nearly every other great Mughal mosque.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: respects,
choices.B: respects, but,
choices.C: respects but
choices.D: respects, but

explanation.why: "It follows the imperial style of the period in most respects" is a complete sentence, and "it has no minarets" is another. Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as "but."
