explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The comma after "but" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces; nothing in that clause needs setting off.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "but" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.D: Correct. A comma plus the conjunction "but" correctly joins the two independent clauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Since the 1960s, the Dead Sea has been shrinking as the rivers that feed it are diverted for farms and cities, and its surface now drops by about a meter a year. As the shoreline retreats, fresh groundwater flows into layers of salt left behind by the lake, dissolving them and opening cavities that collapse without warning. Thousands of sinkholes have appeared, swallowing sections of highway and a stretch of beach. Local councils have put a blunt question to the engineers monitoring the area: can the remaining roads be kept open at ______ answers have been cautious, since no one can predict where the next collapse will occur.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: all? The
choices.B: all, the
choices.C: all the
choices.D: all. The

explanation.why: "Can the remaining roads be kept open at all" is a direct question, quoted as the councils put it, so it must end with a question mark. The next sentence, "The answers have been cautious," then begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Correct. A question mark ends the direct question, and "The answers …" begins a new sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma cannot end the question, and joining it to the next independent clause with a comma alone creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the question runs straight into the next sentence, and "at all the answers" cannot be read clearly.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period cannot end a direct question; "can the remaining roads be kept open at all" asks something, so it needs a question mark.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Aunt Ruth had lost most of her sight the winter Theo turned eleven, and she said the hardest part was not the dark but the way the neighborhood had gone silent in her mind. So Theo made her a map. He walked the eight blocks between her apartment and the park with a notebook, writing down the clatter of the bakery's shutters at six, the bus that sighed at the corner, the loose grate outside the laundry that rang when anyone stepped on ______ read it to her every Sunday, and by the end of the month she could tell him exactly who was passing below.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it, he
choices.B: it he
choices.C: it and he
choices.D: it; he

explanation.why: "He walked the eight blocks … writing down the clatter … the loose grate … that rang when anyone stepped on it" is a complete sentence, and "he read it to her every Sunday" begins another. Two independent clauses need a strong boundary between them, and a semicolon provides one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it; here the missing comma also makes it seem that the grate rang whenever he read.
explanation.D: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins the two independent clauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each spring, Japan's weather services publish forecasts of the "cherry blossom front," the line of first flowering that moves northward from Kyushu in late March to Hokkaido in May. The forecasts matter to millions of people planning picnics and to towns whose economies depend on the visitors. Although the flowering date is set mainly by the warmth of the preceding ______ forecasters must also account for the winter chill that the buds need before they can respond to spring temperatures at all. A mild winter can therefore delay the bloom rather than advance it, a complication that makes the front harder to predict than a reading of the thermometer would suggest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: weeks.
choices.B: weeks,
choices.C: weeks:
choices.D: weeks;

explanation.why: The sentence opens with "Although," so "Although the flowering date is set mainly by the warmth of the preceding weeks" is a dependent clause. The main clause is "forecasters must also account for the winter chill." A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although the flowering date … the preceding weeks" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma links the introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "Although" clause is not one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The stupa at Boudhanath, on the eastern edge of Kathmandu, is one of the largest in the world and a center of Tibetan Buddhist life in Nepal. Its white dome, which pilgrims circle clockwise while turning the prayer wheels set into the surrounding wall, is topped by a square tower painted on each side with a pair of enormous eyes. The eyes, together with the curling mark between them that resembles a question ______ usually explained as the all-seeing gaze of the Buddha and the Nepali numeral one, a symbol of unity. Above the tower rise thirteen gilded steps, said to stand for the stages on the path to enlightenment.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: mark, are
choices.B: mark—are
choices.C: mark are
choices.D: mark; are

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "The eyes," and its verb is "are usually explained." The phrase "together with the curling mark between them that resembles a question mark" is extra information that opens with a comma after "eyes," so it must close with a comma before the verb.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "eyes," setting off the extra information so the subject connects to "are."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it cannot close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "are."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "The eyes, together with … a question mark" has no main verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The theremin, patented in 1928 by the Russian physicist Leon Theremin, is played without being touched. Two metal antennas project from a wooden cabinet, and the performer's hands, moving in the air near them, alter the electrical fields that the circuits inside generate; one hand governs pitch and the other volume. Because there are no keys or frets to guide the fingers, a player must ______ an exact sense of where every note lies in empty space, a steady hand that does not waver, and an ear quick enough to correct a tone that starts to drift. Its wavering sound became a staple of science fiction film scores.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: develop,
choices.B: develop
choices.C: develop;
choices.D: develop:

explanation.why: "Develop" is a verb, and the list "an exact sense …, a steady hand …, and an ear …" is its object: these are the things a player must develop. No punctuation should come between a verb and its object, even when the object is a list.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma cannot separate a verb from its object.
explanation.B: Correct. The verb "develop" leads directly into the list of things that are its object.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and the list "an exact sense … starts to drift" cannot stand alone.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "a player must develop" is left waiting for its object.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. ______ who had been station master at the junction for thirty-one years and had retired on a Friday with a handshake and a clock, was back on the platform the following Monday. He did not wear the uniform. He carried a trowel and a bucket, and he began to dig up the strip of cinders between the waiting room and the fence. The new station master, a young man who kept checking his watch, asked him politely what he was doing. "Planting," said Mr. Okafor, and he did not look up. By June the passengers on the morning train were leaning out of the windows to see the roses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Okafor
choices.B: Okafor;
choices.C: Okafor—
choices.D: Okafor,

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "Mr. Okafor," and its verb is "was." The clause "who had been station master … a handshake and a clock" is extra information about him. It closes with a comma before "was," so it must open with a comma too; the two marks around extra information must match.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the "who" clause is not set off, yet a stray comma then appears before the verb "was."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "Mr. Okafor" alone is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information closes with a comma, so it cannot open with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The opening comma matches the comma before "was," setting off the "who" clause as extra information.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The tuatara, a reptile found only on a few islands off the coast of New Zealand, resembles a lizard but belongs to an order that split from lizards and snakes more than 200 million years ago. Among its most unusual features is a third eye on the top of its head. This parietal eye (which has a lens and a retina of its own but is covered by scales within a few months of ______ is thought to help the animal regulate its daily and seasonal rhythms by sensing changes in light. Tuatara grow slowly and can live for more than a hundred years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: hatching)
choices.B: hatching),
choices.C: hatching);
choices.D: hatching,

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "This parietal eye," and its verb is "is thought." Between them, an opening parenthesis sets off extra information about the eye. That information must be closed with a parenthesis, and nothing may come between the closing parenthesis and the verb.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing parenthesis matches the opening one, and the subject connects directly to "is thought."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The closing parenthesis is right, but the comma after it separates the subject "This parietal eye" from its verb "is thought."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon after the parenthesis would cut the subject off from its verb, and "is thought to help …" cannot stand as an independent clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a parenthesis must close with a parenthesis; a comma does not match the opening mark.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Rani Pokhari, a large rectangular pond in the center of Kathmandu, Nepal, was built in 1670 on the orders of King Pratap Malla. According to tradition, the king had the pond dug to console his queen after the death of one of their sons, and a small temple was raised on an island at its ______ the pond was badly damaged in the earthquake of 2015, its restoration became a subject of public debate, with many residents insisting that the walls be rebuilt in traditional brick and lime mortar rather than concrete. The restored pond reopened in 2020.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: center. When,
choices.B: center, when
choices.C: center. When
choices.D: center when

explanation.why: "According to tradition, the king had the pond dug … and a small temple was raised on an island at its center" is a complete sentence. "When the pond was badly damaged in the earthquake of 2015, its restoration became a subject of public debate" is another complete sentence, made of a "When" clause followed by its main clause. Two complete sentences need a period (or equivalent) between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The period is right, but no comma may separate the subordinating word "When" from the clause it introduces.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join the sentence ending at "center" to the sentence that begins with the "when" clause; this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. The period ends the first sentence, and "When" begins a new sentence whose main clause is "its restoration became a subject of public debate."
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two sentences run together, and the reader cannot tell where the first one ends.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In some forests, the crowns of neighboring trees stop just short of touching, so that from below the canopy looks like a jigsaw puzzle with thin channels of sky between the pieces. Botanists call the pattern crown shyness. Its cause is still debated, and several explanations have been ______ branches may break off when they collide in the wind, buds at the tips of branches may stop growing when they sense light reflected from nearby leaves, or the gaps may limit the spread of leaf-eating insects from one tree to the next. Whatever the mechanism, the gaps allow more light to reach the forest floor.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: proposed:
choices.B: proposed,
choices.C: proposed, including:
choices.D: proposed

explanation.why: "Its cause is still debated, and several explanations have been proposed" is an independent clause. What follows is the list of those explanations, each one a full clause ("branches may break off …," "buds … may stop growing …," "the gaps may limit …"). A colon after an independent clause is the mark that introduces such a list.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces the explanations that the clause promises.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The list that follows is made of independent clauses, so a comma here creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Including" must be followed directly by what it introduces, never by a colon, and it introduces nouns, not full clauses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, "proposed branches may break off" runs together and the list is never introduced.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For forty years, Anselm had rowed the ferry across the river below the mill, and he claimed he could read the water the way other men read a newspaper. His nephew Piet, who had taken over the crossing that spring, did not believe him. The river looked the same to Piet every morning: brown, slow, and ______ the old man would stand on the bank, watch a leaf drift past, and announce that the current had shifted toward the far shore overnight. By midsummer Piet had stopped arguing, because the old man was never wrong.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: indifferent yet
choices.B: indifferent, yet,
choices.C: indifferent: yet
choices.D: indifferent, yet

explanation.why: "The river looked the same to Piet every morning: brown, slow, and indifferent" is an independent clause, and "the old man would stand on the bank …" is another. The coordinating conjunction "yet" can join them, but it needs a comma before it and no punctuation after it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as "yet" need a comma before the conjunction; without it, "indifferent yet the old man" runs the clauses together.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma belongs before "yet," not after it; the second comma cuts the conjunction off from the clause it introduces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon cannot be placed in front of a coordinating conjunction; it would separate "yet" from the clause it belongs to.
explanation.D: Correct. A comma followed by "yet" correctly joins the two independent clauses.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The fort at Galle, on the southwestern coast of Sri Lanka, was first fortified by the Portuguese in the late sixteenth century, but the walls that visitors walk along today were largely built by the Dutch after they captured the town in 1640. The ramparts—constructed from blocks of coral and granite and backed with earth so that they could absorb the impact of cannon ______ proved sturdy enough to shield much of the old town from the tsunami of 2004. Inside the walls, narrow streets lined with Dutch-period houses, churches, and warehouses now hold cafes, galleries, and small hotels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fire
choices.B: fire;
choices.C: fire,
choices.D: fire—

explanation.why: The subject "The ramparts" is followed by a dash that opens a long description of how they were built. That description must be closed with a matching dash before the verb "proved," so that the subject connects to its verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing mark, the description is never set off and "cannon fire proved sturdy" reads as if the fire were the subject.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "The ramparts" from its verb "proved," and neither side is an independent clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash must close with a dash; a comma does not match.
explanation.D: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the description, and "The ramparts … proved sturdy" reads as one clause.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Trams have run through the streets of Kolkata, India, since 1873, when the first cars were pulled by horses along a short route between Sealdah and Armenian Ghat. The system was electrified in 1902 and at its height carried passengers across much of the city. The network that survives after decades of closures and the removal of tracks from many of the city's busiest ______ the oldest operating tram system in Asia and the last one in India. Supporters argue that the trams, which produce no exhaust, deserve new investment rather than gradual retirement.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: streets, is
choices.B: streets; is
choices.C: streets is
choices.D: streets—is

explanation.why: The subject of the third sentence is "The network," and everything from "that survives" to "busiest streets" is a clause that identifies which network. The verb is "is." No punctuation may separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma between the subject "The network …" and its verb "is" breaks the rule that nothing separates a subject from its verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; "is the oldest operating tram system" has no subject of its own.
explanation.C: Correct. The long subject connects directly to its verb "is" with no punctuation in between.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A single dash here would cut the subject off from its verb; dashes set off extra information, but "is the oldest …" is the main verb, not an aside.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before reliable instruments for finding longitude existed, sailors estimated a ship's position by dead reckoning, a method that combined the vessel's known starting point with its speed, heading, and the time elapsed. To measure speed, a crew member threw overboard a flat wooden board attached to a line in which knots had been tied at regular ______ the knots that ran out through his hands while a small sandglass emptied, he could estimate the ship's speed, which is still expressed in knots today. Errors accumulated with every reading, so navigators corrected their reckoning whenever land or a clear sky allowed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: intervals, by counting
choices.B: intervals. By counting,
choices.C: intervals by counting
choices.D: intervals. By counting

explanation.why: "To measure speed, a crew member threw overboard a flat wooden board … at regular intervals" is a complete sentence. "By counting the knots … he could estimate the ship's speed" is another, made of an introductory phrase and a main clause. A period must separate them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma cannot join two complete sentences; here it produces a comma splice, with the "By counting" phrase caught between them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The period is right, but the comma after "counting" separates that verb from its object, "the knots."
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two sentences run together and "at regular intervals by counting the knots" misleads the reader about what the counting does.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the first sentence, and "By counting the knots …" opens the next one, which is completed by "he could estimate the ship's speed."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Flamenco, the music and dance tradition of Andalusia in southern Spain, draws on several elements that performers combine in shifting proportions: the cante, or song, whose most serious form, the cante jondo, deals with grief, longing, and ______ the toque, the guitar playing that supports and answers the singer; and the palmas, the sharp, rhythmic handclaps with which other performers mark the beat. A performance may also include the baile, or dance, and shouts of encouragement called jaleo. Once confined mainly to private gatherings, flamenco spread to cafes and theaters in the nineteenth century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: loss
choices.B: loss,
choices.C: loss:
choices.D: loss;

explanation.why: The sentence lists three elements after the colon, and the items themselves contain commas ("the cante, or song, whose most serious form, the cante jondo, …"). When list items contain commas, the items are separated by semicolons, as the later "; and the palmas" shows. The blank marks the end of the first item, so it needs a semicolon.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without any mark, "loss the toque" runs the first item straight into the second.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The list already uses a semicolon before its last item, and a comma here would make "the toque" look like one more thing the cante jondo deals with, alongside grief, longing, and loss.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon has already introduced the list; a second colon in the middle of the list has nothing to introduce.
explanation.D: Correct. The semicolon separates the first item from the second, matching the semicolon used before the third item.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every autumn a man from the canning company drove out to make my aunt an offer for the orchard, and every autumn she walked him to his car without giving an answer. The trees were old and crooked, and half the apples fell before anyone could pick them. When I asked her why she did not simply sell the land and move into town, she looked at me as if I had asked why she did not sell her own ______ she said finally, "has been something I did not plant." The next spring she taught me to graft a new branch onto an old trunk.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: hands. "Nothing here,"
choices.B: hands, "Nothing here,"
choices.C: hands. "Nothing here"
choices.D: hands. "Nothing here",

explanation.why: The sentence about the aunt's look ends at "hands," so a period is needed there. The quotation "Nothing here … has been something I did not plant" is interrupted by "she said finally," and an interrupting attribution is set off by commas. In American English the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
explanation.A: Correct. The period ends the previous sentence, and the comma inside the quotation marks separates the first part of the quotation from "she said finally."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma after "hands" joins the narrator's sentence to the quotation with nothing but a comma, creating a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When an attribution such as "she said" interrupts a quotation, a comma must separate the quoted words from it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In American English, a comma that follows quoted words is placed inside the closing quotation mark, not after it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1939, the self-taught archaeologist Basil Brown, working at the request of the landowner Edith Pretty, uncovered the outline of a 27-meter ship beneath a mound at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk, England. The wood had rotted away, but rows of iron rivets and a stain in the sand preserved the vessel's shape. In the burial chamber at its center lay gold jewelry, silver dishes from the Byzantine Empire, and the remains of an ornate iron helmet. Many scholars believe that the grave belonged to ______ king of East Anglia who died around 624 CE, though no inscription names its occupant.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Rædwald. A
choices.B: Rædwald, a
choices.C: Rædwald; a
choices.D: Rædwald a

explanation.why: "A king of East Anglia who died around 624 CE" is an appositive: a noun phrase that renames "Rædwald" and adds information about him. An appositive that follows a name at the end of a clause is set off with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period would leave "A king of East Anglia … names its occupant" as a fragment without a main verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the appositive "a king of East Anglia …" to the name it describes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, but "a king of East Anglia who died around 624 CE" has no main verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without punctuation, "Rædwald a king of East Anglia" runs the name and its description together.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Diatoms are single-celled algae that drift in oceans and lakes, and they build cell walls of silica, the same material as glass, which they draw from the surrounding water. Each wall consists of two overlapping halves that fit together like the base and lid of a shallow box, and its surface is pierced by rows of pores in patterns so regular that nineteenth-century microscopists used them to test the quality of their lenses. The pores allow nutrients to pass through the ______ so finely spaced that bacteria and other hazards are kept out. Together, diatoms are thought to produce roughly a fifth of the oxygen generated on Earth each year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: wall: yet they are
choices.B: wall, they are
choices.C: wall, yet they are
choices.D: wall yet, they are

explanation.why: "The pores allow nutrients to pass through the wall" and "they are so finely spaced that bacteria and other hazards are kept out" are both independent clauses. They can be joined by a comma plus the coordinating conjunction "yet," which also signals the contrast between letting nutrients in and keeping hazards out.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon cannot be placed before a coordinating conjunction; "yet" belongs with the clause that follows it, and the colon separates them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "yet" properly links the two independent clauses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The comma must come before "yet," not after it; placed after, it cuts the conjunction off from its clause and leaves the two clauses run together.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The field had to be measured before dark, and the ______ had said perhaps ten words to Tomas since they left the inn that morning, showed no sign of hurrying. He set the tripod, sighted along the brass instrument, and wrote a figure in his book. Tomas, holding the far end of the chain at the edge of a ditch he could no longer quite see, began to suspect that the measurements were already finished and that he was being kept out in the cold for no reason except to learn patience. Then the surveyor waved him forward another twenty links, and the suspicion dissolved.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: surveyor—who
choices.B: surveyor; who
choices.C: surveyor who
choices.D: surveyor, who

explanation.why: The clause "who had said perhaps ten words to Tomas since they left the inn that morning" is extra information about the surveyor, and the text closes it with a comma before the verb "showed." Extra information that closes with a comma must open with a comma, so the subject "the surveyor" connects to "showed" across a matched pair.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Extra information that closes with a comma must open with a comma, not a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "who had said … showed no sign of hurrying" is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no opening comma, the "who" clause reads as essential, and the comma that already follows "morning" then separates the subject from its verb "showed."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma opens the pair of commas that set off the "who" clause, and "the surveyor … showed no sign of hurrying" reads as one clause.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Metal type was too heavy and too costly to cast at the sizes that nineteenth-century posters demanded, so printers turned to wood. In 1827, the New York printer Darius Wells began cutting letters from end-grain maple with a router, and firms such as the Hamilton Manufacturing Company of Two Rivers, Wisconsin, which by the early twentieth century had absorbed most of its ______ wood type to printers across the United States. Although photographic and digital methods later made the blocks obsolete, a growing number of small presses have returned to them, drawn by the slightly uneven impression that worn wooden letters leave on paper.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: competitors, shipped,
choices.B: competitors shipped
choices.C: competitors; shipped
choices.D: competitors, shipped

explanation.why: The subject "firms such as the Hamilton Manufacturing Company of Two Rivers, Wisconsin" is interrupted by the extra information "which by the early twentieth century had absorbed most of its competitors," which opens with a comma after "Wisconsin." That information must close with a comma before the verb "shipped," and the verb must then connect directly to its object, "wood type."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The first comma is right, but the second one separates the verb "shipped" from its object "wood type."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The "which" clause opened with a comma, so it must close with one; without it, the verb "shipped" seems to belong to the "which" clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "firms" from its verb "shipped," and "shipped wood type …" has no subject of its own.
explanation.D: Correct. The comma closes the pair around the "which" clause, and "shipped" leads straight into its object.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The insurance market known as Lloyd's of London takes its name not from a founder but from a coffee house. In the 1680s, Edward Lloyd opened a shop near the Thames that became a favorite meeting place for ship owners, merchants, and the men who, for a fee, agreed to bear part of the loss if a vessel failed to return. Lloyd himself never insured a ______ simply supplied a room, coffee, and reliable shipping news, which he gathered at the docks and later printed in a newsletter. The underwriters who met under his roof eventually formed a society that outlived the coffee house by centuries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ship; he
choices.B: ship, he
choices.C: ship, instead he
choices.D: ship he

explanation.why: "Lloyd himself never insured a ship" and "he simply supplied a room, coffee, and reliable shipping news" are two independent clauses. A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses on its own.
explanation.A: Correct. The semicolon joins the two independent clauses without a conjunction.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Instead" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma plus "instead" still leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Gobelins workshop in Paris began in the fifteenth century as a family dye works on the banks of the Bièvre, a small stream whose waters were prized for the scarlet they helped produce. In 1662, Louis XIV's finance minister bought the premises and gathered there weavers, painters, and metalworkers who would furnish the royal palaces. The weavers worked from the back of the loom, checking the front in mirrors and following painted designs that the painter Charles Le Brun supervised. A single tapestry could occupy a team of weavers for several ______ is why the workshop's output was counted in dozens of pieces per decade rather than hundreds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: years, which
choices.B: years which
choices.C: years; which
choices.D: years. Which

explanation.why: "A single tapestry could occupy a team of weavers for several years" is a complete clause, and "which is why the workshop's output was counted in dozens …" is a nonessential "which" clause that comments on that whole fact. A nonessential "which" clause is attached to the sentence with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma attaches the nonessential "which" clause to the clause it refers to.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A nonessential "which" clause must be set off by a comma; without one, "years which" runs the comment into the clause it comments on.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but a clause that begins with "which" cannot stand on its own.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "Which is why … rather than hundreds" as a fragment, since a "which" clause depends on the sentence before it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Each spring in Patan, Nepal, a towering chariot is built for the Rato Machhindranath festival, which honors a deity associated with rain and a good harvest. The chariot's spire, assembled from bamboo poles bound with cane and vines rather than ______ well above the rooftops of the old town, and the whole structure is hauled from one neighborhood to the next by teams of volunteers over several weeks. On the festival's final day a jeweled vest, the bhoto, is displayed from the chariot; according to a story told in Patan, its ownership was once disputed, and it is shown each year so that the rightful owner may come forward.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: nails, rises
choices.B: nails; rises
choices.C: nails rises
choices.D: nails—rises

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "The chariot's spire," and its verb is "rises." Between them, "assembled from bamboo poles bound with cane and vines rather than nails" is extra information that opens with a comma after "spire," so it must close with a comma before the verb.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "spire," and the subject connects to its verb "rises."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb, and "rises well above the rooftops …" has no subject of its own.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a comma must also close with one; without it, the phrase runs into the verb and "nails rises" reads as if the nails were rising.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The extra information opened with a comma, so it cannot close with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: During Japan's Edo period, the shakuhachi, an end-blown flute cut from the root end of a bamboo stalk, was closely associated with the komuso, wandering monks of a Zen sect who treated playing the instrument as a form of meditation. Several features set these monks apart from other ______ the deep basket hat, woven from reeds, that covered the face entirely and signaled the wearer's withdrawal from the world; the long solo pieces, passed down from teacher to student, that they played while walking from house to house; and the bowl into which listeners dropped coins or rice. After the sect was abolished in 1871, the pieces survived among secular players.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: travelers;
choices.B: travelers:
choices.C: travelers,
choices.D: travelers

explanation.why: "Several features set these monks apart from other travelers" is an independent clause, and what follows is the list of those features, with semicolons separating items that contain commas. A colon after an independent clause introduces such a list.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must have an independent clause after it, but "the deep basket hat, woven from reeds, that covered the face …" is a noun phrase, not a clause.
explanation.B: Correct. The colon follows a complete clause and introduces the list of features that the clause promises.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma would make "the deep basket hat" read as a description of "other travelers" rather than the first item of a list.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without any mark, "other travelers the deep basket hat" runs the clause into the list it introduces.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The house was quiet in the way that houses are quiet when their master is away, and Miss Avery, who had been engaged as governess only a month before, had not yet learned to read its silences. The children's uncle had left for the coast without saying when he would return. Each evening she found herself at the window of the schoolroom, and each evening she asked herself the same thing: whether the carriage would appear on the road before the lamps were ______ never spoke the question aloud, for she suspected that the children, in their own fashion, were asking it too.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: lit? She
choices.B: lit she
choices.C: lit, she
choices.D: lit. She

explanation.why: The sentence reports a question indirectly ("she asked herself … whether the carriage would appear") rather than quoting it, and an indirect question is a statement, so it ends with a period. "She never spoke the question aloud …" is a new sentence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only a direct question takes a question mark; "whether the carriage would appear …" reports the question indirectly, so the sentence is a statement.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without punctuation, two independent clauses run together.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join the sentence ending at "lit" to the independent clause "she never spoke the question aloud"; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the statement containing the indirect question, and "She" begins the next sentence.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Sixty Dome Mosque at Bagerhat, in southwestern Bangladesh, was built in the middle of the fifteenth century by Khan Jahan Ali, a general and governor who turned a stretch of swampy forest into a planned city of mosques, roads, and reservoirs. Its ______ is misleading. The roof of the mosque is in fact carried on seventy-seven domes, and the number in the name more likely refers to the sixty slender stone pillars, arranged in rows, that support the brick arches from inside the hall. The mosque is the best preserved of the monuments of Khan Jahan's city, which was gradually abandoned after his death.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: name, however
choices.B: name; however,
choices.C: name, however,
choices.D: name however,

explanation.why: In "Its name, however, is misleading," the word "however" interrupts the clause between the subject "Its name" and the verb "is." An interrupting word like this is extra information and must be set off by a comma on each side.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The comma before "however" opens the interruption, but a matching comma must close it before the verb "is."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "Its name" is only a subject with no verb, and "however, is misleading" has no subject.
explanation.C: Correct. The pair of commas sets off the interrupting "however," and the subject "Its name" connects to its verb "is."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The interrupting "however" needs a comma before it as well as after it; with only one comma, the subject "Its name however" runs together.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In a kabuki theater, the action is not confined to the stage. A raised walkway called the hanamichi runs from the rear of the auditorium through the audience to the left side of the stage, and some of the most memorable moments in a play take place on it. Why does an actor making a grand entrance stop at a fixed point about seven-tenths of the way along the ______ answer is that the audience can see him from both sides there, so he strikes a pose, delivers a speech, or simply holds still while the house watches. A trapdoor at the same spot lets ghosts and demons rise from below.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: walkway, the
choices.B: walkway? The
choices.C: walkway; the
choices.D: walkway. The

explanation.why: "Why does an actor making a grand entrance stop at a fixed point about seven-tenths of the way along the walkway" is a direct question, worded in question order ("Why does an actor … stop"), so it must end with a question mark. "The answer is that …" begins a new sentence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join the question to the independent clause "the answer is that …," and the question would also lose its question mark.
explanation.B: Correct. The question mark ends the direct question, and a new sentence begins with "The answer."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon cannot stand in for the question mark that a direct question requires.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A direct question that begins "Why does an actor … stop" cannot end with a period; a period would turn the question into a statement that has no sense.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: My uncle bound books in a room above a stationer's shop, and on Saturdays he let me watch. The part I waited for was the marbling. He floated colors on a tray of thickened water, dragged a comb through them until the surface swirled like oil on a puddle, and then laid a sheet of paper on top so lightly that it seemed to rest on air. The ______ he lifted away, each printed with a pattern that would never be repeated, became the endpapers of books I would later find in the shop's window. He did not let me try the comb myself until the winter I turned fourteen.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: sheets, that
choices.B: sheets—that
choices.C: sheets; that
choices.D: sheets that

explanation.why: The clause "that he lifted away" is essential: it tells the reader which sheets became endpapers. A "that" clause is never set off from the noun it limits, so "sheets" connects directly to "that." The only pair of commas in the sentence sets off the separate extra phrase "each printed with a pattern that would never be repeated."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Commas set off nonessential information, but a clause introduced by "that" is essential and is never preceded by a comma.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A dash would set the "that" clause off as an aside, but the clause is essential, and nothing closes the dash before the verb "became."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "The sheets" is only a subject and "that he lifted away … became the endpapers" cannot stand alone.
explanation.D: Correct. The essential "that" clause attaches directly to "sheets" with no punctuation.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the sixteenth century, long before Europeans settled the region, Basque whalers from the ports of northern Spain and southwestern France sailed each summer to the Strait of Belle Isle, between Newfoundland and Labrador, to hunt right and bowhead whales. At Red Bay, on the Labrador shore, the stone ovens in which they rendered blubber into oil (a commodity so valuable in Europe that a single cargo could repay the cost of a ______ still survive, along with barrels, tools, and the wreck of at least one galleon, which sank in the harbor in 1565. The station was identified in the 1970s by a historian working from Spanish archives.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: voyage,
choices.B: voyage),
choices.C: voyage)
choices.D: voyage);

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "the stone ovens," and its verb is "still survive." Between them, a parenthesis opens an aside about the value of whale oil. That aside must close with a parenthesis, and nothing may come between the closing parenthesis and the verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. An aside that opens with a parenthesis must close with a parenthesis, not a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The closing parenthesis is right, but the comma after it separates the subject "the stone ovens" from its verb "still survive."
explanation.C: Correct. The closing parenthesis matches the opening one, and the subject connects directly to "still survive."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon after the parenthesis would cut the subject off from its verb, and "still survive, along with barrels …" cannot stand as an independent clause.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When the first line of the Paris Métro opened in 1900, its street entrances were designed by Hector Guimard, a young architect whose work in the Art Nouveau style had already attracted attention. Guimard's entrances were cast in iron and painted green, with railings that curved like plant stems and lamps held aloft on stalks shaped like the buds of some enormous flower. Although critics at the time found the entrances strange and even unsettling, and dozens were removed in the decades that ______ that remain are now protected as historic monuments. Of the roughly 140 entrances built, fewer than 90 survive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: followed; those
choices.B: followed those
choices.C: followed, those
choices.D: followed. Those

explanation.why: The third sentence begins with "Although," so everything up to "in the decades that followed" is one long dependent clause containing two parts joined by "and." The main clause is "those that remain are now protected as historic monuments." A dependent clause that comes first is joined to its main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent and cannot stand alone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a comma, the long introductory clause runs straight into the main clause, and "that followed those that remain" becomes impossible to read.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma links the introductory "Although" clause to the main clause "those that remain are now protected."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although critics … in the decades that followed" as a fragment with no main clause.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The cave temple at Dambulla, in central Sri Lanka, occupies five chambers hollowed beneath an overhanging granite ridge. According to tradition, a king who had been driven from his throne in the first century BCE sheltered in the caves and, after regaining power, had them turned into a shrine. The roughly 150 statues that the caves ______ images of the Buddha seated, standing, and reclining; figures of two Sri Lankan kings; and several Hindu gods. Most of the murals visible today were repainted in the eighteenth century, when the kingdom of Kandy sponsored a wave of restoration.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: hold include;
choices.B: hold, include
choices.C: hold include:
choices.D: hold include

explanation.why: The subject of the third sentence is "The roughly 150 statues that the caves hold," and its verb is "include." The verb leads directly into the list that is its object. No punctuation may separate a subject from its verb or a verb from its object, even when the object is a long list.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and it cannot separate the verb "include" from the list that is its object.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The comma separates the subject "The roughly 150 statues that the caves hold" from its verb "include."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon may introduce a list only after a complete clause; "The roughly 150 statues that the caves hold include" is not complete until its object follows, so the colon separates the verb from its object.
explanation.D: Correct. The subject, the verb "include," and the list that is its object follow one another with no punctuation between them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: At Hamelin Pool, an arm of Shark Bay in Western Australia, the shallows are dotted with rounded mounds that look like boulders but are alive. They are stromatolites, structures built by mats of cyanobacteria that trap grains of sediment and bind them with lime. The ______ built up layer by layer as each new film of microbes grows over the sediment the last one caught—rise by less than a millimeter a year, so a mound the height of a stool may be a thousand years old. Hamelin Pool's water is roughly twice as salty as the open ocean, which keeps away the snails that would otherwise graze the mats.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: mounds,
choices.B: mounds;
choices.C: mounds—
choices.D: mounds

explanation.why: The subject "The mounds" is followed by the extra information "built up layer by layer as each new film of microbes grows over the sediment the last one caught," which the text closes with a dash before the verb "rise." Extra information that closes with a dash must open with a dash.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The extra information closes with a dash, so it cannot open with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "The mounds" is only a subject with no verb.
explanation.C: Correct. The opening dash matches the closing dash, and the subject "The mounds" connects to its verb "rise."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without an opening mark, "The mounds built up layer by layer" reads as the main clause, and the dash before "rise" is then left unmatched.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Inés had worked the night shift at the railway telegraph office for three weeks, and in that time the machine had chattered perhaps a dozen times, mostly with routine notices about freight. She had learned to doze with one hand resting near the key. On the night of the storm, she woke to a burst of clicks that she could not at first ______ was keying too fast, or the line was carrying some interference from the lightning, and she had to ask twice for the message to be repeated before she understood that a bridge was down. By then she was already reaching for the lamp.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: read the sender
choices.B: read; the sender,
choices.C: read, the sender
choices.D: read. The sender

explanation.why: "On the night of the storm, she woke to a burst of clicks that she could not at first read" is a complete sentence. "The sender was keying too fast, or the line was carrying some interference …, and she had to ask twice …" is another, made of independent clauses properly joined by "or" and "and." A period must separate the two sentences.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without punctuation, "could not at first read the sender" runs the first sentence into the second and changes its meaning.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The semicolon could join the clauses, but the comma after "sender" separates that subject from its verb "was keying."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join the sentence ending at "read" to the independent clause "the sender was keying too fast"; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the first sentence, and "The sender was keying too fast" begins the next one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Tea has been grown on the low hills of Sylhet, in northeastern Bangladesh, since 1854, when the region's first commercial garden was planted at Malnicherra. The district's heavy monsoon rainfall and well-drained slopes suit the tea bush, and today more than a hundred gardens spread across the hills around Srimangal, a town sometimes called the tea capital of the country. Pluckers, most of whom are women and many of whom belong to families that have worked the same garden for ______ move along the rows picking only the top two leaves and the bud of each shoot, which yield the most delicate flavor.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: generations—
choices.B: generations
choices.C: generations;
choices.D: generations,

explanation.why: The subject of the third sentence is "Pluckers," and its verb is "move." Between them, "most of whom are women and many of whom belong to families that have worked the same garden for generations" is extra information that opens with a comma after "Pluckers," so it must close with a comma before the verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The extra information opened with a comma, so it cannot close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off, and "for generations move along the rows" runs the aside into the verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Pluckers" from its verb "move," and "move along the rows …" has no subject of its own.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "Pluckers," and the subject connects to its verb "move."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hydrologists often describe the Indus as one of the great irrigation systems of the world. The river ______ flows about 3,000 kilometers from the Tibetan Plateau to the Arabian Sea, has supported farming along its floodplain for thousands of years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: which
choices.B: . Which
choices.C: , which
choices.D: ; which

explanation.why: "Which flows about 3,000 kilometers ..." is a nonessential clause that adds information about the river, so it needs a comma before it and a comma after it. The sentence then reaches its main verb "has supported."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A nonessential clause needs a comma before it. Without the opening comma, the closing comma after "Sea" splits the subject from its verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period turns the clause into a sentence fragment that starts with "Which" and has no independent clause. The text needs one sentence here.
explanation.C: Correct. The clause "which flows about 3,000 kilometers" adds extra detail, so it is set off by a pair of commas. The main sentence then continues with its verb "has supported."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses. "Which flows..." is a dependent clause, so a semicolon cannot introduce it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Engineers designing a suspension bridge must balance the forces on its cables. Each main cable carries the weight of the deck along its length, and the towers transfer that load into the foundations ______ who test scale models can find weak points before any steel is ordered.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: , engineers
choices.B: engineers
choices.C: ; engineers
choices.D: ; and engineers

explanation.why: Both sides of the blank are independent clauses, so a boundary that joins two of them is needed. A semicolon links them correctly, while a comma alone makes a splice and no punctuation makes a run-on.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma cannot join two independent clauses. Both "the towers transfer that load" and "engineers ... can find weak points" are complete clauses, so the comma creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Two independent clauses with no punctuation between them form a run-on sentence. A semicolon or period is needed.
explanation.C: Correct. A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses. The first clause is complete, and the second begins with its own subject, "engineers."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can be used with a coordinating conjunction only in special cases, and it does not belong before "and" here. A comma is the usual mark before "and" joining clauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Horizontal gene transfer lets bacteria acquire DNA from neighbors rather than receiving it only from their parents, and it is a major route for the spread of antibiotic resistance. Laboratory studies have measured transfer rates in careful detail ______ its patterns in natural settings are hard to predict from genome sequences alone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: , however, its
choices.B: . However its
choices.C: ; however, its
choices.D: however, its

explanation.why: The blank must join two independent clauses that contrast, so the boundary needs a semicolon before "however" and a comma after it. The other options either splice the clauses, omit the comma after "However," or run them together.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma cannot join two independent clauses, and that is what happens here. A conjunctive adverb such as "however" needs a semicolon before it when it links two clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period is acceptable here, but "However" at the start of a sentence needs a comma after it. Without that comma, the sentence breaks a basic rule.
explanation.C: Correct. A semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and "however" is set off by commas. This is the standard pattern for a contrast linked with a conjunctive adverb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Two independent clauses with no punctuation before "however" make a run-on sentence. A semicolon is needed.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians who study merchant networks rely on a small number of surviving documents, and each source is treated with caution. In one family archive, three items proved especially valuable ______ a ledger, a letter, and a map.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ; a ledger
choices.B: , a ledger
choices.C: a ledger
choices.D: : a ledger

explanation.why: The part before the blank is a complete independent clause, and the part after it is a list that explains it. A colon is the correct mark for introducing a list after a complete clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and nothing complete follows. The list is not a clause, so the semicolon is wrong.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma here would separate the verb "proved" from its complement, the list that explains what was valuable. The sentence does not work with a comma.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the list would run into the main clause. A colon is needed to introduce a list after an independent clause.
explanation.D: Correct. A colon introduces a list after a complete independent clause. The clause "three items proved especially valuable" is complete, and the list explains what the items were.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The visitor studied the vase for nearly an hour before speaking to the curator. Then the visitor asked the curator ______ The curator replied that the records were incomplete, so no one could be certain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: whether the glaze on the vase was original.
choices.B: whether the glaze on the vase was original?
choices.C: whether the glaze on the vase was original!
choices.D: whether the glaze on the vase was original,

explanation.why: The blank ends a reported question, which is a sentence that describes what the visitor asked rather than quoting the question itself. Such a sentence takes a period, and the next sentence starts fresh.
explanation.A: Correct. The sentence reports a question indirectly, so it is a statement and ends with a period. The next sentence begins a new independent clause that starts with a capital letter.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A question mark is used only for a direct question. This sentence reports the visitor's question without quoting it, so it ends with a period.
explanation.C: Incorrect. An exclamation point signals strong feeling. A reported question in formal writing ends with a period, not an exclamation point.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma cannot end a complete sentence. With "The curator replied" following, this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most mammals keep their bodies at a steady, warm temperature, but the arctic ground squirrel is a striking exception. During its winter hibernation in Alaska and northern Canada, the squirrel's body temperature can drop below the freezing point of water, the lowest body temperature measured in any mammal. Even so, the animal does not freeze solid: every few weeks it wakes briefly, warms itself up by shivering, and then cools down again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Arctic ground squirrels hibernate for longer periods than any other mammal in the far north.
choices.B: The arctic ground squirrel survives unusually low body temperatures while it hibernates.
choices.C: The arctic ground squirrel wakes every few weeks during winter to warm itself up.
choices.D: Most mammals cannot keep a steady body temperature in very cold climates.

explanation.why: The text opens by calling the arctic ground squirrel "a striking exception" to the steady body temperature of most mammals, then explains that during hibernation its temperature can fall below freezing. The last sentence adds how it survives this. The main idea must cover the whole text: the squirrel endures extremely low body temperatures in hibernation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never compares how long different mammals hibernate.
explanation.B: Correct. Every sentence supports this point: the squirrel is an exception, its temperature drops below freezing, and it still survives.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Waking every few weeks is one detail from the last sentence, not the main point of the whole text.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: most mammals do keep a steady, warm temperature.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, weavers near Dhaka, in what is now Bangladesh, made a cotton cloth so fine and light that it was traded across Asia and Europe. The cloth, known as Dhaka muslin, was spun from a local cotton plant that grew along the banks of the Meghna River. By the early 1900s, however, the craft had disappeared, partly because cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain had replaced it in many markets.
items.stem: According to the text, what was one reason Dhaka muslin stopped being made?

choices.A: Its weavers left the region to look for work in European cities.
choices.B: The local cotton plant used to spin it became too costly to grow.
choices.C: The cloth was too delicate to survive long trade journeys.
choices.D: Cheaper fabric made by machines replaced it in many markets.

explanation.why: The question asks for a reason the craft ended. The last sentence gives it directly: the craft disappeared "partly because cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain had replaced it in many markets." The correct choice restates this in other words.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the cloth was traded to Europe, not that the weavers moved there.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions the local cotton plant but never says it became expensive.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the cloth was traded across Asia and Europe, so it clearly survived long journeys.
explanation.D: Correct. "Cheaper fabric made by machines" restates "cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain," which the text names as a reason the craft disappeared.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Completed in the 120s CE, the dome of the Pantheon in Rome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its builders had no steel bars to strengthen the concrete, so they controlled the dome's weight in other ways. Near the base, where the structure carries the greatest load, the concrete contains heavy stone and the walls are several meters thick. Toward the top, the walls grow thinner, and the builders mixed in pumice, a light volcanic rock, so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did the Pantheon's builders use pumice in the upper part of the dome?

choices.A: To reduce the weight that the top of the dome placed on the parts beneath it
choices.B: To make the upper walls of the dome thicker than the walls near its base
choices.C: To replace the steel bars that Roman builders usually placed in concrete
choices.D: To make the dome larger than any other concrete dome built in Rome at the time

explanation.why: The text says the builders "controlled the dome's weight" without steel. It then explains that they mixed in pumice, "a light volcanic rock, so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below." So the pumice was used to lighten the top of the dome and reduce the load on the lower parts.
explanation.A: Correct. The text states that pumice was used "so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the walls grow thinner toward the top, not thicker.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the builders had no steel bars at all, so pumice could not be replacing a usual practice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text notes the dome's record size but never says pumice was used to achieve it.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Tomás had expected the work at his grandmother's pottery to be quick. On the first morning he shaped six bowls, each one lopsided, and pushed them aside in frustration. His grandmother said nothing; she simply cut the last bowl from the wheel and handed him a fresh lump of clay. By the end of the week, Tomás had made only two bowls, but he had stopped counting. He found himself listening to the hum of the wheel and the soft drag of his fingers through the wet clay, and he no longer glanced at the clock.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Tomás grows frustrated because his grandmother refuses to show him how to use the wheel.
choices.B: Tomás learns to shape bowls much more quickly as the week goes on.
choices.C: Tomás shifts from rushing his work to becoming absorbed in the process of making it.
choices.D: Tomás's grandmother is disappointed by the lopsided bowls he makes on the first morning.

explanation.why: At the start, Tomás expects the work "to be quick," makes six bowls, and is frustrated. By the end of the week he makes fewer bowls, has "stopped counting," and "no longer glanced at the clock." The text as a whole traces this change from hurrying to being absorbed in the work.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The grandmother says nothing, but the text never says she refuses to teach him; she hands him more clay to keep working.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Tomás actually makes fewer bowls by the end of the week (two, compared with six on the first morning).
explanation.C: Correct. This covers both the beginning (expecting quick work, frustration) and the end (stopping counting, ignoring the clock).
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not describe the grandmother's feelings about the bowls, and the point concerns Tomás's change.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the seasonally flooded forests of the Amazon basin, some trees drop their fruit into the water, where it is eaten by fish such as the tambaqui. Because seeds can pass through a fish's gut intact and be released far from the parent tree, ecologists have long suspected that these fish help disperse seeds. Tracking studies now suggest that the largest individuals, which swim farther and hold seeds longer, may carry seeds several kilometers. This finding has an uncomfortable implication: fishing tends to remove precisely the biggest fish, so even where tambaqui remain common, the forest may be losing its most effective long-distance seed dispersers, a loss that population counts alone would not reveal.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Fishing has made tambaqui rare in flooded forests by removing the species' largest individuals.
choices.B: Ecologists have long suspected that fish such as the tambaqui help spread the seeds of flooded-forest trees.
choices.C: Large tambaqui carry seeds farther than any other animal living in the Amazon's flooded forests.
choices.D: Fishing may reduce long-distance seed dispersal in flooded forests even where tambaqui remain common.

explanation.why: The text builds to its final sentence: because the largest tambaqui "may carry seeds several kilometers" and fishing "tends to remove precisely the biggest fish," the forest "may be losing its most effective long-distance seed dispersers" even "where tambaqui remain common." The main idea is this possible hidden effect of fishing on seed dispersal, stated with the text's own caution ("may").
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the loss could happen "even where tambaqui remain common," so it does not claim the fish have become rare.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is background from the second sentence; it leaves out the new finding about large fish and its implication.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text compares large tambaqui only with smaller tambaqui, not with every other animal in the forest.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the text's main point, including its hedge ("may") and the key condition that the fish can still be common.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many illustrated manuscripts produced in the workshop of the Mughal emperor Akbar in the late sixteenth century carry small notes in their margins naming the artists involved. These notes frequently list more than one name for a single painting: one artist is credited with the design of the composition, another with the coloring, and occasionally a third with the faces. For art historians, the inscriptions complicate a habit inherited from the study of European painting, in which a work is attributed to a single master whose personal style it expresses. In Akbar's workshop, the notes suggest, a painting's distinctive qualities may have emerged from collaboration rather than from any one hand.
items.stem: According to the text, what do the notes in the margins of many manuscripts from Akbar's workshop indicate?

choices.A: Artists in Akbar's workshop, like European masters, were each credited with whole paintings.
choices.B: A single painting was often produced by several artists who handled different tasks.
choices.C: European painters had trained many of the artists who worked in Akbar's workshop.
choices.D: Every painting in Akbar's workshop was produced by at least three separate artists.

explanation.why: The text says the notes "frequently list more than one name for a single painting," with different artists credited for the design, the coloring, and "occasionally" the faces. So the notes show that paintings were often made by several artists with different jobs. Watch the qualifiers: "frequently" and "occasionally" rule out any choice that says "every."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The notes show the opposite: paintings were credited to more than one artist, which is why they complicate the European single-master habit.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates "more than one name for a single painting," with separate credits for design, coloring, and sometimes faces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. European painting is mentioned only as the source of art historians' habits, not as an influence on Akbar's artists.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A third artist is credited only "occasionally," and multiple names appear "frequently," not always.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mrs. Halloran had long prided herself on receiving bad news as she received the post: promptly, and without remark. When her brother's letter arrived announcing that the old family house at Kilrush was to be sold, she read it once at the breakfast table, folded it along its original creases, and asked the maid whether the bread had come. Only later, when she found herself in the garden at an hour she never went there, standing before the gooseberry bushes she had grown from cuttings taken at that very house, did she understand that she had been composing, all morning, a reply she had no intention of sending.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mrs. Halloran is secretly relieved that the old family house at Kilrush is finally to be sold.
choices.B: Mrs. Halloran resents her brother for deciding to sell the house without asking her.
choices.C: Mrs. Halloran's calm response to the news hides, even from herself, how much it affects her.
choices.D: Mrs. Halloran's lifelong composure finally gives way when she breaks down in the garden.

explanation.why: Two parts of the text must be read together. At breakfast she reacts "without remark," folding the letter and asking about the bread. Later, standing by bushes grown from the house's cuttings, she realizes she has been "composing, all morning, a reply." The words "Only later ... did she understand" show that her calm surface hid her feelings even from her own awareness.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Her drift to the gooseberry bushes from the old house and her mental reply suggest she is unsettled by the sale, not relieved.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the brother failed to consult her, and it does not reveal what her unsent reply says.
explanation.C: Correct. Her outward calm at breakfast contrasts with her later realization; "only later ... did she understand" shows the feeling was hidden even from her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This overstates the garden scene: she quietly realizes something, but nothing suggests she breaks down.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: That Inca administrators used khipus, arrangements of knotted cords, to record numbers is not in dispute: the position and type of each knot correspond to a decimal system, and many khipus tally census figures or goods owed to the state. Whether some khipus also recorded language is a harder question. Spanish chroniclers of the sixteenth century reported that khipu keepers could "read" histories and family lines from the cords, yet such testimony, offered by observers who could not themselves interpret the cords, establishes only that keepers recited narratives while handling khipus, not that the narratives were encoded in them. A few surviving khipus whose cords vary in color and fiber far more than any numerical purpose would require have therefore drawn particular attention.
items.stem: Based on the text, why have certain surviving khipus drawn particular attention?

choices.A: Their variety of colors and fibers seems to exceed what recording numbers alone would require.
choices.B: They confirm chroniclers' reports that khipu keepers could read histories directly from cords.
choices.C: Their knots, unlike those of the census khipus, do not follow a decimal system of positions.
choices.D: Spanish observers saw keepers reciting narratives while handling these particular khipus.

explanation.why: The text says the chroniclers' reports cannot settle whether khipus recorded language. The last sentence, linked by "therefore," explains why some khipus stand out: their cords vary "far more than any numerical purpose would require." That extra variety is what makes them possible evidence of a non-numerical record.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the final sentence: the variety goes beyond "any numerical purpose," which is why these khipus interest researchers asking whether khipus recorded language.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text calls the question of language open and says the reports prove less than they seem to; nothing confirms them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says these khipus' knots break from the decimal system; it points to color and fiber instead.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text discusses the chroniclers' testimony in general, not observations tied to these particular khipus.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The hoatzin, a pheasant-sized bird of the swampy forests of South America, usually builds its nest on branches that hang over water. When a snake or other predator comes near, a young hoatzin may simply drop out of the nest into the water below and swim away.
