Ancient writers do report that books burned when fires set by Julius Caesar's forces spread through part of the city in 48 BCE. Many historians, however, think the library's end was slower and less dramatic. Over the centuries, royal support for scholars weakened, some scholars were driven out during political conflicts, and fewer new copies were made of the collection's papyrus scrolls, which decay with age.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Papyrus scrolls decay with age unless new copies of them are made.
choices.B: Many historians think the library declined gradually rather than in one fire.
choices.C: The library held more books than any other library in the ancient world.
choices.D: Fires set by Julius Caesar's forces destroyed the entire library in 48 BCE.

explanation.why: The text opens with a popular memory (the library "vanished in a single great fire"), grants that some books did burn in 48 BCE, and then, with "however," gives historians' view that the end "was slower and less dramatic," listing causes over centuries. The main idea is this gradual-decline view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The decay of papyrus is one of several causes listed, not the main point.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures the contrast the text builds: the popular single-fire story versus historians' view of a slow decline.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares the library's size with that of other ancient libraries.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says only that some books burned in 48 BCE; it presents total destruction by one fire as the popular memory historians doubt.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Desert locusts spend much of their lives as solitary insects: shy, green, and inclined to avoid one another. When drought crowds them onto shrinking patches of vegetation, however, repeated contact with other locusts, particularly touches to the hind legs, can trigger a striking transformation. Within hours, crowded individuals become restless and attracted to one another, and over later generations they develop different colors and body proportions. Laboratory work has linked the initial change in behavior to a surge of the chemical messenger serotonin in the nervous system. The finding suggests that the swarms capable of stripping farmland across Africa and Asia are not a separate kind of locust but the same insects responding to the crowded conditions they encounter.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Drought is the main cause of the destructive locust swarms that strip farmland across Africa and Asia.
choices.B: Serotonin causes crowded locusts to change their color and body shape within just a few hours.
choices.C: Swarming locusts appear to be ordinary desert locusts that have changed in response to crowding.
choices.D: Solitary desert locusts are usually green and tend to avoid contact with other locusts.

explanation.why: The text describes how crowding, through repeated contact, switches solitary locusts into a different state, and its last sentence states the conclusion: swarms are "not a separate kind of locust but the same insects responding to the crowded conditions." The main idea must capture that link between crowding and swarming, not just one step in the process.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says drought crowds locusts together, but it presents contact with other locusts, not drought itself, as the trigger, and it never ranks drought as the main cause of swarms.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text links serotonin only to the "initial change in behavior"; changes in color and body proportions come "over later generations," not within hours.
explanation.C: Correct. This matches the text's conclusion that swarms are made up of the same insects transformed by crowded conditions.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes only the solitary phase in the first sentence and leaves out the transformation that the text is about.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: After her husband's death, Agnieszka Wróbel kept the clock shop open chiefly, she told the neighbors, so that the stock would not be wasted. She could not repair a mainspring and had no wish to learn. Yet each evening, once the shutters were drawn, she wound every clock on the walls, though no customer would come before morning to hear them, and set each one by the old regulator that Tadeusz had trusted above the railway time. When the apprentice suggested they let the unsold clocks run down to spare the springs, she told him sharply that a shop of stopped clocks was a shop for sale, and the matter was not raised again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Agnieszka is determined to master the clock repairs that her husband once did.
choices.B: Agnieszka's nightly habits suggest a deeper attachment to the shop than she admits.
choices.C: Agnieszka keeps the shop open mainly so that her husband's stock can be sold off.
choices.D: Agnieszka resents the apprentice for trying to take control of the clock shop from her.

explanation.why: The first sentence gives Agnieszka's stated reason ("she told the neighbors") for keeping the shop open: not wasting the stock. The rest of the text undercuts that reason: she winds every clock each night when no one will hear them, sets them by the regulator her husband trusted, and refuses to let them stop because "a shop of stopped clocks was a shop for sale." Her actions reveal an attachment that her practical explanation does not admit.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says she "had no wish to learn" to repair a mainspring, which contradicts this choice.
explanation.B: Correct. Her careful nightly care for the clocks and her refusal to let them stop show an attachment beyond the practical reason she gives.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This takes her explanation to the neighbors at face value; her nightly winding of clocks no customer will hear shows that more than selling stock is at stake.
explanation.D: Incorrect. She answers the apprentice sharply once, but nothing suggests he is trying to take control of the shop or that she resents him.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The eleven medieval churches of Lalibela, in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, are often described as buildings, but in a strict sense almost none of them was built. Workers, probably in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, began with solid volcanic rock and removed material rather than adding it: they cut deep trenches to isolate a block, then hollowed the block into rooms, windows, and columns. Because nothing could be put back once it was removed, the method left little room for error, and some scholars infer that the plans must have been settled in detail before cutting began. Others caution that irregularities in several interiors suggest that designs were adjusted as the work proceeded.
items.stem: According to the text, why do some scholars infer that the plans for the churches were settled in detail before cutting began?

choices.A: The volcanic rock was too hard to allow any changes once the carving had started.
choices.B: Irregularities in several interiors show that workers kept to a single fixed design.
choices.C: Trenches had to be cut around each block before its interior could be hollowed.
choices.D: Rock removed during carving could not be restored if the workers made a mistake.

explanation.why: The text gives the reason directly with "Because": "nothing could be put back once it was removed," so the method "left little room for error," and from this some scholars infer that the plans were settled in advance. Keep track of who says what: the irregularities are evidence cited by other scholars for the opposite view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never describes the rock as too hard to change; the problem was that removed material could not be replaced.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the irregularities suggest designs "were adjusted as the work proceeded," so they support the other scholars' view, not a fixed design.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is a true step in the method, but it is not the reason the text gives for the scholars' inference.
explanation.D: Correct. This restates the reason the text gives: because carved-away rock could not be put back, mistakes could not be undone.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Sculptures from Gandhara, a region centered on what is now northwestern Pakistan, are frequently cited as proof that Greek art shaped early images of the Buddha: many show robes falling in heavy folds and faces modeled in a manner reminiscent of Hellenistic statues. Yet most of these works date from the first to the fifth centuries CE, long after Greek rulers had lost power in the region, and their nearest stylistic parallels are often found in art of the Roman Empire, with which Gandhara traded. Some art historians therefore argue that "Greek influence" is a misleadingly simple label for a tradition that drew on several Mediterranean and local sources at once.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Some scholars think crediting Gandharan style to Greek art alone oversimplifies its sources.
choices.B: Gandharan sculptors copied Roman statues rather than Greek ones when carving the Buddha.
choices.C: Greek rulers lost power in Gandhara before its trade with the Roman Empire had begun.
choices.D: Gandharan sculptures show heavily folded robes and faces much like those of Hellenistic statues.

explanation.why: The text sets up a common claim (Gandharan sculpture proves Greek influence), then gives two complications: the dates fall "long after Greek rulers had lost power," and the closest parallels are "often" Roman. It concludes that some scholars see "Greek influence" as "a misleadingly simple label" for a tradition with "several Mediterranean and local sources." The main idea is that qualified argument.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the scholars' conclusion, including its scope: the problem is treating Greek art as the single source.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This overstates the text, which says Roman parallels are "often" closest and that the tradition drew on several sources, not that sculptors simply copied Roman statues.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says Greek rulers had lost power before most of the sculptures were made, but it never says when trade with Rome began.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the evidence behind the common claim in the first sentence, not the point the text builds to.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1800, the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt described electric eels in a Venezuelan pool rising from the water to press themselves against horses that local fishers had driven in. For nearly two centuries, many biologists treated the account as an exaggeration, since eels were known to deliver their shocks while fully submerged. Experiments in the 2010s, however, showed that an eel confronting a partly submerged threat will indeed leap up and press its chin against it. Out of the water, the current that would otherwise spread into the surrounding water passes instead through the threat's body, so the shock it receives is stronger. The behavior, researchers suggest, may help eels defend themselves when shrinking dry-season pools leave them exposed.
items.stem: According to the text, why is an eel's shock stronger when the eel leaps up to press against a threat?

choices.A: Shrinking pools in the dry season leave eels more exposed to possible predators.
choices.B: Less current is lost to the surrounding water, so more passes through the threat.
choices.C: The eel can generate more electricity when part of its body is exposed to the open air.
choices.D: The surrounding water carries the eel's current directly into the threat's body.

explanation.why: The fourth sentence explains the mechanism: out of the water, "the current that would otherwise spread into the surrounding water passes instead through the threat's body, so the shock it receives is stronger." The shock is stronger because less current is lost to the water, not because the eel produces more.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the situation in which the behavior may be useful, not the reason the shock is stronger.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates the text's explanation: current that would spread into the water passes through the threat instead.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says the eel produces more electricity in air; it says the same current is directed through the threat instead of spreading into the water.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says the water spreads the current away; leaping out of the water keeps it from doing so.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Accounts of the Ming dynasty's naval expeditions of the early 1400s, led by the admiral Zheng He, credit the largest "treasure ships" with lengths of roughly 120 meters, which would make them several times longer than the ships Columbus sailed decades later. Some historians accept the figure, noting that an enormous rudder post was excavated at the site of a former Ming shipyard. Others point out that the dimensions come from texts written long after the voyages and that wooden hulls of that length would have been extraordinarily difficult to keep from bending and leaking. What both sides agree on is that the fleets were vast overall, with dozens of ships and many thousands of crew members.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Wooden ships cannot be built longer than about 120 meters without bending and leaking.
choices.B: Some historians doubt reports of the ships' length because the reports were written much later.
choices.C: Historians dispute the size of Zheng He's largest ships but agree that his fleets were vast.
choices.D: A huge excavated rudder post has proved that Zheng He's largest ships were about 120 meters long.

explanation.why: The text presents a reported figure, then two camps: some historians accept it (citing the rudder post), and others doubt it (late sources, structural problems). The final sentence adds what "both sides agree on": the fleets were vast. A main idea must cover both the disagreement and the agreement.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says such hulls would have been "extraordinarily difficult" to keep sound, not impossible, and it makes no general claim about all wooden ships.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This gives only one side's argument and leaves out both the opposing view and the point of agreement.
explanation.C: Correct. This covers the whole text: the dispute over the largest ships' size and the shared view that the fleets were enormous.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The rudder post is evidence one side cites, not proof; the text presents the length as disputed.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For thirty-one years Haripada Sen had sorted the letters of Chandpur, and in retirement he had not lost the habit of meeting the morning mail boat. He no longer carried anything back from the landing; he simply stood at its edge while the new clerk, a young man from Comilla, counted out the bundles. Twice that winter the clerk misread a smudged address, and twice Haripada said nothing until the boat had gone, then mentioned, as if recalling an old story, a family by that name who had once lived beyond the tank. The letters reached their owners. The clerk thanked him the second time, and Haripada, embarrassed, spoke of the weather.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A retired postmaster misses the work of carrying the mail back from the landing.
choices.B: A young clerk depends on a retired postmaster to help him sort Chandpur's mail every morning.
choices.C: A retired postmaster quietly helps his successor while avoiding seeming to correct him.
choices.D: A retired postmaster resents the young clerk who has replaced him at the landing.

explanation.why: Haripada waits until the boat has gone, then offers the right information "as if recalling an old story," so his help never looks like a correction. When thanked, he is "embarrassed" and changes the subject. The text centers on this tactful, nearly hidden help.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says he no longer carries anything, but it never says he misses doing so.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Haripada helps only twice and does no sorting; he "simply stood" at the landing's edge.
explanation.C: Correct. His indirect hints and his embarrassment at being thanked show help given without any air of correction.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in his behavior suggests resentment; he helps the clerk and is embarrassed by thanks.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a whale dies in the open ocean, its carcass may sink to a seafloor where food is otherwise scarce. Studies of such "whale falls" describe a sequence of communities. Scavengers such as hagfish and sleeper sharks strip the soft tissue within months to a couple of years; worms and crustaceans then colonize the enriched sediment and exposed bones. The longest stage depends on the skeleton itself: as bacteria break down fats stored in the bones, they release sulfide, which other microbes use as a source of energy, supporting communities of animals for decades. Because some of these animals also live at hydrothermal vents, researchers have proposed that whale falls may serve as stepping stones for vent species spreading across the deep sea.
items.stem: According to the text, what makes it possible for a whale fall to support animals for decades?

choices.A: Animals from hydrothermal vents arrive at the carcass and gradually colonize its bones.
choices.B: Scavengers such as hagfish remove the whale's soft tissue slowly over many years.
choices.C: Microbes draw energy from sulfide released as bacteria break down fats in the bones.
choices.D: Food is otherwise scarce on the deep seafloor where the whale's carcass settles.

explanation.why: The fourth sentence explains the longest stage: bacteria break down fats in the bones and release sulfide, "which other microbes use as a source of energy, supporting communities of animals for decades." The decades-long support comes from this chain of microbial activity in the skeleton.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text only proposes that vent species might use whale falls as stepping stones; it does not say their arrival sustains the community.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says scavengers strip soft tissue "within months to a couple of years," which is quick, not slow over many years.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the mechanism the text gives for the stage that lasts decades.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it explains why a whale fall matters, not what lets it support animals for decades.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In traditional Japanese indigo dyeing, or aizome, the blue does not come from a ready-made dye. Indigo leaves are first composted for months into a dark material called sukumo, which is then placed in a vat with lye made from wood ash. There, bacteria convert the insoluble indigo into a form that can soak into cloth; when the cloth is lifted out, contact with air turns it blue. Because the bacteria must be kept alive, dyers speak of feeding the vat and judge its condition by its smell and the look of its surface foam, and a neglected vat can fail entirely. Chemical agents can perform the same conversion in hours, yet many workshops still prefer the slower method.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Cloth dyed in an aizome vat turns blue only after it is lifted out and exposed to air.
choices.B: Traditional aizome relies on a living fermentation that dyers must tend with great care.
choices.C: The slow aizome method produces deeper shades of blue than any chemical process can.
choices.D: Chemical agents have now largely replaced bacteria in Japan's traditional indigo workshops.

explanation.why: The text explains that aizome depends on bacteria in the vat, which "must be kept alive": dyers "feed" the vat, check its smell and foam, and risk losing it if it is neglected. The last sentence adds that many workshops still choose this slow, living process. The main idea is that aizome depends on carefully tended fermentation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is one step in the process, not the point of the whole text.
explanation.B: Correct. This sums up the text's focus: the bacteria-driven process and the care needed to keep it working.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares the depth of color produced by the two methods.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says many workshops "still prefer the slower method," which contradicts this choice.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, works in cast brass were long the property of the oba, or king. The casters belonged to a hereditary guild, the Igun Eronmwon, whose members lived together in a single quarter of Benin City and worked by royal commission. Between roughly the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, they produced hundreds of rectangular plaques showing court ceremonies, warriors, and foreign visitors, which once covered pillars of the royal palace. Much of the metal arrived as brass bracelets called manillas, traded by Portuguese merchants. The plaques thus record both the kingdom's internal order and its widening commercial ties, though the names of their individual makers have rarely survived.
items.stem: Based on the text, in what way do the plaques reflect the Kingdom of Benin's ties with the wider world?

choices.A: They depict foreign visitors and were cast largely from metal obtained in trade.
choices.B: They depict warriors and court ceremonies that reveal the kingdom's internal order.
choices.C: They covered the pillars of a palace built for Portuguese merchants in Benin City.
choices.D: They were cast by foreign artisans whose individual names have rarely survived.

explanation.why: The text says the plaques record "its widening commercial ties." Two details support that: the plaques show "foreign visitors," and much of their metal came as manillas "traded by Portuguese merchants." Only a choice built on those details answers the question.
explanation.A: Correct. This combines the two details that link the plaques to the outside world: their subject matter and their traded metal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes what the plaques show about the kingdom's internal order, not its outside ties.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The plaques covered pillars of the oba's royal palace; nothing says the palace was built for Portuguese merchants.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The casters were members of a hereditary guild living in Benin City, not foreign artisans.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Pellow had been warned that the parsonage at Thornby was a dull house, and she arrived prepared to find it so. The drawing room was indeed plainly furnished, the curtains faded, and the vicar's welcome brief; yet she observed that every book upon the shelves had been read to softness at the spine, that the children's slates bore not copybook maxims but sums of a difficulty she had herself struggled with at fifteen, and that the youngest girl, introduced as shy, asked within the hour whether the moon had weather. By evening Miss Pellow had revised a good many of her expectations, and had begun, somewhat to her own alarm, to doubt whether she was equal to the place.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A governess finds the parsonage at Thornby just as dull and plain as she had been warned.
choices.B: A governess is charmed by the curiosity of the vicar's shy youngest daughter.
choices.C: A governess resolves to make the shabby parsonage more comfortable for the children.
choices.D: A governess finds a plain household far more intellectually demanding than she expected.

explanation.why: The text moves from expectation to surprise. Miss Pellow expects a "dull house," and the furnishings are plain, "yet" the worn books, difficult sums, and the youngest girl's question reveal lively minds. By evening she doubts "whether she was equal to the place." The main idea is this shift: the plain house turns out to challenge her.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only the furnishings match the warning; the word "yet" introduces evidence that the household is far from dull.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The girl's question is one piece of evidence; it leaves out the books, the sums, and Miss Pellow's self-doubt.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says she plans to improve the house's comfort.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the whole movement from expecting dullness to doubting she can meet the household's demands.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The purple frog of India's Western Ghats was not formally described by scientists until 2003, although people in the region had long known it. Its late recognition reflects its habits more than its rarity: the frog spends most of the year underground, where it feeds mainly on termites with its narrow, pointed snout, and it surfaces for only a few weeks during the monsoon to breed in temporary streams. Genetic studies indicate that its closest living relatives are small frogs found only in the Seychelles, islands in the Indian Ocean. The two lineages are thought to have diverged long ago, when India and the Seychelles were still joined as parts of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is the main reason the purple frog went unrecognized by scientists for so long?

choices.A: It lives underground for most of the year and comes to the surface only briefly.
choices.B: Its closest living relatives are found only on islands in the Indian Ocean.
choices.C: It feeds almost entirely on termites, a food that few other kinds of frogs will eat.
choices.D: It is so rare that few people in the Western Ghats had ever encountered it.

explanation.why: The second sentence answers the question: the frog's late recognition "reflects its habits more than its rarity," and the colon introduces those habits, chiefly that it stays underground most of the year and surfaces "for only a few weeks." A frog that is seldom above ground is easy for scientists to miss.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the habits the text gives as the reason: life underground with only brief appearances.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true according to the text, but it concerns the frog's ancestry, not why scientists overlooked it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says it feeds mainly on termites but never compares its diet with other frogs or links diet to its late discovery.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the late recognition reflects habits "more than its rarity" and that local people "had long known it."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Great frigatebirds can stay aloft over the ocean for weeks at a time, which long raised the question of whether, and how, they sleep. When researchers fitted birds in the Galápagos Islands with small devices that recorded brain activity, they found that the birds did sleep in flight, often letting one half of the brain rest while the other stayed alert. Yet in-flight sleep came in bursts lasting seconds and totaled less than an hour a day, compared with more than twelve hours a day once the birds were back on land. Frigatebirds, it seems, can sleep while flying, but they do remarkably little of it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Frigatebirds rest only one half of the brain at a time whenever they sleep in flight.
choices.B: Frigatebirds sleep in flight, but far less than they sleep once they are back on land.
choices.C: Frigatebirds need more than twelve hours of sleep a day in order to stay aloft for weeks.
choices.D: Recording devices revealed how long frigatebirds sleep after returning to land.

explanation.why: The text answers its opening question in two parts: the birds "did sleep in flight," "yet" that sleep was brief, under an hour a day versus more than twelve on land. The last sentence states both parts together, so the main idea must include both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the birds "often" rested half the brain, not that they always did.
explanation.B: Correct. This keeps both halves of the finding: sleep in flight happens, but it is small compared with sleep on land.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Twelve hours is how much the birds slept on land; the text never says they need that much to stay aloft.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is a single detail and misses the main finding about sleep during flight.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Origami is usually thought of as an art of figures, cranes and frogs folded for their beauty, but some of its patterns have found work in engineering. In the 1970s, the Japanese astrophysicist Koryo Miura developed a fold in which a sheet is creased into a grid of slightly slanted parallelograms rather than squares. The slant makes the creases depend on one another, so that a folded sheet can be opened or closed in a single motion by pulling on two opposite corners rather than being unfolded crease by crease. That property made the pattern attractive for packing large, thin structures, and a version of it was used for a solar panel array on a Japanese satellite launched in 1995.
items.stem: According to the text, what is a result of the slant in the parallelograms of Miura's fold?

choices.A: The folded sheet takes up less space than a sheet that is folded into squares.
choices.B: Origami came to be seen as a branch of engineering rather than as an art form.
choices.C: Each crease in the sheet can be folded on its own, independently of the others.
choices.D: The creases move together, so the whole sheet opens or closes in one motion.

explanation.why: The third sentence states the result: "The slant makes the creases depend on one another, so that a folded sheet can be opened or closed in a single motion." The slant links the creases so they move together.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never compares the space taken up by Miura's fold with a fold of squares.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says only that "some" origami patterns found engineering uses; it never says origami stopped being seen as an art.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says the slant makes the creases "depend on one another."
explanation.D: Correct. This restates the direct result of the slant described in the third sentence.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Dutch "tulip mania" of 1636–1637, when contracts for rare bulbs briefly traded for extraordinary sums, is often retold as a tale of national folly in which a sudden crash ruined thousands. Historians who have examined notarial records and court documents from the period paint a more modest picture. The trade, they find, was concentrated among a fairly small circle of merchants and craftsmen, and they have located few bankruptcies that can be traced to the collapse in prices. Much of the familiar story, these historians suggest, derives from moralizing pamphlets of the time and from later writers who repeated them, so that the episode's reputation as an economic catastrophe owes more to its retelling than to its actual effects.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The tulip crash of 1637 ruined thousands of ordinary Dutch merchants and craftsmen.
choices.B: Moralizing pamphlets of the 1630s were what caused tulip prices to collapse.
choices.C: Contracts for rare tulip bulbs briefly sold for extraordinary sums in the 1630s.
choices.D: Records suggest the tulip mania did far less damage than its reputation implies.

explanation.why: The text contrasts the popular story of a crash that "ruined thousands" with what historians found in records: a small circle of traders and "few bankruptcies." It concludes that the episode's reputation "owes more to its retelling than to its actual effects." The main idea is this correction of an exaggerated reputation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the popular version that the historians' research challenges.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the pamphlets shaped the story told about the crash, not that they caused it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is background from the first sentence and leaves out the historians' reassessment.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the contrast between the archival evidence and the episode's reputation.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Pyotr Ilyich Krasnov read his son's letter standing, as he read invoices, and when he had finished he laid it on the counting-house desk beside the ledger and observed to his clerk that the boy wrote a fair hand. The letter announced that Alexei had left the university at Moscow, had taken employment with a newspaper of which his father had never heard, and was, he wrote, happier than he had been in three years. Krasnov said nothing further about it that day. But the clerk, who had served him for twenty years, noticed that the old man twice entered the same shipment of hemp in the ledger, and that on the second occasion he did not notice his error at all, but sat for some time afterward with the pen lifted, looking not at the page but at the window.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A merchant angrily refuses to discuss his son's news with his longtime clerk.
choices.B: A merchant shows that his accounts matter more to him than his son's future.
choices.C: A merchant is quietly proud that his son has found work that makes him truly happy.
choices.D: A merchant's businesslike calm hides a disturbance that surfaces in his work.

explanation.why: Two parts of the text must be read together. At first Krasnov treats the letter like an invoice, commenting only on the handwriting and saying "nothing further." But the clerk sees him enter the same shipment twice, miss the error, and stare at the window. The contrast shows that the news has unsettled him beneath his composed surface. The text does not say exactly what he feels, so the key names a disturbance without specifying it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. He says nothing more about the letter, but the text shows no anger and no refusal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the clue: his mistakes in the ledger show that the letter has pushed his accounts out of his mind.
explanation.C: Incorrect. His only comment is on the handwriting, and his later distraction suggests unease; nothing in the text shows pride.
explanation.D: Correct. His calm, invoice-like handling of the letter contrasts with the uncharacteristic errors and distraction the clerk observes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ethical constraints prevent researchers from deliberately withholding food from pregnant women, so evidence on how prenatal nutrition shapes adult health has come largely from natural experiments. Few have proved as informative as the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–1945, when a wartime blockade reduced official rations in the western Netherlands to well under 1,000 calories a day. What makes the episode unusual is less its severity than its sharp boundaries: the famine began and ended abruptly in a population that was otherwise reasonably well fed and whose births were carefully recorded. Investigators could therefore compare people exposed during early, middle, or late gestation with siblings and neighbors who were not exposed at all, and they have found that some later health differences depend on when in pregnancy the exposure occurred.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The Dutch Hunger Winter is valuable to researchers chiefly because it was an unusually severe famine.
choices.B: People exposed to the famine late in gestation show the largest differences in health as adults.
choices.C: The famine's abrupt boundaries let researchers link the timing of prenatal exposure to later health.
choices.D: Natural experiments are the only ethical means of studying how nutrition affects human health.

explanation.why: The text says the Hunger Winter is informative not mainly because of its severity but because of "its sharp boundaries." The word "therefore" connects those boundaries to the research design: investigators could compare people exposed at different stages of gestation with unexposed relatives, and they found that outcomes "depend on when in pregnancy the exposure occurred." The main idea joins the famine's sharp timing to this finding about timing.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the episode is unusual "less [for] its severity than its sharp boundaries," which contradicts this choice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says differences depend on timing, but it never says which stage of gestation shows the largest differences.
explanation.C: Correct. This links the feature the text emphasizes, the famine's sharp boundaries, to what that feature allowed researchers to learn.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says evidence on prenatal nutrition has come "largely" from natural experiments; it does not call them the only ethical method for studying nutrition in general.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Excavations at cities of the Indus civilization, which flourished in what are now Pakistan and northwestern India from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, have yielded thousands of small stone weights, most of them carefully cut cubes of chert. Measured against one another, they follow a single scheme: the smaller weights double in sequence, 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on up to 64, after which the larger weights proceed in multiples that are largely decimal. More striking than the scheme itself is its consistency. Weights recovered from sites hundreds of kilometers apart conform to it so closely that some archaeologists infer not merely a shared custom but some form of regulation, since informal traditions passed from trader to trader would be expected to drift over centuries and distances in a way these weights did not.
items.stem: Based on the text, why do some archaeologists think the use of Indus weights may have been regulated?

choices.A: The weights follow a system that combines doubling with decimal multiples.
choices.B: Weights found at distant sites were all produced in a single central workshop.
choices.C: The weights vary less across distant sites than informal practices would likely allow.
choices.D: Customs passed informally from trader to trader tend to stay unchanged over great distances.

explanation.why: The final sentence gives the reasoning: weights from distant sites match the scheme "so closely" that informal traditions, which "would be expected to drift," cannot easily explain them. The inference of regulation rests on consistency, not on the scheme itself, which the text calls less striking.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This describes the scheme, but the text says "More striking than the scheme itself is its consistency"; the inference rests on the consistency.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions where or how the weights were produced.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the archaeologists' reasoning: the weights are more uniform than informal custom could be expected to keep them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text assumes the opposite: informal traditions passed between traders would be expected to drift.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Since the mid-twentieth century, many performers of Baroque music have adopted instruments, tunings, and playing techniques documented from the composer's own era, on the reasonable premise that a sarabande by Bach sounds different on gut strings than on steel. Critics of this "historically informed" movement do not usually dispute that such details matter. Their objection is subtler: even a perfect reconstruction of the sound would reach listeners whose ears have been shaped by two further centuries of music, for whom a harmony that startled an audience in 1720 may pass unnoticed. On this view, the movement can recover what the music sounded like but not how it was heard, and its claims to authenticity should be stated with corresponding modesty.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Critics hold that recovering Baroque music's original sound cannot recover how it was first heard.
choices.B: Critics hold that harmonies in Baroque music no longer surprise audiences as they once did.
choices.C: Critics hold that performers of Baroque music should return to using modern instruments.
choices.D: Critics hold that period instruments and techniques make little real difference to how Baroque music sounds.

explanation.why: The text separates two things: the sound of the music and the experience of hearing it. Critics accept that instruments and techniques affect the sound ("do not usually dispute that such details matter"), but they argue that modern listeners' ears differ, so the movement "can recover what the music sounded like but not how it was heard." The main idea is that distinction and its consequence for claims of authenticity.
explanation.A: Correct. This states the critics' central distinction between reconstructing the sound and reconstructing the listening experience.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the example critics use to support their argument, not the argument itself.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The critics ask only for modesty in claims of authenticity; nothing says they want performers to abandon period instruments.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says critics "do not usually dispute that such details matter," so this reverses their position.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The "island rule" holds that, once isolated on islands, large mammals tend to evolve smaller bodies and small mammals larger ones; the dwarf elephants of several Mediterranean islands and the giant rats of Flores, in Indonesia, are its familiar examples. Proponents explain the pattern by the conditions islands typically impose: limited food favors smaller bodies in large species, while a scarcity of predators and competitors frees small species to grow. Yet these explanations presuppose conditions that vary greatly from island to island, and surveys spanning hundreds of species have found the trend to be strong in some groups and weak or absent in others. Such results suggest that the rule may describe a frequent outcome of particular circumstances rather than a general law of island evolution.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Surveys of hundreds of species show that the island rule does not hold for any mammal group.
choices.B: The island rule may reflect conditions found on some islands rather than a universal pattern.
choices.C: Limited food on islands is the main reason that large mammals evolve smaller bodies there.
choices.D: Mammals isolated on islands generally grow larger because they face few predators there.

explanation.why: The text explains the island rule and its proposed causes, then turns with "Yet": the causes depend on conditions that vary between islands, and the trend is strong in some groups but "weak or absent in others." The final sentence concludes, cautiously, that the rule "may describe a frequent outcome of particular circumstances rather than a general law." The key keeps that hedge and that contrast.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the trend is "strong in some groups," so it does not claim the rule fails everywhere.
explanation.B: Correct. This matches the text's cautious conclusion that the rule depends on particular circumstances rather than holding as a general law.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is part of the proponents' explanation for one half of the pattern, not the text's main point, and the text questions how general that explanation is.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says only small mammals tend to grow larger; large ones tend to shrink, so this overgeneralizes.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Master Fazal Din had prepared for the Inspector's visit as for a siege. The boys' slates were scrubbed, the map of the Punjab rehung so that the damp stain fell behind the cupboard, and the least reliable pupil sent on an errand of indefinite length to the far end of Anarkali Bazaar. The Inspector, a stout gentleman suffering from a cold, heard the recitations without comment and departed within a quarter of an hour. That evening, writing up his day-book, the Master recorded the visit in a single line and then, after some deliberation, crossed out the word "satisfactory" and wrote above it "uneventful," a change that cost him, he afterward admitted to his wife, more thought than all his preparations together.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A schoolmaster resents the Inspector for cutting short his visit to the school.
choices.B: A schoolmaster hides the poor condition of his school by sending away his least reliable pupil.
choices.C: A schoolmaster's elaborate preparations yield a visit so brief that even recording it troubles him.
choices.D: A schoolmaster is greatly relieved when the visiting Inspector praises the recitations of his pupils.

explanation.why: The text sets the Master's siege-like preparations against an anticlimax: the Inspector listens "without comment" and leaves within a quarter hour. The final sentence returns to the Master, who struggles to choose between "satisfactory" and "uneventful," a choice that costs him "more thought than all his preparations." The main idea must include both the buildup and the oddly troubling, uneventful result.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text shows that the Master resents the Inspector or the shortness of his visit.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Sending a pupil away is one of several preparations; it leaves out the visit and the Master's struggle over the day-book.
explanation.C: Correct. This links the two parts of the text: the great preparations and the brief visit whose meaning the Master struggles to put into words.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The Inspector heard the recitations "without comment"; he gives no praise.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Collectors who traveled the English countryside in the early twentieth century, notebooks in hand, preserved thousands of songs that might otherwise have vanished with the elderly singers who knew them. Their published collections, however, are not simple transcripts. Collectors frequently softened or omitted verses they judged indelicate, favored tunes in the old modes over those resembling recent popular music, and passed over the music-hall songs that many of the same singers performed with equal pleasure. Scholars who compare the field notebooks with the printed volumes therefore caution against treating the volumes as a neutral record of rural singing: they document, with considerable accuracy, a portion of what was sung, selected according to the collectors' own idea of what a genuine folk tradition ought to be.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Rural English singers in the early 1900s preferred music-hall songs to the older traditional songs.
choices.B: Early twentieth-century collectors invented many of the folk songs they claimed to record.
choices.C: Printed folk song collections preserve real material but reflect their collectors' selective tastes.
choices.D: Thousands of English folk songs survive only because collectors wrote them down in time.

explanation.why: The text grants the collectors' achievement, then turns with "however" to their choices: softening verses, favoring old tunes, skipping music-hall songs. Its conclusion holds both sides together: the volumes record "with considerable accuracy" only "a portion of what was sung," chosen by the collectors' ideals. The key must keep both the accuracy and the selectivity.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The singers performed music-hall songs "with equal pleasure," which means no preference either way.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the volumes document real singing "with considerable accuracy"; the problem is selection and softening, not invention.
explanation.C: Correct. This keeps both halves of the scholars' judgment: genuine material, chosen and shaped by the collectors' ideals.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This overstates the first sentence ("might otherwise have vanished") and ignores the text's main concern about how the collections were shaped.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The slime mold Physarum polycephalum has no brain or nervous system; for much of its life it is a single, enormous cell that spreads across a surface as a web of branching tubes. In one well-known experiment, researchers set oat flakes, a favored food, in a pattern matching the positions of cities around Tokyo and let the mold grow among them. Within about a day it had connected the food sources with a network that compared well with the region's actual rail system in efficiency and in resilience to the loss of any single link. The mold manages this without any overall plan: tubes through which more fluid flows grow thicker, while those carrying little flow gradually shrink and disappear, so that useful routes are reinforced and redundant ones pruned.
items.stem: Based on the text, what accounts for the slime mold's ability to form a network comparable to the Tokyo rail system?

choices.A: It grows directly along the shortest possible path between each separate pair of food sources.
choices.B: It follows an overall plan for the network, much as the region's rail engineers did.
choices.C: Local changes in its tubes, driven by how much fluid each carries, favor useful routes.
choices.D: Its single, enormous cell can spread across a surface as a web of branching tubes.

explanation.why: The last sentence explains how the mold "manages this": tubes with more flow thicken, tubes with little flow shrink and vanish, so "useful routes are reinforced and redundant ones pruned." The efficient network emerges from these local adjustments, not from any plan.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says the mold finds shortest paths; it describes a gradual process of reinforcing and pruning tubes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the mold works "without any overall plan."
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the mechanism in the final sentence: flow-driven thickening and shrinking of tubes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes the mold's basic form, which makes a network possible, but it does not explain why the network becomes efficient.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Red markings on the walls of several caves in Spain, including lines, dots, and a hand stencil, have been dated to more than 64,000 years ago, which would make them older than any known presence of modern humans in Europe and so, presumably, the work of Neanderthals. The dates were obtained not from the pigment itself but from thin mineral crusts that formed on top of it: since a crust must be younger than what lies beneath it, its age sets a minimum age for the markings. Some geochemists, however, argue that water seeping through such crusts can remove uranium, a process that would make the crusts appear older than they are. The attribution to Neanderthals thus rests on a dating method whose reliability in this setting is itself disputed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A mineral crust that forms over cave markings must be younger than the markings beneath it.
choices.B: Neanderthals, not modern humans, created the earliest cave art that has been found in Europe.
choices.C: The claim that Neanderthals made some Spanish cave markings depends on contested dates.
choices.D: Water seeping through mineral crusts has made the Spanish cave markings seem too old.

explanation.why: The text explains how the markings were dated and why the dates point to Neanderthals, then reports a challenge: seeping water "can" remove uranium and make crusts look older. Its final sentence states the main idea: the attribution "rests on a dating method whose reliability in this setting is itself disputed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the reasoning behind the dating method, a supporting detail rather than the main point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text treats Neanderthal authorship as presumed ("presumably") and disputed, not established.
explanation.C: Correct. This states the text's conclusion: the attribution depends on dates whose reliability is in question.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The geochemists argue that this process "can" happen; the text does not say it has happened in these caves.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every morning for eleven years Inés Ramírez had ridden the funicular down the hill to the port, and every morning she had read the newspaper on the way, so that the city below existed for her chiefly as a pause between the shipping notices and the obituaries. It was only on the day the car stalled halfway, swaying a little on its cable while the operator shouted to someone above, that she lowered the paper and looked. The roofs were red and green and rust, stepped down the slope like a crowd on a staircase; washing moved on a hundred lines; and the bay, which she had known as a word on bills of lading, was simply there, wide and absurdly bright. When the car lurched on, she found she had folded the newspaper and could not remember having done so.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A woman realizes that she dislikes her work at the port and wants to leave it.
choices.B: A woman's fear when the funicular suddenly stalls makes her forget about her newspaper.
choices.C: A woman notices that the roofs of her city are painted in a variety of colors.
choices.D: An unexpected delay leads a woman to truly see a city she had long overlooked.

explanation.why: The first sentence establishes that for eleven years the city was only "a pause" in her reading. The stall makes her lower the paper and look, and the description shows her seeing the roofs, the washing, and the bay as real things rather than words on documents. Her folding the paper without noticing confirms how fully her attention has shifted.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about her feelings toward her work.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing suggests fear; her absorption in the view, not alarm, explains why she folds the paper without noticing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The colored roofs are one detail of what she sees, not the point of the passage.
explanation.D: Correct. This joins the setup (years of ignoring the view) to the change the stall produces.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Appointed in 1904 to head India's meteorological observatories, the British mathematician Gilbert Walker was given a practical task: forecasting the strength of the summer monsoon, on which harvests across the subcontinent depended. Lacking an adequate physical theory of the monsoon, he searched instead for statistical correlations, comparing records of air pressure, temperature, and rainfall from stations around the world. Among the patterns he identified was a seesaw in air pressure between the Pacific and Indian Ocean regions, which he named the Southern Oscillation. His forecasts proved only modestly successful, and some contemporaries regarded correlations without a known cause as of doubtful value. Not until the 1960s did researchers show that the oscillation is coupled to periodic warming of the eastern Pacific, the phenomenon known as El Niño.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did Walker rely on statistical correlations in his work?

choices.A: Records from stations around the world were the only data that his observatories had.
choices.B: Harvests across the subcontinent depended on the strength of the summer monsoon.
choices.C: He had already shown that the Southern Oscillation was linked to El Niño.
choices.D: No adequate physical theory of the monsoon existed on which to base his forecasts.

explanation.why: The second sentence gives the reason: "Lacking an adequate physical theory of the monsoon, he searched instead for statistical correlations." The word "instead" shows that correlations were a substitute for the theory he did not have.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says what other data the observatories held; it says he compared records from around the world.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This explains why forecasting the monsoon mattered, not why Walker used correlations to do it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The link to El Niño was shown "not until the 1960s," by later researchers.
explanation.D: Correct. This restates the reason in the second sentence: correlations took the place of a missing physical theory.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: An influential argument in economics holds that a pasture open to many herders will inevitably be overgrazed, since each herder gains the full benefit of adding an animal while the cost of the damage is shared among all. Field studies of long-lived common pastures, such as the high meadows managed for centuries by villages in the Swiss Alps, have complicated this conclusion. In these cases, the land was held in common but was not open to all: villagers set rules limiting how many animals each household could graze, monitored one another's compliance, and fined violators. The studies do not show that shared resources are never ruined; rather, they indicate that ruin is tied less to common ownership itself than to the absence of rules that the users themselves enforce.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Villages in the Swiss Alps fined herders who grazed more animals than the rules allowed.
choices.B: Herders who share a pasture will always overgraze it unless the land is divided among them.
choices.C: Shared pastures are less likely than privately owned land to be damaged by overgrazing.
choices.D: Studies suggest that overuse of shared land stems from missing rules, not shared ownership.

explanation.why: The text presents an argument that shared pastures are doomed, then field evidence that "complicated this conclusion": Swiss villages kept common land healthy through rules they enforced themselves. The final sentence states the point carefully: the studies do not prove shared resources are never ruined, but they tie ruin to the absence of user-enforced rules rather than to "common ownership itself."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is one piece of evidence about how the villages managed their land, not the main point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the influential argument the field studies challenge, stated even more strongly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares common pastures with privately owned land.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the studies' conclusion about what, rather than common ownership, leads to ruin.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When Greek speakers adopted the Phoenician alphabet, probably in the eighth century BCE, they inherited a script that wrote only consonants, an arrangement well suited to Phoenician, in which a word's consonants carried most of its meaning and readers could supply the vowels. Greek offered no such convenience, since many of its words could be told apart only by their vowels. The Greeks' solution was to reassign several Phoenician letters for consonants that Greek lacked, among them aleph, which stood for a glottal stop, to vowel sounds; aleph thus became alpha. Some scholars doubt that this step required any deliberate insight. Each Phoenician letter's name began with the sound it represented, and a Greek listener who could not hear the initial glottal stop of "aleph" would hear the name as beginning with a vowel.
items.stem: According to the text, why do some scholars doubt that creating Greek vowel letters required deliberate insight?

choices.A: Many Greek words could be told apart only by their vowels, so vowel letters were needed.
choices.B: Greek scribes copied their vowel letters from a script used alongside Phoenician.
choices.C: Greek listeners may have heard some letter names as starting with vowel sounds.
choices.D: The Phoenician alphabet already included letters that its readers used for vowels.

explanation.why: The scholars' reasoning follows "Some scholars doubt": letter names began with the letter's sound, and a Greek listener who could not hear the glottal stop at the start of "aleph" "would hear the name as beginning with a vowel." On this view, vowel values could arise simply from how Greeks heard the names, without a deliberate design.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This explains why Greek needed vowel letters, not why the scholars think creating them took no deliberate insight.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions any other script as a source of Greek vowel letters.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the scholars' explanation: the vowel values could have come from mishearing the letter names.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the Phoenician script "wrote only consonants."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. Ashworth had spent the better part of the dinner describing the improvements he proposed for the shrubbery at Melcombe, which was to be thinned, opened to the south, and furnished with a temple in the Grecian taste, and he concluded by begging Miss Thorne's opinion, as the shrubbery was, after all, hers. Miss Thorne said that she was sure the plan did him great credit. She had walked in that shrubbery every morning since she was eight years old, and knew the precise turning where the laurels closed overhead and the house could no longer be seen; she did not think a temple would improve it, and she did not think Mr. Ashworth had once considered that it might not need improving. But she had learned that a compliment, being so much shorter than an argument, was generally the more prudent reply.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A woman resolves to argue firmly against the changes Mr. Ashworth has in mind.
choices.B: A woman recalls the turning in her shrubbery where the house can no longer be seen.
choices.C: A woman sincerely admires Mr. Ashworth's taste and looks forward to the improvements he plans.
choices.D: A woman disguises her objection to a man's plan for her grounds behind polite praise.

explanation.why: Miss Thorne's spoken reply is a compliment: the plan "did him great credit." The narration then reveals what she does not say: she loves the shrubbery as it is, doubts a temple would improve it, and thinks Mr. Ashworth never considered that it might not need improving. The last sentence explains her choice: a compliment is "more prudent" than an argument. The main idea is the gap between her polite words and her real view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. She chooses a compliment precisely because it is shorter than an argument, so she does not resolve to argue.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This memory is one detail explaining her attachment; it leaves out the conflict between what she thinks and what she says.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Her praise is only prudent politeness; the text says she "did not think a temple would improve it."
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the contrast between her compliment and her private disagreement, along with her reason for keeping quiet.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Readers who come to the Urdu ghazal from European lyric poetry sometimes find it oddly disconnected. Each couplet, or sher, is expected to be complete in itself, so that a single couplet can be quoted, and often is, without the rest of the poem; one couplet may treat longing, the next the passing of time, the next a wry joke at the poet's own expense. What holds the poem together is less a developing argument than a shared form. Every couplet keeps the same meter, and the second line of each ends with the same rhyme followed by a repeated refrain, the radif, so that listeners at a recitation can anticipate the closing words and sometimes say them aloud with the poet. The ghazal's unity, in other words, is one that is heard before it is understood.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Ghazal couplets lack any real unity, which is why readers of European poetry find them disconnected.
choices.B: Audiences at recitations appreciate ghazals more fully than readers of printed poems do.
choices.C: A ghazal's couplets are bound chiefly by shared patterns of sound rather than by a line of thought.
choices.D: Each couplet of a ghazal is complete in itself and can be quoted without the rest of the poem.

explanation.why: The text acknowledges that ghazals can seem "disconnected" because each couplet stands alone, then explains what unifies them: "less a developing argument than a shared form" of meter, rhyme, and refrain. Its final sentence restates this: the unity "is heard before it is understood." The main idea is that the ghazal's unity lies in sound patterns rather than in a continuous argument.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text explains that ghazals do have unity, of a kind that some readers do not expect.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares how fully listeners and readers appreciate ghazals.
explanation.C: Correct. This states the text's central claim that shared meter, rhyme, and refrain, not an argument, hold the poem together.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the feature that makes ghazals seem disconnected, not the text's explanation of what unifies them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most fish die within minutes if they are taken out of water. The mangrove killifish, a small fish of coastal swamps in the Americas, is different. When the shallow pools where it lives dry up or turn foul, the killifish wriggles onto land and settles into damp leaf litter or a crack in a rotting log. There it can survive for weeks, taking in oxygen through its skin, until rain refills the pools.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The mangrove killifish prefers to live inside rotting logs rather than in water.
choices.B: The mangrove killifish dies if the pools it lives in dry up during the hot season.
choices.C: The mangrove killifish can live out of water for weeks when its pools become unlivable.
choices.D: Most fish that live in coastal swamps can breathe through their skin when necessary.

explanation.why: The text opens by contrasting most fish, which die quickly out of water, with the killifish, which "is different." The rest of the text explains the difference: when its pools dry up or turn foul, the fish moves onto land and "can survive for weeks" by breathing through its skin. The main idea must capture this unusual ability.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The killifish uses logs and leaf litter only when its pools dry up or turn foul; the text does not say it prefers them to water.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: the killifish survives on land when its pools dry up.
explanation.C: Correct. Every sentence builds toward this point: the killifish leaves unlivable pools and survives on land for weeks by taking in oxygen through its skin.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text presents the killifish as an exception among fish, not as an example of what most swamp fish can do.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Faiza had never wanted to take the overnight train from Karachi to Lahore. Eighteen hours on a hard bunk, she told her mother, when a flight took two. But once the city lights fell away, she could not sleep. She watched dark fields slide past, the lamps of small stations, a man selling tea on a platform at three in the morning. By sunrise, somewhere past Multan, she had decided to take the train home as well.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Faiza's mother insists that the train is a safer way to travel than flying.
choices.B: Faiza finds the overnight train uncomfortable and regrets not taking a flight.
choices.C: Faiza expects to dislike the train journey but ends up wanting to repeat it.
choices.D: Faiza stays awake all night because the train's bunks are too hard to sleep on.

explanation.why: The text begins with Faiza's reluctance: she "had never wanted to take the overnight train." It then describes what she sees from the window and ends with her decision to "take the train home as well." The main idea is the change from dreading the trip to wanting to do it again.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text mentions what Faiza told her mother, but never says what her mother thinks.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text ends with Faiza choosing the train for her return trip, so she does not regret it.
explanation.C: Correct. This covers both halves of the text: her reluctance at the start and her decision at the end to travel the same way again.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Faiza does lie awake, but the text links this to watching the scenery, not to the hard bunk, and this detail is not the main point.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The world's first underground railway opened in London in January 1863. It ran for about six kilometers, and on its first day it carried tens of thousands of passengers. The trains were pulled by steam locomotives, so the tunnels filled with smoke and steam even though engineers had built openings to let the fumes escape. Passengers complained about the air, yet the line was so popular that other cities soon planned underground railways of their own.
items.stem: According to the text, what was one drawback of the first underground railway?

choices.A: Its tunnels filled with smoke from the steam locomotives.
choices.B: It carried too few passengers to pay for itself.
choices.C: Its trains ran only a short distance outside the city.
choices.D: It had no openings through which fumes could escape.

explanation.why: The question asks for a drawback, so look for a problem named in the text. The third sentence states that because the trains were pulled by steam locomotives, "the tunnels filled with smoke and steam," and the next sentence adds that passengers complained about the air.
explanation.A: Correct. The text says directly that the steam locomotives filled the tunnels with smoke and steam.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the line carried tens of thousands of passengers on its first day and was very popular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The line ran within London between two stations; the text does not describe it as running outside the city.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says engineers had built openings to let fumes escape; the problem was that the tunnels filled with smoke anyway.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Long before movies existed, people could watch pictures move. One popular device of the 1800s was the zoetrope, a short drum with narrow slits cut around its side. A strip of drawings was placed inside the drum, each drawing showing a figure in a slightly different position. When the drum was spun and a viewer looked through the slits, the drawings seemed to blend into a single moving figure, such as a horse galloping or a juggler tossing balls.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The zoetrope created the appearance of motion from a series of still drawings.
choices.B: Drawings of galloping horses were the most common subjects used in the zoetrope.
choices.C: Zoetropes were difficult to use because the viewer had to spin the drum by hand.
choices.D: The zoetrope was the most important invention leading to modern movies.

explanation.why: The text introduces the zoetrope as a device that let people "watch pictures move" before movies existed, and then explains how it worked: a strip of drawings, each slightly different, appeared to blend into a single moving figure when the drum was spun. The main idea is this effect of motion from still pictures.
explanation.A: Correct. The whole text explains how still drawings in a spinning drum appeared to move.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A galloping horse is given only as an example of a moving figure, not as the most common subject.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says the device was difficult to use.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text calls the zoetrope "one popular device" and never ranks it among inventions that led to movies.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The mugger crocodile lives in rivers, lakes, and marshes across South Asia, including parts of Pakistan, India, and Sri Lanka. Like other reptiles, it cannot produce much heat inside its body, so it spends hours basking in the sun. When the weather becomes too hot or too cold, however, the mugger does something few crocodiles do: it digs a burrow into a riverbank, sometimes several meters deep, and rests inside, where the temperature stays steadier than outside.
items.stem: According to the text, why does the mugger crocodile dig burrows?

choices.A: To hide from the animals it hunts along the riverbank
choices.B: To avoid temperatures outside that are too hot or too cold
choices.C: To build a safe place where its eggs can hatch
choices.D: To store food during periods when rivers and lakes dry up

explanation.why: The question asks for the reason given in the text. The last sentence says that "when the weather becomes too hot or too cold," the mugger digs a burrow and rests inside, "where the temperature stays steadier than it does outside." So the burrow is a way of escaping extreme temperatures.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not mention hunting or hiding from prey.
explanation.B: Correct. The text links the burrow directly to weather that is too hot or too cold and to the steadier temperature inside.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Eggs are not mentioned anywhere in the text.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions storing food or rivers drying up.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Ewa had taught her little cousin Piotr to swim, so she expected to teach him to ski as well. On the first morning, though, she fell three times before the slope even began. Piotr, who had skied since he was four, glided back to her, showed her how to angle her skis into a wedge, and waited while she tried again. By afternoon Ewa was sliding slowly down the gentle slope, with Piotr calling out instructions behind her.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Piotr learned to ski at a young age because Ewa taught him.
choices.B: Ewa, used to teaching her cousin, finds herself being taught by him instead.
choices.C: Ewa decides that skiing is too difficult for her to learn in a single day.
choices.D: Piotr refuses to help Ewa because she has always treated him like a small child.

explanation.why: The first sentence sets up Ewa's expectation: she has always been the teacher, so she "expected to teach him to ski as well." The rest of the text reverses this: Piotr shows her how to ski and calls out instructions. The main idea is this switch in roles.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says Piotr has skied since he was four but never says who taught him; Ewa is the one learning to ski.
explanation.B: Correct. This covers the setup (Ewa as the usual teacher) and the turn (Piotr teaching her).
explanation.C: Incorrect. By afternoon Ewa is sliding down the slope with Piotr's help, so she does not give up.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Piotr helps Ewa right away, gliding back to her and showing her what to do.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1700s and early 1800s, stagecoaches carried passengers and mail along the main roads of Britain. A team of horses could not gallop for long without tiring, so the roads were lined with coaching inns about every fifteen kilometers. At each inn, workers led the tired horses away and hitched a fresh team to the coach, often in only a few minutes. Passengers barely had time to stretch their legs before the coach rolled on.
items.stem: According to the text, what happened at coaching inns?

choices.A: Passengers stayed overnight while their horses rested.
choices.B: Mail was sorted and handed over to local carriers.
choices.C: Tired horses were replaced with a fresh team.
choices.D: Coaches were repaired before continuing along the road.

explanation.why: The question asks for what the text says happened at the inns. The third sentence states it directly: "workers led the tired horses away and hitched a fresh team to the coach, often in only a few minutes."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says passengers "barely had time to stretch their legs" before moving on, so they did not stay overnight.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says coaches carried mail but never describes sorting or handing it over at inns.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the text's description of workers swapping the tired horses for a fresh team.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not mention repairs to the coaches.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The narwhal, an Arctic whale, is famous for the long spiral "horn" on the front of its head. The horn is not a horn at all but a tooth. In most males, one upper tooth grows straight out through the lip, sometimes reaching nearly three meters. The tusk is not solid like an elephant's: it is full of tiny channels and nerve endings, so some scientists suggest that it helps the narwhal sense changes in the surrounding water.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Narwhals use their tusks mainly to fight other males during the mating season.
choices.B: The narwhal's famous tusk is actually a tooth that may serve as a sense organ.
choices.C: Elephant tusks and narwhal tusks are made of the same solid material.
choices.D: A narwhal's tusk can grow to nearly three meters in length.

explanation.why: The text corrects a common impression: the narwhal's "horn" is "not a horn at all but a tooth." It then describes how the tooth grows and ends with the idea that its nerve endings may let the narwhal sense its surroundings. The main idea must include both points.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions fighting or mating.
explanation.B: Correct. This combines the two main points: the tusk is a tooth, and it may work as a sense organ.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: the narwhal tusk is "not solid like an elephant's."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The length of the tusk is a single detail, not the point of the whole text.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The tabla, a pair of hand drums played across Pakistan and northern India, is tuned with care. In the center of each drumhead is a black circle called the syahi, a paste of iron filings and rice flour applied in many thin layers. The syahi adds weight to the middle of the skin, which gives the drum a clear, bell-like pitch instead of a dull thud. Players adjust that pitch by tapping small wooden blocks up or down the sides of the drum.
items.stem: According to the text, what effect does the syahi have on the sound of a tabla?

choices.A: It gives the drum a clear pitch rather than a dull sound.
choices.B: It softens the sound so that the drum does not overpower the singer.
choices.C: It makes the drum loud enough to be heard over other instruments.
