explanation.D: Incorrect. The worms retreat below the surface on a daily schedule, before the sun warms the ice; the text does not say a warmed worm can escape by burrowing.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: At seventy-one, two years after her husband's death, Ingrid Solberg enrolled in the beginners' swimming class at the town pool. Her children assumed she was conquering a fear; the instructor assumed she wished to be safe on the ferry to the island where she spent her summers. Ingrid let them think what they liked. The truth was simpler and harder to explain. For fifty years she had been half of a pair; everything she knew how to do she had learned beside Anders or for him. Floating on her back in the shallow end, she was doing the first thing in decades that belonged to her alone, that no one had asked of her and no one would share, and she did not mind the loneliness of it at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Ingrid finds that learning to swim helps her feel closer to the husband she has lost.
choices.B: Ingrid takes up swimming as something entirely her own after a lifetime of shared experience.
choices.C: Ingrid struggles to explain to her children why she wants to learn to swim after her husband's death.
choices.D: Ingrid takes swimming lessons to overcome a fear of water that she has hidden from her family.

explanation.why: The text lists other people's explanations (fear, safety on the ferry) and then gives "the truth": for fifty years everything she did was "beside Anders or for him," and swimming is "the first thing in decades that belonged to her alone." The main idea is this claiming of something that is hers only.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not say swimming connects her to Anders; it is valued precisely because it is not shared with anyone.
explanation.B: Correct. Swimming is the first thing that "belonged to her alone" after fifty years as "half of a pair."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says she "let them think what they liked"; the difficulty of explaining is a passing detail, not the point.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Conquering a fear is what her children assume; the text says "the truth was simpler."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. Pennington prided himself upon being a man of independent views, and he was never more conscious of the distinction than at dinner, where he was accustomed to deliver them. On this particular evening he spoke at length upon the folly of the new harbor scheme, the decline of the drama, and the character of the Bishop, and he observed with satisfaction that Mrs. Ashby, who was known to read, had twice nodded. It was only afterward, in the smoking room, when he took up that morning's paper to pass the quarter hour before the carriages came, that his eye fell upon the leading article, and he read, with a sensation he could not immediately name, his three opinions set out in order, in very nearly the words he had used, by a writer he had never met and would, he reflected, have described as a hack.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mr. Pennington's opinions are so widely shared that a journalist has printed them in the newspaper.
choices.B: Mr. Pennington is embarrassed when Mrs. Ashby reveals that she has read the same article he has.
choices.C: Mr. Pennington discovers that the views he believed were his own had been supplied by the morning's newspaper.
choices.D: Mrs. Ashby's nods convince Mr. Pennington that his opinions are well founded.

explanation.why: The text first establishes Mr. Pennington's pride in his "independent views" and his satisfaction in delivering them. The ending undercuts that pride: in "that morning's paper" he finds "his three opinions set out in order, in very nearly the words he had used." The reader is meant to see that he had absorbed the article and repeated it as his own.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the direction of borrowing: the article was written before dinner, so the newspaper did not print his opinions; he repeated the newspaper's.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Mrs. Ashby reveals nothing; she only nods, and the discovery happens when he is alone in the smoking room.
explanation.C: Correct. The opinions he delivered as his own appear in the morning paper he had evidently read, which is the irony the whole text builds toward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Her nods are a passing detail of his satisfaction at dinner, not the point of the text.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many birds can sleep with one half of the brain at a time, keeping open the eye connected to the waking half. The ability has long been assumed to guard against predators, but testing that idea requires showing that birds use it more when danger is greater. In one experiment, researchers arranged mallard ducks in a row of four and recorded their brain activity and eyes as they slept. Ducks at the two ends of the row, each with an exposed side, spent far more of their sleep with one hemisphere awake than ducks in the middle, and the open eye was almost always the one facing outward, away from the group. When the positions were switched, the behavior switched too. The birds were not simply sleeping lightly; they appeared to be allocating sleep to each half of the brain according to where a threat could come from.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Birds that keep one eye open while sleeping are simply sleeping more lightly than birds with both eyes closed.
choices.B: Mallard ducks prefer to sleep in the middle of a group because that position lets both halves of the brain rest.
choices.C: Ducks at the ends of a row were unable to sleep because of their exposed position.
choices.D: The experiment suggests that ducks adjust which half of the brain sleeps, and how much, according to their exposure to danger.

explanation.why: The text frames the experiment as a test of whether half-brain sleep is "a guard against predators." The results support that idea: end ducks used it more, their open eye faced outward, and the pattern followed the birds when positions changed. The last sentence draws the conclusion that the ducks were "allocating sleep to each half of the brain according to where a threat could come from."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text explicitly rejects this: "The birds were not simply sleeping lightly."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never discusses which position the ducks prefer; the researchers placed them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The end ducks did sleep; they simply kept one hemisphere awake more often, so this overstates the finding.
explanation.D: Correct. This states the conclusion the experiment supports, with the text's own caution ("appeared").

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Geography of Claudius Ptolemy, compiled in Alexandria in the second century, gave the latitude and longitude of some 8,000 places, and when it reached Western Europe in the early 1400s, mapmakers adopted its coordinates almost unaltered. Among its errors, one proved unusually durable: Ptolemy stretched the Mediterranean to roughly 62 degrees of longitude, about half again its true length. The mistake did not persist for lack of travel; sailors crossed the sea constantly. It persisted because there was no reliable way to measure longitude. Latitude could be fixed by observing the sun or the pole star, but east-west position rested on estimates of distance traveled, and such guesses could not overturn a figure as authoritative as Ptolemy's. Only in the late 1600s, when astronomers learned to fix longitude by timing the eclipses of Jupiter's moons from different cities, did the Mediterranean shrink on maps to its real size.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did Ptolemy's error about the length of the Mediterranean survive for so long?

choices.A: No one could measure east-west position accurately enough to challenge a figure that carried Ptolemy's authority.
choices.B: Mapmakers of the 1400s were unable to read the coordinates in Ptolemy's text correctly.
choices.C: Few Europeans traveled far enough across the sea to notice that its mapped length was wrong.
choices.D: Ptolemy's latitudes were so accurate that mapmakers assumed his longitudes were equally sound.

explanation.why: The text rules out one explanation ("did not persist from lack of travel") and gives another: "there was no reliable way to measure longitude," so rough estimates of distance "could not overturn a figure as authoritative as Ptolemy's." The correct choice combines the measurement problem with Ptolemy's authority.
explanation.A: Correct. Without a reliable way to measure longitude, no one could produce evidence strong enough to displace Ptolemy's figure.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Mapmakers adopted the coordinates "almost unaltered"; nothing suggests they misread them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says "sailors crossed the sea constantly."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says latitude could be measured, but it never claims that Ptolemy's latitudes earned trust for his longitudes.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In the weeks after Mr. Perera's funeral, his widow took up the accounts, which he had always kept himself in a ledger she had never been invited to read. She had been prepared for the careful figures; he had been a careful man, careful to the point, she had sometimes felt, of meanness, and she had resented the small economies of their life in Colombo more than she had said. What she had not been prepared for was the column headed only with initials, and the modest sums entered against them month after month for twenty years. One set of initials belonged to a boy down the lane whose school fees, she learned when she asked, had been paid since his father's death. With the ledger open before her, Mrs. Perera could not decide whether she was more ashamed of her husband's secrecy or of her own resentment.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mrs. Perera learns that her husband's careful bookkeeping concealed debts that will now fall to her.
choices.B: Mrs. Perera decides to continue paying the school fees of the boy her husband had been supporting.
choices.C: Discovering her husband's hidden generosity, Mrs. Perera must revise the resentment she had felt toward his frugality.
choices.D: Mrs. Perera resents the small economies that her husband imposed on their household for twenty years.

explanation.why: Two parts of the text work together. First, Mrs. Perera had resented her husband's "small economies" as meanness. Then the ledger reveals twenty years of quiet payments, including a boy's school fees. The final sentence shows the effect: she is torn between shame at his secrecy and shame at "her own resentment," which the discovery has made unfair.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the discovery: the sums were gifts her husband paid out, not debts he owed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text describes no decision about future payments.
explanation.C: Correct. This joins the earlier resentment with the discovery and the shame that follows.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Her resentment is the starting point, not the main idea; the text is about how the ledger unsettles it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Oulipo, a group of writers and mathematicians founded in Paris in 1960, set itself an unusual program: to invent formal constraints and then write under them. A novel composed without the letter e, a poem whose lines recombine into an astronomical number of sonnets, a story structured on the moves of a chess knight: each obeys a rule that has nothing to do with its subject. Critics have sometimes taken this as a game, or as a confession that the writers had nothing to say. The group's own account is nearly the opposite. Ordinary writers, its members have argued, already obey constraints, such as grammar and genre, that they do not notice and therefore cannot choose. A constraint adopted deliberately is at least visible, and in forcing a writer away from the first phrase that comes to mind, it can produce sentences that habit would never have supplied.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The Oulipo's experiments were a playful admission that its members had little of substance to say.
choices.B: The Oulipo held that deliberately chosen constraints, unlike unnoticed ones, could push writers toward invention rather than limit them.
choices.C: The Oulipo's members believed that grammar and genre should be abandoned in favor of mathematical rules.
choices.D: A novel written without the letter e shows that a formal constraint need have no connection to a work's subject.

explanation.why: The text describes the Oulipo's practice, notes the critics' view (a game, or a confession of having nothing to say), and then presents the group's own account as "nearly the opposite": all writers obey unnoticed constraints, and a chosen constraint "can produce sentences that habit would never have supplied." The main idea is this defense of constraint as a source of invention.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the critics' view, which the text says the group's account nearly reverses.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures the contrast between unnoticed and chosen constraints and the claim that chosen ones spur invention.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says members argued that writers already obey grammar and genre without noticing; it never says these should be abandoned.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is one example and one observation from the text, not its central argument.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A plant root grows downward, and the mechanism by which it senses which way is down has been debated for more than a century. The leading explanation points to a cluster of cells at the root's tip that contain dense, starch-filled grains. Within minutes of a root being turned on its side, these grains settle to the new bottom of each cell, and the shift is thought to trigger the signals that redirect growth. The hypothesis predicts that a root without such grains should be unable to sense gravity. Yet mutant plants whose cells cannot make starch, and whose grains are therefore too light to settle properly, still bend downward when tilted, only more slowly and less reliably than normal roots. The result does not overturn the explanation so much as complicate it: the settling grains evidently sharpen the root's sense of gravity, but they are not its only source.
items.stem: Based on the text, what do the experiments with starchless mutant plants indicate?

choices.A: The debate over how roots sense gravity has been settled by the discovery of starchless mutants.
choices.B: Starchless mutants sense gravity through a cluster of cells located far from the root tip.
choices.C: Starch-filled grains are the only means by which a root detects the direction of gravity.
choices.D: The settling of the grains improves a root's response to gravity but does not entirely account for it.

explanation.why: The hypothesis predicts that roots without settling grains "should be unable to sense gravity," yet the starchless mutants "still bend downward," only "more slowly and less reliably." The text's conclusion is that the grains "sharpen the root's sense of gravity, but they are not its only source." The correct choice restates this partial role.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the result "complicate[s]" the explanation rather than settling the debate.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says where the mutants' remaining sense of gravity comes from.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the finding: the mutants still respond, so the grains are "not its only source."
explanation.D: Correct. The grains improve the response (mutants are slower and less reliable) but are not the whole mechanism.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Pompeii worm lives in papery tubes on the chimneys of hydrothermal vents on the Pacific seafloor, where superheated water pours out. Early temperature readings taken near its tubes suggested that the worm's tail rested in water of about 80 degrees Celsius while its head, extended into the open, lay in water of around 20 degrees, which would make it the most heat-tolerant animal known. Those readings, however, came from probes placed beside the tubes rather than inside them, and the worms were almost impossible to study, since they died on the trip to the surface. When researchers later succeeded in keeping some alive in pressurized tanks, the animals thrived in moderate warmth but died within hours once the water passed about 50 degrees. The worm remains remarkably hardy, but the figure that made it famous now looks like a measurement of its surroundings, not of the worm.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Laboratory evidence suggests that the Pompeii worm tolerates far less heat than early readings near its tubes implied.
choices.B: Pompeii worms cannot be studied alive because they die on the journey from the seafloor to the surface.
choices.C: The Pompeii worm is the most heat-tolerant animal known, surviving water of about 80 degrees Celsius.
choices.D: Researchers have abandoned the idea that any animal can live close to hydrothermal vents.

explanation.why: The text presents the famous 80-degree figure, then undermines it: the readings were taken "beside the tubes rather than inside them," and worms kept alive in tanks "died within hours once the water passed about 50 degrees." The final sentence states the conclusion: the figure "now looks like a measurement of its surroundings rather than of the worm."
explanation.A: Correct. This states the revision the text argues for, with the text's own caution ("suggests").
explanation.B: Incorrect. This was true of early attempts, but the text says researchers "later succeeded in keeping some alive," and it is a detail in any case.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is the early claim that the rest of the text calls into question.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the worm "remains remarkably hardy" and lives at the vents; it questions only the 80-degree figure.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Tomasz had met his grandfather perhaps six times, always in the same stiff parlor, and had known him chiefly as a silence at the end of the table. So he was unprepared, when he came to the town after the funeral to help clear the house, for the way it recognized him. The woman at the bakery looked up and said his grandfather's name before she caught herself. The old man at the hardware shop asked whether he still took his coffee black, laughed at his own mistake, and then said, more quietly, that it was the way Tomasz stood in the doorway, one shoulder against the frame. By the third day Tomasz had begun to notice the habit in himself, and he could not have said whether he had always had it or whether he had, somewhere between the bakery and the hardware shop, decided to keep it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Through strangers' recognition, Tomasz discovers a likeness to his grandfather that he begins, perhaps deliberately, to make his own.
choices.B: Tomasz is annoyed that the people of the town keep confusing him with a grandfather he barely knew.
choices.C: The townspeople mistake Tomasz for his grandfather because of the way he stands in doorways.
choices.D: Tomasz resolves to rid himself of the mannerisms that remind the townspeople of his grandfather.

explanation.why: The text opens with how little Tomasz knew his grandfather and then shows the town "recognizing" the old man in him. The last sentence is the key: Tomasz notices the habit "in himself" and cannot say whether he always had it or has "decided to keep it." The main idea joins the strangers' recognition with Tomasz's half-conscious choice to hold on to the likeness.
explanation.A: Correct. This covers both the recognition by strangers and Tomasz's possible decision to keep what they saw in him.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no sign of annoyance; he is "unprepared" and then begins to adopt the habit.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The doorway is one explanation offered by one shopkeeper; it is a detail, not the point of the text.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the ending, in which he may have "decided to keep" the mannerism.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Japanese lacquerware owes its depth and durability to urushi, the sap of a tree native to East Asia, applied in many thin coats over a wooden core. The word "drying" is often used for what happens to each coat, but it is misleading. Urushi does not harden by losing moisture; it hardens by absorbing it. An enzyme in the sap uses oxygen and water from the air to drive a reaction that links the sap's molecules into a hard, cross-linked film, and the reaction proceeds only within a narrow band of warmth and high humidity. A coat left in a dry room will stay tacky for weeks. Craftsmen therefore place freshly coated pieces in a wooden cabinet whose walls have been dampened, where each layer cures for a day or more before it can be polished and the next applied. A fine piece may pass through this cycle thirty times.
items.stem: According to the text, why are freshly lacquered pieces placed in a dampened cabinet?

choices.A: The sap hardens through a reaction that needs moisture from the air and stalls in dry conditions.
choices.B: The cabinet keeps dust from settling on the surface before it can be polished.
choices.C: The moisture keeps the thin coats of urushi from cracking as they lose water.
choices.D: The enclosed space traps the sap's fumes, which speed the hardening of each coat.

explanation.why: The text corrects a common misunderstanding: urushi "does not harden by losing moisture; it hardens by absorbing it," through an enzyme reaction that needs "oxygen and water from the air" and "high humidity." A coat in a dry room "will stay tacky for weeks," which is why ("therefore") pieces go into the dampened cabinet.
explanation.A: Correct. The cabinet supplies the humidity that the hardening reaction requires.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions dust.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says the sap hardens by absorbing moisture, not by losing it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about fumes; the reaction depends on water and oxygen from the air.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In towns across Catalonia, in northeastern Spain, teams of several hundred people build human towers called castells, some rising ten levels, with a child of six or seven climbing to the top. Spectators naturally watch the climb. Within the tradition, however, the climb is only half the task. A tower is counted as fully achieved only when it has been taken down in the same order it was built, each level descending in turn, without a fall; a tower that reaches its full height and then collapses is recorded in a separate and lesser category. The rule reflects a conviction that strength and daring are the easy virtues. Controlled descent demands that the people at the top, already exhausted and often frightened, perform their most exact movements last, and that the hundreds pressed together at the base hold their positions when the cheering suggests the work is over.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Castells are dangerous because the children who climb to the top are too young to come down safely.
choices.B: A castell that reaches its full height is counted as a success even if it collapses afterward.
choices.C: The people at the base of a castell do the hardest work, though spectators rarely notice them.
choices.D: A castell's success is judged by its orderly dismantling as much as its height, reflecting the value placed on control.

explanation.why: The text turns on "however": spectators watch the climb, but within the tradition "the climb is only half the task," and a tower counts fully only when it is taken down in order. The text then explains the value behind the rule: strength and daring are "the easy virtues," while controlled descent demands exactness and discipline. The main idea joins the rule with the value it expresses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not discuss danger to the children or their age as a problem.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the rule: a tower that collapses after reaching full height is recorded in a "lesser category."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The base is mentioned as one of two groups whose discipline the descent requires; this is a detail, and the text never says the base does the hardest work.
explanation.D: Correct. This covers the rule about dismantling and the conviction about control that the text says the rule reflects.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Basil is a warm-season herb, so gardeners often wonder how warm the soil should be before they plant it. Horticulturist Lucía Ferreira sowed 50 basil seeds in each of four trays, kept each tray at a different soil temperature, and recorded how many seeds sprouted. In her test, the greatest number of seeds sprouted at a soil temperature of ______

data.title: Basil Seeds Sprouted at Four Soil Temperatures (50 seeds per tray)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 25°C, where 46 of the 50 seeds sprouted.
choices.B: 30°C, where seeds sprouted in an average of 4.8 days.
choices.C: 15°C, where 21 of the 50 seeds sprouted.
choices.D: 35°C, where nearly all of the 50 seeds sprouted.

explanation.why: The statement is about which temperature produced the greatest number of sprouted seeds, so look at the "Seeds sprouted" column and find the largest value. The largest number is 46, in the 25°C row.
explanation.A: Correct. At 25°C, 46 of 50 seeds sprouted, more than at any other temperature in the table.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 30°C gave the fastest sprouting time, but the statement is about how many seeds sprouted, and 44 is fewer than 46.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 15°C produced the fewest sprouted seeds, not the most.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table does not include a tray kept at 35°C.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At the start of March 2023, a community library in Kathmandu, Nepal, opened a reading corner with low shelves and floor cushions for children. Librarian Sushila Thapa counted how many books were borrowed each month to see whether the new space made a difference. The graph suggests that borrowing increased after the reading corner opened: ______

data.title: Books Borrowed per Month at a Kathmandu Community Library, 2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: borrowing was highest in January, when about 410 books were borrowed.
choices.B: most of the extra books borrowed were picture books for young children.
choices.C: monthly borrowing rose from about 400 books to more than 650 books.
choices.D: about 410 books were borrowed in January and about 400 in February.

explanation.why: The statement says borrowing increased after the corner opened in March, so the choice must compare the months before (January and February) with the months after (March and April). The graph shows about 400 books in each of the first two months and more than 650 in each of the last two.
explanation.A: Incorrect. January is one of the lowest months on the graph; April is the highest.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The graph shows only the total number of books borrowed, not what kinds of books they were.
explanation.C: Correct. Borrowing went from about 400 books per month in January and February to 655 and 731 books in March and April.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These numbers are accurate, but they describe only the months before the corner opened, so they do not show an increase.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Museum visitors often spend only a few seconds in front of a painting. Curator Ingrid Solberg suspected that this was partly because wall labels give only basic facts, such as a work's title and date. She hypothesized that adding a short card telling the story behind a painting would increase viewing time for every painting in her test, not just for the most popular ones.

data.title: Average Time Visitors Spent Viewing Each Painting

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Solberg's hypothesis?

choices.A: Visitors spent 38 seconds viewing Portrait of a Weaver with a story card, longer than they spent on any other painting.
choices.B: Still Life with Lemons received less viewing time than any other painting, with or without a story card.
choices.C: Visitors viewed The Orchard Wall for longer when it had only a label than when it also had a story card.
choices.D: Each of the four paintings was viewed longer on average with a story card than with only a label.

explanation.why: Solberg's hypothesis is that story cards increase viewing time for every painting, not only the popular ones. Support must therefore compare the two columns for all four paintings. In every row, the "Label and story card" time is greater than the "Label only" time.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one painting and does not compare its time with the label-only time, so it cannot show an effect on every painting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares paintings with one another instead of comparing each painting with and without a story card.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The Orchard Wall was viewed for 26 seconds with a story card and only 18 seconds with a label alone, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Correct. All four paintings gained viewing time with a story card (14 to 31, 22 to 38, 9 to 17 and 18 to 26 seconds), which is what "every painting" requires.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A green roof is covered with soil and low plants, which shade the surface and release water vapor that cools the air around them. Engineer Rangi Parata measured the surface temperature of a green roof and a conventional black roof in Auckland, New Zealand, every three hours on a sunny summer day. Parata found that the gap between the two roofs was largest in the afternoon: ______

data.title: Roof Surface Temperature over One Summer Day

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: at 6 p.m., the black roof was 44°C, while the green roof was 30°C.
choices.B: at 3 p.m., the black roof reached 66°C, while the green roof reached only 35°C.
choices.C: at 3 p.m., the green roof reached 66°C, while the black roof reached only 35°C.
choices.D: at 9 a.m., the green roof was more than 10°C cooler than the black roof.

explanation.why: The statement needs the afternoon time when the difference between the two lines is greatest. At 3 p.m. the gap is 66 − 35 = 31°C, larger than at noon (28°C) or 6 p.m. (14°C). The choice must also give the values the right way around: the black roof is the hotter one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. These values are accurate, but the gap at 6 p.m. is only 14°C, much smaller than the gap at 3 p.m.
explanation.B: Correct. At 3 p.m. the black roof (66°C) was 31°C hotter than the green roof (35°C), the largest gap shown.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This swaps the two roofs; the graph shows the black roof, not the green roof, reaching 66°C.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The 11°C gap at 9 a.m. is real, but 9 a.m. is morning, and the gap then is far smaller than in the afternoon.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When a midsize city expanded its bike-share network between 2019 and 2023, officials celebrated the rise in total trips as evidence that residents were embracing cycling for leisure. Urban planner Tomás Iturralde reads the same records differently. Because the new docking stations were placed mostly near offices and transit hubs, he argues, the growth in ridership came overwhelmingly from people riding on workdays, while recreational weekend use stayed nearly flat. In his view, the network had become chiefly a commuting tool.

data.title: Bike-Share Trips in a Midsize City

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Iturralde's argument?

choices.A: Total trips rose from 600,000 in 2019 to 905,000 in 2023.
choices.B: Weekday trips rose by 280,000 from 2019 to 2023, while weekend trips rose by only 25,000.
choices.C: Weekend trips increased in every year shown, from 190,000 in 2019 to 215,000 in 2023.
choices.D: Weekday trips more than doubled between 2019 and 2023, while weekend trips did not.

explanation.why: Iturralde does not dispute that total trips grew; his claim is about where the growth came from: mostly weekday trips, with weekend trips nearly flat. Support therefore has to compare the change in the two columns. Weekday trips rose from 410 to 690 thousand (+280,000), while weekend trips rose from 190 to 215 thousand (+25,000).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but officials and Iturralde both accept that total trips grew; the total does not show which kind of trip produced the growth.
explanation.B: Correct. It compares the growth in the two columns and shows that nearly all of the increase came from weekday trips.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes weekend trips alone and stresses their growth, which does not show that weekday trips drove the increase.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Weekday trips rose from 410,000 to 690,000, which is less than double, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In parts of Bangladesh, flash floods can leave young rice plants completely underwater for days, and many conventional varieties die if submerged for much longer than a week. Agronomist Farzana Haque compared a conventional variety with a flood-tolerant variety by holding seedlings of each underwater for different lengths of time and then counting the survivors. Haque concluded that although the tolerant variety offers only a slight benefit in brief floods, its advantage over the conventional variety grows considerably as flooding lasts longer.

data.title: Rice Seedling Survival after Submergence

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Haque's conclusion?

choices.A: The tolerant variety had a higher survival rate than the conventional variety after every flooding period tested.
choices.B: Survival rates for both varieties declined as the number of days underwater increased.
choices.C: Between 3 and 14 days underwater, the tolerant variety's survival rate fell by more percentage points than the conventional variety's did.
choices.D: The tolerant variety's survival rate was 3 percentage points higher than the conventional variety's after 3 days but 55 points higher after 14 days.

explanation.why: Haque's conclusion has two parts: the tolerant variety's advantage is small in short floods, and that advantage grows as floods last longer. Support must show the gap between the two bars at a short and a long flooding period. The gap is 95 − 92 = 3 points at 3 days and 64 − 9 = 55 points at 14 days.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that the tolerant variety always did better, not that its advantage was slight at first and then grew.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes both varieties together and says nothing about the difference between them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The tolerant variety fell 31 points (95 to 64), while the conventional variety fell 83 points (92 to 9), so this reverses the data.
explanation.D: Correct. A 3-point gap after a short flood and a 55-point gap after a long one shows both parts of the conclusion: a slight early benefit and a much larger later one.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Because lizards cannot generate much body heat internally, they were long described as being at the mercy of their surroundings, warming and cooling with the air. Herpetologist Elif Karaca, who fitted Mediterranean wall lizards in a rocky hillside population with miniature temperature sensors and recorded their average body temperature every two hours through a clear summer day, rejects that characterization. By shuttling between sunlit rock and shaded crevices, she contends, the lizards confine their body temperature to a band considerably narrower than the daily swing in the temperature of the air around them, rather than simply tracking that swing.

data.title: Air Temperature and Average Lizard Body Temperature over One Day

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Karaca's claim?

choices.A: Between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., the lizards' body temperature stayed within about 10°C, whereas air temperature spanned nearly 20°C.
choices.B: At every time of day shown, the lizards' average body temperature was higher than the temperature of the surrounding air.
choices.C: From 8 a.m. to noon, the temperature of the air rose by fewer degrees than the lizards' body temperature did.
choices.D: The lizards spent more of the hottest afternoon hours in shaded crevices than they did in the cool early morning.

explanation.why: Karaca's specific claim is about range: body temperature varies within a narrower band than air temperature does. To support it, compare the spread of each line across the day. Body temperature runs from 25°C to 35°C (about 10 degrees), while air temperature runs from 14°C to 33°C (19 degrees).
explanation.A: Correct. Comparing the two ranges, about 10°C for the lizards versus about 19°C for the air, shows exactly the narrower band Karaca describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but being warmer than the air is a different claim; a lizard could be warmer than the air at every hour and still swing as widely as the air does.
explanation.C: Incorrect. From 8 a.m. to noon the air warmed by 15°C (14 to 29), while the lizards warmed by only 10°C (25 to 35), so this reverses the data.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Shuttling into shade fits Karaca's explanation, but the graph shows only temperatures, not where the lizards spent their time.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In a fishing town on the coast of Galicia, in northwestern Spain, older residents use a rich set of local words for particular winds and sea conditions, words that younger residents rarely say aloud. One might assume that this vocabulary is simply being forgotten. Linguist Xoana Castro, who surveyed residents of four age groups, proposes a different account: younger speakers, she argues, still know the traditional words about as well as their grandparents do but choose standard terms instead, so the shift reflects a change in preference rather than a loss of knowledge.

data.title: Survey of Traditional Wind and Sea Words in a Galician Fishing Town

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Castro's account?

choices.A: The share of speakers who regularly used the traditional words fell steadily from 88% in the oldest group to 23% in the youngest group.
choices.B: Among speakers aged 65 and older, 88% regularly used the traditional words and 97% recognized them.
choices.C: Speakers aged 15–24 used the traditional words at roughly a quarter of the rate of those 65 and older, yet recognized them at nearly the same rate.
choices.D: Recognition of the traditional words fell about as sharply from the oldest to the youngest group as regular use of the words did.

explanation.why: Castro's account has two parts that must both appear: younger speakers use the words much less than older speakers, and yet they know the words about as well. That requires comparing the youngest and oldest groups in both columns. Use falls from 88% to 23% (about a quarter), while recognition changes only from 97% to 90%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a drop in use is what both explanations accept; without the recognition figures it cannot show that the words are not being forgotten.
explanation.B: Incorrect. These figures are accurate and use both columns, but they describe only the oldest speakers, while Castro's account is about what younger speakers know.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows a large gap in use (23% versus 88%) alongside a small gap in recognition (90% versus 97%), which is exactly the pattern a change in preference would produce.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Recognition fell only 7 points (97% to 90%), while use fell 65 points (88% to 23%), so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On hydroponic farms, lettuce grows in nutrient-rich water instead of soil, often under lamps that growers can switch on and off. Grower Tobias Lindqvist raised lettuce under four daily lighting schedules in a greenhouse in Sweden and weighed the heads at harvest. In his trial, the heaviest heads of lettuce grew with ______

data.title: Lettuce Grown under Four Daily Lighting Schedules

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 16 hours of light per day, which produced the quickest harvest.
choices.B: 18 hours of light per day, which produced heads heavier than any others.
choices.C: 10 hours of light per day, which produced heads averaging 142 grams.
choices.D: 14 hours of light per day, which produced heads averaging 205 grams.

explanation.why: The statement asks which schedule produced the heaviest heads, so look at the "Average head mass" column and find the largest value. The largest mass is 205 grams, in the 14-hour row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The 16-hour schedule did give the quickest harvest (34 days), but its heads averaged 198 grams, less than 205 grams.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table does not include an 18-hour schedule.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The 10-hour schedule produced the lightest heads in the table, not the heaviest.
explanation.D: Correct. Lettuce given 14 hours of light averaged 205 grams, more than under any other schedule.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2024, a public library in Islamabad, Pakistan, began opening on Sundays in addition to its usual six days. Librarian Farah Qureshi wanted to know whether the new Sunday hours would attract readers, so she counted visitors on each day of one week in May. Her count suggests that the Sunday hours were popular: ______

data.title: Library Visitors on Each Day of One Week in May 2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: about 520 people visited on Sunday, more than on any other day of the week.
choices.B: on Friday, the library had about 260 visitors, fewer than on any other day.
choices.C: most Sunday visitors were students who could not come during the school week.
choices.D: about 455 people visited on Saturday, more than on any other day of the week.

explanation.why: The statement says the Sunday hours were popular, so the choice must show how Sunday compared with the other days. The Sunday bar, at about 520 visitors, is the tallest on the graph.
explanation.A: Correct. Sunday had about 520 visitors, more than any other day, which shows the new hours were popular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Friday did have the fewest visitors, but this says nothing about Sunday, the day the statement is about.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph shows only how many people visited, not who they were or why they came on Sunday.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This misreads the graph: Saturday had about 455 visitors, fewer than Sunday's 520.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In a pond, algae and water plants release oxygen into the water during daylight through photosynthesis. At night, photosynthesis stops, but the pond's living things keep using oxygen. Student researcher Amara Osei measured the oxygen in a pond in Ghana every four hours for one day. Her readings show that the oxygen level was lowest ______

data.title: Oxygen Dissolved in a Pond over One Day

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: at 4 a.m., when it was about 4 milligrams per liter.
choices.B: at noon, when the algae were releasing the most oxygen.
choices.C: at 4 p.m., when it reached about 10 milligrams per liter.
choices.D: at midnight, when it had dropped to about 5.6 milligrams per liter.

explanation.why: The statement asks when the oxygen level was lowest, so find the lowest point on the line. The line dips to about 4.1 milligrams per liter at 4 a.m., lower than at any other time shown.
explanation.A: Correct. The reading at 4 a.m., about 4 milligrams per liter, is the lowest point on the graph.
explanation.B: Incorrect. At noon the reading was about 8.3 milligrams per liter, well above the lowest value, and the graph does not show when algae released the most oxygen.
explanation.C: Incorrect. At 4 p.m. the oxygen level was at its highest, not its lowest.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The level did drop to about 5.6 at midnight, but it fell even lower, to about 4.1, by 4 a.m.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A marionette theater in Prague, Czech Republic, presents the same puppet show in several languages for residents and tourists. To plan the next season, manager Petra Nováková recorded the number of performances in each language and the average audience at those performances during the summer. According to her records, the language with the largest average audience was ______

data.title: Marionette Show Performances by Language, Summer Season

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: German, which had an average audience of 72 people per performance.
choices.B: English, which was used in more performances than any other language.
choices.C: Italian, with an average of 95 people at each performance.
choices.D: Czech, which had an average audience of 61 people per performance.

explanation.why: The statement is about the largest average audience, so the "Average audience" column is the one to check, not the "Performances" column. The largest value there is 95, for Italian.
explanation.A: Incorrect. German performances averaged 72 people, fewer than both English and Italian performances.
explanation.B: Incorrect. English had the most performances (40), but its average audience of 88 was smaller than Italian's 95.
explanation.C: Correct. Italian performances averaged 95 people, the largest average audience in the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Czech performances had the smallest average audience in the table, not the largest.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mulch is a layer of material spread over soil to slow the loss of water. Gardener Rosa Delgado covered four garden beds in Tucson, Arizona, with different mulches and left a fifth bed bare. Two days after watering all five beds, she measured how much water remained in the soil of each. Her results show that the soil held the most water under ______

data.title: Soil Moisture Two Days after Watering

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: bare soil, where soil moisture was about 11 percent.
choices.B: wood chips, which also kept weeds from growing in the bed.
choices.C: cardboard, where soil moisture was about 22 percent.
choices.D: straw, where soil moisture was about 24 percent.

explanation.why: The statement asks which covering left the most water in the soil, so look for the tallest bar. The straw bar, at about 24 percent, is taller than all the others.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Bare soil held the least water of the five beds, not the most.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The graph shows only soil moisture; it gives no information about weeds.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Cardboard did keep about 22 percent moisture, but that is less than straw's 24 percent.
explanation.D: Correct. The soil under straw held about 24 percent moisture, the highest value on the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Members of a farming cooperative near Nakuru, Kenya, share equipment and sell their crops together. In 2025, cooperative officer Wanjiru Kamau recorded how many hectares each crop covered and how large each harvest was. Her records show that the crop planted on the most land was ______

data.title: Crops Grown by a Cooperative near Nakuru, Kenya, 2025

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: potatoes, which produced the largest harvest of any crop.
choices.B: beans, which were planted on 31 hectares.
choices.C: maize, which was planted on 46 hectares.
choices.D: wheat, which was planted on more land than maize.

explanation.why: The statement is about the crop planted on the most land, so check the "Land planted" column, not the harvest column. The largest value there is 46 hectares, for maize.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Potatoes gave the largest harvest (396 metric tons), but they were planted on only 22 hectares.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Beans were planted on 31 hectares, which is less land than maize's 46 hectares.
explanation.C: Correct. Maize covered 46 hectares, more land than any other crop in the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table does not include wheat at all.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Tea bushes grow best with plenty of rain, and many tea estates in Sri Lanka keep their own rainfall records. Estate manager Dilani Perera measured the rain that fell on her estate, in the southwest of the country, during the first six months of 2025. Her measurements show that the wettest of these months was ______

data.title: Monthly Rainfall at a Tea Estate in Southwestern Sri Lanka, 2025

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: April, when the rain helped the tea bushes grow fastest.
choices.B: February, when about 105 millimeters of rain fell.
choices.C: May, when about 470 millimeters of rain fell.
choices.D: June, when about 400 millimeters of rain fell.

explanation.why: The wettest month is the one with the highest rainfall, so find the highest point on the line. The line peaks at about 470 millimeters in May.
explanation.A: Incorrect. April had about 310 millimeters, less than May, and the graph says nothing about how fast the tea bushes grew.
explanation.B: Incorrect. February had the least rain of the six months, so it was the driest, not the wettest.
explanation.C: Correct. About 470 millimeters fell in May, more than in any other month shown.
explanation.D: Incorrect. June was very wet, with about 400 millimeters, but May had even more rain.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: At a youth music camp in Cape Town, South Africa, each of 163 campers chose one instrument to study for the week. Camp director Thandiwe Mokoena expected the guitar to be the most popular choice. However, the camp's records show that the instrument chosen by the most campers was ______

data.title: Instruments Chosen by Campers

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the marimba, which was chosen by 34 campers.
choices.B: the guitar, which was chosen by 41 campers.
choices.C: the keyboard, which was chosen by 47 campers.
choices.D: the drums, which most campers had already played at school.

explanation.why: The word "However" signals that the most popular instrument was not the guitar, as the director expected. The tallest bar on the graph is the keyboard, chosen by 47 campers.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The marimba was chosen by 34 campers, fewer than both the keyboard and the guitar.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The guitar was the director's expectation, but its 41 campers are fewer than the keyboard's 47, and "However" signals a different answer.
explanation.C: Correct. The keyboard was chosen by 47 campers, more than any other instrument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph does not show what campers had played before, and the drums drew only 29 campers.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ice in a cooler melts more slowly when the cooler's walls let less heat pass through. For a consumer magazine, product tester Daniel Hirsch placed 5 kilograms of ice in each of four coolers, kept them in a 30°C room, and recorded how long the ice took to melt completely. In his test, the ice lasted longest in ______

data.title: Time for 5 Kilograms of Ice to Melt in Four Coolers at 30°C

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: Cooler Y, where the ice took 72 hours to melt completely.
choices.B: Cooler Z, where the ice took 14 hours to melt completely.
choices.C: Cooler X, which had the thickest foam walls of the four coolers.
choices.D: Cooler W, the lightest and least expensive of the four coolers.

explanation.why: The statement asks where the ice lasted longest, so look at the "Hours until all ice melted" column. The largest value is 72 hours, for cooler Y.
explanation.A: Correct. The ice in cooler Y took 72 hours to melt, longer than in any other cooler.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Cooler Z's ice melted fastest, so it lasted the shortest time, not the longest.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Cooler X did have the thickest foam walls, but its ice melted in 58 hours, sooner than cooler Y's.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table gives no information about weight or price, and cooler W's ice melted in only 31 hours.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2019, volunteers in a coastal town in Maine finished restoring an old lighthouse and opened it as a small museum. Town historian Ruth Callahan has kept a record of how many people visit the museum each year. Her records show that the museum's lowest yearly attendance came in ______

data.title: Yearly Visitors to a Lighthouse Museum in Maine

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2021, when about 1,400 people visited the museum.
choices.B: 2024, the year with the highest attendance shown.
choices.C: 2019, when about 3,200 people visited the museum.
choices.D: 2020, when about 1,900 people visited the museum.

explanation.why: The statement asks for the year of lowest attendance, so find the lowest point on the line. The line drops to about 1,900 visitors in 2020, its lowest value.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the graph: about 4,100 people visited in 2021, not about 1,400.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 2024 had the highest attendance, which is the opposite of what the statement describes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. About 3,200 people did visit in 2019, but that is more than the roughly 1,900 who visited in 2020.
explanation.D: Correct. About 1,900 people visited in 2020, fewer than in any other year shown.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A public library in Montreal, Canada, lends comic books in several languages. Librarian Sophie Tremblay counted the comic books borrowed in each language during 2025. She found that more comic books were borrowed in French than in any other language, followed by ______

data.title: Comic Books at a Montreal Public Library, 2025

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: English, with 3,150 comic books borrowed.
choices.B: Spanish, with 1,410 comic books borrowed.
choices.C: Arabic, with more than 3,000 comic books borrowed.
choices.D: Mandarin, with 690 comic books borrowed.

explanation.why: "Followed by" means the language with the second-largest number of loans. In the "Comic books borrowed" column, French is first with 4,820, and English is second with 3,150.
explanation.A: Correct. English, with 3,150 loans, is second only to French.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Spanish had 1,410 loans, far fewer than English, so it was not second.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This misreads the table: Arabic had 1,260 loans, not more than 3,000.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Mandarin had the fewest loans of any language, not the second most.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Different birds prefer different seeds, so the food in a feeder affects which birds visit it. In a backyard in Ohio, birdwatcher Grace Whitfield filled four identical feeders with four kinds of seed and counted bird visits over one week. The seed that drew the most visits was ______

data.title: Bird Visits to Four Backyard Feeders over One Week

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: black-oil sunflower seed, which drew 412 visits.
choices.B: safflower, which drew 167 visits.
choices.C: millet, which drew birds of six different species.
choices.D: Nyjer seed, which drew 238 visits.

explanation.why: The statement is about the most visits, so check the "Bird visits" column. The largest number there is 412, for black-oil sunflower seed.
explanation.A: Correct. Black-oil sunflower seed drew 412 visits, more than any other seed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Safflower drew the fewest visits of the four seeds, not the most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is about the number of species, not the number of visits, and millet drew only 189 visits.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nyjer drew 238 visits, the second-highest number, but fewer than sunflower seed's 412.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When ocean water stays unusually warm for weeks, corals expel the algae living in their tissues and turn white, a process called bleaching. Marine biologist Keoni Kahale surveyed two reefs off the island of Hawai'i during 2025: one in a sheltered bay and one on an exposed point where cooler water rises from the deep. Kahale reported that the exposed reef appeared to be partly protected from bleaching, noting that ______

data.title: Percentage of Corals Bleached at Two Reefs, 2025

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: in September, about 47% of the exposed reef's corals were bleached, versus about 18% in the bay.
choices.B: at both reefs, a larger share of corals was bleached in September than in June.
choices.C: bleaching at the exposed reef began only after the water there warmed past 29°C.
choices.D: in September, about 18% of the exposed reef's corals were bleached, versus about 47% in the bay.

explanation.why: To show that the exposed reef was partly protected, the choice must compare the two reefs and show less bleaching at the exposed point. At the peak in September, the exposed point line is at about 18% and the sheltered bay line is at about 47%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This swaps the two reefs; the graph shows the sheltered bay, not the exposed point, at about 47%.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes a change over time at both reefs and does not compare the exposed reef with the sheltered one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph shows the percentage of corals bleached, not water temperatures.
explanation.D: Correct. The exposed reef had far less bleaching than the sheltered reef in September (about 18% versus 47%), but some bleaching, which fits "partly protected."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2021, a sports academy in Karachi, Pakistan, began offering free cricket coaching to girls on weekend mornings. The academy had long trained mostly boys, and its boys' program continued alongside the new one. Each year, the academy recorded how many boys and girls were enrolled. Coach Sana Baig claims that girls now make up a much larger proportion of the academy's players than they did when the girls' program began.

data.title: Players Enrolled at a Karachi Cricket Academy, 2021-2025

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Baig's claim?

choices.A: More girls than boys were enrolled at the academy in 2025.
choices.B: Girls were about 12% of players in 2021 but about 38% in 2025.
choices.C: The academy enrolled 118 girls in 2025, more than in any other year shown.
choices.D: The number of boys enrolled at the academy was higher in 2025 than in 2021.

explanation.why: Baig's claim is about proportion: the share of all players who are girls. A rising number of girls alone does not prove this, since the number of boys could rise too. In 2021 girls were 24 of 204 players (about 12%), and in 2025 they were 118 of 314 (about 38%).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the table: in 2025 there were 196 boys and only 118 girls.
explanation.B: Correct. The girls' share of all players roughly tripled, from about 12% to about 38%, which directly supports a claim about proportion.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives only a number of girls, not their share of all players, so it cannot show that the proportion grew.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (196 versus 180), but it is about boys and does not show the girls' share growing.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Brazilian publishers translate far more fiction from English than from any other language. Literary scholar Helena Barros counted the novels translated into Portuguese by Brazilian publishers in 2015 and in 2025, grouping them by the language in which each novel was first written. Her counts cover five common source languages. She argues that although English remained dominant, translations from some Asian languages grew especially quickly over the decade, noting, for example, that ______

data.title: Novels Translated into Portuguese by Brazilian Publishers

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the number of novels translated from English rose from 410 in 2015 to 455 in 2025.
choices.B: translations from Japanese fell from 49 novels in 2015 to 14 novels in 2025.
choices.C: translations from Korean grew from 3 novels in 2015 to 37 novels in 2025.
choices.D: Korean novels translated in 2025 sold more copies than French novels did.

explanation.why: The blank must give an example of an Asian language whose translations grew especially quickly. Korean and Japanese are the Asian languages on the graph, and Korean translations rose from 3 to 37, more than tenfold.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but English is not an Asian language, and a rise from 410 to 455 is modest growth.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the years: Japanese translations rose from 14 in 2015 to 49 in 2025.
explanation.C: Correct. Korean is an Asian language, and its translations grew from 3 to 37 novels, an especially fast increase.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows how many novels were translated, not how many copies were sold.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many garden plants sold in nurseries are cultivars bred for showy blooms, and some ecologists suspect that such breeding can reduce the nectar and pollen that bees rely on. Ecologist Mateus Oliveira compared four groups of plants in a botanical garden in the midwestern United States, counting bee visits to a native species and to an ornamental cultivar in each group. He concluded that, in his study, the native plants were more attractive to bees than the cultivars.

data.title: Average Bee Visits per Plant in One Hour

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Oliveira's conclusion?

choices.A: The ornamental cultivars were sold in more local nurseries than the native species were.
choices.B: The ornamental bee balm received more bee visits per hour than the native bee balm did.
choices.C: In all four plant groups, the native species drew more bee visits than the cultivar.
choices.D: The native aster received 31 bee visits per hour, more than any other plant in the study.

explanation.why: Oliveira's conclusion is a general comparison of native plants and cultivars, so the best support compares the two columns across every group. In each row, the native species' number is larger than the cultivar's.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table gives no information about which plants nurseries sell.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This misreads the table: the native bee balm received 18 visits and the cultivar only 15.
explanation.C: Correct. Native species drew more visits in every group (31 to 12, 24 to 9, 18 to 15 and 27 to 6), which supports the conclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes a single plant and does not compare it with a cultivar, so it cannot support a general conclusion.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For decades, a car ferry was the only way to cross a fjord near a small town in western Norway. In 2022, a bridge opened across the fjord, and planners predicted that use of the ferry, which still stops at two island villages, would keep shrinking year after year. Transport researcher Ola Haugen's data show that ferry use did drop sharply in 2022 but that the rest of the prediction was wrong: ______

data.title: Yearly Ferry Passengers across a Fjord in Western Norway

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the ferry carried about 410,000 passengers in 2019, more than in any later year shown.
choices.B: after 2022, ferry use rose slightly each year, reaching about 185,000 passengers in 2025.
choices.C: the new bridge carried more than a million vehicles in its first full year of operation.
choices.D: by 2025, the ferry was again carrying about 400,000 passengers a year, as it had before 2022.

explanation.why: Planners predicted that ferry use would keep shrinking every year. The graph shows a sharp drop in 2022, but after that the line rises a little each year, from about 160,000 to about 185,000, which contradicts the prediction.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the years before the bridge opened and says nothing about what happened after 2022.
explanation.B: Correct. After the drop, ferry use grew slightly every year, so it did not keep shrinking as planners predicted.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph shows only ferry passengers, not traffic on the bridge.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This misreads the graph: ferry use in 2025 was about 185,000, far below the roughly 400,000 of earlier years.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Oil pressed from the seeds of the neem tree is used by many farmers in Pakistan as a natural pest spray. At a research farm in Sindh, agricultural scientist Imran Soomro sprayed aphid-infested chili plants with water only, a 1% neem solution, or a 2% neem solution and counted aphids per leaf on the day of spraying and ten days later. Soomro concluded that the stronger neem solution worked better than the weaker one, pointing out that ______

data.title: Aphids on Chili Plants Sprayed with Water or Neem Solution

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: after ten days, the 1% plants had about 9 aphids per leaf and the 2% plants about 23.
choices.B: plants sprayed with water only had more aphids per leaf after ten days than at the start.
choices.C: plants sprayed with the 1% solution had far fewer aphids after ten days than at the start.
choices.D: after ten days, the 2% plants had about 9 aphids per leaf and the 1% plants about 23.

explanation.why: Soomro's conclusion compares the two neem strengths, so the choice must compare the 2% and 1% plants. Both groups started with similar numbers (about 41 and 44), but ten days later the 2% plants had about 9 aphids per leaf and the 1% plants about 23.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This swaps the two solutions; the graph shows the 2% plants, not the 1% plants, with about 9 aphids per leaf.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (42 rose to 58), but it is about the water-only plants and does not compare the two neem solutions.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that the weaker solution worked, not that the stronger one worked better.
explanation.D: Correct. Starting from similar levels, the 2% plants ended with far fewer aphids than the 1% plants, so the stronger solution worked better.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: At a film festival in Lyon, France, four foreign-language films were each shown twice: once with French subtitles and once dubbed into French. Festival organizer Camille Roux asked audience members to rate each screening on a scale from 1 to 10. The two screenings of each film drew audiences of similar size. Roux noted that audiences did not prefer the same version of every film: ______

data.title: Average Audience Ratings for Subtitled and Dubbed Screenings

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: The Salt Road scored higher subtitled, but Paper Moons scored higher dubbed.
choices.B: every film was rated higher in its subtitled version than in its dubbed one.
choices.C: North Wind scored higher dubbed, but Winter Kitchen scored higher subtitled.
choices.D: both versions of Winter Kitchen received ratings above 7.5.

explanation.why: Roux's point is that the preferred version differed from film to film, so the choice must name one film rated higher subtitled and another rated higher dubbed. The Salt Road scored 8.4 subtitled and 7.1 dubbed, while Paper Moons scored 6.8 subtitled and 7.5 dubbed.
explanation.A: Correct. The Salt Road was preferred subtitled and Paper Moons was preferred dubbed, so audiences did not favor the same version every time.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Paper Moons was rated higher dubbed (7.5) than subtitled (6.8), so not every film was preferred subtitled, and this would contradict Roux's point.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This misreads the table: North Wind scored higher subtitled (8.1) than dubbed (6.9).
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (7.9 and 7.6), but it concerns one film only and shows no difference in which version audiences preferred.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In mountain streams fed by melting snow, water flow usually peaks in late spring or early summer. Hydrologist Erin Castillo compared the flow of a stream in the Colorado Rockies in 2023, after a winter of heavy snowfall, and in 2024, after a winter of light snowfall. She found that in the low-snow year, the stream not only carried less water at its peak but also peaked earlier: ______

data.title: Average Monthly Flow of a Snow-Fed Stream in Colorado

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the flow peaked in May in 2023 but did not peak until June in 2024.
choices.B: the flow peaked in June 2023 at about 14.5 but in May 2024 at only about 7.4.
choices.C: in both years, the stream's flow was lower in August than it had been in June.
choices.D: in 2024, the flow rose from about 2.9 cubic meters per second in April to about 7.4 in May.

explanation.why: Castillo's finding has two parts: in 2024 the peak was lower and came earlier. The choice must give both years' peaks. The 2023 line peaks in June at about 14.5, and the 2024 line peaks in May at about 7.4, a smaller peak one month earlier.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This swaps the years: the 2023 flow peaked in June and the 2024 flow peaked in May.
explanation.B: Correct. The 2024 peak (about 7.4 in May) was both smaller and a month earlier than the 2023 peak (about 14.5 in June).
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares August with June and says nothing about the size or timing of each year's peak.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only 2024 and does not compare its peak with the 2023 peak.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Night markets in Bangkok, Thailand, attract both residents and tourists. Urban geographer Niran Chaiyaporn counted the stalls of each type at two night markets, one near a business district popular with visitors and one in a residential neighborhood. He hypothesized that the residential market would devote a much larger share of its stalls to everyday goods, such as fresh produce and household items, than the business district market would.

data.title: Stalls at Two Bangkok Night Markets

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chaiyaporn's hypothesis?

choices.A: Most shoppers at the residential market said they lived within a short walk of it and visited weekly.
choices.B: The business district market had more prepared-food stalls than the residential market had, 120 compared with 95.
choices.C: The residential market had more clothing and souvenir stalls than the business district market, 140 compared with 30.
choices.D: About 48% of stalls at the residential market sold produce or household goods, versus 13% at the other market.

explanation.why: The hypothesis is about the share of each market's stalls selling everyday goods. The residential market has 60 + 55 = 115 such stalls out of 240 (about 48%), while the business district market has 15 + 25 = 40 out of 300 (about 13%).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table counts stalls; it contains no information about shoppers.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but prepared food is not one of the everyday goods named in the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This swaps the markets: the business district market had 140 clothing and souvenir stalls, and the residential market had 30.
explanation.D: Correct. Everyday goods filled about 48% of the residential market's stalls but only about 13% of the business district market's, as the hypothesis predicts.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On mussel farms, young mussels grow on ropes that hang down into the water from floating lines. Aquaculture researcher Fiona MacLeod hung ropes in a sea loch in western Scotland and measured how much the mussels' shells grew at three depths over each of two years. MacLeod argues that mussels grow faster closer to the surface, where the tiny algae they eat are most plentiful. Her measurements are consistent with this view: ______

data.title: Average Shell Growth of Mussels at Three Depths

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: in both years, mussels at 10 meters grew more than mussels at 2 meters did.
choices.B: in both years, growth was greatest at 2 meters and least at 10 meters.
choices.C: in 2025, mussels at 6 meters grew about 30 millimeters, slightly more than in 2024.
choices.D: in both years, the water at 2 meters held more algae than the water at 10 meters.

explanation.why: MacLeod's view is that mussels grow faster the closer they are to the surface. The graph should therefore show growth decreasing with depth. In both years the 2-meter bar is tallest and the 10-meter bar is shortest.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the graph: mussels at 2 meters grew about twice as much as those at 10 meters.
explanation.B: Correct. In both years, shell growth was largest at the shallowest depth and smallest at the deepest, as MacLeod's view predicts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares one depth across years rather than comparing depths, so it says nothing about growth near the surface.
explanation.D: Incorrect. MacLeod says algae are most plentiful near the surface, but the graph measures shell growth, not the amount of algae.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A monthly Urdu poetry magazine published in Lahore, Pakistan, began posting each issue online in 2019 while continuing to sell printed copies. Editor Ayesha Rana reported that within a few years the magazine's online readers outnumbered its print buyers, even though print sales fell only slightly. According to the graph, the first year in which online readers outnumbered print copies sold was ______

data.title: Average Monthly Readership of an Urdu Poetry Magazine

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2019, when print sales were about 12,000 copies.
choices.B: 2021, when online readers reached about 10,400.
choices.C: 2024, when online readers reached about 21,000.
choices.D: 2022, when online readers reached about 13,900.

explanation.why: The question asks for the first year the online line rose above the print line. In 2021 online readers (about 10,400) were still below print copies (about 11,500), but in 2022 online readers (about 13,900) passed print copies (about 11,100).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but in 2019 print copies far outnumbered online readers (about 12,000 versus 2,500).
explanation.B: Incorrect. In 2021 online readers were about 10,400, still fewer than the roughly 11,500 print copies sold.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Online readers did outnumber print copies in 2024, but they had already done so in 2022 and 2023, so 2024 was not the first year.
explanation.D: Correct. 2022 is the first year the online line is above the print line: about 13,900 online readers versus about 11,100 print copies.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many fruit-eating birds swallow seeds whole and later pass them in their droppings. Some ecologists have proposed that passing through a bird's gut also helps seeds sprout. Botanist Lucas Ferraz tested this idea in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, comparing seeds of four tree species collected from bird droppings with seeds taken directly from fruit. Ferraz concluded that the effect depends on the species: gut passage helped some kinds of seeds sprout but not others.

data.title: Percentage of Seeds That Sprouted, by Source

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ferraz's conclusion?

choices.A: For all four species, seeds from droppings sprouted at a higher rate than seeds taken from fruit.
choices.B: Guava seeds sprouted far more often after passing through a bird, but pitanga seeds did not.
choices.C: Guava seeds from droppings sprouted at a higher rate, 81%, than seeds of any other species did.
choices.D: Seeds passed by birds were carried farther from the parent tree than seeds that fell in fruit.

explanation.why: Ferraz's conclusion has two sides: gut passage helped some species and not others. Support must show one species that benefited and one that did not. Guava seeds sprouted at 81% from droppings versus 39% from fruit, while pitanga seeds sprouted at 55% versus 57%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the table: pitanga and embaúba seeds sprouted slightly less often from droppings than from fruit.
explanation.B: Correct. Gut passage roughly doubled guava's sprouting rate but did not raise pitanga's, so the effect depended on the species.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares species with one another and shows only that guava did well, not that the effect differed among species.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table shows sprouting rates, not how far seeds were carried.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In many rural parts of Central America, families have traditionally cooked over wood fires. In 2015, a program in a highland town in Guatemala began offering low-cost bottled-gas stoves. Economist Lucía Ajanel surveyed households about their main cooking fuel in 2015 and again in 2025. She found that gas had become much more common but had not come close to replacing wood.

data.title: Main Cooking Fuel of Households in a Guatemalan Highland Town

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Ajanel's finding?
