choices.A: The share of households cooking mainly with electricity rose from 4% to 6% over the decade.
choices.B: By 2025, more households cooked mainly with bottled gas than cooked mainly with wood.
choices.C: The share of households cooking mainly with wood dropped from 78% in 2015 to 51% in 2025.
choices.D: Gas became the main fuel for 41% of households, up from 12%, yet 51% still used mainly wood.

explanation.why: Ajanel's finding has two parts: gas became much more common, and wood remained widely used. The choice must show both. Gas rose from 12% to 41% of households, while wood was still the main fuel for 51% in 2025.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it concerns electricity, not gas or wood.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This misreads the graph: in 2025, 51% of households used mainly wood and 41% used mainly gas.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true and shows that wood remained common, but it does not show that gas in particular became more common.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows gas rising sharply (12% to 41%) and wood still the main fuel for about half of households (51%), covering both parts of the finding.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Crushed waste glass can replace some of the sand in concrete, which keeps glass out of landfills. Civil engineer Hana Novak made concrete samples in which 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, or 40% of the sand was replaced with glass and measured the pressure each sample could withstand after 28 days. She found that replacing up to 20% of the sand had little effect on strength, but that ______

data.title: Strength of Concrete Made with Crushed Glass in Place of Sand

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: the concrete with 10% glass was slightly stronger than the concrete with no glass.
choices.B: strength dropped to about 35 megapascals at 30% glass and to about 31 at 40%.
choices.C: the concrete with 40% glass cost less to produce than the concrete with no glass.
choices.D: strength rose steadily as more glass was added, reaching its highest point at 40%.

explanation.why: "But" signals a contrast with "little effect on strength" up to 20%, so the blank must describe a clear loss of strength at higher amounts of glass. Strength stays near 40 megapascals up to 20% glass, then falls to 35.1 at 30% and 30.6 at 40%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (40.8 versus 40.2), but it describes the range where glass had little effect and does not provide the contrast that "but" requires.
explanation.B: Correct. Beyond 20%, strength fell clearly, to about 35 and then about 31 megapascals, which contrasts with the small changes at lower amounts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The table gives no information about cost.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the trend: the 40% sample was the weakest in the table, not the strongest.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Since the late 2000s, vinyl records have made a comeback among music buyers. Marcus Bell, who owns an independent music store in Austin, Texas, tracked how many vinyl records and CDs his store sold each year from 2018 to 2024. Bell observes that the growth in vinyl sales at his store more than made up for the decline in CD sales: although CD sales fell every year, ______

data.title: Vinyl Records and CDs Sold Each Year at an Austin Music Store

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: most of the store's vinyl buyers had never bought CDs there.
choices.B: CD sales in 2024 were less than half of what they had been in 2018.
choices.C: vinyl sales first rose above CD sales in 2019.
choices.D: vinyl sales rose by about 4,100 while CD sales fell by about 2,500.

explanation.why: Bell's claim is that vinyl's gain was larger than the CDs' loss. From 2018 to 2024, vinyl sales rose from about 3,100 to about 7,200 (a gain of about 4,100), while CD sales fell from about 4,800 to about 2,300 (a loss of about 2,500).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The graph shows sales totals, not who bought the records.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (2,300 is less than half of 4,800), but it only describes the CD decline and does not compare it with the vinyl gain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This misreads the graph: in 2019 the store sold about 3,600 records and about 4,300 CDs; vinyl first passed CDs in 2020.
explanation.D: Correct. The vinyl gain of about 4,100 is larger than the CD loss of about 2,500, so vinyl more than made up for the decline.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sugarcane needs large amounts of water, and in the Indian state of Maharashtra many fields have traditionally been watered through furrows, shallow channels between rows. Agronomist Priya Deshmukh compared furrow watering with drip irrigation, which delivers water through tubes directly to plant roots, on test plots over one growing season. She concluded that drip irrigation did more than simply save water: it let farmers grow more cane while using less water.

data.title: Water Use and Sugarcane Yield under Three Irrigation Methods

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Deshmukh's conclusion?

choices.A: The alternate-row furrow plots yielded more cane per hectare than the drip plots did, 92 versus 118 metric tons.
choices.B: Drip plots used less water than every-row furrow plots yet grew more cane: 118 versus 99 metric tons per hectare.
choices.C: The drip plots used about 1,500 millimeters of water, roughly 750 millimeters less than the every-row furrow plots.
choices.D: The alternate-row furrow plots used 1,800 millimeters of water, less than the 2,250 used by every-row furrow plots.

explanation.why: Deshmukh claims that drip irrigation did more than save water: it gave a larger harvest with less water. Support must therefore show both less water and a higher yield for drip. Drip used 1,500 millimeters and yielded 118 metric tons per hectare; every-row furrows used 2,250 millimeters and yielded 99.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the table: 92 is less than 118, so the alternate-row plots yielded less cane than the drip plots.
explanation.B: Correct. Drip plots used less water and produced more cane than every-row furrow plots, which is exactly what Deshmukh concluded.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that drip saved water, which is the part Deshmukh says is not the whole story.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares two furrow methods and says nothing about drip irrigation.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Many libraries now lend e-books as well as printed books. Information scientist Wei Ling Tan studied loans at a public library in Singapore from 2021 to 2025 to see whether readers of different ages were moving to e-books at the same rate. She found that e-books made up a growing share of loans for both adults and teenagers but that the change was much faster among adults: ______

data.title: E-Books as a Share of All Loans at a Singapore Library

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: the e-book share of teen loans rose from 15% to 21%, a larger rise than among adults.
choices.B: teenagers borrowed more printed books than adults did in every year from 2021 to 2025.
choices.C: the adult e-book share rose 16 percentage points, while the teen share rose only 6.
choices.D: in 2025, e-books made up 38% of adult loans, the highest share shown in the table.

explanation.why: The claim compares how fast the e-book share grew for the two age groups, so the choice must compare the change in each column. The adult share went from 22% to 38% (16 points), and the teen share went from 15% to 21% (6 points).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The teen share did rise from 15% to 21%, but that 6-point rise is smaller than the adults' 16-point rise, not larger.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table shows only percentages, not the number of printed books each group borrowed.
explanation.C: Correct. The adult share grew by 16 points and the teen share by only 6, so the change was much faster among adults.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives one year's figure for adults only and does not compare how fast the two groups changed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Male fireflies flash light in patterns to attract mates, and like many insect behaviors, their flashing tends to speed up in warm weather. Entomologist Rachel Kim recorded how often males of two firefly species flashed at different air temperatures in a meadow in Tennessee. Kim noted that both species flashed faster as the temperature rose, but that one species was far more sensitive to temperature than the other: ______

data.title: Flash Rates of Male Fireflies of Two Species

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: species X went from about 6 to 14 flashes per minute, but species Y only from about 10 to 13.
choices.B: at 25°C, males of both species flashed about 12 times per minute.
choices.C: females of species Y answered fewer flashes as the air grew warmer.
choices.D: species Y went from about 6 to 14 flashes per minute, but species X only from about 10 to 13.

explanation.why: The claim is that one species' flash rate changed much more with temperature than the other's. Between 16°C and 28°C, species X more than doubled its rate (6 to 14), while species Y changed only a little (10 to 13).
explanation.A: Correct. Species X's rate rose by about 8 flashes per minute across the temperatures shown, compared with only about 3 for species Y, so X was far more sensitive.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes a single temperature and does not show how either species' rate changed as temperatures rose.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph shows only males' flash rates; it says nothing about how females responded.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This swaps the species: species X, not species Y, went from about 6 to about 14 flashes per minute.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A history museum in Vienna, Austria, offers its audio guide in five languages. Curator Lena Hofer recorded how many visitors rented the guide in each language during 2023. She was surprised to find that, although German is the main language of Austria, visitors chose English more often than any other language, German included: ______

data.title: Audio Guide Rentals by Language at a Vienna History Museum, 2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: French rentals exceeded English rentals by more than 6,000 during the year.
choices.B: English rentals reached 24,310, while German, the next most popular, had 18,450.
choices.C: Japanese rentals, at 3,940, were the lowest of the five languages offered.
choices.D: German rentals, at 18,450, were greater than Italian and French rentals combined.

explanation.why: The statement says English was chosen more often than any other language, including German. The choice must show English at the top and compare it with the next-highest language. The table shows 24,310 English rentals and 18,450 German rentals, with every other language far lower.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table shows French at 5,180 and English at 24,310, so French rentals were far lower, not higher.
explanation.B: Correct. English had 24,310 rentals, more than German's 18,450, and German was the second most popular language.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but which language was least popular does not show that English was the most popular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (18,450 is more than 6,920 + 5,180), but it compares German with other languages and says nothing about English.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Alappuzha, in the Indian state of Kerala, visitors rent houseboats to cruise the region's network of lagoons and canals. The monsoon, which brings heavy rain from June to September, has long been treated as the off-season. Tourism researcher Anjali Nair argues that the monsoon months now depend heavily on travelers from within India: when the rains come, she notes, bookings by international visitors fall much more sharply than bookings by domestic visitors.

data.title: Houseboat Bookings in Alappuzha, Kerala, by Month

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Nair's claim?

choices.A: In December, domestic bookings (about 3,600) were greater than international bookings (about 2,900) by roughly 700.
choices.B: From January to July, domestic bookings fell from about 3,200 to 2,400; international ones fell from 2,600 to 300.
choices.C: Domestic bookings were higher in July than in any other month shown in the graph.
choices.D: International bookings were higher in October, at about 1,500, than in April, at about 1,100.

explanation.why: Nair claims that international bookings drop much more sharply than domestic ones during the monsoon. Support must compare the change in both series between a dry-season month and a monsoon month. From January to July, domestic bookings fell by about a quarter, while international bookings fell by almost 90%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. December is not a monsoon month, so this comparison says nothing about how bookings change when the rains come.
explanation.B: Correct. Between January and July, international bookings fell far more steeply than domestic bookings, just as Nair claims.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Domestic bookings were lowest, not highest, in July (about 2,400).
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is accurate, but neither April nor October is a monsoon month, and the choice ignores domestic bookings.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Colombo, Sri Lanka, has tested lanes reserved for buses on some of its busiest roads during the morning rush hour. Supporters hoped the lanes would speed up bus trips, while critics feared they would slow everyone else by leaving fewer lanes for other traffic. Transport planner Dilini Perera compared average trip times on one route before and during a trial. She concluded that the lane greatly helped bus riders while making trips only a little slower for people traveling by car.

data.title: Average Morning Rush-Hour Trip Time on One Colombo Route (minutes)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Perera's conclusion?

choices.A: Car trips became faster during the trial, with their average time falling from 44 to 41 minutes.
choices.B: Bus trips fell from 52 to 38 minutes during the trial, while car trips rose only from 41 to 44 minutes.
choices.C: During the trial, an average bus trip (38 minutes) was shorter than an average car trip on the route (44 minutes).
choices.D: Three-wheeler trips changed by only one minute during the trial, from 33 minutes to 34 minutes.

explanation.why: Perera's conclusion has two parts: buses became much faster, and cars became only slightly slower. The choice must report the change for both buses and cars. Bus trips dropped by 14 minutes, while car trips grew by just 3 minutes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table shows car trips rising from 41 to 44 minutes, not falling.
explanation.B: Correct. Buses gained 14 minutes while cars lost only 3, which supports both parts of Perera's conclusion.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This compares buses and cars during the trial only; it does not show how much either changed, so it cannot show that cars were only slightly slowed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Three-wheelers are not part of Perera's conclusion, which concerns buses and cars.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Brick kilns in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley burn large amounts of coal. After many kilns were damaged in the 2015 earthquake, a number of owners rebuilt them with a zigzag design, in which hot air winds back and forth through the stacked bricks instead of flowing in a straight line, so that more of its heat reaches the bricks. Engineer Bikash Shrestha tracked kilns of both designs over five firing seasons and argues that the zigzag design cuts coal use by more than a quarter.

data.title: Coal Used per 1,000 Bricks in Kathmandu Valley Kilns

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Shrestha's argument?

choices.A: Zigzag kilns used more coal per 1,000 bricks in 2020 than they had in 2016, the first season shown.
choices.B: Coal use in traditional kilns fell slightly over the five seasons, from about 208 to about 196 kilograms per 1,000 bricks.
choices.C: In every season, zigzag kilns used about 140 kilograms of coal per 1,000 bricks, while traditional kilns used about 200.
choices.D: In 2018, traditional kilns used about 201 kilograms of coal for every 1,000 bricks they fired.

explanation.why: Shrestha's claim compares the two designs: zigzag kilns should use at least a quarter less coal than traditional ones. The choice must compare the two lines. Zigzag kilns used about 140 kilograms per 1,000 bricks while traditional kilns used about 200, a reduction of about 30%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The graph shows zigzag kilns' coal use falling, from about 146 to about 138 kilograms, not rising.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes only the traditional kilns, so it cannot show how the zigzag design compares.
explanation.C: Correct. About 140 is roughly 30% less than about 200, more than a quarter, and the gap held in every season.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This gives a single value for traditional kilns and makes no comparison with zigzag kilns.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many lakes in Bengaluru, India, were once choked with sewage and weeds. When one lake was restored, workers not only cleaned the water but also reshaped its edges into wide, shallow margins where the water is only a few centimeters deep. Ecologist Shreya Raghavan, who counted birds at the lake before and after the work, argues that the new margins mainly benefited wading birds such as herons and egrets, which feed by walking in shallow water. Other groups, she says, gained far less.

data.title: Average Bird Counts at a Bengaluru Lake Before and After Restoration

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Raghavan's argument?

choices.A: Dabbling ducks increased by a greater number of birds than wading birds did after the restoration.
choices.B: Before the restoration, diving birds were the most numerous of the four groups of birds counted.
choices.C: Every group of birds counted was more numerous after the restoration than it had been before.
choices.D: Wading birds more than tripled, from 34 to 112, while no other group of birds even doubled.

explanation.why: Raghavan argues that wading birds gained far more than other groups. The choice must compare wading birds' increase with the other groups' increases. Wading birds rose from 34 to 112, more than tripling, while diving birds, dabbling ducks, and kingfishers rose by about 50% or less.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Dabbling ducks rose by only 6 birds (40 to 46), while wading birds rose by 78.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (58 was the largest count before), but it describes only the starting numbers, not which group gained most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows that all groups gained, not that wading birds gained far more than the others.
explanation.D: Correct. Wading birds more than tripled, while the largest gain among the other groups was kingfishers' rise from 6 to 9.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Barn owls cough up pellets of fur and bone from the prey they swallow whole, so researchers can learn what the owls eat by examining the pellets. Ecologist Thomas Wright collected pellets from farms in eastern England, some of which leave strips of rough grass along the edges of their fields. Field voles, the owls' preferred prey, thrive in such grass. Wright argues that owls hunting on farms with grass strips catch more voles and therefore depend less on shrews, a less nourishing prey.

data.title: Prey Found in Barn Owl Pellets on Farms in Eastern England

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Wright's argument?

choices.A: At both kinds of farms, prey in the "Other" category made up less than a tenth of all prey items.
choices.B: At farms without grass strips, shrews and field voles made up nearly equal shares of the owls' prey.
choices.C: Wood mice made up a larger share of the owls' prey at farms with grass strips than they did at farms without them.
choices.D: Voles were 58% of prey at farms with grass strips but 34% at farms without, while shrews were 18% and 35%.

explanation.why: Wright's argument has two linked parts: owls at farms with grass strips eat more voles and fewer shrews. The choice must compare both prey types across the two kinds of farms. Voles rise from 34% to 58% and shrews drop from 35% to 18% where grass strips are present.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (8% and 9%), but other prey has nothing to do with the voles and shrews in Wright's argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (35% and 34%), but it describes only one kind of farm, so it cannot show the effect of grass strips.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Wood mice were 16% of prey at farms with grass strips and 22% at farms without, so the share was smaller, not larger.
explanation.D: Correct. Owls at farms with grass strips ate a much larger share of voles and a much smaller share of shrews, as Wright argues.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In Iceland, greenhouses heated with water from hot springs allow tomatoes to be grown year-round, but in the darkest months there may be only four or five hours of daylight. Many growers therefore add electric lamps above their plants. Horticulturist Ásta Gunnarsdóttir compared tomato yields in a greenhouse with lamps and one without. She argues that the lamps are most valuable in midwinter: their advantage, she says, shrinks as the days lengthen toward spring.

data.title: Monthly Tomato Yield in Two Icelandic Greenhouses (kilograms per square meter)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Gunnarsdóttir's argument?

choices.A: The lamps added 1.5 kilograms per square meter to the yield in December but only 0.6 kilograms in March.
choices.B: The yield of plants grown without lamps tripled between December and March, from 0.6 to 1.8 kilograms.
choices.C: In every month shown, plants grown without lamps produced more tomatoes than plants grown with them.
choices.D: Plants grown with lamps produced their highest monthly yield of the study, 2.4 kilograms per square meter, in March.

explanation.why: Gunnarsdóttir's argument concerns the size of the lamps' advantage, the gap between lit and unlit yields, and how that gap changes from winter to spring. The choice must compare the gap in a dark month with the gap in a brighter month. The gap was 1.5 kilograms (2.1 minus 0.6) in December and 0.6 kilograms (2.4 minus 1.8) in March.
explanation.A: Correct. The lamps' advantage fell from 1.5 kilograms in December to 0.6 kilograms in March, shrinking as the days lengthened.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the unlit plants and does not compare them with lit plants.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The table shows lit plants yielding more than unlit plants in every month, not less.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes only the lit plants; it does not show how the lamps' advantage over unlit plants changed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Maple syrup is made from sap collected through taps drilled into sugar maple trees in early spring. Forester Claire Dubois recorded daily temperatures and the sap collected per tap over six days in March at a stand of maples in Quebec, Canada. She argues that sap flows strongly only when a night below freezing is followed by a day above freezing; if either the night stays mild or the day stays frozen, she says, the flow almost stops.

data.title: Temperatures and Sap Collected over Six Days in March

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Dubois's argument?

choices.A: Day 5 had the coldest night of the six days, with the temperature falling to −8°C.
choices.B: Days 1, 2, and 6, each with a frozen night and a thawing day, gave about 2 liters per tap; days 3 and 5 gave almost none.
choices.C: The amount of sap collected per tap on day 4, when the night was barely below freezing, was less than half that on day 1.
choices.D: Day 3, which had the highest daytime temperature of the six days, also produced the most sap per tap.

explanation.why: Dubois claims that strong flow needs both a freezing night and a day above freezing, and that missing either condition stops the flow. Support must contrast days with both conditions against days lacking one of them. Days 1, 2, and 6 meet both conditions and yield about 2 liters, while day 3 (mild night) and day 5 (frozen day) yield 0.2 and 0.0 liters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives only the night temperature on one day and says nothing about sap flow.
explanation.B: Correct. Days with both conditions gave about 2 liters per tap, while days missing either condition gave almost nothing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (0.9 versus 1.9 liters), but day 4 had both a frozen night and a thawing day, so the comparison does not show what happens when a condition is missing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Day 3 produced only 0.2 liters, among the least sap of the six days, not the most.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Millions of birds die each year after flying into windows, because they see reflected sky and trees rather than glass. Glass printed with small dots can make windows visible to birds. To test different patterns, biologist Naomi Kessler fitted panels of several kinds to the walls of a research building and counted bird collisions over one autumn. She argues that the spacing of the dots matters a great deal: dots placed 5 centimeters apart, she concludes, prevent far more collisions than dots placed 10 centimeters apart.

data.title: Bird Collisions with Different Glass Panels over One Autumn

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Kessler's conclusion?

choices.A: Panels with dots 10 centimeters apart had fewer collisions than plain glass, 31 compared with 48.
choices.B: Panels with dots 10 centimeters apart had fewer collisions than panels with dots 5 centimeters apart.
choices.C: Panels with dots 5 centimeters apart had 7 collisions, compared with 31 for panels with dots 10 centimeters apart.
choices.D: Glass with a special coating that reflects ultraviolet light had fewer collisions than plain glass did, 26 versus 48.

explanation.why: Kessler's conclusion compares two dot spacings, 5 centimeters and 10 centimeters. The choice must compare those two bars. Panels with closer dots had 7 collisions, while panels with wider spacing had 31.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares one dot spacing with plain glass rather than comparing the two spacings.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The graph shows 31 collisions for 10-centimeter spacing and only 7 for 5-centimeter spacing, so this reverses the data.
explanation.C: Correct. Closer dots led to far fewer collisions (7) than wider dots (31), which is the comparison Kessler's conclusion makes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but the coating is not a dot pattern, so it says nothing about dot spacing.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Leeds, England, volunteers run a community fridge where anyone may leave spare food or take what they need. Organizer Priya Malhotra noticed that the fridge was often empty by Sunday afternoon and studied a month of records to find out why. She concluded that the problem was not unusually heavy use on weekends; rather, donations fell sharply on Saturdays and Sundays while the number of items people took stayed about the same as on weekdays.

data.title: Average Daily Use of a Leeds Community Fridge over One Month

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Malhotra's conclusion?

choices.A: Daily donations were higher from Monday through Thursday than on Friday, Saturday, or Sunday, the other days of the week.
choices.B: On Fridays, people took more items from the fridge (131) than donors left in it (122).
choices.C: Donations fell from about 130 a day on weekdays to about 60 on weekend days, while items taken stayed near 128.
choices.D: Far fewer items were taken from the fridge on Saturdays and Sundays than on weekdays.

explanation.why: Malhotra's conclusion has two parts: donations dropped on weekends, and the number of items taken did not change much. The choice must cover both columns. Donations fell from about 130 per day to 64 and 58, while items taken stayed between 127 and 131 throughout the week.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that donations were highest early in the week; it does not show that items taken stayed steady.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it concerns Friday, a weekday, and does not show what changed on weekends.
explanation.C: Correct. Weekend donations were about half the weekday level, while the number of items taken stayed nearly constant, which matches both parts of the conclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table shows 129 and 127 items taken on Saturday and Sunday, about the same as on weekdays.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Bat houses, wooden boxes mounted on poles or buildings, give roosting bats a place to shelter, and many guides advise painting them dark so that they absorb the sun's heat. Wildlife biologist Marcus Ortega checked hundreds of bat houses in the United States to see which were occupied. He argues that the best color depends on climate: dark paint helps where summers are cool, he says, but in hot regions light-colored houses are more likely to attract bats, perhaps because dark ones overheat.

data.title: Occupancy of Bat Houses by Paint Color and Climate

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Ortega's argument?

choices.A: Dark houses were occupied more often than light-colored houses in both the cool regions and the hot regions.
choices.B: In cool regions, 68% of dark houses were occupied, while only 31% of light-colored houses were occupied.
choices.C: Dark houses did better in cool regions (68% versus 31%), but light houses did better in hot ones (54% versus 22%).
choices.D: Light-colored houses in hot regions were occupied more often than light-colored houses in cool regions, 54% versus 31%.

explanation.why: Ortega argues that the better color switches with climate: dark wins in cool regions, light wins in hot regions. Support must show both halves of that pattern. In cool regions dark houses were occupied far more often, and in hot regions light houses were.
explanation.A: Incorrect. In hot regions, light-colored houses were occupied more often (54%) than dark ones (22%), so this misreads the graph.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it covers only cool regions, so it cannot show that the best color depends on climate.
explanation.C: Correct. The better color reverses between cool and hot regions, which is exactly Ortega's argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is accurate (54% versus 31%), but it compares one color across regions instead of comparing the two colors within each region.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many railway stations in Europe now have public pianos that anyone may play. Musicologist Elena Varga counted how many people played the pianos at two stations in Budapest, Hungary: one used mainly by commuters and one used mainly by tourists. She found that at the commuter station, people seem to avoid playing when the station is most crowded: ______

data.title: People Playing Public Pianos at Two Budapest Stations

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: at the commuter station, only 2 to 4 people played per hour at 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., but 11 to 14 at midday.
choices.B: at the commuter station, the piano was played by 9 people per hour at 7 p.m., more than at 5 p.m.
choices.C: at the tourist station, the number of players stayed between 9 and 12 per hour throughout the day.
choices.D: at the commuter station, more people played the piano at 5 p.m. than at any other time of the day.

explanation.why: The statement says commuter-station players avoid the busiest times. For a commuter station, the busiest times are the morning and evening rush hours, so the choice must compare those hours with quieter ones. The commuter line drops to 2 to 4 players at 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. and rises to 11 to 14 at midday.
explanation.A: Correct. Playing dropped sharply during the morning and evening rush hours and peaked in the quieter middle of the day.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but comparing two evening hours does not show that players avoid both rush hours compared with quieter times.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the tourist station, not the commuter station the statement is about.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows only 4 players at 5 p.m. at the commuter station, one of its lowest values, not its highest.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Brown trout, first brought to the Swat River in northern Pakistan in the early twentieth century, are still raised in hatcheries and released into the river for anglers. Fisheries officer Imran Yousafzai found that far fewer stocked trout survive their first year in the lower river than upstream. Some anglers blame fishing pressure, but Yousafzai argues that warm summer water is the main cause, since trout need cool water to thrive.

data.title: Stocked Brown Trout in Three Sections of the Swat River

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Yousafzai's argument?

choices.A: The lower section had the fewest angler-days (900) but the lowest survival (7%) and the warmest July water (22°C).
choices.B: The middle section had more than twice as many angler-days per year as the upper section, 2,900 compared with 1,200.
choices.C: The middle section had the most angler-days and also the lowest one-year survival of the three sections.
choices.D: The upper section, at the highest elevation, had the highest one-year survival of stocked trout, at 46%.

explanation.why: Yousafzai and the anglers disagree about whether water temperature or fishing pressure causes low survival. Support must separate the two. The lower section had the least fishing of all three sections but the worst survival and the warmest water, so fishing cannot explain its losses, while temperature can.
explanation.A: Correct. The section with the least fishing had the lowest survival and the warmest water, which points to temperature rather than fishing pressure.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it concerns only fishing pressure and says nothing about water temperature or survival.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The lowest survival (7%) was in the lower section, not the middle section, which had 29%.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but the upper section had both the coolest water and little fishing, so it does not show which factor matters.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On the tea estates of Sylhet, in northeastern Bangladesh, the first leaves of the season are plucked in March, and growth depends heavily on spring rain. Agronomist Nusrat Jahan compared monthly yields on one estate in a year with normal spring rain and in a year when the spring was unusually dry. She argues that the dry spring cut yields only early in the season: once the monsoon rains arrived in June, she says, the bushes caught up.

data.title: Monthly Tea Leaf Yield on a Sylhet Estate (kilograms per hectare)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Jahan's argument?

choices.A: The dry year trailed the normal year by 70 to 130 kilograms from March to May but nearly matched it in June and July.
choices.B: In both years, the estate's yield of tea leaves rose in every single month from March through July, peaking each year in July.
choices.C: In March, the yield in the dry year was higher than the yield in the year with normal spring rain.
choices.D: In the normal year, the yield in July was more than twice the yield in April.

explanation.why: Jahan's argument has two parts: the dry year fell behind early in the season, and it caught up after June. The choice must compare the two years in both periods. From March to May the dry year was 70 to 130 kilograms per hectare lower, but in June and July the two years were within about 10 kilograms of each other.
explanation.A: Correct. The dry year lagged well behind from March to May and then nearly matched the normal year in June and July.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but steady growth in both years does not show that the dry year fell behind and then caught up.
explanation.C: Incorrect. In March the dry year yielded 110 kilograms per hectare, less than the normal year's 180, not more.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (470 versus 320), but it describes only the normal year.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Kente, a cloth woven in narrow strips that are sewn together, has long been made in the town of Bonwire, Ghana, where weaving was traditionally done by men. In 2019, one Bonwire workshop began selling its cloth online. Historian Abena Owusu, who examined the workshop's records, argues that the rise in the number of young people training there since then has come almost entirely from women joining the craft.

data.title: Apprentices at a Kente Weaving Workshop in Bonwire, Ghana

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Owusu's argument?

choices.A: From 2016 to 2022, female apprentices rose from 2 to 14, while male apprentices stayed between 14 and 16.
choices.B: In 2022, the workshop had a total of 29 apprentices, more than in any other year shown in the table.
choices.C: The number of male apprentices at the workshop roughly doubled between 2016 and 2022.
choices.D: In every year shown in the table, the workshop had at least as many male apprentices as female apprentices.

explanation.why: Owusu argues that nearly all of the growth in apprentices came from women. The choice must show both that the number of women rose and that the number of men did not. Female apprentices grew from 2 to 14, while male apprentices barely changed.
explanation.A: Correct. Women accounted for the increase, rising from 2 to 14, while the number of men stayed nearly level.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (15 + 14 = 29), but a total does not show whether the growth came from women or men.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Male apprentices went from 14 to 15, so their number barely changed rather than doubling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it does not show which group's numbers grew over time.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Lisbon's Tram 28 winds through the old hilltop neighborhoods of the Portuguese capital and has become one of the city's most famous tourist attractions. As crowds of visitors packed its small cars, some residents complained that they could no longer ride the line at all. Urban planner Marta Sousa counted riders over several weeks and argues that residents have adapted rather than abandoned the tram: they now ride it mostly at the times of day when tourists are few.

data.title: Average Riders per Hour on Lisbon's Tram 28

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Sousa's argument?

choices.A: From 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., tourist riders outnumbered resident riders by more than three to one.
choices.B: Tourist ridership on the tram was highest from 1 to 3 p.m., at about 560 riders per hour.
choices.C: Residents' ridership was highest from 1 to 3 p.m., the same two-hour period in which tourist riders were most numerous.
choices.D: Residents' riding peaked from 7 to 9 a.m. and from 5 to 7 p.m., the two periods with the fewest tourist riders.

explanation.why: Sousa argues that residents ride mainly when tourists are few. Support must connect the times of residents' heaviest riding with the times of lightest tourist riding. Residents' two highest bars (about 410 and 380) fall in exactly the two periods with the fewest tourists (about 60 and 210).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (about 520 versus 150), but it shows only that residents are scarce at midday, not that they ride mainly at the quieter times.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only tourists and does not show when residents ride.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Residents' ridership was among its lowest from 1 to 3 p.m. (about 140), not its highest.
explanation.D: Correct. Residents rode most in the early morning and early evening, when tourist ridership was at its lowest, which matches Sousa's argument.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many people listen to podcasts while traveling to work, so it might seem that the longer a person's commute, the more podcasts that person will hear. Media researcher Inês Carvalho surveyed commuters in Porto, Portugal, and argues that this is true only for people who ride public transit. For drivers, she found, the length of the commute makes little difference, perhaps because drivers must keep their attention on the road and often switch to music or the radio instead.

data.title: Weekly Podcast Listening by Commute Length in Porto

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Carvalho's argument?

choices.A: Drivers' weekly listening rose more steeply as commutes grew longer than transit riders' weekly listening did.
choices.B: Drivers with the shortest commutes listened to more podcasts each week than transit riders with the shortest commutes did.
choices.C: Transit riders with commutes of more than 60 minutes listened to more podcasts than any other group surveyed.
choices.D: As commutes lengthened, transit riders' weekly listening rose from 40 to 230 minutes; drivers' stayed between 70 and 85.

explanation.why: Carvalho's argument contrasts two groups: listening rises with commute length for transit riders but not for drivers. Support must describe how both lines change as commutes get longer. The transit line climbs from 40 to 230 minutes, while the driver line stays nearly flat between 70 and 85.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The drivers' line is nearly flat, while the transit riders' line rises steeply, so this reverses the data.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (70 versus 40 minutes), but it compares only the shortest commutes and says nothing about how listening changes with commute length.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but a single high value does not show that drivers' listening stays flat while transit riders' rises.
explanation.D: Correct. Listening rose steadily with commute length for transit riders but barely changed for drivers, the contrast Carvalho describes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the ger districts of Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, many families live in gers, round felt-covered tents, and heat them with coal stoves through winters in which temperatures often fall below −30°C. Adding layers of felt to a ger's walls reduces the amount of coal needed. Energy engineer Bat-Erdene Ganbold measured daily coal use in gers with different numbers of felt layers. He argues that each extra layer saves less coal than the one before it, so that the first additional layer is by far the most worthwhile.

data.title: Coal Use in Ulaanbaatar Gers with Different Numbers of Felt Layers

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ganbold's argument?

choices.A: Gers with four layers of felt used the least coal of any group, about 20 kilograms per day.
choices.B: Adding a second layer cut daily coal use by 12 kilograms, but adding a third cut it by only 4 kilograms.
choices.C: Every additional layer of felt reduced the amount of coal that a ger used each day, from 38 kilograms down to 20.
choices.D: Adding a third layer of felt saved more coal per day than adding a second layer did.

explanation.why: Ganbold argues that the savings shrink with each added layer. Support must compare the savings from one added layer with the savings from the next. Going from one to two layers saved 12 kilograms (38 to 26), but going from two to three saved only 4 (26 to 22).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives only the lowest value and does not show how the savings change from layer to layer.
explanation.B: Correct. The saving fell from 12 kilograms for the second layer to 4 for the third, showing smaller savings with each layer.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that each layer helps, not that each layer helps less than the one before.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The third layer saved 4 kilograms, far less than the 12 kilograms saved by the second layer.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each winter, caves form inside the edges of Iceland's Vatnajökull glacier, and guided tours lead visitors through their blue ice. Because the caves are safe to enter only when the ice is cold and firm, the tour season depends on the weather. Guide Einar Pálsson compared monthly visitor numbers for two seasons eight years apart. He argues that warmer conditions have shortened the season at both its beginning and its end, even though demand in the middle of winter has held steady.

data.title: Monthly Visitors on Vatnajökull Ice Cave Tours

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Pálsson's argument?

choices.A: In both seasons shown, January had more visitors than December did.
choices.B: The total number of visitors over the whole season was greater in 2023–24 than in 2015–16.
choices.C: In the 2023–24 season, the number of visitors peaked in January, at about 16,000, slightly above the 2015–16 season's peak.
choices.D: Visitors fell from about 9,000 to 3,000 in November and 11,000 to 5,000 in March but held steady from December to February.

explanation.why: Pálsson's argument has two parts: the early and late months lost visitors, and the midwinter months did not. Support must compare the two seasons at the edges and in the middle. November and March dropped sharply between the seasons, while December through February stayed within about 1,000 visitors of the earlier season.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares two midwinter months and says nothing about the start or end of the season.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The 2023–24 season had fewer visitors in total (about 52,000) than the 2015–16 season (about 65,000).
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but a peak in one season does not show how the season's length changed.
explanation.D: Correct. The early and late months lost many visitors while the midwinter months held steady, matching both parts of the argument.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Cyclists in Dutch cities often leave their bicycles on sidewalks near train stations, blocking pedestrians. In early 2020, one midsize Dutch city opened a large new bicycle garage beside its main station. Critics predicted that the garage would simply attract more cyclists while doing little about the clutter outside. City official Sanne de Vries argues, however, that the garage mainly drew bicycles off the sidewalks: most of the bikes parked in the garage, she says, would otherwise have been left outside.

data.title: Average Daily Bicycles Parked near a Dutch City's Main Station

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support de Vries's argument?

choices.A: From 2019 to 2020, sidewalk parking fell by about 2,500 bikes, while garage parking rose by about 3,000.
choices.B: Garage parking rose by far more than sidewalk parking fell, so the total number of parked bikes nearly doubled.
choices.C: In every year shown, more bicycles were parked in station garages than on the sidewalks.
choices.D: The number of bicycles parked on sidewalks changed little between 2020 and 2021.

explanation.why: De Vries claims that the new garage mostly moved bikes from the sidewalks rather than adding new ones. Support must compare the drop in sidewalk parking with the rise in garage parking when the garage opened. Sidewalk parking fell by about 2,500 while garage parking rose by about 3,000, so most of the garage's gain matches the sidewalks' loss.
explanation.A: Correct. The fall in sidewalk parking nearly equals the rise in garage parking, so most bikes in the new garage would otherwise have been on the sidewalks.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The total rose only from about 12,100 to 12,600 bikes, not nearly doubling, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it was also true before the new garage opened, so it says nothing about where the garage's bikes came from.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the year after the opening and does not compare the sidewalk drop with the garage gain.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Seagrass meadows trap large amounts of carbon in the sediment beneath them, and studies have often found that meadows in deeper water store less carbon than shallow ones. Marine ecologist Ana Ribeiro, who sampled five meadows off the coast of Portugal, argues that depth itself is not the cause. Because less light reaches deeper water, she points out, seagrass there usually grows more sparsely, and it is the density of the shoots, she contends, rather than the depth of the water, that determines how much carbon a meadow stores.

data.title: Five Seagrass Meadows off the Coast of Portugal

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ribeiro's argument?

choices.A: Site 4, at 6 meters, stored more carbon than the shallower Sites 2 and 3 and had denser shoots than either.
choices.B: Stored carbon fell with every increase in depth, from the shallowest site to the deepest one.
choices.C: Site 5, the deepest of the five sites, stored the least carbon, about 58 tonnes per hectare.
choices.D: Site 1, the shallowest of the five sites, had both the densest growth of shoots and the most carbon stored in its sediment.

explanation.why: Ribeiro must show that shoot density, not depth, controls carbon storage. In most sites, depth and density change together, so they cannot be told apart. Site 4 breaks the pattern: it is deeper than Sites 2 and 3 but has denser shoots, and it stores more carbon than both, just as Ribeiro's argument predicts.
explanation.A: Correct. Site 4 is deeper but denser than Sites 2 and 3 and stores more carbon, so density rather than depth tracks carbon storage.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Carbon did not fall at every step: Site 4 (6 meters) stored more than Sites 2 and 3, which are shallower.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Site 5 is both the deepest and the sparsest, so this fits either explanation equally well.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Site 1 is both the shallowest and the densest, so its high carbon fits the depth explanation as well as Ribeiro's; it cannot tell them apart.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Since the 1990s, Welsh has been a required subject in schools across Wales, and in many areas pupils are taught largely through Welsh. Sociolinguist Carys Llywelyn surveyed residents of a town in Gwynedd, a county in northwest Wales where the language is widely spoken. She argues that the schools have been very successful at teaching young people to speak Welsh but have done much less to make it a language used at home, and that the gap between the two is clearest among the town's youngest residents.

data.title: Welsh Speaking and Home Use by Age in a Gwynedd Town

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Llywelyn's argument?

choices.A: Daily home use of Welsh was higher among 5- to 15-year-olds than among any older age group in the town.
choices.B: Residents aged 65 and older were the most likely of any age group to speak Welsh daily at home.
choices.C: Among 5- to 15-year-olds, 82% could speak Welsh but only 31% used it daily at home, the widest gap of any age group.
choices.D: The 5- to 15-year-olds had a higher share of residents able to speak Welsh than any other age group surveyed in the town.

explanation.why: Llywelyn's argument is about the gap between being able to speak Welsh and using it at home, and she says that gap is widest for the youngest group. The choice must give both figures for the youngest group and compare its gap with the others. The gap is 51 points for ages 5 to 15, compared with 33, 22, 19, and 17 points for the older groups.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only 31% of 5- to 15-year-olds used Welsh daily at home, the second-lowest share; the 30–49, 50–64, and 65+ groups were all higher.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (47%), but it describes home use among the oldest residents rather than the gap among the youngest.
explanation.C: Correct. The youngest group shows a 51-point gap between ability and home use, wider than any other group's gap.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This shows the schools' success in teaching Welsh, but it leaves out home use, so it says nothing about the gap.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, Missouri, was the largest city in North America north of Mexico around 1100 CE, home to thousands of people who built enormous earthen mounds. By 1350 it had been largely abandoned. Archaeologist Daniel Whitehorse, who dated houses excavated in both the city's central precinct and its outlying neighborhoods, argues that the decline did not begin everywhere at once: people began leaving the outlying neighborhoods while the central precinct was still growing.

data.title: Houses Dated to Each Period at Cahokia (CE)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Whitehorse's argument?

choices.A: The outlying neighborhoods lost half their houses between 1050–1100 and 1150–1200, falling from 520 to 260.
choices.B: From 1050–1100 to 1100–1150, outlying houses fell from 520 to 410, while central houses rose from 340 to 360.
choices.C: The outlying neighborhoods had more houses than the central precinct in each of the first three periods shown.
choices.D: The number of houses in the central precinct began to fall before the number in the outlying neighborhoods did.

explanation.why: The argument has two parts that must hold at the same time: the outlying neighborhoods were losing houses while the central precinct was still gaining them. The choice must compare both areas over the same span. From 1050–1100 to 1100–1150, outlying houses dropped from 520 to 410 while central houses rose from 340 to 360.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the outlying neighborhoods; over that same span the central precinct also shrank slightly (340 to 330), so it does not show the center still growing.
explanation.B: Correct. During the same period, the outlying neighborhoods declined while the central precinct grew, exactly as Whitehorse argues.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares the sizes of the two areas, not when each began to decline.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The central precinct kept growing until 1100–1150, after the outlying neighborhoods had already begun to decline, so this reverses the order.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the early nineteenth century, steamboats turned towns at landings along the Mississippi and Ohio Rivers into busy centers of trade. Historian Ruth Callahan compared the average populations of eight river-landing towns and eight inland towns in one Midwestern region. She acknowledges that the river towns grew faster for decades, but she argues that once railroads reached the region's inland towns in the early 1850s, the inland towns became the faster-growing group.

data.title: Average Population of River-Landing and Inland Towns in One Midwestern Region

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Callahan's argument?

choices.A: From 1850 to 1870, inland towns added about 3,100 residents, more than twice the river towns' gain of about 1,300.
choices.B: In 1870, the average river-landing town was still larger than the average inland town, about 6,100 residents to 5,200.
choices.C: From 1830 to 1850, river towns added about 3,400 residents, while inland towns added only about 1,300.
choices.D: From 1850 to 1870, the river towns added more residents, on average, than the inland towns did.

explanation.why: Callahan's claim concerns growth after the railroads arrived in the early 1850s: inland towns should then grow faster than river towns. The choice must compare the two groups' growth after 1850. Inland towns rose from about 2,100 to 5,200 (about 3,100 people), while river towns rose from about 4,800 to 6,100 (about 1,300).
explanation.A: Correct. After 1850, inland towns grew by more than twice as many people as river towns did, which shows they had become the faster-growing group.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares the towns' sizes in one year, not their growth; a larger town can still be growing more slowly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the years before the railroads arrived, which Callahan already grants were the river towns' advantage.
explanation.D: Incorrect. From 1850 to 1870, river towns gained about 1,300 residents and inland towns about 3,100, so this reverses the data.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the ancient Mediterranean, wine traveled in amphorae, tall clay jars with two handles. Potters on the island of Rhodes and in the city of Knidos often stamped the handles with the names of officials who held office for a single year, which allows archaeologists to date the handles closely. Archaeologist Eleni Stavrou studied stamped handles excavated in Alexandria, Egypt, and argues that during the second century BCE, wine from Knidos increasingly took the place of Rhodian wine in the city's markets.

data.title: Stamped Amphora Handles Found in Alexandria, by Period

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Stavrou's argument?

choices.A: The number of Rhodian handles fell by 2,400 between the periods 180–150 BCE and 120–90 BCE.
choices.B: Knidian wine was sold at a lower price than Rhodian wine, which made it more attractive to buyers in Alexandria.
choices.C: As Rhodian handles fell from 3,100 to 700 after 180–150 BCE, Knidian handles rose from 650 to 1,650.
choices.D: Rhodian handles outnumbered Knidian handles in every period shown except the last, 120–90 BCE.

explanation.why: Stavrou's claim is that Knidian wine replaced Rhodian wine, which requires two trends at once: Rhodian handles falling and Knidian handles rising over the same periods. Only a choice reporting both trends together supports a replacement. From 180–150 BCE to 120–90 BCE, Rhodian handles dropped from 3,100 to 700 while Knidian handles rose from 650 to 1,650.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a fall in Rhodian handles alone could mean that Alexandria simply imported less wine; it does not show Knidian wine taking its place.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table gives only numbers of handles, not prices, so it cannot support this statement.
explanation.C: Correct. Rhodian handles declined while Knidian handles increased over the same periods, the pattern a replacement would produce.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares the two kinds of handles period by period without showing that one rose as the other fell.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Bakers describe a dough's hydration as the weight of its water compared with the weight of its flour, so a dough with 75% hydration contains 75 grams of water for every 100 grams of flour. Wetter doughs often rise higher in the oven, but only up to a point, beyond which they spread instead. Baker and food scientist Henrik Dahl argues that this point depends on the flour: bread flour, which contains more of the proteins that form gluten, can hold more water before it stops rising than all-purpose flour can.

data.title: Height of Sourdough Loaves at Different Dough Hydrations

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Dahl's argument?

choices.A: At every hydration level tested, the bread-flour loaves were taller than the all-purpose loaves.
choices.B: At 85% hydration, loaves made with either kind of flour were shorter than at 80% hydration.
choices.C: Bread-flour loaves were tallest at 80% hydration, while all-purpose loaves were tallest at 75%.
choices.D: All-purpose loaves reached their greatest height at a higher hydration than bread-flour loaves did.

explanation.why: Dahl claims that the hydration at which loaves stop rising higher is greater for bread flour than for all-purpose flour. The choice must compare where each flour's loaves reach their peak height. Bread-flour loaves peak at 80% (10.1 centimeters), while all-purpose loaves peak at 75% (8.9 centimeters).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that bread flour makes taller loaves, not that it reaches its peak at a higher hydration.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the drop after 80% and does not show that the two flours peak at different hydrations.
explanation.C: Correct. Bread flour kept rising up to 80% hydration, while all-purpose flour peaked at 75%, so bread flour can hold more water before it stops rising.
explanation.D: Incorrect. All-purpose loaves peaked at 75% and bread-flour loaves at 80%, so this reverses the data.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Arctic char, cold-water relatives of salmon, live in many lakes in Greenland. In some lakes the char stay small, feeding mostly on insect larvae and tiny crustaceans, while in others a few individuals grow very large. Many ecologists have assumed that lake size explains the difference, since bigger lakes offer more food of every kind. Freshwater ecologist Aaju Lynge, who netted fish in five lakes, argues instead that what allows char to grow large is the presence of sticklebacks, small fish that large char can eat.

data.title: Largest Arctic Char Caught in Five Greenland Lakes

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Lynge's argument?

choices.A: Lake 2 had larger char than Lake 1, even though the two lakes were almost exactly the same size.
choices.B: Lake 4, the smallest of the five lakes and one without sticklebacks, also had the smallest char, at 24 centimeters.
choices.C: Lake 3, the largest of the five lakes sampled, also had the largest char, at 71 centimeters.
choices.D: Lakes 1 and 2 were nearly equal in size, but their largest char were 58 cm with sticklebacks and 31 cm without them.

explanation.why: Lynge must show that sticklebacks matter apart from lake size. Because larger lakes in the table also tend to have sticklebacks, the best evidence compares lakes of the same size that differ only in whether sticklebacks are present. Lakes 1 and 2 are almost identical in size, yet the lake with sticklebacks has char nearly twice as long.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The largest char in Lake 2 (31 cm) were smaller than those in Lake 1 (58 cm), not larger.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Lake 4 is small and lacks sticklebacks, so its small char fit either explanation equally well.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Lake 3 is large and has sticklebacks, so its big char fit the lake-size explanation as well as Lynge's.
explanation.D: Correct. With lake size held nearly equal, only the lake with sticklebacks produced large char, which points to sticklebacks rather than size.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Some theaters set aside certain performances as pay-what-you-can nights, when audience members choose their own ticket price. Critics have suggested that such nights mostly give discounts to older regular theatergoers, many of whom live on fixed incomes. Theater manager Olivia Chen, who surveyed audiences at a theater in Vancouver, Canada, argues that the nights do something different: compared with regular-price performances, she says, they draw a much younger audience.

data.title: Age of Audience Members at a Vancouver Theater

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Chen's argument?

choices.A: People aged 65 and older made up a larger share of pay-what-you-can audiences than of regular-price audiences.
choices.B: Under-30s were 14% of regular-price audiences but 38% of pay-what-you-can ones; people 65 and older were 26% and 11%.
choices.C: On pay-what-you-can nights, people under 30 made up a larger share of the audience than people aged 30 to 49 did, 38% to 33%.
choices.D: On regular-price nights, people aged 50 to 64 made up a larger share of the audience than any other age group did.

explanation.why: Chen's claim is comparative: pay-what-you-can audiences are much younger than regular-price audiences. The choice must compare the age makeup of the two kinds of performances. The youngest group's share nearly triples and the oldest group's share falls by more than half on pay-what-you-can nights.
explanation.A: Incorrect. People 65 and older made up 11% of pay-what-you-can audiences and 26% of regular-price audiences, so their share was smaller, not larger.
explanation.B: Correct. Compared with regular-price nights, pay-what-you-can nights had a much larger share of young people and a much smaller share of older people.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (38% versus 33%), but it describes only pay-what-you-can nights; without a comparison to regular-price nights it cannot show that those nights draw a younger crowd.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (31%), but it describes only regular-price nights.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Japanese has absorbed thousands of words from English, usually written in the katakana script, such as konpyūtā ("computer"). Linguist Haruto Sato counted English loanwords in articles from a major Tokyo newspaper over five decades. He acknowledges that some kinds of coverage have always used more loanwords than others, but he argues that the growth in loanwords since 1990 has come overwhelmingly from technology and business reporting, while other kinds of coverage have changed little.

data.title: English Loanwords in a Tokyo Newspaper by Type of Coverage

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Sato's argument?

choices.A: From 1990 to 2020, loanwords in culture coverage increased more than loanwords in technology and business coverage did.
choices.B: From 1990 to 2020, technology and business coverage gained 140 loanwords per 10,000 words; culture gained 11 and politics 12.
choices.C: In 2020, technology and business coverage used more English loanwords per 10,000 words than either of the other two kinds of coverage.
choices.D: In 1970, culture coverage used more English loanwords per 10,000 words than technology and business coverage did.

explanation.why: Sato's argument concerns growth since 1990, not the level of loanwords in any single year. The choice must compare how much each kind of coverage changed from 1990 to 2020. Technology and business rose from 110 to 250 (a gain of 140), while culture rose from 75 to 86 and politics from 29 to 41.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Culture coverage gained only 11 loanwords per 10,000 words, far fewer than the 140 gained in technology and business coverage.
explanation.B: Correct. Almost all of the growth since 1990 occurred in technology and business coverage, while the other two lines barely rose.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives only the 2020 levels; it does not show that the increase since 1990 came from technology and business coverage.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (60 versus 45), but it describes a single year before 1990 and says nothing about growth since then.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In many cities, wealthier neighborhoods are cooler on summer afternoons than poorer ones. Climate researcher Jamal Bennett measured afternoon surface temperatures in five neighborhoods of a large city in the United States. He argues that income itself is not what keeps a neighborhood cool. Instead, he contends, tree canopy, the share of the ground shaded by trees, explains the difference, and wealthier neighborhoods tend to be cooler mainly because they usually have more trees.

data.title: Income, Tree Canopy, and Summer Temperature in Five Neighborhoods

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Bennett's argument?

choices.A: Neighborhood C, with under half of B's median income, had 39% tree canopy and was nearly 7°C cooler than B.
choices.B: Neighborhood A had both the highest median household income and the lowest afternoon surface temperature of the five.
choices.C: Neighborhood C was hotter than Neighborhood B, even though C had far more tree canopy than B did.
choices.D: Neighborhood D had both the lowest median household income and the highest afternoon surface temperature.

explanation.why: Bennett must separate canopy from income, since in most neighborhoods the two go together. The best evidence is a neighborhood where they point in opposite directions. Neighborhood C has much lower income than B but far more canopy, and it is the cooler of the two (31.8°C versus 38.6°C), so canopy, not income, matches temperature.
explanation.A: Correct. C is poorer than B but shadier, and it is much cooler, which shows canopy rather than income tracking temperature.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Neighborhood A is high in both income and canopy, so its low temperature fits an income explanation just as well as Bennett's.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Neighborhood C (31.8°C) was much cooler than Neighborhood B (38.6°C), not hotter.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Neighborhood D is low in both income and canopy, so its high temperature cannot show which factor matters.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hummingbirds feed on flower nectar, which is mostly sugar dissolved in water. To learn which sugar mixture ruby-throated hummingbirds prefer, biologist Nadia Kowalczyk hung four feeders in a garden in Ontario, Canada, each filled with a different mixture, and counted the birds' visits over one week. The feeder that received the most visits held a mixture that was ______

data.title: Hummingbird Visits to Four Feeders over One Week

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 30 percent sugar, which received 211 visits.
choices.B: 20 percent sugar, which received 211 visits.
choices.C: taken from wild flowers, which received the most visits.
choices.D: 10 percent sugar, which received 84 visits.

explanation.why: The statement asks which mixture was in the feeder with the most visits, so find the largest number in the "Visits" column. That number is 211, in the 20% row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The 30% feeder received 167 visits; the 211 visits belong to the 20% feeder, so this misreads the table.
explanation.B: Correct. The 20% feeder received 211 visits, the largest number in the "Visits" column.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The table lists only sugar mixtures in feeders; it gives no data about wild flower nectar.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The 10% feeder received the fewest visits, not the most.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2019, education officials in Bahawalpur District, Pakistan, began fitting rooftop solar panels to government schools that often lost electricity during the day. Engineer Faisal Qureshi recorded how many schools in the district had panels at the end of each year. According to the graph, from 2019 to 2022 the number of schools with solar panels ______

data.title: Schools with Rooftop Solar Panels in Bahawalpur District

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: fell every year, from 245 schools to 35 schools.
choices.B: rose every year, from 35 schools to 245 schools.
choices.C: stayed at about 90 schools in every year.
choices.D: rose fastest among schools for girls.

explanation.why: The statement describes how the number of schools changed from 2019 to 2022, so read the bars from left to right. They rise from 35 in 2019 to 90, then 160, then 245 in 2022.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the graph: 35 schools is the 2019 value and 245 is the 2022 value.
explanation.B: Correct. The bars grow taller each year: 35, 90, 160 and 245 schools.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only 2020 shows about 90 schools; the other years show 35, 160 and 245.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows only the total number of schools; it does not separate schools for girls and boys.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In June 2024, a small community theater in Buenos Aires, Argentina, began offering half-price tickets to students. Theater manager Julieta Ramos wanted to know whether audiences grew afterward, so she recorded the number of tickets sold each month from March to August. According to the graph, monthly ticket sales first rose above 1,500 in ______

data.title: Tickets Sold per Month at a Community Theater in Buenos Aires, 2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: March, when 1,150 tickets were sold.
choices.B: May, when 1,180 tickets were sold.
choices.C: August, when 1,910 tickets were sold.
choices.D: June, when 1,640 tickets were sold.

explanation.why: The statement asks for the first month in which sales were above 1,500, so read the line from left to right and stop at the first point higher than 1,500. March, April and May are all under 1,200; June is 1,640.
explanation.A: Incorrect. 1,150 is below 1,500, so sales had not yet passed that level in March.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 1,180 is below 1,500; May was the last month before sales rose above that level.
explanation.C: Incorrect. August's sales were above 1,500, but they had already passed that level in June and July, so August was not the first such month.
explanation.D: Correct. March, April and May are all below 1,500, and June, at 1,640, is the first month above it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Earthworms loosen and mix soil, so park managers often want to know which ground covers suit them. Soil scientist Grace Liu marked out plots of 1 square meter under four different covers in a park in Melbourne, Australia, and counted the earthworms she dug up in each plot. She found the fewest earthworms under ______

data.title: Earthworms Found in 1-Square-Meter Plots under Four Ground Covers

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: bare soil, where only 9 earthworms were counted.
choices.B: wood chips, where 52 earthworms were counted.
choices.C: leaf litter, where 64 earthworms were counted.
choices.D: grass lawn, where soil moisture was the lowest.

explanation.why: The statement is about the fewest earthworms, so look for the smallest number in the "Earthworms counted" column. That number is 9, in the bare soil row.
explanation.A: Correct. Bare soil had 9 earthworms, the smallest number in the "Earthworms counted" column.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 52 earthworms is more than the counts for the grass lawn and bare soil, so wood chips did not have the fewest.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Leaf litter had the most earthworms, not the fewest.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Bare soil, at 14%, had the lowest soil moisture, and the grass lawn did not have the fewest earthworms.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Shea butter, made from the nuts of the shea tree, is sold around the world for use in foods and skin creams. In northern Ghana, much of it is produced by women who work together in cooperatives. Economist Abena Owusu followed one cooperative in Tamale from 2019 to 2023. According to the graph, the cooperative's membership in 2023 was twice its membership in ______

data.title: Members of a Shea Butter Cooperative in Tamale, Ghana

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2019, when the cooperative had 120 members.
choices.B: 2021, when the cooperative had 190 members.
choices.C: 2018, before the study began.
choices.D: 2020, when the cooperative had 145 members.

explanation.why: The 2023 bar shows 240 members, so the statement needs the year with half that number, 120. The 2019 bar shows 120 members.
explanation.A: Correct. The cooperative had 240 members in 2023, and 240 is twice 120, the 2019 total.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Twice 190 is 380, far more than the 240 members in 2023.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph begins in 2019, so it gives no membership figure for 2018.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Twice 145 is 290, not 240, so 2023's membership was less than twice the 2020 figure.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mangoes picked while still green ripen in storage, and the temperature of the storeroom affects how quickly they do so. Food scientist Hina Baloch stored four batches of Chaunsa mangoes from Multan, Pakistan, at different temperatures and recorded how many days each batch took to ripen. The batch that ripened the fastest was stored at ______

data.title: Ripening of Chaunsa Mangoes at Four Storage Temperatures (40 fruits per batch)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 30°C, where the mangoes ripened in 5 days.
choices.B: 15°C, where the fewest fruits spoiled.
choices.C: 15°C, where the mangoes took 14 days to ripen.
choices.D: 25°C, where the mangoes ripened in 4 days.

explanation.why: "Ripened the fastest" means the fewest days to ripen, so look for the smallest number in the "Days to ripen" column. That number is 5, in the 30°C row.
explanation.A: Correct. At 30°C the mangoes took 5 days, the smallest number in the "Days to ripen" column.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It is true that only 1 fruit spoiled at 15°C, but the statement is about ripening speed, and that batch took the longest to ripen.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 14 days is the longest ripening time in the table, so this batch ripened the slowest, not the fastest.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The 25°C batch ripened in 6 days; the 4 is the number of fruits that spoiled, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Since 2017, a children's magazine in Wellington, New Zealand, has held a yearly poetry contest for students aged 8 to 14. In 2020, the contest began accepting poems written in te reo Māori as well as in English. According to the graph, the number of entries rose the most from one year to the next between ______

data.title: Entries in a Children's Poetry Contest, 2017–2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2022 and 2023, when entries rose from 640 to 705.
choices.B: 2020 and 2021, when entries rose from 410 to 590.
choices.C: 2017 and 2018, when entries rose from 340 to 365.
choices.D: 2019 and 2020, when entries rose from 352 to 410.
