explanation.why: The statement asks where the number of entries rose by the largest amount in a single year. Subtract each pair of neighboring years: the largest jump is from 410 in 2020 to 590 in 2021, a rise of 180.
explanation.A: Incorrect. 2023 had the most entries in total, but the rise from 2022 was only 65.
explanation.B: Correct. Entries rose by 180 from 2020 to 2021, more than in any other one-year step.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This rise was only 25 entries, one of the smallest on the graph.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 2020 is the year the rule changed, but entries rose by only 58 from 2019 to 2020, far less than the next year's rise.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many insects gather around white streetlights at night, and some bats hunt them there. To see whether the color of the light matters, ecologist Pieter de Vries placed bat detectors under streetlights of four colors along a country road in the Netherlands and counted bat calls each night. The detectors recorded the most bat calls under ______

data.title: Average Bat Calls Recorded per Night under Streetlights of Four Colors

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: green lights, with about 410 calls per night.
choices.B: red lights, with about 120 calls per night.
choices.C: amber lights, with about 190 calls per night.
choices.D: white lights, with about 410 calls per night.

explanation.why: The statement asks which light color had the most bat calls, so find the tallest bar. The white bar, at 412 calls per night, is taller than the green (365), amber (188) and red (121) bars.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Green lights recorded about 365 calls per night; the bar near 410 is the white one, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Red lights recorded the fewest calls, not the most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Amber lights recorded fewer calls than white or green lights.
explanation.D: Correct. The white bar is the tallest, at 412 calls per night.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Early in 2022, a town in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco gave every household free low-flow taps, which release less water per minute. Water engineer Youssef Amrani compared average household water use in the summer of 2021, before the program, with use in the summer of 2022. Of the three months shown, average daily water use fell the most in ______

data.title: Average Water Use per Household (liters per day)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: September, when it dropped by more than 100 liters.
choices.B: June, when it dropped from 412 to 351 liters.
choices.C: July, when it dropped from 455 to 372 liters.
choices.D: August, when it dropped from 470 to 401 liters.

explanation.why: To find where use fell the most, subtract the 2022 value from the 2021 value for each month: June 61, July 83 and August 69 liters. The largest drop is in July.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table gives no data for September.
explanation.B: Incorrect. June's drop of 61 liters was the smallest of the three months.
explanation.C: Correct. Use fell by 83 liters in July, more than in June (61 liters) or August (69 liters).
explanation.D: Incorrect. August had the highest use in both years, but it fell by only 69 liters, less than July's 83.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth. With very little water vapor in the air to hold heat, the desert cools quickly once the sun goes down. Geographer Camila Rojas recorded the air temperature every three hours over one day in March. The lowest temperature of the day occurred at ______

data.title: Air Temperature over One Day in the Atacama Desert

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 6 a.m., when it was about 4°C.
choices.B: 3 p.m., when it was about 27°C.
choices.C: 12 a.m., when it fell below 0°C.
choices.D: 9 p.m., soon after sunset, when it was about 12°C.

explanation.why: The statement asks when the temperature was lowest, so find the lowest point on the line. That point is at 6 a.m., at about 4°C.
explanation.A: Correct. The line reaches its lowest point, about 4°C, at 6 a.m.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 3 p.m. was the warmest time of the day, not the coldest.
explanation.C: Incorrect. At 12 a.m. the temperature was about 9°C, and no point on the graph is below 0°C.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The air was cooling at 9 p.m., but it kept falling for several more hours and was colder at 12 a.m., 3 a.m. and 6 a.m.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A music school in Kolkata, India, lends instruments to students who cannot afford their own. At the end of 2023, administrator Ananya Ghosh counted how many times each instrument had been borrowed that year. According to the graph, the instrument borrowed most often was the ______

data.title: Times Each Instrument Was Borrowed, 2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: harmonium, which was borrowed 112 times.
choices.B: tabla, which was borrowed 88 times.
choices.C: sarod, which was borrowed 23 times.
choices.D: sitar, which costs the most to buy.

explanation.why: To find the instrument borrowed most often, look for the tallest bar. The harmonium bar, at 112, is taller than every other bar.
explanation.A: Correct. The harmonium bar is the tallest, at 112.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The tabla was borrowed often, but 88 is less than the harmonium's 112.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sarod was borrowed the fewest times, not the most.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows how often instruments were borrowed, not what they cost.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For a school science fair in Toronto, Canada, Mei Lin Zhou folded paper airplanes in four designs and threw each one ten times from the same spot. She recorded how far each design flew and how long it stayed in the air, on average. According to her results, the design that flew the farthest was the ______

data.title: Average Flight of Four Paper Airplane Designs (10 throws each)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: dart, which flew 9.4 meters on average.
choices.B: glider, which stayed in the air for 3.2 seconds.
choices.C: square-wing, which flew 5.6 meters on average.
choices.D: delta, which flew 9.4 meters on average.

explanation.why: "Flew the farthest" refers to distance, so look for the largest number in the "Distance (meters)" column. That number is 9.4, in the dart row.
explanation.A: Correct. 9.4 meters is the largest number in the "Distance" column.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The glider stayed up the longest, but the statement is about distance, and the glider flew only 7.1 meters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 5.6 meters is the shortest distance in the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The delta flew 8.2 meters; 9.4 meters belongs to the dart, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Officials in a neighborhood of Valparaíso, Chile, wanted to know which materials residents recycled most. For one year, environmental planner Diego Fuentes weighed the material collected from recycling bins and from regular trash bins. According to the table, the material collected for recycling in the largest amount was ______

data.title: Waste Collected in One Year in a Valparaíso Neighborhood (metric tons)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: paper and cardboard, with 340 metric tons.
choices.B: food scraps, with 500 metric tons.
choices.C: metal cans, with 45 metric tons.
choices.D: plastic, with 410 metric tons.

explanation.why: The statement is about material collected for recycling, so use only the "Collected for recycling" column and find its largest value. That value is 340 metric tons, for paper and cardboard.
explanation.A: Correct. 340 metric tons is the largest number in the "Collected for recycling" column.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Food scraps do not appear in the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 45 metric tons is the smallest amount collected for recycling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 410 metric tons of plastic was thrown away as trash; only 90 metric tons was collected for recycling, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sunflowers can grow remarkably quickly in early summer. Working at a field station in central Ukraine, agronomist Olena Kovalenko measured the height of one sunflower plant at the end of each week after it sprouted. According to the graph, by the end of week 6 the plant had reached a height of ______

data.title: Height of a Sunflower Plant in the Eight Weeks after Sprouting

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: about 120 centimeters.
choices.B: about 80 centimeters.
choices.C: about 170 centimeters.
choices.D: about 45 centimeters.

explanation.why: Find week 6 on the horizontal axis and read the height of that point. It is at about 120 centimeters, between the week 5 value of 80 and the week 7 value of 155.
explanation.A: Correct. The point for week 6 is at about 120 centimeters.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 80 centimeters is the plant's height at week 5, one week earlier.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 170 centimeters is the plant's height at week 8, the end of the study, not at week 6.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 45 centimeters is the plant's height at week 4, not week 6.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ethio-jazz, a style that blends Ethiopian musical scales with jazz and funk, flourished in Addis Ababa in the late 1960s and early 1970s. An archive in the city has been copying old reel-to-reel tapes of the music into digital files. Archivist Selam Tesfaye recorded how many recordings were copied each year. The archive copied the most recordings in ______

data.title: Recordings Copied into Digital Files by an Addis Ababa Archive

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2022, when 210 recordings were copied.
choices.B: 2020, when the fewest tapes needed repair.
choices.C: 2019, when 140 recordings were copied.
choices.D: 2021, when 210 recordings were copied.

explanation.why: The statement asks when the archive copied the most recordings, so look for the largest number in the "Recordings copied" column. That number is 210, in the 2021 row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The archive copied 185 recordings in 2022; the 210 belongs to 2021, so this misreads the table.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It is true that 2020 had the fewest repairs, but it also had the fewest recordings copied, so it does not complete the statement.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 140 is less than the totals for 2021 and 2022, so 2019 was not the busiest year.
explanation.D: Correct. 210 is the largest number in the "Recordings copied" column.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Coffee is often grown in full sun to maximize harvests, but some farmers in Colombia plant it beneath taller shade trees. Agronomist Luis Cárdenas compared plots grown in full sun, light shade and heavy shade. He concluded that shade involves a trade-off: shaded plots produce smaller harvests, but a greater share of their beans are large, a quality that coffee buyers value.

data.title: Coffee Plots Grown under Three Levels of Shade

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Cárdenas's conclusion?

choices.A: Heavy-shade plots yielded 1,240 kg per hectare to full sun's 1,850 kg, but 63 percent of their beans were large, versus 38 percent.
choices.B: Plants under heavy shade grew to an average of 2.4 meters, taller than the 1.9 meters reached in full sun.
choices.C: Plots under light shade yielded more beans per hectare than plots in full sun did, and a larger share of their beans were large.
choices.D: Plots in full sun yielded 1,850 kg of beans per hectare, more than the plots under either light shade or heavy shade.

explanation.why: A trade-off has two sides, so support for Cárdenas's conclusion must show both a smaller harvest and a larger share of large beans under shade. Only one choice compares both columns for shaded and unshaded plots.
explanation.A: Correct. It shows both halves of the trade-off: heavy shade produced a smaller harvest than full sun but a larger share of large beans.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but plant height is not part of the trade-off Cárdenas describes, which concerns harvest size and bean size.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Light-shade plots yielded 1,620 kg per hectare, less than the 1,850 kg from full-sun plots, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true and shows that shade lowers the harvest, but it says nothing about bean size, so it supports only half of the trade-off.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Bangladesh, mobile banking services let people send, receive and save money using a basic phone. Economist Tahmina Akter surveyed villages in Rangpur Division in 2018 and again in 2022. She reports that younger adults were still the most likely to use mobile banking in 2022, but that the gap between age groups narrowed because use grew fastest among adults aged 50 and older.

data.title: Village Residents Using Mobile Banking in Rangpur Division, by Age Group

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Akter's explanation of why the gap narrowed?

choices.A: The share of residents aged 18–29 who used mobile banking rose by more percentage points between 2018 and 2022 than did the share of any other age group.
choices.B: In 2022, 74 percent of residents aged 18–29 used mobile banking, the highest share of any age group that year.
choices.C: In both 2018 and 2022, residents aged 30–49 used mobile banking at a higher rate than residents aged 50 and older.
choices.D: The share of residents aged 50 and older who used mobile banking rose from 12 percent to 41 percent, a larger increase than in either younger age group.

explanation.why: Akter explains the narrowing gap by saying that use grew fastest among adults aged 50 and older, so the support must compare the increases of the age groups. The oldest group rose from 12 to 41 percent (29 points), more than the 18–29 group (16 points) or the 30–49 group (19 points).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The 18–29 group rose by only 16 points, the smallest increase of the three, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true and matches Akter's point that younger adults were still the most likely users, but it does not show why the gap narrowed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes a difference that existed in both years; it does not show which group's use grew fastest.
explanation.D: Correct. The oldest group rose by 29 percentage points, compared with 16 for ages 18–29 and 19 for ages 30–49, which shows that use grew fastest among older adults.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On many lakes in Finland, local observers have written down the dates of freezing and thawing for well over a century. Limnologist Aino Virtanen used such records from one lake to find the average number of days per winter that it stayed covered with ice in each decade since the 1950s. She argues that the lake's ice cover has not simply declined but that the decline has sped up in recent decades.

data.title: Average Days of Ice Cover per Winter on a Finnish Lake, by Decade

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Virtanen's argument?

choices.A: In the 1990s, the lake was covered with ice for an average of 165 days per winter, more than in the 2000s.
choices.B: Average ice cover fell by about the same number of days from each decade to the next across the whole record.
choices.C: Average ice cover fell by 5 days in total from the 1950s to the 1970s but by 11 days from the 2000s to the 2010s alone.
choices.D: The lake was covered with ice for an average of 182 days per winter in the 1950s and 146 days in the 2010s.

explanation.why: Virtanen claims more than a decline: she says the decline sped up. Support must therefore compare the size of the drop in an earlier period with the size of the drop in a recent one. From the 1950s to the 1970s ice cover fell from 182 to 177 days, but from the 2000s to the 2010s it fell from 157 to 146 days.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a single comparison between two decades says nothing about whether the rate of decline changed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The drops grew from 2 days (1950s to 1960s) to 11 days (2000s to 2010s), so they were not about the same.
explanation.C: Correct. A 5-day drop over two decades early on, compared with an 11-day drop in a single recent decade, shows that the decline has sped up.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true and shows that ice cover declined, but comparing only the first and last decades cannot show whether the decline sped up.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Some orchestras offer short talks before concerts to introduce the music. At four concerts in Lyon, France, arts researcher Camille Fournier recorded the share of listeners who returned to their seats after intermission, comparing those who had attended the talk with those who had not. The table lists the programs from most familiar to least familiar to typical audiences. Fournier concluded that the talks mattered most for the least familiar music.

data.title: Listeners Who Returned after Intermission at Four Concerts in Lyon

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Fournier's conclusion?

choices.A: Listeners who attended the talk returned after intermission at a lower rate for the Boulez concert than for any other concert.
choices.B: Among listeners who skipped the talk, a higher share returned at the Messiaen concert than at the Stravinsky concert.
choices.C: At every concert, listeners who attended the talk returned after intermission at a higher rate than listeners who did not.
choices.D: The gap between the two groups' return rates was 5 percentage points for Debussy and Ravel but 25 points for Boulez.

explanation.why: Fournier's conclusion is about where the talks mattered most, so the support must compare the gap between the two groups across programs. The gap is 5 points for Debussy and Ravel, 9 for Stravinsky, 18 for Messiaen and 25 for Boulez, growing as the music becomes less familiar.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one group and does not compare talk attendees with other listeners.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Only 72 percent returned at the Messiaen concert, compared with 84 percent at the Stravinsky concert, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true and suggests that the talks helped, but it does not show that they helped most for the least familiar music.
explanation.D: Correct. The gap between the groups grows from 5 points for the most familiar program to 25 points for the least familiar one, so the talks made the biggest difference where the music was least familiar.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In England, many farmers now sow strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields to provide food for pollinating insects. Ecologist Hannah Mercer counted bumblebees on four farms, comparing field edges sown with wildflowers and edges left as grass. She claims that the wildflower strips benefited bumblebees on every farm, though the size of the benefit differed greatly from one farm to another.

data.title: Bumblebees Counted along Field Edges on Four Farms

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Mercer's claim?

choices.A: Wildflower strips had more bumblebees than grass edges on all four farms, by 6 at Bramley but by 39 at Calder.
choices.B: More bumblebees were counted along wildflower strips than along grass edges on only three of the four farms.
choices.C: The grass edges had between 9 and 18 bumblebees, so the number of bumblebees varied from farm to farm.
choices.D: The wildflower strip at Calder had 48 bumblebees, more than any other strip or grass edge in the study.

explanation.why: Mercer's claim has two parts: the strips helped on every farm, and the size of the help varied. The support must compare the two bars for each farm. Wildflower strips beat grass edges everywhere, by 22 at Ashcombe, 6 at Bramley, 39 at Calder and 9 at Dunmore.
explanation.A: Correct. It shows a benefit on every farm and that the benefit ranged from 6 to 39 bumblebees, which covers both parts of Mercer's claim.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Wildflower strips had more bumblebees on all four farms, so this misreads the graph and would weaken the claim about every farm.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the grass edges; it does not compare them with the wildflower strips, so it cannot show a benefit.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes one farm only and does not show a benefit on every farm.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: After many office workers in Melbourne, Australia, began working from home several days a week, economist Ravi Chandrasekaran studied cafés in the city center, where many customers had once been office workers buying coffee and lunch. He hypothesized that these cafés depended heavily on such customers, so their sales would have fallen much more on weekdays than on weekends.

data.title: Average Daily Sales at City-Center Cafés in Melbourne (dollars)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chandrasekaran's hypothesis?

choices.A: Average sales fell by $700 to $1,100 on each weekday shown but by only $50 on each weekend day.
choices.B: Average sales fell by more on Saturdays than on Wednesdays between 2019 and 2023.
choices.C: Average sales on Wednesdays were higher than on any other day shown, in both 2019 and 2023.
choices.D: Average sales on Sundays were lower than on any other day shown, in both 2019 and 2023.

explanation.why: The hypothesis predicts a larger drop in sales on weekdays than on weekends, so the support must compare the changes from 2019 to 2023. Weekday sales fell by $1,100 (Monday), $700 (Wednesday) and $1,100 (Friday), while Saturday and Sunday sales each fell by only $50.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares the drop on weekdays with the drop on weekends, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Saturday sales fell by only $50, while Wednesday sales fell by $700, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares days within each year and does not show how much sales fell.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it does not compare the change in sales on weekdays with the change on weekends.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Air generally becomes cooler as altitude increases. In the Langtang Valley of Nepal, glaciologist Pemba Sherpa installed weather stations at five elevations and recorded the average air temperature at each one during July. She found that, along this valley, the temperature fell by roughly 6°C for every 1,000 meters of elevation gained. For example, the average July temperature was ______

data.title: Average July Air Temperature at Five Stations in the Langtang Valley

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: about 16°C at 2,500 meters and about 4°C at 3,500 meters.
choices.B: below freezing at 5,500 meters, the highest station.
choices.C: about 22°C at 1,500 meters, the warmest of the five stations.
choices.D: about 16°C at 2,500 meters and about 10°C at 3,500 meters.

explanation.why: Sherpa's finding is about a rate of change, so the example must give temperatures at two elevations and show a drop of about 6°C for each 1,000 meters. The stations at 2,500 and 3,500 meters average about 16°C and 10°C, a drop of about 6°C over 1,000 meters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The 3,500-meter station averaged about 10°C; about 4°C was recorded at 4,500 meters, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives only one station's temperature and does not show a drop of about 6°C per 1,000 meters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but a single temperature cannot show how much the temperature falls as elevation increases.
explanation.D: Correct. These two stations are 1,000 meters apart, and the temperature falls by about 6°C between them, which is an example of the pattern Sherpa describes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Swahili, spoken across much of East Africa, developed along a coast where traders from Arabia, Persia, India and, later, Portugal and Britain did business for centuries. Linguist Neema Mwakyusa traced the origins of 400 Swahili words related to trade and seafaring. She concluded that, in this vocabulary, words borrowed from Arabic outnumber the words borrowed from all other foreign languages combined.

data.title: Origins of 400 Swahili Words Related to Trade and Seafaring

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Mwakyusa's conclusion?

choices.A: Words of Bantu origin, at 180, made up the largest single group among the 400 words in the sample.
choices.B: Arabic contributed 150 of the words, far more than the 20 words that came from Portuguese.
choices.C: Persian, Indian languages, Portuguese and English together contributed more of the words than Arabic did.
choices.D: Arabic contributed 150 of the words, while Persian, Indian languages, Portuguese and English together contributed 70.

explanation.why: Mwakyusa compares Arabic with all other foreign languages combined, so add up the bars for Persian (20), Indian languages (15), Portuguese (20) and English (15): 70 words. Arabic's 150 words are more than that total, and only one choice makes this comparison.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but Bantu words are native to Swahili, not borrowed, so they are not part of Mwakyusa's comparison.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares Arabic with only one other language, not with all the other foreign languages combined.
explanation.C: Incorrect. These four sources together contributed 70 words, fewer than Arabic's 150, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.D: Correct. It compares Arabic with all the other foreign sources combined (20 + 15 + 20 + 15 = 70), which is the comparison the conclusion makes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Gardeners sometimes release lady beetles, which eat aphids, to protect plants without using pesticides. In a rose garden in Seville, Spain, horticulturist Sofía Navarro released lady beetles onto some rosebushes and left others untreated, then counted aphids every week. She concluded that the beetles reduced aphid numbers at first but that the effect had nearly disappeared within a few weeks.

data.title: Average Aphids per Rose Shoot after Lady Beetles Were Released

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Navarro's conclusion?

choices.A: One week after release, bushes with beetles had 14 aphids per shoot, far fewer than the 46 on untreated bushes.
choices.B: In week 1, bushes with beetles had 14 aphids per shoot to untreated bushes' 46, but by week 4 they had 47 to 52.
choices.C: Most of the lady beetles released onto the rosebushes had flown away to other parts of the garden by week 3.
choices.D: By week 4, bushes with beetles had more aphids per shoot than untreated bushes had in the same week.

explanation.why: Navarro's conclusion has two parts: an early drop in aphids and a later fading of that effect. The support must compare the two columns at an early week and at a late week. In week 1 the gap was 32 aphids per shoot (14 versus 46), but by week 4 it was only 5 (47 versus 52).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true and shows the early reduction, but it does not show that the effect later nearly disappeared.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows both a large early reduction and a small difference by week 4, matching both parts of the conclusion.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The table counts aphids only; it gives no information about where the beetles went.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In week 4, bushes with beetles had 47 aphids per shoot and untreated bushes had 52, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Geographer Chidi Okonkwo mapped the stalls of a large open-air market in Lagos, Nigeria, in 2012 and again in 2022. He reports that stalls selling mobile phones and accessories grew in number by far more than any other kind of stall over the decade, even though fabric and clothing sellers still held more stalls than any other group in 2022.

data.title: Stalls in an Open-Air Market in Lagos, by Goods Sold

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Okonkwo's report?

choices.A: Fabric and clothing stalls were the most common type of stall in the market in both 2012 and 2022.
choices.B: Household goods stalls increased by more than phone and accessory stalls did between 2012 and 2022.
choices.C: In 2022, the market had 260 phone and accessory stalls and 330 food and spice stalls, out of 1,310 stalls in all.
choices.D: Phone and accessory stalls rose by 215, yet fabric and clothing stalls, at 405, were still the most common type in 2022.

explanation.why: Okonkwo reports two things: phone stalls grew by far the most, and fabric and clothing stalls were still the most numerous in 2022. The support must show both. Phone stalls rose from 45 to 260 (an increase of 215), and fabric and clothing, at 405, remained the largest group.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true and supports the second part of the report, but it says nothing about the growth of phone stalls.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Household goods stalls rose by only 25, while phone stalls rose by 215, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. These numbers are accurate, but they describe 2022 only and do not show how much any type of stall grew.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows both parts of the report: the largest increase (215, compared with at most 25 for any other type) and fabric and clothing still in first place.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Wheat in Pakistan's Punjab province is harvested in April and May, so an unusually hot March, when the grains are filling, can shrink the crop. Plant breeder Rubina Chaudhry compared a widely grown older variety with a newer variety bred to tolerate heat. She argues that the new variety's advantage is not constant: it matters most in years when March is especially hot.

data.title: Wheat Yields of Two Varieties at a Research Farm in Punjab, Pakistan

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chaudhry's argument?

choices.A: The newer variety produced a higher yield than the older variety in every year from 2019 through 2023.
choices.B: The gap between the yields of the two varieties was smaller in 2022 than in any other year shown.
choices.C: The newer variety outyielded the older one by 0.9 metric tons per hectare in 2022, the hottest March, but by only 0.1 in 2019, the coolest.
choices.D: The older variety's yield was highest in 2019, when it produced 3.4 metric tons of wheat per hectare.

explanation.why: Chaudhry claims that the newer variety's advantage depends on March temperature, so the support must compare the gap between the varieties in hot and cool years. The gap was 0.1 metric tons per hectare in 2019 (24.1°C) but 0.9 in 2022 (28.9°C), and it was larger in 2021 and 2022, the two hottest years, than in any other year.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true and shows that the newer variety did better, but it does not show that its advantage was largest in hot years.
explanation.B: Incorrect. In 2022 the gap was 0.9 metric tons per hectare, the largest of any year, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Correct. The newer variety's advantage was largest in the hottest year and smallest in the coolest one, which shows that its advantage grows when March is hot.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the older variety and does not compare the two varieties.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In 2016, a city in central Mexico began paying for murals on public walls. Art historian Paloma Ortiz argues that a rule added in 2019, which gave grants to murals designed together with neighborhood residents, changed the program's character: before the rule, most of its murals were the work of invited professional artists, but afterward, most were designed with residents.

data.title: Murals Painted per Year through a City Mural Program

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Ortiz's argument?

choices.A: The program produced more murals in 2022, a total of 29, than in any earlier year shown on the graph.
choices.B: Murals by invited artists outnumbered murals designed with residents in every year shown, from 2016 through 2022.
choices.C: The number of murals designed with residents rose sharply after the 2019 rule, from 3 in 2018 to 13 in 2019.
choices.D: Invited artists painted most murals from 2016 through 2018, but resident-designed murals were the majority every year from 2019 on.

explanation.why: Ortiz claims that the majority switched from invited artists' murals to resident-designed murals after 2019, so the support must compare the two lines before and after that year. Invited artists led in 2016–2018, and resident-designed murals led in every year from 2019 to 2022.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (29 murals), but it concerns the total number of murals, not who designed them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. From 2019 on, murals designed with residents outnumbered those by invited artists, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one line; without comparing it with the invited artists' murals, it cannot show which kind made up most of the murals before and after 2019.
explanation.D: Correct. In 2016–2018 invited artists led (12 to 2, 14 to 3, 15 to 3), and from 2019 on resident-designed murals led (13 to 9, 15 to 8, 18 to 7, 21 to 8), which is the change Ortiz describes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In sea turtles, whether an egg hatches as a male or a female depends on the temperature of the sand around the nest: warmer nests produce more females. On a beach in Bahia, Brazil, biologist Mariana Teixeira found that nests in open sand were warmer than nests shaded by coastal plants. She argues that if the shaded parts of the beach are cleared for development, the beach will produce an even higher share of female hatchlings.

data.title: Female Hatchlings from Sea Turtle Nests on a Beach in Bahia, Brazil

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Teixeira's argument?

choices.A: Nests shaded by plants produced 42 percent female hatchlings, while nests in open sand produced 93 percent.
choices.B: Most of the hatchlings from partly shaded nests, 71 percent, were female rather than male.
choices.C: Nests in open sand produced a smaller share of female hatchlings than nests shaded by plants did.
choices.D: More turtles laid their eggs in open sand than in the shaded parts of the beach, where plants grow.

explanation.why: Teixeira's argument depends on shaded nests producing fewer females than open-sand nests, so that removing shade would raise the share of females. The graph shows 42 percent females from shaded nests and 93 percent from open-sand nests.
explanation.A: Correct. Shaded nests produced far fewer females than open-sand nests, so losing the shaded areas would leave mostly nests that produce females.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (71 percent), but it does not compare shaded nests with open-sand nests, which is what the argument about losing shade depends on.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Open-sand nests produced 93 percent females, compared with 42 percent for shaded nests, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows the share of female hatchlings, not how many nests were in each location.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When a regional railway in Poland introduced a smartphone ticket app in 2021, transport researcher Agnieszka Wróbel tracked how passengers at one station bought their tickets. She found that the app did not mainly replace the ticket counter, as many staff had feared. Instead, its growth came mostly at the expense of the station's ticket machines, while the counter's share fell only slightly.

data.title: Share of Tickets Sold at One Station, by Method (%)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Wróbel's finding?

choices.A: The share of tickets bought through the app rose in every year after the app was introduced in 2021.
choices.B: From 2020 to 2023, the machines' share fell from 62 to 26 percent, while the counter's share fell only from 38 to 34 percent.
choices.C: From 2020 to 2023, the counter's share of ticket sales fell by more percentage points than the machines' share did.
choices.D: In 2023, 40 percent of tickets were bought through the app, more than through either of the other methods.

explanation.why: Wróbel's finding is about where the app's growth came from, so the support must compare how much the counter and the machines each lost. The machines dropped from 62 to 26 percent, while the counter dropped only from 38 to 34 percent.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the app alone and does not compare the losses of the counter and the machines.
explanation.B: Correct. The machines lost 36 percentage points while the counter lost only 4, which shows that the app's growth came mostly from the machines.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The counter's share fell by 4 points and the machines' share by 36 points, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only how popular the app became, not which method lost the most sales to it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In winter, a layer of snow acts like a blanket, slowing the loss of heat from the ground beneath it. Near Fairbanks, Alaska, soil scientist Ivan Petrov measured soil temperatures 10 centimeters below the surface in plots kept clear of snow and in plots left under natural snow cover. He concluded that the insulating effect of snow was strongest during the coldest months.

data.title: Average Monthly Temperatures near Fairbanks, Alaska (°C)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Petrov's conclusion?

choices.A: Snow-covered soil was 12°C warmer than cleared soil in January, the coldest month, but only 4°C warmer in March, the mildest.
choices.B: In every month shown, the soil under natural snow was warmer than the air above it, often by more than 10°C.
choices.C: The difference between cleared soil and snow-covered soil was largest in March, the mildest month shown.
choices.D: The soil under natural snow stayed between −2°C and −4°C from November through March, while the air ranged from −10°C to −24°C.

explanation.why: The insulating effect of snow is the difference between soil under snow and soil without snow. Petrov's conclusion requires that this difference be largest in the coldest months. The difference is 12°C in January (−4 versus −16), when the air was coldest, but only 4°C in March (−3 versus −7).
explanation.A: Correct. The snow made the biggest difference in the coldest month and a much smaller one in the mildest, which is what Petrov concluded.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares snow-covered soil with the air, not with cleared soil, so it does not show when the snow's insulating effect was strongest.
explanation.C: Incorrect. In March the difference was only 4°C, the smallest of any month, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it never compares snow-covered soil with cleared soil, so it cannot show when the snow's insulating effect was strongest.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On hot summer days, unshaded sidewalks in Seville, Spain, can become far hotter than the air above them, and the city has planted street trees partly to counter this effect. Urban climatologist Lucía Ferrer measured the surface temperature of sidewalks beneath tree canopy and of nearby sidewalks with no shade at four times of day during a series of cloudless July days. Ferrer concluded that the cooling the canopy provides is not constant over the course of the day; instead, she argues, it is largest in the afternoon, at roughly the time when exposed pavement reaches its peak temperature.

data.title: Average Sidewalk Surface Temperature on Cloudless July Days in Seville

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Ferrer's conclusion?

choices.A: Between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., shaded sidewalks warmed by more degrees than unshaded sidewalks did.
choices.B: Shade cooled sidewalks by 3°C at 9 a.m. but by 15°C at 3 p.m., when unshaded pavement was hottest.
choices.C: At each of the four times measured, sidewalks beneath tree canopy were cooler than sidewalks with no shade.
choices.D: Unshaded sidewalks were 11°C hotter at 6 p.m. than they had been at 9 a.m.

explanation.why: Ferrer does not claim only that shade cools sidewalks; she claims the cooling changes over the day and is largest in the afternoon, when unshaded pavement peaks. Support must therefore compare the gap between the two bars at different times. The gap is 31 − 28 = 3°C at 9 a.m. but 51 − 36 = 15°C at 3 p.m., the hottest reading for unshaded sidewalks.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Shaded sidewalks warmed 8°C (28 to 36), while unshaded sidewalks warmed 20°C (31 to 51), so this reverses the data.
explanation.B: Correct. It compares the cooling effect at two times and shows it is much larger at 3 p.m., exactly when unshaded pavement is hottest.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that shade always helps, not that its cooling effect changes and peaks in the afternoon.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (42 − 31 = 11), but it describes unshaded sidewalks alone and says nothing about how much the canopy cools them.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Chennai, India, receives most of its rain between October and December and then endures a long dry season, during which many households buy water delivered by tanker trucks. Many buildings in the city now collect rain from their rooftops in storage tanks, and some observers have expected this storage to free households from buying water. Urban geographer Kavitha Raman, who tracked tanker purchases in one neighborhood, offers a more limited assessment. Households with storage, she finds, buy far less tanker water than other households early in the dry season, but by its final months, once their stored water is used up, the two groups buy nearly the same amount.

data.title: Average Tanker Water Purchased per Household in One Chennai Neighborhood

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Raman's assessment?

choices.A: In February, households with storage bought 1,500 fewer liters than households without it, but in May they bought only 50 fewer.
choices.B: Households without rooftop storage bought more tanker water than households with storage in every month shown.
choices.C: The difference between the two groups' tanker purchases grew larger from February to May.
choices.D: Tanker purchases by households with storage rose in each month from February to May, reaching 2,050 liters.

explanation.why: Raman's assessment has two parts: households with storage buy far less early in the dry season, and by the end the two groups buy nearly the same amount. Support must compare the two columns at the start and at the end. In February the gap is 1,800 − 300 = 1,500 liters; in May it is 2,100 − 2,050 = 50 liters.
explanation.A: Correct. It shows a large gap early in the dry season and almost none at its end, matching both parts of Raman's assessment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that storage always helps somewhat; it does not show the advantage shrinking to almost nothing by May.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The difference shrank from 1,500 liters in February to 50 liters in May, so this reverses the data.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only households with storage; without the other column it cannot show the two groups converging.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Honeybees and bumblebees often visit the same flowers, but their daily schedules can differ. Because bumblebees are large and densely furred, they can fly in air too cool for many smaller bees. Pollination ecologist Saskia de Vries counted visits by each kind of bee to plots of flowering clover in the Netherlands on a series of cool spring days. She argues that bumblebees dominate the clover in the early morning, while temperatures are still low, but that this difference largely disappears by midday, when honeybees become at least as active as bumblebees.

data.title: Average Bee Visits to Clover Plots on Cool Spring Days

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support de Vries's argument?

choices.A: Honeybee visits peaked at noon and then declined slightly by 2 p.m.
choices.B: Bumblebees made more visits to the clover plots than honeybees did at every time of day shown.
choices.C: Both kinds of bees made fewer visits per hour at 6 a.m. than they did at noon.
choices.D: At 6 a.m., bumblebees made 38 more visits per hour than honeybees did, but at noon honeybees made 3 more.

explanation.why: De Vries's argument contrasts two times of day: bumblebees dominate early, but by midday honeybees are at least as active. Support must compare the two lines at an early time and at midday. At 6 a.m. the counts are 42 versus 4, a 38-visit gap in favor of bumblebees; at noon they are 63 versus 66, with honeybees slightly ahead.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes honeybees alone, so it cannot show how the two kinds of bees compare at different times.
explanation.B: Incorrect. At noon (66 versus 63) and 2 p.m. (64 versus 60) honeybees made more visits, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes both bees together and says nothing about how they compare with each other.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows a large early-morning gap favoring bumblebees and a midday reading in which honeybees match or slightly exceed them.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Over the past two decades, English-language readers have encountered far more fiction translated from Korean than they once did. To some critics, this rise is simply one part of a broader boom in translated fiction of all kinds. Literary scholar Ines Halvorsen, who maintains a database of novels and story collections published in English translation, disagrees. The growth in Korean titles, she argues, has been so much faster than the growth of translated fiction as a whole that a general boom alone cannot account for it.

data.title: Fiction Titles Published in English Translation, Halvorsen Database

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Halvorsen's argument?

choices.A: From 2008 to 2023, translated fiction as a whole grew at a faster rate than fiction translated from Korean.
choices.B: From 2008 to 2023, Korean titles grew more than sevenfold, while all translated titles grew by about 15%.
choices.C: The number of titles translated from Korean increased between each pair of years shown.
choices.D: In every year shown, titles translated from Korean made up a small fraction of all translated titles.

explanation.why: Halvorsen's argument is a comparison of growth rates: Korean titles grew much faster than translated fiction overall. Support must therefore compare the growth of the two columns. Korean titles rose from 9 to 66, more than seven times as many, while all translated titles rose from 512 to 590, an increase of about 15%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Korean titles grew more than sevenfold, while the total grew only about 15%, so this reverses the data.
explanation.B: Correct. It compares the growth of the two columns and shows Korean titles growing far faster than translated fiction as a whole.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes Korean titles alone; steady growth could still be part of a general boom if the total grew just as fast.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but the size of Korean fiction's share in any one year says nothing about how fast it grew compared with the whole.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In many rural homes in Nepal, meals are cooked over open wood fires that fill kitchens with fine smoke particles. Improved cookstoves, which burn wood more completely and vent smoke through a chimney, are designed to reduce this pollution. Environmental engineer Anjana Shrestha measured particle levels during cooking in kitchens using traditional fires and improved stoves. She found that the improved stoves lowered particle levels in every kind of kitchen she studied, but she argues that their benefit is greatest in poorly ventilated kitchens, where smoke from a traditional fire has the fewest ways to escape.

data.title: Average Particle Levels during Cooking in Rural Nepali Kitchens

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Shrestha's argument?

choices.A: Improved stoves cut particle levels by 580 micrograms per cubic meter in kitchens with no windows but by 140 in kitchens with two or more.
choices.B: With either kind of stove, kitchens with two or more windows had lower particle levels than kitchens with no windows.
choices.C: With improved stoves, particle levels were similar in every type of kitchen, ranging only from 190 to 240.
choices.D: Improved stoves lowered particle levels by roughly the same amount in each type of kitchen shown.

explanation.why: Shrestha's argument concerns the size of the stoves' benefit: it is largest in the least ventilated kitchens. The benefit is the difference between the two bars for each kitchen type, so support must compare those differences. In kitchens with no windows the reduction is 820 − 240 = 580; in kitchens with two or more windows it is 330 − 190 = 140.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares the reduction in the least and most ventilated kitchens and shows the benefit is far larger where ventilation is poorest.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows that windows reduce smoke, not that the improved stove helps more in kitchens without them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the improved stove alone; without the traditional-fire levels, it does not show how much the stove reduced pollution.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The reductions were 580, 300, and 140, which are far from equal, so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2023, a midsize city in northern Portugal stopped charging fares on its buses. Ridership rose, and the city's mayor credited the policy with persuading commuters to leave their cars at home. Transport economist Rui Valente is skeptical of that interpretation. Comparing average weekday ridership in 2022 and 2023, he argues that the growth came largely from trips taken in the middle of the day, such as errands and visits, while ridership during the morning and evening rush hours, when most commuting occurs, barely changed.

data.title: Average Weekday Bus Riders by Time of Day

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Valente's argument?

choices.A: Ridership rose by about 1,500 in each period from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. but by only about 300 in each rush-hour period.
choices.B: In both years, more people rode between 7 and 9 a.m. than during any other time period shown.
choices.C: More people rode the buses in 2023 than in 2022 during every time period shown.
choices.D: The largest increase in ridership from 2022 to 2023 occurred between 5 and 7 p.m.

explanation.why: Valente accepts that ridership rose; his point is about where the growth came from: midday trips grew, while rush-hour trips barely changed. Support must compare the change in midday periods with the change in rush-hour periods. Ridership rose 1,500 from 9 a.m. to noon (2.1 to 3.6 thousand) and from noon to 3 p.m. (2.4 to 3.9), but only 300 from 7 to 9 a.m. (5.2 to 5.5) and from 5 to 7 p.m. (4.8 to 5.1).
explanation.A: Correct. It compares the gains in midday and rush-hour periods and shows that the growth came mostly in the middle of the day.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares time periods within each year rather than showing how ridership changed after fares ended.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but the mayor and Valente both accept that ridership grew; it does not show which trips produced the growth.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The 5–7 p.m. period rose by only 300 riders, one of the smallest increases, so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many home bakers assume that keeping bread dough warm is always an advantage, since warm dough rises faster. Food scientist Amaka Obi tested that assumption by letting identical batches of yeast dough rise at four temperatures and then measuring both the time each batch took to double in size and the volume of the baked loaves. Obi agrees that warmth speeds rising, but she argues that beyond a moderate temperature, the time saved comes at a cost: the finished loaves are noticeably smaller.

data.title: Rising Time and Loaf Volume at Four Dough Temperatures

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Obi's argument?

choices.A: At 20°C, the dough took more than three hours to double in size.
choices.B: Rising time decreased with each increase in dough temperature shown in the table.
choices.C: Loaf volume was greatest at 20°C and decreased with each increase in dough temperature.
choices.D: Raising the temperature from 24°C to 32°C halved the rising time but shrank loaf volume from 1,480 to 1,290 cubic centimeters.

explanation.why: Obi's argument has two linked parts: above a moderate temperature, dough rises faster, but the loaves are smaller. Support must use both columns over the same temperature change. From 24°C to 32°C, rising time fell from 2.0 to 1.0 hours while loaf volume fell from 1,480 to 1,290 cubic centimeters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives one reading at the coolest temperature and shows neither a trade-off nor what happens above a moderate temperature.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it supports only the point Obi already grants (warmth speeds rising) and says nothing about the cost in loaf size.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Loaf volume was greatest at 24°C (1,480), not at 20°C (1,450), so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows both the time saved and the loss in volume when the temperature rises beyond a moderate level, which is exactly the trade-off Obi describes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Opera is usually sung in its original language, which many audience members do not understand. When a regional opera company in Canada began projecting English translations above the stage at the start of its 2013 season, its managers hoped the change would make performances in Italian, German, and French more welcoming. Arts administrator Grace Whitfield, who studied the company's ticket records, concludes that the change mattered mainly to newcomers: it drew a wave of first-time operagoers but did little to alter attendance among people who had attended the company's performances before.

data.title: Attendance at a Regional Opera Company by Season

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Whitfield's conclusion?

choices.A: After the translations were introduced in 2013, returning attendance rose by more than first-time attendance did.
choices.B: First-time attendance increased in every season shown, from 3,900 in 2011 to 7,300 in 2014.
choices.C: Returning attendees outnumbered first-time attendees by a wide margin in every season shown.
choices.D: From 2012 to 2013, first-time attendance rose by about 2,700, but returning attendance rose by only about 500.

explanation.why: Whitfield's conclusion has two parts tied to the moment the translations began in 2013: first-time attendance surged, but returning attendance barely changed. Support must compare the change in both series across that moment. From 2012 to 2013, first-time attendance rose from 4,100 to 6,800 (about 2,700), while returning attendance moved only from 21,100 to 21,600 (about 500).
explanation.A: Incorrect. From 2012 to 2013, first-time attendance rose about 2,700, while returning attendance rose about 500, so this reverses the data.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it covers first-time attendees only, and the rise from 2011 to 2012 came before the translations began.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but which group was larger says nothing about how each responded to the translations.
explanation.D: Correct. It compares both groups across the 2013 change and shows a large jump for newcomers and little change for returning attendees.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Lichens, partnerships between fungi and algae, absorb water and nutrients directly from the air, so many species are harmed by the pollutants that vehicles emit. Ecologist Henrik Aalto surveyed trees at several distances from a busy highway in southern Finland, recording whether each tree carried leafy lichens, which are generally sensitive to pollution, and crust lichens, which are generally tolerant of it. Aalto argues that the highway's influence shows up in the sensitive lichens alone: crust lichens are about equally common at every distance, whereas leafy lichens become common only well away from the road.

data.title: Trees Carrying Lichens at Different Distances from a Highway

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Aalto's argument?

choices.A: At every distance measured, crust lichens grew on a larger share of trees than leafy lichens did.
choices.B: Crust lichens grew on 70% to 75% of trees at every distance, while leafy lichens grew on 4% of trees at the road and 64% at 800 meters.
choices.C: Leafy lichens grew on a larger share of trees at 800 meters from the highway than at any other distance measured.
choices.D: The share of trees carrying crust lichens fell steadily as distance from the highway increased.

explanation.why: Aalto's argument contrasts the two kinds of lichen: crust lichens stay about equally common at all distances, while leafy lichens become common only far from the road. Support must describe both lines across distance. Crust lichens stay between 70% and 75%, while leafy lichens climb from 4% at the road to 64% at 800 meters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but which lichen is more common overall does not show how each changes with distance from the road.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows the flat pattern for tolerant crust lichens alongside the steep rise for sensitive leafy lichens, which is exactly Aalto's contrast.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes leafy lichens alone and says nothing about whether crust lichens were unaffected by the road.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The crust-lichen line stays between 70% and 75% with no steady decline, so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the highlands of southern Peru, many families raise alpacas and sell the animals' fiber, which is graded by fineness: the finer the fiber, the more it is worth. Some herders sell to traveling buyers on their own, while others sell through a cooperative that pools members' fiber into large, sorted lots. Economist Rosa Quispe argues that the cooperative helps herders mainly by raising the prices of the finest grades, since buyers pay a substantial premium for fine fiber only when they can purchase it in large, consistent lots.

data.title: Average Price Paid to Herders for Alpaca Fiber

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Quispe's argument?

choices.A: The cooperative paid herders more than independent buyers did for every grade of fiber shown.
choices.B: Fine and extra-fine fiber sold for more than coarse or medium fiber, whether or not it was sold through the cooperative.
choices.C: The gap between independent and cooperative prices was roughly the same for all four grades of fiber.
choices.D: The cooperative raised the price of extra-fine fiber by 20 soles per kilogram but that of coarse fiber by only 1 sol.

explanation.why: Quispe's argument is about where the cooperative's advantage is concentrated: in the finest grades. The advantage is the difference between the two price columns, so support must compare that difference for fine and coarse fiber. For extra-fine fiber it is 66 − 46 = 20 soles; for coarse fiber it is 13 − 12 = 1 sol.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that the cooperative always pays more, not that its advantage is mainly in the finest grades.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that finer fiber is worth more, which the text already states, not that the cooperative helps most with fine grades.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The gaps were 1, 5, 14, and 20 soles, which grow sharply with fineness, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Correct. It compares the cooperative's advantage for the finest and coarsest grades and shows that the gain is concentrated in the finest fiber.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In a no-take marine reserve, all fishing is banned, and fish are often more plentiful inside such reserves than in nearby waters. Marine ecologist Talia Moana compared fish biomass, the total weight of fish in a given area, inside a reserve off the coast of New Zealand's North Island and at similar reefs outside it. She argues that the reserve's advantage lies mainly with large predatory fish, which are the chief targets of local fishers, rather than being spread evenly across the reef's fish community.

data.title: Fish Biomass Inside and Outside a No-Take Reserve

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Moana's argument?

choices.A: Small reef fish had a greater biomass outside the reserve than inside it.
choices.B: Plant-eating fish had the greatest biomass of any group both inside and outside the reserve.
choices.C: The combined biomass of all three groups was greater inside the reserve than outside it.
choices.D: Predatory fish biomass was more than four times as great inside the reserve as outside, while plant-eating fish biomass was about 20% greater.

explanation.why: Moana's argument is that the reserve's advantage is concentrated in predatory fish rather than shared evenly. Support must compare the inside-versus-outside difference for predatory fish with that for another group. Predatory fish biomass is 410 versus 90 (more than four times as great), while plant-eating fish biomass is 520 versus 430 (about 21% greater).
explanation.A: Incorrect. Small reef fish biomass was 180 inside and 170 outside, so this reverses the graph.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but which group weighs the most says nothing about where the reserve's advantage is concentrated.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (1,110 versus 690), but a larger total could come from an advantage spread evenly across all groups, which is what Moana denies.
explanation.D: Correct. It compares the reserve's effect on two groups and shows a far larger advantage for predatory fish than for plant-eating fish.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Mangoes from Pakistan have long been sent abroad by air, because ripe fruit spoils quickly. Refrigerated shipping containers, however, can keep mangoes fresh for the weeks needed to cross the sea, and they cost far less per tonne than air freight. Trade economist Bilal Qureshi, who examined records kept by an association of mango exporters in Multan, argues that the growth in the association's exports after 2010 came almost entirely from sea freight, while the quantity of mangoes its members sent by air hardly changed.

data.title: Mangoes Shipped Abroad by Members of a Multan Exporters' Association

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Qureshi's argument?

choices.A: Total shipments rose from about 52,000 tonnes in 2010 to about 89,000 tonnes in 2018.
choices.B: In every year shown, members shipped more mangoes by sea than they did by air.
choices.C: From 2010 to 2018, air shipments and sea shipments increased by similar amounts.
choices.D: Sea shipments more than doubled from 2010 to 2018, while air shipments stayed between 21,000 and 24,000 tonnes.

explanation.why: Qureshi's argument is about the source of the growth: sea freight grew while air freight stayed nearly flat. Support must describe how each line changed. Sea shipments rose from 30 to 66 thousand tonnes, more than double, while air shipments stayed between 21 and 24 thousand tonnes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that exports grew, which Qureshi takes for granted; it does not show which kind of shipping produced the growth.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but sea freight could exceed air freight every year without being the source of the growth.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Sea shipments rose by 36,000 tonnes, while air shipments rose by only 1,000, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows strong growth in sea shipments alongside nearly flat air shipments, which is exactly the pattern Qureshi describes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Piano teachers often debate how students should divide their practice time. Music educator Camille Okafor had beginning piano students practice a new piece for the same total number of minutes each week, either in short daily sessions or in a single long session, and then tested how accurately they played it. Okafor reports that the two schedules produced nearly identical results while practice continued, but she argues that the daily schedule had an advantage that emerged only later: students who had practiced that way retained far more of the piece after a month without playing it.

data.title: Accuracy Playing a New Piece (percent of notes correct)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Okafor's argument?

choices.A: After two weeks of practice, students in the weekly group played slightly more accurately than students in the daily group.
choices.B: After the month without practice, the weekly group was more accurate than the daily group.
choices.C: Both groups played more accurately after four weeks of practice than they had after two weeks.
choices.D: After four weeks of practice the groups differed by 1 point, but a month later the daily group scored 18 points higher.

explanation.why: Okafor's argument has two parts: the schedules gave nearly identical results during practice, and the daily group retained far more a month later. Support must compare the two columns at the end of practice and again after the break. At four weeks the scores are 86 and 85 (1 point apart); after the month without practice they are 80 and 62 (18 points apart).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it fits only the first part of the argument and says nothing about the later advantage of daily practice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. After the break the daily group scored 80 and the weekly group 62, so this reverses the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows that both groups improved, not that the two schedules differed in how well students retained the piece.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows a near tie at the end of practice and a large gap after the break, matching both parts of Okafor's argument.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The shells of the grove snail, a common European land snail, range from pale yellow to dark brown. Dark shells absorb more sunlight than pale ones, so in exposed places they can cause their owners to overheat. Evolutionary biologist Marta Lindqvist marked hundreds of snails of each color, released them in three habitats on the Danish coast, and later recorded how many survived. She argues that the advantage of pale shells depends on exposure to the sun: it is substantial in open dunes but shrinks as the habitat becomes more shaded, nearly vanishing in woodland.

data.title: Survival of Marked Grove Snails by Shell Color and Habitat

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Lindqvist's argument?

choices.A: Pale shells' survival advantage was 27 points in open dunes, 11 points at the dune edge, and 2 points in woodland.
choices.B: Dark-shelled snails survived at a higher rate in woodland than they did in open dunes.
choices.C: Pale-shelled snails survived at a higher rate than dark-shelled snails in open dunes, at the dune edge, and in woodland.
choices.D: In woodland, dark-shelled snails survived at a higher rate than pale-shelled snails did.

explanation.why: Lindqvist's argument is about the size of the pale shells' advantage: large in open dunes, smaller with more shade, and nearly gone in woodland. The advantage is the gap between the two bars in each habitat. The gaps are 68 − 41 = 27 points, 61 − 50 = 11 points, and 57 − 55 = 2 points.
explanation.A: Correct. It tracks the gap between pale and dark shells across the three habitats and shows it shrinking from 27 points to almost nothing.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (55% versus 41%), but it describes dark shells alone and does not compare them with pale shells in each habitat.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that pale shells always did better, not that their advantage shrinks as shade increases.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In woodland, pale shells survived at 57% and dark shells at 55%, so this reverses the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Ancient merchant ships in the Mediterranean carried wine and olive oil in amphorae, clay jars whose shapes reveal what they held. Because sunken wrecks preserve these cargoes, archaeologists can use them to trace changes in trade. Studying wrecks found off the coast of southern France, archaeologist Giulia Ferri argues that between the first century BCE and the second century CE, olive oil did not merely join wine as a major cargo but displaced it: as oil cargoes became more common, wine cargoes became correspondingly rarer.

data.title: Wrecks off Southern France by Main Cargo

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ferri's argument?

choices.A: Wrecks carrying mainly olive oil outnumbered those carrying mainly wine in the first century CE, the middle period shown.
choices.B: More of the wrecks carried mainly olive oil than mainly wine in the second century CE.
choices.C: From the first century BCE to the second century CE, wine wrecks fell from 48 to 14 as oil wrecks rose from 9 to 37.
choices.D: The total number of wrecks in each period stayed between about 50 and 60.

explanation.why: Ferri claims not just that oil became common but that it displaced wine: oil cargoes rose while wine cargoes fell. Support must show both columns changing in opposite directions over time. Wine wrecks fell from 48 to 14, while oil wrecks rose from 9 to 37.
explanation.A: Incorrect. In the first century CE, 31 wrecks carried mainly wine and 22 mainly oil, so this reverses the table.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (37 versus 14), but a single period cannot show a change over time, let alone that wine declined as oil rose.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows wine cargoes declining while oil cargoes increased over the same span, which is the displacement Ferri describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (57, 53, and 51), but the total number of wrecks says nothing about which cargo was replacing which.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The flowers of a night-blooming cactus in the Sonoran Desert open at dusk and remain open until the following midmorning, so they are available both to hawk moths, which fly at night, and to bees, which begin foraging after sunrise. Botanist Inés Carrillo hypothesizes that the plant depends almost entirely on the moths for pollination and that the bees' morning visits, though frequent, contribute little to its seed production. To test this, she covered flowers with mesh bags during different periods, preventing visits at those times, and then recorded seed set. The results support Carrillo's hypothesis: ______

data.title: Seed Set in Cactus Flowers under Four Bagging Treatments

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: flowers open only at night set seed nearly as often as fully open flowers, while morning-only flowers rarely did.
choices.B: flowers open to all visitors had the highest seed set of any treatment, with 78% producing seed.
choices.C: flowers open only at night produced more seeds per fruit than flowers open to all visitors did.
choices.D: flowers open only in the morning were four times as likely to produce seed as flowers bagged throughout.

explanation.why: Carrillo's hypothesis has two parts: moths (night visitors) account for almost all pollination, and bees (morning visitors) add little. Support therefore needs the night-only treatment to come close to the fully open flowers and the morning-only treatment to fall far short. Night-only flowers set seed 71% of the time, close to the 78% for fully open flowers, while morning-only flowers did so only 12% of the time.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares each partial treatment with the fully open flowers and shows that night visits alone nearly match full access, while morning visits alone accomplish little.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but fully open flowers receive both moths and bees, so their seed set cannot show which visitor matters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Night-only flowers averaged 389 seeds per fruit, fewer than the 412 for fully open flowers, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (12% versus 3%), but it highlights a contribution from morning visitors rather than showing that the plant depends almost entirely on moths.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When the public library system of a midsize American city stopped charging fines for overdue items in January 2014, critics warned that, without a penalty, borrowers would grow careless about returning items on time. Supporters had argued that fines mostly drove away the borrowers least able to pay them. Librarian and researcher Marisol Castellanos, analyzing the system's records, concludes not only that the critics' fear went unrealized but that the policy accomplished what its supporters had intended: ending fines drew back borrowers who had stayed away, many of them because of unpaid fines, without making borrowers any more likely to return items late.

data.title: Records of a City Library System

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Castellanos's conclusion?

choices.A: After fines ended, active borrowers rose from about 41,000 to nearly 51,000, while late returns stayed near 9% of items.
choices.B: The number of active borrowers increased in every year from 2012 to 2016.
choices.C: The share of items returned late was higher in 2014, the first full year without fines, than it had been in 2013, before fines ended.
choices.D: Active borrowers increased more from 2013 to 2014 than in any other one-year period shown.

explanation.why: Castellanos's conclusion joins two claims: ending fines brought borrowers back, and it did not make late returns more common. Support must use both columns across the change in 2014. Active borrowers rose from 40,600 in 2013 to 50,800 in 2016, while the share of late items stayed between 8.8% and 9.3% throughout.
explanation.A: Correct. It shows the rise in borrowers after 2013 together with a late-return rate that stayed near 9%, supporting both halves of the conclusion.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Active borrowers fell from 41,200 in 2012 to 40,600 in 2013, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (9.3% versus 8.8%), but it seems to favor the critics, and it ignores the borrower figures and the return to about 9% afterward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (a rise of 6,300), but it addresses only the return of borrowers and says nothing about whether late returns became more common.

items.subject: science
items.passage: White-tailed deer in a Pennsylvania state park share their range with hikers, whose numbers on the park's trails more than triple on weekends. One might expect the deer simply to abandon the areas near the trails when hikers are most numerous. Wildlife biologist Owen Sutherland, who analyzed photographs from motion-triggered cameras placed along the trails, proposes a different account. The deer, he argues, do not so much leave the area on weekends as rearrange their schedules, avoiding the trails during the hours when hikers are present and making up for that avoidance after dark.

data.title: Average Deer Detections per Camera along Park Trails

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Sutherland's account?

choices.A: Summed across all six times shown, deer were detected less often on weekends, when hikers were most numerous, than on weekdays.
choices.B: Weekend detections peaked at 2 a.m., the time when weekday detections were at their lowest.
choices.C: On weekends, deer were detected less often than on weekdays at 6 a.m., 10 a.m., and 2 p.m.
choices.D: Weekend detections fell below weekday detections from 6 a.m. through 6 p.m. but rose above them at 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.

explanation.why: Sutherland's account is not merely that deer avoid the trails on weekends (the simple expectation he rejects) but that they shift their activity: fewer weekend detections during the day and more after dark. Support must compare the two lines in both daytime and nighttime hours. Weekend detections are lower at every time from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., but at 10 p.m. (17 versus 10) and 2 a.m. (15 versus 7) they exceed weekday detections.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (46 versus 58), but a lower weekend total, taken alone, fits the abandonment view that Sutherland rejects rather than his own account.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Weekend detections peaked at 10 p.m. (17), and weekday detections were lowest at 2 p.m. (6), so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but daytime avoidance alone fits the simple expectation that deer abandon the area; it does not show them making up for it after dark.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows both halves of the shift: lower weekend activity during hiking hours and higher weekend activity at night.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In northwestern Bangladesh, wheat is often sown after the rice harvest, so when the rice comes in late, so does the wheat.
