Late-sown wheat fills its grain during the hot weeks of March, and heat at that stage lowers yields. Agronomist Nusrat Jahan grew a standard wheat variety and a newer heat-tolerant variety side by side at four sowing dates. Jahan argues that farmers who sow early gain nothing by switching to the tolerant variety, but that for farmers who sow late, its advantage over the standard variety becomes larger the later the crop is sown.

data.title: Wheat Yields by Sowing Date in Northwestern Bangladesh

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Jahan's argument?

choices.A: From the earliest sowing date to the latest, the tolerant variety's yield fell by less than half as much as the standard variety's did.
choices.B: The tolerant variety produced a higher yield than the standard variety at every sowing date tested.
choices.C: Both varieties produced lower yields when sown on December 25 than when sown on November 10.
choices.D: The tolerant variety yielded no more than the standard one when sown in November but 0.4 and 0.7 tonnes more when sown in December.

explanation.why: Jahan's argument has two parts: the tolerant variety offers no gain at early sowing dates, and its advantage widens with later sowing. Support must compare the two bars at each date. In November the tolerant variety yields 3.5 versus 3.6 and 3.4 versus 3.4 (no gain), while in December it leads by 3.2 − 2.8 = 0.4 and then 2.9 − 2.2 = 0.7 tonnes per hectare.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (a drop of 0.6 versus 1.4), but comparing only the first and last dates cannot show that the tolerant variety offers no gain when sown early, the first half of Jahan's claim.
explanation.B: Incorrect. On November 10 the tolerant variety yielded less (3.5 versus 3.6), and on November 25 the yields were equal, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows that late sowing hurts both varieties, not how the tolerant variety compares with the standard one.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows no advantage at the November dates and a growing advantage at the December dates, supporting both parts of Jahan's argument.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Until the early 1950s, most jazz recordings were issued on 78-rpm discs, which held only about three minutes of music per side, so musicians often had to trim their performances to fit. Once the long-playing record, or LP, became common, recorded performances grew much longer. Musicologist Rafael Oyelaran, who timed the sections of hundreds of studio recordings, argues that the added length was not distributed evenly across a performance: musicians devoted nearly all of the new time to improvised solos, while the written themes that open and close a piece remained about as long as they had been.

data.title: Average Length of Sections in Studio Jazz Recordings (minutes)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Oyelaran's argument?

choices.A: The average track recorded in 1955–1959 was more than twice as long as the average track recorded in 1945–1949.
choices.B: Of the 4.4 minutes added to the average track between 1945–1949 and 1955–1959, solos accounted for 4.2.
choices.C: In every period shown, musicians spent more time on improvised solos than they did on theme statements.
choices.D: Solos took up a larger share of the average track in 1945–1949 than they did in 1955–1959.

explanation.why: Oyelaran accepts that tracks got longer; his claim is about where the added time went: almost all of it to solos, with themes nearly unchanged. Support must compare the growth of the solo and theme columns with the growth of the whole track. From 1945–1949 to 1955–1959, tracks grew by 7.4 − 3.0 = 4.4 minutes, solos by 6.1 − 1.9 = 4.2 minutes, and themes by only 0.2 minutes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that tracks got longer, which the text already accepts, not which sections absorbed the added time.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows that nearly all of the added time went to solos, leaving theme statements almost unchanged.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but solos could outweigh themes in every period even if both had grown by similar amounts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Solos made up about 63% of a track (1.9 of 3.0 minutes) in 1945–1949 but about 82% (6.1 of 7.4) in 1955–1959, so this reverses the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Desert sunlight makes arid regions attractive for solar power, but dust that settles on panels blocks light and lowers their output, and washing panels is costly where water is scarce. At a test site in southern Jordan, engineer Dalia Haddad compared panels that were cleaned every week with panels that were never cleaned at all. Apart from one storm, the study period was entirely dry. At the end of April, the site received the only heavy rain of the six-month study. Haddad's data suggest that this single storm did much of the work of a cleaning crew: ______

data.title: Average Monthly Output of Test Panels in Southern Jordan

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the output of the panels cleaned every week stayed between 94% and 96% of rated output in every month, both before and after the storm.
choices.B: the never-cleaned panels' output was higher in June than it had been in May.
choices.C: the never-cleaned panels' output, which trailed that of the cleaned panels by 20 points in April, came within 2 points of it in May.
choices.D: the never-cleaned panels' output fell by 7 percentage points in each month from January to April.

explanation.why: The statement claims that the late-April storm acted like a cleaning, so the data must show the uncleaned panels catching up with the cleaned panels right after the rain. That requires comparing the two lines before and after the storm. In April the gap was 94 − 74 = 20 points; in May it was 95 − 93 = 2 points.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the cleaned panels and shows nothing about what the storm did to the uncleaned ones.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Output of the never-cleaned panels fell from 93% in May to 86% in June, so this reverses the graph.
explanation.C: Correct. It compares the two kinds of panels just before and just after the storm and shows the uncleaned panels nearly matching the cleaned ones once the rain had fallen.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (95, 88, 81, 74), but it shows the damage done by dust before the storm, not the recovery that the rain produced.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians have long debated how much the arrival of the railway shaped the growth of towns in nineteenth-century Germany, where thousands of kilometers of track were laid between 1840 and 1880. Skeptics point out that in one western region, towns without a railway station added more residents between 1850 and 1880 than towns with one did. Historian Wiebke Lorenz considers this comparison misleading, because the towns without stations were far larger to begin with. Measured relative to their starting size, she argues, the towns that had gained a station by 1855 grew about twice as fast as those that had not.

data.title: Average Population of Towns in One Western German Region

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Lorenz's argument?

choices.A: In every year shown, towns without a station were larger on average than towns with a station.
choices.B: From 1850 to 1880, towns with a station added more residents than towns without a station did.
choices.C: From 1850 to 1880, towns with a station grew by about 64%, while towns without one grew by about 33%.
choices.D: From 1850 to 1880, towns without a station added about 3,200 residents, while towns with a station added about 2,700.

explanation.why: Lorenz rejects comparing the number of residents added and instead compares growth relative to starting size, so support must express each group's growth as a percentage. Towns with a station grew from 4,200 to 6,900, an increase of 2,700, or about 64%; towns without one grew from 9,600 to 12,800, an increase of 3,200, or about 33%. The first rate is roughly twice the second.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it supports only Lorenz's point about starting size, not her claim about how fast each group grew.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Towns with a station added 2,700 residents, fewer than the 3,200 added by towns without one, so this reverses the table.
explanation.C: Correct. It compares growth relative to each group's starting size and shows towns with a station growing at about twice the rate of the others.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it is the skeptics' comparison of residents added, which Lorenz calls misleading; it says nothing about growth relative to size.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A mushaira is a gathering at which Urdu poets recite their work before a live audience, which traditionally responds aloud to favorite lines. When a literary society in Karachi began streaming its annual mushaira online in 2015, some members worried that the stream would empty the hall. Cultural historian Sadia Mirza, who examined the society's attendance and viewing figures, argues that those worries proved unfounded and that the stream's growing audience came mainly from viewers outside Pakistan rather than from people in Pakistan who might otherwise have attended in person.

data.title: Audience for a Karachi Literary Society's Annual Mushaira

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Mirza's argument?

choices.A: In-person attendance rose in each year shown, from 3,100 in 2015 to 3,300 in 2019.
choices.B: In 2019, the mushaira's online viewers outnumbered its in-person attendees by more than seven to one.
choices.C: From 2015 to 2019, viewers abroad increased by about 16,000 and those in Pakistan by fewer than 2,000, while in-person attendance did not decline.
choices.D: Online viewers in Pakistan outnumbered online viewers abroad in every year shown.

explanation.why: Mirza's argument has two parts: the stream did not empty the hall, and the stream's growth came mainly from abroad rather than from within Pakistan. Support needs all three series. Viewers abroad rose from 2,200 to 18,500 (about 16,000), viewers in Pakistan rose from 4,000 to 5,900 (1,900), and in-person attendance went from 3,100 to 3,300.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it addresses only the first part of Mirza's argument, not where the stream's growing audience came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (24,400 versus 3,300), but the size of the online audience says nothing about where its growth came from or whether the hall emptied.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows that growth abroad far outpaced growth in Pakistan and that the hall did not empty, covering both parts of Mirza's argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Viewers abroad outnumbered viewers in Pakistan in 2017 (9,800 versus 5,100) and 2019 (18,500 versus 5,900), so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: science
items.passage: After Pacific salmon spawn and die, their decaying bodies release nitrogen carried from the ocean into the streams, and some of that nitrogen reaches the trees along the banks. Ecologist Hana Kowalczyk hypothesizes that this marine nitrogen speeds tree growth. Because waterfalls prevent salmon from swimming farther upstream, she compared trees below and above the falls on two Alaskan streams. She measured the share of leaf nitrogen that came from the ocean and, since soil moisture also affects growth, the moisture of the soil as well. Kowalczyk's data support her hypothesis while making soil moisture an unlikely alternative explanation: ______

data.title: Streamside Trees below and above Waterfalls on Two Alaskan Streams

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: trees below the falls on Stream 1 grew faster than trees in any other section of either stream, and their leaves held the most ocean nitrogen.
choices.B: on both streams, soil moisture was higher above the falls, where salmon cannot reach, than below the falls.
choices.C: trees along Stream 1 grew faster, on average, than trees along Stream 2 did.
choices.D: on both streams, trees below the falls grew faster and held more ocean nitrogen, yet soil there was moister on only one stream.

explanation.why: The statement makes two claims: the data support a link between marine nitrogen and growth, and they rule out soil moisture as the explanation. The completion must therefore show growth tracking nitrogen on both streams while moisture does not. Below the falls, growth (2.4 and 2.1 mm) and ocean nitrogen (22% and 18%) exceed the figures above the falls (1.5 and 1.4 mm; 3% and 2%), but soil was moister below the falls only on Stream 1 (31% versus 30%), not on Stream 2 (27% versus 33%).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a single section cannot show a pattern across both streams, and it says nothing about soil moisture.
explanation.B: Incorrect. On Stream 1, soil moisture was 31% below the falls and 30% above them, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (averages of 1.95 and 1.75 mm), but comparing the two streams ignores the below-versus-above comparison that the hypothesis depends on.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows growth and ocean nitrogen rising together below the falls on both streams while soil moisture follows no consistent pattern, which supports the hypothesis and undercuts the alternative.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Women now make up more than half of the medical students at a large public university in Chile but only about a quarter of its engineering students, and observers often cite the contrast as evidence that engineering has resisted change. Sociologist Paula Briones, examining the university's enrollment records since 1980, argues that this familiar contrast between the two fields conceals a reversal in their recent trajectories. Medicine, where women's share climbed rapidly from 1980 to 2000, has changed relatively little since then, she contends, whereas engineering, where change was slow over those two decades, has since gained more ground than medicine has.

data.title: Women's Share of Students in Two Fields at a Public University in Chile

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Briones's argument?

choices.A: Women's share of engineering students nearly tripled between 1980 and 2020.
choices.B: In every year shown, women made up a larger share of medical students than of engineering students.
choices.C: Women's share of medical students grew more from 2000 to 2020 than it had from 1980 to 2000.
choices.D: Medicine gained 23 points from 1980 to 2000 and then 4 points by 2020; engineering gained 7 points and then 9.

explanation.why: Briones's claim is about a reversal: medicine gained faster than engineering from 1980 to 2000, but engineering has gained more since 2000. Support must compare the gains of both fields in both periods. Medicine rose 23 points (28 to 51) and then 4 (51 to 55); engineering rose 7 points (9 to 16) and then 9 (16 to 25).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (9% to 25%), but it describes engineering over the whole period and cannot show that its pace overtook medicine's after 2000.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it is the familiar contrast that Briones says conceals the real pattern; it says nothing about how fast each field changed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Medicine gained 23 points from 1980 to 2000 but only 4 from 2000 to 2020, so this reverses the graph.
explanation.D: Correct. It gives both fields' gains in both periods and shows medicine ahead before 2000 and engineering ahead after, which is the reversal Briones describes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Tadpoles of many frog species grow deeper tails when predators are near, a change that helps them escape. Because dragonfly larvae prey on tadpoles, one might suppose that the mere presence of the larvae is enough to trigger the change. Ecologist Kwame Asante doubts this. He argues that tadpoles respond chiefly to chemical cues released when a predator eats other tadpoles, not to the presence of a predator as such, and still less to general disturbance. To test this, he raised tadpoles under four conditions and measured them after three weeks.

data.title: Tadpole Measurements after Three Weeks under Four Conditions

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Asante's argument?

choices.A: Stirring the water every day increased tail depth by only 0.1 mm compared with the control.
choices.B: Tadpoles kept near caged dragonfly larvae had deeper tails than control tadpoles, whether the larvae were fed snails or fed tadpoles.
choices.C: Tadpoles near larvae fed tadpoles had the shortest bodies but not the deepest tails of any group.
choices.D: Tails were 1.2 mm deeper with tadpole-fed larvae than with snail-fed larvae, more than twice the gap between snail-fed and control.

explanation.why: Asante's key claim is that the response comes chiefly from cues released when predators eat tadpoles, not from the predator's presence. The test of that is to compare the two predator conditions, which differ only in what the larvae ate, and to set that difference against the effect of presence alone. Larvae fed tadpoles produced tails 5.8 − 4.6 = 1.2 mm deeper than larvae fed snails, while snail-fed larvae raised tail depth only 4.6 − 4.1 = 0.5 mm above the control.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it rules out only general disturbance; it says nothing about whether presence or diet cues drive the response.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it treats both predator conditions alike, and the snail-fed result shows that presence alone has some effect, which does not help show that diet cues matter most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Tadpoles near larvae fed tadpoles had the deepest tails (5.8 mm) of any group, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Correct. It isolates the effect of what the predator ate and shows that this effect is much larger than the effect of the predator's mere presence.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Painters in the seventeenth-century Dutch Republic turned out landscapes in enormous numbers, often working quickly in standardized formats, and in estate inventories from Amsterdam a landscape was, by the 1680s, valued at only a small fraction of what a history painting, depicting a scene from the Bible, mythology, or the past, would fetch. Art historian Femke Dijkstra, who compiled the values recorded in hundreds of such inventories, argues that this widening gap reflected changes in the market for landscapes alone: landscapes grew steadily cheaper, she contends, while the prices of history paintings scarcely moved.

data.title: Average Values of Paintings in Amsterdam Estate Inventories

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Dijkstra's argument?

choices.A: The average value of landscapes fell in every decade from the 1630s to the 1680s.
choices.B: The gap between the two kinds of painting widened mainly because history paintings became more expensive over the period.
choices.C: Landscapes fell from 24 to 11 guilders on average, while history paintings stayed between 58 and 63 guilders.
choices.D: History paintings were valued at least twice as highly as landscapes on average in every decade shown.

explanation.why: Dijkstra's argument explains the widening gap by pointing to one series only: landscapes fell while history paintings held steady. Support must describe both lines, showing a decline in one and stability in the other. Landscapes dropped from 24 to 11 guilders, while history paintings stayed between 58 and 63 guilders throughout.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it covers only half of the argument; the gap could also have widened partly because history paintings rose.
explanation.B: Incorrect. History paintings were worth 60 guilders in both the 1630s and the 1680s, so the gap widened because landscapes fell, the opposite of this choice.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows the decline in landscape values alongside nearly flat values for history paintings, which is exactly the pattern Dijkstra describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but a constant ratio of at least two to one says nothing about which kind of painting changed in value.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the hills of central Nepal, the red flowers of the tree rhododendron, Nepal's national flower, have long marked the arrival of spring. Botanist Prakash Gurung compiled records of first flowering at two sites in the Annapurna region, one at 2,000 meters above sea level, among terraced farmland, and one at 3,200 meters, in high forest. Gurung argues that although rhododendrons now bloom earlier at both elevations than they did in 1990, the shift has been far greater at the higher site, a pattern he attributes to faster warming at high elevations.

data.title: Average First Flowering Date of Tree Rhododendrons in the Annapurna Region

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Gurung's argument?

choices.A: At the lower site, rhododendrons first flowered earlier in 2020 than in any other year shown.
choices.B: In every year shown, rhododendrons at the higher site first flowered later in the year than those at the lower site.
choices.C: From 1990 to 2020, first flowering came 22 days earlier at the higher site but only 7 days earlier at the lower one.
choices.D: The gap between the first flowering dates at the two sites widened from 1990 to 2020.

explanation.why: Gurung's argument compares the size of the shift at the two sites: both now bloom earlier, but the higher site has shifted far more. Support must compare how much each line changed. A lower day number means earlier flowering: the higher site moved from day 128 to day 106 (22 days earlier), while the lower site moved from day 75 to day 68 (7 days earlier).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the lower site and gives no comparison with the higher site.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it is expected at a colder site and says nothing about how much flowering has shifted at each elevation.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows that flowering moved earlier at both sites and that the shift at the higher site was about three times as large.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The gap shrank from 53 days (128 − 75) to 38 days (106 − 68), so this reverses the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1840s and 1850s, travelers between Liverpool and New York could cross the Atlantic either on a sailing packet, a sailing ship that departed on a fixed schedule, or on a steamship. Because the prevailing winds over the North Atlantic blow from west to east, sailing ships took much longer on the westbound voyage to New York than on the eastbound return. Historian Aurelio Pinto argues that steam's advantage was therefore uneven: steamships saved travelers far more time on the westbound crossing, where sailing ships fought the wind, than on the eastbound one.

data.title: Average Crossing Times between Liverpool and New York (days)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Pinto's argument?

choices.A: In both decades, steamships saved 21 or 22 days westbound but only 9 or 10 days eastbound.
choices.B: Sailing packets took 13 to 14 days longer to cross westbound than eastbound in both decades.
choices.C: Both kinds of ships made faster crossings in both directions in the 1850s than they had in the 1840s.
choices.D: In the 1850s, steamships' time advantage over sailing packets was greater eastbound than westbound.

explanation.why: Pinto's claim concerns the time steamships saved, which is the difference between packet and steamship times in each direction. Support must compute that saving for both directions and compare them. Westbound, steamships saved 37 − 16 = 21 days in the 1840s and 35 − 13 = 22 in the 1850s; eastbound, they saved only 23 − 14 = 9 and 22 − 12 = 10 days.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares the time steamships saved in each direction and shows the saving was more than twice as large westbound.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it repeats the premise about sailing ships and the wind; it does not compare sailing ships with steamships, which Pinto's claim requires.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but improvement over time says nothing about whether steam's advantage differed by direction.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In the 1850s steamships saved 10 days eastbound but 22 days westbound, so this reverses the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the fynbos, the shrubland of South Africa's Western Cape, many plants keep seeds dormant in the soil for years and germinate only after a fire. Fires return to most patches of fynbos at intervals of a decade or more. A fire offers buried seeds two distinct signals: the heat that passes into the soil and the chemicals carried in smoke. Botanist Thandiwe Ndlovu exposed seeds of two fynbos plants, a reedlike restio and a legume, to heat alone, smoke alone, both, or neither. She concluded that the two species respond to different fire cues: ______

data.title: Germination of Two Fynbos Species after Four Treatments

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: both species germinated at their highest rates when their seeds were exposed to heat and smoke together rather than to either cue alone.
choices.B: smoke alone raised the restio's germination from 6% of seeds to 48% of seeds.
choices.C: smoke alone raised the restio's germination from 6% to 48% but barely affected the legume's, whereas heat alone did the reverse.
choices.D: heat alone raised the restio's germination by more percentage points than smoke alone did.

explanation.why: Ndlovu's conclusion is a contrast: each species responds to a different cue. The completion must show each cue working for one species but not the other, which means comparing the single-cue bars with the untreated bars for both species. Smoke alone lifted the restio from 6% to 48% but the legume only from 4% to 5%, while heat alone lifted the legume from 4% to 55% but the restio only from 6% to 7%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (51% and 57%), but it shows the two species behaving alike, which does nothing to show that they respond to different cues.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes one species and one cue; without the legume's results it cannot show that the species respond differently.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows smoke working for the restio but not the legume and heat working for the legume but not the restio, which is exactly the contrast Ndlovu draws.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Heat alone raised the restio only from 6% to 7%, while smoke alone raised it to 48%, so this reverses the graph.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Radishes grow quickly, which makes them useful for testing how much water a crop needs. Gardener Hanna Virtanen planted 40 radish seeds in each of four raised beds in Tampere, Finland, and watered each bed on a different schedule for five weeks. She then weighed all the radishes harvested from each bed. In her trial, the heaviest total harvest came from the bed watered ______

data.title: Radish Harvest under Four Watering Schedules (40 seeds per bed)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: every 7 days, which produced the smallest number of radishes.
choices.B: every 3 days, which produced the heaviest radishes.
choices.C: every 2 days, which produced 3.9 kilograms of radishes.
choices.D: every day, when 36 radishes were harvested.

explanation.why: The statement is about the heaviest total harvest, so look at the "Total harvest (kg)" column and find the largest value. The largest is 3.9 kilograms, in the "Every 2 days" row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The bed watered every 7 days gave the lightest harvest (1.4 kilograms), not the heaviest.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table has no bed watered every 3 days.
explanation.C: Correct. The bed watered every 2 days produced 3.9 kilograms, more than any other bed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This number is accurate, but it counts radishes rather than weighing them, and the daily-watered bed's 3.1 kilograms is less than 3.9.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2023, officials in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, installed lamps along a cycle track in a city park that had been unlit after sunset. Planner Nadia Akhtar counted the cyclists using the track during the same two-hour evening period on one weekday in each month, both before and after the lamps were switched on in April. Akhtar reports that evening use of the track rose sharply once the lighting was installed: ______

data.title: Evening Cyclists Counted on a Rawalpindi Park Track, 2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the count was lower in June than it had been in February.
choices.B: the count rose from 38 cyclists in February to 42 in March.
choices.C: the count rose from about 40 cyclists before April to well over 100 afterward.
choices.D: most of the cyclists counted after April were commuters returning from work.

explanation.why: The statement says use rose sharply after the lamps were installed in April, so the choice must compare the months before April with the months after. The graph shows 38 and 42 cyclists in February and March and 117 and 131 in May and June.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The graph shows 131 cyclists in June and only 38 in February, so June was much higher, not lower.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Both of these months come before the lamps were installed, so this small rise says nothing about the effect of the lighting.
explanation.C: Correct. The counts went from about 40 per evening before the lighting to 117 and 131 after it, a sharp rise.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows only how many cyclists were counted, not why they were riding.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Potters know that the temperature inside a kiln affects how finished pieces turn out. Ceramics instructor Teodora Ilić fired 30 identical clay bowls at each of four temperatures in her studio in Belgrade, Serbia, and counted how many bowls came out cracked. She also noted how the glaze looked on the bowls that survived. According to her results, the fewest bowls cracked when the kiln was set to ______

data.title: Results of Firing 30 Clay Bowls at Four Kiln Temperatures

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 1,100°C, where only 2 of the 30 bowls cracked.
choices.B: 1,300°C, the highest temperature in the test.
choices.C: 900°C, where 7 of the 30 bowls cracked.
choices.D: 1,200°C, which produced a glossy finish on the bowls.

explanation.why: The statement asks for the temperature at which the fewest bowls cracked, so find the smallest number in the "Bowls cracked" column. That number is 2, in the 1,100°C row.
explanation.A: Correct. Only 2 bowls cracked at 1,100°C, fewer than at any other temperature in the table.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table does not include a firing at 1,300°C; the highest temperature tested was 1,200°C.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The most bowls cracked at 900°C, so this is the opposite of what the statement needs.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The glaze at 1,200°C was glossy, but 6 bowls cracked at that temperature, more than the 2 that cracked at 1,100°C.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Seabird biologists count penguin nests each year to track how colonies are changing. Biologist Rafael Benítez surveyed Magellanic penguin colonies on two small islands off the coast of Argentina every breeding season from 2020 to 2023. He noted that the two colonies did not follow the same trend over those years: ______

data.title: Magellanic Penguin Nests Counted on Two Islands, 2020–2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the Isla Sur colony shrank because fish became scarcer in the waters around the island.
choices.B: Isla Norte had more nests than Isla Sur in every year from 2020 to 2023.
choices.C: the number of nests on Isla Sur grew each year, while the number on Isla Norte fell each year.
choices.D: the number of nests on Isla Norte grew each year, while the number on Isla Sur fell each year.

explanation.why: The statement says the two colonies did not follow the same trend, so the choice must describe how each colony changed over time. The Isla Norte line rises every year (1,450 to 1,690), while the Isla Sur line falls every year (980 to 870).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The graph shows nest counts only; it says nothing about the fish supply.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares the sizes of the colonies rather than their trends, so it does not show that they changed differently.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This swaps the two islands: Isla Norte is the colony that grew, and Isla Sur is the one that shrank.
explanation.D: Correct. Isla Norte rose from 1,450 to 1,690 nests while Isla Sur fell from 980 to 870, so the two colonies moved in opposite directions.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Quito, Ecuador, is built on steep hillsides, and residents of some high neighborhoods ride cable cars to reach the city center. Transportation researcher Lucía Andrade recorded how many passengers rode one cable car line on each day of a week in March 2024. She observed that the line carried far more passengers on weekdays than on the weekend: ______

data.title: Daily Passengers on a Quito Cable Car Line, One Week in March 2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: ridership on Sunday was about 4,100, more than on any weekday.
choices.B: about 10,000 passengers rode on each weekday, compared with about 5,200 on Saturday and 4,100 on Sunday.
choices.C: ridership was highest on Thursday, when about 10,300 passengers rode the line.
choices.D: most weekday passengers were traveling to jobs in the city center.

explanation.why: The statement compares weekdays with the weekend, so the choice must give figures for both. The bars for Monday through Friday are all close to 10,000, while Saturday is about 5,200 and Sunday about 4,100.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Sunday was the lowest day on the graph, not the highest.
explanation.B: Correct. Every weekday bar is near 10,000 passengers, roughly double Saturday's 5,200 and more than double Sunday's 4,100.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes only one day and does not compare weekdays with the weekend.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows how many people rode, not where they were going.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Students sometimes cram all of their studying into one long session the night before a test. Psychology instructor Daniel Okoro asked 60 students in Abuja, Nigeria, to learn a list of 40 unfamiliar words. Half of the students studied for 60 minutes in one session, and the other half studied for 20 minutes on each of three days. Each group was tested right after its last session and again one week later. Okoro's results favored the group that spread out its studying: ______

data.title: Words Recalled by Two Study Groups (40 words on the list)
columns: Average words recalled right after studying
Average words recalled one week later

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: students in the three-session group reported feeling less nervous before the test.
choices.B: the one-session group recalled an average of 26 words one week later, compared with 17 for the three-session group.
choices.C: the one-session group recalled an average of 31 words right after studying.
choices.D: the three-session group recalled an average of 26 words one week later, compared with 17 for the one-session group.

explanation.why: The statement says the results favored the group that spread out its studying, so the choice must show that group doing better. In the "one week later" column, the three-session group recalled 26 words and the one-session group only 17.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table reports only words recalled; it says nothing about how students felt.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This swaps the two groups: it was the three-session group that recalled 26 words one week later.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes only the one-session group and, if anything, shows that group doing slightly better right after studying.
explanation.D: Correct. One week later, the three-session group remembered 26 words on average and the one-session group only 17, so spreading out the studying paid off.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Chitwan National Park in southern Nepal is home to greater one-horned rhinoceroses. Park ranger Bikram Tamang recorded rhino sightings in two sectors of the park during monthly patrols in early 2024, making one patrol in each sector every month. He reported that the riverside sector consistently produced more sightings than the hill sector: ______

data.title: Rhino Sightings per Monthly Patrol in Two Sectors of Chitwan National Park, 2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: sightings in the hill sector rose from 6 in January to 8 in March.
choices.B: in every month, the riverside sector produced at least 14 sightings, while the hill sector never produced more than 8.
choices.C: rhinos in the riverside sector were drawn by the tall grass growing along the water.
choices.D: in April, the patrol recorded 19 sightings in the hill sector and 7 in the riverside sector.

explanation.why: The statement says the riverside sector consistently had more sightings, so the choice must compare the two sectors across all the months. The riverside bars are 14, 17, 15 and 19, and the hill bars are 6, 5, 8 and 7, so the riverside sector was higher every month.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes a change within the hill sector and does not compare the two sectors.
explanation.B: Correct. The lowest riverside count (14) is higher than the highest hill count (8), so the riverside sector led in every month.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph records only how many rhinos were seen, not why they were there.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This swaps the sectors: the riverside sector had 19 sightings in April, and the hill sector had 7.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Coastal sand dunes protect the land behind them from storms, but foot traffic can flatten them. In 2021, a town on the west coast of Denmark fenced off one section of its beach dunes while leaving a neighboring section open to walkers. Geographer Mette Sørensen measured the average height of the dunes in each section every summer. Her measurements suggest that the fence helped the dunes grow: ______

data.title: Average Dune Height in Two Sections of a Danish Beach, 2021–2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the fenced dunes rose from 2.1 meters to 3.1 meters between 2021 and 2024, while the open dunes fell from 2.0 meters to 1.7 meters.
choices.B: the fenced dunes and the open dunes were almost exactly the same height in 2021, the year the fence was put up.
choices.C: beach grass spread across the fenced dunes within two years, holding the sand in place.
choices.D: the open dunes rose from 2.0 meters to 3.1 meters between 2021 and 2024, while the fenced dunes stayed the same.

explanation.why: To suggest that the fence helped, the choice must show the fenced dunes growing while the unfenced dunes did not. The fenced line climbs from 2.1 to 3.1 meters, and the open line drops from 2.0 to 1.7 meters.
explanation.A: Correct. The fenced section grew by a full meter while the open section lost height, which is what the statement needs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the starting point only and says nothing about what happened after the fence went up.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph measures only dune height; it says nothing about grass.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This swaps the two sections: it was the fenced dunes that rose to 3.1 meters, and the open dunes that stayed low.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Sialkot, Pakistan, produces a large share of the world's hand-stitched soccer balls. Industrial researcher Farhan Qureshi visited a workshop that stitches balls both by hand and with sewing machines and recorded the output of each method over one week. He found that a worker using a machine finished far more balls in a day than a hand stitcher did: ______

data.title: Output of Two Stitching Methods at a Sialkot Workshop
columns: Balls finished per worker per day

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 5 percent of the machine-stitched balls were rejected for flaws.
choices.B: machine stitchers were paid more per day than hand stitchers.
choices.C: a hand stitcher finished 11 balls per day, compared with 4 for a machine stitcher.
choices.D: a machine stitcher finished 11 balls per day, compared with 4 for a hand stitcher.

explanation.why: The statement compares how many balls each kind of worker finished in a day, so look at the "Balls finished per worker per day" column. Machine stitching shows 11 and hand stitching shows 4.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes flaws rather than how many balls were finished.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table shows the price of each ball, not what the workers were paid.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This swaps the two methods: the machine stitcher is the one who finished 11 balls a day.
explanation.D: Correct. A machine stitcher finished 11 balls a day, nearly three times the 4 finished by a hand stitcher.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Arctic foxes on the islands of Svalbard, Norway, raise their cubs in dens dug into hillsides, and the same dens may be used for many years. Ecologist Ingvild Haugen checked 25 known dens each summer from 2019 to 2023 and recorded how many were occupied by foxes with cubs. She noted that the number of occupied dens varied greatly from year to year: ______

data.title: Arctic Fox Dens Checked Each Summer on Svalbard (25 dens)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: the average number of cubs per occupied den was highest in 2020.
choices.B: fewer dens were occupied in years when the geese that foxes hunt were scarce.
choices.C: the number of occupied dens rose steadily from 9 in 2019 to 16 in 2023.
choices.D: as few as 4 dens were occupied in 2021, while 16 were occupied in 2020.

explanation.why: The statement is about how much the number of occupied dens changed from year to year, so the choice should contrast a low year with a high year in the "Dens occupied" column. The lowest value is 4 (2021) and the highest is 16 (2020).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it concerns cubs per den, not the number of dens occupied.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table says nothing about geese or any other food supply.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The number of occupied dens did not rise steadily; it was 16 in 2020, 4 in 2021 and 7 in 2023.
explanation.D: Correct. Occupancy ranged from only 4 dens in 2021 to 16 dens in 2020, a very large difference between years.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On the Greek island of Crete, olives are picked from late autumn into winter, and growers debate when to harvest. Agronomist Eleni Papadakis pressed olives picked from the same grove on four dates during one season and recorded how much oil each 100 kilograms of olives produced. A tasting panel also rated the oil from each date. Her results show that the oil yield was greatest for olives picked in ______

data.title: Oil Yield and Taste Rating of Olives Picked on Four Dates

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: February, after the olives had fully ripened on the trees.
choices.B: January, when each 100 kilograms of olives yielded 20 liters of oil.
choices.C: December, when each 100 kilograms of olives yielded 21 liters of oil.
choices.D: October, when the oil received the highest taste rating.

explanation.why: The statement asks when the oil yield was greatest, so look for the largest number in the "Oil per 100 kg" column. That is 21 liters, for the December 10 harvest.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table does not include a February harvest.
explanation.B: Incorrect. January's yield of 20 liters was close, but December's 21 liters was higher.
explanation.C: Correct. Olives picked on December 10 yielded 21 liters per 100 kilograms, more than on any other date.
explanation.D: Incorrect. October's oil did get the best taste rating, but its yield of 14 liters was the lowest in the table.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Public swimming pools give city residents a place to cool off, so their use may rise when temperatures climb. Officials in Madrid, Spain, recorded the number of visitors to one outdoor pool on each day of a week in July 2024, along with each day's highest temperature. The figures suggest that pool attendance followed the heat: ______

data.title: Visitors to a Madrid Outdoor Pool during One Week in July 2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: the two hottest days, Wednesday and Thursday, also drew the most visitors, 1,180 and 1,310.
choices.B: the pool stayed open for more hours on Thursday than on any other day of the week.
choices.C: attendance was lowest on Monday, when the high was 31°C, and highest on Tuesday, when it was 33°C.
choices.D: the high temperature rose from 31°C on Monday to 33°C on Tuesday.

explanation.why: The statement says attendance followed the heat, so the choice must link the temperature column to the visitor column. The hottest days, Wednesday (38°C) and Thursday (40°C), had the largest visitor counts, 1,180 and 1,310.
explanation.A: Correct. The highest temperatures and the highest visitor counts fall on the same two days, which is exactly what "followed the heat" means.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table gives no information about opening hours.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Monday was indeed the lowest day, but the highest attendance was on Thursday (1,310), not Tuesday (720).
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it mentions temperatures only, without the visitor numbers that the statement is about.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Reindeer calves born in spring must survive their first winter, when snow can bury the lichens they eat. Sámi herders in northern Sweden told ecologist Anna Lindgren that deep snow is less dangerous for calves than a hard crust of ice over the snow, which forms when rain falls in midwinter and then freezes. Lindgren compared calf survival across four winters in one herd. The herders' view is consistent with her data: ______

data.title: Winter Conditions and Reindeer Calf Survival in One Herd

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: the two winters with the most ice-crust days had the lowest calf survival, even though their snow was shallower than in the other two winters.
choices.B: calf survival was above 75 percent in two of the four winters and below 55 percent in the other two.
choices.C: calf survival was lowest in 2022–23, the winter with the shallowest snow of the four.
choices.D: the winter of 2021–22 had the deepest snow, 110 centimeters, and only 4 days with an ice crust.

explanation.why: The herders claim that ice crust, not deep snow, is the danger. Supporting data must show survival falling with crust days and not with snow depth. The winters with 19 and 23 crust days had survival of 54% and 49%, while the two deep-snow winters (95 and 110 cm) with few crust days had survival of 81% and 78%.
explanation.A: Correct. This links low survival to the ice-crust winters and shows that snow depth did not matter in the way one might expect, which is exactly the herders' point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it does not connect the survival figures to either snow depth or ice crust, so it cannot support the herders' explanation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The shallowest snow (60 cm) was in 2020–21, not 2022–23, so this misreads the table, and it points to snow depth rather than ice crust.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes a single winter and does not mention calf survival at all.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Bangladesh grows much of the world's jute, a plant fiber used for sacks and bags, and the government restricts thin plastic shopping bags. Economist Tahmina Rahman surveyed 40 grocery shops in Dhaka to learn what kind of bag each shop mainly gave customers in 2019 and again in 2023, after enforcement of the restrictions was tightened. She concluded that although plastic bags had become much less common, shops had replaced them mainly with paper bags rather than with jute ones: ______

data.title: Main Type of Bag Given to Customers by 40 Dhaka Grocery Shops

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: the number of shops mainly using paper bags rose from 6 to 19, while the number using jute bags rose only from 4 to 8.
choices.B: by 2023, more shops mainly used jute bags than paper bags, although plastic bags were still the most common.
choices.C: the number of shops mainly using thin plastic bags fell from 28 to 9, while the number using cloth bags rose from 2 to 4.
choices.D: the number of shops mainly using jute bags doubled, from 4 in 2019 to 8 in 2023.

explanation.why: Rahman's conclusion has two parts: plastic became rarer, and the replacement was mainly paper, not jute. The choice must therefore compare the growth of paper with the growth of jute. Paper went from 6 shops to 19 (up 13), while jute went from 4 to 8 (up only 4).
explanation.A: Correct. Paper gained 13 shops while jute gained only 4, which shows that shops turned mainly to paper.
explanation.B: Incorrect. In 2023, 19 shops mainly used paper and only 8 used jute, and plastic (9 shops) was no longer the most common.
explanation.C: Incorrect. These figures are accurate, but they concern plastic and cloth and say nothing about paper or jute, which the conclusion is about.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but on its own it shows jute growing and never mentions paper, so it cannot show that paper, not jute, took plastic's place.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Publishers often assume that listeners give up on long audiobooks more readily than readers give up on long books. Reading researcher Olivia Brennan tested this idea with records from a library app in Dublin, Ireland, that tracks how far users get in both e-books and audiobooks. For each range of book lengths, she calculated the share of borrowers who finished the book. Brennan found that the assumption held only for the longest books: ______

data.title: Share of Library App Borrowers Who Finished a Book, by Format and Length

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: audiobook borrowers finished books in every length range at a lower rate than e-book borrowers did.
choices.B: for books over 500 pages, only 41 percent of e-book borrowers and 29 percent of audiobook borrowers finished.
choices.C: the share of borrowers finishing fell as books got longer for both e-books and audiobooks.
choices.D: audiobook borrowers finished at equal or higher rates than e-book borrowers for books up to 500 pages, but at a much lower rate for books over 500 pages.

explanation.why: The statement says the assumption (that listeners give up more readily) held only for the longest books, so the choice must show both halves: no audiobook disadvantage for shorter books and a clear one for the longest. For the first three rows the audiobook rate is higher (74 vs. 71, 65 vs. 63, 54 vs. 52); for books over 500 pages it is much lower (29 vs. 41).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the table: for the three shorter ranges, audiobook borrowers finished at a slightly higher rate, not a lower one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This shows the longest books only, so it supports the assumption without showing that it failed for shorter books, which "only" requires.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes length alone and never compares the two formats, which is what the assumption is about.
explanation.D: Correct. This shows that audiobooks matched or beat e-books up to 500 pages and fell far behind only for the longest books, exactly what the statement needs.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Seed vaults keep crop seeds in cold storage so that old varieties can be regrown decades later. Plant scientist Yusuf Demir tested wheat seeds that had been stored at a research institute in Ankara, Turkey, for different lengths of time, some at 4°C and some at −18°C. He planted 100 seeds from each batch and counted how many sprouted. Demir concluded that the colder storage, which costs more to maintain, is worth the expense mainly for seeds kept for very long periods: ______

data.title: Wheat Seeds That Sprouted after Storage at Two Temperatures (100 seeds planted per batch)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: seeds stored at −18°C sprouted several days sooner after planting than seeds stored at 4°C.
choices.B: seeds stored at −18°C sprouted in greater numbers than seeds stored at 4°C after every length of storage.
choices.C: after 45 years in storage, 90 of the seeds kept at 4°C sprouted, compared with only 42 of the seeds kept at −18°C.
choices.D: the gap between the two temperatures was only 1 seed after 5 years of storage but grew to 48 seeds after 45 years.

explanation.why: Demir's conclusion is that the colder storage matters mainly for long storage periods, so the choice must show a small difference for short periods and a large one for long periods. After 5 years the difference is 97 − 96 = 1 seed; after 45 years it is 90 − 42 = 48 seeds.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table counts how many seeds sprouted, not how quickly they did so.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it suggests that colder storage helps at every period, which does not support the idea that it is worth the cost mainly for long storage.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This swaps the two temperatures: it was the seeds at −18°C that sprouted 90 times after 45 years.
explanation.D: Correct. A difference of 1 seed after 5 years versus 48 seeds after 45 years shows that the colder storage pays off mainly over very long periods.

items.subject: science
items.passage: City beekeeping is sometimes dismissed as a hobby that cannot produce much honey. Beekeeper and researcher Jonas Weber weighed the honey taken each month from hives on rooftops in Berlin, Germany, and from hives on a farm outside the city during one summer. He argued that rooftop hives are as productive over a season as rural ones, because the city's gardens and street trees keep flowering through late summer, after farm fields have finished blooming.

data.title: Honey Harvested per Hive from Rooftop and Farm Hives, One Summer

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Weber's argument?

choices.A: Farm hives produced slightly more honey per hive than rooftop hives did in both May and June.
choices.B: Rooftop hives produced less honey per hive than farm hives did in July and August.
choices.C: Rooftop hives produced their largest monthly harvest, 10 kilograms per hive, in June.
choices.D: Although farm hives produced slightly more honey in May and June, rooftop hives produced far more in July and August, when farm hives yielded only 4 and 2 kilograms.

explanation.why: Weber argues two things: rooftop hives match rural ones over the season, and the reason is that the city keeps flowering into late summer. Support must show the rooftop hives holding up in July and August while the farm hives drop off. Rooftop hives gave 9 and 7 kilograms in those months against 4 and 2 for the farm, which more than makes up for the farm's slight lead in May and June (totals: 34 kilograms rooftop, 26 farm).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows the farm hives doing better, so by itself it works against Weber rather than for him.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the graph: in July and August the rooftop hives produced more, not less.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This describes only one month for the rooftop hives and makes no comparison with the farm hives.
explanation.D: Correct. This shows the rooftop hives pulling well ahead in late summer, which is both why their season total matches the farm's and the pattern Weber's explanation predicts.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Bronze is made by mixing copper with a small amount of tin, and in the late Bronze Age both metals were shipped around the eastern Mediterranean in the form of ingots. Archaeologist Nikos Alexandrou catalogued the cargo of a merchant ship that sank off the coast of southern Turkey around 1300 BCE. He argued that the ship was carrying metal in roughly the proportions needed to make bronze, rather than whatever metal its crew happened to obtain, since bronze typically contains about ten parts copper to one part tin.

data.title: Cargo Recovered from a Late Bronze Age Shipwreck

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Alexandrou's argument?

choices.A: The ship carried nearly five times as many copper ingots as tin ingots.
choices.B: The ship carried 220 copper ingots, more pieces than of any other item in its cargo.
choices.C: The ship carried about 5,200 kilograms of copper and about 520 kilograms of tin, a ratio of roughly ten to one.
choices.D: The glass ingots on the ship weighed more in total than the tin ingots did.

explanation.why: Alexandrou's argument rests on the proportion of copper to tin matching the ten-to-one recipe for bronze. Proportions of metal are a matter of mass, so compare the "Total mass" figures: 5,200 kilograms of copper to 520 kilograms of tin is exactly ten to one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is accurate, but the ratio of pieces (220 to 48) is about 4.6 to 1, not 10 to 1; the ingots differ in size, so only their mass shows the proportion of metal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is accurate, but counting copper ingots against glass and resin says nothing about the ratio of copper to tin.
explanation.C: Correct. The masses of copper and tin stand in a ten-to-one ratio, which is the proportion bronze requires, just as Alexandrou claims.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This misreads the table: the glass ingots weighed 110 kilograms in total and the tin ingots 520 kilograms.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The railway between Colombo and Kandy in Sri Lanka climbs through hill country on a line opened in the nineteenth century. In 2022, the railway replaced old hand-operated signals on part of the route with an electronic system. Transport analyst Dilshan Perera compared the punctuality of the daily express trains in the year before and the year after the change. He concluded that the new signals helped, but that they addressed only part of the problem, since many delays were caused by landslides and track repairs rather than by signaling.

data.title: Delayed Express Trains on the Colombo–Kandy Line, by Cause of Delay
data.note: The electronic signals were installed during 2022.

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Perera's conclusion?

choices.A: Delays caused by landslides and track repairs fell sharply after the new signals were installed.
choices.B: The number of trains delayed by signal failures fell from 142 in 2021 to 31 in 2023.
choices.C: Delays from signal failures dropped from 142 to 31, but delays from landslides and track repairs stayed at about 120.
choices.D: The total number of delayed trains fell from 361 in 2021 to 250 in 2023.

explanation.why: Perera's conclusion has two parts: the signals helped, and they fixed only part of the problem because other causes remained. The support must show both: signal delays fell from 142 to 31, while landslide and track-repair delays stayed almost unchanged (118 and 121).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the table: landslide and track-repair delays went from 118 to 121, so they did not fall at all.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that the signals helped; it says nothing about the delays the signals could not fix.
explanation.C: Correct. This pairs the sharp drop in signal delays with the unchanged landslide and repair delays, supporting both halves of the conclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These totals are correct, but they show overall improvement without separating what the signals fixed from what they did not.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Kestrels, small falcons that hunt voles in open fields, nest in holes in trees and buildings, which are scarce on modern farmland. Ornithologist Petra Nováková placed nest boxes on 30 farms in the Czech Republic early in 2020 and recorded how many were used by kestrels each year, along with the average number of chicks that flew from each used box. She reported that kestrels took several years to adopt the boxes, but that once a box was in use, it produced chicks at a steady rate.

data.title: Kestrel Use of 30 Farm Nest Boxes, 2020–2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Nováková's report?

choices.A: The number of chicks fledged per used box rose steadily as more boxes came into use.
choices.B: Fewer than a third of the boxes were in use in 2021, the second year of the project.
choices.C: The total number of chicks fledged from all the boxes rose each year from 2020 to 2023.
choices.D: The number of boxes used climbed from 4 in 2020 to 23 in 2023, while chicks fledged per used box stayed near 4 every year.

explanation.why: The report has two parts: adoption was slow (the number of boxes used grew over several years) and output per box was steady. The support must use both columns: boxes used went 4, 9, 17, 23, while chicks per used box stayed between 3.8 and 4.1.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the table: chicks per used box did not rise steadily; it went 3.9, 4.1, 3.8, 4.0.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (9 of 30), but it describes a single year and says nothing about chicks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but a rising total only reflects more boxes being used; it does not show whether each box produced chicks at a steady rate.
explanation.D: Correct. The rising count of boxes used shows gradual adoption, and the nearly constant chicks per box shows the steady rate, so this supports both parts.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Peat bogs store large amounts of carbon, but many bogs in Ireland were drained for farming or fuel, and drained peat dries out and releases carbon dioxide. In 2018, conservationists blocked the drainage ditches on part of a bog in County Offaly to raise the water table. Soil scientist Ciara Doyle measured the water table and the carbon dioxide released from the soil each summer on both the restored section and an unrestored section. Doyle's data support the view that raising the water table reduces carbon release: ______

data.title: Water Table and Carbon Dioxide Release on Two Sections of an Irish Bog
data.note: Ditches on the restored section were blocked in autumn 2018.

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: in 2018, before the ditches were blocked, the two sections released almost the same amount of carbon dioxide.
choices.B: the restored section's water table rose from 48 to 9 centimeters below the surface and its carbon dioxide release fell from 6.2 to 1.4 tonnes, while the unrestored section changed little.
choices.C: in 2023, the water table in the unrestored section was 55 centimeters below the surface, deeper than it had been in 2018.
choices.D: carbon dioxide release from the restored section rose between 2018 and 2023 as its water table climbed toward the surface.

explanation.why: To show that raising the water table reduces carbon release, the choice must pair the rise in the restored section's water table with its falling carbon dioxide figures, and ideally contrast that with the unrestored section. From 2018 to 2023 the restored water table went from 48 to 9 centimeters below the surface while its release fell from 6.2 to 1.4 tonnes; the unrestored section stayed near 50 centimeters and 6.5 tonnes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the starting point before restoration and shows no effect of raising the water table.
explanation.B: Correct. This links the rising water table to the fall in carbon dioxide and uses the unrestored section to show that nothing similar happened without restoration.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes only the unrestored section's water table and never mentions carbon dioxide.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the data: carbon dioxide release from the restored section fell from 6.2 to 1.4 tonnes; it did not rise.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Editors at literary magazines often say that poetry is the hardest category in which to be published, because so many poems are submitted for so few pages. Editor Marguerite Dubois examined the submissions received by a quarterly magazine in Montreal, Canada, during 2023 to see whether this was true at her own magazine. She found that poetry was indeed the most competitive category, though not because it received the most submissions: ______

data.title: Submissions and Acceptances at a Montreal Literary Magazine, 2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: translations had the highest acceptance rate because the magazine struggled to find enough translators.
choices.B: short fiction received 2,840 submissions, more than any other category, and had the lowest acceptance rate.
choices.C: poetry had the lowest acceptance rate, 0.6 percent, even though short fiction received far more submissions.
choices.D: poetry received 1,960 submissions, the second-largest number of any category.

explanation.why: "Most competitive" means the smallest share of submissions accepted, so look at the acceptance rate column: poetry's 0.6 percent is the lowest. The statement adds that this was not because poetry had the most submissions, so the choice must also note that short fiction received more (2,840 versus 1,960).
explanation.A: Incorrect. Translations did have the highest rate, but the table offers no reason for it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Short fiction did receive the most submissions, but its acceptance rate (0.8 percent) was not the lowest; poetry's (0.6 percent) was.
explanation.C: Correct. Poetry's acceptance rate was the lowest of the four categories even though short fiction had far more submissions, which matches both parts of the statement.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but the number of submissions alone does not show how competitive a category is, and the statement says submissions were not the reason.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Salt marshes along the coast of Georgia, in the United States, are feeding grounds for wading birds such as herons and egrets. In 2019, a conservation group removed an old earthen dike from one marsh so that tides could flow across it again. Ecologist Darnell Whitaker counted wading birds on the restored marsh and on a nearby marsh that had never been diked during the same week each spring. He argued that the restored marsh was recovering, though it had not yet caught up with the undiked marsh: ______

data.title: Wading Birds Counted on Two Georgia Salt Marshes, 2019–2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the restored marsh had more wading birds than the undiked marsh by 2023, after rising every year since 2019.
choices.B: the undiked marsh had roughly 70 wading birds in every year from 2019 to 2023, with no clear trend.
choices.C: bird counts on the restored marsh rose from 12 in 2019 to 52 in 2023, still below the undiked marsh's roughly 70.
choices.D: bird counts on the restored marsh rose every year, from 12 in 2019 to 52 in 2023.

explanation.why: Whitaker's statement has two parts: the restored marsh is recovering (counts rising) and it has not yet caught up (still below the undiked marsh). The choice must give both: the restored line climbs from 12 to 52, while the undiked line stays near 70, so 52 is still well short of it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the graph: in 2023 the restored marsh had 52 birds, still below the undiked marsh's 70.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes only the undiked marsh and says nothing about whether the restored marsh is recovering.
explanation.C: Correct. The rise from 12 to 52 shows recovery, and the comparison with roughly 70 on the undiked marsh shows the gap that remains.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This shows the recovery but leaves out the comparison with the undiked marsh, so it does not support the "not yet caught up" part.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ancient Greek theaters were built as bowls of stone seats rising around a circular performance space, and visitors today still remark that an unamplified voice carries to the top rows. Acoustics researcher Sofia Karamanlis tested this reputation at a theater built in the fourth century BCE. She played recorded speech from the performance space and asked listeners seated in different rows to write down the words they heard. Her results show that clarity fell with distance, but only slightly, and that even the highest rows remained easy to understand: ______

data.title: Words Correctly Identified by Listeners in an Ancient Greek Theater

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: listeners in row 5 sat 15 meters from the performance space and identified 98 percent of the words correctly.
choices.B: listeners in row 5 identified fewer of the words correctly than listeners in row 45, who were 62 meters away.
choices.C: listeners in row 45, 62 meters away, identified 91 percent of the words correctly, compared with 98 percent for listeners in row 5.
choices.D: the theater's rows of seats rise far more steeply than the seating in a modern concert hall does.

explanation.why: The statement makes two claims: clarity dropped only slightly with distance, and the top rows were still easy to understand. The choice must compare a near row with a far one: 98 percent in row 5 versus 91 percent in row 45, a drop of only 7 points that still leaves the far rows above 90 percent.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it gives one row only, so it cannot show how clarity changed with distance.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the data: row 5 listeners identified more words (98 percent), not fewer, than row 45 listeners (91 percent).
explanation.C: Correct. Comparing 98 percent at 15 meters with 91 percent at 62 meters shows both the small decline and the high clarity in the top rows.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table says nothing about how steep the seating is or about concert halls.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Date palms in Khairpur District, in Pakistan's Sindh province, are traditionally watered by flooding the ground around each tree with canal water. Drip irrigation, which delivers water slowly through tubes to each tree's roots, is more expensive to install. Agricultural engineer Sana Soomro compared the two methods on neighboring plots of the same date variety for three seasons. She concluded that drip irrigation used far less water without reducing the harvest: ______

data.title: Water Use and Date Harvest under Two Irrigation Methods, per Tree

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: drip-irrigated trees used about 4,000 liters of water per season, less than half the amount used by flooded trees.
choices.B: flooded trees produced about 10,000 kilograms of fruit per tree each season, more than drip-irrigated trees did.
choices.C: drip-irrigated trees used less than half as much water as flooded trees each season, yet produced about the same amount of fruit, 70 to 74 kilograms per tree.
choices.D: drip-irrigated trees produced dates that sold for a higher price at market than those from flooded trees.

explanation.why: Soomro's conclusion has two parts: far less water and no loss of harvest. The support must use both the water and the fruit columns. Drip trees used 4,000 to 4,300 liters against 9,600 to 10,300 for flood trees, and their fruit (74, 70, 73 kilograms) was within a couple of kilograms of the flood trees' (72, 68, 75).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it covers only the water saving and never mentions the harvest, so it cannot show that yields were unaffected.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This misreads the table: about 10,000 is the number of liters of water a flooded tree used, not kilograms of fruit; the fruit figures are 68 to 75 kilograms.
explanation.C: Correct. This pairs the large water saving with nearly identical harvests, supporting both halves of the conclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table says nothing about prices.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Smart electricity meters can send readings to a small display in the home that shows how much power is being used at that moment. Energy researcher Callum Reid wanted to know whether simply seeing this information leads households to use less electricity. In Glasgow, Scotland, he recruited 400 households with smart meters and gave half of them a display at the end of January 2024; the other half received none. He then compared the two groups' average monthly electricity use. Reid reported that the display produced a modest saving that persisted through the year: ______

data.title: Average Monthly Electricity Use of Two Groups of Glasgow Households, 2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: households with a display used more electricity than households without one in every month after January.
choices.B: from March to November, households with a display used roughly 20 kilowatt-hours less per month than households without one.
choices.C: households with a display used about 310 kilowatt-hours in January, nearly the same as households without one.
choices.D: both groups used the most electricity in January and the least in July.

explanation.why: The statement needs a difference between the two groups that is modest and lasts through the year. Before the displays were installed (January) the groups were nearly equal; from March onward the "with display" line sits about 17 to 21 kilowatt-hours below the other line in every month shown.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the graph: after January, households with a display used less electricity, not more.
explanation.B: Correct. A steady gap of about 20 kilowatt-hours in every month from March to November is exactly a modest saving that persisted.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is accurate, but January is before the displays were handed out, so it shows no effect of the display.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the seasonal pattern shared by both groups and says nothing about the difference between them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the haors, the vast seasonal wetlands of northeastern Bangladesh, many families keep flocks of ducks that feed on snails and insects in the flooded fields. Agricultural economist Mahbub Hossain recorded egg production and feed purchases for a group of flocks over one year. He observed that the ducks laid best during the monsoon months, when the wetlands were flooded and the ducks could find their own food, and that this was also when families spent the least on purchased feed: ______

data.title: Egg Production and Feed Purchases for Haor Duck Flocks, per Duck
data.note: The wetlands are flooded from roughly June to September.

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: families bought the most feed in December, when they spent 48 taka per duck.
choices.B: in June and August, ducks laid 21 and 23 eggs per month, while families spent 45 and 48 taka per duck on feed.
choices.C: egg production rose from 12 eggs per duck in February to 14 in April.
choices.D: in June and August, ducks laid 21 and 23 eggs per month, the most of any months, while feed spending fell to 12 and 8 taka per duck, the least.

explanation.why: The statement links the monsoon months to two things: the most eggs and the least feed spending. The choice must give both for June and August, the flooded months in the table: 21 and 23 eggs (the highest values) and 12 and 8 taka (the lowest).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes feed spending in a dry month only and says nothing about eggs or the monsoon.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This misreads the feed column: 45 and 48 taka are the February and December figures; in June and August feed spending was 12 and 8 taka.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is accurate, but both months are before the monsoon, and it mentions neither the peak months nor feed spending.
explanation.D: Correct. The two monsoon months had the highest egg counts and the lowest feed spending, which is exactly what Hossain observed.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Obsidian, a volcanic glass that can be chipped into sharp blades, was prized by ancient toolmakers, and each volcanic source has a chemical signature that lets archaeologists trace a tool back to its origin. Archaeologist Rosa Mendieta analyzed obsidian tools from a settlement in central Mexico across four periods of its occupation. She argued that the settlement's trade links reached farther over time, as tools made from distant sources made up a growing share of the total.

data.title: Origin of Obsidian Tools from a Settlement in Central Mexico, by Period

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Mendieta's argument?

choices.A: Obsidian from distant sources was of higher quality than obsidian from sources near the settlement.
choices.B: Tools from sources within 100 kilometers made up the majority of the tools analyzed in every period.
choices.C: The share of tools from sources within 100 kilometers rose steadily across the four periods.
