choices.D: The share of tools from sources more than 300 kilometers away rose from 2 percent in the earliest period to 19 percent in the latest.

explanation.why: Mendieta's argument is that distant sources supplied a growing share of tools over time. The support must track a far-source share across the periods: the share from sources over 300 kilometers away rose from 2 to 6 to 12 to 19 percent (and the 100–300 kilometer share also grew).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table shows where tools came from, not how good the obsidian was.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it emphasizes how much local obsidian was used and says nothing about whether distant sources grew.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the data: the local share fell from 88 percent to 52 percent; it did not rise.
explanation.D: Correct. A share rising from 2 percent to 19 percent across the four periods shows distant sources becoming more important, as Mendieta argues.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A free telephone homework-help line in Toronto, Canada, is staffed by volunteer teachers on weekday evenings. Coordinator Priya Raman reviewed the call logs for one school term to decide how to schedule volunteers with different specialties. She found that math calls made up the largest share of calls in every hour, but that the balance shifted later in the evening, when science questions became much more common: ______

data.title: Calls to a Homework-Help Line during One Term, by Hour and Subject

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: English calls were most common in the 6–7 p.m. hour, when 48 English calls were received.
choices.B: math calls outnumbered science calls in every hour, but science calls rose from 22 in the 5–6 p.m. hour to 72 in the 8–9 p.m. hour.
choices.C: math calls peaked in the 6–7 p.m. hour, when 118 math calls were received.
choices.D: science calls outnumbered math calls in the 8–9 p.m. hour, the only hour in which math was not the largest category.

explanation.why: The statement makes two claims: math led in every hour, and science grew much more common later in the evening. The choice must show both. Math is the largest column in all four rows, and science climbs from 22 to 35 to 61 to 72 across the evening.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but English calls are not part of the statement, which concerns math and science.
explanation.B: Correct. Math leading in all four hours and science rising from 22 to 72 calls support both halves of the statement.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes math alone and says nothing about the rise in science calls.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This misreads the table: in the 8–9 p.m. hour there were 85 math calls and 72 science calls, so math still led.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Radio dramas, serialized plays performed for broadcast, remain popular in Ghana, where many listeners follow them on local stations. Media researcher Kofi Mensah surveyed 1,200 people in Accra about one drama that a station broadcast twice a day, at 7 a.m. and at 8 p.m., and also posted online. He expected the morning broadcast to attract the most listeners, since many people listen to the radio while traveling to work, but the survey showed otherwise: ______

data.title: How 1,200 Survey Respondents in Accra Followed a Radio Drama

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: respondents who followed the drama online heard an average of 2.6 episodes a week.
choices.B: the morning broadcast attracted more respondents than the evening broadcast and the online version combined.
choices.C: the evening broadcast attracted 610 respondents, more than twice as many as the morning broadcast's 290.
choices.D: 290 of the respondents followed the drama through the morning broadcast.

explanation.why: Mensah expected the morning broadcast to have the most listeners, and the statement says the survey showed otherwise. The choice must therefore show that another option beat the morning broadcast: 610 respondents followed the evening broadcast, compared with 290 for the morning one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it concerns how many episodes online followers heard, not which broadcast attracted the most listeners.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the table: the morning broadcast's 290 is far below the evening broadcast's 610 alone.
explanation.C: Correct. The evening broadcast's 610 respondents far exceed the morning broadcast's 290, which contradicts Mensah's expectation just as the statement says.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is accurate, but on its own it does not show that any other option drew more listeners than the morning broadcast.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On steep hillside farms in the highlands of Guatemala, heavy rains can wash topsoil away from fields left bare between harvests. Agronomist Rosa Menchú compared plots left bare after the maize harvest with plots sown with velvet bean, a cover crop that blankets the soil, measuring how much soil each kind of plot lost during the rainy season over three years. She concluded that the cover crop greatly reduced erosion on these slopes and that its protective effect held up even in the wettest year of the study.

data.title: Soil Loss on Hillside Plots during the Rainy Season
columns: Soil lost, bare plots (tons per hectare)
Soil lost, cover-crop plots (tons per hectare)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Menchú's conclusion?

choices.A: In 2022, the wettest year, bare plots lost 41 tons of soil per hectare while cover-crop plots lost only 9 tons.
choices.B: Cover-crop plots lost more soil in 2023 than they had lost in 2022.
choices.C: The cover crop also raised maize yields on the hillside plots in each of the three years.
choices.D: Bare plots lost the most soil in 2022, the year with the highest rainy-season rainfall.

explanation.why: Menchú's conclusion has two parts: the cover crop greatly reduced erosion, and the effect held up even in the wettest year. The support should compare bare and cover-crop plots in the year with the most rain. In 2022, rainfall was highest (1,420 mm), and bare plots lost 41 tons per hectare against 9 tons for cover-crop plots.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares the two kinds of plot in the wettest year and shows a large reduction, which supports both parts of the conclusion.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Cover-crop plots lost 8 tons in 2023 and 9 tons in 2022, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The table records rainfall and soil loss, not maize yields, so the data cannot support this.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes bare plots only; without the cover-crop figure it cannot show that the cover crop reduced erosion.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: For more than a century, a music publisher in Vienna, Austria, has sold printed sheet music for piano, much of it to students and amateur players. When the firm began selling digital downloads of the same scores in 2018, some employees feared that downloads would simply replace printed sales, leaving total sales unchanged. Business historian Lukas Pichler, who examined the firm's records, argues otherwise: in his view, the downloads reached customers whom the printed scores had never reached, so that total sales grew substantially while printed sales held nearly steady.

data.title: Piano Scores Sold by a Viennese Music Publisher

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Pichler's argument?

choices.A: In 2023, downloads outsold printed scores for the first time.
choices.B: Between 2017 and 2023, downloads grew from zero to 57 thousand while printed sales changed by only 3 thousand, so total sales nearly doubled.
choices.C: Downloads sold rose in every period shown, reaching 57 thousand in 2023.
choices.D: Most customers who bought downloads had never bought a printed score from the firm.

explanation.why: Pichler's argument is that downloads added sales rather than replacing printed ones. Supporting it requires both columns: printed sales must stay roughly level while downloads grow. Printed sales went from 62 to 59 thousand, downloads from 0 to 57 thousand, so total sales rose from 62 to 116 thousand.
explanation.A: Incorrect. In 2023 downloads (57 thousand) were still slightly below printed scores (59 thousand), so this misreads the table.
explanation.B: Correct. Nearly steady printed sales alongside strong download growth is exactly the pattern that shows downloads added to total sales rather than replacing printed ones.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but growth in downloads alone is consistent with the employees' fear; only the printed column shows that downloads did not replace printed sales.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is Pichler's explanation, but the table reports only numbers sold, not who the buyers were.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Oyster reefs once lined the shores of Chesapeake Bay, in the eastern United States, but harvesting and disease reduced many of them to scattered shells. Coastal engineer Dana Whitfield helped rebuild a reef along an eroding shoreline in Virginia and measured wave heights on both sides of it during storms. Because the reef lies below the surface at high tide, some of her colleagues expected it to protect the shore only at low tide. Whitfield reports instead that the reef lowered wave heights at every tide level she measured, though its effect was strongest when the water was lowest.

data.title: Storm Wave Heights on Either Side of a Rebuilt Oyster Reef

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Whitfield's report?

choices.A: Waves seaward of the reef were higher at high tide than they were at low tide.
choices.B: At high tide, waves shoreward of the reef were 38 cm, nearly as high as the 48 cm waves seaward of it.
choices.C: Shoreward waves were lower than seaward waves at all three tide levels, by 27 cm at low tide but only 10 cm at high tide.
choices.D: The reef reduced wave height by a greater amount at high tide than at low tide.

explanation.why: Whitfield's report makes two claims: the reef lowered waves at every tide level, and its effect was strongest at low tide. The evidence must compare the seaward and shoreward columns at all three levels. The reductions are 27 cm at low tide (42 to 15), 18 cm at mid tide, and 10 cm at high tide.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares seaward waves at different tides and says nothing about what the reef did to them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes high tide alone and stresses how small the effect was there, which does not show that the reef worked at every tide level.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows a reduction at all three levels and that the reduction was largest at low tide, supporting both parts of the report.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The reduction was 10 cm at high tide and 27 cm at low tide, so this reverses the pattern in the table.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In many towns in Bangladesh, drivers of pedal-powered three-wheelers have switched to battery-powered versions, which are faster and less tiring to operate but must be rented at a higher daily rate from the vehicles' owners. Critics argued that the switch mainly benefits the owners, since drivers hand over so much more in rent. Economist Farhana Chowdhury, who surveyed drivers in a district town, argues that the drivers themselves come out ahead: although their rental payments rise and they must pay to charge the batteries, she contends, the extra fares they collect more than cover these costs, leaving them with higher daily earnings than before.

data.title: Average Daily Figures Reported by Three-Wheeler Drivers in a District Town

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chowdhury's argument?

choices.A: Drivers of battery-powered vehicles paid three times as much daily rent as drivers of pedal-powered ones.
choices.B: After rent and charging costs, drivers of battery-powered vehicles kept about 680 taka a day, compared with about 550 taka for pedal-powered drivers.
choices.C: Battery-powered vehicles brought in 1,100 taka in fares per day, 450 taka more than pedal-powered vehicles did.
choices.D: Daily charging costs alone exceeded the extra rent that battery-powered drivers paid.

explanation.why: Chowdhury's claim concerns what drivers keep after costs, so the evidence must combine all three rows. A pedal driver keeps 650 minus 100, or 550 taka; a battery driver keeps 1,100 minus 300 minus 120, or 680 taka. Only the choice that completes this calculation shows that drivers come out ahead.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (300 versus 100 taka), but higher rent is the critics' point; on its own it suggests drivers are worse off.
explanation.B: Correct. Subtracting rent and charging from fares shows battery-powered drivers keeping 130 taka more per day, which is exactly what Chowdhury argues.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but extra fares alone do not show that drivers come out ahead, since the extra fares must cover 200 taka more rent and 120 taka of charging.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Charging cost 120 taka, while the extra rent was 200 taka, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In Phoenix, Arizona, summer asphalt can reach temperatures far above that of the air. City engineers coated several residential streets with a pale, reflective sealant in the hope of cooling the neighborhoods around them. Urban climatologist Marisol Vega measured surface and air temperatures on coated streets and on nearby untreated streets over several afternoons. She concludes that the coating works as a surface treatment but not as a neighborhood one: it lowers the temperature of the pavement itself substantially, she argues, while the air a pedestrian actually breathes, at head height, is scarcely any cooler.

data.title: Afternoon Measurements on Coated and Untreated Streets in Phoenix
rows: Air temperature at 1.5 m above pavement (°C)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Vega's conclusion?

choices.A: Air temperature at 1.5 meters was lower on coated streets than on untreated streets.
choices.B: On coated streets, the pavement surface was cooler than the air 1.5 meters above it.
choices.C: Coated streets reflected nearly three times as much sunlight as untreated streets did.
choices.D: Coated streets had pavement surfaces 12°C cooler than untreated streets but air at 1.5 meters only 0.4°C cooler.

explanation.why: Vega's conclusion contrasts a large effect on the pavement with a negligible effect on the air at head height. The evidence must report both differences: surface temperature fell from 64°C to 52°C, a 12-degree drop, while air temperature fell from 41.0°C to 40.6°C, less than half a degree.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it states only that the air was cooler; without the size of the difference it cannot show that the air was 'scarcely any cooler.'
explanation.B: Incorrect. The coated surface was 52°C and the air above it 40.6°C, so the surface was warmer, not cooler.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but reflectivity explains why the coating might work; it does not show what happened to either temperature.
explanation.D: Correct. It sets the large surface difference beside the tiny air difference, which is precisely the contrast Vega draws.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When a school district in the midwestern United States moved its high school start time from 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 a.m., some parents predicted that students would simply go to bed an hour later and gain no sleep at all. Sleep researcher Anika Rao, who had students log their bedtimes and wake times for two weeks before the change and two weeks after it, argues that the prediction was only partly borne out: students did stay up somewhat later, she acknowledges, but they shifted their bedtimes by much less than the full hour, so that their average nightly sleep still grew.

data.title: Student Sleep Logs before and after a Later School Start Time

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Rao's argument?

choices.A: Average bedtime shifted later by 20 minutes, far less than the hour the start time moved, and average sleep rose from 7.2 to 7.8 hours.
choices.B: Students reported feeling more alert in morning classes after the start time changed.
choices.C: Students went to bed later after the change, which left their average nightly sleep unchanged.
choices.D: Students' average wake time moved from 6:20 a.m. to 7:15 a.m. after the start time changed.

explanation.why: Rao concedes that bedtimes moved later but argues that the shift was much smaller than an hour and that sleep therefore increased. The evidence must show both the size of the bedtime shift (11:05 to 11:25 p.m., 20 minutes) and the gain in sleep (7.2 to 7.8 hours).
explanation.A: Correct. A 20-minute shift against a 60-minute change in start time, together with the rise in sleep, is exactly what Rao describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table reports bedtimes, wake times, and hours of sleep, not how alert students felt.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Average sleep rose from 7.2 to 7.8 hours, so it did not stay unchanged.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but a later wake time is simply what the new start time allows; it does not show whether students gave the gain back by staying up later.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Hand-knotted carpets from the Kashmir Valley are woven from a talim, a coded script that tells the weaver the color of every knot. Learning to read it is slow, and workshop owners often say that a weaver is not fully productive until several years into the trade. Textile scholar Nighat Mir, who timed weavers of different experience at a workshop near Srinagar, agrees that speed rises with experience, but she argues that most of the gain comes early: the largest jump, she contends, occurs within the first two years, after which weavers improve only gradually.

data.title: Weaving Speed by Experience at a Kashmiri Carpet Workshop

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Mir's argument?

choices.A: Weavers with under 1 year of experience tied fewer than half as many knots per hour as those with more than 10 years.
choices.B: Knots per hour rose by roughly equal amounts from each experience group to the next.
choices.C: Knots per hour rose by 310 between the first year and the second, but by only 160 across all the more experienced groups combined.
choices.D: Weavers with more than 10 years of experience tied the most knots per hour, 880.

explanation.why: Mir does not dispute that experienced weavers are faster; her specific claim is about timing: the big jump comes in the first two years and later gains are gradual. To support it, compare the size of the increases between rows. From under 1 year to 1–2 years, speed rises 410 to 720 (310 knots); from 1–2 years to more than 10, it rises only 720 to 880 (160 knots).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (410 versus 880), but a comparison of the two extremes shows that speed rises with experience, not that most of the rise happens early.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The increases are 310, 70, 60, and 30 knots, which are far from equal.
explanation.C: Correct. A 310-knot jump in the first two years against a 160-knot rise over all the later years shows that most of the improvement comes early.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but the most experienced group being fastest is what the workshop owners also believe; it says nothing about when the gains occur.

items.subject: science
items.passage: White storks that nest in Portugal once flew to Africa every autumn, but since open landfills began offering food all year, many have stopped migrating. Some ornithologists suspected that the birds which stay behind are those too weak for the journey and that they fare poorly in winter. Ecologist Inês Carvalho, who tracked storks fitted with transmitters over three winters, proposes the opposite: storks that winter in Portugal near landfills, she argues, survive the season about as well as migrants do and begin breeding earlier in spring, which gives them an advantage.

data.title: Winter Survival and Breeding of Tracked White Storks
rows: Stayed in Portugal, near a landfill
Stayed in Portugal, far from landfills

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Carvalho's proposal?

choices.A: Storks that migrated to Africa survived the winter at a higher rate than either group that stayed in Portugal.
choices.B: Storks near landfills laid their first eggs earlier than migrants because they did not need to recover from a long flight.
choices.C: Storks near landfills laid their first eggs about two weeks later than migrants did.
choices.D: Storks wintering near landfills survived at 90%, nearly matching the migrants' 91%, and laid their first eggs almost three weeks earlier.

explanation.why: Carvalho's proposal concerns one group, storks near landfills, and makes two claims about it: survival about equal to migrants' and earlier breeding. The evidence must compare that row with the migrants' row in both columns: 90% versus 91% survival, and March 14 versus April 2, about 19 days earlier.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (91% against 90% and 78%), but it stresses the migrants' advantage; the one-point gap with landfill storks is what Carvalho calls 'about as well,' and the choice ignores breeding dates.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The earlier egg date is in the table, but the table gives no reason for it; the explanation about recovering from a flight is not shown by the data.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Storks near landfills laid on March 14, before the migrants' April 2, so this reverses the table.
explanation.D: Correct. It compares the landfill group with the migrants on both survival and breeding date, supporting both parts of the proposal.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before railways, long-distance travelers in England rode stagecoaches on turnpike roads, which were maintained by trusts that collected tolls at gates. Historians have often assumed that a railway's arrival ruined the turnpikes in its path almost at once. Transport historian Eleanor Whitcombe, who studied the account books of one turnpike trust in the English Midlands, offers a more gradual picture: in her reading, the trust's income from stagecoaches collapsed within a few years of the railway's opening in 1838, but tolls from farm wagons and local carts held up, so total receipts declined far more slowly than the stagecoach figures alone would suggest.

data.title: Annual Toll Receipts of a Midlands Turnpike Trust

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Whitcombe's reading?

choices.A: Stagecoach tolls fell from £1,420 in 1836 to £180 in 1844, yet total tolls fell by only about a third, because wagon and cart tolls stayed near £2,000.
choices.B: By 1844, stagecoach tolls made up less than a tenth of the trust's total receipts.
choices.C: Tolls from wagons and carts declined steadily as farmers shifted their goods to the railway.
choices.D: Total tolls were lower in each year shown than in the year before the railway opened.

explanation.why: Whitcombe's reading combines three facts: stagecoach tolls collapsed, wagon and cart tolls held up, and so total receipts fell only slowly. The evidence must draw on all three columns. Stagecoach tolls fell from £1,420 to £180; wagon and cart tolls stayed between £2,030 and £2,110; total tolls fell from £3,470 to £2,210, about 36 percent.
explanation.A: Correct. It shows the collapse in stagecoach tolls, the steadiness of wagon and cart tolls, and the resulting modest fall in the total, supporting the whole reading.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (£180 of £2,210), but it shows only how far stagecoach tolls had collapsed, not that other tolls held up.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Wagon and cart tolls went £2,050, £2,110, £2,030, which is not a steady decline, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but a falling total is also what the 'immediate ruin' view predicts; without the breakdown by traffic it cannot show that the decline was gradual.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Roads divide hedgehog populations, and many hedgehogs are killed crossing them. In the Netherlands, wildlife tunnels beneath roads are usually built for badgers, and some ecologists doubted that hedgehogs, which are far smaller, would enter these wide tunnels. Ecologist Bram Vermeulen placed cameras at tunnel entrances and counted hedgehog crossings for a year along two stretches of road, one fitted with a few badger tunnels and one with small tunnels designed for hedgehogs. He argues that hedgehogs will use whatever tunnel is available, but that small tunnels placed close together serve them better than a few large ones do.

data.title: Hedgehog Use of Wildlife Tunnels along Two Stretches of Road
columns: Hedgehog crossings recorded in one year

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Vermeulen's argument?

choices.A: Hedgehogs crossed through the badger tunnels 212 times, but the section with small tunnels every 300 meters recorded 655 crossings.
choices.B: The badger tunnels were spaced three times as far apart as the small tunnels were.
choices.C: Hedgehogs used only the small tunnels, avoiding the badger tunnels entirely.
choices.D: Far fewer hedgehogs were killed on the road along Section 2 than along Section 1.

explanation.why: Vermeulen's argument has two parts: hedgehogs use even badger tunnels, and closely spaced small tunnels serve them better. The evidence must show substantial use of the badger tunnels (212 crossings) together with much heavier use of the closely spaced small tunnels (655 crossings).
explanation.A: Correct. The 212 crossings show that hedgehogs do use badger tunnels, and the 655 crossings show that the closely spaced small tunnels serve far more animals.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (900 meters versus 300), but spacing alone says nothing about how many hedgehogs used either kind of tunnel.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The badger tunnels recorded 212 crossings, so hedgehogs did not avoid them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This may be what Vermeulen hopes, but the table records tunnel crossings, not deaths on the road.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the hot, dry spring of interior Sindh, in Pakistan, chili growers raise seedlings in open nursery beds before transplanting them to the fields, and many seedlings wither under the midday sun. Horticulturist Saba Khaskheli compared open beds with beds covered by shade nets that block 30 percent or 50 percent of sunlight, recording how many seedlings survived to transplanting and how thick their stems grew, since thin-stemmed seedlings often fail after transplanting. She concludes that moderate shade is best: the 30 percent net raised survival at almost no cost to stem thickness, she argues, whereas the denser net saved about as many seedlings but left them noticeably thinner and weaker.

data.title: Chili Seedlings Raised under Different Levels of Shade

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Khaskheli's conclusion?

choices.A: Stem thickness was greatest under the 30 percent net.
choices.B: The 30 percent net raised survival from 61 to 84 percent while stem thickness barely changed, but under the 50 percent net stems were nearly a millimeter thinner.
choices.C: Both shade nets raised survival well above the 61 percent recorded in the open bed.
choices.D: Seedlings under the 50 percent net survived at the highest rate of the three beds.

explanation.why: Khaskheli's conclusion weighs two measures against each other: survival and stem thickness. The 30 percent net raised survival from 61 to 84 percent while thickness fell only from 3.1 to 3.0 mm; the 50 percent net raised survival only slightly further, to 86 percent, but thickness dropped to 2.2 mm. Only a choice using both columns for both nets can support this trade-off.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Stems were thickest in the open bed (3.1 mm), slightly above the 30 percent net (3.0 mm).
explanation.B: Correct. It shows the gain in survival with little loss of thickness under moderate shade and the sharp loss of thickness under dense shade.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it covers only survival; without stem thickness it cannot show why the 30 percent net is preferable.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (86 percent), but survival alone makes the denser net look best, which is the opposite of what Khaskheli concludes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Graphic designers are often told that a poster with strong contrast between lettering and background is remembered better than one in subtle, low-contrast colors. Design researcher Ewa Lisowska suspected that this rule ignores how posters are actually seen. She showed volunteers posters for an imaginary concert in two versions, high contrast and low contrast, either for a glance of two seconds or for a full twenty seconds, and later tested their recall of the concert's date and venue. She argues that contrast matters only for brief exposure: given time to read, she contends, viewers remember a low-contrast poster about as well as a high-contrast one.

data.title: Recall of Poster Details by Contrast and Viewing Time

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Lisowska's argument?

choices.A: At 2 seconds the high-contrast poster led by 27 percentage points, but at 20 seconds the gap shrank to 3 points.
choices.B: At 20 seconds, the low-contrast poster was recalled slightly better than the high-contrast one.
choices.C: Viewers recalled more details from the high-contrast poster than from the low-contrast one at both viewing times.
choices.D: Recall of the low-contrast poster more than doubled when viewing time rose from 2 to 20 seconds.

explanation.why: Lisowska's argument is about how the gap between the two posters changes with viewing time: large at a glance, nearly gone with time to read. The evidence must compare the gap at each time: 58 minus 31 is 27 points at 2 seconds, while 81 minus 78 is 3 points at 20 seconds.
explanation.A: Correct. A 27-point gap after a glance and a 3-point gap after twenty seconds shows contrast mattering only for brief exposure.
explanation.B: Incorrect. At 20 seconds the high-contrast poster was recalled slightly better (81 versus 78 percent), so this reverses the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but stating that high contrast won both times leaves out the size of each gap, which is what distinguishes her view from the usual rule.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (31 to 78 percent), but it describes the low-contrast poster alone; it does not compare the two posters at 20 seconds.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Ladakh, in the high mountains of northern India, herders move their yaks between pastures through the year. In some villages, families have long rotated among several high summer pastures, grazing each for only a few weeks; in others, herds remain on a single large summer pasture. Rangeland scientist Tsering Dolkar surveyed grass cover at the end of the grazing season on summer pastures of both kinds over four years. She argues that rotation protects the land: pastures grazed in rotation keep more of their grass cover and, unlike pastures under continuous grazing, show no steady decline from one year to the next.

data.title: Grass Cover on Summer Pastures at the End of the Grazing Season

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Dolkar's argument?

choices.A: Rotated pastures kept grass cover between 66 and 69 percent in every year, while continuously grazed pastures fell from 61 to 48 percent.
choices.B: Grass cover on rotated pastures rose steadily from 2019 to 2022.
choices.C: Yaks on rotated pastures gained more weight over the summer than yaks on continuously grazed pastures.
choices.D: In 2022, grass cover on continuously grazed pastures was 19 points lower than on rotated pastures.

explanation.why: Dolkar's argument has two parts: rotated pastures keep more cover, and they show no steady decline, unlike continuously grazed ones. The evidence must describe both lines across the years. The rotated line stays within 66–69 percent; the continuous line falls every year, from 61 to 48 percent.
explanation.A: Correct. It shows the rotated pastures holding steady and the continuously grazed pastures declining year after year, which supports both parts of the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The rotated line goes 68, 66, 69, 67, which is level, not a steady rise.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph shows grass cover only; it records nothing about the animals' weight.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (67 against 48), but a single year's gap cannot show that one kind of pasture is declining and the other is not.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Many primary schools in Glasgow, Scotland, run breakfast clubs that open before the school day and serve a free meal. The clubs are usually justified on grounds of nutrition, but education researcher Callum Fraser suspected that they also change when children arrive. At four schools that opened clubs in the autumn of 2022, he compared the share of pupils arriving late in the term before the clubs opened with the share in the following term, and he did the same at four similar schools without clubs. He argues that the clubs reduced lateness and that the change cannot be explained by a general trend affecting all schools that year.

data.title: Pupils Arriving Late at Eight Glasgow Primary Schools
columns: Pupils late, term before clubs opened (%)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Fraser's argument?

choices.A: In the term after the clubs opened, 8.1 percent of pupils at those schools arrived late, compared with 13.5 percent at the comparison schools.
choices.B: Pupils who attended the breakfast clubs performed better in reading tests than pupils who did not.
choices.C: Lateness at schools with new clubs fell from 14.2 to 8.1 percent, while at the comparison schools it barely changed, from 13.8 to 13.5 percent.
choices.D: Lateness fell at both groups of schools by similar amounts across the two terms.

explanation.why: Fraser makes two claims: lateness fell at the club schools, and the fall was not part of a general trend. Showing both requires the change over time in each group. Club schools dropped 6.1 points (14.2 to 8.1); comparison schools dropped only 0.3 points (13.8 to 13.5).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but comparing the two groups in one term alone cannot show that lateness fell; the club schools might simply have had less lateness all along.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table records lateness only; it says nothing about reading tests.
explanation.C: Correct. A large drop at the club schools beside an almost flat line at similar schools supports both the reduction and the ruling out of a general trend.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The comparison schools' lateness changed by only 0.3 points against 6.1 points at the club schools, so the amounts were not similar.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ground beetles that live in the hedgerows at the edges of farm fields prey on slugs, which damage young wheat. Because these beetles walk rather than fly, entomologist Hugo Lindqvist expected their benefit to fade with distance from the hedge. He trapped beetles and recorded slug damage at set distances into fields bordered by hedgerows and in a field with no hedgerow. His results, he argues, show a sharp boundary rather than a gradual fade: beetle numbers and protection from slugs are both high within about 20 meters of the hedge, but beyond that distance beetles are scarce and slug damage climbs to the level seen where there is no hedgerow at all.

data.title: Ground Beetles and Slug Damage at Increasing Distances from a Hedgerow

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Lindqvist's argument?

choices.A: Slug damage decreased steadily as distance from the hedgerow increased.
choices.B: At every distance sampled, the fields with hedgerows had less slug damage than the field with no hedgerow.
choices.C: Between 20 and 40 meters from the hedgerow, beetles per trap fell from 24 to 7 and slug damage rose from 8 to 19 percent, close to the 22 percent seen without a hedgerow.
choices.D: Beetle numbers were highest 5 meters from the hedgerow, at 31 per trap.

explanation.why: Lindqvist's specific claim is that the change is abrupt and located at about 20 meters, after which conditions match a field with no hedge. The evidence must show a small change between 5 and 20 meters, a large change between 20 and 40 meters, and values beyond 40 meters near the no-hedgerow figures (beetles 7 and 5 against 4; damage 19 and 21 against 22).
explanation.A: Incorrect. Damage rose with distance, from 6 to 21 percent, so this reverses the table.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true in the narrowest sense (21 percent at 80 meters against 22), but it suggests the hedge helps everywhere, whereas Lindqvist's point is that beyond 20 meters the benefit is essentially gone.
explanation.C: Correct. It locates the sharp drop in beetles and rise in damage between 20 and 40 meters and shows that beyond it damage nearly matches the field with no hedgerow.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but one reading near the hedge cannot show where the beetles' benefit ends or how sharply.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Owners of secondhand bookshops often say that literary fiction sells slowly while crime novels fly off the shelves, so a shop should take in all the crime it can. Bookseller Tomasz Nowicki, who kept detailed records at his shop in Kraków, Poland, questions the second half of that advice. Crime novels do sell faster, he acknowledges, but they are also what customers most often bring in to sell, so his shop acquires crime titles far more quickly than it can sell them and the shelves fill with unsold copies. Literary fiction, though slower to sell, arrives in such modest numbers that what comes in is roughly matched by what goes out.

data.title: Secondhand Books Bought and Sold at a Kraków Bookshop, 2023
columns: Average days on shelf before sale

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Nowicki's view?

choices.A: The shop sold nearly twice as many crime novels as literary fiction titles in 2023.
choices.B: Literary fiction was the only genre for which the shop sold more copies than it bought in.
choices.C: Crime novels sold after an average of 38 days on the shelf, less than half the time literary fiction took.
choices.D: The shop took in 750 more crime novels than it sold in 2023, whereas copies of literary fiction bought and sold were nearly equal.

explanation.why: Nowicki accepts that crime sells faster; his point is about the balance between what comes in and what goes out. The evidence must compare the 'bought in' and 'sold' columns for both genres: crime 2,400 in against 1,650 out (750 left over), literary fiction 900 in against 870 out (only 30 left over).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (1,650 against 870), but sales alone cannot show that crime piles up; that depends on how many copies came in.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Every genre sold fewer copies than it bought in (870 against 900 for literary fiction), so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (38 against 95 days), but it shows only that crime sells faster, which both Nowicki and the other owners accept.
explanation.D: Correct. The large surplus of unsold crime novels beside the near balance for literary fiction is exactly the pattern Nowicki describes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Beginning in 2013, a wasting disease killed most ochre sea stars along the Pacific coast of North America. Sea stars eat mussels, and in their absence mussel beds spread across rocks that had been open to other species. Marine ecologist Priya Natarajan, who has monitored tide pools on the Oregon coast since before the outbreak, argues that recovery is under way but incomplete in an important sense: the sea stars returning to her sites are overwhelmingly small juveniles, and because juveniles eat far fewer mussels than adults do, mussel cover has yet to fall even where sea star numbers have climbed back toward their earlier levels.

data.title: Sea Stars and Mussel Cover at Oregon Tide Pool Sites

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Natarajan's argument?

choices.A: Sea star numbers fell from 48 per 100 square meters in 2012 to 6 in 2015, when mussel cover rose to 35 percent.
choices.B: By 2021 sea star numbers were near their 2012 level, but about 70 percent were juveniles and mussel cover stayed at 45 percent, double the 2012 figure.
choices.C: Mussel cover began to decline once sea star numbers rose above their 2015 level.
choices.D: Juvenile sea stars at the sites grew more slowly than juveniles had before the outbreak.

explanation.why: Natarajan's argument links three facts: sea star numbers have nearly recovered, most of those sea stars are juveniles, and mussel cover has not fallen. The evidence must use all three columns for the recent years: 42 per 100 square meters in 2021 against 48 in 2012, 71 percent juveniles, and mussel cover at 45 percent against 22 percent in 2012.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the outbreak and its immediate effect, not the recovery that Natarajan is characterizing.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows recovered numbers, a juvenile-dominated population, and mussel cover still at its high level, which together support the argument.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Mussel cover rose from 35 to 44 and then 45 percent as sea star numbers recovered, so it did not decline.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table gives the share of juveniles, not how fast they grew.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: On the trekking routes of the Annapurna region of Nepal, porters carry visitors' baggage, and trekking companies generally limit the load a porter they employ may carry to 25 kilograms. Porters hired directly by independent trekkers are not bound by company rules, and some observers assumed that these porters simply carry whatever they are offered. Labor researcher Pemba Sherpa, who weighed porters' loads at a checkpoint on a popular route, argues that the company limit shapes expectations even where it does not apply: directly hired porters do carry more than company porters on average, he finds, but the difference is modest, and most of them still stay within the 25-kilogram limit.

data.title: Loads Carried by Porters Weighed at a Checkpoint in the Annapurna Region
data.note: Average load: company-hired porters 21.3 kg; directly hired porters 23.6 kg.

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Sherpa's argument?

choices.A: Seven percent of directly hired porters carried more than 30 kilograms, while no company-hired porter did.
choices.B: Directly hired porters averaged 23.6 kilograms against 21.3 for company-hired porters, and 74 percent of them still carried 25 kilograms or less.
choices.C: Most directly hired porters carried loads heavier than the 25-kilogram company limit.
choices.D: Directly hired porters were paid more per trip than company-hired porters were.

explanation.why: Sherpa's argument concedes a difference but insists it is modest and that most directly hired porters stay within the limit. The evidence must give both the size of the average difference (23.6 against 21.3 kilograms) and the share of directly hired porters at or under 25 kilograms (24 plus 50, or 74 percent).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it highlights the heaviest loads, which is the observers' picture; it says nothing about what most directly hired porters carry.
explanation.B: Correct. A difference of about two kilograms in the averages and a clear majority within the limit are exactly the two points Sherpa makes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only 26 percent of directly hired porters (19 plus 7) carried more than 25 kilograms, so most did not.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table records loads, not pay.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Great spotted woodpeckers excavate a fresh nest hole nearly every spring, leaving earlier holes empty. Many birds that cannot dig their own cavities, such as tits and starlings, nest in these abandoned holes. Ornithologist Katrin Hoffmann inspected old woodpecker holes of known age in a forest in Germany each spring and recorded whether another bird species was nesting inside. Some foresters assume that the holes decay quickly and are useful for only a season or two. Hoffmann argues instead that the holes remain in demand for years: occupancy by other species, she finds, is actually lowest in the first spring after excavation and rises as holes age, before eventually declining in the oldest holes.

data.title: Occupancy of Abandoned Woodpecker Holes by Other Bird Species
columns: Holes occupied by other bird species (%)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Hoffmann's argument?

choices.A: Occupancy fell steadily as holes aged, from 25 percent in the first year.
choices.B: Occupancy of holes more than 10 years old was about the same as occupancy of one-year-old holes.
choices.C: Holes aged 3 to 5 years were the most numerous in the sample and also the most often occupied.
choices.D: Only 25 percent of one-year-old holes were occupied, compared with 62 percent of holes aged 3 to 5 years and 55 percent of those aged 6 to 10.

explanation.why: Hoffmann's argument is that holes stay useful for years, with occupancy lowest at first and higher in older holes. The evidence must compare the occupancy of young holes with that of holes several years old: 25 percent at one year against 62 percent at 3–5 years and 55 percent at 6–10 years.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Occupancy rose from 25 to 48 and then 62 percent before falling, so it did not decline steadily.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (27 against 25 percent), but comparing the two ends says nothing about the high occupancy of holes in between, which is Hoffmann's point.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The number of holes inspected reflects how many Hoffmann could find, not how birds used them, and the choice does not compare occupancy across ages.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows the low occupancy of new holes and the much higher occupancy of holes that are several years old, which is the pattern Hoffmann describes.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Residents of a neighborhood in Bogotá, Colombia, asked the city to install speed humps on a street that through traffic used as a shortcut. Traffic engineer Camila Restrepo measured vehicle speeds and traffic volume before the humps were installed and again six months afterward. Opponents had predicted that drivers would slow for each hump and then accelerate hard between them, so that speeds along most of the street would barely change while the street grew noisier. Restrepo argues that the humps achieved what residents wanted: speeds dropped substantially along the whole street, she reports, and a good part of the shortcut traffic disappeared altogether, presumably to other routes.

data.title: Traffic on a Bogotá Residential Street before and after Speed Humps

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Restrepo's argument?

choices.A: Traffic volume fell slightly while speeds between the humps stayed close to their earlier level.
choices.B: After installation, drivers traveled faster midway between the humps than at the humps themselves.
choices.C: Speeds midway between the humps fell from 49 to 31 km/h, and weekday traffic dropped from 3,900 to 2,700 vehicles.
choices.D: Average speed at the humps fell from 47 to 18 km/h after they were installed.

explanation.why: Restrepo's two claims are that speeds fell along the whole street, not just at the humps, and that some traffic left the street. The opponents' prediction concerned the stretches between humps, so the evidence must show the drop there (49 to 31 km/h) together with the fall in volume (3,900 to 2,700 vehicles).
explanation.A: Incorrect. Speeds between the humps fell from 49 to 31 km/h, and traffic fell by nearly a third, so neither part of this is accurate.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (31 against 18 km/h), but it fits the opponents' picture of slowing and speeding up; it does not show the overall drop or the fall in traffic.
explanation.C: Correct. A large fall in speed between the humps and a sizable fall in traffic volume support both parts of Restrepo's argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but a drop at the humps themselves is what the opponents expected; it does not show that speeds fell along the whole street.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each spring, great crested newts leave the woodland where they overwinter and travel to ponds to breed, and where a road lies between the two, many are crushed. A common remedy is a low fence along the road that guides the animals to tunnels passing beneath it. Herpetologist Jonas Albrecht, who monitored a fenced crossing in Bavaria, Germany, for four springs, cautions that the usual measure of success, the number of newts recorded using the tunnels, can mislead. The relevant question, he argues, is what share of the migrating population gets through: at his site, tunnel use grew impressively over the four years, but so did the number of newts found dead on the road, and the fraction of the population completing the crossing through the tunnels hardly improved at all.

data.title: Spring Newt Migration at a Fenced Road Crossing in Bavaria
columns: Newts found dead on the road

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Albrecht's argument?

choices.A: The number of newts recorded using the tunnels rose in every year of the study.
choices.B: Newts using the tunnels rose from 180 to 320 between 2020 and 2023, but the population leaving the woodland grew almost as fast, so the share crossing through the tunnels stayed near 30 percent.
choices.C: Newts found dead on the road made up a smaller share of the migrating population each year.
choices.D: In 2023, more newts used the tunnels than were found dead on the road.

explanation.why: Albrecht's point is that raw tunnel counts rose only because the population rose, so the share getting through did not improve. The evidence must set tunnel use against the migrating population: 180 of 620 in 2020 is 29 percent, 240 of 780 is 31 percent, 280 of 910 is 31 percent, and 320 of 1,050 is 30 percent.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a rising count of tunnel users is the very measure Albrecht says is misleading; on its own it suggests the crossing is improving.
explanation.B: Correct. Dividing tunnel use by the migrating population shows that the share stayed at about 30 percent despite the growth in raw numbers, which is exactly the contrast Albrecht draws.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The share found dead was about 15, 17, 16, and 17 percent, which did not shrink each year, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (320 against 175), but a single year's comparison of two columns says nothing about whether the share getting through improved over time.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the mid-nineteenth century, many English novels first reached readers in monthly magazine installments, and a magazine's editor could ask a novelist to lengthen or shorten a part so that it fit the issue. Literary historian Margaret Ashdown, who measured every installment of three novels serialized in one magazine during the 1860s, challenges the assumption that such pressure made each installment roughly the same length. The constraint operated, she argues, only at the extremes: installments varied considerably in length within a single novel, yet across all three novels none fell below about 6,000 words or rose above about 11,000, which suggests that the editor enforced a floor and a ceiling rather than a target.

data.title: Installment Lengths of Three Novels Serialized in One Magazine, 1860s

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ashdown's argument?

choices.A: The average installment lengths of the three novels differed from one another by no more than 600 words.
choices.B: Installments of the novel with the most parts were the most uniform in length.
choices.C: Within each novel the longest installment exceeded the shortest by at least 3,400 words, yet no installment in any novel was shorter than 6,100 or longer than 10,800 words.
choices.D: The editor shortened installments more often than he lengthened them.

explanation.why: Ashdown's argument has two halves: wide variation within each novel, and firm limits that no installment crossed. The evidence must show both the spread within novels (10,800 minus 6,200, 9,900 minus 6,500, and 10,600 minus 6,100 give 4,600, 3,400, and 4,500 words) and the overall minimum and maximum (6,100 and 10,800 words).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (8,100 to 8,700 words), but similar averages, if anything, suggest a common target, which is the view Ashdown rejects; averages also hide the variation within each novel.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Novel 3 has the most parts (20) but a range of 4,500 words; Novel 2 has the narrowest range (3,400), so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Correct. The large gap between shortest and longest in each novel shows the variation, and the shared limits show the floor and ceiling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table gives only lengths; it records nothing about what the editor asked for.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In a town near Sylhet, Bangladesh, a group of women who had been sewing garments at home formed a cooperative in 2021, renting a shared workshop and taking orders jointly. A common worry about such arrangements is that pooling work merely redistributes a fixed quantity of orders, so that members who previously had the most customers lose out to those who had few. Development economist Rumana Haque, who followed the earnings of the founding members, argues that the cooperative expanded the work available rather than redistributing it: the members who had earned least before joining gained the most, she acknowledges, but even the members who had earned the most saw their incomes rise.

data.title: Average Monthly Earnings of a Tailoring Cooperative's Founding Members
columns: Members grouped by earnings before joining

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Haque's argument?

choices.A: By 2023, the gap in average earnings between the lowest and highest thirds had narrowed to 2,500 taka.
choices.B: The lowest third gained 3,900 taka a month on average, but the highest third, far from losing customers, also gained 1,500 taka.
choices.C: Average earnings of the highest third declined slightly after the cooperative formed.
choices.D: The lowest third's average earnings more than doubled between 2020 and 2023.

explanation.why: The worry Haque answers is that the highest earners lose when work is pooled. Her argument therefore needs the highest third's earnings to have risen, alongside the larger gains of the lowest third. The lowest third went from 3,200 to 7,100 taka (up 3,900); the highest third went from 8,100 to 9,600 (up 1,500).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (9,600 minus 7,100), but a narrowing gap is also what redistribution would produce; it does not show that the top earners gained.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows the large gain at the bottom and, crucially, a gain rather than a loss at the top, which is what distinguishes expansion from redistribution.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The highest third's earnings rose from 8,100 to 9,600 taka, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (3,200 to 7,100), but it describes the group everyone expects to gain; the dispute is about the highest third.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mangrove planting projects along the north coast of Java, Indonesia, often report success by counting seedlings planted, yet many seedlings die within a year, usually because they are set out on mudflats too low and exposed for the species chosen. Restoration ecologist Dewi Rahayu tested two approaches on adjacent sites: dense planting of nursery-raised seedlings of a single fast-growing species, and sparse planting behind low brushwood fences that trap sediment and calm the water, allowing seedlings of several species to establish on their own as well. She argues that the fenced approach is the more productive one, even though it begins with far fewer seedlings in the ground, because after three years it supports more living trees and a wider range of species.

data.title: Two Mangrove Restoration Approaches on the North Coast of Java
columns: Living trees per hectare after 3 years

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Rahayu's argument?

choices.A: The dense approach began with four times as many seedlings per hectare as the fenced approach.
choices.B: Although the fenced site began with 2,500 seedlings per hectare against 10,000, after three years it held 3,100 living trees of four species, compared with 1,400 trees of one species.
choices.C: Only 14 percent of the densely planted seedlings were still alive after three years.
choices.D: After three years, the fenced site held more trees per hectare than the dense site but fewer species.

explanation.why: Rahayu's argument contrasts a modest starting point with a better outcome on two counts, trees and species. The evidence must compare the two sites on all three columns: 2,500 planted against 10,000, yet 3,100 living trees against 1,400, and four species against one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it is the point Rahayu concedes; on its own it suggests the dense approach was the larger effort, not the less productive one.
explanation.B: Correct. It acknowledges the smaller start and then shows the fenced site ahead in both living trees and species, which is the whole of Rahayu's argument.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (1,400 of 10,000), but it shows only that dense planting fared badly; it says nothing about how the fenced site did.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The fenced site had four species against one, so it had more species, not fewer.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians of eighteenth-century Britain have generally held that tea overtook coffee as the preferred hot drink gradually, as the price of tea fell across the century. Economic historian Thomas Reade, who transcribed the customs ledgers of one provincial English port for the years 1700 to 1760, argues that in that port at least the change was neither gradual nor driven simply by cheapness. Coffee imports, he notes, continued to grow for decades; what changed was that tea imports grew far faster, so that tea overtook coffee in volume within a single twenty-year span even though, pound for pound, tea remained the dearer commodity throughout.

data.title: Coffee and Tea Imports Recorded at a Provincial English Port
columns: Price of tea per lb as a multiple of coffee

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Reade's argument?

choices.A: By 1760, the port imported roughly three times as much tea as coffee.
choices.B: Coffee imports rose from 42 to 71 thousand pounds over the period, but tea imports rose from 30 to 96 thousand between 1720 and 1740 alone, overtaking coffee while still costing nearly twice as much per pound.
choices.C: Coffee imports declined after 1720 as merchants shifted their trade to tea.
choices.D: Tea remained more expensive than coffee per pound in every year shown.

explanation.why: Reade's argument has three parts: coffee kept growing, tea grew much faster and overtook coffee within twenty years, and tea stayed dearer. The evidence must draw on all three columns: coffee 42 to 71 thousand pounds; tea 30 to 96 thousand between 1720 and 1740, passing coffee's 68 thousand; tea still 1.9 times the price of coffee in 1740.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (210 against 71 thousand pounds), but the end point alone cannot show how quickly tea overtook coffee or that coffee kept growing.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows coffee growing, tea leaping past it within a single twenty-year span, and tea remaining the costlier drink at that moment, supporting every part of the argument.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Coffee imports rose in every period shown, from 55 thousand pounds in 1720 to 71 thousand in 1760.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it supports only the smallest part of Reade's argument and says nothing about how tea overtook coffee.

items.subject: science
items.passage: House sparrows have declined sharply in many European cities since the 1980s, and the causes remain debated. One explanation blames the loss of nesting cavities as old buildings are renovated; another blames a shortage of the insects that sparrows need to feed their chicks. Urban ecologist Sven Lindgren, who counted sparrows and flying insects and surveyed nesting cavities across twelve neighborhoods of a Scandinavian city, argues that his data favor the second explanation. Neighborhoods with abundant cavities but few insects, he observes, hold scarcely more sparrows than neighborhoods lacking both, whereas insect-rich neighborhoods support many sparrows even where cavities are comparatively scarce.

data.title: Nesting Cavities, Insects, and Sparrows in Twelve City Neighborhoods

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Lindgren's argument?

choices.A: Neighborhoods with many cavities and many insects had the highest sparrow count, 31 per kilometer of street.
choices.B: Neighborhoods with few cavities held fewer sparrows than those with many cavities regardless of insect abundance.
choices.C: Neighborhoods with many cavities but few insects held only 6 sparrows per kilometer, barely above the 4 found where both were scarce, while insect-rich neighborhoods with few cavities held 24.
choices.D: Renovation of old buildings removed more nesting cavities in insect-poor neighborhoods than in insect-rich ones.

explanation.why: To favor one explanation over the other, Lindgren needs neighborhoods where cavities and insects point in different directions. The evidence must compare the two mixed rows: plenty of cavities but few insects gives 6 sparrows per kilometer, close to the 4 where both are scarce, while few cavities but many insects gives 24.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a neighborhood rich in both cavities and insects fits either explanation equally well, so it cannot show which factor matters.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Neighborhoods with few cavities but many insects held 24 sparrows per kilometer, far more than the 6 in neighborhoods with many cavities but few insects.
explanation.C: Correct. Cavities without insects yield almost no sparrows, while insects without cavities yield many, which is exactly the pattern that favors the insect explanation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table reports how many cavities exist, not how or why any were lost.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Teachers who ask children to learn poems by heart often favor rhymed verse on the grounds that rhyme makes lines easier to remember. Literary scholar Beatriz Cardoso, who studied memorization in classrooms in Porto, Portugal, suggests that this belief runs together two distinct effects. In her study, children aged nine and ten learned either a rhymed or an unrhymed poem of equal length and were tested on word-for-word recall after one day and again after four weeks. Rhyme, she argues, chiefly protects what has already been learned against forgetting: it offered the children little advantage when they were tested the next day, but a substantial one a month later.

data.title: Word-for-Word Recall of a Rhymed and an Unrhymed Poem

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Cardoso's argument?

choices.A: Recall of the unrhymed poem fell by 32 percentage points over the four weeks.
choices.B: Children recalled the rhymed poem better than the unrhymed poem at both tests.
choices.C: After one day the rhymed poem led by only 4 percentage points, but after four weeks it led by 23 points, because recall of the rhymed poem fell far less.
choices.D: After four weeks, children recalled the unrhymed poem almost as well as they had after one day.

explanation.why: Cardoso's argument is about the difference between the two poems at each test: small after a day, large after a month. The evidence must compare both bars at both times: 74 against 70 after one day (a 4-point gap) and 61 against 38 after four weeks (a 23-point gap), with the rhymed poem losing 13 points and the unrhymed poem 32.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (70 to 38), but it describes only the unrhymed poem, so it cannot show how rhyme changed the pattern.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but saying rhyme helped both times is the ordinary belief; Cardoso's point is that the help was negligible at first and large later.
explanation.C: Correct. A tiny initial gap that grows to a large one, driven by the rhymed poem's smaller loss, shows rhyme working mainly against forgetting.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Recall of the unrhymed poem dropped from 70 to 38 percent, so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Repair cafés, where volunteers help visitors mend broken household items free of charge, are often praised for keeping goods out of landfills. Skeptics counter that the items brought in are mostly cheap and simple, so the cafés fix little that would not otherwise be replaced for a few dollars, while the complex electronics that make up much of discarded household waste are rarely repaired successfully. Sociologist Hanna Berglund, who recorded every item brought to a repair café in Gothenburg, Sweden, over two years, argues that the skeptics underestimate the cafés' reach: electrical appliances and electronics, she reports, were the most common category brought in, and most of them left working.

data.title: Items Brought to a Gothenburg Repair Café over Two Years

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Berglund's argument?

choices.A: Electrical appliances and electronics were brought in more often than any other category, with 412 items.
choices.B: Electrical appliances and electronics were the largest category, 412 of 863 items, and 268 of them, about 65 percent, were repaired successfully.
choices.C: Fewer than half of the electrical appliances and electronics brought in were repaired successfully.
choices.D: Clothing and textiles had the highest repair success rate of any category, at about 91 percent.

explanation.why: Berglund's reply to the skeptics has two parts: electronics were the most common category, and most of them were fixed. The evidence must give both the count (412 of 863 items) and the success rate for that category (268 of 412, about 65 percent).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it supports only the first half of the argument; the skeptics could grant it and still say electronics are rarely fixed.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows electronics as the largest category and shows that most of them were repaired successfully, answering both halves of the skeptics' claim.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 268 of 412 electrical items were repaired, which is about 65 percent, well over half.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (214 of 236), but the dispute is about electronics, not clothing; this choice says nothing about the category the skeptics doubt.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Elephants that leave protected areas in Kenya to feed on crops are a danger to farmers and, because of the conflicts that follow, to themselves. Since elephants avoid African honeybees, some farmers have hung beehives at intervals along a wire fence around their fields, so that an elephant pushing against the fence sets the hives swinging and the bees flying. Conservation biologist Naomi Wanjiru, who compared fields protected by beehive fences with nearby fields protected by thorn-bush barriers over three growing seasons, argues that the fences deter elephants substantially but not completely, and that their value depends on the hives actually being occupied: fences whose hives stood empty, she finds, were little better than thorn bushes.

data.title: Elephant Visits to Fields with Different Kinds of Protection
columns: Elephant visits per field per season
Visits in which crops were damaged (%)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Wanjiru's argument?

choices.A: Occupied hives also provided the farmers with honey that they could sell.
choices.B: Fields with empty hives received more elephant visits per season than fields protected by thorn bushes.
choices.C: Fields fenced with occupied hives received 2.1 elephant visits per season against 9.4 for thorn-bush fields, while fields with empty hives received 7.8.
choices.D: Elephants damaged crops in fewer than a quarter of their visits to fields with occupied hives.

explanation.why: Wanjiru's argument has three parts: occupied beehive fences cut visits sharply, they do not stop visits altogether, and empty hives barely help. The evidence must compare all three rows: 2.1 visits with occupied hives (far fewer than 9.4, but not zero) and 7.8 with empty hives, close to the thorn-bush figure.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Honey may be a real benefit, but the table records only elephant visits and damage.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Fields with empty hives received 7.8 visits per season, fewer than the 9.4 for thorn-bush fields.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows the large reduction with occupied hives, the visits that still occur, and the near-thorn-bush result for empty hives, supporting every part of the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (24 percent), but it describes only what happened during visits to one kind of field; it cannot show that the fences reduced visits or that empty hives failed.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In eighteenth-century English towns, a boy entering a trade signed an indenture binding him to a master for a term of years, and the town's guild recorded each agreement, noting where the apprentice's father lived. Historians have used these records to ask how far young people traveled for training. Social historian Anne Fairley, who examined indentures from one county town across the century, argues that the familiar story of a widening catchment, in which towns drew apprentices from ever farther afield as roads improved, does not hold for the most prestigious trades. Among apprentices to the lucrative trades of goldsmith and mercer, she finds, the share coming from distant parishes barely changed, while among apprentices to humbler trades it grew markedly.

data.title: Apprentices from Parishes More Than 30 Miles Away, by Trade Group

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Fairley's argument?

choices.A: Across all trades, the share of apprentices from more than 30 miles away rose from 19 to 32 percent over the century.
choices.B: Prestigious trades charged higher fees, which only wealthy families from distant parishes could afford.
choices.C: The share of distant apprentices among goldsmiths and mercers stayed between 38 and 40 percent, while among carpenters and blacksmiths it tripled from 9 to 28 percent.
choices.D: Goldsmiths and mercers drew a smaller share of their apprentices from distant parishes than carpenters and blacksmiths did in every period.

explanation.why: Fairley accepts the widening-catchment story for humbler trades but denies it for prestigious ones, so the evidence must contrast the two trade rows across the periods. Goldsmiths and mercers moved only from 38 to 40 to 39 percent; carpenters and blacksmiths went from 9 to 17 to 28 percent.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but the combined figure is the familiar story itself; it hides the difference between trades that is Fairley's point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The table records where apprentices came from, not what trades charged or what families could afford.
explanation.C: Correct. A flat line for the prestigious trades beside a sharp rise for the humbler ones is exactly the contrast Fairley describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Goldsmiths and mercers drew a larger share from distant parishes in every period (38, 40, 39 percent against 9, 17, 28), so this reverses the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants of the same species can look quite different depending on where they grow. On windy hilltops, for example, they tend to be shorter and have thicker stems than plants in sheltered valleys. Botanist Lena Fischer thinks the wind itself causes this difference. She hypothesizes that when a plant's stem is bent again and again, the plant responds by growing shorter and sturdier.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Fischer's hypothesis?

choices.A: Plants on windy hilltops produce fewer flowers than plants of the same species growing in valleys.
choices.B: Plants growing on windy hilltops are often damaged by strong storms during the winter.
choices.C: Indoor plants bent gently each day grew shorter and thicker than identical plants left alone.
choices.D: Valley soils hold more water than hilltop soils, which allows valley plants to grow taller.

explanation.why: Fischer's hypothesis is that repeated bending of the stem causes plants to grow shorter and sturdier. The strongest support would be a test in which bending is the only difference between two groups of plants. If the bent plants turn out shorter and thicker, bending is shown to cause the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Flower numbers have nothing to do with stem bending, height, or thickness.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Storm damage is a different effect of weather and says nothing about how bending changes growth.
explanation.C: Correct. Bending was the only difference between the two groups, and the bent plants grew shorter and thicker, just as Fischer predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This offers a different cause (water in the soil) for the height difference, so it would weaken the hypothesis rather than support it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the mid-1800s, trips to the seaside became common among British factory workers for the first time. Historian Kwame Asante argues that the main cause was cheap railway fares rather than rising wages. In his view, many workers could already afford a day away from work, but they had no affordable way to reach the coast until trains made the journey short and inexpensive.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Asante's argument?

choices.A: Where cheap trains to the coast already ran, workers' seaside trips became common only after wages rose.
choices.B: Seaside trips by workers increased sharply in towns soon after cheap train service to the coast began.
choices.C: Wealthy families had visited seaside resorts for many decades before railway lines reached the coast.
choices.D: Many seaside towns built new hotels and piers to attract the large numbers of visitors who arrived by train.

explanation.why: Asante claims that cheap trains, not higher wages, made seaside trips common. A finding weakens this if it shows that trains were not enough on their own and that wages made the difference. If trips stayed rare where cheap trains already ran and grew only once wages rose, wages look like the main cause.
explanation.A: Correct. Cheap trains were available but trips did not become common until wages rose, which points to wages, not fares, as the main cause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Trips rising right after cheap trains arrived would support Asante's argument, not weaken it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The argument is about factory workers; the habits of wealthy families do not bear on it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How resorts responded to visitors says nothing about whether fares or wages caused workers to travel.

items.subject: science
items.passage: House sparrows were once a familiar sight in South Asian cities, but residents of some neighborhoods in Karachi say they now see far fewer of them than in the past. Ornithologist Farah Siddiqui suspects that the main cause is a shortage of places to nest. Older houses had gaps under roofs and holes in walls where sparrows built their nests, whereas the smooth concrete and glass of newer buildings offer few such spaces.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Siddiqui's hypothesis?

choices.A: Sparrows in Karachi feed mainly on seeds and insects found in gardens and markets.
choices.B: Sparrow numbers fell by similar amounts in neighborhoods of older houses and in neighborhoods of new buildings.
choices.C: Several other bird species have also become less common in Karachi in recent decades.
choices.D: Sparrow numbers rose in an area after nest boxes were added to its new buildings but not in nearby areas.

explanation.why: Siddiqui's hypothesis is that sparrows declined because newer buildings offer few places to nest. If adding nesting places brings sparrows back in one area but not in similar areas without them, then a lack of nest sites was holding their numbers down. That is direct support.
explanation.A: Incorrect. What sparrows eat is unrelated to the hypothesis, which is about nesting sites.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If old houses with many nesting gaps lost sparrows just as fast, nest sites would not explain the decline; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Declines in other species could have many causes and do not show that sparrows lack nesting places.
explanation.D: Correct. Providing nest sites raised sparrow numbers only where they were added, which points to a shortage of nest sites as the cause.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When two languages come into close contact, speakers often borrow words from each other. Linguist Ngozi Eze has studied a coastal town where speakers of two languages have traded with each other for generations. She hypothesizes that the words most likely to be borrowed are those for things that were new to one community when the contact began, such as unfamiliar tools or foods, rather than words for familiar everyday ideas.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Eze's hypothesis?

choices.A: Speakers in the town use borrowed words more often when talking with traders than with family.
