explanation.why: Memon's argument is about who keeps the natural-dye revival going: outside buyers rather than local wearers. Support must compare who buys the natural-dyed cloth. If most of it goes to city shops and foreign buyers while local customers prefer synthetic-dyed cloth, the revival depends on outsiders.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A quality advantage might explain why anyone buys natural-dyed cloth, but it does not show which buyers sustain the revival.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Growth in the workshops shows the revival is doing well, not who is paying for it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If local customers bought most of the natural-dyed cloth, the revival would rest on them, which weakens the argument.
explanation.D: Correct. Natural-dyed cloth is bought mainly by outside buyers, while locals mostly buy synthetic-dyed cloth, exactly as Memon argues.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The hull of a modern Venetian gondola is asymmetrical: its left side curves outward more than its right. Because the gondolier stands near the stern and rows with a single oar on the right, a symmetrical boat would tend to turn with each stroke, and the extra curve on the left helps the gondola run straight. Maritime historian Paolo Venier argues that boatbuilders refined this design in the nineteenth century mainly to cut costs: by making it practical for one oarsman to handle a gondola that had often been rowed by two, the design lowered the expense of operating the boat.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Venier's argument?

choices.A: The share of gondolas rowed by two oarsmen stayed about the same as asymmetrical hulls became common.
choices.B: Asymmetrical hulls first appeared on gondolas built for racing rather than on the gondolas that carried paying passengers.
choices.C: Gondolas with asymmetrical hulls are slightly heavier than older gondolas of the same length.
choices.D: Owners' account books show that switching to an asymmetrical gondola usually meant paying one rower instead of two.

explanation.why: Venier claims the asymmetrical design was adopted mainly to save money by letting one oarsman do the work of two. Support must tie the new hull both to fewer rowers and to lower costs. Account books showing that owners paid one rower instead of two after switching connect the design directly to that saving.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If two-oarsman gondolas remained just as common, the design did not lead owners to use fewer rowers; this weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A racing origin would suggest the design was meant for speed rather than for saving on rowers' wages.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A difference in weight does not show that the design reduced the number of rowers or the cost of operating the boat.
explanation.D: Correct. The switch to the new hull went along with paying one rower rather than two, which is the cost saving Venier describes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Young five-lined skinks, small lizards of eastern North America, have bright blue tails, while the rest of the body is dark with pale stripes. Like many lizards, a skink can shed its tail when a predator grabs it and later grow a new one, though regrowing a tail costs energy. Herpetologist Mei Takahashi hypothesizes that the blue color protects young skinks by drawing predators' attacks toward the tail, which the lizard can afford to lose, and away from the head and body, where an attack is more likely to be fatal.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Takahashi's hypothesis?

choices.A: Predators attacked clay skink models with blue tails about as often as models with brown tails.
choices.B: On clay skink models placed outdoors, blue tails received a larger share of predator strikes than brown tails did.
choices.C: Young five-lined skinks spend more of their time in open, sunny areas than adult skinks do.
choices.D: On clay skink models, predator strikes hit the head and body just as often whether the model's tail was blue or brown.

explanation.why: Takahashi's hypothesis is about where attacks land: a blue tail should pull strikes toward itself and away from the head and body. Support must compare where strikes fall on blue-tailed and brown-tailed models. If blue tails receive a larger share of strikes, the color is redirecting attacks.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The hypothesis concerns where attacks land, not how many there are, so equal attack rates neither support nor weaken it.
explanation.B: Correct. A larger share of strikes went to blue tails than to brown ones, so the blue color drew attacks toward the part the skink can lose.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Where young skinks spend their time does not show whether the blue tail redirects attacks.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If tail color did not change how often the head and body were hit, the blue tail would not be drawing attacks away from them; this weakens the hypothesis.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Antarctic krill, small shrimplike animals eaten by whales, seals, and penguins, often gather in dense swarms that rise toward the surface at night and sink to deeper water during the day. Biological oceanographer Lucía Ferraro hypothesizes that the swarms do not descend to a fixed depth each day. Instead, she proposes, they sink only as far as needed to stay below a certain level of brightness, which keeps them hard to spot for predators that hunt by sight.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferraro's hypothesis?

choices.A: During daylight hours, swarms stayed at shallower depths on heavily overcast days than on clear days.
choices.B: Swarms that rose to the surface at night fed on more algae than swarms that stayed in deeper water all day.
choices.C: Swarms descended to about the same depth each day, whether the sky was clear or heavily overcast.
choices.D: Krill swarms are larger in summer, when the algae they eat are plentiful, than they are in winter.

explanation.why: Ferraro claims that krill track a level of brightness rather than a fixed depth. If so, the swarms should stay shallower when less light reaches the water, as on overcast days. A finding that daytime depth changes with cloud cover in this way supports her directly.
explanation.A: Correct. On dim, overcast days the swarms did not need to go as deep to stay below the same brightness, just as the hypothesis predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This explains why krill might rise at night to feed, not how far they sink during the day.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A depth that stays the same whatever the light suggests a fixed depth, which weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Swarm size by season has nothing to do with how deep the swarms go in daylight.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Sri Lanka, texts were long written on ola, strips of dried palm leaf. A scribe scratched letters into a leaf with a metal stylus and then rubbed the surface with a dark mixture, often of soot and oil, so that the letters stood out. In the island's humid climate, a leaf manuscript rarely lasts more than a few centuries, so a text survived only if it was copied onto fresh leaves again and again. Historian Nirmala Perera argues that which texts were recopied depended largely on whether they were used for teaching in monastery schools.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Perera's argument?

choices.A: Ola manuscripts kept wrapped in cloth inside closed wooden boxes lasted longer than those stored on open shelves.
choices.B: Texts listed in records of monastery teaching survive in far more copies than untaught texts of similar age.
choices.C: Many surviving ola manuscripts contain notes that later readers added in the margins of the leaves.
choices.D: Texts never used in teaching were recopied about as often as the texts most widely used in teaching.

explanation.why: Perera's argument links a text's survival through recopying to its use in teaching. Support must compare taught and untaught texts. If texts used in teaching survive in many more copies than comparable untaught texts, teaching use was driving the recopying.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How storage affected the life of a manuscript does not show which texts scribes chose to recopy.
explanation.B: Correct. Taught texts survive in far more copies than untaught texts of similar age, which fits the idea that teaching use drove recopying.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Notes in the margins show that manuscripts were read, but not that teaching use decided which texts were copied.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If untaught texts were recopied as often as taught ones, teaching use would not explain the choice; this weakens the argument.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the shores of the Hawaiian Islands, people built loko kuapa, fishponds enclosed by walls of stacked stone and coral on shallow reef flats. Wooden gates in the walls let small fish swim in from the sea but kept the larger, fattened fish from escaping, so the ponds could yield fish all year. Many historians link the building of such ponds to the ambitions of powerful chiefs, who controlled the ponds' harvests. Archaeologist Keoni Kamaka argues, however, that along one stretch of coast new ponds were built mainly in response to the growing number of people living nearby.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kamaka's argument?

choices.A: The dates of new ponds along that coast closely track increases in the number of house sites near the shore.
choices.B: The fish raised in the ponds were mostly mullet and milkfish, both of which feed on algae growing in the water.
choices.C: Fishpond walls along that stretch of coast were rebuilt several times after being damaged by storms.
choices.D: Most new ponds along that coast were built within a few years after a new chief took control of the area.

explanation.why: Kamaka connects the building of new ponds to a rising local population rather than to chiefs' ambitions. Support must show that pond building rose and fell with the number of people. If the dates of new ponds track increases in nearby house sites, pond building followed population growth.
explanation.A: Correct. New ponds appeared as house sites near the shore increased, linking pond building to a growing local population.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The kinds of fish raised do not show whether population growth or chiefly power led to new ponds.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Repairs after storms say nothing about why new ponds were built in the first place.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Ponds built soon after new chiefs took power would support the usual explanation that Kamaka disputes; this weakens his argument.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the high Andes of Peru and Bolivia, farmers have long made chuño, potatoes preserved by leaving them out to freeze on cold nights, trampling them to squeeze out moisture, and drying them in the sun. Properly made chuño can be stored for years. Some highland potato varieties contain bitter compounds that make them unpleasant to eat fresh, but freezing and soaking reduce this bitterness. Archaeologist Rosa Mamani hypothesizes that, at an ancient village she is excavating, chuño was made mainly from these bitter varieties, while the milder varieties were eaten fresh.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mamani's hypothesis?

choices.A: Tests show that freeze-dried potato remains at the site are mostly bitter varieties, while fresh-cooked ones are mostly mild.
choices.B: Bitter and mild varieties appear in roughly equal numbers among the freeze-dried potato remains found at the village.
choices.C: The village lies high enough that nights below freezing occur there for several months of each year.
choices.D: Chuño found at the village had been stored in straw-lined pits dug beneath the floors of houses.

explanation.why: Mamani's hypothesis matches potato type to use: bitter varieties were freeze-dried, mild ones eaten fresh. Support must show which varieties ended up in each form. Test results showing mostly bitter varieties among freeze-dried remains and mostly mild ones among fresh-cooked remains fit the hypothesis on both counts.
explanation.A: Correct. The freeze-dried remains are mostly bitter and the fresh-cooked remains mostly mild, exactly the division Mamani proposes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If bitter and mild potatoes were freeze-dried equally, chuño was not made mainly from bitter varieties; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Cold nights show only that villagers could make chuño, not which varieties they used for it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How chuño was stored does not reveal which potato varieties it was made from.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Silent films told much of their stories through intertitles, frames of printed text inserted between scenes to show dialogue or explain the action. Because intertitles were simply filmed cards, a foreign distributor could replace them without changing the rest of a film. Film historian Yara Haddad has compared original prints of American films from the 1920s with the versions shown in Brazil. She argues that Brazilian distributors treated two kinds of films differently: in comedies they freely rewrote the intertitles to suit local tastes, whereas in dramas they stayed close to the original wording.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's argument?

choices.A: Intertitles in the Brazilian drama prints depart from the original meaning about as often as those in the Brazilian comedy prints.
choices.B: Brazilian versions of both comedies and dramas often contained more intertitles than the original American prints did.
choices.C: Most joke intertitles in the Brazilian comedies differ in meaning from the originals, but most drama intertitles match closely.
choices.D: Brazilian audiences of the 1920s attended American comedies more often than they attended American dramas.

explanation.why: Haddad's argument is a contrast: comedy intertitles were freely rewritten, drama intertitles were kept close to the original. Support must compare the two kinds of films. A finding that comedy jokes usually changed in meaning while drama intertitles usually matched shows exactly that difference.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If dramas were changed as often as comedies, there would be no difference in treatment; this weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes a change made to both kinds of films alike, so it does not show that comedies were treated differently from dramas.
explanation.C: Correct. Comedy intertitles were often changed in meaning while drama intertitles were not, which is the difference Haddad describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Which films audiences preferred does not show how distributors handled the intertitles.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Germany's Bauhaus school, founded in 1919, aimed to unite art and craft, and its weaving workshop became one of its most productive. In the school's early years, weaving students made mostly unique, pictorial wall hangings. By the late 1920s, however, they were increasingly designing plain, durable fabrics that could be manufactured in quantity. Design historian Greta Lindqvist acknowledges that many weavers had come to admire industrial production for its own sake, but she argues that the shift was driven mainly by the school's need for the income it earned from licensing fabric designs to manufacturers.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's argument?

choices.A: The workshop produced about as many industrial designs in years without licensing contracts as in years with them.
choices.B: The workshop's output of designs for industrial fabric rose and fell with its income from licensing contracts.
choices.C: Several weavers wrote essays in the late 1920s praising the clean, simple look of factory-made fabric.
choices.D: Pictorial wall hangings from the workshop's early years now sell for high prices when they come to auction.

explanation.why: Lindqvist grants that some weavers admired industry, but her main claim is that the need for licensing income drove the shift. Support must link the amount of industrial design work to that income. If output rose and fell along with licensing income, the income was steering the workshop.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If licensing contracts made no difference to output, income would not be driving the shift; this weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Correct. Industrial design work tracked licensing income, which fits the claim that the need for that income drove the change.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Weavers' admiration for factory fabric is the factor Lindqvist acknowledges but says mattered less, so this does not support her main claim.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Present-day auction prices say nothing about why the workshop changed what it made in the 1920s.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In the professional theaters of Shakespeare's London, female roles were played by boys and young men, usually apprentices attached to an acting company. At any one time, a company might have only a few apprentices skilled enough for demanding parts. Theater historian Rowan Ashby argues that this limitation shaped the plays themselves. Playwrights writing for a particular company, she contends, kept the number of large female roles in a play no greater than the number of skilled apprentices that company had at the time.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ashby's argument?

choices.A: The number of large female roles in new plays stayed about the same whenever companies gained or lost skilled apprentices.
choices.B: Several apprentices who played female roles went on to become leading actors in adult male roles.
choices.C: Female characters in the plays of this period speak, on average, far fewer lines than male characters do.
choices.D: Plays for two-apprentice companies rarely had over two large female roles, but plays for four-apprentice companies often did.

explanation.why: Ashby ties the number of large female roles in a play to the number of skilled apprentices in the company it was written for. Support must compare companies with different numbers of apprentices. If plays for two-apprentice companies seldom exceed two large female roles while plays for four-apprentice companies often do, the roles track the apprentices.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If the number of roles did not change as companies' apprentices changed, the link would not hold; this weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Apprentices' later careers do not bear on how many female roles playwrights wrote.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Female characters having fewer lines overall does not show that their number depended on how many skilled apprentices a company had.
explanation.D: Correct. The number of large female roles rose with the number of skilled apprentices, exactly the link Ashby proposes.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, watchmaking spread through the villages of the Jura Mountains in western Switzerland, where many farm families made watch parts at home and sold them to merchants who organized the trade. Historians often explain this spread by the region's thin, rocky soils, which made farming alone a poor living. Historian Lukas Meier argues that a different feature of the mountains mattered more: the long winters, when deep snow halted farm work for months and left families with time to fill.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Meier's argument?

choices.A: Families in the villages with the poorest soils earned the largest share of their yearly income from making watch parts.
choices.B: Watch parts made in Jura farmhouses were sold to merchants based in Geneva and other towns.
choices.C: Snowy villages took up watchmaking early even with good soils, while poor-soiled villages with mild winters took it up late.
choices.D: Many Jura watchmakers specialized in making a single kind of part, such as springs or small gears.

explanation.why: Meier contrasts two causes, winter idleness and poor soils, and says winters mattered more. Support must separate the two. Villages with long winters but good soils adopted watchmaking early, while villages with poor soils but mild winters adopted it late, so winter length, not soil, predicts the spread.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A link between poor soils and watchmaking income supports the usual explanation that Meier disputes, not his argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Where the parts were sold does not show why families took up the work.
explanation.C: Correct. Watchmaking followed winter length even when soil quality pointed the other way, which supports Meier over the usual explanation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How the work was divided among workers says nothing about why watchmaking spread.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud," a poem by William Wordsworth first published in 1807 and revised for an 1815 edition, recalls a walk on which the speaker came upon a great crowd of daffodils beside a lake. Much of the poem lingers on the scene itself: the flowers' numbers, their motion in the breeze, and the sparkling water beside them. Yet the speaker also suggests that the encounter did not end on the day of the walk, since the daffodils return to him afterward, when he is by himself, and continue to affect him.
items.stem: Which quotation from "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "I gazed—and gazed—but little thought / What wealth the show to me had brought:"
choices.B: "They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude;"
choices.C: "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way,"
choices.D: "The waves beside them danced; but they / Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:"

explanation.why: The claim has two parts: the daffodils come back to the speaker later, and they do so when he is alone. The quotation must show both. In "They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude," the flowers reappear in his memory (his "inward eye") during "solitude."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This hints that the scene was worth more than the speaker realized at the time, but it does not show the flowers returning to him when he is alone.
explanation.B: Correct. The daffodils reappear in the speaker's memory, his "inward eye," and the lines place that moment in "solitude," so both parts of the claim are shown.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This line describes the daffodils as they looked during the walk, comparing them to stars; it says nothing about their returning to him later.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These lines describe the scene during the walk, comparing the flowers with the waves; they do not show the encounter continuing afterward.

source.author: William Wordsworth
source.work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: From the fourteenth century onward, merchants of the Hanseatic League, an alliance of mainly German trading towns, dominated commerce in Bergen, Norway. Their chief export from the city was stockfish, cod caught off northern Norway and dried in the open air until it would keep for years. In return, the northern fishing communities, where cold, short summers made growing grain difficult, received grain shipped from Baltic ports. Historians usually explain the Hanseatic grip on Bergen by the merchants' control over the sale of stockfish to continental markets. Historian Solveig Hansen argues instead that their power rested mainly on grain: because the fishers depended on imported grain to survive, she contends, they had little choice but to sell their fish to the merchants who supplied it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hansen's argument?

choices.A: Hanseatic merchants in Bergen shipped more stockfish to German and Baltic ports than all other merchants there combined.
choices.B: Northern fishers sold their stockfish to whichever merchants paid the most for it, whether or not those merchants supplied grain.
choices.C: When English traders offered more for stockfish but brought no grain, northern fishers still sold mostly to Hanseatic merchants.
choices.D: Grain grew so poorly in northern Norway that few fishing families there could raise enough to last the winter.

explanation.why: Hansen claims that the merchants' power came from supplying grain the fishers depended on, not from controlling stockfish sales. The best support would show fishers choosing the grain suppliers even when another buyer offered more for their fish. That behavior makes sense only if the need for grain, not price, bound the fishers to the Hanseatic merchants.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This shows how large the merchants' stockfish trade was, which fits the usual explanation as well as Hansen's; it does not show that grain was the source of their power.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If fishers simply sold to the highest bidder regardless of grain, grain would not be the basis of the merchants' power; this weakens the argument.
explanation.C: Correct. The fishers passed up better prices from traders who had no grain, which shows that dependence on grain tied them to the Hanseatic merchants.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This explains why fishers needed imported grain, a point the text already makes, but it does not show that the need decided whom they sold to.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In 1912, Rabindranath Tagore published Gitanjali: Song Offerings, a volume of English prose poems that he had translated himself from his Bengali verse; the following year he became the first non-European to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. Readers who know both languages have long observed that the English poems are often much shorter and plainer than the Bengali originals. Some critics attribute this mainly to the difficulty of carrying Bengali rhyme and meter into English. Literary scholar Priyanka Sen argues, however, that many of the cuts reflect a deliberate choice about audience: Tagore, she contends, removed above all the details that would have been unfamiliar to English readers.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sen's argument?

choices.A: On average, the English poems are less than half as long as the Bengali poems from which they were translated.
choices.B: References to Bengali seasons, plants, and festivals were dropped far more often than widely shared images of sky and light.
choices.C: Images of Bengali seasons, plants, and festivals were dropped no more often than widely shared images of sky, light, and rain.
choices.D: The English poems rarely keep the patterns of rhyme that run throughout the Bengali originals.

explanation.why: Sen argues that Tagore's cuts targeted details unfamiliar to English readers. To support this, a finding must show that the cuts fell unevenly, landing mostly on culturally specific material. If references to Bengali seasons, plants, and festivals were dropped far more often than images any reader would know, the pattern of cuts reflects the audience.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This confirms that the English poems are shorter, which both Sen and the critics accept; it does not show what kind of material was removed.
explanation.B: Correct. Culturally specific details were removed far more often than familiar images, which is the pattern Sen's argument predicts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If unfamiliar Bengali details were cut no more often than familiar images, the cuts would not reflect a choice about audience; this weakens the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Losing the rhyme fits the critics' view about the difficulty of English verse; it does not show that unfamiliar details were the main target of the cuts.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When dry sand avalanches down the steep face of certain desert dunes, it can produce a loud, low hum that lasts a minute or more and is sometimes heard kilometers away. Each such dune tends to hum at its own characteristic pitch, and researchers disagree about what sets it. One view holds that the dune's internal structure is responsible: a dry surface layer resting on firmer, moister sand may trap sound waves, so that the layer's thickness determines the tone. Physicist Omar Benali rejects this view, arguing that the pitch depends on the size of the sand grains themselves, which collide in step with one another as they slide.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Benali's argument?

choices.A: After heavy rain changed the moisture of a dune's deeper sand, its pitch shifted, though its surface grains were unchanged.
choices.B: Sand from several dunes, avalanched in a lab chute with no layering, hummed at its home dune's pitch, lower for coarser sand.
choices.C: Dunes made of coarse sand tend to have thicker dry surface layers than dunes made of fine sand, and they hum at lower pitches.
choices.D: Humming is heard only when sand slides down a dune's steep face, never when wind blows sand across its gentler slope.

explanation.why: Benali and his opponents disagree about whether grain size or the dune's layering sets the pitch. The best support must separate the two causes. In a lab chute there is no layering at all, so if each sand still hums at its home dune's pitch, and coarser sand hums lower, the sand grains alone must set the tone.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A pitch change caused by moisture in the deeper sand, with the grains unchanged, points to the dune's structure; this weakens Benali's argument.
explanation.B: Correct. With layering removed, each sand kept its dune's pitch and the pitch followed grain size, showing that the grains, not the dune's structure, set the tone.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Grain size and layer thickness vary together here, so the lower pitch could come from either; the finding cannot decide between the two views.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes when humming occurs, not what determines its pitch, so it does not bear on the disagreement.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Because the date of placement is carved into a gravestone, cemeteries allow ecologists to estimate how fast lichens grow on stone. In a cemetery in an English industrial city, lichenologist Hannah Pryce found something puzzling: the largest lichen patches on headstones from the 1890s were scarcely bigger than those on headstones from the 1960s. Pryce hypothesizes that heavy air pollution from coal burning, which most lichens tolerate poorly, killed off earlier growth throughout the cemetery, so that nearly all the patches now present began growing only after the city's air became cleaner in the 1960s.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Pryce's hypothesis?

choices.A: Lichens on the city's headstones now grow at about the same yearly rate as lichens on headstones in rural cemeteries.
choices.B: Records show that the city's air was no smokier between 1890 and 1960 than it has been since the 1970s.
choices.C: Lichens in the city cemetery grow more slowly on smooth, polished granite than on rough sandstone.
choices.D: In a rural cemetery that escaped the city's smoke, 1890s headstones carry far larger lichen patches than 1960s ones.

explanation.why: Pryce explains the city's puzzle with a local cause: pollution wiped out early growth, so every patch started around the same time. The strongest support would show that, where that cause was absent, older stones do carry much larger lichens. A smoke-free rural cemetery with far larger patches on its 1890s stones shows that the city's pattern is not normal and points to the city's smoke.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This shows only that the city's air is clean enough for lichens today; it says nothing about whether pollution killed earlier growth.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If the air was no smokier before 1960 than afterward, pollution could not explain the missing early growth; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Differences between types of stone do not explain why old and newer stones of the city carry patches of similar size.
explanation.D: Correct. Without the city's smoke, older stones have much larger patches, so the city's similar-sized patches point to growth being wiped out by pollution there.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the seventeenth century, the English and Dutch East India Companies began shipping large quantities of chintz, painted and printed cotton cloth from India, to Europe, where it quickly became fashionable for clothing and furnishings. Indian dyers fixed their colors with mordants, metallic salts that bind dye to fiber, using techniques for cotton that European craftspeople had not yet mastered, so Indian reds and blues survived repeated washing. Many accounts attribute chintz's success to the novelty of its flowering designs. Historian Meera Iyer argues instead that its appeal rested mainly on the durability of its colors, which no European cotton cloth of the time could match.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Iyer's argument?

choices.A: Once European printers learned to make cotton colors that survived washing, demand for Indian chintz stayed just as strong.
choices.B: Buyers paid far more for Indian chintz than for European prints that copied its patterns exactly but faded when washed.
choices.C: Imports of Indian chintz into England rose sharply in the 1680s, before new laws restricted its sale.
choices.D: European trading companies sent sample patterns to Indian workshops so that the cloth would suit European tastes.

explanation.why: Iyer claims that chintz sold because of its lasting colors, not its designs. Support must hold the design constant and vary the colorfastness. If buyers paid far more for Indian chintz than for exact copies of its patterns that faded, the extra value lay in the colors.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If demand for Indian chintz held steady even after European cloth matched its colorfastness, durable color would not explain its appeal; this weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Correct. With the patterns identical, buyers still paid far more for the Indian cloth, so its lasting colors, not its designs, explain the higher value.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Rising imports show that chintz was popular, not why it was popular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This shows that designs were adjusted for European buyers, but it does not show that colorfastness was the main source of the cloth's appeal.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Medieval Icelanders built their houses with thick walls of stacked turf, since the island had few trees for timber. The earliest farmhouses were long halls warmed by a central hearth, but over the following centuries many were replaced by houses of several small rooms joined by a passage. Some archaeologists attribute this change to a growing shortage of timber, because small rooms need only short roof beams. Archaeologist Sigrún Ólafsdóttir argues instead that it was a response to a cooling climate: small, clustered rooms, she contends, were easier to keep warm than a single long hall.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ólafsdóttir's argument?

choices.A: Iceland's birch woodlands had been largely cleared within a few centuries of the island's settlement.
choices.B: Small clustered rooms had lower ceilings than long halls, so each room's hearth had less air to heat than a hall's hearth did.
choices.C: Driftwood-rich farms switched to clustered rooms as early as timber-poor farms, and first where winters were harshest.
choices.D: Houses with clustered rooms used more turf for each square meter of floor than the earlier long halls did.

explanation.why: Ólafsdóttir and her opponents offer competing causes: cold or timber shortage. Support must separate them. If farms with plenty of driftwood for beams changed as early as timber-poor farms, timber shortage cannot explain the change, and if the change came first where winters were harshest, cold is the likely cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Cleared woodlands would make timber scarce, which fits the rival explanation rather than Ólafsdóttir's; this weakens her argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This explains why small rooms might be warmer, but it does not show that the change actually happened in response to a cooling climate rather than a lack of timber.
explanation.C: Correct. Timber supply made no difference to the timing, while harsh winters did, which points to climate rather than timber shortage as the cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The amount of turf used does not tell us whether cold or timber shortage drove the change in house plans.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Through most of the seventeenth century, church organs in northern Europe were commonly tuned in meantone temperament, a system that makes the most frequently used keys sound especially sweet but makes keys with many sharps or flats sound harshly out of tune. Retuning an organ was slow and costly work, so an organist usually had to accept whatever tuning his instrument already had. Musicologist Anke Brandt notes that organ music by northern German composers of the 1600s rarely uses those remote keys. She argues that this pattern reflects the limits of the instruments the composers played rather than a shared taste for simpler keys.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's argument?

choices.A: Organists whose instruments were retuned to newer systems soon began writing organ works in remote keys.
choices.B: Meantone tuning was also common on church organs in Italy and England during the 1600s.
choices.C: Most northern German organ music of the 1600s is written in keys that have few sharps or flats.
choices.D: The same composers' unaccompanied choral works, which were free of any fixed tuning, also avoided remote keys.

explanation.why: Brandt says the composers avoided remote keys because their organs could not play them well, not because they disliked such keys. The best support would show the composers' choices changing when only the instrument's tuning changed. Organists who began using remote keys once their organs were retuned show that the tuning, not their taste, had held them back.
explanation.A: Correct. When the tuning limit was removed, the same organists began writing in remote keys, showing that the instruments, not taste, had restricted them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Where else meantone tuning was used says nothing about why these composers avoided remote keys.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This simply restates the pattern Brandt is trying to explain; it does not show whether the instruments or the composers' taste caused it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Avoiding remote keys even where no tuning limited them would suggest a shared taste for simpler keys; this weakens the argument.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Edo, the city now called Tokyo, suffered frequent great fires during the period of Tokugawa rule, since most of its buildings were made of wood and paper. Over time, many merchants built kura, storehouses with thick walls of clay and plaster that could survive a fire with their contents unharmed. The government at times issued orders encouraging fire-resistant building, and some historians credit these orders with the spread of kura. Historian Kenji Mori argues instead that kura spread mainly because merchants judged for themselves that protecting their stock was worth the considerable cost.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mori's argument?

choices.A: Merchants in districts never covered by building orders rarely built kura, even after fires had destroyed shops nearby.
choices.B: After many great fires, the government ordered that wide firebreaks be cleared between some city districts.
choices.C: Kura spread as fast in districts without building orders as in districts with them, mostly just after nearby fires.
choices.D: A kura cost a merchant several times as much to build as a wooden storehouse of the same size.

explanation.why: Mori credits merchants' own choices, not government orders, with the spread of kura. Support must show kura spreading where no order applied, and ideally show merchants reacting to the risk themselves. Equal spread in districts without orders, concentrated just after nearby fires, does both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If merchants built kura only where orders applied, the orders would explain the spread; this weakens Mori's argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Firebreaks were another government fire measure; they say nothing about why merchants built kura.
explanation.C: Correct. Kura spread just as fast where no order applied, and especially after nearby fires reminded merchants of the risk, which points to merchants' own judgment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The high cost explains why the decision was serious, but it does not show whether merchants or government orders drove the spread.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Mali and neighboring parts of West Africa, griots, hereditary specialists in speech and music, have long recited the genealogies of the families they serve, tracing their patrons' ancestry back many generations, sometimes to figures in the epic of Sunjata, the thirteenth-century founder of the Mali Empire. Scholars once treated such genealogies as fixed records passed down unchanged. Historian Aminata Keïta argues that they are better understood as living documents: the ancestors a griot names for a family, she contends, shift over time to match that family's present standing in its community.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Keïta's argument?

choices.A: Recitations recorded decades apart left the ancestors unchanged for families whose standing had risen, as for all others.
choices.B: Different griots serving the same family sometimes name somewhat different ancestors for that family.
choices.C: In recitations recorded decades apart, prominent new ancestors appeared mainly for families whose standing had risen.
choices.D: Patrons who won local office often gave larger gifts than before to the griots who praised them.

explanation.why: Keïta claims more than that genealogies change: she says they change to match a family's current standing. Support must link changes in the recited ancestors to changes in standing. If prominent ancestors were added mainly for families that had risen in the meantime, the genealogies were tracking standing.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If rising families kept the same ancestors, the genealogies would not be shifting with standing; this weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Variation between griots shows the genealogies are not perfectly fixed, but it does not connect the differences to a family's standing.
explanation.C: Correct. Prominent ancestors were added mainly for families that had gained standing, which is the link Keïta describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Larger gifts might give griots a motive to flatter, but the finding does not show that the genealogies actually changed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Gray squirrels bury thousands of nuts each fall, placing them one at a time in separate spots scattered across a wide area. Months later, during the winter, they dig many of them up again. Biologist Rosa Delgado thinks squirrels find these nuts mainly by remembering where they buried them, not simply by sniffing out any buried nut that happens to be nearby.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Delgado's hypothesis?

choices.A: Squirrels dug up far more of their own buried nuts than nuts that researchers had buried nearby in similar spots.
choices.B: Many of the buried nuts that squirrels never dig up later sprout in the spring and grow into new trees.
choices.C: Squirrels bury more nuts in years when oak and hickory trees produce especially large crops of acorns and nuts.
choices.D: Squirrels dug up nuts that researchers had buried nearby just as often as the nuts they had buried themselves.

explanation.why: Delgado says squirrels rely on memory of their own hiding spots rather than on smell alone. If smell were enough, a squirrel would find any nearby nut equally well. A finding that squirrels recover their own nuts far more often than similar nuts buried by someone else points to memory.
explanation.A: Correct. The researchers' nuts smelled just as much like nuts, so finding mostly their own shows the squirrels remembered where they had dug.
explanation.B: Incorrect. What happens to forgotten nuts does not show whether the recovered ones were found by memory or by smell.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How many nuts squirrels bury says nothing about how they find them again.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Finding other nuts just as often suggests smell, not memory, is doing the work, so this would weaken the hypothesis.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Mumbai, India, workers known as dabbawalas deliver around 200,000 home-cooked lunches to offices every working day, and very few boxes ever go to the wrong place. Many dabbawalas have had little schooling and do not read long written addresses. Researcher Priya Kulkarni argues that the system works so well mainly because of a short code of colors, letters, and numbers painted on each lunch box, which tells every worker where the box must go next.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kulkarni's argument?

choices.A: In a trial, boxes marked only with full written addresses were misdelivered far more often than coded boxes.
choices.B: Dabbawalas usually travel between neighborhoods on Mumbai's crowded suburban trains, carrying dozens of boxes at once.
choices.C: Many office workers in Mumbai say that they prefer home-cooked lunches to meals bought from nearby restaurants.
choices.D: In a trial, boxes with missing codes reached the right offices just as often as boxes with complete codes.

explanation.why: Kulkarni credits the painted code for the system's accuracy. To support her, a finding should show that accuracy depends on the code. If boxes without the code but with full addresses are misdelivered much more often, the code is clearly what keeps deliveries correct.
explanation.A: Correct. When the code was replaced by written addresses, mistakes rose sharply, which shows the code is what makes the system accurate.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How dabbawalas travel does not show what keeps the boxes going to the right place.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Why customers like home-cooked food has nothing to do with how the boxes are sorted.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If boxes without codes did just as well, the code would not matter, so this would weaken the argument.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Folktales often change as they pass from one storyteller to another. Folklorist Amara Nwosu has been studying a West African tale in which a clever hare outwits a shark along the seashore. She proposes that storytellers adapt such tales to their own surroundings, keeping the basic plot but changing details so that the story takes place somewhere their listeners know well.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nwosu's proposal?

choices.A: Many listeners in the villages Nwosu visited said they enjoy tales about clever animals more than other tales.
choices.B: In inland versions, the hare outwits a crocodile at a riverbank instead of a shark at the sea.
choices.C: Storytellers in inland villages tell the tale with the same seashore setting that coastal storytellers use.
choices.D: The tale about the hare is among the oldest stories still told in the coastal villages that Nwosu visited.

explanation.why: Nwosu predicts that the plot stays the same while the setting shifts to match each storyteller's surroundings. Inland villages are far from the sea, so her idea predicts that their versions would replace the sea with something local. A version with the same plot set at a river does exactly that.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Listeners' favorite kinds of tales say nothing about how storytellers change a tale's details.
explanation.B: Correct. The plot stays the same, but the setting and animal change to match an inland landscape, just as Nwosu proposes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If inland storytellers keep the seashore setting, the tale is not being adapted to their surroundings, so this would weaken the proposal.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The age of the tale does not show whether storytellers change its details to fit where they live.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many songbirds that live in cities sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species living in quiet forests. Ecologist Johan Lindqvist suspects that city birds raise their pitch so that their songs can be heard over the low rumble of traffic. He also thinks that individual birds can adjust their pitch from moment to moment, depending on how noisy their surroundings are.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's hypothesis?

choices.A: Individual city birds sang at a higher pitch during noisy rush hours than during quiet weekend mornings.
choices.B: City songbirds often begin singing earlier in the morning than forest songbirds of the same species do.
choices.C: City birds living beside quiet parks sang at the same high pitch as city birds living beside busy roads.
choices.D: City songbirds tend to build their nests higher off the ground than forest songbirds of the same species.

explanation.why: Lindqvist links high pitch to traffic noise and says each bird can change its pitch as the noise level changes. The best support would show the same birds singing higher when it is noisy and lower when it is quiet.
explanation.A: Correct. The same birds sang higher when traffic was loud and lower when it was quiet, which shows them adjusting their pitch to the noise.
explanation.B: Incorrect. When birds start singing is a different question from what pitch they use.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If birds near quiet parks sing just as high as birds near busy roads, noise does not seem to matter, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nest height has nothing to do with the pitch of the birds' songs.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Many medieval cathedrals in Europe took more than a century to finish, and work on them often stopped for years at a time. Historian Claire Moreau argues that these long pauses happened mainly because the people in charge of building ran out of money, not because of wars or other outside events.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Moreau's argument?

choices.A: Some skilled builders traveled from city to city, working on several cathedrals during their careers.
choices.B: Building records show that work usually stopped soon after the money collected for construction was spent.
choices.C: Many medieval cathedrals have stained-glass windows showing stories that were familiar to local people.
choices.D: Building records show that work usually stopped when wars broke out, even while donations kept arriving.

explanation.why: Moreau claims the pauses came mainly from a lack of money rather than from wars. A finding weakens her if it shows work stopping because of war at times when money was still available.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Builders moving between cities does not show what caused the long pauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Work stopping when the money ran out fits Moreau's argument, so this would support it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The windows' subjects say nothing about why construction stopped.
explanation.D: Correct. Work stopped during wars even though donations kept coming in, so a lack of money cannot explain these pauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In parts of Sri Lanka, wild Asian elephants sometimes wander onto farms and eat the crops. Some farmers have begun hanging beehives along the fences around their fields, and elephants seem to stay away from these fences. Wildlife biologist Nirmala Perera thinks the elephants avoid the fences because they are frightened by the sound of buzzing bees.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Perera's hypothesis?

choices.A: Elephants walked away when researchers played recordings of buzzing bees but not recordings of wind.
choices.B: Fences with beehives cost farmers less to build and repair than electric fences do.
choices.C: Elephants stayed away just as often from fences hung with empty hive boxes that made no sound.
choices.D: Elephants in Sri Lanka raid farms most often during dry months, when wild food is hard to find.

explanation.why: Perera's hypothesis is specifically about sound: elephants avoid the fences because buzzing frightens them. The best support would show elephants reacting to the buzzing itself and not to other sounds.
explanation.A: Correct. The elephants left only when they heard bees, not when they heard another sound, so the buzzing itself seems to scare them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The cost of the fences says nothing about why elephants avoid them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If silent, empty hives work just as well, the buzzing cannot be the reason, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When elephants raid farms does not explain why they avoid the beehive fences.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Willa Cather spent much of her childhood in the small prairie town of Red Cloud, Nebraska. Her novel My Ántonia (1918) follows Jim Burden, who grows up on the Nebraska prairie alongside Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a family of immigrants from Bohemia. Literary scholar Tomás Herrera argues that many of the novel's characters were based on real people Cather knew in Red Cloud, rather than being entirely invented.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Herrera's argument?

choices.A: My Ántonia sold well when it first appeared and is now often taught in American literature classes.
choices.B: Several of Cather's other novels are also set on the prairie and describe the hard work of farming there.
choices.C: Cather once wrote that she had always avoided basing characters on people she had actually met.
choices.D: Cather's letters describe a Red Cloud neighbor whose life closely matches the life of the character Ántonia.

explanation.why: Herrera claims that Cather drew her characters from real people in Red Cloud. The strongest support would link a specific character to a specific person Cather knew there.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The novel's sales and its place in classrooms say nothing about where its characters came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This concerns the setting of other novels, not whether this novel's characters were based on real people.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Cather saying she avoided real people as models would weaken Herrera's argument, not support it.
explanation.D: Correct. A real neighbor whose life matches Ántonia's is direct evidence that at least one major character was based on someone Cather knew.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Arctic foxes grow a thick white coat each fall and change to a thinner brown or gray coat in the spring. Zoologist Ingrid Solberg hypothesizes that the main signal that starts the change to a white coat is the shortening of the days in fall, not the drop in temperature that comes at the same time of year.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Solberg's hypothesis?

choices.A: Foxes kept in a warm room under shortening days still grew their white coats at the usual time.
choices.B: A thick white coat both keeps a fox warm and helps hide it from its prey against the snow.
choices.C: Arctic foxes sometimes follow polar bears in winter to feed on what is left of the bears' meals.
choices.D: Foxes kept in a cold room with long, summer-length days still grew their white coats at the usual time.

explanation.why: Solberg says shorter days, not colder weather, are the main trigger for the white coat. To weaken her, a finding should show the coat changing without shorter days. If foxes in long days but cold air still turn white, cold alone seems to be enough.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Foxes turning white with short days but no cold fits Solberg's hypothesis, so this would support it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This explains why a white coat is useful, not what signal starts the change.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How foxes find food in winter has nothing to do with what triggers the coat change.
explanation.D: Correct. The days never got shorter, yet the foxes turned white in the cold, which suggests temperature, not day length, triggers the change.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the last years of his life, the French painter Claude Monet suffered from cataracts, a condition that clouds the lens of the eye and can make colors look dull and yellowish. His late paintings of his garden show blurred shapes and strong reddish and brownish tones. Art historian Elena Ruiz argues that these features were caused by his failing eyesight rather than by a deliberate change in his style.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ruiz's argument?

choices.A: Monet's late paintings of his garden include some of the largest canvases he ever produced.
choices.B: Paintings Monet made years before his eyesight began to fail already show the same blurred shapes and reddish tones.
choices.C: Monet complained in letters that he could no longer tell some colors apart as his cataracts grew worse.
choices.D: Many visitors traveled to Monet's home at Giverny to see the garden that appears in his paintings.

explanation.why: Ruiz says Monet's late blurring and reddish colors came from his cataracts. If the same features appear in paintings made while his eyes were still healthy, his eyesight cannot be what produced them, which weakens her argument.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The size of the canvases says nothing about why the shapes are blurred or the colors reddish.
explanation.B: Correct. The same features appear before his eyesight failed, so they are more likely a choice of style than a result of cataracts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Monet's trouble seeing colors fits Ruiz's argument, so this would support it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Visitors to the garden have nothing to do with the cause of the paintings' features.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the coast of Kerala, India, fishers sell their catch at beach markets. Before the late 1990s, a boat usually landed at its nearest market, so on the same day fish could be very expensive at one market and very cheap at another. Economist Arjun Menon argues that mobile phones made prices more even, because fishers still at sea could call several markets and then sail to the one paying the most.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Menon's argument?

choices.A: After mobile phones arrived, nearly every boat still landed at its nearest market, just as before.
choices.B: Before mobile phones arrived, some markets sold fish caught by boats from several different villages.
choices.C: After mobile phones arrived, many fishers also began using them to talk with their families while at sea.
choices.D: After mobile phones arrived, boats often sailed past their nearest market to sell at one paying more.

explanation.why: Menon's explanation depends on a change in behavior: with phones, fishers chose the best-paying market instead of the nearest one. A finding that boats really did start sailing past their nearest market to sell elsewhere supports that explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If boats kept landing at the nearest market, phones did not change where fish were sold, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes markets before phones and says nothing about how phones changed prices.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Calling family members does not show that phones changed where fishers sold their catch.
explanation.D: Correct. This shows fishers using information to choose the higher-paying market, which is exactly how Menon says prices became more even.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a group of meerkats searches for food in the Kalahari Desert, one animal often climbs onto a rock or bush and keeps watch for eagles and jackals while the others dig. Biologist Hannah Botha hypothesizes that a meerkat takes on this guard role mainly when it has already eaten enough, so that it can afford to stop feeding for a while.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Botha's hypothesis?

choices.A: Meerkats that researchers gave extra food stood guard no more often than meerkats given no extra food.
choices.B: Meerkats that researchers gave extra food stood guard more often than meerkats given no extra food.
choices.C: Meerkats live in groups that can include more than twenty animals.
choices.D: A meerkat on guard gives one alarm call for eagles and a different one for jackals.

explanation.why: Botha links guarding to how full a meerkat is. If her hypothesis is right, meerkats that have eaten more should guard more often. A test in which well-fed meerkats guard more than others would support her.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If extra food made no difference, being well fed would not explain guarding, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.B: Correct. The meerkats given extra food guarded more often, which shows that being well fed leads to taking the guard role.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The size of meerkat groups does not show when an individual chooses to stand guard.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The kinds of alarm calls describe what guards do, not why a meerkat becomes a guard.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Great Zimbabwe, a city known for its massive stone walls, was the center of a powerful state in southern Africa from about 1200 to 1450 CE. Archaeologist Thandiwe Moyo argues that much of the city's wealth came from long-distance trade, in which gold from the region was carried to ports on the East African coast and exchanged for goods from distant lands.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moyo's argument?

choices.A: Excavations at Great Zimbabwe have found almost no objects that were made outside the surrounding region.
choices.B: Excavations at Great Zimbabwe have uncovered glass beads from Persia and pieces of pottery from China.
choices.C: The stone walls of Great Zimbabwe were built without mortar, using carefully shaped blocks of granite.
choices.D: Many families living near Great Zimbabwe grew crops such as sorghum and kept herds of cattle.

explanation.why: Moyo claims the city grew rich through trade that reached faraway lands. Objects made in distant places, found at the site itself, would show that such trade really reached Great Zimbabwe.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If almost nothing at the site came from outside the region, there is little sign of long-distance trade, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.B: Correct. Goods from Persia and China at the site are direct evidence that Great Zimbabwe was connected to long-distance trade.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How the walls were built says nothing about where the city's wealth came from.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Local farming describes everyday life near the city, not long-distance trade.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Bread left out on a kitchen counter turns hard within a few days. Baker Liam O'Connor claims that bread goes stale mainly because water escapes from the loaf into the surrounding air, leaving the inside of the bread dry. For that reason, he tells his customers to keep their loaves tightly wrapped at all times.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken O'Connor's claim?

choices.A: Loaves sealed in airtight bags lost almost no water but became hard just as quickly as unwrapped loaves.
choices.B: Bread made with extra sugar or butter usually stays soft for a day or two longer than plain bread.
choices.C: Loaves left unwrapped on the counter lost water and also became hard within a few days.
choices.D: Many of O'Connor's customers prefer to buy fresh bread every day rather than store it at home.

explanation.why: O'Connor says bread hardens mainly because it loses water. If bread that keeps almost all its water still hardens just as fast, water loss cannot be the main cause, so that finding weakens his claim.
explanation.A: Correct. The sealed loaves kept their water but still went stale at the same speed, so something other than water loss must be the main cause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is about ingredients, not about whether losing water is what makes bread stale.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Unwrapped loaves losing water and hardening fits O'Connor's claim, so this would support it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Customers' shopping habits do not show why bread becomes hard.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Kantha is a style of embroidery from Bangladesh and eastern India in which several layers of old cotton saris are stitched together with rows of small running stitches. Today many kantha quilts are richly decorated with flowers, animals, and scenes from daily life. Textile historian Farida Rahman argues that kantha began mainly as a practical way to reuse worn cloth, and that its decoration developed later.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Rahman's argument?

choices.A: The oldest surviving kanthas are covered with detailed scenes stitched in many different colors.
choices.B: The oldest surviving kanthas are made of worn, patched cloth and have very little decoration.
choices.C: Today, kantha quilts are sold in shops around the world and are popular with collectors.
choices.D: Running stitches are also used in many other embroidery traditions in different parts of Asia.

explanation.why: Rahman says kantha started as a plain, practical craft and became decorative only later. The oldest examples are the best test: if they are mostly patched, worn cloth with little decoration, her account is supported.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Richly decorated early kanthas would suggest decoration was there from the start, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.B: Correct. The earliest kanthas are practical and plain, which fits the idea that decoration came later.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Kantha's popularity today says nothing about how the craft began.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The use of running stitches elsewhere does not show why kantha began.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Chameleons are famous for their ability to change color. In a popular book about animals, nature writer Paolo Ricci claims that a chameleon changes color mainly to match whatever it happens to be sitting on, so that predators passing by cannot see it. He describes the chameleon as a living camouflage that copies the colors around it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ricci's claim?

choices.A: Chameleons placed on a bright green leaf turned green within a few minutes.
choices.B: Chameleons placed on green, brown, and gray backgrounds stayed the same color on all three.
choices.C: Chameleons catch insects by shooting out a sticky tongue that can be longer than their bodies.
choices.D: Many species of chameleon live only on Madagascar, an island off the southeastern coast of Africa.

explanation.why: Ricci says chameleons change color mainly to match their surroundings. If chameleons put on very different backgrounds do not change color at all, matching the background cannot be the main reason they change, so that finding weakens his claim.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A chameleon turning green on a green leaf fits Ricci's claim, so this would support it.
explanation.B: Correct. The chameleons did not change to match any of the three backgrounds, which goes against the idea that they change color to blend in.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How chameleons catch food has nothing to do with why they change color.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Where chameleons live does not show why they change color.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Some orb-weaving spiders add bright zigzag bands of silk, called decorations, to the centers of their webs. Because spinning these bands costs the spider both silk and energy, biologists have long asked what purpose they serve. Arachnologist Mei-Ling Chou argues that their main purpose is to warn birds: a bird that notices the bright bands can swerve away in time instead of flying straight through the web and destroying it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Chou's argument?

choices.A: Some spider species add decorations to their webs only while the spiders are young.
choices.B: Decorated webs are built most often by spiders that hunt during the day, when birds are most active.
choices.C: Orb-weaving spiders often eat their old webs and reuse the silk to spin new ones.
choices.D: Birds flew through webs with decorations just as often as through similar webs without them.

explanation.why: Chou claims the decorations exist mainly to keep birds from flying into webs. If that were true, decorated webs should be hit by birds less often. A finding that birds hit decorated and undecorated webs equally often shows the decorations are not doing that job, which weakens her argument.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Knowing that only young spiders of some species decorate does not show whether decorations warn birds.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Decorations being most common where birds are active fits Chou's argument, so this would support it rather than weaken it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Reusing silk explains how spiders save material, not what the decorations are for.
explanation.D: Correct. If decorations did not reduce how often birds broke through webs, they cannot be serving mainly as a warning to birds.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1291, the government of Venice ordered the city's glassmakers to move their furnaces to Murano, a small island nearby. The official reason was safety: Venice was crowded with wooden buildings, and glass furnaces could easily start fires. Historian Paolo Benedetti, however, argues that the order was mainly meant to protect the city's valuable glassmaking methods by gathering the craftsmen in one place where they could be closely watched.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Benedetti's argument?

choices.A: Glassmakers who moved to Murano were forbidden to leave Venetian lands or to teach their methods to outsiders.
choices.B: In the centuries after the move, Murano glassmakers developed new kinds of especially clear glass.
choices.C: Several serious fires had broken out in Venice in the decades before the glassmakers were ordered to move.
choices.D: Glass made on Murano became famous and was sold to wealthy buyers in cities across Europe.

explanation.why: Benedetti's claim is about the government's motive: keeping glassmaking secrets inside Venice, rather than preventing fires. Rules that stopped the glassmakers from leaving or sharing their methods would show that controlling the craftsmen and their knowledge was a central aim.
explanation.A: Correct. Forbidding glassmakers to leave or to teach outsiders shows that the government was focused on keeping their methods from spreading.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Later improvements in glassmaking do not reveal the government's reason for the move in 1291.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Earlier fires would make the official safety reason more believable, which works against Benedetti's argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Murano glass becoming famous shows the craft was valuable but not why the glassmakers were moved.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In Ladakh, a high, dry region of northern India, villages depend on meltwater from glaciers to water their fields in spring, but many of the glaciers there are shrinking. Some villages now build "ice stupas": tall cones of ice made in winter by spraying stream water into the freezing air. Engineer Stanzin Dolma argues that the cone shape is what lets this ice last into late spring, because a cone exposes much less of its surface to direct sunlight than a flat sheet of ice holding the same amount of water.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Dolma's argument?

choices.A: At the same site, ice cones lasted several weeks longer than flat sheets of ice made from equal amounts of water.
choices.B: Ice stupas built at higher, colder sites lasted longer than ice stupas built lower in the same valleys.
choices.C: At the same site, flat sheets of ice lasted just as long as ice cones made from equal amounts of water.
choices.D: Ladakh receives very little rain or snow, so its farmers have long relied on melting glacier ice.

explanation.why: Dolma credits the shape of the ice, not just the cold, for how long it lasts. A fair test would compare a cone and a flat sheet with the same amount of water in the same place, so that only the shape differs. If the cones last much longer, shape is shown to matter.
explanation.A: Correct. Only the shape differed between the two kinds of ice, and the cones lasted weeks longer, just as Dolma predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This shows that colder sites help the ice last, which is about location and temperature, not about the cone shape.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If flat sheets lasted just as long, the cone shape would not matter, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This explains why villages need meltwater, not why cone-shaped ice lasts longer.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In recent decades, the instrumental introductions of popular songs have grown much shorter, and many hit songs now reach the singer's voice within a few seconds. Musicologist Daniel Okafor links this change to music streaming services, which typically count a song as played only if a listener stays with it for about thirty seconds. He argues that songwriters began shortening their intros so that listeners would not skip ahead before reaching that point.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okafor's argument?

choices.A: Most of the shortening of intros took place years before streaming services became widely used.
choices.B: Some popular songs released in recent years still begin with intros longer than thirty seconds.
choices.C: Short intros have become common in songs written for films as well as in popular music.
choices.D: On streaming services, listeners are most likely to skip a song during the first few seconds of its intro.

explanation.why: Okafor claims streaming caused songwriters to shorten intros. A cause must come before its effect, so if most of the shortening had already happened before streaming was common, streaming cannot be the main cause.
explanation.A: Correct. If intros mostly shrank before streaming spread, the change must have had a different main cause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Okafor describes an overall trend; a few long intros today do not show that streaming was not behind the trend.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Short intros in film songs do not show what caused the change, so this neither confirms nor undercuts the streaming explanation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Listeners skipping during intros gives songwriters a reason to shorten them, so this fits Okafor's argument.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein (1818) in June 1816 near Lake Geneva in Switzerland. That summer was unusually cold and stormy across Europe, partly because a huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia the year before had filled the sky with ash. Literary scholar Inés Navarro argues that the strange weather of that summer directly shaped the bleak, icy, and storm-filled settings that dominate much of the novel.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Navarro's argument?

choices.A: The ghost-story contest that led Shelley to begin the novel was proposed by the poet Lord Byron, who was staying nearby.
choices.B: Many novels written in warmer, calmer years of the period also feature bleak, icy, and storm-filled settings.
choices.C: Shelley's journal from that summer describes storms over the lake in words that closely match scenes in the novel.
choices.D: Frankenstein became much more widely known in the 1820s after it was adapted into a play for the London stage.

explanation.why: Navarro claims the weather of summer 1816 directly shaped the novel's settings. The best support would connect what Shelley actually experienced that summer to what she wrote. Journal descriptions of the storms that closely match scenes in the book make that connection.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Who proposed the contest explains how the novel started, not where its stormy settings came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If such settings were common in novels written in calm years, they may simply have been a fashion of the time, which would weaken Navarro's argument.
explanation.C: Correct. Matching language shows Shelley drawing on the storms she saw that summer when she wrote the novel's scenes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The novel's later fame on the stage says nothing about what shaped its settings.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the Namib Desert of southwestern Africa, where rain almost never falls, some darkling beetles climb to the tops of sand dunes on foggy mornings. There they lean forward with their backs raised into the wind, and fog droplets gather on their bodies and roll down toward their mouths. Some researchers suspect this headstand mainly helps the beetles cool down, but ecologist Yusuf Adeyemi argues that its main purpose is to collect drinking water.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Adeyemi's argument?

choices.A: Several other desert animals, including some lizards, also get water from fog in their own ways.
choices.B: Beetles in the headstand position lost body heat faster than beetles resting flat on the sand.
choices.C: On clear mornings just as cool as foggy ones, the beetles almost never took the headstand position.
choices.D: The beetles' dark bodies warm up quickly once the sun rises higher over the dunes.

explanation.why: Two explanations compete: cooling and water collection. To favor Adeyemi's, a finding must separate them. Comparing mornings with the same temperature but with and without fog does this: if the beetles do the headstand only when there is fog to catch, water is the likely purpose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Other animals using fog says nothing about the purpose of this beetle's posture.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Losing heat faster in the headstand fits the cooling explanation, so this would favor the researchers Adeyemi disagrees with.
explanation.C: Correct. With temperature held the same, the beetles did the headstand only when fog was present, which points to collecting water rather than cooling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How fast the beetles warm in the sun does not show why they do the headstand on foggy mornings.

items.subject: history_social
