explanation.D: Correct. When a mask did not need to be worn, carvers chose heavier wood, which shows that lightness was the reason for choosing kaduru for dance masks.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The children's author Harriet Lowe published more than twenty novels between 1920 and 1950 and received many letters from young readers. Literary scholar Tomas Varga claims that Lowe sometimes changed the endings of her books in response to these letters, giving readers the happier conclusions they asked for.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Varga's claim?

choices.A: Several of Lowe's later novels end less happily than her earlier ones, despite their popularity with readers.
choices.B: A manuscript shows one novel's original sad ending replaced after several readers wrote asking Lowe to let the main character survive.
choices.C: Lowe's publisher repeatedly asked her to make her endings happier so that the books would sell better in bookstores.
choices.D: Lowe replied personally to nearly every letter she received from a young reader, often within a few days.

explanation.why: Varga's claim has two parts: Lowe changed endings, and she did so because of readers' letters. The best support shows both parts together: a changed ending and the letters that prompted it. A choice that gives another cause for happier endings, or that says nothing about letters, cannot support the claim.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A trend toward sadder endings does not show that letters from readers ever changed an ending.
explanation.B: Correct. The manuscript shows an ending being changed, and the change came after readers asked for it, which is exactly what Varga claims.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This offers a different reason for happier endings, pressure from the publisher, so it does not support the idea that readers' letters caused the changes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Answering letters shows that Lowe valued her readers, but not that she changed her endings because of them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Male silk moths find females by following a scent that the females release into the air. The males detect the scent with their large, feathery antennae. Entomologist Rosa Delgado hypothesizes that a male does not simply fly toward wherever the scent is strongest. Instead, once he detects any scent at all, he turns to face the wind and flies upwind, because the scent must be coming from that direction.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Delgado's hypothesis?

choices.A: Males with larger antennae detected the scent at much lower concentrations than males with smaller antennae did.
choices.B: Males always flew toward the spot where the scent was most concentrated, even when that meant flying downwind.
choices.C: In a wind tunnel, males flew upwind as soon as they detected the scent and circled in place when the fan was turned off.
choices.D: Female moths release the scent mostly at night, when the air is usually calmer and the scent spreads more slowly.

explanation.why: Delgado's hypothesis is that the wind, not the strength of the scent, tells a male which way to fly. The clearest support is an experiment showing that males head upwind after detecting scent and lose direction when there is no wind. A finding that males follow the strongest scent would contradict her.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This concerns how sensitive the antennae are, not how a male chooses which way to fly.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the behavior Delgado argues against: following the strongest scent instead of the wind.
explanation.C: Correct. The moths used the wind to choose a direction and lost their way without wind, which is just what Delgado predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When the scent is released does not show how males navigate toward it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Urban planner Felix Osei has noticed that some streets in his city are busy with people on foot while similar streets nearby are nearly empty. He hypothesizes that the difference is shade: on hot days, people choose to walk along streets lined with trees and avoid streets that have no shade.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Osei's hypothesis?

choices.A: On every street surveyed, counts of walkers were higher on weekends than on weekdays throughout the year.
choices.B: Residents who were surveyed said that they liked the look of trees on their streets and wanted more planted.
choices.C: Tree-lined streets in the city tend to have more shops, cafes, and other attractions than streets without trees do.
choices.D: On hot afternoons, tree-lined streets had far more walkers than treeless streets; on cool, cloudy days, the difference nearly vanished.

explanation.why: Osei thinks people pick shady streets on hot days. To support that, a finding should show that tree-lined streets are busier specifically when it is hot. If the difference appears on hot days but disappears on cool days, shade is the likely reason. A choice offering a different cause for the busy streets, such as shops, would not support Osei.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Weekend crowds say nothing about why some streets are busier than others.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Liking the look of trees is not the same as choosing to walk in their shade on hot days.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This suggests a different reason for the busier streets, shops rather than shade, so it does not support Osei's explanation.
explanation.D: Correct. The tree-lined streets drew more walkers only when it was hot, which shows that people were seeking shade.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most blue whales migrate long distances each year, feeding in cold waters near the poles in summer and moving to warmer waters in winter. The blue whales seen off the southern coast of Sri Lanka, however, are spotted in every month of the year. Marine biologist Nuwan Jayasinghe hypothesizes that these whales do not migrate at all but stay in the waters around Sri Lanka all year.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Jayasinghe's hypothesis?

choices.A: Photographs of individual whales, identified by tail shape, show the same animals off Sri Lanka in both summer and winter.
choices.B: Tourist boats that take visitors to see the whales operate mostly between November and April, when the sea is calm.
choices.C: Whales photographed off Sri Lanka in summer have never been seen there again in any later season.
choices.D: Blue whales off Sri Lanka feed mainly on shrimplike animals that are plentiful in the area throughout the year.

explanation.why: The fact that whales are seen in every month could mean that the same whales stay or that different whales pass through. Jayasinghe claims the first. The best support is evidence that the very same individuals are present in different seasons, which photographs of recognizable tails can provide.
explanation.A: Correct. Seeing the same individual whales in different seasons shows that they stay rather than migrate.
explanation.B: Incorrect. When tourists go whale watching has nothing to do with where the whales spend the year.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If the summer whales are never seen again, different whales are passing through, which suggests migration rather than staying.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Plentiful food might make staying possible, but it does not show that the whales actually stay.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ancient Egyptian craftworkers made beads and small figures from faience, a paste of crushed quartz that develops a shiny blue-green glaze when it is fired. Archaeologist Mariam Haddad is studying a workshop site where thousands of unfinished beads were found. She hypothesizes that the workers shaped the beads by pressing the paste into molds rather than rolling each bead by hand.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's hypothesis?

choices.A: The beads from the site vary widely in size, and many of them bear fingerprints pressed into the paste.
choices.B: The workshop also produced faience bowls, amulets, and small figures of animals in a range of sizes.
choices.C: The beads from the site are nearly identical in size and shape, and clay molds with bead-shaped hollows were found nearby.
choices.D: The blue-green color of the beads came from a small amount of copper mixed into the quartz paste before firing.

explanation.why: Haddad's hypothesis is about a method: molds instead of hand-rolling. Molds would produce beads that look alike, and the molds themselves might survive. A finding that reports both uniform beads and actual molds supports her directly, while varied, fingerprinted beads would suggest hand-rolling instead.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Varied sizes and fingerprints point to beads rolled by hand, the opposite of what Haddad proposes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Other products of the workshop do not show how the beads were shaped.
explanation.C: Correct. Identical beads and molds found at the site are exactly what molding, rather than hand-rolling, would leave behind.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The source of the color has nothing to do with whether molds were used.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Houseplants are often said to clean the air inside homes. The idea comes from experiments in which plants placed in small sealed chambers removed certain pollutants from the air over several hours. Based on these results, a popular magazine claims that keeping a few houseplants in a room will noticeably improve the air that people breathe there.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the magazine's claim?

choices.A: People who keep houseplants often report that they feel more relaxed and cheerful at home.
choices.B: In ordinary rooms, outside air leaking in through windows and doors replaces the room's air far faster than plants can clean it.
choices.C: Rooms with many houseplants were found to have lower pollutant levels than similar rooms with no plants at all.
choices.D: Plants in sealed chambers removed more pollutants when the chambers were brightly lit than when they were dim.

explanation.why: The magazine moves from sealed chambers to real rooms. The claim is weakened by a finding that shows why the chamber results do not carry over: in an ordinary room, fresh air replaces the room's air much faster than plants can act, so the plants' effect would be too small to notice.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Feeling relaxed is a different benefit and says nothing about air quality.
explanation.B: Correct. If the room's air is replaced before plants can clean it, a few houseplants would make no noticeable difference, which undercuts the claim.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This would support the magazine's claim, not weaken it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This adds detail about the chamber experiments but does not show whether plants help in a real room.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In medieval Europe, people who traveled to holy sites often brought home small metal badges showing the saint or shrine they had visited. Thousands of these badges have been found, many of them in rivers. Historian Ingrid Halvorsen hypothesizes that the badges were made and sold at the shrines themselves rather than produced in a few large cities and shipped out.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Halvorsen's hypothesis?

choices.A: Written records show that badge makers in one large city supplied shrines across an entire region with badges.
choices.B: Most of the badges were made of a cheap mixture of tin and lead that melted easily and could be cast quickly.
choices.C: Stone molds for casting badges have been excavated at several shrines, each mold matching that shrine's own badges.
choices.D: Badges from many different shrines have been found together in the mud of a single stretch of river in London.

explanation.why: Halvorsen's hypothesis concerns where the badges were made. The strongest support is physical evidence of badge making at the shrines, such as molds that match each shrine's own badges. Evidence about the metal or about where badges were later lost does not answer that question.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This describes badges made in a city and shipped out, the opposite of what Halvorsen proposes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The metal used does not show where the badges were made.
explanation.C: Correct. Molds found at the shrines, each for that shrine's own badges, show that the badges were made where they were sold.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Where badges were lost after travelers brought them home says nothing about where they were made.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In a rural district of Sindh, Pakistan, many families once fetched water from a river several kilometers away. In 2019, a charity installed hand pumps in a number of villages. Economist Sana Baloch hypothesizes that the pumps mainly benefited girls, since fetching water had been their job and the time saved could now be spent at school.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Baloch's hypothesis?

choices.A: After the pumps were installed, school attendance by girls in the villages rose, while attendance by boys stayed about the same.
choices.B: Families in the villages with pumps reported that the pump water tasted better and was clearer than river water.
choices.C: Before the pumps were installed, boys in the villages were more likely than girls to be enrolled in school.
choices.D: Villages that did not receive pumps saw girls' school attendance rise just as much over the same period.

explanation.why: Baloch claims that the pumps helped girls in particular by freeing their time for school. The best support compares girls with boys after the pumps arrived and shows that girls' attendance rose while boys' did not. A finding that attendance rose equally in villages without pumps would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.A: Correct. A rise in attendance for girls only is just what Baloch's hypothesis predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Better-tasting water is a benefit for everyone and says nothing about girls and school.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This describes the situation before the pumps and does not show what the pumps changed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If attendance rose equally where there were no pumps, the pumps cannot be the reason for the rise.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The novelist Edwin Marsh set most of his books in Hollins, a fictional mill town. Marsh himself grew up in Dunford, a real mill town in northern England. Literary scholar Aiko Tanaka claims that Hollins is closely modeled on Dunford and that Marsh changed little more than the name.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tanaka's claim?

choices.A: Marsh wrote in a letter that he had invented Hollins so that no reader would recognize any real place.
choices.B: Maps of Dunford from Marsh's childhood match the streets, bridges, and mills of the Hollins novels almost exactly.
choices.C: Many novels of the period were set in fictional industrial towns with invented names.
choices.D: Marsh moved away from Dunford at eighteen and rarely returned to the town for the rest of his life.

explanation.why: Tanaka's claim is that the fictional Hollins copies the real Dunford in nearly every detail. The strongest support compares the two directly and finds them matching. A letter in which Marsh says he invented the town would weaken the claim rather than support it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A statement that Hollins was invented to avoid resembling any real place works against Tanaka's claim.
explanation.B: Correct. If the real town's layout matches the fictional one almost exactly, Hollins is indeed Dunford with a new name.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A general fashion for fictional towns says nothing about whether this particular town was based on Dunford.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Leaving Dunford does not show whether Marsh used it as the model for Hollins.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Some damselfish that live on coral reefs tend small patches of algae, chasing away other fish that try to graze there. These patches are dominated by a single kind of fine red algae that the damselfish eat. Marine ecologist Hana Yoshida hypothesizes that the damselfish actively weed their patches, removing other kinds of algae so that the red algae can thrive, rather than the red algae simply growing best in the spots the fish happen to defend.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Yoshida's hypothesis?

choices.A: Red algae growing inside the patches contain more protein than the same algae growing outside the territories do.
choices.B: Damselfish defend their patches far more fiercely against large grazing fish than against small ones that eat little.
choices.C: The red algae grow faster than other kinds of algae in the sunny, shallow spots where damselfish usually set up their territories.
choices.D: Damselfish were observed pulling up other kinds of algae that sprouted in their patches and carrying them beyond their territories.

explanation.why: The passage sets up two explanations for the red algae patches: the fish weed them, or the red algae simply grow best there. Yoshida favors weeding, so the best support is a direct observation of the fish removing other algae. A finding that the red algae naturally outgrow other algae in those spots would favor the rival explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The quality of the algae does not show how the patches came to be dominated by it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How hard the fish defend their patches against grazers says nothing about whether they remove unwanted algae.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This supports the alternative explanation that the red algae simply grow best in those spots, so it works against Yoshida's hypothesis.
explanation.D: Correct. The fish deliberately removing other algae is weeding, exactly the behavior Yoshida proposes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many reef corals contain proteins that glow green or orange when light strikes them, a property called fluorescence. One long-standing hypothesis holds that these proteins act as a sunscreen: by absorbing harmful high-energy light and releasing it as harmless lower-energy light, they protect the coral and the algae living inside it from damage in bright, shallow water.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the sunscreen hypothesis?

choices.A: Shallow-water corals kept in shaded tanks gradually produced less and less fluorescent protein over several weeks.
choices.B: Fluorescent proteins in corals were first described by scientists in the middle of the twentieth century, decades after fluorescence in other animals.
choices.C: Some fish that live among the corals can see the fluorescent glow, which is invisible to people without special filters.
choices.D: Corals in deep, dim water, where little harmful light reaches, make as much fluorescent protein as shallow-water corals or more.

explanation.why: The sunscreen hypothesis predicts that corals make fluorescent proteins to cope with strong light. A finding that corals in dim deep water, where strong light is not a problem, make just as much or more of the protein does not fit that prediction and so weakens the hypothesis. A finding that production falls in the shade would fit the prediction and support it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Producing less protein when light is reduced fits the sunscreen idea and would support the hypothesis rather than weaken it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. When the proteins were discovered has no bearing on what they do.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Whether fish can see the glow does not tell us whether the proteins protect the coral from light.
explanation.D: Correct. If corals that need no protection from strong light make just as much of the protein, protection from light is unlikely to be its purpose, which weakens the hypothesis.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pokkali is a variety of rice grown in low-lying coastal fields in Kerala, India, where seawater seeps in and makes the soil salty. Most rice varieties die in such conditions, but pokkali plants grow tall and produce grain. Agricultural scientist Reshma Pillai hypothesizes that pokkali survives because its roots keep salt out, letting far less salt into the plant than other varieties do, rather than because the plant can tolerate high levels of salt in its tissues.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Pillai's hypothesis?

choices.A: Farmers in Kerala often raise prawns in the same fields during the months of the year when rice is not growing there.
choices.B: Pokkali plants grow taller than most other rice varieties even in fields that contain no salt at all, and their grain is coarser.
choices.C: Pokkali plants grown in salty water contained as much salt in their leaves as other varieties but showed far less leaf damage.
choices.D: Grown side by side in salty water, pokkali plants contained much less salt in their stems and leaves than other varieties did.

explanation.why: Pillai contrasts two explanations: keeping salt out versus tolerating salt inside. Her hypothesis is the first, so the best support measures salt inside the plants and finds less in pokkali. A finding of equal salt inside but less damage would support the rival explanation instead.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The farming cycle has nothing to do with how pokkali handles salt.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Height in salt-free fields says nothing about how the plant deals with salt.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Equal salt inside the plant with less damage would mean the plant tolerates salt in its tissues, the explanation Pillai rejects.
explanation.D: Correct. Less salt inside the plant under the same conditions shows that pokkali's roots are keeping salt out, as Pillai proposes.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, merchants from across Europe gathered at a cycle of trade fairs in the Champagne region of France. Each fair lasted several weeks and ended with a period set aside for settling payments. Economic historian Paolo Ferrante argues that most of the trade at these fairs was settled not with coins but by canceling debts against one another, so that a merchant who owed money to one trader and was owed money by another paid only the difference.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferrante's argument?

choices.A: The fairs declined in the fourteenth century as sea routes between Italy and Flanders improved and grew safer.
choices.B: Local officials in Champagne charged merchants a fee to set up stalls at each fair and taxed the goods they sold.
choices.C: Merchants' account books from the fairs list long columns of debts crossed out against one another, with only small sums paid in coin.
choices.D: Merchants traveling to the fairs often hired armed guards to protect the heavy chests of coins they carried with them.

explanation.why: Ferrante's argument is about the method of payment: canceling debts rather than handing over coins. The most direct support is the merchants' own records showing debts being canceled against each other and little coin changing hands. Evidence that merchants hauled chests of coins to the fairs would point the other way.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Why the fairs later declined says nothing about how payments were settled.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Stall fees are a detail of how the fairs were run, not of how merchants paid one another.
explanation.C: Correct. Debts canceled against each other with only small amounts paid in coin is precisely the system Ferrante describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Merchants carrying large amounts of coin suggests that coins, not canceled debts, settled most trade.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ancient Greek marble statues are usually displayed today as pure white stone, and for centuries many admirers assumed that this was how the Greeks had intended them to look. Art historian Sofia Katsaros argues instead that the statues were originally painted in bright colors and that their present whiteness is simply the result of the paint wearing away over time.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Katsaros's argument?

choices.A: Greek writers of the period praised sculptors for the lifelike quality of their marble figures and the skill of their carving.
choices.B: Under ultraviolet light, traces of red, blue, and yellow pigment appear in the deep folds of carved clothing on many statues.
choices.C: Some Roman copies of Greek statues were carved from colored stone, such as green or red marble, rather than white.
choices.D: Chemical tests on the surfaces of several famous statues found only marble and the residue of modern cleaning agents.

explanation.why: Katsaros claims the statues were painted and the paint later wore off. The best support is physical evidence of paint that survives where wear was least, which both shows that paint was there and explains why most of it is gone. Praise for lifelike sculpture or colored stone copies does not establish paint on the originals.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Praise for lifelike figures could refer to the carving itself and does not show that the statues were painted.
explanation.B: Correct. Pigment surviving exactly where it was most sheltered shows that the statues were once painted and that the color has worn away elsewhere.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Colored stone used by later copyists says nothing about paint on the Greek originals.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Finding no trace of pigment at all would work against the argument that the statues were once painted.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: "Ozymandias" is an 1818 sonnet by Percy Bysshe Shelley. In it, a traveler describes the ruined statue of an ancient king lying in an empty desert. The king's power is long gone, and his boastful inscription now seems absurd. Yet the poem suggests that something has outlasted the king: the skill of the sculptor, whose carving still conveys the king's arrogance and cruelty centuries after the king himself and everything he ruled have vanished.
items.stem: Which quotation from "Ozymandias" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "'My name is Ozymandias, king of kings: / Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!'"
choices.B: "Tell that its sculptor well those passions read / Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,"
choices.C: "Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desert."
choices.D: "Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away."

explanation.why: The claim is that the sculptor's skill has outlasted the king by preserving the king's character in stone. The right quotation must mention the sculptor and the survival of what he captured. Only the lines about the sculptor reading the king's "passions," which "yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things," do both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the king's boast. It shows his arrogance but does not say that the sculptor's art has survived.
explanation.B: Correct. These lines say that the sculptor understood the king's "passions" and that they "yet survive" in the stone, which is the claim that the sculptor's skill outlasted the king.
explanation.C: Incorrect. These lines describe the broken statue but say nothing about the sculptor or what his work preserved.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These lines show that the king's empire has vanished, which is only part of the claim; they do not mention the sculptor's skill surviving.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Robert Frost's 1916 poem "The Road Not Taken" is often read as a celebration of bold, independent choices. The speaker, standing where two roads split in a wood, picks one and later says that the choice changed his life. But a closer reading shows that the speaker himself admits, in the middle of the poem, that the two roads were in fact nearly identical.
items.stem: Which quotation from "The Road Not Taken" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "I shall be telling this with a sigh / Somewhere ages and ages hence:"
choices.B: "I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference."
choices.C: "Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, / And sorry I could not travel both"
choices.D: "Though as for that the passing there / Had worn them really about the same,"

explanation.why: The claim is that the speaker admits the two roads were nearly the same. The quotation must contain that admission. Only the lines saying the roads had been worn "really about the same" do so; the famous closing lines insist on a difference, which is the opposite.
explanation.A: Incorrect. These lines look ahead to the speaker retelling the story; they say nothing about how similar the roads were.
explanation.B: Incorrect. These lines claim that one road was "less traveled," which is the opposite of admitting that the roads were nearly identical.
explanation.C: Incorrect. These lines set the scene and express regret, but they do not say that the roads were alike.
explanation.D: Correct. Here the speaker concedes that the two roads had been worn "really about the same," which is the admission that they were nearly identical.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Many companies have replaced private offices and cubicles with open-plan workspaces in which employees sit at shared tables with no walls between them. Supporters argue that removing the walls increases face-to-face conversation among coworkers, since people can see one another and simply walk over to talk. Management researcher Leila Haddad calls this the open interaction hypothesis.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the open interaction hypothesis?

choices.A: Employees in open-plan offices reported that they could overhear their coworkers' conversations throughout the working day.
choices.B: At a company that switched to an open plan, employees were observed walking over to colleagues' desks several times each hour.
choices.C: After one company switched to an open plan, sensors worn by employees recorded a sharp drop in face-to-face conversation.
choices.D: Open-plan offices cost less to build and maintain than offices divided into private rooms, and they hold more workers.

explanation.why: The hypothesis predicts more face-to-face conversation once walls are removed. To weaken it, a finding must show that face-to-face conversation did not increase, or actually fell, after a switch to an open plan. Measurements showing a sharp drop in conversation do exactly that.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Overhearing others is not the same as talking with them more, so this does not test the hypothesis.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Frequent visits to colleagues' desks would support the hypothesis rather than weaken it.
explanation.C: Correct. Less face-to-face conversation after the walls came down is the opposite of what the hypothesis predicts, so this finding weakens it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Cost has nothing to do with whether people talk face-to-face more often.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At Mamallapuram, on the coast of Tamil Nadu in southern India, the Pallava kings of the seventh and eighth centuries had temples and sculptures carved directly out of granite outcrops. Many of the monuments were never completed: carvings stop partway, and some surfaces show only rough outlines. Archaeologist Kavitha Sundaram hypothesizes that the monuments were carved at the same time by many crews working at once, rather than one after another over many decades.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sundaram's hypothesis?

choices.A: Stone chips and worn tools discarded during carving lie in one thick layer across the site rather than in separate layers.
choices.B: Several of the completed monuments at the site were later used as landmarks by sailors approaching the coast from the east.
choices.C: The granite at Mamallapuram is extremely hard, so carving even a small shrine would have required many months of work.
choices.D: The style of the carving changes noticeably from one monument to the next, in a sequence that matches changes in Pallava sculpture over a century.

explanation.why: Sundaram's hypothesis is about timing: many crews at once, not one project after another. Debris from carving is a good test, because work done at the same time leaves one layer while work spread over decades leaves layers. A sequence of changing styles would instead suggest work spread out over time.
explanation.A: Correct. A single layer of carving debris across the whole site is what many crews working at once would leave, while work spread over decades would leave layered deposits.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The later use of the monuments has nothing to do with how the carving was organized.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How long each shrine took does not show whether the crews worked at the same time or in sequence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A sequence of styles spanning a century suggests that the monuments were carved one after another, which goes against the hypothesis.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In late spring, patches of mountain snow sometimes turn pink or red. The color comes from microscopic algae that live in the snow and produce a red pigment. Biologist Marek Nowak hypothesizes that the pigment acts as a sunscreen, shielding the algae's cells from the intense sunlight reflected by the snow, and that the algae make more of it when the light is stronger.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nowak's hypothesis?

choices.A: The red pigment absorbs some of the sun's energy, warming the surrounding snow and causing it to melt slightly faster.
choices.B: The algae are green during the winter and turn red only after the snow begins to melt in the spring, when they multiply.
choices.C: Algae from snow on shaded, north-facing slopes contained far less red pigment than algae from nearby sunlit slopes.
choices.D: Algae from shaded slopes contained just as much red pigment as algae from slopes that lay in full sun all day.

explanation.why: Nowak predicts that pigment production rises with the strength of sunlight. The cleanest support compares algae in bright and shaded places and finds more pigment in the bright ones. Equal pigment in both places would weaken the hypothesis, and effects of the pigment on the snow do not test it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This describes an effect of the pigment on the snow, not whether the algae make more of it in stronger light.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The timing of the color change could have many causes and does not link pigment to the strength of light.
explanation.C: Correct. Less pigment where there is less light is what Nowak's hypothesis predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Equal pigment regardless of light would go against the idea that the algae make more pigment when light is stronger.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Several medieval cathedrals in France have a labyrinth, a winding path laid out in colored stone in the floor of the central aisle. No document from the time explains what the labyrinths were for. Historian Beatrice Lemoine hypothesizes that worshippers walked the labyrinth's path as a substitute for a long journey to a distant holy site, a journey that most of them could never afford to make.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lemoine's hypothesis?

choices.A: Labyrinth patterns similar to those in the cathedrals appear on ancient Greek coins and on Roman floor mosaics across Europe.
choices.B: Records show that the labyrinths were used mainly for a ceremonial ball game played by the clergy at Easter each year.
choices.C: The labyrinth at one cathedral was removed in the eighteenth century because it distracted worshippers during services.
choices.D: Church records from one cathedral town note that people unable to travel to a distant shrine were told to walk the labyrinth instead.

explanation.why: Lemoine's hypothesis is about purpose: the labyrinth replaced a journey people could not make. The passage says no contemporary document explains the labyrinths, so a record describing exactly this use would be the most direct support. A record describing a different main use would weaken her hypothesis.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The pattern's older history says nothing about how medieval worshippers used it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A different main purpose, a clergy game, works against the idea that the labyrinths stood in for a journey.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Why a labyrinth was later removed does not show what it was originally for.
explanation.D: Correct. A record of the labyrinth being walked in place of a journey to a distant shrine is direct evidence for Lemoine's explanation.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Paubha are devotional paintings on cloth made by the Newar people of the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal. The brilliant blues in many old paubha resemble ultramarine, a costly pigment made from lapis lazuli mined far away in what is now Afghanistan. Art conservator Sabina Shrestha hypothesizes that the painters used cheaper blue minerals for most of each painting and reserved ultramarine for the small areas that mattered most, such as the faces and robes of the central figures.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Shrestha's hypothesis?

choices.A: Pigment analysis of several old paubha found ultramarine throughout the sky and background as well as on the central figures.
choices.B: Newar painters traditionally worked in family workshops and passed their techniques and recipes to the next generation.
choices.C: Pigment analysis of several old paubha found ultramarine only on the central figures, with a cheaper blue in the sky and background.
choices.D: Trade caravans carrying lapis lazuli regularly passed through the Kathmandu Valley on their way from Afghanistan to Tibet.

explanation.why: Shrestha's hypothesis predicts a specific pattern: expensive ultramarine on the central figures, cheaper blue elsewhere. The best support is a pigment analysis that finds that pattern. An analysis finding ultramarine everywhere would weaken it, and facts about trade or training do not test it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Ultramarine used everywhere would mean the painters did not save it for the most important areas, which goes against the hypothesis.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How the craft was taught does not show which pigments were used where.
explanation.C: Correct. Ultramarine confined to the central figures and a cheaper blue elsewhere is exactly the pattern Shrestha predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Lapis lazuli being available locally does not show that painters limited its use to the central figures.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pied kingfishers, black-and-white birds found near rivers and lakes in Africa and Asia, catch fish by diving from the air. Sometimes a kingfisher dives from a perch such as an overhanging branch; sometimes it hovers in place above the water, beating its wings rapidly, before plunging. Ornithologist Amadou Diallo hypothesizes that hovering costs far more energy than perching, so kingfishers hover only when no suitable perch is available.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Diallo's hypothesis?

choices.A: Kingfishers hovering over the river were seen more often in the early morning than at midday, regardless of the weather.
choices.B: Kingfishers caught fish on a higher proportion of dives made from a hover than of dives made from a perch.
choices.C: Where overhanging branches had been cleared, kingfishers hovered far more often; where artificial perches were added, they hovered less.
choices.D: Pied kingfishers are among the largest birds able to hover in still air for more than a few seconds at a time.

explanation.why: Diallo's hypothesis links hovering to the absence of perches. The best support changes the number of perches and watches hovering change in the opposite direction. A finding that hovering is actually more successful would suggest birds hover by preference, weakening the hypothesis.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The time of day of hovering does not link hovering to the availability of perches.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If hovering gives better results, the birds might hover by choice rather than only when forced to, which works against the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Correct. Hovering rising when perches are removed and falling when perches are added shows that the birds hover only when they lack a perch.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The bird's ability to hover does not show when or why it chooses to hover.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Downtown shop owners often oppose raising the price of street parking, fearing that higher prices will drive customers away. Transportation economist Mei-Ling Chen argues the opposite: that higher prices on the busiest blocks free up spaces by discouraging drivers from parking all day, so that more shoppers can find a spot and the shops gain customers.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Chen's argument?

choices.A: After a city raised prices on its busiest downtown blocks, the average parking stay fell by half and shops there reported more customers.
choices.B: Most drivers surveyed said that they would rather pay more for parking than spend time circling the block looking for a space.
choices.C: Shops on blocks where prices were raised reported fewer customers, and many parking spaces sat empty for most of the day.
choices.D: After the price rise, drivers who had parked downtown all day began parking on nearby residential streets and walking the rest of the way.

explanation.why: Chen's argument has a chain: higher prices lead to shorter stays, shorter stays free up spaces, and more shoppers reach the shops. The most direct support reports both ends of the chain after a real price rise: shorter stays and more customers. A finding of fewer customers would support the shop owners instead.
explanation.A: Correct. Shorter stays and more customers after the price rise are exactly the two effects Chen predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. What drivers say they prefer does not show what actually happened to parking turnover or to the shops.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Fewer customers and empty spaces would support the shop owners' fear, not Chen's argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Where the all-day parkers went does not show whether shops gained customers.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The rich cod fishing grounds off Newfoundland became widely known in Europe after John Cabot's voyage of 1497. Historian Iñaki Etxeberria hypothesizes that Basque fishermen from northern Spain were already catching cod there some years before Cabot sailed, and that they kept the location quiet to protect their catch from competitors.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Etxeberria's hypothesis?

choices.A: Cod were plentiful off Newfoundland because cold currents carry nutrients to the shallow banks there, supporting vast schools.
choices.B: Account books from a Basque port in the early 1490s record ships returning with salted cod after voyages far longer than trips to any European fishing ground.
choices.C: Basque whalers had established seasonal stations on the coast of Labrador by the middle of the 1500s, with furnaces for rendering whale oil.
choices.D: The earliest Basque documents that mention Newfoundland by name date from the 1510s, more than a decade after Cabot's voyage.

explanation.why: The hypothesis is about timing: Basque fishing at Newfoundland before 1497. Support must come from before that date and point to a distant ground. Records of unusually long cod voyages in the early 1490s do that. Evidence from the 1500s, or about why the fishing was good, does not establish an earlier presence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Why the fishing was good has nothing to do with who got there first.
explanation.B: Correct. Long cod voyages dated before 1497 fit the idea that the Basques were already fishing a distant ground such as Newfoundland.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Stations set up decades after 1497 do not show that the Basques were in the region before Cabot.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If the earliest mentions come only after Cabot's voyage, that points against an earlier Basque presence.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The novelist Clara Whitfield, writing in the 1890s, set several books in India and Egypt and described their streets, markets, and landscapes in vivid detail. Reviewers of her time assumed that she had traveled widely, and literary scholar Daniel Okafor accepts this view, arguing that the settings must be based on her own journeys because no writer who stayed at home could have captured such specific detail.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okafor's argument?

choices.A: Many of Whitfield's descriptions repeat, sometimes almost word for word, passages from a popular travel guidebook of the 1880s.
choices.B: Whitfield's diary records a voyage to Egypt in 1888, two years before the publication of her first novel set there.
choices.C: Several reviewers complained that Whitfield's plots were far less convincing than her settings and her minor characters.
choices.D: Whitfield's novels set in England describe their settings in far less detail than her novels set in India and Egypt do.

explanation.why: Okafor reasons that such detail could only come from travel. The argument is weakened by showing another source for the detail. If the descriptions closely follow a popular guidebook, Whitfield could have written them without leaving home. A diary recording a real voyage would strengthen his view instead.
explanation.A: Correct. If the details came from a guidebook, a writer who stayed at home could have produced them, which removes the basis for Okafor's argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A recorded voyage would support the idea that she drew on her own travels, not weaken it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Opinions about the plots have nothing to do with the source of the settings.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A difference in the amount of detail does not show where the foreign details came from.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Purple-faced langurs are monkeys found only in Sri Lanka. In forests they eat mostly leaves, but groups living in the gardens of suburban Colombo feed heavily on cultivated fruits such as jackfruit and mango. Primatologist Ruwan Fernando hypothesizes that the garden langurs eat fruit not because they prefer it but because the gardens contain too few trees with leaves the monkeys can eat.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Fernando's hypothesis?

choices.A: Garden langurs weighed more than forest langurs of the same age and sex and had thicker, glossier coats.
choices.B: Garden langurs spend less time traveling each day than forest langurs do and rest for longer periods.
choices.C: Langur groups in gardens ate mostly fruit even when native leaf-bearing trees were plentiful within their home ranges.
choices.D: Langurs in gardens with many native leaf-bearing trees ate mostly leaves; those in gardens dominated by fruit trees ate mostly fruit.

explanation.why: Fernando contrasts two reasons for fruit eating: preference or a shortage of edible leaves. His hypothesis is the second. The best support compares gardens with and without leaf-bearing trees and shows that the monkeys eat leaves when they can. Eating fruit even when leaves are plentiful would point to preference instead.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Body weight does not show why the garden monkeys eat fruit.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How far the monkeys travel says nothing about what drives their choice of food.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Choosing fruit even when leaves are plentiful would suggest a preference for fruit, the explanation Fernando rejects.
explanation.D: Correct. When edible leaves are available in gardens, the monkeys eat leaves, which shows that scarcity of leaves, not preference, drives the fruit eating.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Roosters famously crow at dawn. Some scientists believe that crowing is triggered simply by the first light of morning. Animal behaviorist Yusuf Demir rejects this view. He hypothesizes that roosters crow according to an internal clock that tells them when dawn is near, so that they would start crowing at about the usual time even if no light appeared.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Demir's hypothesis?

choices.A: The highest-ranking rooster in a group is usually the first to crow each morning, followed by the others in order of rank.
choices.B: Roosters kept in constant dim light for several days still began crowing at roughly 24-hour intervals, shortly before the time of sunrise outside.
choices.C: Roosters often crow during the day in response to the crowing of other roosters nearby or to sudden loud noises.
choices.D: Roosters kept in constant dim light for several days crowed only when a lamp was switched on, at whatever hour that happened to be.

explanation.why: Demir predicts that roosters will crow at the usual time even without light. A finding that weakens this must show roosters failing to crow at the usual time when light is absent and crowing only when light appears. Roosters crowing on schedule in constant dim light would support him instead.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Which rooster crows first does not show whether light or an internal clock sets the time.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Crowing at the usual time without any dawn light is what an internal clock would produce, so this supports Demir rather than weakening him.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Daytime crowing in reply to other roosters says nothing about what triggers the dawn crowing.
explanation.D: Correct. Crowing that depends entirely on a light being switched on, with no crowing at the usual time, shows that light rather than an internal clock triggers it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Some sea urchins pick up shell fragments, pebbles, and scraps of seaweed with their tube feet and hold them over their bodies like a loose coat. The behavior has usually been explained as a disguise that hides the urchin from fish and other predators. Marine biologist Ines Carvalho hypothesizes instead that the covering mainly shields urchins from strong sunlight, which can damage their tissues in shallow water. In her view, an urchin decides how much to cover itself based on how much light reaches it, not on whether predators are nearby.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Carvalho's hypothesis?

choices.A: Urchins in tanks covered themselves more heavily within minutes of predator scent being added to the water.
choices.B: Urchins graze mainly on algae that grow on the sunlit rocks of shallow reefs.
choices.C: Urchins in brightly lit tanks covered themselves far more than urchins in dim tanks, whether or not a predator was present.
choices.D: Urchins that had covered themselves moved across the tank floor as quickly as uncovered urchins.

explanation.why: Carvalho's hypothesis is that urchins cover themselves in response to light, not to predators. A finding supports it if covering rises with brightness and does not depend on predators. Urchins covering more in bright tanks than in dim ones, regardless of whether a predator was present, shows exactly that.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Covering up in response to predator scent would support the disguise explanation that Carvalho rejects.
explanation.B: Incorrect. What urchins eat says nothing about why they cover themselves.
explanation.C: Correct. Covering tracked light level and was unaffected by predators, which is what Carvalho's hypothesis predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How fast covered urchins move does not reveal what the covering is for.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many insect-eating bats hunt around streetlamps, where moths and other insects gather in dense swarms. Two explanations have been offered for why the lamps help the bats. One is that the light itself makes individual insects easier to catch, since moths dazzled by the glare perform fewer of the evasive dives and loops they use in darkness. Ecologist Tomasz Wrona favors a different explanation: in his view, lamps benefit bats mainly by concentrating prey in a small space, so that a bat spends far less time and energy searching for its next meal, while the difficulty of catching any single insect is unchanged.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Wrona's explanation?

choices.A: Moths captured by bats near lamps were larger on average than moths captured in dark areas.
choices.B: Bats hunting at lamps made far fewer passes between captures than bats in dark areas, but the share of attacks that succeeded was the same in both places.
choices.C: Bats hunting at lamps succeeded on a larger share of their attacks than bats in dark areas, while the time between captures was unchanged.
choices.D: Insect numbers around lamps were highest during the first hour after dark and fell steadily afterward.

explanation.why: Wrona says lamps help by shortening the search for prey, not by making each capture easier. The two explanations predict different things: his predicts less searching with no change in success per attack; the rival predicts more success per attack. A finding of fewer passes between captures and the same success rate matches Wrona's prediction and not the rival's.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The size of the moths caught does not show whether lamps shorten the search or make captures easier.
explanation.B: Correct. Less searching between captures with no change in capture success is exactly what Wrona's explanation predicts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Higher success per attack with no change in search time is what the rival explanation predicts, so this would count against Wrona.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When insects are most numerous around lamps says nothing about which explanation is right.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Antlion larvae dig cone-shaped pits in loose sand and wait buried at the bottom; an ant that steps over the rim slides down the wall into the larva's jaws. Larvae given a choice of sands consistently build their pits in the finest grains available. The usual explanation is simply that fine sand is easier to dig. Entomologist Rina Kaur hypothesizes that something else matters more: walls made of fine grains sit closer to the point of collapse, so even a small insect's steps set off a slide that carries it to the bottom. On her view, larvae choose fine sand because pits built in it trap prey more reliably, not because they are easier to build.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kaur's hypothesis?

choices.A: Larvae still chose fine sand when it had been dampened so that digging it took longer than digging the coarse sand beside it, and their pits there caught more of the ants that entered.
choices.B: Pits built in fine sand and pits built in coarse sand reached the same depth and width and held the same number of larvae.
choices.C: Larvae completed pits in fine sand in about half the time they needed to complete pits of the same size and depth in coarse sand.
choices.D: Ants that entered pits built in coarse sand were caught just as often as ants that entered pits built in fine sand.

explanation.why: Kaur's hypothesis separates two possible reasons for the preference: ease of digging and effectiveness at trapping. To support her, a finding must show that larvae prefer fine sand even when it is not easier to dig, and that fine-sand pits trap better. The dampened-sand result does both: digging was harder, the preference remained, and the pits caught more prey.
explanation.A: Correct. With the digging advantage removed, the larvae still chose fine sand, and the pits trapped more prey, which is what Kaur predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Equal size says nothing about which sand traps prey better or why larvae prefer it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Faster digging in fine sand supports the usual explanation that Kaur is arguing against.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If coarse-sand pits trapped just as well, trapping could not explain the preference; this would weaken Kaur's hypothesis.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the Waitomo caves of New Zealand, the larvae of a small fly glow blue-green on the cave ceilings and hang sticky silk threads beneath them. Flying insects drawn toward the lights blunder into the threads and are hauled up and eaten. Biologist Hemi Walker proposes that each larva adjusts its brightness according to its hunger: a larva that has not eaten for some time glows more brightly, drawing more prey toward its threads, while a well-fed larva dims to save energy. The proposal would explain why the glow of a single larva can vary from night to night.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Walker's proposal?

choices.A: Larvae that hung a greater number of threads caught more prey over a month than larvae with fewer threads.
choices.B: Insects in the cave were strongly attracted to artificial lights of the same color as the larvae's glow.
choices.C: Larvae glowed most brightly in sections of the cave where flying insects were scarcest.
choices.D: Larvae that had just been fed glowed as brightly over the following nights as larvae that had gone without food for two weeks.

explanation.why: Walker's proposal predicts that hunger raises brightness and feeding lowers it. A finding weakens it if brightness turns out not to depend on hunger at all. If recently fed larvae glow just as brightly as larvae starved for two weeks, hunger is not controlling the glow, and the proposal fails.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The link between thread number and catch says nothing about whether brightness depends on hunger.
explanation.B: Incorrect. That insects are drawn to this color explains why glowing works, not whether larvae adjust it according to hunger.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Brighter glowing where prey are scarce, and larvae presumably hungrier, is consistent with Walker's proposal.
explanation.D: Correct. If feeding makes no difference to brightness, hunger cannot be what controls the glow, which is the core of Walker's proposal.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When threatened, many squids release a cloud of dark ink and jet away. Some species, however, release something more specific: a compact blob of ink, held together by mucus, that is roughly the size and shape of the squid itself. Marine biologist Daniel Okoro argues that this blob, called a pseudomorph, works as a decoy. On his account, a predator mistakes the blob for the squid and attacks it, buying the real squid a few seconds to escape; the ink's value in these cases lies in being mistaken for the animal, not in screening the animal from view the way a diffuse cloud would.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okoro's argument?

choices.A: Squids released larger pseudomorphs when the approaching predator was larger and faster.
choices.B: In tank trials, fish that met a pseudomorph struck at the blob itself while the squid that released it escaped untouched.
choices.C: Fish that swam into a diffuse ink cloud usually lost track of the squid that had released it.
choices.D: In tank trials, fish ignored the pseudomorph entirely and pursued the fleeing squid instead.

explanation.why: Okoro's claim is that the pseudomorph works by being mistaken for the squid and attacked in its place. The most direct support is a predator actually treating the blob as the squid. Fish striking at the blob while the squid escapes is that behavior observed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Blob size changing with predator size does not show that predators mistake the blob for the squid.
explanation.B: Correct. Predators attacking the blob while the squid gets away is the decoy effect Okoro describes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This shows how a diffuse cloud works by screening the squid, which is the mechanism Okoro says the pseudomorph does not rely on.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Predators ignoring the blob is the opposite of a decoy working, so this would weaken Okoro's argument.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pitcher plants trap insects in cup-shaped leaves filled with digestive fluid and draw nitrogen from the remains. One large species found in the mountains of Borneo has an unusual feature: the lid of its pitcher produces a sugary secretion, and tree shrews climb onto the pitcher to lick it, often leaving droppings in the cup as they do. Botanist Ananya Rao hypothesizes that in this species the pitcher has become primarily a collector of droppings rather than a trap: its main source of nitrogen, she suggests, is the shrews' waste, and insect capture has become a minor sideline.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Rao's hypothesis?

choices.A: The pitchers of this species captured as many insects per week as the pitchers of related species that shrews do not visit.
choices.B: Tree shrews visit the pitchers mainly in the early morning, when the secretion is most plentiful.
choices.C: The pitchers of this species contain the same digestive fluid found in the pitchers of related species.
choices.D: Chemical analysis showed that most of the nitrogen in the plant's tissues came from the shrews' droppings rather than from insects.

explanation.why: Rao's hypothesis is specific: the plant gets most of its nitrogen from droppings, and insects contribute little. The direct test is where the plant's nitrogen actually comes from. Analysis showing that most of it comes from droppings confirms the hypothesis.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Capturing as many insects as its relatives suggests the trap is still fully in use, which works against the idea that insect capture is a minor sideline.
explanation.B: Incorrect. When the shrews visit does not tell us how much of the plant's nitrogen their droppings supply.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Having digestive fluid shows the plant can still digest something, not where most of its nitrogen comes from.
explanation.D: Correct. Nitrogen coming mostly from droppings is exactly what Rao claims.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Traces of pigment have been detected in some fossil dinosaur eggshells, including the blue-green and brown-spotted colors found in the eggs of many living birds. Paleontologist Lukas Meier argues that egg color in dinosaurs evolved as camouflage and therefore depended on nesting habits. Species that laid their eggs in open nests, where eggs lay exposed to the eyes of predators, would have gained from colored, spotted shells, he reasons, while species that buried their eggs in sand or soil, where color could serve no purpose, would have kept plain white shells.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Meier's argument?

choices.A: Species that buried their eggs show the same shell pigments as species that nested in the open.
choices.B: Among living birds, species that nest in dark burrows or tree holes usually lay plain white eggs.
choices.C: Pigment was found in the eggshells of species whose nests were open, and absent in species whose eggs were buried.
choices.D: Pigmented eggshells have been identified in several different groups of dinosaurs that lived on different continents.

explanation.why: Meier's argument predicts a match between nesting habit and egg color in dinosaurs: color in open nesters, none in buriers. A finding supports it most directly if it shows that very pattern in dinosaur fossils. Pigment present in open nesters and absent in buriers is that pattern.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The same pigments in buriers and open nesters would break the link Meier proposes, so this would weaken his argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The pattern in living birds suggests the idea is reasonable, but it is not evidence about dinosaurs, which is what Meier's argument concerns.
explanation.C: Correct. Pigment tracking nesting habit in the fossils is the exact prediction Meier makes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Finding pigment in several groups says nothing about whether color matched nesting habits.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Excavations at cities of the Indus Valley civilization, which flourished in present-day Pakistan and northwestern India between about 2600 and 1900 BCE, have turned up hundreds of small cubical stone weights. Remarkably, the weights follow the same system of proportions at sites hundreds of kilometers apart. Archaeologist Nadia Qureshi argues that such uniformity could only have been achieved by city authorities that set the standard and enforced it in the markets, rather than by merchants gradually copying one another's weights until a common system emerged.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Qureshi's argument?

choices.A: Sets of weights were found in buildings beside the gates of several cities, where goods entering may have been checked.
choices.B: Weight systems with similar proportions were used centuries later in parts of Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf.
choices.C: Weights following the standard proportions appear in small settlements that date from centuries before the large cities were built.
choices.D: Weights from different Indus cities were cut from the same type of banded stone and polished in the same way.

explanation.why: Qureshi claims that the uniform system required city authorities to set and enforce it. If the standard was already in use in small settlements long before there were cities or administrative buildings, it cannot have been created by city authorities, and a gradual, informal origin becomes more likely. That directly undercuts her argument.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Weights kept where goods entered cities fit the idea of official checking, which would support Qureshi.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Later systems elsewhere say nothing about how the Indus system came to be uniform.
explanation.C: Correct. A standard in place before the cities existed could not have been imposed by city authorities, which is what Qureshi's argument requires.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A shared stone type is consistent with either central control or gradual copying, so it does not weaken the argument.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Navigators of the Marshall Islands, in the central Pacific, once made charts from the ribs of palm fronds, lashed into lattices with small shells tied on to mark islands. The curved and straight sticks represented the ocean swells that bend and cross around islands, patterns a skilled navigator could feel through the hull of a canoe. Because the charts seem so practical, early European visitors assumed they were carried on voyages. Anthropologist Peter Lind argues otherwise: the charts, he contends, were instruments for teaching and memorizing swell patterns on land, and a navigator who had mastered a chart had no further need of it at sea.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lind's argument?

choices.A: Canoes of the period had a space beside the steersman's position where a chart could be lashed in place.
choices.B: Navigators interviewed in the early twentieth century said they studied the charts on shore with a teacher and knew every pattern by heart before a voyage began.
choices.C: Several surviving charts show swell patterns that closely match measurements made around the same islands with modern instruments.
choices.D: Charts made on different atolls used noticeably different arrangements of sticks to represent the same swell patterns around the same islands.

explanation.why: Lind's claim has two parts: the charts were used for learning on land, and they were not needed at sea. Navigators' own accounts of studying the charts on shore and memorizing them before sailing bear on both parts and give the most direct support.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A place to lash a chart on board suggests charts were carried to sea, which would work against Lind.
explanation.B: Correct. Studying on shore and memorizing before sailing is the use Lind describes, and it explains why the charts were not needed at sea.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Accuracy shows the charts recorded real patterns but not where or how they were used.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Local differences in design say nothing about whether the charts were used on land or at sea.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Several studies have reported that shoppers in supermarkets buy more when slow background music is playing than when the music is fast. Consumer researcher Maya Lindqvist argues that the effect works entirely through walking pace and without the shoppers' awareness: slow music makes people move more slowly, slower movement means more time in the aisles, and more time in the aisles means more items noticed and picked up. On her account, the music need not be noticed at all; a shopper who never registers it is just as affected as one who does.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Lindqvist's argument?

choices.A: Shoppers walked more slowly on weekends than on weekdays, whatever music was playing.
choices.B: When questioned after leaving the store, most shoppers could not say whether any music had been playing during their visit.
choices.C: During slow-music sessions, only shoppers who reported noticing the music bought more than usual; those who had not noticed it bought their usual amount.
choices.D: Sales rose during slow-music sessions mainly in the aisles nearest the entrance, where shoppers spend the first minutes of a visit.

explanation.why: Lindqvist's argument rests on the claim that the effect does not depend on noticing the music. A finding weakens it if the effect appears only in shoppers who did notice. If unaware shoppers bought no more than usual, awareness is doing the work, contrary to her account.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Walking pace varying by day of the week is unrelated to how music produces its effect.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Shoppers failing to notice the music fits Lindqvist's claim that awareness is not required.
explanation.C: Correct. If the extra buying occurred only among shoppers who noticed the music, the effect depends on awareness, which Lindqvist's argument denies.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Where in the store sales rose does not show whether awareness of the music mattered.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For more than a century, jute grown in the Bengal delta, in what is now Bangladesh and eastern India, supplied most of the world's sacks for grain, sugar, coffee, and fertilizer. From the 1960s onward, demand fell steeply. Two causes are usually named: cheap sacks woven from synthetic fibers, which were lighter and did not rot, and the spread of bulk handling, in which grain and other goods were poured loose into ships, trucks, and silos, so that no sacks were needed at all. Economic historian Farhana Chowdhury argues that synthetic sacks, not bulk handling, were by far the larger cause of the decline.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Chowdhury's argument?

choices.A: Demand for jute sacks fell sharply even for goods, such as sugar and fertilizer, that were still packed in sacks rather than handled in bulk.
choices.B: Demand for jute fell most steeply in exactly the years when bulk handling of grain spread most rapidly through the world's ports.
choices.C: Synthetic sacking was first manufactured on a commercial scale in the 1950s, a decade before jute demand began to fall.
choices.D: Jute mills in Bangladesh and India continued to employ hundreds of thousands of workers through the 1980s, well after the decline began.

explanation.why: Chowdhury's argument weighs two causes against each other. The decisive test is what happened to jute demand where only one cause could operate. If jute sales collapsed even for goods that were still packed in sacks, bulk handling cannot explain that loss; those sacks must have switched to synthetics.
explanation.A: Correct. A sharp fall in jute demand for goods still packed in sacks can only be explained by a switch to another kind of sack, which supports Chowdhury.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The decline matching the spread of bulk handling would point to bulk handling as the main cause, the opposite of Chowdhury's view.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When synthetic sacks first appeared does not show how much of the decline they caused.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Continued employment in the mills says nothing about which cause reduced demand.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Thousands of rune stones were raised in Sweden during the eleventh century, most of them inscribed with a simple formula: a named person raised the stone in memory of a named relative, usually with the relationship stated. They are generally read as memorials. Historian Astrid Holm argues that for many sponsors the memorial purpose was secondary. In a society that kept no written records of property, she contends, a stone that announced in public exactly how the sponsor was related to the dead person served to declare the sponsor's right to inherit that person's land.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Holm's argument?

choices.A: Stones raised by heirs whose claims were most open to challenge, such as a widow or a brother, carry unusually detailed statements of kinship.
choices.B: Most inscriptions close with a short prayer or a wish for the dead person's soul.
choices.C: The carvers of some stones added their own names to the inscriptions, sometimes alongside a short boast about their skill.
choices.D: Many stones stand beside roads and bridge crossings where large numbers of travelers would have passed and could read them.

explanation.why: Holm's claim is that the statements of kinship were there to establish rights to inherit. If the sponsors with the weakest claims took the most care to spell out their kinship, the inscriptions were doing the work of establishing claims, as she argues. That is the pattern her reading predicts.
explanation.A: Correct. The sponsors who most needed to prove a claim gave the fullest kinship statements, which is what Holm's inheritance reading predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Prayers for the dead point to the memorial purpose Holm regards as secondary, so this would not help her case.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Carvers signing their work tells us nothing about why sponsors stated their kinship.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Placing stones where people pass fits a memorial just as well as a declaration of inheritance.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A storeroom attached to a medieval synagogue in Cairo preserved thousands of letters exchanged by merchants who traded between the Mediterranean and India in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The merchants routinely entrusted valuable goods to partners in distant ports. Historian Yusuf Haddad argues that this trust rested not on enforceable contracts but on reputation within a close-knit community: a partner who cheated could expect to be shut out of future dealings by everyone who heard of it, and that threat, rather than any court, kept partners honest.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Haddad's argument?

choices.A: When a partner failed to deliver goods or payment, merchants routinely brought written contracts before a court and obtained judgments enforcing them.
choices.B: Most of the letters were written in Arabic using Hebrew letters.
choices.C: Many of the merchants dealt in spices and dyes brought from the coast of India.
choices.D: The letters frequently pass along news of which merchants had behaved dishonestly in other ports.

explanation.why: Haddad's argument is that reputation, not enforceable contracts, secured honest dealing. If merchants in fact used written contracts and obtained court judgments against partners who failed them, then enforcement did exist and was relied on, which directly contradicts his claim.
explanation.A: Correct. Routine use of courts to enforce contracts shows that formal enforcement, not only reputation, kept partners honest.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The script the letters used is unrelated to how merchants secured honest dealing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. What goods were traded says nothing about how trust between partners was maintained.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Spreading news of dishonest merchants is how a reputation system works, so this would support Haddad.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ceramics made in the town of Iznik for the Ottoman court in the sixteenth century are prized for a bright red that stands up from the surface in slight relief. The color came from an iron-rich clay that potters applied in a thick layer beneath the glaze. Art historian Selin Aydın argues that the thickness was an aesthetic decision: potters built up the red so that it would catch the light and stand out from the flat blues and greens around it. Others have proposed a technical reason instead, suggesting that the clay simply could not produce the color unless applied thickly.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Aydın's argument?

choices.A: Raised red appears both on tiles made for mosques and on dishes made for everyday use.
choices.B: Writers of the period praised the red of Iznik ware for seeming to rise from the surface.
choices.C: Test firings show that the same red clay, applied in a thin layer, fires to a dull brown rather than a bright red.
choices.D: On the same tiles, the blue and green pigments were applied thinly and lie flat under the glaze.

explanation.why: Aydın claims the thickness was chosen for its visual effect. The rival view is that thickness was technically necessary for the color. A finding that thin layers do not produce the red at all shows that potters had no choice, which removes the basis for calling the thickness an aesthetic decision.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Where the raised red appears does not show whether its thickness was chosen or required.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Praise for the raised effect suggests it was valued, which fits Aydın's view rather than undermining it.
explanation.C: Correct. If a thin layer cannot produce the red, the thick application was a technical necessity, not an aesthetic choice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. That other colors were applied thinly tells us nothing about why the red was applied thickly.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The trucks that carry goods across Pakistan are famous for their painted decoration: panels of flowers, birds, landscapes, and calligraphy covering nearly every surface. The painting is done in workshops in cities such as Karachi and Rawalpindi. Ethnographer Bilal Shaikh argues that the people who paint the trucks are regarded, by owners and by one another, as individual artists rather than as anonymous craftworkers. As his main evidence he points to the signatures that appear on many painted panels, which he reads as artists claiming credit for their own work.
