items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Shaikh's argument?

choices.A: The signatures on the panels are the names of workshop owners, who manage the business and rarely paint, not of the painters.
choices.B: The lettering on a truck is usually done by a different worker from the one who paints the pictures and borders.
choices.C: Some truck owners travel long distances to have their trucks painted by one particular painter whose work they admire.
choices.D: Most painters learned the craft as apprentices in the same workshop where they still work, often beginning as boys.

explanation.why: Shaikh's conclusion rests on reading the signatures as painters claiming credit. If the signatures name workshop owners who do not paint, they are business labels, not artists' claims, and his main evidence no longer supports his conclusion.
explanation.A: Correct. If the signatures belong to workshop owners rather than painters, they do not show painters claiming credit, which undercuts Shaikh's evidence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The division of work between lettering and pictures is unrelated to how painters are regarded.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Owners seeking out a particular painter suggests painters are valued as individuals, which supports Shaikh.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How painters were trained does not show whether they are seen as individual artists.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A large historical dictionary of English, begun in the second half of the nineteenth century, set out to document every word with dated quotations showing it in use. Its editors could not read everything themselves, so they recruited hundreds of volunteers who read books and mailed in slips, each bearing a quotation and the word it illustrated. Historian of language Clara Benson argues that the volunteers' tastes shaped the dictionary: because readers were drawn to rare and striking words and passed over ordinary ones, the editors ended up with abundant evidence for unusual words and thin evidence for the commonest words in the language.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Benson's argument?

choices.A: Letters from the editors complain of receiving hundreds of slips for words used only once or twice in English but almost none for "do" and "make."
choices.B: The editors sent volunteers lists of books from particular periods that they wished to have read and excerpted.
choices.C: The editors shortened many quotations before printing them to save space in the finished volumes.
choices.D: The volunteers included people from many occupations and from several countries, and a few of them sent in many thousands of slips each.

explanation.why: Benson's claim is that volunteer readers oversupplied rare words and undersupplied common ones. The editors' own complaints about piles of slips for rare words and almost none for "do" and "make" are direct evidence of exactly that imbalance in what the volunteers sent.
explanation.A: Correct. The editors' complaints document the imbalance Benson describes: plenty of slips for rare words, almost none for common ones.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Guidance about which books to read does not show which words the readers picked out of them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Editing quotations for length is unrelated to which words the volunteers supplied evidence for.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Who the volunteers were does not show what kinds of words they chose to record.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: "Remember" is an 1862 sonnet by Christina Rossetti. The speaker, anticipating her own death, addresses the person she loves. The first eight lines are a plea: she asks to be remembered when she is gone and can no longer be held by the hand or hear plans for a shared future. In the final six lines the poem turns. The speaker's wish to be remembered gives way to a greater concern for the beloved's happiness, so that she ends by placing his peace of mind above her own place in his memory.
items.stem: Which quotation from "Remember" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "Remember me when no more day by day / You tell me of our future that you plann'd:"
choices.B: "Yet if you should forget me for a while / And afterwards remember, do not grieve:"
choices.C: "Remember me when I am gone away, / Gone far away into the silent land;"
choices.D: "Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad."

explanation.why: The claim is that the speaker ends by valuing the beloved's happiness above being remembered. The quotation must show her preferring his happiness even at the cost of being forgotten. Only the closing lines say that outright: forgetting with a smile is "better by far" than remembering with sadness.
explanation.A: Incorrect. These lines continue the plea and recall the shared future; they do not put the beloved's happiness first.
explanation.B: Incorrect. These lines begin the turn by excusing a temporary lapse of memory, but they stop at "do not grieve" and do not yet state that his happiness matters more than being remembered.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is the opening plea to be remembered, the wish the poem later sets aside.
explanation.D: Correct. The speaker says plainly that the beloved forgetting and smiling is better than remembering and being sad, which places his happiness above her own memory.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The novelist Thomas Allard set his books of the 1860s and 1870s among farming families and wrote their speech in dialect spelling, dropping letters and respelling words to capture local pronunciation. In editions published after 1885, much of this spelling was replaced with standard forms. Literary scholar Hannah Brooks argues that Allard himself made the change, yielding to reviewers who had complained that the dialect made his books tiring to read, rather than the publisher imposing it without his knowledge, as some have assumed.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brooks's argument?

choices.A: The editions published after 1885 also corrected a number of printing errors found in the early editions.
choices.B: Allard's own copies of the early editions survive with the dialect spellings crossed out and standard spellings written in beside them in his handwriting.
choices.C: Allard's publisher issued the later editions in a cheaper format aimed at a wider public.
choices.D: Reviews of the early editions praised the dialect speech as the most lifelike feature of the books.

explanation.why: Brooks claims the author made the change himself. The most direct evidence would show Allard revising the dialect in his own hand. His marked-up copies with standard spellings written in do exactly that, and they rule out the idea that the publisher acted without his knowledge.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Correcting printing errors is routine and does not show who changed the dialect spelling.
explanation.B: Correct. Revisions in Allard's own handwriting show that he, not the publisher alone, made the change.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The format of the later editions does not reveal who decided to alter the spelling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Reviewers praising the dialect runs against the premise that complaints prompted the change, so this does not support Brooks.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The Dastan-e Amir Hamza, a cycle of adventure tales about the hero Hamza, was performed for centuries by professional storytellers in the cities of northern India, who could hold an audience for many evenings. In the late nineteenth century a press in Lucknow issued a printed Urdu version that ran to dozens of thick volumes. Scholar Rukhsana Mirza argues that this enormous length simply records the storytellers' practice of expanding each episode on demand to keep patrons listening; the press, in her view, set down the performers' material rather than adding new matter of its own.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Mirza's argument?

choices.A: The printed volumes were sold to readers by subscription, one volume at a time.
choices.B: Much shorter written versions of the tales had circulated in Persian for several centuries.
choices.C: Storytellers of the period are recorded as stretching a single episode over several evenings when the audience was large.
choices.D: The press's account books record payments to hired writers for composing new episodes for the printed version.

explanation.why: Mirza's argument is that the printed length came from the storytellers, not from the press adding material. A finding weakens it if it shows the press generating new content. Payments to writers for composing new episodes show exactly that.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How the volumes were sold does not show where their contents came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Earlier short versions in another language say nothing about whether the press added material to this one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Storytellers stretching episodes is the practice Mirza relies on, so this would support her view.
explanation.D: Correct. If the press paid writers to compose new episodes, the printed version contains matter the press added, which Mirza denies.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The classical Tamil poems known as Sangam literature, composed in southern India roughly two thousand years ago, include hundreds of short love poems. Later commentators sorted these poems into five landscapes, such as mountain, seashore, and farmland, each tied to a stage of love, a season, and a flower. Some scholars suspect that this neat system was the commentators' invention, imposed on poems that had been composed without it. Literary historian Kavitha Raman argues instead that the system was already a shared code when the poems were written, so that a poet who named a flower or a landscape could count on listeners to supply the mood that went with it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Raman's argument?

choices.A: Many Sangam poems concern kings, warfare, and the praise of patrons rather than love between individuals.
choices.B: Commentators writing centuries after the poems disagreed with one another about which landscape some poems belong to.
choices.C: The flowers associated with the five landscapes all grow in southern India and still carry the same names in Tamil today.
choices.D: In the earliest poems, just as in the latest, a poem's mood can be predicted from the landscape it names, with no exceptions.

explanation.why: Raman's claim is that the landscape code was in force when the poems were composed. If the pairing of landscape and mood is already consistent in the earliest poems and never violated, the poets were using the system, not having it imposed on them later. That is the direct support her claim needs.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The existence of poems on other subjects says nothing about whether the love poems followed a shared code.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Later disagreement about classifying some poems suggests the fit was imperfect, which would help the view Raman argues against.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Where the flowers grow does not show whether poets and listeners treated them as a code.
explanation.D: Correct. A consistent landscape-mood pairing from the earliest poems onward shows the poets themselves were working within the system.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most vultures have bare, featherless skin on the head and neck, a feature long explained by hygiene: a bird that pushes its head into carcasses would foul any feathers there, and bare skin is more easily cleaned by sun and rain. Ornithologist Grace Mwangi proposes that the bare skin serves chiefly to regulate body temperature. Vultures, she notes, move within minutes between cold air at soaring altitude and scorching ground beside a carcass; bare skin, richly supplied with blood, could shed heat quickly when exposed and conserve it when the head is drawn down into the feathers of the body. On this view, posture should change with temperature in a predictable way.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mwangi's proposal?

choices.A: Vulture species that feed mainly on small carcasses, and so seldom push the head inside a body, nevertheless have heads as bare as other vultures.
choices.B: Vultures resting in midday heat hold the neck fully stretched out, exposing the bare skin, while in cold morning air they hunch with the head drawn into the body feathers.
choices.C: Bare-headed vultures bathe and preen more often after feeding than feathered scavengers such as crows and gulls do.
choices.D: The bare skin on a vulture's head flushes a deeper color when the bird is excited or alarmed, for example during disputes over food.

explanation.why: Mwangi's proposal predicts specific behavior: vultures should expose the bare skin when hot and cover it when cold. A finding that posture tracks temperature in exactly that way is direct confirmation of her prediction. Findings that merely cast doubt on the hygiene explanation are less direct, since the bare skin might have some third purpose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This weakens the hygiene explanation, but it does not show that the bare skin regulates temperature; some other function could be involved.
explanation.B: Correct. Exposing bare skin in heat and tucking it away in cold is precisely the posture change Mwangi's proposal predicts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Frequent bathing after feeding points to cleanliness as the concern, which fits the hygiene explanation rather than Mwangi's.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Color change with excitement suggests signaling, not temperature control.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Experiments in which a large tree is supplied with carbon that carries a detectable label have found that some of that carbon later turns up in shaded seedlings nearby, whose roots are linked to the tree's by a shared fungal network. Many have concluded that trees feed their neighbors' offspring with sugar through the fungus. Forest ecologist Hanna Berglund objects that the evidence does not show this. The fungus, she points out, takes sugar from the tree for its own use and grows inside the seedlings' roots; labeled carbon found in a seedling's root could simply be fungal tissue lodged there, with no sugar ever handed over to the seedling itself.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Berglund's objection?

choices.A: Labeled carbon from the large tree was found in the seedlings' new leaves and stems, tissues that the fungus does not enter.
choices.B: The same fungal species also forms connections with shrubs and grasses growing in the forest.
choices.C: Within the seedlings' roots, the labeled carbon was concentrated in the root tips where the fungus lives.
choices.D: Seedlings whose fungal connections were left intact survived their first summer at higher rates than seedlings whose connections had been severed.

explanation.why: Berglund's objection is that the labeled carbon may never have left the fungus. It fails if the carbon appears in parts of the seedling the fungus cannot reach. Carbon in new leaves and stems must have been taken up by the seedling itself, which is what her objection says has not been shown.
explanation.A: Correct. Carbon in tissues the fungus never enters must have passed into the seedling, so Berglund's alternative explanation cannot account for it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Which other plants the fungus connects to says nothing about whether carbon reached the seedlings.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Carbon concentrated where the fungus lives is exactly what Berglund would expect if the carbon is still fungal tissue, so this supports her objection.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Better survival with intact connections could result from water or minerals supplied by the fungus; it does not show that sugar from the tree reached the seedling, which is the point Berglund disputes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The giraffe's neck is usually explained as an adaptation for feeding: a taller animal can reach leaves that other browsers cannot. A competing account points to a behavior called necking, in which male giraffes fight by swinging their heads and necks at one another; on this account, longer necks evolved because they won fights and therefore mates, and the feeding advantage was a byproduct. Zoologist Kwame Boateng acknowledges that necking is real but argues that feeding remains the better explanation of why the neck grew so long in the first place.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Boateng's argument?

choices.A: In the dry season, when food is scarcest, giraffes of both sexes take most of their food from branches above the reach of any other browser.
choices.B: The giraffe's neck contains the same seven bones found in the necks of almost all other mammals, each one greatly elongated.
choices.C: Males with longer necks win more of their fights and father a larger share of calves than males with shorter necks do.
choices.D: Female giraffes, which do not fight with their necks, have necks noticeably shorter in proportion to their bodies than males have.

explanation.why: Boateng's claim is that reaching high food drove the neck's evolution. The strongest support shows the neck actually delivering that advantage when it matters most: in the lean season, both sexes depend on food that only a long neck can reach. Findings about fighting success point the other way, and findings about anatomy do not bear on either explanation.
explanation.A: Correct. Both sexes relying on food that only a long neck can reach, exactly when food is scarce, is direct evidence that feeding is what the neck is for.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The number of neck bones is true of giraffes but says nothing about why the neck became long.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Longer necks winning fights and mates is the evidence the necking account relies on, so this works against Boateng.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If only the fighting sex had the longer necks, fighting would seem to be driving neck length, which supports the competing account.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the waterfront of Kochi, on the southwestern coast of India, stand large fishing nets suspended from wooden frames that are lowered into the water and raised by counterweights. They are known locally as Chinese nets, and a popular account holds that they were introduced directly by Chinese traders who visited the coast in the early 1400s. Historian Anil Menon argues for a less direct path: in his view, the nets reached Kochi more than a century later with the Portuguese, who had encountered such nets at their trading post at Macau, on the Chinese coast, and brought the design to their settlements in India.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Menon's argument?

choices.A: The frames of the Kochi nets are built from teak and bamboo that grow locally, and the counterweights are blocks of local stone.
choices.B: Chinese ceramics dating from the early 1400s have been excavated at several points along the Kochi waterfront and in the old town behind it.
choices.C: The Kochi nets closely resemble shore-mounted nets illustrated in Chinese sources from the 1300s, including the counterweights used to raise them.
choices.D: The earliest written description of such nets at Kochi is a Portuguese account of the 1570s; detailed accounts of the port from the 1400s never mention them.

explanation.why: Menon's argument concerns timing and route: the nets arrived with the Portuguese in the 1500s, not with Chinese visitors in the 1400s. Support must bear on when the nets appeared. Their absence from detailed descriptions of the port in the 1400s, together with their first appearance in a Portuguese source of the 1570s, fits Menon's timing and not the popular account's.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Local building materials would be used whichever route the design took, so this does not favor either account.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Chinese goods at Kochi in the 1400s show that Chinese traders came, which supports the popular account rather than Menon's.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A Chinese origin for the design is accepted by both accounts; the question is who carried it to Kochi and when, which this does not address.
explanation.D: Correct. The nets' absence from fifteenth-century descriptions of the port and their first mention in a Portuguese source match the later, Portuguese route Menon proposes.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In many medieval European villages, a family's farmland was not a single block but a collection of narrow strips scattered across the village's great fields, sometimes dozens of strips lying far apart. Walking between them wasted hours, and historians have long asked why the arrangement persisted. One explanation is inheritance: holdings divided among heirs over many generations would naturally become fragmented. Economic historian Lucía Ortega argues that the scattering was instead a deliberate strategy for spreading risk: strips on different soils, slopes, and drainage meant that a frost, flood, or drought that ruined one part of the fields would spare another, so that a family rarely lost its whole harvest at once.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ortega's argument?

choices.A: In villages where all the land lay on one uniform soil with no differences in flooding or frost risk, holdings were just as scattered as elsewhere.
choices.B: Because strips lay side by side in the same fields, villagers had to agree on common dates for plowing, sowing, and harvest each year.
choices.C: Families that traded strips with neighbors to consolidate their land into one block suffered total crop failures more often than families that kept their land scattered.
choices.D: The boundaries between neighboring strips were marked by narrow ridges of unplowed turf that were renewed each spring.

explanation.why: Ortega's explanation predicts that scattering should be found where it does some good: where land varies enough for different strips to face different risks. If holdings were equally scattered in villages whose land was uniform, where scattering could spread no risk, then risk-spreading cannot be what produced the pattern, and her argument loses its support.
explanation.A: Correct. Scattering just as common where it brought no risk-spreading benefit indicates that something other than risk explains it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Coordinating field work is a consequence of the strip system, not evidence about why it arose.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Consolidated families suffering more total failures is what Ortega's argument predicts, so this would support her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How the strips were marked off has no bearing on why holdings were scattered.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Bronze bells cast in China more than two thousand years ago have a cross section shaped like an almond rather than a circle, and each bell can sound two distinct notes, one when struck at the center of its face and another when struck near the edge. Some scholars regard the second note as an accident of the shape, which the casters neither intended nor controlled. Musicologist Wei Lin argues that the two-tone property was understood, planned, and tuned: casters, in her view, shaped each bell so that its two notes would stand at a chosen interval, and adjusted the bells after casting to bring that interval into line.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lin's argument?

choices.A: Bells of the same almond shape cast with the same bronze produce two notes, while round bells cast in the same workshops with the same bronze produce only one.
choices.B: On bells buried together as a set, the inner surfaces show grinding marks at exactly the spots where removing metal alters the second note, and the interval between the two notes is the same on nearly every bell.
choices.C: Written texts of the period refer to each bell by a single note name and give no name to any second note.
choices.D: Bells found together as a set vary widely in size and weight, from a few kilograms to well over a hundred.

explanation.why: Lin's claim has two parts: the two tones were controlled by adjustment, and they were set to a chosen interval. Grinding marks at the spots that change the second note show adjustment, and a consistent interval across a set shows a chosen target. Together they support both parts of her claim.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This shows that the shape produces two notes, which the accidental view already accepts; it does not show that casters planned or tuned the second note.
explanation.B: Correct. Marks of deliberate adjustment at the second-note spots, together with a consistent interval across the set, show that the two tones were planned and tuned.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Naming each bell by one note suggests that the second note was not treated as part of the design, which works against Lin.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Differences in size are expected in any set of bells of different pitches and say nothing about the second note.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Several of Shakespeare's plays survive in two forms: a short early printing, often garbled, and a much longer, more polished later text. The short versions have traditionally been explained as memorial reconstructions, texts pieced together from memory by an actor who had played a minor part and then sold the result to a printer. Scholar Eleanor Whitcombe challenges this account. She argues that the short texts are deliberate abridgments, prepared so that a small company could perform the play while touring, and that their roughness reflects hasty cutting rather than faulty recall.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Whitcombe's argument?

choices.A: In one short text, the lines of a single minor character are reproduced almost perfectly, while the speeches of the leading characters are loosely paraphrased throughout.
choices.B: The cuts in the short texts fall mostly within long speeches and in scenes requiring many actors on stage, while the passages that remain match the longer texts nearly word for word.
choices.C: Small companies of actors are recorded as performing plays in towns across England during the years when the short texts were printed and sold.
choices.D: The short texts were issued by printers who also published other plays of the period, including several that survive in only one version.

explanation.why: The two accounts predict different kinds of damage. Memorial reconstruction predicts uneven accuracy, best in the lines the reconstructing actor knew. Abridgment for a small company predicts cuts aimed at length and at scenes needing many actors, with the retained material accurate. A pattern of cuts in long speeches and crowded scenes, with the rest preserved word for word, is the abridgment pattern.
explanation.A: Incorrect. One minor part reproduced accurately while the rest is paraphrased is the signature of memorial reconstruction, which Whitcombe disputes.
explanation.B: Correct. Cuts targeting length and crowd scenes, with the remainder accurate, match deliberate abridgment for a small touring company rather than faulty memory.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Touring companies existing shows that such abridgments could have been needed, but it does not show that these texts were abridgments.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Who printed the texts does not reveal how they came to be short.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: "Ulysses," a poem by Alfred Tennyson published in 1842, is spoken by the hero of Homer's Odyssey years after his return home. Now an aging king, he looks back on his voyages and ahead to what remains of his life. Readers often take the poem as a celebration of restless adventure, but its view of age is more exacting than that. The speaker treats old age not as a time of rest that has been earned, but as a time that still demands worthwhile labor: being old, in his view, does not excuse a man from the obligation to accomplish something before he dies.
items.stem: Which quotation from "Ulysses" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "Tho' much is taken, much abides; and tho' / We are not now that strength which in old days / Moved earth and heaven, that which we are, we are;"
choices.B: "This is my son, mine own Telemachus, / To whom I leave the sceptre and the isle,"
choices.C: "I am a part of all that I have met; / Yet all experience is an arch wherethro' / Gleams that untravell'd world whose margin fades / For ever and for ever when I move."
choices.D: "Old age hath yet his honour and his toil; / Death closes all: but something ere the end, / Some work of noble note, may yet be done,"

explanation.why: The claim is specific: old age still demands worthwhile labor, and being old does not excuse a man from accomplishing something. The quotation must link old age with work still owed. Only the lines that give old age "his toil" and insist that "some work of noble note, may yet be done" before death say this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. These lines admit lost strength and affirm that the speaker's identity endures, but they say nothing about work still to be done; they express persistence, not obligation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. These lines hand over the kingdom to the speaker's son and concern his departure, not the demands of old age.
explanation.C: Incorrect. These lines express the speaker's hunger for new experience, not the idea that old age carries an obligation to labor.
explanation.D: Correct. The lines assign old age its own "toil" and insist that "some work of noble note" remains to be done before death, which is the claim exactly.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: A great many novels published in Britain during the nineteenth century appeared anonymously or under a pen name, so reviewers often had to guess at the author's identity, and in particular at the author's sex. Literary historian Joanna Reyes argues that those guesses governed the verdicts. Qualities that reviewers admired as vigorous and frank in a book they believed to be a man's, she contends, were condemned as coarse and improper when the same reviewers believed a book to be a woman's; the words on the page mattered less than the sex the reviewer had assigned to the hand that wrote them.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Reyes's argument?

choices.A: Reviewers applied the same standards to anonymous novels whether or not they took the author to be a woman, and said so in their reviews.
choices.B: Reviewers of the period guessed wrongly about the sex of anonymous authors in a large share of cases, and often admitted as much in print.
choices.C: After a novel reviewed as a man's work was revealed to be by a woman, reviews of its next edition condemned as unsuitable the very scenes the earlier reviews had admired for their frankness.
choices.D: Novels known to be by women sold in numbers comparable to novels known to be by men throughout the period.

explanation.why: Reyes's claim is that the same text drew different verdicts depending on the sex reviewers assigned to its author. The cleanest support holds the text constant and changes only the assumed sex. Reviews of the same scenes turning from admiration to condemnation once the author was known to be a woman is exactly that comparison.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Reviewers using the same standards regardless of assumed sex is the opposite of what Reyes claims.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Reviewers guessing wrongly shows that they guessed, but not that their guesses changed how they judged a book.
explanation.C: Correct. The same scenes judged differently once the author's sex was known shows that the assumed sex, not the text, drove the verdict.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Sales reflect readers' choices, not how reviewers judged the writing.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Popular books about nursery rhymes often claim that these short verses preserve hidden accounts of political events: a rhyme about a tumbling egg or a falling bridge is said to mock a disgraced minister or record a royal quarrel, with the real names disguised. Folklorist Martin Hale argues that nearly all such readings are modern inventions. The rhymes themselves, he contends, were nonsense verses and children's games whose supposed secret meanings were attached long after the events they are said to describe, by writers who wanted the rhymes to be more interesting than they are.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hale's argument?

choices.A: Many nursery rhymes survive in several versions with different words, different numbers of lines, and different characters.
choices.B: Rhymes said to carry political meanings are no more widely known among children today than rhymes that are not.
choices.C: For most rhymes, the political reading first appears in print in the twentieth century, while the rhyme itself was recorded a century or more earlier with no hint of such a meaning.
choices.D: A few rhymes can be traced to street songs that openly mocked named public figures of their day by name and office.

explanation.why: Hale's claim is about timing and origin: the political meanings were added long after the rhymes, by later writers. Support must show that the meanings came late and were not present early. Political readings first appearing in print long after the rhymes were recorded without any such meaning is just that evidence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Variation between versions is common in oral tradition and does not show when or whether political meanings were attached.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How widely known the rhymes are today has no bearing on whether their political meanings are genuine.
explanation.C: Correct. The political readings appearing only long after the rhymes were recorded, with no earlier trace of the meaning, supports Hale's view that they were later inventions.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Rhymes traceable to songs mocking real figures would show that some rhymes did carry political meaning from the start, which works against Hale.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For many years, a popular explanation held that zebras' black-and-white stripes help them escape lions. When a herd runs together, the idea went, the moving stripes blur into a confusing pattern, making it hard for a predator to pick out a single animal.
items.passage_b: Biologists testing the purpose of zebra stripes have found support for a different explanation. In one experiment, horses wearing striped coats had far fewer biting flies land on them than horses wearing plain coats. The researchers concluded that the stripes' main benefit is protection from these insects, which can spread disease.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that evidence points to a different main purpose for zebra stripes
choices.B: By agreeing that the main purpose of zebra stripes is to confuse lions
choices.C: By arguing that zebras are rarely hunted by lions or other predators
choices.D: By pointing out that biting flies are most common where lions live

explanation.why: Text 1 says stripes help zebras escape lions. Text 2 describes an experiment in which striped coats kept flies away and concludes that the stripes' "main benefit is protection from these insects." So the author of Text 2 would answer that the evidence supports a different purpose.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 presents experimental evidence that stripes mainly protect zebras from biting flies, a different explanation from the one in Text 1.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the main benefit is protection from insects, not from lions, so it would not agree.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about how often lions hunt zebras.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares where biting flies and lions are found.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Pakistan, many trucks are covered in brightly painted flowers, birds, and mountain scenes, along with lines of poetry and jingling metal chains. For drivers who may spend weeks on the road, a richly decorated truck is a source of pride and a kind of home.
items.passage_b: Pakistani truck art is also a major trade. Workshops in cities such as Karachi and Rawalpindi employ painters, metalworkers, and woodcarvers who may spend weeks decorating a single truck. Today these artists also paint the same designs on furniture and other objects that are sold to collectors around the world.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the description of truck art in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that truck art matters only as a business, not as a source of pride
choices.B: By adding that truck art is also an important source of work for skilled artists
choices.C: By claiming that truck art is found only in Karachi and Rawalpindi
choices.D: By noting that the designs on trucks were first created for furniture

explanation.why: Text 1 describes truck art from the drivers' point of view: it is "a source of pride." Text 2 adds another side, saying truck art "is also a major trade" that employs "painters, metalworkers, and woodcarvers." Text 2 builds on Text 1 rather than disagreeing with it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says truck art is "also" a trade, which adds to Text 1's point rather than denying that drivers take pride in it.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 adds that truck art provides work for painters, metalworkers, and woodcarvers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 names Karachi and Rawalpindi as examples ("cities such as"), not as the only places truck art is found.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says artists now paint truck designs on furniture, so the designs moved from trucks to furniture, not the other way around.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Norse settlers lived in Greenland from about 985 CE but had abandoned their farms by the mid-1400s. A common explanation is that they clung to European ways of life, raising cattle and sheep as the climate grew colder, and failed to adopt the hunting practices that allowed Inuit communities in the region to thrive.
items.passage_b: Chemical analysis of Norse skeletons from Greenland shows that, over the centuries, the settlers' diets came to rely heavily on seals and other marine animals. Archaeologist Hanne Sørlie argues that the settlers' departure is better explained by the falling value of walrus ivory, their main export to Europe, than by a refusal to change.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting it but adding that the settlers also exported walrus ivory
choices.B: By suggesting that the settlers left mainly because their farms could no longer feed them
choices.C: By questioning it, citing evidence that the settlers did change how they obtained food
choices.D: By arguing that a change in the settlers' diet caused them to abandon Greenland

explanation.why: Text 1 says the Norse "failed to adopt" new ways of getting food. Text 2 reports that their diets "came to rely heavily on seals and other marine animals" and that their departure is better explained by falling ivory prices "than by a refusal to change." So Text 2 doubts Text 1's explanation and offers evidence of adaptation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not accept Text 1's explanation; it says the departure is better explained by something other than "a refusal to change."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not blame failing farms; it points to the falling value of walrus ivory.
explanation.C: Correct. The evidence that settlers shifted toward eating seals challenges Text 1's claim that they failed to adapt.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In Text 2 the diet change is evidence that the settlers adapted, not the cause of their leaving; the cause it proposes is the falling value of ivory.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In one experiment, researchers played recorded sounds of bees' wings to evening primrose flowers. Within minutes, the sugar concentration of the flowers' nectar increased. The researchers suggest that the bowl-shaped petals vibrate in response to such sounds, allowing the plant to detect nearby pollinators and offer them a sweeter reward.
items.passage_b: Studies showing that plants react to sound are intriguing, but the word "hearing" can mislead. Plants have no nervous system, so any response must arise from cells physically disturbed by vibration. Moreover, a single experiment, however striking, needs to be repeated by other laboratories before biologists can be confident that the effect is real.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Plants hear sounds in much the same way that animals do.
choices.B: The evening primrose results have already been confirmed by other laboratories.
choices.C: Evening primrose nectar becomes sweeter when the flowers are exposed to bee sounds.
choices.D: Any response of plants to sound would depend on plant parts being physically moved.

explanation.why: Text 1 explains the flowers' response through petals that "vibrate in response to such sounds." Text 2 says any plant response "must arise from cells physically disturbed by vibration." Both authors connect a plant's reaction to sound with physical movement of its parts.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 warns that the word "hearing" can mislead because plants have no nervous system, so its author would not agree.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the experiment still "needs to be repeated by other laboratories," and Text 1 mentions no repetition.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 1 reports this result, but Text 2 says biologists cannot yet be "confident that the effect is real," so only one author clearly accepts it.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 1 relies on vibrating petals, and Text 2 says responses must come from cells "physically disturbed by vibration," so both would agree.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Iliad and the Odyssey are thick with repeated phrases, such as "swift-footed Achilles" and "rosy-fingered Dawn," that once struck readers as mere padding. In the 1930s, scholars who studied living oral poets in the Balkans showed that such stock phrases are the working tools of singers who compose as they perform, fitting ready-made units to the meter. The density of these formulas in Homer, the scholars concluded, is the signature of poetry composed without writing.
items.passage_b: That the Homeric poems emerged from a tradition of oral composition is now hard to dispute. What the formulas cannot establish is how the particular texts we possess came to be fixed. A singer trained in oral techniques might well have dictated a performance to a scribe, or even revised it in writing, without abandoning the formulaic style in which he had learned to think. The formulas tell us about the poet's training, not about the circumstances of the poems' final composition.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting that the formulas reflect an oral tradition while denying that they show how the surviving poems were composed
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that the Homeric poems have any connection to a tradition of oral composition
choices.C: By arguing that the formulas were inserted into the poems by the scribes who later copied them
choices.D: By agreeing that the poems were composed without writing while doubting that Balkan poets are a valid comparison

explanation.why: Text 2 grants that the poems "emerged from a tradition of oral composition," which accepts part of Text 1. But it says the formulas "cannot establish" how the surviving texts were fixed, since a poet trained orally might have dictated or revised in writing. So Text 2 accepts the oral tradition but rejects the step from formulas to "composed without writing."
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 agrees the formulas point to an oral tradition and the poet's "training" but denies that they reveal how the final texts were composed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 calls an oral tradition behind the poems "hard to dispute," so it does not reject that connection. This choice exaggerates its disagreement.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says scribes may have taken down a performance, not that scribes added the formulas.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not agree that the poems were composed without writing; that is exactly the conclusion it questions. It also never criticizes the Balkan comparison.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Because snow leopards are rarely seen, ecologists often count them with camera traps: motion-triggered cameras placed along the ridges and trails the cats use. Each leopard's spot pattern is unique, so researchers can tell individuals apart in the photographs. Using this method over one winter in a valley in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan region, a team led by ecologist Sana Mirza identified nine adults and concluded that the valley supports a small but stable population.
items.passage_b: Camera-trap counts of snow leopards are valuable, but a single survey can say little about trends. As zoologist Arjun Thapa points out, photographs taken over a few months show which individuals were present during that time; they cannot reveal whether the population is growing, shrinking, or holding steady. Only surveys repeated over several years in the same area can support such a judgment.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By doubting that the photographs could reliably tell individual leopards apart
choices.B: By arguing that the valley most likely contains more than nine adult leopards
choices.C: By accepting the count of individuals but questioning the claim that the population is stable
choices.D: By suggesting that the population's stability could be confirmed by a longer survey in another valley

explanation.why: Text 2 calls camera-trap counts "valuable" and says photographs show "which individuals were present," so it accepts the count. But it says a single survey "cannot reveal whether the population is growing, shrinking, or holding steady." Text 1's claim that the population is "stable" is exactly the kind of judgment Text 2 says needs repeated surveys.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 calls camera-trap counts "valuable" and does not question the use of spot patterns to identify individuals.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not say the count is too low; its concern is about trends over time, not the number of leopards.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts what the photographs show about who was present but says one survey cannot show that a population is stable.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says only surveys repeated "in the same area" can support a judgment about trends, so a survey in another valley would not confirm this valley's stability.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Why did mechanized industry first take hold in eighteenth-century Britain? One influential answer is economic. British wages were high relative to the cost of capital and of coal, which was abundant and cheap. Under those conditions, machines that replaced costly labor with cheap energy were profitable to adopt in Britain, whereas the same machines, even if they had been available elsewhere, would not have repaid their cost in regions where labor was cheaper and fuel more expensive.
items.passage_b: Explanations grounded in relative prices are persuasive about why British manufacturers were eager to buy labor-saving machines; they are less persuasive about why such machines were invented and steadily improved there in the first place. Prices create an incentive, but an incentive does not by itself produce the tinkerers, instrument makers, and networks of correspondence through which technical knowledge was shared and refined. Those owed as much to a culture that prized practical experiment as to any ledger of costs.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the economic answer in Text 1?

choices.A: By disputing the claim that British wages were high compared with the cost of coal
choices.B: By conceding that it explains why British firms adopted machines but not why they were invented there
choices.C: By arguing that cultural values, rather than prices, explain why British manufacturers chose to buy machines
choices.D: By questioning whether economic incentives played any part in Britain's technological development

explanation.why: Text 2 says explanations based on prices "are persuasive about why British manufacturers were eager to buy labor-saving machines," which concedes part of Text 1. It then says they are "less persuasive about why such machines were invented and steadily improved there," pointing to a culture of practical experiment. Text 2 accepts the answer for adoption but finds it incomplete for invention.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 never disputes the facts about wages and coal; it questions only how much those facts explain.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 grants that prices explain why machines were bought but says they do not explain why the machines were invented and improved in Britain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that prices explain the eagerness to buy machines; it turns to culture only to explain invention and improvement.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says "Prices create an incentive" and that invention owed to culture "as much as" to costs, so it does not deny that incentives mattered.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Jane Austen's Persuasion (1817) is often read as a novel about the dangers of yielding to others. Eight years before the story begins, Anne Elliot broke off her engagement to Frederick Wentworth on the advice of her older friend Lady Russell, and the novel dwells on the cost of that decision: years of quiet regret, and a reunion that comes about only because Wentworth's feelings, like Anne's, proved more durable than the advice that divided them. On this reading, the book's title names the error its heroine must outgrow.
items.passage_b: Readers who take Persuasion as a warning against being persuaded must contend with its final chapters. There Anne, reflecting on the broken engagement, tells Wentworth that Lady Russell's advice was mistaken but that she herself was right to follow it, given what duty then required of a young woman in her position. Austen, in other words, separates the soundness of the advice from the rightness of submitting to it, a distinction that the title, read as a simple caution, tends to obscure.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of Persuasion in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the reading on the grounds that Text 1 misstates why Anne ended her engagement
choices.B: By arguing that Lady Russell's advice was sound and that Anne was right to accept it
choices.C: By claiming that the novel endorses following others' advice whenever duty seems to require it
choices.D: By contending that the reading overlooks Anne's view that following mistaken advice was nonetheless right

explanation.why: Text 1 treats being persuaded as "the error its heroine must outgrow." Text 2 points to the final chapters, where Anne says Lady Russell's advice "was mistaken but that she herself was right to follow it." Text 2's author would say Text 1's reading misses this distinction between bad advice and a right decision to submit to it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that Anne ended the engagement on Lady Russell's advice; it challenges what the novel concludes about that choice, not the facts of the plot.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says Anne calls the advice "mistaken," so the author would not argue that the advice was sound.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses Anne's judgment about one decision "given what duty then required of a young woman in her position"; it does not claim the novel recommends obeying advice in general.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 argues that Text 1 misses Anne's own judgment that the advice was wrong but that submitting to it was right.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many cat owners believe that a purring cat is always a happy cat. Cats often purr while being stroked or while resting in a warm lap, so it seems natural to treat the sound as a sign of contentment.
items.passage_b: Veterinarians report that cats also purr in situations that are anything but pleasant, such as when they are injured, giving birth, or close to death. According to animal behaviorist Ingrid Solberg, purring may sometimes help a cat calm itself during stress rather than simply express pleasure.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By noting that cats also purr when they are hurt or under stress
choices.B: By arguing that cats purr only when they are in pain or afraid
choices.C: By claiming that cats purr most often when they are being stroked
choices.D: By agreeing that purring is a reliable sign that a cat is content

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the belief that "a purring cat is always a happy cat." Text 2 reports that cats also purr when they are "injured, giving birth, or close to death" and that purring may help a cat "calm itself during stress." So the author of Text 2 would point out that purring does not always mean contentment.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 lists painful and stressful situations in which cats purr, which challenges the idea that purring always means a cat is happy.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says purring may "sometimes" help a cat calm itself; it does not say cats purr only when in pain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares how often cats purr in different situations.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 gives examples of cats purring in unpleasant situations, so its author would not call purring a reliable sign of contentment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Sri Lanka, once called Ceylon, is famous around the world for its tea. Visitors to the island's green hill country see slopes covered with neat rows of tea bushes, and many assume that tea has been the island's main crop for as long as anyone can remember.
items.passage_b: In fact, tea became Ceylon's leading crop only in the late 1800s. Before then, much of the hill country was covered with coffee plantations. In the 1870s, a fungus called coffee rust spread through the plantations and destroyed most of the crop. Planters then turned to tea, which soon took coffee's place.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By pointing out that few visitors travel to the hill country to see its farms
choices.B: By explaining that tea replaced an earlier crop that was destroyed by disease
choices.C: By agreeing that tea has always been the island's most important crop
choices.D: By arguing that coffee grows better than tea on the island's steep hill slopes

explanation.why: Text 1 says many people assume tea has been the island's main crop "for as long as anyone can remember." Text 2 says tea became the leading crop "only in the late 1800s," after a fungus destroyed the coffee plantations that came before it. So the author of Text 2 would correct the assumption by explaining this history.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about how many visitors go to the hill country.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 explains that coffee was the main crop until coffee rust destroyed it and planters "turned to tea."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says tea became the leading crop only in the late 1800s, so its author would not agree that tea was always the main crop.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says coffee was destroyed by a fungus; it never compares how well coffee and tea grow on the slopes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Some teachers argue that listening to an audiobook is not really reading. In their view, students who listen to a story instead of looking at the printed words will understand and remember less of it.
items.passage_b: Psychologist Tomás Ferreira tested this idea with a group of adult volunteers. Half of them read a short history book in print, and half listened to a recording of the same book. On a test given afterward, the two groups answered about the same number of questions correctly. Ferreira concluded that, at least for this kind of book, listening and reading led to similar understanding.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view of the teachers in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that schools should replace printed books with recordings
choices.B: By noting that in one test, listeners understood a book as well as readers
choices.C: By arguing that audiobooks are better than print for every type of book
choices.D: By agreeing that people who listen to books remember less than readers do

explanation.why: The teachers in Text 1 claim that listeners "will understand and remember less." In Text 2, Ferreira's listeners and readers "answered about the same number of questions correctly," so he concluded that listening and reading led to "similar understanding." The author of Text 2 would answer the teachers by pointing to this result.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not recommend replacing printed books; it only compares understanding.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 reports that listeners and readers did about equally well on the test, which challenges the teachers' claim.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 found similar results, not better ones, and limits its conclusion to "this kind of book."
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the teachers' view in Text 1; Text 2's test found that the two groups did about equally well.

items.subject: science
items.passage: After a heavy rain, sidewalks are often covered with earthworms. A common explanation is that the worms come to the surface to escape drowning, since rainwater fills the tunnels where they live.
items.passage_b: Researchers have found that earthworms can survive for days underwater, because they breathe through their moist skin and can take in oxygen that is dissolved in water. Biologist Chen Yiming suggests a different reason for their behavior: wet ground lets worms travel long distances across the surface without drying out, so rain gives them a rare chance to move to new areas.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that worms leave their tunnels to avoid drowning
choices.B: By claiming that worms rarely come to the surface after rain
choices.C: By arguing that heavy rain usually harms earthworms badly
choices.D: By doubting it, because worms can live underwater for days

explanation.why: Text 1 says worms surface after rain "to escape drowning." Text 2 reports that earthworms "can survive for days underwater" and offers "a different reason": rain lets them travel across the surface. So the author of Text 2 would doubt the drowning explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 offers "a different reason," so its author would not agree with the drowning explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that worms come to the surface after rain; it disagrees only about why.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 presents rain as giving worms "a rare chance" to move, not as harming them.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2's evidence that worms survive underwater for days casts doubt on the idea that they surface to avoid drowning.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In movies, cartoons, and costumes, Viking warriors are almost always shown wearing helmets with large horns. This image has become so familiar that many people assume it reflects how the Vikings really dressed for battle.
items.passage_b: Archaeologists have found no evidence that Vikings wore horned helmets. The only nearly complete Viking helmet ever discovered, found in Norway, is a simple rounded iron cap with no horns. Historians trace the popular image largely to the 1800s, when costume designers for operas and plays added horns to make Viking characters look dramatic.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that Vikings never wore helmets of any kind at all
choices.B: By arguing that the familiar image is not supported by evidence
choices.C: By suggesting that horned helmets were common in 1800s Norway
choices.D: By agreeing that Vikings often wore horned helmets in battle

explanation.why: Text 1 says many people assume the horned helmet "reflects how the Vikings really dressed." Text 2 says archaeologists "have found no evidence" of horned helmets and traces the image to costume designers of the 1800s. So the author of Text 2 would say the assumption lacks support.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 describes a real Viking helmet, a "rounded iron cap," so it does not say Vikings wore no helmets.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 explains that no horned Viking helmets have been found and that the image came from 1800s stage costumes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says costume designers in the 1800s added horns for the stage, not that horned helmets were common in Norway then.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says there is "no evidence" that Vikings wore horned helmets.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Today, Aesop's fables, such as the story of the tortoise and the hare, are usually printed in picture books for young children, often in shortened form. Yet in ancient Greece, these short animal tales were often told by adults. Speakers used them in arguments to make a point in a memorable way.
items.passage_b: The fables reached modern readers through many hands. Over the centuries, collectors gathered and rewrote the tales, and many of the neat moral lessons that now end each story were added by these later editors. The fables we read today are therefore not exactly the ones first told in Greece.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Aesop's fables were first created mainly to entertain young children.
choices.B: The moral lessons at the end of each fable were part of the first versions.
choices.C: Picture books have made the fables more popular than they have ever been.
choices.D: The fables as people know them today differ from the ancient Greek versions.

explanation.why: Text 1 says the fables are now printed for children "often in shortened form," while in ancient Greece adults used them in arguments. Text 2 says later editors rewrote the tales and added many of the morals, so modern fables are "not exactly the ones first told in Greece." Both authors describe ways the fables have changed since ancient times.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 1 says the tales were "often told by adults" in ancient Greece, so its author would not agree.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says many of the morals "were added by these later editors," not that they were in the first versions.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Neither text compares how popular the fables are now with how popular they were in the past.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 1 notes shortened children's versions, and Text 2 notes rewriting and added morals; both show that today's fables differ from the originals.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the early 1900s, only a few dozen greater one-horned rhinoceroses may have survived in the area that is now Kaziranga National Park in northeastern India. Today the park holds more than 2,000 of them. Wildlife officials usually credit this recovery to strict protection: armed guards patrol the park, and hunting rhinos for their horns is severely punished.
items.passage_b: Protection from poachers has clearly been essential, but ecologist Rupa Bordoloi argues that it tells only part of the story. Every year, the Brahmaputra River floods much of Kaziranga, leaving fresh silt that renews the tall grasslands rhinos depend on for food. Without these floods, she notes, the grasslands would slowly turn into woodland that could support far fewer rhinos.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation offered by wildlife officials in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the floods, not protection from hunters, explain the recovery
choices.B: By accepting that protection mattered while arguing that yearly floods also helped
choices.C: By questioning whether the number of rhinos in the park has truly increased
choices.D: By suggesting that the floods threaten rhinos by destroying their grasslands

explanation.why: Text 1 credits the rhinos' recovery to "strict protection." Text 2 calls protection "clearly... essential" but says it "tells only part of the story," because the Brahmaputra's floods renew the grasslands rhinos feed on. So the author of Text 2 would accept the officials' explanation as incomplete and add the role of flooding.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 calls protection "essential"; it adds floods as another factor rather than replacing protection with them.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 agrees that protection was essential and adds that floods keep the rhinos' grasslands from turning into woodland.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 does not question the population figures in Text 1.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the floods renew the grasslands, the opposite of destroying them.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Impressionists are often described as rebels shut out by the art world of nineteenth-century Paris. According to this account, the official Salon, the city's most important exhibition, rejected their loose brushwork and everyday subjects, so the painters had no choice but to organize their own independent show in 1874.
items.passage_b: Art historian Odile Marchand points out that the story is less tidy than it seems. Several future Impressionists, including Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, had paintings accepted by the Salon in the 1860s. Their rejections were real but inconsistent, and Marchand argues that the 1874 exhibition reflected a wish to show their work on their own terms as much as a lack of other options.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the account in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the Salon accepted nearly every painting the Impressionists sent in
choices.B: By agreeing that the painters held their own show only because the Salon refused them
choices.C: By noting that some of the painters had earlier found success at the Salon
choices.D: By claiming that the Impressionists' brushwork was less loose than critics believed

explanation.why: Text 1 says the painters "had no choice" but to hold their own show because the Salon rejected them. Text 2 notes that Monet and Renoir "had paintings accepted by the Salon in the 1860s" and calls the rejections "real but inconsistent." So the author of Text 2 would complicate the account by pointing to these earlier successes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the rejections "were real," so it does not claim the Salon accepted nearly everything.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 argues that the 1874 show reflected a wish to show work "on their own terms" as much as a lack of options, so it does not agree with "only."
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 points out that several future Impressionists had paintings accepted by the Salon, which complicates the story of total exclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not discuss the painters' brushwork.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Napoleon Bonaparte is often remembered as a very short man, and the term "Napoleon complex" is still used for the idea that short people make up for their height with aggressive behavior. Many people assume that Napoleon's own drive for power came from a similar sense of being physically small.
items.passage_b: Historians who have examined records from Napoleon's lifetime estimate that he stood about 1.69 meters (5 feet 7 inches) tall, close to average for a Frenchman of his era. The belief that he was tiny may come partly from French inches, which were longer than English ones, and partly from British cartoonists, who mocked him by drawing him as a small, angry figure.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that Napoleon was unusually short for a man of his time
choices.B: By claiming that British cartoonists invented the term "Napoleon complex"
choices.C: By questioning its basis, since Napoleon was likely of average height
choices.D: By arguing that Napoleon was in fact taller than most men in France

explanation.why: The assumption in Text 1 depends on Napoleon being "physically small." Text 2 says historians estimate he was "close to average for a Frenchman of his era" and explains where the idea that he was tiny came from. So the author of Text 2 would question the starting point of the assumption.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says Napoleon's height was close to average, so its author would not call him unusually short.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says British cartoonists drew Napoleon as small; it does not say they created the term.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 shows that Napoleon was probably of average height, which undercuts an assumption built on his being small.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says he was "close to average," not taller than most men.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For much of the twentieth century, many people believed that dogs see the world only in shades of black, white, and gray. Because dogs rely so heavily on their sense of smell, it seemed reasonable to assume that color vision would be of little use to them.
items.passage_b: The retina contains cone cells, which allow animals to detect color. Humans typically have three types of cones, while dogs have two. Studies in which dogs were trained to choose between colored panels show that they can tell blue from yellow but have trouble telling red from green. Their color vision, in other words, resembles that of a person with red-green color blindness.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that dogs are unable to distinguish any colors at all
choices.B: By noting that dogs see some colors, though fewer than most people
choices.C: By suggesting that dogs actually depend more on sight than on smell
choices.D: By arguing that dogs see colors just as well as most humans can

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the belief that dogs see "only in shades of black, white, and gray." Text 2 says dogs have two types of cones and "can tell blue from yellow" but struggle with red and green. So the author of Text 2 would say dogs do see color, but a narrower range than most humans.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says dogs can tell blue from yellow, so they can distinguish some colors.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 explains that dogs distinguish blue from yellow but not red from green, so they see some colors but fewer than most people.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 does not compare how much dogs rely on sight and on smell.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says dogs have fewer cone types than humans and have trouble with red and green.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is often read as a warning about science. In this reading, Victor Frankenstein's mistake is the experiment itself: by trying to create life, he oversteps the proper limits of human knowledge, and the disasters that follow are his punishment.
items.passage_b: Some critics locate Victor's failure elsewhere. Moments after the creature comes to life, Victor flees in horror and leaves it to fend for itself. The creature, who at first seeks kindness, turns violent only after being rejected again and again. For these critics, the novel is less concerned with whether Victor should have made the creature than with his refusal to care for it once he had.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the novel in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that it overlooks the importance of Victor's abandonment of the creature
choices.B: By suggesting that Victor deserved a harsher punishment than he received
choices.C: By claiming that the creature was violent from the moment it came to life
choices.D: By agreeing that the novel's main concern is the danger of scientific experiment

explanation.why: Text 1 says Victor's mistake is "the experiment itself." Text 2's critics "locate Victor's failure elsewhere": he abandons the creature, which turns violent "only after being rejected." They argue the novel cares more about Victor's "refusal to care for it" than about whether he should have made it.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 shifts the focus from the experiment to Victor's abandonment of the creature, which the reading in Text 1 does not consider.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not discuss whether Victor's punishment was severe enough.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the creature "at first seeks kindness" and turns violent only later.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the novel is "less concerned" with whether Victor should have made the creature, so it does not agree with this reading.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A survey of 3,000 schoolchildren found that those who took music lessons scored higher on math tests, on average, than those who did not. Education writer Grace Nwosu argues that the finding shows that learning an instrument strengthens mathematical skills, and she urges schools to expand music programs for that reason.
items.passage_b: Children who take music lessons tend to differ from other children in many ways: their families are often wealthier, for example, and may spend more time helping with schoolwork at home. When psychologist Lars Eklund randomly assigned children either to music lessons or to another activity, the two groups' math scores rose by about the same amount.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Nwosu in Text 1?

choices.A: By questioning whether the music lessons caused the higher math scores
choices.B: By arguing that schools should spend less on math programs and more on music
choices.C: By arguing that music lessons actually lower children's scores on math tests
choices.D: By agreeing that schools should expand music programs to raise math scores

explanation.why: Nwosu concludes from a survey that music lessons strengthen math skills. Text 2 notes that children who take lessons "tend to differ from other children in many ways," and that when children were randomly assigned, math scores "rose by about the same amount" in both groups. So the author of Text 2 would doubt that the lessons themselves caused the higher scores.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 offers other explanations for the survey result and describes an experiment in which lessons gave no extra math benefit.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 makes no recommendation about how schools should divide their spending.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 reports that both groups' scores rose by about the same amount, not that lessons lowered scores.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2's evidence undercuts the reason Nwosu gives for expanding music programs.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Beekeepers in many countries have reported losing unusually large numbers of honeybee colonies in recent decades. Entomologist Kofi Asante argues that the main cause is the Varroa mite, a parasite that feeds on bees and spreads viruses through a hive. Colonies left untreated for the mites, he notes, often die within a few years.
items.passage_b: Research on honeybee losses suggests that no single factor is to blame. Biologist Elena Vidal points out that bees weakened by poor nutrition or by exposure to certain pesticides are less able to survive infections, including those spread by parasites. In her view, colony losses result from several stresses acting together.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Parasites can contribute to the deaths of honeybee colonies.
choices.B: Beekeepers have exaggerated the number of colonies they have lost.
choices.C: The Varroa mite alone accounts for most honeybee colony losses.
choices.D: Pesticides are the main reason that so many honeybee colonies have died.

explanation.why: Asante blames the Varroa mite, a parasite, for colony losses. Vidal argues that several stresses act together, including "infections, including those spread by parasites." Both authors therefore treat parasites as one cause of colony deaths, even though they disagree about whether it is the main cause.
explanation.A: Correct. Asante says the Varroa mite kills colonies, and Vidal lists parasite-spread infections among the stresses that act together.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Neither text questions the beekeepers' reports.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is Asante's view, but Vidal says "no single factor is to blame."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Asante names the mite as the main cause, and Vidal names pesticides as only one of several stresses.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At Lothal, an Indus Valley Civilization site in Gujarat, India, archaeologists in the 1950s uncovered a large brick-lined basin more than 200 meters long. Because the town lay near a river that once connected to the sea, the excavators concluded that the basin was a dockyard where boats were loaded with goods for trade.
items.passage_b: Some archaeologists find the dockyard idea doubtful. They argue that the evidence linking the basin to boats is thin, and they note that ancient communities in dry regions often built large tanks to hold water. Archaeologist Meera Pillai suggests that the basin may instead have been a reservoir storing fresh water for the town, though she agrees that Lothal was an important center of trade.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the basin was most likely used for loading boats with goods
choices.B: By proposing another use for the basin while accepting Lothal's role in trade
choices.C: By claiming that the basin was built long after the town had been abandoned
choices.D: By arguing that the town of Lothal played no part in trade of any kind

explanation.why: Text 1's excavators concluded that the basin was "a dockyard." Text 2 calls this idea "doubtful" and suggests the basin "may instead have been a reservoir," while Pillai "agrees that Lothal was an important center of trade." So Text 2 offers a different purpose for the basin without denying Lothal's trade.
