explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 argues that the amounts are small and the route unproven, so the results do not show that the networks nourish seedlings in any meaningful way.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not agree that the networks feed seedlings; it says that has not been shown.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 states that labeled carbon "does move from tree to seedling."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions the soil only as one possible route for the labeled carbon; it makes no claim about where seedlings get most of their carbon.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before printing, every copy of a book was made by hand, and each scribe introduced errors of his own, so that no two manuscripts of a long text were identical. Historian Gérard Lemaire argues that the printing press, introduced in Europe in the mid-fifteenth century, changed this by fixing texts. Once type was set, hundreds of copies could be pulled from it in the time a scribe needed for one, and readers in distant cities could, for the first time, cite the same words on the same page.
items.passage_b: Printing did make it possible to produce many copies far faster than any scribe could. But early printed editions were less uniform than they appear. Printers routinely corrected errors while a sheet was being run, without discarding the sheets already printed, and then bound corrected and uncorrected sheets together. Surviving copies of a single edition, such as Shakespeare's First Folio of 1623, therefore often differ from one another. The stability we associate with print was a slow achievement of later practice, not an immediate effect of the press.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Early printers seldom corrected errors once a book's type had been set.
choices.B: The stability of printed texts developed gradually through later printing practices.
choices.C: Copies of a single early printed edition were usually identical to one another.
choices.D: Printing allowed copies of a book to be produced far more quickly than by hand.

explanation.why: Text 1 says hundreds of copies could be printed "in the time a scribe needed for one." Text 2 agrees that printing made it possible "to produce many copies far faster than any scribe could." The authors disagree about whether early print fixed texts, but both accept that printing was much faster than hand copying.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says printers "routinely corrected errors" during a print run.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is Text 2's view; Text 1 presents fixed texts as an effect of the press itself.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 1 implies this, but Text 2 says copies of one edition "often differ from one another."
explanation.D: Correct. Both texts state that printing produced copies much faster than scribes could.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a honeybee colony outgrows its hive, thousands of bees leave with the old queen and cluster on a branch while scouts search for a new home. Returning scouts perform waggle dances advertising the sites they have found, and bees that have inspected a better site dance for it longer. Over several days, dances for inferior sites die out. Biologist Rafael Moreno argues that the swarm reaches its decision when the dancers achieve consensus, all advertising the same site, at which point the swarm takes flight.
items.passage_b: The dances clearly do the work of comparing sites: better sites recruit more inspectors. But the trigger for departure lies elsewhere. Scouts visiting a candidate site keep track, apparently by how often they encounter one another, of how many bees are present there. Once that number passes a threshold, they return and begin preparing the swarm to fly, sometimes while dances for rival sites are still under way. The choice is settled by a quorum at the site, not by unanimity on the cluster.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the account of how the swarm reaches its decision in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that dances for inferior sites always continue until the swarm takes flight
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that waggle dances help the swarm compare possible nest sites
choices.C: By agreeing that dances compare sites but locating the decision in a quorum at the site
choices.D: By arguing that a swarm departs only after every scout has inspected the chosen site

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that "The dances clearly do the work of comparing sites." But it says departure is triggered when the number of scouts at one site "passes a threshold," "sometimes while dances for rival sites are still under way." So the decision comes from a quorum at the site, not the consensus among dancers that Moreno describes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says rival dances continue only "sometimes"; it does not say they always last until departure.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the dances "clearly do the work of comparing sites."
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 keeps the dances' role in comparing sites but argues that a quorum of scouts at a site, not unanimous dancing, settles the choice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says a threshold number of bees at the site is enough; it never requires every scout to visit.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Where did human language begin? Psychologist Naomi Adler argues that it began in the hands. Chimpanzees and other great apes, she notes, use dozens of gestures flexibly: an individual adjusts its gestures to the attention of its audience and repeats or changes them when it is not understood. Their vocal calls, by contrast, appear largely fixed and tied to emotional states. Because flexible, intentional signaling is a precondition for language, Adler concludes that language must have first emerged as gesture and only later shifted to speech.
items.passage_b: The contrast between flexible ape gestures and rigid ape calls was once widely accepted, but it has softened. Field studies now show that chimpanzees produce some calls selectively, calling more when companions seem unaware of a danger than when they already know of it, and captive orangutans have learned to produce new sounds by imitation. If vocal signaling in apes is more controllable than once thought, the case for a gesture-only stage loses its main support, and language may have drawn on hand and voice together from the start.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion reached by Adler in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that great apes adjust their gestures to the attention of their audience
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that flexible, intentional signaling is a necessary precondition for language
choices.C: By claiming that human language began as speech and only later came to include gesture
choices.D: By arguing that it rests on a contrast between gesture and voice that newer evidence weakens

explanation.why: Adler's conclusion depends on the contrast between flexible gestures and "largely fixed" calls. Text 2 says that contrast "has softened," citing chimpanzees that call selectively and orangutans that learn new sounds, so "the case for a gesture-only stage loses its main support." Text 2 attacks the premise about ape calls rather than the importance of flexible signaling.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that ape gestures are flexible; it questions only how rigid their calls are.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions this premise; it disputes the claim that only gestures met it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 suggests hand and voice worked "together from the start," not that speech came first.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 argues that apes' calls are more controllable than Adler assumes, which undercuts the contrast her conclusion relies on.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Anton Chekhov's story "The Lady with the Dog" (1899) begins with Dmitri Gurov, a jaded Moscow banker who regards women with contempt, starting an affair at a seaside resort that he expects to forget within weeks. Instead, back in Moscow, he cannot stop thinking of Anna, and by the end he recognizes that only now, as his hair turns gray, has he truly fallen in love. Critic Elif Arslan reads the story as a tale of redemption: love has transformed a cynic into a man capable of tenderness.
items.passage_b: Gurov's change of heart is genuine; Chekhov leaves no doubt that he has come to love Anna. What the story withholds is any sense that this love has delivered him. Its final scene finds the lovers in a Moscow hotel room, still meeting in secret, still married to others, and still unable to imagine how they might live openly. They feel that a solution must be near, yet both understand that the hardest part has barely begun. A reading that ends in redemption completes a story that Chekhov deliberately leaves open.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the story in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that Gurov comes to feel genuine love for Anna by the end of the story
choices.B: By suggesting that the story's open ending reveals Chekhov's disapproval of the affair
choices.C: By granting that Gurov changes but denying that the story resolves his situation
choices.D: By claiming that the lovers find a way to live together openly in the story's final scene

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that "Gurov's change of heart is genuine," accepting part of Arslan's reading. It objects that the story "withholds any sense that this love has delivered him": the lovers are still hiding, and "the hardest part has barely begun." A redemption reading, Text 2 says, "completes a story that Chekhov deliberately leaves open."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says Chekhov "leaves no doubt that he has come to love Anna."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the ending is open, but it never says Chekhov disapproves of the affair.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts that Gurov truly changes but says calling it redemption imposes an ending that the open final scene withholds.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the lovers are "still unable to imagine how they might live openly."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many people believe that cracking your knuckles will give you arthritis later in life. The loud pop certainly sounds like something being damaged, and parents and teachers have warned children against the habit for generations.
items.passage_b: The pop of a cracked knuckle comes from a gas bubble forming in the fluid that surrounds the joint, not from bone or cartilage being harmed. Studies that compared longtime knuckle crackers with people who never crack their knuckles found no difference in how often the two groups developed arthritis in their hands.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that arthritis in the hands is caused mainly by injuries
choices.B: By explaining the source of the sound and noting that crackers get arthritis no more often than others
choices.C: By warning that cracking knuckles can weaken a person's grip over time
choices.D: By agreeing that the popping sound shows that the joints are being damaged

explanation.why: Text 1 reports the belief that knuckle cracking causes arthritis and that the sound suggests damage. Text 2 says the pop is a gas bubble, "not from bone or cartilage being harmed," and that studies found "no difference" in arthritis between crackers and non-crackers. So the author of Text 2 would answer the belief with an explanation of the sound and the evidence from those studies.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about what does cause arthritis.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 explains that the pop is a harmless gas bubble and cites studies showing no extra arthritis among knuckle crackers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never mentions grip strength.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the sound comes from a gas bubble, not from damage, so its author would not agree.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The bagpipe is the national instrument of Scotland. It is played at Scottish weddings, parades, and military ceremonies, and a lone piper on a hillside is one of the most familiar images of the country. Many people therefore assume that the instrument was invented there.
items.passage_b: Instruments made of a bag and a set of pipes were played in many parts of the world long before Scotland became known for them. Roman writers mention a bagpipe, and medieval paintings show pipers across Europe. Today bagpipes are still part of folk music in Spain, Italy, Bulgaria, and parts of the Middle East. The Scottish Highland pipe is one member of a large family.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that bagpipes are no longer played anywhere except Scotland
choices.B: By agreeing that the instrument was first invented in Scotland
choices.C: By pointing out that bagpipes have long been played in many places outside Scotland
choices.D: By arguing that Scottish bagpipes sound better than those of other countries

explanation.why: Text 1 says people assume the bagpipe "was invented" in Scotland. Text 2 replies that bagpipes were played "in many parts of the world long before Scotland became known for them" and are still played in Spain, Italy, Bulgaria, and the Middle East. The author of Text 2 would answer the assumption by pointing to this wider history.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the opposite: bagpipes are "still part of folk music" in several other countries.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says bagpipes existed elsewhere long before Scotland became known for them, so its author would not agree.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 gives examples of bagpipes in ancient Rome, medieval Europe, and modern folk music in several countries.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares how the instruments sound.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ostriches are often seen with their heads held low, close to the ground. A common story says that a frightened ostrich buries its head in the sand, as if not seeing danger would make it go away. The phrase "burying your head in the sand" comes from this idea.
items.passage_b: An ostrich with its head buried in sand could not breathe. What people see is something else: ostriches dig shallow nests in the sand and lower their heads to turn their eggs, and they bend down to swallow pebbles that help them grind food. A frightened ostrich does not hide; it runs, or it lies flat with its neck stretched out.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: An ostrich's best defense against danger is its sharp eyesight.
choices.B: Ostriches can hold their breath for several minutes while underground.
choices.C: Ostriches bury their heads in order to hide from danger.
choices.D: Ostriches sometimes lower their heads close to the ground.

explanation.why: Text 1 opens by saying ostriches "are often seen with their heads held low, close to the ground." Text 2 explains that they "lower their heads to turn their eggs" and "bend down to swallow pebbles." Both authors accept that ostriches put their heads near the ground; they differ only on why.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Neither text mentions eyesight.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Neither text says anything about holding breath; Text 2 says a buried ostrich could not breathe at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 1 calls this "a common story," and Text 2 rejects it, saying a frightened ostrich "does not hide" and could not breathe with its head buried.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 1 says ostriches are seen with heads held low, and Text 2 describes them bending down to tend eggs and swallow pebbles.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In a bullfight, the matador waves a red cape, and the bull charges at it. Because of this, many people believe that the color red makes bulls angry. The idea is so widely accepted that a person who provokes someone is sometimes said to be waving a red flag at a bull.
items.passage_b: Cattle have only two kinds of color-sensing cells in their eyes, and they cannot tell red from green. What a bull reacts to is the movement of the cloth. Matadors also use a much larger cape that is pink on one side and yellow on the other, and bulls charge at it just as readily. The cape is red for the audience, not for the bull.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the color red makes bulls especially angry
choices.B: By noting that bulls can see more colors than people can
choices.C: By suggesting that bulls charge only when they feel threatened
choices.D: By explaining that the bull reacts to the cape's movement rather than its color

explanation.why: Text 1 says people believe "the color red makes bulls angry." Text 2 answers that bulls "cannot tell red from green" and that "what a bull reacts to is the movement of the cloth," adding that bulls charge a pink-and-yellow cape just as readily. So the author of Text 2 would reply that movement, not color, draws the charge.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says bulls cannot even tell red from green, so its author would not agree.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says cattle have only two kinds of color-sensing cells, which means they see fewer colors, not more.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never discusses whether bulls feel threatened.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 says bulls cannot see red and react to the cloth's movement.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At the end of a meal in a Chinese restaurant in the United States, diners are usually given fortune cookies: crisp, folded cookies with a slip of paper inside that carries a short message. Because the cookies are served in Chinese restaurants, many diners assume they are an old Chinese tradition.
items.passage_b: Fortune cookies were being made by Japanese bakers in California in the early 1900s, based on a folded cracker from Kyoto that also carried a paper message. Chinese restaurants in the United States adopted the cookies later, and they spread across the country after World War II. In China itself, fortune cookies were almost unknown until recent decades.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that fortune cookies were first made in Kyoto by Chinese cooks
choices.B: By explaining that the cookie began with Japanese bakers in the United States
choices.C: By arguing that Chinese restaurants should stop serving fortune cookies
choices.D: By agreeing that fortune cookies have been eaten in China for centuries

explanation.why: Text 1 says diners assume fortune cookies are "an old Chinese tradition." Text 2 traces them instead to "Japanese bakers in California in the early 1900s" and notes that in China they "were almost unknown until recent decades." So the author of Text 2 would correct the assumption with this history.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the Kyoto cracker was Japanese and that the cookies were made in California, not in Kyoto by Chinese cooks.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 says the cookies started with Japanese bakers in California and were adopted by Chinese restaurants later.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 gives a history; it does not tell restaurants what to serve.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the cookies were almost unknown in China until recently, so its author would not agree.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In Delhi, India, an iron pillar more than seven meters tall has stood outdoors for about 1,600 years. Although it is soaked by rain every monsoon season, it has barely rusted. Many visitors conclude that the ancient smiths who made it knew a secret of metalworking that has since been lost.
items.passage_b: Metallurgists who studied the pillar found that its iron contains an unusually large amount of phosphorus. When the surface reacts with air, the phosphorus helps form a thin, hard layer that seals the metal from further rust. Delhi's climate, dry for most of the year, also slows the process. The pillar's survival comes from the chemistry of its iron and its surroundings, not from a lost secret.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion reached by visitors in Text 1?

choices.A: By explaining that the pillar's resistance to rust comes from the chemistry of its iron
choices.B: By suggesting that the pillar is much younger than visitors think
choices.C: By arguing that the pillar has in fact rusted badly in recent years
choices.D: By agreeing that the method used to make the pillar has been completely lost

explanation.why: Text 1 says visitors conclude that the smiths "knew a secret of metalworking that has since been lost." Text 2 explains that the iron's high phosphorus content forms a protective layer and that the dry climate helps, concluding that the survival is explained "by the chemistry of its iron and its surroundings, not by a lost secret."
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 points to the phosphorus in the iron, which forms a sealing layer, together with the dry climate.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not question the pillar's age.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the protective layer seals the metal from rust; it never says the pillar has rusted badly.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the survival is "not" explained by a lost secret.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: According to a popular legend, coffee was discovered by an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi. He noticed that his goats became lively after eating the red berries of a certain shrub, tried the berries himself, and felt the same energy. The story is repeated in countless cafés and coffee histories as the origin of the drink.
items.passage_b: The Kaldi story first appears in print in 1671, in a book by a European writer, several centuries after coffee drinking was already well established. The earliest reliable records show Sufi communities in Yemen drinking coffee in the 1400s to stay awake during night prayers. The legend is charming, but it tells us more about Europeans' curiosity about the new drink than about where coffee actually came from.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the legend in Text 1?

choices.A: By noting that the story was written down long after coffee drinking was established
choices.B: By arguing that coffee was first drunk in Europe rather than in Africa or Arabia
choices.C: By claiming that goats are not affected by eating coffee berries
choices.D: By accepting the story as the most reliable account of coffee's discovery

explanation.why: Text 1 presents the Kaldi legend as the usual story of coffee's origin. Text 2 says the story "first appears in print in 1671," centuries after coffee drinking "was already well established" in Yemen, and that it reveals Europeans' curiosity rather than coffee's origins. So the author of Text 2 would respond by pointing to the late date of the story.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 dates the first printed version to 1671, centuries after coffee was already being drunk.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 places the earliest coffee drinking in Yemen, not Europe.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about the effect of coffee berries on goats.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the "earliest reliable records" are from Yemen and treats the legend as a later European tale, so it would not call the story reliable.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Children are often told never to touch a baby bird that has fallen from its nest. The warning rests on a widely repeated belief: if the parents smell a human on their chick, they will reject it and let it starve. According to this view, the best thing to do with a bird on the ground is to leave it alone.
items.passage_b: Ornithologist Teodora Vlahović notes that most songbirds have a weak sense of smell and do not reject a chick that a person has handled. Still, she agrees that a young bird on the ground is usually best left where it is, because a fledgling with feathers is normally being fed by parents nearby and is learning to fly. A featherless nestling, however, can safely be placed back in its nest.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: A young bird found on the ground should often be left where it is.
choices.B: A baby bird found on the ground should be taken to a wildlife center.
choices.C: Featherless nestlings can safely be returned to their nests.
choices.D: Parent birds abandon chicks that carry a human scent.

explanation.why: Text 1 concludes that "the best thing to do with a bird on the ground is to leave it alone." Text 2 "agrees that a young bird on the ground is usually best left where it is," though for a different reason. Both authors therefore accept that leaving the bird is often right.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 1 says to leave the bird alone, and Vlahović agrees that a young bird is usually best left where it is.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Neither text mentions wildlife centers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only Text 2 says this; Text 1 says never to touch a baby bird.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the belief in Text 1, but Text 2 says most songbirds have a weak sense of smell and do not reject handled chicks.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa is the most famous painting in the world, and most visitors to the Louvre assume that its fame rests on its artistic qualities: the soft, smoky shading that blurs every edge, the mysterious half-smile, and the way the sitter's eyes seem to follow the viewer around the room.
items.passage_b: In the nineteenth century, the Mona Lisa was admired, but it was not more admired than many other paintings in the Louvre. That changed in 1911, when the painting was stolen from the museum and disappeared for two years. Newspapers around the world covered the theft, crowds lined up to stare at the empty space on the wall, and when the painting was recovered in 1913, it returned as a celebrity. Its qualities are real, but its fame owes at least as much to a crime.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that the painting was little known until it was stolen a second time
choices.B: By agreeing that the painting's fame rests entirely on its artistic qualities
choices.C: By arguing that a famous crime did as much as the painting's qualities to make it known
choices.D: By denying that the painting shows any unusual skill

explanation.why: Text 1 says visitors assume the painting's fame "rests on its artistic qualities." Text 2 says that before the 1911 theft it was "not more admired than many other paintings" and that its fame "owes at least as much to a crime." So the author of Text 2 would respond that the theft, not just the painting's qualities, explains its fame.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 describes only one theft, in 1911.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the fame owes at least as much to the theft, so its author would not agree.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 argues that the 1911 theft and the coverage it received made the painting a celebrity.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the painting's "qualities are real"; it questions only whether they explain its fame.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island (1883), the one-legged ship's cook Long John Silver is the villain. He lies to the ship's owners, secretly leads the pirates' mutiny, and kills to get his way. Many readers take him as a warning that charm can hide treachery: the friendlier Silver seems, the more dangerous he is.
items.passage_b: Long John Silver is a liar and a killer, yet he is also the most alive character in the book. The young narrator, Jim Hawkins, cannot help admiring him, and Stevenson allows Silver to slip away at the end with a bag of coins instead of facing the gallows. The novel condemns what Silver does, but it never stops enjoying him.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view of Silver in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that Silver takes part in the mutiny against the ship's officers
choices.B: By arguing that Jim Hawkins, not Silver, is the novel's true villain
choices.C: By granting that Silver is treacherous but arguing that the novel treats him with affection
choices.D: By claiming that Silver is punished for his crimes at the end of the novel

explanation.why: Text 1 reads Silver as a villain and "a warning that charm can hide treachery." Text 2 accepts that he is "a liar and a killer" but adds that he is "the most alive character," that Jim admires him, and that the novel "never stops enjoying him." So the author of Text 2 agrees about Silver's crimes but not about the novel's attitude toward him.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 calls Silver a liar and a killer and never questions his role in the mutiny.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says Jim admires Silver; it never calls Jim a villain.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 concedes Silver's treachery but argues that the novel enjoys him and lets him escape.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says Silver slips away "with a bag of coins instead of facing the gallows."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, a pattern of sound unlike that of any other dolphin in its group. Researchers who played recordings of these whistles found that a dolphin responded most strongly to a copy of its own. Some scientists describe the whistles as names, much as a person turns when called.
items.passage_b: Marine biologist Anwar Haddad finds the comparison with names tempting but overstated. A signature whistle is produced mostly by the dolphin itself, to announce who and where it is, whereas people rarely go around saying their own names. Other dolphins do sometimes copy a companion's whistle, but evidence that they use the copy to address that individual is still thin. The whistles identify, Haddad says, but it is not clear that they call.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the comparison of whistles to names in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that dolphins cannot tell one whistle from another
choices.B: By suggesting that dolphins use whistles only to warn one another of danger
choices.C: By claiming that every dolphin in a group shares the same whistle
choices.D: By accepting that the whistles identify individuals but doubting that they work like names

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that scientists describe signature whistles as names. Haddad calls the comparison "tempting but overstated": a whistle is mostly self-produced, and evidence that dolphins use copies to address others is "still thin." He concludes that the whistles "identify" but may not "call," which accepts part of Text 1 and doubts the rest.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that dolphins copy particular whistles, which requires telling them apart.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says whistles announce identity and location; it never mentions danger.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Both texts treat each whistle as belonging to one dolphin.
explanation.D: Correct. Haddad agrees that whistles announce identity but doubts that they are used to address individuals the way names are.

items.subject: science
items.passage: During the 1990s, populations of several vulture species in India and Pakistan fell by more than 95 percent. Vultures had been a familiar sight at cattle carcasses for centuries, and their sudden disappearance alarmed farmers and conservationists. Many observers assumed that the cause was the usual one: loss of habitat, combined with poisoning from agricultural pesticides.
items.passage_b: Researchers who examined dead vultures found no sign of pesticide poisoning. Instead, nearly all of the birds had died of kidney failure, and the cause was traced to diclofenac, a painkiller that veterinarians had begun giving to cattle. When a treated animal died and vultures ate its remains, the drug killed them within days. The drug's use in cattle was banned in several South Asian countries, and vulture numbers have since begun to stabilize.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that pesticides were the main reason for the decline
choices.B: By identifying a drug given to cattle, rather than habitat loss or pesticides, as the cause
choices.C: By arguing that the decline in vultures was smaller than first reported
choices.D: By suggesting that cattle, not vultures, were harmed by the drug

explanation.why: Text 1 says observers assumed the decline came from habitat loss and pesticides. Text 2 reports that dead vultures showed "no sign of pesticide poisoning" and that the deaths were traced to diclofenac, a painkiller given to cattle whose remains the vultures ate. So the author of Text 2 would respond by naming a different cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the birds showed no sign of pesticide poisoning.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 identifies diclofenac in cattle carcasses as the cause of the vultures' deaths.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 does not question the size of the decline; it explains the cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the drug was given to cattle as a painkiller and killed the vultures that ate treated animals.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1600s and 1700s, the Dutch East India Company controlled the coasts of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, largely for one reason: cinnamon. Company officials claimed a monopoly on the spice, which was peeled from wild trees in the island's forests. Unauthorized peeling was punished severely, and by limiting the supply sent to Europe the Company kept prices high.
items.passage_b: Historian Dilani Weerasinghe argues that the Company's control of cinnamon was never as complete as its records suggest. Much of the forest where the best trees grew lay inside the inland kingdom of Kandy, beyond Dutch reach, and smuggling along the coast was constant. The clearest sign of the Company's difficulty came in the 1760s, when it began planting its own cinnamon gardens near Colombo because the wild supply could not be relied on.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the account of the cinnamon monopoly in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the Company fully controlled the island's cinnamon trade
choices.B: By denying that the Company punished unauthorized peeling
choices.C: By suggesting that cinnamon lost its value in Europe during the 1700s
choices.D: By arguing that the Company's control of cinnamon was weaker than Text 1 suggests

explanation.why: Text 1 describes a Company monopoly that controlled supply and prices. Weerasinghe argues that control "was never as complete as its records suggest," citing forests beyond Dutch reach, constant smuggling, and the Company's turn to planting its own gardens because the wild supply "could not be relied on." So she would respond that the monopoly was weaker than Text 1 implies.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 argues the opposite, that control was incomplete.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never disputes that punishments existed; it questions how effective Dutch control was.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about cinnamon prices in Europe.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 gives several reasons to think the Company's grip on cinnamon was limited.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many textbooks include a diagram called the tongue map. It shows the tongue divided into zones, each responsible for one taste: sweet at the tip, bitter at the back, and sour and salty along the sides. Generations of students have tested the map by touching sugar or salt to different parts of their tongues.
items.passage_b: The tongue map is based on a misreading of a study published in Germany in 1901. That study found only slight differences in sensitivity between regions of the tongue, but a later summary turned the small differences into an all-or-nothing diagram. In fact, every region of the tongue that has taste buds can detect all of the basic tastes. The map persists because it is simple and easy to draw, not because it is accurate.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the diagram described in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that each taste is detected in only one region of the tongue
choices.B: By claiming that there are more basic tastes than the diagram shows
choices.C: By explaining that the diagram rests on a misreading of an early study
choices.D: By arguing that bitter tastes cannot be detected anywhere on the tongue

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the tongue map as a diagram found in textbooks. Text 2 says the map "is based on a misreading of a study published in Germany in 1901," in which small differences were turned into "an all-or-nothing diagram," and that every region can detect all the basic tastes. So the author of Text 2 would respond by explaining the map's mistaken origin.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says every region with taste buds detects all the basic tastes, so its author would not agree.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not discuss how many basic tastes there are.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 traces the map to a misreading of a 1901 study whose small differences were exaggerated.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says all basic tastes can be detected across the tongue.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1752, Benjamin Franklin flew a kite during a thunderstorm and drew sparks from a key tied to the string, showing that lightning is a form of electricity. The experiment is one of the most famous in the history of science and is retold in nearly every account of Franklin's life.
items.passage_b: Historian Olumide Bankole points out how thin the evidence for the kite experiment is. Franklin's own account, printed in a newspaper, is brief, gives no date, and never plainly states that he carried out the experiment himself; the detailed version most people know was published fifteen years later by another writer. Bankole does not call the story false, but he notes that a kite struck directly by lightning would likely have killed its flier. If Franklin flew a kite, he drew a small charge from the storm cloud, not a lightning bolt.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the account of the experiment in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that Franklin ever studied electricity
choices.B: By agreeing that Franklin's kite was struck directly by lightning
choices.C: By questioning how well the famous story is documented
choices.D: By arguing that another writer, not Franklin, performed the experiment

explanation.why: Text 1 presents the kite experiment as established fact. Bankole points out "how thin the evidence" is: Franklin's account is brief and undated, and the detailed version came fifteen years later from someone else. He does not say the story is false, so the author of Text 2 would respond by questioning the documentation rather than rejecting the story outright.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 questions only the kite story, not Franklin's work on electricity in general.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says a direct strike would likely have killed Franklin and that he would have drawn only a small charge.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 focuses on the weakness of the evidence for the experiment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The other writer published the detailed account; Text 2 never says he performed the experiment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, developed in Germany around 1450, made books far cheaper and more plentiful than handwritten copies had ever been. The flood of printed books that followed is often credited with creating readers: as books became common, more people had reason to learn to read, and literacy spread across Europe.
items.passage_b: Historian Agnieszka Dobrowolska argues that the usual story gets cause and effect partly backward. In the decades before Gutenberg, demand for books was already rising: universities were growing, merchants kept written accounts, and workshops of scribes were producing books in surprising quantity. Printing succeeded because readers already existed to buy its products. The press certainly multiplied readers later, but it did not create the first of them.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim that printing created readers in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that existing readers made printing possible, even if printing later increased their number
choices.B: By denying that printing had any effect on the number of readers
choices.C: By claiming that handwritten books were cheaper than printed ones
choices.D: By agreeing that printing created the first readers in Europe

explanation.why: Text 1 credits printed books with "creating readers." Dobrowolska says this "gets cause and effect partly backward": demand for books was already rising, and printing "succeeded because readers already existed." She adds that the press "certainly multiplied readers later." So she accepts part of Text 1 while reversing the order of cause and effect.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 argues that readers came first and made printing succeed, while granting that printing later increased their number.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the press "certainly multiplied readers later."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares the prices of handwritten and printed books.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says printing "did not create the first" readers.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Rabindranath Tagore's short story "Kabuliwala" (1892) is usually read as a tale of friendship across the widest possible gap. Rahmun, a dried-fruit seller from Kabul, befriends Mini, the five-year-old daughter of a Calcutta writer, and the two trade the same jokes every day. For critic Ayesha Rahim, the story's charm lies in this bond between a large, rough stranger and a chattering child, which neither age, nor language, nor the suspicion of Mini's mother can break.
items.passage_b: The friendship between Mini and the peddler is the story's surface, not its center. Its decisive moment belongs to the narrator, Mini's father, who has treated Rahmun with amused tolerance at best. When Rahmun returns after years in prison and unfolds a worn paper bearing the inked print of his own small daughter's hand, the narrator understands for the first time that the man before him is a father like himself. The money he then gives Rahmun for the journey home is taken from Mini's wedding expenses, and the story's real bond is the one between the two fathers.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the story in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the story's deepest bond is between the narrator and the peddler as fathers
choices.B: By denying that Mini and the peddler are genuinely fond of each other
choices.C: By agreeing that the friendship between Mini and the peddler is the story's main subject
choices.D: By claiming that the narrator distrusts the peddler until the story's final scene

explanation.why: Rahim reads the story as centered on the friendship between Mini and Rahmun. Text 2 calls that friendship "the story's surface, not its center" and locates the decisive moment in the narrator's recognition that Rahmun "is a father like himself," concluding that "the story's real bond is the one between the two fathers." So the author of Text 2 would redirect attention from the child's friendship to the fathers.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 argues that the narrator's recognition of Rahmun as a fellow father is the story's center.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts the friendship as real; it calls it the story's "surface," not a pretense.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 explicitly says the friendship is "not its center."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the narrator treated Rahmun with "amused tolerance," not distrust, before the final scene.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Were dinosaurs warm-blooded, like birds and mammals, or cold-blooded, like lizards? Paleontologist Rosa Benavides argues for warm-blooded. Thin slices of dinosaur bone show tissue packed with channels for blood vessels, a pattern found in fast-growing mammals, and growth rings indicate that some species went from hatchling to a multi-ton adult in two or three decades. No living reptile grows at anything like that rate, and such growth, Benavides concludes, requires the high, steady metabolism of a warm-blooded animal.
items.passage_b: The growth evidence is sound, but it need not force a choice between two categories. When growth rates are plotted against metabolic rates for hundreds of living species, dinosaurs fall neither with lizards nor with mammals but between them, alongside animals such as tuna and leatherback turtles, which generate their own heat without holding a fixed body temperature. For such animals, biologists have coined the term mesotherm. Asking whether dinosaurs were warm- or cold-blooded may simply be asking the wrong question.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion reached by Benavides in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that bone structure can reveal anything about an animal's metabolism
choices.B: By suggesting that tuna and leatherback turtles are more closely related to dinosaurs than birds are
choices.C: By arguing that dinosaur growth rates were no faster than those of modern reptiles
choices.D: By accepting the growth evidence but arguing that it points to an intermediate kind of metabolism

explanation.why: Benavides concludes from growth rates that dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Text 2 agrees that "the growth evidence is sound" but says it "need not force a choice between two categories": plotted against living species, dinosaurs fall "between" lizards and mammals, like tuna and leatherback turtles. So the author of Text 2 accepts the evidence and rejects the either-or conclusion.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 calls the bone-based growth evidence "sound."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 compares dinosaurs' metabolism with that of tuna and leatherback turtles; it says nothing about how closely related they are.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts the growth evidence and places dinosaurs above living reptiles, not level with them.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 grants the evidence but argues that it places dinosaurs in a middle category, the mesotherms.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In a well-known experiment from the 1970s, young children were offered one treat immediately or two if they could wait alone for several minutes. Years later, the children who had waited longer tended to score higher on academic tests and to report fewer difficulties as adolescents. Psychologist Marcus Lindqvist takes the finding as evidence that self-control in early childhood is a key to later success, and he argues that teaching children to delay gratification could improve their prospects.
items.passage_b: A later study that repeated the task with a far larger and more varied group of children found the link to later achievement much weaker. Once the researchers accounted for family income and the home environment, how long a child waited predicted little on its own. Children from secure homes have every reason to trust a promised second treat; children who have learned that promises fall through may sensibly take what is on the table. Waiting, in other words, may reflect a child's circumstances as much as a trait.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the recommendation made by Lindqvist in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the idea that early childhood has any bearing on later outcomes
choices.B: By claiming that children who waited longer in the original study later fared worse
choices.C: By suggesting that waiting may reflect children's circumstances more than a trait that can be taught
choices.D: By arguing that the original sample was large and varied enough to settle the question

explanation.why: Lindqvist recommends teaching children to delay gratification because waiting predicts success. Text 2 reports that in a larger study the link weakened once family income and home environment were considered, and that waiting "may reflect a child's circumstances as much as a trait." The author of Text 2 would therefore doubt that teaching waiting addresses what really drives the results.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 stresses the role of children's home circumstances, which is itself an early-childhood influence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the link became "much weaker," not that it reversed.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 argues that circumstances such as income and trust in promises explain much of the waiting, which undercuts a recommendation based on teaching a trait.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 contrasts the original study with a "far larger and more varied" one, implying the original was smaller.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Anton Chekhov insisted that The Cherry Orchard (1904) was a comedy, "in places even a farce," and he was dismayed when Konstantin Stanislavski's company in Moscow staged it as a solemn tragedy about a family losing its estate. Critic Jonas Hallgrímsson sides with the playwright. The family ignores every warning that the orchard will be sold, the servants are clowns, and the characters' self-absorption is laughable rather than pitiable. Played straight, the play loses the irony that gives it life.
items.passage_b: An author's label for a play need not bind its audiences, and in this case comedy and grief are not rivals. The final act gives us the sound of axes already at work in the orchard and the old servant Firs, forgotten, lying down in the locked and empty house. Audiences laugh at these people and then find that the loss is real anyway. The play's power lies in its refusal to settle the matter, and a production that chooses either comedy or tragedy alone throws half of it away.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim that Chekhov was right in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the family's self-absorption makes the play purely comic
choices.B: By denying that Chekhov ever described the play as a comedy
choices.C: By insisting that Stanislavski's tragic staging was the only correct interpretation
choices.D: By arguing that the play's comic and tragic elements coexist rather than one canceling the other

explanation.why: Hallgrímsson sides with Chekhov in calling the play a comedy. Text 2 says "comedy and grief are not rivals," points to the axes and the forgotten Firs, and argues that the play "refuses to settle the matter," so that a production choosing "either comedy or tragedy alone throws half of it away." The author of Text 2 would say Chekhov's label captures only part of the play.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the loss "is real anyway" and that the play is not purely one thing.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that the author gave the play a label; it argues only that the label need not bind audiences.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says a production choosing tragedy alone, like one choosing comedy alone, loses half the play.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 argues that laughter and genuine loss coexist in the play.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Mughal emperor Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri, near Agra, as his capital in the early 1570s and left it only about fourteen years later. The standard explanation is environmental. The city drew its water from an artificial lake, and once the lake began to shrink, the supply could not sustain a court and a city of that size. On this account, Fatehpur Sikri was abandoned because it ran dry.
items.passage_b: Historian Farrukh Siddiqui doubts that water decided the matter. The city's wells, channels, and waterworks continued to function for decades after the court departed, and the lake survived into the nineteenth century. What happened in 1585 was political: Akbar moved to Lahore to deal with unrest on the empire's northwestern frontier, and a court that traveled with its ruler simply never came back. The story of the failed lake, Siddiqui suggests, is a tidy explanation invented after the fact for a departure that had nothing to do with the city itself.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the standard explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the lake dried up before the court departed
choices.B: By arguing that the court's departure had political causes rather than a failing water supply
choices.C: By denying that Akbar intended Fatehpur Sikri as a capital
choices.D: By claiming that the city was never fully occupied

explanation.why: Text 1 attributes the abandonment to a shrinking water supply. Siddiqui says the waterworks "continued to function for decades" and that the departure "was political": Akbar moved to Lahore for frontier reasons and the mobile court never returned. He calls the lake story an explanation "invented after the fact." So he would respond by replacing the environmental cause with a political one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the lake "survived into the nineteenth century."
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 argues that the move to Lahore for political reasons, not water, ended Fatehpur Sikri's time as capital.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions what Akbar intended; it questions why the court left.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about how fully the city was occupied.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The peacock's enormous train, spread into a fan studded with eyespots, is the textbook example of a trait shaped by female choice. In one long-running field study, peahens mated most often with the males whose trains carried the most eyespots, and when researchers trimmed some eyespots from a male's train, his success with females fell. Biologist Henrike Vossberg concludes that peahens count, in effect, and that the eyespots are what they are judging.
items.passage_b: A seven-year study of a free-ranging peacock population found no relationship between the number of eyespots and a male's mating success. The reason may be simple: nearly every adult male had between 165 and 170 eyespots, far too little variation for females to base a choice on. Peahens evidently attend to something, perhaps the vigor of the display or the shimmer of the feathers when the train is shaken, but eyespot number may once have mattered and now sit at a ceiling that every healthy male reaches.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion reached by Vossberg in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that trimming eyespots reliably reduces a male's success with females
choices.B: By arguing that peahens prefer the males with the fewest eyespots
choices.C: By denying that peahens choose among males at all
choices.D: By questioning whether eyespot number still varies enough to guide peahens' choices

explanation.why: Vossberg concludes that peahens judge eyespot number. Text 2 reports a study that found "no relationship" between eyespots and mating success and suggests why: nearly all males had 165 to 170 eyespots, "far too little variation for females to base a choice on." The author of Text 2 accepts that females choose but doubts that eyespot counts can now be the basis.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only Text 1 reports the trimming result; Text 2 does not endorse it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 found no relationship either way, not a preference for fewer eyespots.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says peahens "evidently attend to something," so it accepts that they choose.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 argues that eyespot numbers barely vary among healthy males, so they cannot be what females currently judge.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the margins of manuscripts made in northern Europe between about 1290 and 1340, an odd scene appears again and again: an armored knight confronting a snail. Sometimes the knight charges, sometimes he kneels in apparent surrender. Art historian Beatriz Olalde reads the motif as satire. A warrior cowering before the slowest creature imaginable mocks the pretensions of chivalry, and the joke would have landed with readers who knew knights mainly as a class that collected rents.
items.passage_b: The search for the one meaning of the snail knight may be misguided. The image appears in prayer books, legal texts, and romances, in England, France, and Flanders, drawn by dozens of artists over half a century. A motif that travels so far and lasts so long is best understood as a convention passed from workshop to workshop, a shape that illuminators enjoyed drawing, whose significance, if it ever had a single one, shifted with each hand that copied it. Asking what the snail means may be like asking what a doodle means.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading proposed by Olalde in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the images were meant to ridicule cowardly knights
choices.B: By arguing that the snail stands for a specific group that medieval writers mocked
choices.C: By suggesting that the motif's spread and variety make a single intended meaning unlikely
choices.D: By claiming that the images were drawn by a single artist over many years

explanation.why: Olalde reads the snail knight as a satire of chivalry. Text 2 says the search for "the one meaning" may be misguided, because the motif appears in many kinds of books, in several regions, by "dozens of artists over half a century," and so is better seen as a convention whose meaning "shifted with each hand." The author of Text 2 would respond that the motif's spread argues against any single intended meaning.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not endorse the satire reading; it questions whether any one reading fits.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not propose any specific target; it doubts that there is one.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 cites the motif's range of books, places, artists, and years as reasons to doubt a single meaning.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the images were drawn by "dozens of artists."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Between roughly 1300 and 1850, average temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere fell in a period known as the Little Ice Age. Its coldest decades, in the seventeenth century, brought shortened growing seasons, repeated harvest failures, and hunger across much of Europe. Historian Tomasz Wieczorek argues that the wave of revolts and wars that historians call the crisis of the seventeenth century cannot be understood apart from this climate.
items.passage_b: The Dutch Republic reached the height of its wealth and power in exactly the decades Wieczorek describes. Historian Ingeborg Nystrand argues that the cold, far from harming the Dutch, worked in their favor: shifts in prevailing winds sped their ships to Asia, herring moved south into waters their fleets controlled, and their grain stores and canal networks let them profit from scarcity elsewhere. Climate shaped the century, Nystrand concludes, but what it did to any society depended on how that society was organized.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: The Dutch suffered more than other peoples during the Little Ice Age.
choices.B: Changes in prevailing winds were the main cause of harvest failures.
choices.C: Cold weather harmed every European society during the seventeenth century.
choices.D: The cooler climate of the seventeenth century affected European societies.

explanation.why: Wieczorek says the century's upheavals "cannot be understood apart from this climate." Nystrand says the cold "worked in their favor" for the Dutch and that "climate shaped the century." Both authors accept that the cooler climate had real effects on European societies; they differ over whether those effects were uniformly harmful.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nystrand says the Dutch reached the height of their wealth and that the cold worked in their favor.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 1 links harvest failures to shortened growing seasons; Text 2 mentions winds only as a benefit to Dutch shipping.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nystrand argues that the cold benefited the Dutch, so she would reject "every."
explanation.D: Correct. Both authors treat the climate as a force that shaped seventeenth-century societies.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When caterpillars chew on a plant's leaves, the plant releases a cloud of volatile chemicals into the air. Neighboring plants exposed to those chemicals begin producing their own defensive compounds before any caterpillar reaches them. Ecologist Priyanka Deshmukh describes this as a warning system: a plant under attack alerts its neighbors, and she argues that the ability to send such warnings evolved because it protects the surrounding community.
items.passage_b: The word "warning" smuggles in an assumption. A plant's neighbors are also its competitors for light and water, so a plant that spent resources alerting them would be helping its rivals. A more likely account is that the volatiles are messages a plant sends to its own distant leaves, which the air carries faster than the plant's internal channels can; neighbors simply eavesdrop. The neighbors' response is real enough, but the intention implied by "warning" has not been shown.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the description of a warning system in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting that neighbors respond to the chemicals but doubting that alerting them is the chemicals' function
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that plants respond to airborne chemicals at all
choices.C: By agreeing that plants release the chemicals in order to protect their neighbors
choices.D: By arguing that the chemicals attract predators of the attacking caterpillars

explanation.why: Deshmukh calls the volatiles a warning system that evolved to protect neighbors. Text 2 says the word "warning" assumes an intention that "has not been shown," proposes that the chemicals are messages to the plant's own leaves, and notes that neighbors "simply eavesdrop," while granting that "the neighbors' response is real enough." So the author of Text 2 accepts the effect but not the purpose Deshmukh assigns to it.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 grants that neighbors respond but argues that the chemicals most likely serve the emitting plant itself.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the neighbors' response "is real enough."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 argues that helping neighbors would mean helping competitors, so it rejects this purpose.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about predators of caterpillars.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Shakespeare's sonnets reached print in 1609 in an edition issued by the publisher Thomas Thorpe, who also wrote its cryptic dedication. Nothing suggests the poet took part. A decade earlier, a contemporary had described the sonnets circulating in manuscript "among his private friends," and scholar Lucia Ferrante argues that Thorpe's edition most likely reflects the order in which he gathered such copies. Readers who trace a story across the sequence, she warns, are reading a design that may be the publisher's accident rather than the poet's intention.
items.passage_b: Whatever Thorpe's role, the 1609 arrangement displays more shape than accident can account for. The opening seventeen sonnets, all urging a young man to marry, form an unmistakable block; the one hundred twenty-sixth, with twelve lines instead of fourteen, reads as a deliberate farewell before the sequence turns to a very different addressee; linked pairs and echoed images run through the whole. An unauthorized edition is not the same thing as a random one. Some ordering hand, and plausibly the poet's, was at work before the copies reached the printer.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the warning issued by Ferrante in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that the sonnets circulated in manuscript before 1609
choices.B: By granting that the edition may be unauthorized while arguing that its order is nonetheless deliberate
choices.C: By agreeing that the sequence reflects only the order in which Thorpe obtained the poems
choices.D: By insisting that Shakespeare himself prepared the 1609 edition for publication

explanation.why: Ferrante warns that the 1609 order may be the publisher's accident. Text 2 begins "Whatever Thorpe's role" and states that "an unauthorized edition is not the same thing as a random one," citing the marriage block, the twelve-line sonnet 126, and linked pairs as evidence of design. So the author of Text 2 sets aside the question of authorization and disputes the claim of accident.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 refers to "the copies" reaching the printer and never disputes manuscript circulation.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 concedes the edition may be unauthorized but argues from its internal structure that the order was deliberate.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 argues the opposite, that the order shows deliberate shape.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says only that "some ordering hand, and plausibly the poet's," was at work; it does not claim the poet prepared the edition.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In Henry James's The Turn of the Screw (1898), a young governess becomes convinced that the two children in her care are being visited by the ghosts of two former servants, Peter Quint and Miss Jessel. Critic Adaeze Nwosu takes the ghosts as real. The governess describes a man she has seen in detail before anyone has told her about Quint, and the housekeeper, Mrs. Grose, identifies him from that description. James himself, in a later preface, called the tale a ghost story designed to catch readers who are not easily caught.
items.passage_b: The identification Nwosu relies on cuts both ways: the governess supplies a description, and Mrs. Grose supplies the name, so the reader never sees the two matched independently. Everything we know, moreover, comes from the governess's own manuscript, read aloud years afterward; no other character ever admits to seeing a ghost, and the children never confess to anything. James's preface does say the story was built to catch readers. It does not say which readers, and a story that catches those who believe in the ghosts has caught someone too. The tale is constructed so that the question cannot be closed.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Nwosu in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that the children openly admit to seeing the ghosts
choices.B: By arguing that the same evidence Nwosu cites can be read as the governess's own construction
choices.C: By asserting that James's preface proves the ghosts were meant to be imaginary
choices.D: By pointing out that Mrs. Grose herself later sees the ghosts

explanation.why: Nwosu argues that the ghosts are real, citing Mrs. Grose's identification and James's preface. Text 2 answers that the identification "cuts both ways," that everything comes from "the governess's own manuscript," and that the preface "does not say which readers" it means to catch. The author of Text 2 does not declare the ghosts imaginary but shows that Nwosu's evidence supports the opposite reading equally well.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says "the children never confess to anything."
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 reinterprets each piece of Nwosu's evidence to show that it is consistent with the governess constructing the ghosts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the preface "does not say which readers" it traps, and it concludes that the question "cannot be closed," not that the ghosts are imaginary.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says "no other character ever admits to seeing a ghost."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Across the twentieth century, average scores on intelligence tests rose in country after country by roughly three points per decade, a pattern so steady that test makers periodically had to make their tests harder. Psychologist Dmitri Volkov holds that the best explanation is biological: better nutrition, fewer childhood infections, and smaller families allowed brains to develop more fully than in earlier generations. He notes that the gains were largest in countries where diets improved most dramatically.
items.passage_b: Nutrition cannot carry the whole explanation. In wealthy countries, improvements in diet had largely leveled off by the middle of the century, yet scores kept climbing for decades afterward. More telling is the shape of the gains. They were smallest on tests of vocabulary and arithmetic, exactly the areas in which better-fed children should also have improved, and largest on tests of abstract pattern-finding, the kind of thinking that extended schooling and modern work demand. The century did not merely feed people better; it trained them to think in the way the tests reward.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation offered by Volkov in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that nutrition played no role in rising scores anywhere
choices.B: By denying that scores on intelligence tests rose during the twentieth century
choices.C: By arguing that the pattern of gains across kinds of tests fits schooling better than nutrition
choices.D: By suggesting that scores rose fastest on tests of vocabulary and arithmetic

explanation.why: Volkov explains rising scores through nutrition and health. Text 2 says nutrition "cannot carry the whole explanation," because gains continued after diets leveled off and, "more telling," were smallest in vocabulary and arithmetic and largest in abstract pattern-finding, "the kind of thinking that extended schooling and modern work demand." So the author of Text 2 would respond that the profile of the gains points to training rather than biology.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says nutrition cannot be "the whole explanation," which leaves it some role.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that scores "kept climbing for decades."
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 argues that the uneven pattern of gains, concentrated in abstract reasoning, is better explained by schooling and modern work than by diet.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says gains were "smallest" on vocabulary and arithmetic.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: From the 1580s, Jesuit missions to the court of the Mughal emperor Akbar brought engravings of European religious paintings, and the court's painters began copying them. The copies are so faithful, down to the folds of a Madonna's robe and the receding lines of a European street, that art historian Caterina Vidal speaks of a conversion: within a generation, she argues, Mughal painters had adopted European ways of seeing, above all perspective and the modeling of forms with light and shadow.
items.passage_b: The borrowing was real but selective. Mughal painters took what served them, receding landscapes in the distance and softly shaded faces, and left the rest. The raised viewpoint, the flattened architecture seen from several angles at once, and the crowded, patterned surfaces of the Persian tradition all survive, and European figures appear inside such compositions as motifs rather than as organizing principles. The painters acquired a vocabulary; they did not adopt a grammar. To call the result a conversion mistakes a set of quotations for a change of faith.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim that a conversion took place in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the idea that European prints had any effect on Mughal painting
choices.B: By suggesting that European painters, in turn, borrowed from Mughal art
choices.C: By arguing that painters adopted European devices piecemeal within a framework that remained their own
choices.D: By claiming that Persian traditions were abandoned in favor of European ones

explanation.why: Vidal argues that Mughal painters underwent a conversion to European ways of seeing. Text 2 calls the borrowing "real but selective": painters took landscapes and shaded faces but kept the Persian viewpoint, architecture, and surfaces, so that they "acquired a vocabulary" but "did not adopt a grammar." The author of Text 2 would answer that the European elements were absorbed into a structure that stayed Mughal.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 calls the borrowing "real"; it disputes only how deep it went.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about European painters borrowing from Mughal art.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 describes selective borrowing of devices within compositions that remained Persian in structure.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the Persian traditions "all survive."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Within a span of perhaps twenty-five million years beginning about 540 million years ago, nearly every major group of animals alive today makes its first appearance in the fossil record, an episode known as the Cambrian explosion. Paleontologist Keiko Arimura regards the fossils as testimony to a genuine burst of evolutionary invention, perhaps triggered by rising oxygen levels or by the arrival of the first predators, which forced prey into an arms race of shells, spines, and speed.
items.passage_b: Molecular clock analyses, which estimate when lineages diverged by comparing the DNA of living animals and calibrating the differences against dated fossils, place the origins of the major animal groups tens of millions of years before the Cambrian. Such estimates are imprecise, and different methods disagree about the dates, but they agree in putting the divergences well before the first recognizable fossils. The explosion in the rocks may record, at least in part, the moment when animals became large and hard enough to fossilize rather than the moment they came into being.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: The first predators appeared only after all the major animal groups had evolved.
choices.B: The fossil record cannot be trusted to show when any group of animals evolved.
choices.C: Many major animal groups first appear in the fossil record during the Cambrian.
choices.D: The major animal lineages originated during the Cambrian period.

explanation.why: Arimura describes the Cambrian as the time when nearly every major animal group "makes its first appearance in the fossil record." Text 2 does not dispute this; it speaks of "the first recognizable fossils" and "the explosion in the rocks," arguing only that lineages diverged earlier than they fossilized. Both authors accept the fossil pattern and disagree about what it records.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 1 proposes predators as a possible trigger of the explosion; neither text says they came after all groups had evolved.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the fossil record may be misleading "at least in part" about origins, and it still uses dated fossils to calibrate its clocks; neither author rejects the record wholesale.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 1 states it directly, and Text 2 accepts the appearance of fossils in the Cambrian while reinterpreting what it means.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 1 implies this, but Text 2 places the origins "tens of millions of years before the Cambrian."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: At exactly noon, the old clocks in Mr. Adeyemi's repair shop ______ all at once, filling the narrow room with chimes, bells, and the cry of a wooden cuckoo. His new apprentice, Tunde, still jumps at the sound every day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: rings
choices.B: ring
choices.C: is ringing
choices.D: has rung

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "clocks," which is plural; "in Mr. Adeyemi's repair shop" only tells where the clocks are. A plural subject needs a plural verb, and the rest of the passage is in the simple present ("jumps"), so "ring" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Rings" is singular and agrees with "shop," but the subject is the plural "clocks."
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "ring" agrees with the plural subject "clocks."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Is ringing" is singular, but the subject "clocks" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Has rung" is singular, but the subject "clocks" is plural.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Louvre in Paris first opened as a public museum in 1793, during the French Revolution. Today, ______ collection holds hundreds of thousands of objects, so only a small fraction of them can be displayed at any one time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it's
choices.B: their
choices.C: its
choices.D: its'

explanation.why: The blank must show that the collection belongs to the Louvre, a single museum. The possessive form of "it" is "its," with no apostrophe.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "It's" is a contraction of "it is" or "it has"; "it is collection" makes no sense.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Their" is plural, but it refers to the Louvre, which is singular.
explanation.C: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive pronoun, showing the collection belongs to the Louvre.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its'" is not a word in Standard English; the possessive "its" never takes an apostrophe.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, records a single royal decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic, and ancient Greek. Because the scholars who studied it could already read Greek, the stone gave ______ a way to work out the meaning of the other two scripts, though fully deciphering the hieroglyphs still took more than twenty years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them
choices.B: it
choices.C: they
choices.D: him

explanation.why: The ones who were given a way to work out the other scripts are "the scholars," a plural noun. The pronoun is also the object of "gave," so it must be the plural object pronoun "them."
explanation.A: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "scholars," and is the object form needed after "gave."
