His skill so impressed the court of Kublai Khan that he spent the rest of his life in China, where he designed the White Stupa that still stands in Beijing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: he
choices.B: him
choices.C: they
choices.D: it

explanation.why: The person who traveled to Tibet is Araniko, a single man, and the pronoun is the subject of "traveled." The next sentence confirms this with "His skill" and "he spent." So the singular subject pronoun "he" is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "He" is singular, refers to Araniko, and is the subject form needed before "traveled."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Him" is an object pronoun; the subject of "traveled" needs the subject form "he."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "They" is plural, but the antecedent is the one artist Araniko; the craftsmen are mentioned only afterward, as the people he traveled with.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It" is used for things, not for a person such as Araniko.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The toco toucan of South America has a bright orange beak that can be a third as long as the bird itself. Although it looks heavy, a ______ beak is mostly hollow and surprisingly light. Scientists have found that the bird also uses it to release heat, sending extra blood into the beak when its body gets too warm.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: toucan's
choices.B: toucans
choices.C: toucans'
choices.D: toucan

explanation.why: The beak belongs to a toucan, so a possessive is needed. The article "a" shows that one bird is meant, so the singular possessive "toucan's" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. "Toucan's" is the singular possessive that fits "a."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Toucans" is a plain plural with no apostrophe and does not show possession; it also does not fit after "a."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Toucans'" is a plural possessive, but "a" shows that a single bird is meant.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Toucan" has no apostrophe, so "a toucan beak" does not show that the beak belongs to the bird.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The first modern Olympic Games ______ in Athens, Greece, in April 1896. Athletes from about a dozen countries competed in events such as running, swimming, and wrestling, and the marathon was won by a Greek runner named Spyridon Louis, who became a national hero.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: take place
choices.B: took place
choices.C: are taking place
choices.D: will take place

explanation.why: The sentence gives a specific finished time in the past, "in April 1896," and the following sentence uses past-tense verbs ("competed," "was won," "became"). So the simple past "took place" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present tense "take place" does not fit an event dated to 1896.
explanation.B: Correct. The simple past "took place" matches "in April 1896" and the past-tense verbs around it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present progressive "are taking place" describes something happening now, not an event in 1896.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The future "will take place" does not fit an event that happened in 1896.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: George Frideric Handel composed much of his music at great speed. Written in only about three weeks in the summer of 1741, ______ The piece soon became one of the most frequently performed works in English choral music.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the first performance of Messiah took place in Dublin in April 1742.
choices.B: Dublin hosted the first performance of Messiah in April 1742.
choices.C: Handel first presented Messiah in Dublin in April 1742.
choices.D: his oratorio Messiah was first performed in Dublin in April 1742.

explanation.why: The opening phrase "Written in only about three weeks" describes the piece of music, so the music must be the subject right after the comma. Only choice D makes "his oratorio Messiah" the subject.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject here is "the first performance," but a performance is not written; the music is.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject here is "Dublin," but a city was not written in three weeks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject here is "Handel," so the sentence wrongly says that Handel was written in three weeks.
explanation.D: Correct. "His oratorio Messiah" is the thing that was written, and it directly follows the modifier.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every spring, Mateo and his cousins build kites out of bamboo strips and colored paper in their grandfather's courtyard. Every one of the kites that they make ______ a different name, usually chosen by the youngest cousin, and the names are painted along the tail in black ink.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are given
choices.B: get
choices.C: have
choices.D: gets

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "Every one," which is singular; "of the kites that they make" only describes which one. A singular subject needs the singular verb "gets."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are given" is plural, but the subject "Every one" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Get" is plural and would agree with "kites," but the subject is the singular "Every one."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have" is plural, but the subject "Every one" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "gets" agrees with the singular subject "Every one."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hoolock gibbons live in the forests of northeastern India, Bangladesh, and Myanmar. A pair of gibbons spends most of its life together high in the trees. Each morning, the two sing a loud duet that can be heard more than a kilometer away, and scientists think ______ use the song to tell other gibbons that the territory is taken.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them
choices.B: he
choices.C: they
choices.D: it

explanation.why: The ones who use the song are "the two" gibbons that sing the duet, a plural antecedent, and the pronoun is the subject of "use." So the plural subject pronoun "they" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Them" is an object pronoun; the subject of "use" needs the subject form "they."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "He" is singular and would refer to one animal, but both gibbons sing the duet.
explanation.C: Correct. "They" is plural, matching "the two," and is the subject form needed before "use."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but the antecedent "the two" is plural.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Flamenco, a style of music and dance from southern Spain, uses the feet of the dancers as a kind of drum. In a duet, both ______ shoes have rows of small nails hammered into the toes and heels, so that every tap and stamp rings out sharply on the wooden floor. Skilled performers can produce a rapid burst of taps in just a second or two.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: dancers'
choices.B: dancer's
choices.C: dancers's
choices.D: dancers

explanation.why: The shoes belong to the dancers, so a possessive is needed, and "both" shows there are two dancers, so the plural possessive "dancers'" (apostrophe after the s) is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. "Dancers'" is the plural possessive, matching "the dancers" in the first sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "dancer's" is a singular possessive, but "both" tells us there are two dancers, so the plural possessive is needed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Dancers's" is not a standard form; a plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Dancers" has no apostrophe, so it does not show that the shoes belong to the dancers.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each spring, horseshoe crabs crawl out of the sea onto the beaches of Delaware Bay, on the east coast of the United States, to lay their eggs. Since 1990, teams of volunteers ______ the crabs on these beaches on certain nights in May and June. Their records are now one of the longest-running counts of a marine animal anywhere.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: will count
choices.B: count
choices.C: have counted
choices.D: counted

explanation.why: The phrase "Since 1990" describes an action that began in the past and continues to the present, which is what the present perfect expresses. So "have counted" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The future "will count" does not fit an action that began in 1990.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The simple present "count" does not fit with "Since 1990," which requires a perfect tense.
explanation.C: Correct. The present perfect "have counted" fits "Since 1990," an action that started in the past and continues.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The simple past "counted" suggests a finished action, but "Since 1990" means the counting is still going on.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the village of Henawala, near Kandy in central Sri Lanka, families have made Dumbara mats for generations. Woven from plant fibers dyed in deep reds, blacks, and yellows, ______ Today the weavers also make bags and wall hangings using the same patterns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: rows of birds, elephants, and geometric shapes decorate the mats.
choices.B: weavers decorate the mats with rows of birds, elephants, and geometric shapes.
choices.C: the mats show rows of birds, elephants, and geometric shapes.
choices.D: the village is known for mats showing rows of birds, elephants, and geometric shapes.

explanation.why: The opening phrase "Woven from plant fibers" describes the mats, so "the mats" must be the subject that comes right after the comma. Only choice C does this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject here is "rows of birds, elephants, and geometric shapes," but these are patterns, not the woven mats themselves.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject here is "weavers," so the sentence wrongly says the weavers are woven from plant fibers.
explanation.C: Correct. "The mats" directly follows the phrase that describes them, so the modifier is not dangling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject here is "the village," but a village is not woven from plant fibers.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1978, archaeologists in Hubei Province, China, opened the tomb of a ruler known as Marquis Yi of Zeng, who died around 433 BCE. Among the treasures inside was a set of bronze bells. The set of bells, arranged in three rows on a wooden frame, ______ sixty-five bells, each able to produce two different notes depending on where it is struck.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: include
choices.B: are including
choices.C: have included
choices.D: includes

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "set," which is singular; "of bells" and "arranged in three rows on a wooden frame" only describe the set. A singular subject needs the singular verb "includes."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Include" is plural and would agree with "bells" or "rows," but the subject is the singular "set."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Are including" is plural, but the subject "set" is singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have included" is plural, but the subject "set" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "includes" agrees with the singular subject "set."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Yusuf and his sister Lena reached the bakery just as the shutters were going up. The baker, who had known the two of them since they were small, handed ______ two warm loaves wrapped in paper and waved away the coins Yusuf held out.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: they
choices.B: it
choices.C: them
choices.D: him

explanation.why: The baker handed the loaves to Yusuf and Lena, two people, so the pronoun must be plural. It is also the object of "handed," so the plural object pronoun "them" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "They" is a subject pronoun; after the verb "handed," the object form "them" is needed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "It" is singular and is used for things, not for the two children.
explanation.C: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "Yusuf and his sister Lena," and is the object form needed after "handed."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Him" is singular and refers only to Yusuf, but the baker gave the loaves to both children.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The baya weaver is a small yellow bird found across Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka. The male builds a nest shaped like a hanging flask by weaving hundreds of strips of grass and palm leaf. A ______ nest hangs from a thin branch, often over water, so that snakes and other predators have trouble reaching it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: weavers
choices.B: weaver
choices.C: weavers'
choices.D: weaver's

explanation.why: The nest belongs to a weaver bird, so a possessive form is needed. The article "A" shows that one bird is meant, so the singular possessive "weaver's" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Weavers" is a plain plural with no apostrophe and does not show possession; it also does not fit after "A."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Weaver" has no apostrophe, so "A weaver nest" does not show that the nest belongs to the bird.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Weavers'" is a plural possessive, but "A" shows that a single bird is meant.
explanation.D: Correct. "Weaver's" is the singular possessive that fits "A."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world and holds about a fifth of the planet's unfrozen fresh water. The Baikal seal, the only seal species that spends its entire life in fresh water, along with hundreds of other animals found nowhere else on Earth, ______ in the lake's cold, clear waters. How the seals' ancestors reached a lake so far from any ocean remains a puzzle.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have lived
choices.B: live
choices.C: are living
choices.D: lives

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "The Baikal seal," which is singular. The long phrase "along with hundreds of other animals found nowhere else on Earth" is not part of the subject; "along with" does not make a subject plural the way "and" would. So the singular verb "lives" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Have lived" is plural, but the subject "The Baikal seal" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Live" is plural and would agree with "animals," but "along with" sets that phrase aside; the subject is the singular "seal."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are living" is plural, but the subject "The Baikal seal" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "lives" agrees with the singular subject "The Baikal seal."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Between the 1790s and the 1930s, several generations of the Stevenson family of Edinburgh designed most of the lighthouses along the coast of Scotland. Because sailors needed to tell one light from another at night, each of the lighthouses the family built was given ______ own pattern of flashes, so that a captain could identify it from a chart.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: his
choices.B: their
choices.C: its
choices.D: it's

explanation.why: The pronoun refers to "each of the lighthouses," and "each" is singular; the verb "was given" confirms this. A lighthouse is a thing, so the singular possessive "its" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "His" refers to a male person, but the antecedent is a lighthouse.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Their" is plural and would agree with "lighthouses," but the subject is "each," which is singular.
explanation.C: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive that agrees with "each" and refers to a thing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It's" means "it is"; the possessive form "its" has no apostrophe.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In many Japanese elementary schools, students themselves clean the classrooms. They spend about fifteen minutes each day sweeping floors, wiping desks, and emptying bins, usually in small groups that rotate through the tasks. Teachers say that the ______ daily cleaning builds a sense of responsibility for shared spaces that lasts long after they leave school.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: children's
choices.B: childrens'
choices.C: children
choices.D: childrens

explanation.why: The daily cleaning is done by the children, so a possessive form is needed. "Children" is already plural and does not end in s, so its possessive is formed by adding an apostrophe and s: "children's."
explanation.A: Correct. "Children's" is the correct possessive of the irregular plural "children."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Childrens'" wrongly treats "children" as if it ended in s; the plural does not take an added s.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Children" has no apostrophe, so "the children daily cleaning" does not show whose cleaning it is.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Childrens" is not a word; "children" is already plural, and no apostrophe shows possession.

items.subject: science
items.passage: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft was launched from Florida in January 2006 on a mission to Pluto. By the time it flew past the dwarf planet in July 2015, the spacecraft ______ for more than nine years and covered nearly five billion kilometers, and it had spent much of that long cruise in a low-power sleep mode to protect its instruments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: will have traveled
choices.B: travels
choices.C: has traveled
choices.D: had traveled

explanation.why: The sentence describes an action completed before another past event: the traveling was finished "by the time it flew past" Pluto in 2015. An action completed before a past moment takes the past perfect, "had traveled," which also matches "had spent" later in the sentence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The future perfect "will have traveled" refers to a future point, but the flyby happened in 2015.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present tense "travels" does not fit an action completed before a past event in 2015.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present perfect "has traveled" links an action to the present, but the sentence measures the travel up to a past moment, July 2015.
explanation.D: Correct. The past perfect "had traveled" shows that the traveling was complete by the past moment "it flew past the dwarf planet."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Having waited all year for the first real snow, ______ Their mother called after them that breakfast was on the table, but by then the two of them were already halfway up the hill behind the house, the sled bumping along behind.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Teo and his sister's sled was out of the shed before breakfast.
choices.B: Teo and his sister had the sled out of the shed before breakfast.
choices.C: the sled was dragged out of the shed by Teo and his sister before breakfast.
choices.D: breakfast could not keep Teo and his sister from the shed where the sled was stored.

explanation.why: The opening phrase "Having waited all year for the first real snow" describes the people who waited, so they must be the subject right after the comma. Only choice B makes "Teo and his sister" the subject.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject here is "sled" (Teo and his sister's sled), not the children who waited.
explanation.B: Correct. "Teo and his sister" directly follow the phrase that describes them, so the modifier is not dangling.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject here is "the sled," so the sentence wrongly says the sled waited all year for snow.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject here is "breakfast," which cannot have waited for snow.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Qawwali is a form of devotional music performed in Pakistan and northern India, usually by a group of eight or nine musicians seated on the floor. The lead singer, together with a chorus of performers who clap in rhythm and repeat his lines, ______ a single verse for many minutes, raising the intensity little by little until the whole audience is swaying.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are stretching
choices.B: have stretched
choices.C: stretches
choices.D: stretch

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "The lead singer," which is singular. The phrase "together with a chorus of performers who clap in rhythm and repeat his lines" is set off by commas and does not make the subject plural; only "and" would do that. So the singular verb "stretches" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are stretching" is plural, but the subject "The lead singer" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have stretched" is plural, but the subject "The lead singer" is singular.
explanation.C: Correct. The singular verb "stretches" agrees with the singular subject "The lead singer."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Stretch" is plural and would agree with "performers," but "together with" sets that phrase aside; the subject is the singular "lead singer."

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1925, at the Harvard College Observatory, Cecilia Payne completed a doctoral thesis ______ conclusion, that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, contradicted the common view that they resembled Earth in composition. Senior astronomers at first persuaded her to describe the result as probably mistaken, but within a few years other researchers confirmed it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: whose
choices.B: who
choices.C: which
choices.D: who's

explanation.why: The blank must show that the conclusion belongs to the thesis: the thesis's conclusion contradicted the common view. The relative pronoun that shows possession is "whose," which in English can refer to things as well as people.
explanation.A: Correct. "Whose conclusion" shows that the conclusion belongs to the thesis.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Who" is used for people and does not show possession; "who conclusion" is not grammatical.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Which conclusion" does not show possession; "which" would have to stand for the thesis itself, so "conclusion" is left hanging and the clause makes no sense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Who's" means "who is"; it is not a possessive.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: On December 28, 1895, the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten short films to a paying audience in the basement of a café in Paris, using a machine of their own design that could both record and project moving pictures. The ______ screening lasted only about twenty minutes, yet within months their machine was being shown in cities around the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: brothers
choices.B: brother's
choices.C: brothers's
choices.D: brothers'

explanation.why: The screening was put on by the two brothers, so a plural possessive is needed. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe: "brothers'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Brothers" has no apostrophe, so it does not show that the screening was theirs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Brother's" is a singular possessive, but the text speaks of two brothers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Brothers's" is not a standard form; a plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Correct. "Brothers'" is the plural possessive, matching "the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mira had thrown the letter away the same evening it arrived, telling herself that her old teacher's advice no longer mattered. Now, sitting on the train with the acceptance papers in her lap, she wished that she ______ it, if only to read the last line once more.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has kept
choices.B: will keep
choices.C: had kept
choices.D: keeps

explanation.why: Mira is wishing about something in the past that cannot be changed: she threw the letter away earlier. A wish about a past action uses the past perfect, "had kept," which also matches "had thrown" at the start of the passage.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present perfect "has kept" is not used after "wished" for a past regret; the past perfect is needed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The future "will keep" does not fit a regret about a letter already thrown away.
explanation.C: Correct. "Had kept" is the past perfect, the form used for a wish about something that already happened.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The present tense "keeps" does not fit a wish about an action that is already in the past.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The element iridium was identified in 1803 by the English chemist Smithson Tennant, who found it in the residue left after platinum ore was dissolved in acid. Named for Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because of the many colors of its compounds, ______ It is also one of the densest elements known and resists corrosion better than almost any other metal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: iridium's compounds were a striking sight to early chemists.
choices.B: chemists prize iridium for its hardness and brittleness.
choices.C: the hardness and brittleness of iridium make it difficult to work.
choices.D: iridium is a hard, brittle, silvery-white metal.

explanation.why: The opening phrase "Named for Iris" describes the element, so "iridium" must be the subject right after the comma. Only choice D makes iridium the subject of the main clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject here is "compounds," but it was the element, not its compounds, that was named for Iris.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject here is "chemists," so the sentence wrongly says the chemists were named for Iris.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject here is "the hardness and brittleness," which were not named for Iris.
explanation.D: Correct. "Iridium" directly follows the phrase that describes it, so the modifier is not dangling.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mice rely on their whiskers to find their way in the dark, sweeping them back and forth to sense walls and objects. To test how much the animals depend on this sense, a research team trimmed the ______ whiskers on one side of the face and then watched them explore a dim maze. The mice bumped into obstacles on the trimmed side far more often than before.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: mouse's
choices.B: mice's
choices.C: mices'
choices.D: mice

explanation.why: The whiskers belong to the mice, so a possessive form is needed. "Mice" is already plural and does not end in s, so its possessive is formed by adding an apostrophe and s: "mice's."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Mouse's" is singular, but the team worked with several mice ("the animals," "them").
explanation.B: Correct. "Mice's" is the correct possessive of the irregular plural "mice."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Mices'" wrongly treats "mice" as if it ended in s; the plural does not take an added s.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Mice" has no apostrophe, so "the mice whiskers" does not show whose whiskers they are.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Construction of the Appian Way, the first great Roman road, began in 312 BCE under the official Appius Claudius Caecus. The road, which eventually ______ more than 500 kilometers from Rome to the port of Brindisi on the Adriatic coast, was paved with tightly fitted blocks of stone and remained in use for centuries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: having stretched
choices.B: stretched
choices.C: to stretch
choices.D: stretching

explanation.why: The clause beginning with "which" needs a complete verb of its own. The passage is in the past tense ("began," "was paved," "remained"), so the finite past-tense verb "stretched" is needed; the -ing, to-, and having- forms cannot serve as the main verb of a clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Having stretched" is a participle phrase, not a finite verb, so the clause is incomplete.
explanation.B: Correct. "Stretched" is a finite past-tense verb, completing the "which" clause and matching the other past-tense verbs.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To stretch" is an infinitive and cannot act as the main verb of the "which" clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Stretching" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the "which" clause would have no main verb.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sundews are small carnivorous plants that grow in bogs where the soil holds little nitrogen. Each leaf is covered with hair-like tentacles, and the sticky droplet at the tip of these tentacles ______ like a bead of nectar to a passing insect. Once the insect lands and gets stuck, the tentacles slowly bend inward, pressing it against the leaf surface, where digestive enzymes break it down over several days.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have looked
choices.B: looks
choices.C: are looking
choices.D: look

explanation.why: Find the subject of the blank: "the sticky droplet at the tip of these tentacles." The head noun is the singular "droplet"; "tentacles" is only part of a phrase describing where the droplet sits. A singular subject needs the singular verb "looks."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Have looked" is plural; the subject "droplet" is singular.
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "looks" agrees with the singular subject "droplet."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are looking" is plural; the subject "droplet" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Look" is plural and seems to agree with the nearby "tentacles," but the subject is the singular "droplet."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Chaukhandi tombs, a cluster of graves on the outskirts of Karachi, Pakistan, were built mostly between the fifteenth and eighteenth centuries. The tombs are made of sandstone slabs stacked in stepped layers and carved with dense geometric and floral patterns. Historians note that many stones also show horses, swords, or jewelry; because ______ appear on the graves of men and women in different combinations, these details may have signaled the rank or trade of the person buried below.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it
choices.B: one
choices.C: they
choices.D: this

explanation.why: The things that "appear on the graves ... in different combinations" are the "horses, swords, or jewelry" just mentioned, a plural set. The verb "appear" is also plural, so the blank needs the plural subject pronoun "they."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but the antecedent ("horses, swords, or jewelry") and the verb "appear" are plural.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "One" is singular and would need "appears"; it also leaves unclear which single item is meant.
explanation.C: Correct. The plural pronoun "they" refers to the horses, swords, and jewelry and agrees with "appear."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "This" is singular and does not fit the plural verb "appear" or the plural antecedent.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Katsushika Hokusai was already in his seventies when he began Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, a series of woodblock prints published in Japan in the early 1830s. The series shows the mountain from different places and seasons: behind a huge curling wave, above rice fields, through the frame of a wooden barrel. Because the prints sold so well, the publisher ______ ten more designs, so that the finished series actually contains forty-six views.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: added
choices.B: is adding
choices.C: adds
choices.D: will add

explanation.why: The sentence reports something that happened in the early 1830s: the prints "sold" well, so the publisher "added" more designs. The verb describing that finished past event must be in the simple past, matching "sold."
explanation.A: Correct. The simple past "added" matches "sold" and the 1830s setting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Is adding" describes something happening now, but the addition is a finished past event.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present "adds" does not fit an action completed in the 1830s and clashes with the past "sold."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The future "will add" cannot describe an event that is already complete ("the finished series actually contains").

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The waiting room outside the audition hall was so quiet that Ayesha could hear the clock on the far wall. She had practiced the piece every evening for three months, and still her fingers felt cold and stiff. Gripping the neck of the violin a little too tightly, ______ The accompanist smiled at her, and the first note came out clearer than she had expected.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: she walked through the door when the examiner called her name.
choices.B: the door opened and her name was called by the examiner.
choices.C: the examiner called her name, and she walked through the door.
choices.D: her name was called by the examiner, and the door opened.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Gripping the neck of the violin a little too tightly" describes Ayesha. An introductory modifier attaches to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be "she."
explanation.A: Correct. "She" (Ayesha) comes right after the introductory phrase, so she is the one gripping the violin.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject after the comma is "the door," so the sentence says the door was gripping the violin; the modifier dangles.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "the examiner," so the sentence wrongly says the examiner was gripping Ayesha's violin.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "her name," which cannot grip a violin.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Visitors to Pompeii, the Roman town buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, can still see dozens of shops called thermopolia, where hot food and drinks were sold to people who had no kitchen of their own. The row of large clay jars set into the counter of each shop ______ to hold the dishes on offer, a bit like the trays in a modern cafeteria. Many residents of the crowded town seem to have eaten most of their meals this way.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: was used
choices.B: were used
choices.C: are used
choices.D: have been used

explanation.why: The subject of the blank is "The row," a singular noun; "jars," "counter," and "shop" belong to phrases describing the row. The text also describes the shops in the past ("were sold"), so the singular past "was used" is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. The singular past "was used" agrees with "row" and matches "were sold."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Were used" is plural and seems to agree with "jars," but the subject is the singular "row."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are used" is plural and in the present tense, but the subject is singular and the practice belongs to the past.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have been used" is plural, and the present perfect does not fit a practice that ended in 79 CE.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The okapi, a shy animal of the rainforests of central Africa, has striped legs like a zebra, but its closest living relative is actually the giraffe. The two animals share a long, dark tongue that can strip leaves from branches, and both have skin-covered horns. Biologists who have studied okapis in the wild suggest that the stripes may help calves keep sight of ______ mothers in the dim light under the forest canopy.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: they're
choices.C: their
choices.D: there

explanation.why: The mothers belong to "calves," a plural noun, so the blank needs the plural possessive "their." Watch for the sound-alike forms: "they're" means "they are" and "there" points to a place.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its" is singular, but the owners of the mothers are the plural "calves."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "They're" is a contraction of "they are" and cannot show possession.
explanation.C: Correct. "Their" is the plural possessive and refers to "calves."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "There" refers to a place; it is not a possessive.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The tabla, a pair of hand drums, is the main rhythm instrument of North Indian classical music. For much of the twentieth century it was treated as a supporting instrument, keeping time for singers and string players. Ustad Alla Rakha, born in 1919 in the Jammu region, helped change that. By the time he ______ at large music festivals in the United States in the late 1960s, audiences had begun to hear the tabla as a solo voice capable of dazzling speed and wit.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: performs
choices.B: has performed
choices.C: performed
choices.D: will perform

explanation.why: The clause describes a definite past time, "in the late 1960s," and the main clause uses the past perfect "had begun." A finished action at a stated past time takes the simple past: "performed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present "performs" does not fit "in the late 1960s" or the past-tense main clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present perfect "has performed" is not used with a specific finished time such as "the late 1960s."
explanation.C: Correct. The simple past "performed" fits the stated past time and the surrounding past tenses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The future "will perform" cannot describe events of the 1960s.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1920, Bessie Coleman could not find a single flying school in the United States that would accept her as a student, because she was both a woman and African American. So she learned French, saved her earnings from a job as a manicurist, and sailed to France. In June 1921 she earned an international pilot's license, and she returned home to perform at air shows. Newspapers covered the ______ loops and dives with admiration, and large crowds came to watch her fly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: pilots'
choices.B: pilots
choices.C: pilot's
choices.D: pilots's

explanation.why: The loops and dives belong to one person, Coleman, the pilot. A singular noun shows possession with an apostrophe and s, so "pilot's loops and dives" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Pilots'" is a plural possessive, but the text describes a single pilot.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Pilots" is a plain plural; without an apostrophe it cannot show that the loops and dives were hers.
explanation.C: Correct. "Pilot's" is the singular possessive, matching the one pilot, Coleman.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Pilots's" is not a standard form, and the owner here is singular anyway.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the early 1950s, chemist Rosalind Franklin used X-rays to study the structure of DNA at King's College London. By passing X-rays through carefully prepared fibers of DNA and recording the pattern they made on film, ______ The image, later known as Photo 51, showed a cross-shaped pattern that pointed to a helical structure, and it became an important clue for the model of DNA that James Watson and Francis Crick published in 1953.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: 1952 brought Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling an unusually sharp image.
choices.B: the laboratory of Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling produced an unusually sharp image in 1952.
choices.C: Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling obtained an unusually sharp image in 1952.
choices.D: an unusually sharp image was obtained by Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling in 1952.

explanation.why: The opening phrase "By passing X-rays through ... and recording the pattern" describes what the researchers did. The subject right after the comma must therefore be the people who did it: "Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "1952," a year, which could not have passed X-rays through fibers.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the laboratory," a place, rather than the people who performed the actions in the modifier.
explanation.C: Correct. "Franklin and her student" directly follows the modifier, so they are the ones passing X-rays and recording the pattern.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "an unusually sharp image," so the sentence says the image was passing X-rays through DNA; the modifier dangles.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China, struck fragments of a life-size clay soldier. Excavations soon revealed an army of thousands of such figures buried near the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 BCE. Each of the soldiers, which stand in long rows facing east with their hands positioned to hold real weapons, ______ a slightly different face, and traces of paint show that they were once brightly colored.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are having
choices.B: having
choices.C: have
choices.D: has

explanation.why: The subject of the blank is "Each," which is always singular; "of the soldiers" and the long "which" clause only describe it. A singular subject takes the singular verb "has."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are having" is plural; the subject "Each" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having" is not a finite verb, so the clause would have no main verb at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have" is plural and seems to agree with "soldiers," but the subject is the singular "Each."
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "has" agrees with the singular subject "Each."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The bus pulled away before Rafael realized that his suitcase was still on the rack above the seat. He ran a few steps after it, waving, then stopped and laughed at himself; the driver could not possibly see him. At the ticket window, a clerk with tired eyes listened to his story and nodded as if she heard it every day. "Lost luggage comes back to this office," she said, "and I will set it aside for you when ______ arrives."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: they
choices.B: them
choices.C: its
choices.D: it

explanation.why: The thing that will arrive is Rafael's suitcase, referred to just before as "it" ("set it aside"). The blank is the subject of the singular verb "arrives," so the singular subject pronoun "it" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "They" is plural and does not agree with the singular verb "arrives" or the single suitcase.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Them" is an object pronoun and plural; the blank needs a singular subject.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Its" is a possessive and cannot stand alone as the subject of "arrives."
explanation.D: Correct. "It" is the singular subject pronoun, matching "arrives" and referring to the suitcase.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In December 1995, astronomers pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny, apparently empty patch of sky in the constellation Ursa Major and kept it there for ten days. Some scientists had worried that the project would waste valuable telescope time. Instead, the combined exposure, known as the Hubble Deep Field, ______ about 3,000 galaxies, some of them so distant that their light had been traveling for most of the history of the universe.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: revealed
choices.B: having revealed
choices.C: revealing
choices.D: to reveal

explanation.why: The sentence beginning "Instead, the combined exposure ..." needs a main verb, or it is not a complete sentence. Only "revealed" is a finite verb; the other choices are participles or an infinitive, which cannot serve as the main verb on their own.
explanation.A: Correct. The simple past "revealed" is a finite verb and matches the 1995 setting and the past tense of the passage.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having revealed" is a participle phrase and leaves the sentence without a main verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Revealing" is a participle, not a complete verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "To reveal" is an infinitive; the sentence would be a fragment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Kangchenjunga, on the border of Nepal and the Indian state of Sikkim, is the third-highest mountain in the world. When British climbers George Band and Joe Brown made the first ascent in 1955, they stopped a few steps below the top, keeping a promise made to the ruler of Sikkim that the summit, which local people regarded as sacred, would not be stepped on. Many ______ later expeditions have honored the same tradition, turning back just short of the highest point.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: climber's
choices.B: climbers'
choices.C: climbers
choices.D: climbers's

explanation.why: The later expeditions belong to many climbers, so a plural possessive is needed. A plural noun ending in s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s: "climbers' later expeditions."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Climber's" is singular, but "Many" shows that more than one climber is meant.
explanation.B: Correct. "Climbers'" is the plural possessive, matching "Many."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Climbers" has no apostrophe, so it cannot show that the expeditions belong to the climbers; "Many climbers later expeditions" does not make sense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Climbers's" is not a standard form; a plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: During the Second World War, the British code-breaking center at Bletchley Park faced a daily problem: the German Enigma machine changed its settings every twenty-four hours, and finding the new settings by hand could take longer than a day. Designed by mathematician Alan Turing and improved by his colleague Gordon Welchman, ______ The first of these machines began work in 1940, and more than two hundred were eventually built.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: thousands of possible settings an hour could be tested by an electromechanical device called the bombe.
choices.B: Bletchley Park used an electromechanical device called the bombe to test thousands of possible settings an hour.
choices.C: an electromechanical device called the bombe tested thousands of possible settings an hour.
choices.D: the problem was attacked by an electromechanical device called the bombe, which tested thousands of possible settings an hour.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Designed by ... Turing and improved by ... Welchman" describes the machine. The subject that follows the comma must therefore be the device itself, "an electromechanical device called the bombe."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "thousands of possible settings," which Turing did not design.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "Bletchley Park," which was not designed by Turing.
explanation.C: Correct. "An electromechanical device" directly follows the modifier, so it is what Turing designed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "the problem," so the sentence says the problem was designed by Turing; the modifier dangles.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Mumbai's largest railway station, opened in 1888 as Victoria Terminus and now called Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, took about ten years to build. Its architect, Frederick William Stevens, combined the pointed arches and turrets of Victorian Gothic buildings with domes, carved stonework, and animal sculptures drawn from Indian traditions. Stone carvers trained at a local art school ______ much of the decoration, which includes peacocks, monkeys, and a lion and a tiger guarding the gates.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have produced
choices.B: produced
choices.C: producing
choices.D: produce

explanation.why: The passage describes the building of a station finished in 1888, using past-tense verbs ("took," "combined"). The carvers' work was part of that finished construction, so the simple past "produced" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present perfect "have produced" suggests an action continuing to now, but the decoration was finished with the building in 1888.
explanation.B: Correct. The simple past "produced" matches the other past-tense verbs and the historical setting.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Producing" is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The present "produce" does not fit work completed in the 1880s and clashes with "took" and "combined."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Alhambra, a palace complex built by the Nasrid rulers of Granada, Spain, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, is famous for a kind of ceiling decoration called muqarnas. Hundreds of small plaster cells, each shaped like a tiny niche, hang in layered rows so that the ceiling resembles a honeycomb or a cave of dripping stalactites. The effect of these overlapping cells, especially when sunlight from the windows below ______ across them, is to make the heavy ceiling seem to float.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: move
choices.B: moves
choices.C: have moved
choices.D: are moving

explanation.why: In the clause "when sunlight from the windows below ______ across them," the subject is "sunlight," a singular noun; "from the windows below" only says where the light comes from. A singular subject takes the singular verb "moves."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Move" is plural and seems to agree with "windows," but the subject is "sunlight."
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "moves" agrees with the singular subject "sunlight."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have moved" is plural; the subject "sunlight" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are moving" is plural; "sunlight" is singular.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pigeons that settle on the grass courts of a major tennis tournament in London are more than a nuisance: they interrupt play and leave droppings on the playing surface. For well over a decade, the tournament has relied not on netting or noise machines but on a trained Harris's hawk, flown over the grounds each morning before the gates open. The strategy works because the mere sight of a predator, together with the memory of earlier encounters that the pigeons appear to retain for days, ______ the birds to feed elsewhere. The hawk is rarely allowed to catch anything; its job is simply to be seen.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are persuading
choices.B: have persuaded
choices.C: persuades
choices.D: persuade

explanation.why: The subject of the blank is "the mere sight of a predator," whose head noun "sight" is singular. The phrase "together with the memory of earlier encounters ..." is an add-on set off by commas, not a second subject joined by "and," so it does not make the subject plural. The verb must be the singular "persuades."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are persuading" is plural; the subject "sight" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have persuaded" is plural and seems to agree with "encounters" or "pigeons," which are not the subject.
explanation.C: Correct. The singular "persuades" agrees with the singular subject "sight."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Persuade" is plural, but "together with" does not create a compound subject; the subject is still the singular "sight."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the early 1800s, women were not admitted to the École Polytechnique in Paris, so the self-taught mathematician Sophie Germain obtained lecture notes from male students and submitted her own work under the name of a former student, Monsieur Le Blanc. She kept the pseudonym when she began writing to the German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss about number theory in 1804. Learning the true identity of his correspondent only in 1807, when Germain arranged for his protection during a French military occupation, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: her courage and talent were praised by Gauss, whose letters took on a new tone of respect.
choices.B: a new tone of respect entered the letters of Gauss, who praised her courage and talent.
choices.C: the letters took on a new tone of respect, as Gauss praised her courage and talent.
choices.D: Gauss praised her courage and talent, and his letters took on a new tone of respect.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Learning the true identity of his correspondent only in 1807" describes the person who learned it: Gauss. The subject right after the comma must therefore be "Gauss."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "her courage and talent," which could not have learned anything.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "a new tone of respect," not the person who learned the identity.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "the letters," so the sentence says the letters learned the identity; the modifier dangles.
explanation.D: Correct. "Gauss" directly follows the modifier, so he is the one who learned his correspondent's identity.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A tandoor is a tall clay oven, open at the top, used across South and Central Asia to bake flatbreads such as naan. A fire at the bottom heats the thick walls to well over 400°C, and the bread is slapped directly onto the inside surface, where it bakes in under two minutes. The ______ ability to hold heat explains both the speed and the texture of the result: the clay radiates steadily even as the fire dies down, so the bread puffs quickly and develops a blistered crust that a metal oven rarely produces.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ovens'
choices.B: ovens's
choices.C: ovens
choices.D: oven's

explanation.why: The ability to hold heat belongs to the oven, which the passage treats as one singular thing ("A tandoor is a tall clay oven"). A singular noun shows possession with an apostrophe and s: "oven's."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Ovens'" is a plural possessive, but the text is about one oven ("a tandoor," "the inside surface").
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Ovens's" is not a standard form, and the owner is singular in any case.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Ovens" is a plain plural without an apostrophe, so it cannot show that the ability belongs to the oven.
explanation.D: Correct. "Oven's" is the singular possessive, matching the single oven the passage describes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: For much of his career, Antonio Vivaldi taught violin at the Ospedale della Pietà, a Venetian institution that raised orphaned and abandoned girls. The best musicians among them formed an orchestra and choir whose concerts, given from behind a screen, drew visitors from across Europe. Many of the hundreds of concertos that Vivaldi wrote ______ for these performers, and the unusual difficulty of some solo parts suggests just how skilled the young women had become. Several of them, known to audiences only by a first name and an instrument, were celebrated in their own right.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: were intended
choices.B: intended
choices.C: was intended
choices.D: intending

explanation.why: The subject is "Many of the hundreds of concertos," which is plural, and the sentence needs a finite verb to be complete. The concertos did not intend anything themselves; they were intended for the performers, so the passive plural "were intended" is required.
explanation.A: Correct. "Were intended" is a finite, plural, passive verb: the concertos were meant for these performers.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Intended" on its own reads as a participle here, leaving the clause without a main verb; the concertos themselves could not have intended anything.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Was intended" is singular, but the subject "Many" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Intending" is not a finite verb, so the clause would have no main verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the wetlands around Sylhet, in northeastern Bangladesh, weavers make shital pati, smooth mats whose name means "cool mat" in Bengali. The mats are woven from thin strips of the murta, a reed-like plant that grows along canals and ponds. The strips are split, boiled, and sometimes dyed before being woven so tightly that the finished surface feels almost like cloth. Because the murta stalks must be cut and processed soon after harvesting, the weavers, most of whom are women working at home, organize ______ year around the plant's growing season. In 2017 the craft was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: their
choices.B: one's
choices.C: her
choices.D: its

explanation.why: The year being organized belongs to "the weavers," a plural noun. The phrase "most of whom are women" describes the weavers but does not change their number, so the plural possessive "their" is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Their" is plural and refers to "the weavers."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "One's" is a general pronoun with no antecedent in the text; the sentence names specific weavers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Her" is singular; it is tempting because of "women," but the antecedent "weavers" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its" is singular and refers to things, but the owners are the plural "weavers."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Sixth Symphony of Gustav Mahler, first performed in 1906, calls for a set of cowbells to be rung offstage. The sound of these bells, drifting into the hall during quiet passages for strings and woodwinds, ______ meant to suggest a herd grazing on a distant mountainside, far from the turmoil of the rest of the work. Some early listeners found the device odd, and critics debated whether ordinary farm objects belonged in a concert hall at all. Yet other composers, Richard Strauss among them, have since written for cowbells to similar pastoral effect.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: were
choices.B: is
choices.C: are
choices.D: have been

explanation.why: Strip away the modifiers and the sentence reads "The sound ... is meant to suggest a herd." The subject is the singular "sound"; "bells," "passages," "strings," and "woodwinds" all sit inside phrases describing it. The passage uses the present tense for the score ("calls for"), so "is" fits.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Were" is plural; the subject "sound" is singular.
explanation.B: Correct. The singular "is" agrees with "sound" and matches the present tense used for the score.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are" is plural and seems to agree with "bells," but the subject is the singular "sound."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural; the subject "sound" is singular.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Gond painting takes its name from the Gond people of central India, among whom it began as a tradition of decorating house walls with images of animals, trees, and local stories. In the 1980s, the artist Jangarh Singh Shyam began working on paper and canvas, and the style quickly found a wider audience. What makes these works recognizable at a glance is the way each figure is filled with its own pattern: a deer's body may be built from rows of dashes, a tree's crown from rings of dots. ______ signature patterns are now so individual that collectors can often identify a painting's maker without seeing a name.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Artist's
choices.B: Artists'
choices.C: Artists's
choices.D: Artists

explanation.why: The signature patterns belong to the artists in general, a plural group ("collectors can often identify a painting's maker" implies many makers). A plural noun ending in s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s: "Artists' signature patterns."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Artist's" is singular; standing alone without "an," it cannot refer to the many painters the sentence describes.
explanation.B: Correct. "Artists'" is the plural possessive: the patterns of many artists.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Artists's" is not a standard form; a plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Artists" has no apostrophe, so it cannot show that the patterns belong to the artists.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The night bus to Karachi left the depot an hour late, and by then Imran had given up hope of sleeping. The passenger beside him, an elderly man with a wool cap pulled low, had already begun to snore. Outside, the lights of roadside tea stalls flashed past and then gave way to a darkness so complete that the window became a mirror. Pressing his forehead against the cool glass and watching his own reflection, ______ It was the first time he had traveled so far alone, and the thought was both frightening and strangely pleasant.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Imran's thoughts drifted to the morning ahead and the city he had never seen.
choices.B: the morning ahead and the city he had never seen filled Imran's thoughts.
choices.C: Imran let his thoughts drift to the morning ahead and the city he had never seen.
choices.D: the hours seemed to Imran to stretch out without end.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Pressing his forehead against the cool glass and watching his own reflection" describes Imran. The subject after the comma must be Imran himself, not his thoughts or the hours.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "Imran's thoughts," not Imran; thoughts cannot press a forehead to glass.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the morning ahead and the city," which cannot watch a reflection.
explanation.C: Correct. "Imran" directly follows the modifier, so he is the one pressing his forehead to the glass.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "the hours," so the sentence says the hours were pressing a forehead against the glass; the modifier dangles.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Seventeen colossal stone heads, carved by the Olmec people of Mexico's Gulf Coast between roughly 1200 and 400 BCE, are among the oldest monumental sculptures in the Americas. Each was cut from a single block of basalt, and the largest weigh more than thirty tons. The nearest source of that basalt lies in the Tuxtla Mountains, which means that the Olmec, who had neither wheeled vehicles nor draft animals, ______ some of the blocks more than eighty kilometers over land and water. How exactly they did so remains an open question.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: must move
choices.B: must be moving
choices.C: must had moved
choices.D: must have moved

explanation.why: The sentence draws a conclusion about something the Olmec did more than two thousand years ago. A confident conclusion about a past action is expressed with "must have" plus the past participle: "must have moved."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Must move" refers to the present or future, but the blocks were moved in the distant past.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Must be moving" describes an action happening now, not one finished centuries ago.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Must had moved" is not a Standard English form; after "must," the past is formed with "have," never "had."
explanation.D: Correct. "Must have moved" expresses a conclusion about a completed past action.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The upturned bell of Dizzy Gillespie's trumpet, now the jazz musician's most recognizable trademark, began as an accident. In January 1953, at a party, a guest fell against the instrument, which had been left on a stand, and bent its bell upward at a sharp angle. Rather than discard the damaged horn, Gillespie played it that night and found that he could hear ______ more clearly and that the sound reached the back of a room faster. He soon had a trumpet made to the same odd shape and used the design for the rest of his career.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: him
choices.B: itself
choices.C: his
choices.D: himself

explanation.why: The person doing the hearing and the person being heard are the same: Gillespie heard his own playing. When the object of a verb is the same as its subject ("he ... could hear ..."), the reflexive pronoun "himself" is required.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Him" would refer to a different male person, but the text mentions no one else Gillespie could be hearing.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Itself" would have to refer back to the subject "he," but "he" is a person, not a thing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "His" is a possessive and cannot stand alone as the object of "hear."
explanation.D: Correct. "Himself" is the reflexive form, used because Gillespie is both the one hearing and the one heard.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Khaju Bridge in Isfahan, Iran, completed around 1650 under the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas II, was never only a bridge. Its lower level contains sluice gates that could be closed to raise the river behind it for irrigation, its stepped bases served as a place to sit beside the water, and a pavilion at the center gave the ruler a shaded spot from which to watch festivities. This combination of dam, meeting place, and royal viewing stand, together with the twenty-three arches whose tiled faces are reflected in the river below, ______ the bridge one of the most studied works of Persian engineering.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are making
choices.B: makes
choices.C: make
choices.D: have made

explanation.why: The subject of the blank is "This combination," a singular noun. The list "of dam, meeting place, and royal viewing stand" describes the combination, and "together with the twenty-three arches" is an add-on set off by commas, not a second subject joined by "and." A singular subject takes the singular verb "makes."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are making" is plural; the subject "combination" is singular.
explanation.B: Correct. The singular "makes" agrees with the singular subject "combination."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Make" is plural, tempting because of the list and the "arches," but the subject is the singular "combination."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have made" is plural; "together with" does not turn the subject into a plural compound.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Farah had expected the clay to obey her. For two weeks she had watched the older students at the studio draw tall vases out of spinning lumps as easily as pulling a thread, and she had assumed the trick was simply confidence. Now the wheel hummed under her hands and the clay wobbled, leaned, and collapsed into a gray puddle for the third time. The instructor, passing behind her, said nothing; he had seen that first bowl fail a hundred times. "Your ______ are fighting each other," he finally said, pressing his own palms together. "Let one lead."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: hand
choices.B: hands
choices.C: hands'
choices.D: hand's

explanation.why: The blank is the subject of "are fighting each other," so it must be a plain plural noun: Farah's two hands. No possession is shown here (the hands do not own anything in this sentence), so no apostrophe is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Hand" is singular, but the plural verb "are" and the phrase "each other" require more than one hand.
explanation.B: Correct. "Hands" is the plain plural subject that agrees with "are fighting" and makes sense with "each other."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Hands'" is a plural possessive, but the hands are the subject of the verb, not the owners of something.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Hand's" is a singular possessive; the sentence needs a plural subject for "are" and "each other," and nothing is possessed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Before the 1930s, knowledge of India's birds rested largely on the notes of British officers and on specimens shipped to museums in Europe. The ornithologist Sálim Ali changed that by spending years in the field, often camping for months in remote districts to record which species lived where and in what numbers. Carrying out systematic surveys of several princely states, including Hyderabad and Travancore, on behalf of the Bombay Natural History Society, ______ The Book of Indian Birds, which he published in 1941 for ordinary readers, drew on those surveys and remains in print today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Ali's reports built up a picture of the subcontinent's bird life region by region.
choices.B: a picture of the subcontinent's bird life was built up by Ali region by region.
choices.C: the subcontinent's bird life was mapped region by region in Ali's reports.
choices.D: Ali built up a picture of the subcontinent's bird life region by region.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Carrying out systematic surveys ..." describes the person doing the surveying, Ali. The subject right after the comma must therefore be "Ali," not his reports or the picture they produced.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "Ali's reports"; the reports did not carry out the surveys, Ali did.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "a picture," so the sentence says the picture carried out the surveys; the modifier dangles.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "the subcontinent's bird life," which did not carry out surveys.
explanation.D: Correct. "Ali" directly follows the modifier, so he is the one carrying out the surveys.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The hairy frog of Central Africa owes its name to the hair-like strands of skin that males grow along their flanks during the breeding season, but its most remarkable feature is hidden in its hind feet. When the frog is threatened, the tips of its toe bones break away from the rest of the skeleton and push out through the skin, forming sharp claws. The questions of how the bones return to their original position afterward and whether the skin heals completely ______ unanswered, since no one has yet observed a frog recovering in the wild.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has remained
choices.B: remains
choices.C: is
choices.D: remain

explanation.why: Strip away the modifiers and the sentence reads "The questions … remain unanswered." The subject is the plural noun "questions"; "position" and "skin" sit inside the phrases that describe those questions. A plural subject needs the plural verb "remain."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Has remained" is singular, but the subject "questions" is plural.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Remains" is singular and seems to agree with the nearby "skin," but the subject of the sentence is the plural "questions."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Is" is singular, but the subject "questions" is plural.
explanation.D: Correct. The plural verb "remain" agrees with the plural subject "questions."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Chausath Yogini temple at Mitaoli, in the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh, stands on a low hill and is built as a ring: sixty-four small chambers open inward onto a circular courtyard, at the center of which a separate shrine stands under the open sky. An inscription dates the temple to the fourteenth century, and the chambers once housed the sixty-four goddesses ______ images gave the temple its name. Nearly all of those images have since disappeared, so historians rely on better-preserved yogini temples elsewhere in India to imagine how this one originally looked.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: their
choices.B: whom
choices.C: which
choices.D: whose

explanation.why: The blank must connect "the sixty-four goddesses" to the clause "images gave the temple its name" and show that the images belonged to the goddesses. Only the relative possessive pronoun "whose" does both jobs: "the goddesses whose images gave the temple its name."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Their" is a possessive, but it is not a relative pronoun, so it leaves two clauses run together with nothing joining them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Whom" is an object pronoun and cannot show that the images belonged to the goddesses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Which" cannot show possession; "the goddesses which images" does not make sense.
explanation.D: Correct. The relative pronoun "whose" links the clause to "goddesses" and shows that the images were theirs.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Although it is called the Bayeux Tapestry, the eleventh-century work that depicts the events leading to the Norman conquest of England in 1066 is not a tapestry at all: its images are not woven into the cloth but embroidered on it in colored wool. Nearly seventy meters long, it was probably stitched in England within a generation of the conquest, most likely in a workshop at Canterbury. Because the hanging was produced by several embroiderers, scholars have studied the ______ techniques closely, noting small differences in the way figures are outlined and filled that may show where one worker's section ends and another's begins.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: embroiderers's
choices.B: embroiderers
choices.C: embroiderers'
choices.D: embroiderer's

explanation.why: The techniques belonged to "several embroiderers," so the word in the blank must be plural and possessive. A plural noun ending in s forms its possessive by adding only an apostrophe: "embroiderers'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "embroiderers's" is not standard.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Embroiderers" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it does not show that the techniques belonged to them.
explanation.C: Correct. "Embroiderers'" is the plural possessive, showing that the techniques belonged to the several embroiderers.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Embroiderer's" is the possessive of one embroiderer, but the text says several embroiderers produced the hanging.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the early 1950s, the geochemist Clair Patterson set out to determine the age of Earth by measuring the ratios of lead isotopes in meteorites, which formed at the same time as the planets. His early measurements kept coming out wrong, and he eventually realized why: lead from the laboratory's air, dust, and glassware was contaminating every sample. Only after he built one of the first ultra-clean laboratories did he obtain consistent results. The age that Patterson announced in 1956, about 4.55 billion years, derived from a meteorite that had struck Arizona some 50,000 years earlier and refined by later work on other meteorites, ______ the accepted figure today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: to remain
choices.B: having remained
choices.C: remains
choices.D: remaining

explanation.why: The subject of the final sentence is "The age that Patterson announced in 1956"; everything from "about 4.55 billion years" to "other meteorites" describes that age, and the verbs inside it ("announced," "had struck") belong to smaller clauses. The sentence still needs its own main verb, so the blank must be a finite verb: "remains."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "To remain" is an infinitive, which cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having remained" is a participle phrase, not a main verb, so the subject "The age" would be left without a verb.
explanation.C: Correct. The present-tense verb "remains" gives the subject "The age" its main verb and fits "today."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Remaining" is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The globe had stood on the corner of Miss Okafor's desk for eleven years, and in that time the Pacific had faded to the color of weak tea and a long crack had opened across Siberia. The children had stopped noticing it, the way one stops noticing a clock, but she had not. Unwilling to ask the district for a replacement that would take months to arrive, ______ The next morning the crack was nearly invisible, and the oceans, if not blue, were at least no longer brown.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the art room lent Miss Okafor a box of paints, and she stayed after the last bell with a tube of glue and a sheet of fine sandpaper.
