choices.B: a tube of glue, a sheet of fine sandpaper, and a box of paints borrowed from the art room were gathered by Miss Okafor after the last bell.
choices.C: Miss Okafor's repair began after the last bell with a tube of glue, a sheet of fine sandpaper, and a box of paints borrowed from the art room.
choices.D: Miss Okafor stayed after the last bell with a tube of glue, a sheet of fine sandpaper, and a box of paints borrowed from the art room.

explanation.why: The sentence opens with the modifier "Unwilling to ask the district for a replacement," which describes a person who is unwilling. The main clause must therefore begin with that person, Miss Okafor, as its subject. Only one choice does so.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "the art room" the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that the art room was unwilling to ask the district.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes the glue, sandpaper, and paints the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that they were unwilling to ask the district.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "Miss Okafor's repair" the subject, so the modifier wrongly describes the repair, not Miss Okafor, as unwilling.
explanation.D: Correct. "Miss Okafor" is the subject right after the modifier, so it is she who is unwilling to ask for a replacement.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The rock garden at Ryoanji, a Zen temple in Kyoto, consists of fifteen stones arranged in five groups on a rectangular bed of white gravel that the monks rake into patterns each day. The garden was laid out in the late fifteenth century, though its designer is unknown and its meaning has been debated for generations. One feature is often remarked on by visitors: from any point on the wooden veranda that runs along the garden's edge, at least one of the stones is hidden behind the others, so that the full set of fifteen ______ never visible at once.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is
choices.B: were
choices.C: have been
choices.D: are

explanation.why: The subject of the final clause is "the full set," a singular noun; "fifteen" and "the stones" earlier in the sentence describe what is in the set but are not the subject. A singular subject needs the singular verb "is," and the present tense matches the rest of the sentence.
explanation.A: Correct. The singular verb "is" agrees with the singular subject "set" and fits the present tense of the sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Were" is plural and past tense; the subject "set" is singular and the sentence is in the present tense.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, but the subject "set" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are" is plural and seems to agree with "fifteen" or "stones," but the subject is the singular "set."

items.subject: science
items.passage: The hangul, or Kashmir stag, survives today almost entirely within Dachigam National Park, a reserve of forested slopes and alpine meadows a short distance from Srinagar. Fewer than three hundred of the animals are thought to remain. In summer the herds climb to high pastures, and in winter they descend to the sheltered lower valleys, a pattern that park staff track through annual counts. Because each stag sheds and regrows ______ antlers every year, researchers cannot rely on antler shape to identify individuals, and they have turned instead to camera traps and to the patterns of pale spots on the animals' coats.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: there
choices.C: it's
choices.D: their

explanation.why: The pronoun in the blank refers to "each stag," which is singular, and it must show that the antlers belong to that stag. The singular possessive pronoun "its" does this.
explanation.A: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive pronoun and agrees with the singular antecedent "each stag."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "There" is an adverb of place, not a possessive pronoun, so it cannot show whose antlers are meant.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "It's" is the contraction of "it is," not a possessive; "each stag regrows it is antlers" makes no sense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Their" is plural, but the antecedent "each stag" is singular; "each" always takes a singular pronoun.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1978, researchers working with the paleoanthropologist Mary Leakey uncovered a trail of footprints preserved in hardened volcanic ash at Laetoli, in northern Tanzania. The ash had fallen about 3.6 million years ago, and a light rain had evidently turned it to a soft paste before it set; at least two individuals had walked across it, leaving prints that show a rounded heel, an arch, and a big toe aligned with the others. Because the trail predates the earliest known stone tools by more than a million years, the ______ discovery provided strong evidence that walking upright evolved before toolmaking did.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: researchers
choices.B: researchers'
choices.C: researcher's
choices.D: researchers's

explanation.why: The discovery was made by "researchers," plural, so the word in the blank must be plural and possessive. A plural noun ending in s shows possession by adding only an apostrophe: "researchers'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Researchers" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it cannot show whose discovery it was.
explanation.B: Correct. "Researchers'" is the plural possessive, showing that the discovery belonged to the researchers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Researcher's" is the possessive of one researcher, but the text says that several researchers made the discovery.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "researchers's" is not standard.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the late 1960s, the Chinese pharmacologist Tu Youyou joined a government project to find new treatments for malaria, which had grown resistant to existing drugs. Her team screened hundreds of remedies from traditional medicine, and an extract of sweet wormwood showed promise, but the results were inconsistent. Noticing that a fourth-century handbook advised soaking the plant in cold water and wringing out the juice rather than boiling it, ______ Tested in 1971, the new extract cleared malaria parasites from infected animals, and its active compound, later named artemisinin, became the basis of the most effective antimalarial drugs in use today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Tu suspected that heat was destroying the active ingredient and switched to a low-temperature method of extraction.
choices.B: the active ingredient, Tu suspected, was being destroyed by heat, and she switched to a low-temperature method of extraction.
choices.C: heat, Tu suspected, was destroying the active ingredient, so a low-temperature method of extraction was adopted.
choices.D: Tu's suspicion was that heat was destroying the active ingredient, and a low-temperature method of extraction replaced boiling.

explanation.why: The sentence opens with the modifier "Noticing that a fourth-century handbook advised…," which describes someone who noticed. The main clause must begin with that person, Tu, as its subject. Only one choice does.
explanation.A: Correct. "Tu" is the subject right after the modifier, so it is she who noticed the handbook's advice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes "the active ingredient" the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that the ingredient noticed the advice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "heat" the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that heat noticed the handbook's advice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "Tu's suspicion" the subject, so the modifier wrongly describes the suspicion, not Tu, as noticing the advice.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When the box came down from the top of the wardrobe, it held less than Nadia had hoped: a packet of letters tied with ribbon, a single photograph of her grandmother as a young woman, and a brass key that fit no lock in the house. Her mother said the key had been there as long as she could remember. Nadia read the letters twice through. Neither the letters nor the photograph ______ any help with the key, and in the end she hung it on a string around her neck, less because she thought it would open anything than because nobody could explain it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: were
choices.B: was
choices.C: have been
choices.D: are

explanation.why: When two subjects are joined by "neither … nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. Here the closer subject is the singular "photograph," and the story is told in the past tense, so the verb must be "was."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Were" is plural and seems to agree with "letters," but with "neither … nor" the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the singular "photograph."
explanation.B: Correct. "Was" is singular, agreeing with the nearer subject "photograph," and past tense, matching the rest of the story.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural and present perfect; the nearer subject "photograph" is singular and the story is in the past tense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are" is plural and present tense; the nearer subject is singular and the story is in the past tense.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In 1884 the city of Calais commissioned Auguste Rodin to make a monument to an episode from 1347, when, according to the chronicler Jean Froissart, six leading citizens offered their lives to the English king Edward III in exchange for the lifting of a siege. The city expected a single heroic figure on a tall pedestal. Rodin instead modeled all six men, ______ he showed not as triumphant heroes but as exhausted and uncertain figures walking toward what they believed was their execution, and he wanted the group set at ground level so that viewers could walk among them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: whom
choices.B: whose
choices.C: which
choices.D: who

explanation.why: The blank introduces a clause describing "all six men," and within that clause the pronoun is the object of the verb "showed" (he showed them). An object pronoun referring to people is "whom."
explanation.A: Correct. "Whom" is the object form, correct here because the pronoun is the object of "showed" ("he showed them").
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Whose" shows possession, but nothing in the clause belongs to the men; the pronoun is the object of "showed."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Which" refers to things, not to people such as the six men.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Who" is the subject form, but the clause already has its subject, "he"; the pronoun is the object of "showed."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Every winter, cod migrate from the Barents Sea to spawn in the waters around the Lofoten Islands, off the northwest coast of Norway, and for at least a thousand years people have gathered there to catch them. The fish were split and hung on wooden racks to dry in the cold wind, producing stockfish that was traded as far away as Italy. Because the fishery drew fishermen from along the whole coast for only a few months each year, rows of small cabins called rorbuer were built at the water's edge to house them; the ______ quarters were cramped, with bunks for a full boat crew in a single room.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fishermens
choices.B: fishermens'
choices.C: fishermen's
choices.D: fisherman's

explanation.why: The quarters belonged to the "fishermen" who came from along the coast, so the blank needs a plural possessive. "Fishermen" is already plural (an irregular plural that does not end in s), so its possessive is formed by adding an apostrophe and s: "fishermen's."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Fishermens" is not a word, and it has no apostrophe to show possession.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Fishermens" is not a word; "fishermen" is already plural, so the possessive is "fishermen's."
explanation.C: Correct. "Fishermen's" is the possessive of the irregular plural "fishermen": apostrophe plus s, because the plural does not end in s.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Fisherman's" is the possessive of a single fisherman, but the cabins housed crews of many fishermen.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Caral, in the Supe Valley about 180 kilometers north of Lima, is among the oldest cities in the Americas: its stepped pyramids and sunken circular plazas were built around 2600 BCE, roughly when the first pyramids of Egypt were rising. Its age was not appreciated until systematic excavation began. Since 1994, when the Peruvian archaeologist Ruth Shady started work there, the site ______ a wealth of material, including reed bags used to carry stones, flutes made of bird bones, and knotted cords that may be an early form of record keeping; no pottery has been found, which supports the early date.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has yielded
choices.B: is yielding
choices.C: had yielded
choices.D: yielded

explanation.why: The phrase "Since 1994" describes an action that began in the past and continues to the present, and the sentence later uses "has been found." An action stretching from a past starting point up to now takes the present perfect: "has yielded."
explanation.A: Correct. The present perfect "has yielded" fits "Since 1994," which marks a period running from the past up to the present.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present progressive "is yielding" describes only what is happening now and cannot be used with "Since 1994," which covers the whole period from then until now.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The past perfect "had yielded" would place the action before some other past event, but the sentence gives none; the work continues to the present.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The simple past "yielded" describes a finished action, which does not fit "Since 1994," a period that continues to the present.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The great cannon known as Zamzama stands today on a platform in the middle of the Mall in Lahore, opposite the museum. Cast in the city in 1757 from copper and brass, it is more than four meters long and was among the largest guns of its age in South Asia. It changed hands repeatedly over the next century as rulers captured and lost it in turn, and by the 1800s it had become more a trophy than a weapon. Familiar to readers of English fiction through the opening scene of Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim (1901), in which a boy sits astride it, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the cannon is still sometimes called Kim's Gun by visitors to the city.
choices.B: Kipling's readers still sometimes hear the cannon called Kim's Gun by visitors to the city.
choices.C: visitors to the city still sometimes call the cannon Kim's Gun.
choices.D: the name Kim's Gun is still sometimes used for the cannon by visitors to the city.

explanation.why: The sentence opens with the modifier "Familiar to readers of English fiction through the opening scene of … Kim," which describes the thing that appears in that scene: the cannon. The main clause must begin with "the cannon" as its subject. Only one choice does.
explanation.A: Correct. "The cannon" is the subject right after the modifier, so it is the cannon that is familiar to readers of Kim.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes "Kipling's readers" the subject, so the modifier absurdly says that the readers are familiar to readers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "visitors" the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that the visitors are familiar to readers through the novel's opening scene.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "the name" the subject, but the opening scene of the novel features the cannon itself, not a name that the novel never uses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The titan arum, a plant native to the rainforests of Sumatra, produces one of the largest flowering structures in the world: a central spike that can rise nearly three meters, wrapped in a single frilled sheath that opens to reveal a deep red interior. The bloom lasts only a day or two, during which the plant releases a smell resembling rotting meat and warms the tip of its spike to roughly human body temperature, which helps carry the odor to the beetles and flies that pollinate it. The combination of rarity, scale, and stench ______ crowds to botanical gardens whenever a specimen is about to open.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: draws
choices.B: have drawn
choices.C: draw
choices.D: are drawing

explanation.why: The subject of the final sentence is "The combination," a singular noun; "rarity, scale, and stench" are inside the phrase "of rarity, scale, and stench" and are not the subject. A singular subject needs the singular verb "draws."
explanation.A: Correct. The singular verb "draws" agrees with the singular subject "combination."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have drawn" is plural, but the subject "combination" is singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Draw" is plural and seems to agree with "rarity, scale, and stench," but those nouns are part of a prepositional phrase; the subject is the singular "combination."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are drawing" is plural, but the subject "combination" is singular.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A camel's reputation for going without water rests on several adaptations that work together: it can lose a quarter of its body weight in water without serious harm, its body temperature can rise by several degrees during the day so that it sweats less, and its kidneys produce highly concentrated urine. Less obvious is the camel's nose. Its long nasal passages absorb heat from inhaled air during the day and then, cooling at night, recover moisture from the air the animal breathes out. Among the reasons the camel loses so little water through breathing, then, ______ the scrolled bony structures inside the nose, whose large surface makes this exchange efficient.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: was
choices.B: has been
choices.C: are
choices.D: is

explanation.why: The sentence is inverted: it opens with the phrase "Among the reasons…," and the subject comes after the verb. That subject is "the scrolled bony structures," which is plural, so the verb must be the plural "are." The nearby singular nouns "camel" and "breathing" are not the subject.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Was" is singular and past tense; the subject "structures" is plural and the passage is in the present tense.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Has been" is singular, but the subject "structures" is plural.
explanation.C: Correct. The plural verb "are" agrees with the plural subject "structures," which follows the verb in this inverted sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Is" is singular and seems to agree with "camel" or "breathing," but the real subject, which follows the verb, is the plural "structures."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. Halloran had kept the shop on Carver Street for forty years, and in that time he had sold fewer than a third of the books that passed through his hands. The rest he gave away. A student who lingered too long over a volume she could not afford would find it wrapped in brown paper by the door the next day; a retired engineer who mentioned bridges went home with a crate. His daughter, who kept the accounts, pointed out more than once that a man who gave books to ______ asked for them could not expect to stay in business, and he agreed every time and changed nothing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: whoever
choices.B: whomever
choices.C: whom
choices.D: who

explanation.why: The pronoun is the subject of the verb "asked" (whoever asked for them), and the whole clause "whoever asked for them" is the object of the preposition "to." Because the pronoun does the asking, it takes the subject form "whoever," even though it follows "to."
explanation.A: Correct. "Whoever" is the subject of "asked"; the entire clause, not the pronoun alone, is the object of "to."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Whomever" is an object form, but the pronoun is the subject of the verb "asked" inside its own clause; the preposition "to" governs the whole clause, not the pronoun.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Whom" is an object form and, without "-ever," has no antecedent here; the pronoun must be the subject of "asked."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Who" is the right case but needs an antecedent to refer to; there is none, so the sentence needs the indefinite "whoever."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Padshahnama, an official chronicle of the first decade of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan's reign, survives in its finest form in a manuscript now kept at Windsor Castle in England, where it arrived in 1799 as a gift to King George III from the ruler of Awadh. Its forty-four paintings record court ceremonies, sieges, and processions with hundreds of figures whose faces are individual enough to be portraits. Several of the paintings bear the names of the artists who made them, and specialists have used these signed pages to recognize the same ______ hands in the unsigned ones, matching the handling of textiles, horses, and faces.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: painters's
choices.B: painters'
choices.C: painters
choices.D: painter's

explanation.why: The hands belong to the "artists" who signed several paintings, plural, so the blank needs a plural possessive. A plural noun ending in s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone: "painters'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "painters's" is not standard.
explanation.B: Correct. "Painters'" is the plural possessive, showing that the hands belong to the several painters who signed the pages.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Painters" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it does not show that the hands belong to them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Painter's" is the possessive of a single painter, but the text refers to "the artists who made them," plural.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In December 1938, the chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, working in Berlin, found that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium, an element barely half as heavy, a result that made no sense under the physics of the day. Hahn described the finding in a letter to his longtime collaborator Lise Meitner, who had fled Germany for Sweden earlier that year. Discussing the letter with her nephew, the physicist Otto Frisch, during a walk through the snow near the town of Kungälv, ______ The two published the explanation in February 1939, and Frisch gave the process its name: fission.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the uranium nucleus, Meitner realized, must have split into two smaller nuclei, releasing an enormous amount of energy in the process.
choices.B: it became clear to Meitner that the uranium nucleus must have split into two smaller nuclei, releasing an enormous amount of energy in the process.
choices.C: Meitner realized that the uranium nucleus must have split into two smaller nuclei, releasing an enormous amount of energy in the process.
choices.D: Meitner's realization was that the uranium nucleus must have split into two smaller nuclei, releasing an enormous amount of energy in the process.

explanation.why: The sentence opens with the modifier "Discussing the letter with her nephew … during a walk," which describes the person who was discussing. The main clause must begin with that person, Meitner, as its subject. Only one choice does.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "the uranium nucleus" the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that the nucleus was discussing the letter.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes the empty pronoun "it" the subject, so the modifier has no one to describe; Meitner is only an indirect object.
explanation.C: Correct. "Meitner" is the subject right after the modifier, so it is she who was discussing the letter during the walk.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "Meitner's realization" the subject, so the modifier wrongly describes the realization, not Meitner, as discussing the letter.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Tsar Bell, which stands on a stone pedestal in the Moscow Kremlin, is the largest bell in the world, at roughly two hundred tons, and it has never been rung. Cast in 1735 by Ivan Motorin and his son Mikhail, it was still sitting in its casting pit two years later when a fire swept the Kremlin; water thrown on the hot metal caused a piece weighing some eleven tons to crack away. Lifted out only in 1836, the bell, together with the broken fragment that now leans against its base, ______ one of the Kremlin's most photographed sights, a monument to ambition rather than to sound.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: remains
choices.B: remain
choices.C: have remained
choices.D: are

explanation.why: The subject of the final sentence is "The bell," which is singular. The phrase "together with the broken fragment…" adds information but, unlike "and," does not make the subject plural. A singular subject needs the singular verb "remains."
explanation.A: Correct. The singular verb "remains" agrees with the singular subject "bell"; "together with" does not create a plural subject.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Remain" is plural, as if "the bell" and "the fragment" were joined by "and," but "together with" leaves the subject singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have remained" is plural, but the subject "bell" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are" is plural, but the subject "bell" is singular.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 2000, miners drilling nearly three hundred meters below the surface at Naica, in the Mexican state of Chihuahua, broke into a chamber filled with crystals of selenite, a form of gypsum, some of them longer than a bus. The crystals had grown over hundreds of thousands of years in water kept just above the temperature at which gypsum crystallizes by heat from magma far below, conditions so stable that the crystals, ______ slow growth required that the water never cool or drain, reached a size found nowhere else on Earth. Since pumping stopped in 2015, the chamber has flooded again.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: of which
choices.B: their
choices.C: which
choices.D: whose

explanation.why: The blank must introduce the clause "slow growth required that the water never cool or drain" and show that the slow growth belonged to "the crystals." The relative possessive pronoun "whose" does both: "the crystals, whose slow growth required…."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Of which" cannot stand directly before the noun it modifies in this way; "of which slow growth required" is not standard English.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Their" is a possessive but not a relative pronoun, so it leaves the clause "their slow growth required…" jammed into the sentence with nothing to connect it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Which" cannot show possession, and "the crystals, which slow growth required…" is not a grammatical clause.
explanation.D: Correct. "Whose" links the clause to "the crystals" and shows that the slow growth was theirs.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Newgrange, a great mound of earth and stone in the valley of the River Boyne in Ireland, was built around 3200 BCE by farming communities that left no written record. A narrow passage leads to a central chamber under a corbeled stone roof that has kept the interior dry for five thousand years. Above the entrance sits a small opening, the roof-box, whose purpose was confirmed only in 1967, when the archaeologist Michael O'Kelly stood in the chamber at dawn on the winter solstice and watched sunlight travel up the passage. The ______ precision in aligning the opening with the midwinter sunrise has changed assumptions about the societies of Neolithic Europe.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: builder's
choices.B: builders
choices.C: builders's
choices.D: builders'

explanation.why: The precision belonged to the people who built Newgrange, the "farming communities" of the first sentence, so the blank needs a plural possessive. A plural noun ending in s shows possession with an apostrophe alone: "builders'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Builder's" is the possessive of a single builder, but the text says the mound was built by whole communities.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Builders" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it cannot show whose precision is meant.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "builders's" is not standard.
explanation.D: Correct. "Builders'" is the plural possessive, showing that the precision was that of the many people who built the mound.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The letter from the shipping office reached the house on a Tuesday, though it had been posted the previous Thursday and had evidently spent the interval in several puddles. By the time Eleanor opened it, the berth it offered her brother on the Castlebar had been given to someone else, the ship had cleared the harbor, and her brother, who had packed his trunk three times that week, had gone back to the mill without a word. Had the letter arrived even a day sooner, she ______ him to the docks herself, and the whole shape of the following year, she later thought, would have been different.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: had walked
choices.B: will have walked
choices.C: would walk
choices.D: would have walked

explanation.why: "Had the letter arrived even a day sooner" is an inverted way of saying "If the letter had arrived," a condition contrary to what actually happened in the past. The result of such a condition takes "would have" plus a past participle, and the sentence's own second result, "would have been different," confirms the pattern: "would have walked."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Had walked" is the form used in the condition itself ("had the letter arrived"), not in the result; two past perfects leave the sentence without a conditional result.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Will have walked" is a future form and cannot express the result of a past condition that did not occur.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Would walk" expresses a present or future possibility, but the condition is about the past and did not happen.
explanation.D: Correct. "Would have walked" is the correct form for the result of a past condition that did not happen, matching "would have been different" later in the sentence.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Bhai Ram Singh, born in 1858 in the village of Rasulnagar in Punjab, entered the Mayo School of Art in Lahore as a student of woodcarving and rose to become its principal, the first Indian to hold the post. His buildings, among them the Lahore Museum and parts of Aitchison College, combined Mughal and Sikh ornament with European planning. His best-known commission, however, lies far from Punjab. Invited to England in 1890 to decorate a new banqueting hall at Osborne House, Queen Victoria's residence on the Isle of Wight, ______ Every surface of the Durbar Room, as it came to be called, carries his designs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: intricate plasterwork modeled on the ornament of Mughal and Sikh buildings was what Ram Singh used to cover the ceiling and walls.
choices.B: Ram Singh covered the ceiling and walls with intricate plasterwork modeled on the ornament of Mughal and Sikh buildings.
choices.C: the ceiling and walls were covered by Ram Singh with intricate plasterwork modeled on the ornament of Mughal and Sikh buildings.
choices.D: Ram Singh's intricate plasterwork, modeled on the ornament of Mughal and Sikh buildings, covered the ceiling and walls.

explanation.why: The sentence opens with the modifier "Invited to England in 1890 to decorate a new banqueting hall," which describes the person who was invited. The main clause must begin with that person, Ram Singh, as its subject. Only one choice does.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "intricate plasterwork" the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that the plasterwork was invited to England.
explanation.B: Correct. "Ram Singh" is the subject right after the modifier, so it is he who was invited to England.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "the ceiling and walls" the subject, so the modifier wrongly says that the ceiling and walls were invited to England.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "Ram Singh's intricate plasterwork" the subject, so the modifier wrongly describes the plasterwork, not Ram Singh, as having been invited.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The hamper had been packed by their aunt with the thoroughness of a woman who had once been caught in the rain without an umbrella. Tomas, who was eight and considered himself the expedition's leader, insisted on carrying it across the meadow himself and set it down at the top of the hill with the air of someone who had crossed a continent. His sister unbuckled the straps. Beneath the folded cloth ______ a loaf still warm from the oven and a bottle of lemonade wrapped in newspaper, and beneath those, to the children's astonishment, a second, smaller cloth folded over a cake.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is
choices.B: were
choices.C: has been
choices.D: was

explanation.why: The final sentence is inverted: it begins with the phrase "Beneath the folded cloth," and the subject comes after the verb. That subject is "a loaf … and a bottle of lemonade," two things joined by "and," so it is plural and the verb must be "were." The singular "cloth" just before the blank is not the subject.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Is" is singular and present tense; the subject is plural and the story is told in the past tense.
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "were" agrees with the compound subject "a loaf … and a bottle," which follows the verb, and matches the past tense of the story.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Has been" is singular and present perfect; the subject is plural and the story is told in the past tense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Was" is singular and seems to agree with "cloth" or "a loaf," but the subject is the pair "a loaf … and a bottle," which is plural.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On the coast of Kutch, in the Indian state of Gujarat, a breed of camel does something that camels elsewhere never do: it swims. Kharai camels wade and then paddle across tidal creeks to reach islands of mangrove, where they feed on the salty leaves for days before returning. The herders who keep them, from communities that have lived on this coast for generations, follow the animals in small boats or wait on shore. Although the breed was formally recognized only in 2015, the ______ knowledge of the tides, the creeks, and the mangrove stands reaches back far longer, and conservationists argue that protecting the camels means protecting the mangroves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: herders's
choices.B: herders
choices.C: herders'
choices.D: herder's

explanation.why: The knowledge belongs to "the herders who keep them," plural, so the blank needs a plural possessive. A plural noun ending in s shows possession with an apostrophe alone: "herders'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "herders's" is not standard.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Herders" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it cannot show that the knowledge is theirs.
explanation.C: Correct. "Herders'" is the plural possessive, showing that the knowledge belongs to the herders as a group.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Herder's" is the possessive of a single herder, but the text describes many herders from whole communities.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The British chemist Dorothy Hodgkin used X-ray crystallography, in which the pattern of X-rays scattered through a crystal reveals the arrangement of atoms inside it, to determine the structures of molecules far more complex than most contemporaries thought possible. Her map of penicillin, completed in 1945, and her solution of vitamin B12 in 1956 earned her the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964. The structure of insulin, which she had first photographed as a young researcher in 1934 and which required more than three decades of refinement and the arrival of electronic computers before it yielded, ______ in 1969, a year that she regarded as the fulfillment of her career.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: finally appeared
choices.B: finally appearing
choices.C: to appear finally
choices.D: having finally appeared

explanation.why: The subject of the final sentence is "The structure of insulin"; the two "which" clauses that follow describe it, and their verbs ("had photographed," "required," "yielded") belong to those clauses. The sentence still needs its own main verb, so the blank must be a finite verb: "finally appeared."
explanation.A: Correct. The past-tense verb "appeared" gives the subject "The structure of insulin" its main verb and fits the date 1969.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Appearing" is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To appear" is an infinitive, which cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Having appeared" is a participle phrase, not a main verb, so the subject "The structure of insulin" would be left without a verb.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The collection of amber fragments from Myanmar, which includes several insect species that were previously unknown to science, ______ held in a university vault for decades before anyone catalogued it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are
choices.B: were
choices.C: have been
choices.D: has been

explanation.why: The sentence's subject is "collection," a singular noun. The long phrase that follows contains plural nouns, but they do not change the verb's number. The sentence needs the singular "has been."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are" is a plural present-tense verb and cannot follow a singular subject here. The passage describes an event that began in the past.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "collection," which is singular. The plural "were" agrees with the nearby plural noun "species," not with the true subject.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have" is plural. It agrees with "species" in the nonessential phrase, but the verb must agree with the singular subject "collection."
explanation.D: Correct. The subject is the singular noun "collection," and the phrase "which includes several insect species" only adds information. The singular helping verb "has" agrees with it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The hydrologists spent three weeks ______ water samples along the Ravi River before the first monsoon rains arrived. Their data later showed that nitrate levels rose sharply in the weeks after the rains.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: to collect
choices.B: collecting
choices.C: collect
choices.D: collects

explanation.why: The verb "spent" must be followed by an -ing form that names the activity. The only option with that form is "collecting," which completes the phrase "spent three weeks collecting."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The verb "spent" is followed by an -ing form, not by "to" plus a verb. "Spent to collect" is not standard English.
explanation.B: Correct. The verb "spend" takes an -ing form when it is followed by an activity, so "spent three weeks collecting water samples" is the standard structure.
explanation.C: Incorrect. After "spent," the next verb must take the -ing form. A bare verb like "collect" does not fit the structure of the sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A finite verb such as "collects" cannot follow "spent" directly. The structure needs a non-finite -ing form.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Two independent field teams measured soil loss on the same north-facing slope, using different methods. Both ______ data pointed to the same conclusion: the topsoil on the slope had been thinning for decades.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: teams's
choices.B: team's
choices.C: teams
choices.D: teams'

explanation.why: The data belong to two teams, so the word must be the plural of "team" in the possessive form. A plural noun that ends in s takes an apostrophe alone, giving "teams'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to form the possessive. Adding another s is not standard English.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Team's" is the singular possessive, which would mean that one team owns the data. The passage describes two teams, so the plural possessive is needed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without an apostrophe, "teams" is a plain plural noun. It cannot show that the data belong to the two teams.
explanation.D: Correct. "Teams" is plural, and the data belong to the two teams. A plural noun that ends in s takes an apostrophe after the s to show possession.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The population of shorebirds that refuel in coastal wetlands during their spring migration, despite decades of conservation effort along the flyway, ______ declined sharply since the 1990s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have
choices.B: were
choices.C: are
choices.D: has

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun "population." The plural nouns in the phrases between the subject and the verb do not control agreement, so the verb must be "has declined."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Have" is plural and agrees with "wetlands" or "efforts," which sit in the phrases between the subject and the verb. The subject itself is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Were" is a plural past form and cannot agree with the singular subject "population." It also does not combine with "declined" as a present perfect.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are" is a plural present form. It does not agree with the singular subject "population," and it cannot combine with "declined" in this structure.
explanation.D: Correct. The subject is "population," which is singular, and the long phrase about wetlands and conservation does not change that. The singular "has" agrees with it, and "has declined" matches the present perfect.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores in their leaves called stomata, but water vapor escapes through the same pores. Most plants open their stomata during the day. Many cacti, however, open their stomata only at night, when the desert air is cooler and more humid. Since less water evaporates into cool, humid air, this habit most likely helps cacti ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: survive without taking in any carbon dioxide at all.
choices.B: grow taller than plants that open their stomata in daylight.
choices.C: lose less water than they would by opening their stomata during the day.
choices.D: lose more water at night than they do during the hot daytime hours.

explanation.why: The text gives two facts: water escapes through open stomata, and less water evaporates into cool, humid air. Cacti open their stomata only at night, when the air is cool and humid, so this timing must reduce how much water they lose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says plants take in carbon dioxide through their stomata; cacti still open them, just at night.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how tall cacti grow compared with other plants.
explanation.C: Correct. Opening the stomata only in cool, humid air means less water escapes than would escape in daytime heat.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the logic; the cool, humid night air reduces water loss rather than increasing it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In many earlier European churches, thick walls had to hold back the heavy outward push of stone ceilings, so windows had to stay small; large openings would have weakened the walls. In the late twelfth century, builders began using flying buttresses, stone arches on the outside of a building that carry much of that push down to supports beyond the walls. With less force pressing on the walls, builders could ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: make the walls even thicker than they had been before.
choices.B: cut larger window openings without weakening the walls.
choices.C: build the ceilings out of wood instead of heavy stone.
choices.D: place every window in the ceiling rather than the walls.

explanation.why: The text explains that windows stayed small because large openings would weaken walls that were resisting the push of heavy ceilings. Flying buttresses took much of that force off the walls, so the reason for keeping windows small was removed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Less force on the walls means they need less thickness, not more.
explanation.B: Correct. Once the walls bore less force, larger openings would no longer weaken them dangerously.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions changing the material of the ceilings.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives no reason to move windows into the ceiling; it is about openings in the walls.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Archaeologists working at sites of the Indus Valley Civilization, which flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE in what is now Pakistan and northwestern India, have found hundreds of small stone cubes that were used as weights. The cubes follow the same system of sizes whether they come from Harappa, from Mohenjo-daro, or from settlements hundreds of kilometers away. Because the civilization's writing has never been deciphered, no surviving text explains how this system was kept in place. Even so, the uniformity of the weights suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: people in widely separated settlements shared common standards for measuring goods.
choices.B: every one of the weights was produced in a single workshop in Mohenjo-daro.
choices.C: scholars have learned how the weights were used by reading Indus inscriptions.
choices.D: trade between distant Indus settlements was rare and of little importance.

explanation.why: The key fact is that weights from many distant sites follow the same system of sizes. Even without written records, matching weights across far-apart places point to a shared standard that people in those places followed.
explanation.A: Correct. Identical weight systems in settlements hundreds of kilometers apart indicate shared measuring standards.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about where the weights were made; uniform sizes could result from many makers following one standard.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the Indus writing has never been deciphered, so no one can read such inscriptions.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A shared system of weights across distant places suggests that exchange mattered, not that it was rare.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Bloodroot, a woodland wildflower of eastern North America, produces seeds with a small fatty attachment called an elaiosome. Native ants carry the seeds to their nests, eat the elaiosomes, and discard the intact seeds in waste piles, where many later sprout. Ecologist Anneke de Vries compared two forests: one with plenty of native ants and one where those ants had been replaced by an invasive ant species that ignores the seeds. Bloodroot seeds sprouted equally well in both forests, but in the second forest nearly every seedling grew within half a meter of a parent plant. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the invasive ants eat bloodroot seeds, which keeps most of the seeds from sprouting.
choices.B: bloodroot seeds can sprout only after native ants have placed them in waste piles.
choices.C: bloodroot will soon disappear from every forest that the invasive ants have entered.
choices.D: native ants help bloodroot spread to new spots but are not needed for its seeds to sprout.

explanation.why: Two findings must be combined. Seeds sprouted equally well with or without native ants, so ants are not needed for sprouting. But without native ants, seedlings stayed right next to parent plants, so the ants are what move seeds to new places.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the invasive ants ignore the seeds, and seeds sprouted equally well in both forests.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Seeds sprouted just as well in the forest without native ants, so they do not need the waste piles to sprout.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text shows only that seedlings stayed near parent plants, not that the species will disappear.
explanation.D: Correct. It matches both findings: equal sprouting in both forests, but movement away from parent plants only where native ants were present.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Prussian blue, often described as the first modern synthetic pigment, was first made in Berlin in the early 1700s and was unavailable to painters before then. A landscape in a private collection bears an inscription dating it to 1690, yet conservator Hiroshi Tanabe detected Prussian blue in its sky. That detection alone would not settle the matter, since restorers routinely repaint damaged areas with pigments of their own era. Tanabe's cross-sections, however, place the Prussian blue in the lowest layer of paint, beneath layers that show no sign of having been scraped away or disturbed. Taken together, these observations suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the date in the inscription is unlikely to reflect when the landscape was actually painted.
choices.B: a later restorer added the Prussian blue when repairing a damaged area of the sky.
choices.C: the landscape was most likely painted in Berlin, where Prussian blue was first produced.
choices.D: the inscription was added to the landscape by someone other than the artist who painted it.

explanation.why: The pigment did not exist before the early 1700s, so a 1690 date is suspicious. The text then rules out the other explanation, a later restoration, because the blue sits in the very first layer under undisturbed paint. The blue was therefore part of the original painting, which means the painting was probably made after 1690.
explanation.A: Correct. If the original paint contains a pigment not available until the early 1700s, the 1690 date is probably not the true date of the painting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the explanation the cross-sections rule out: the blue lies in the lowest layer, beneath undisturbed paint, so it was not added during a repair.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Knowing where the pigment was invented says nothing about where this painting was made; the pigment could have been sold elsewhere.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The evidence shows only that the date is probably wrong; the artist could have written the inaccurate date, so who added the inscription is not established.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The transit method detects a planet by the slight dimming that occurs when it passes in front of its star. Such a passage is visible only if the planet's orbit happens to be tilted so that, from Earth, the planet crosses the face of its star. For a giant planet orbiting very close to a sunlike star, only about one orbit in ten is tilted this way, and the fraction is far smaller for planets on wider orbits. Surveying 50,000 sunlike stars, astronomer Chidi Nwosu's team detected transits by close-orbiting giant planets around 26 of them, roughly one star in 2,000. Assuming these detections are accurate, the results imply that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: about one in ten of the stars the team surveyed has a close-orbiting giant planet.
choices.B: most close-orbiting giant planets went undetected because they were too small to dim their stars.
choices.C: considerably more of the surveyed stars have close-orbiting giant planets than the team directly detected.
choices.D: the transit method is unable to detect any planet that orbits far from its star.

explanation.why: Only about one in ten close-orbiting giant planets has an orbit tilted so that it transits. So for each such planet the team saw, roughly nine others around surveyed stars would have produced no transit at all. The true number of stars with these planets must therefore be well above the 26 detected.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "One in ten" is the share of orbits that are tilted the right way, not the share of stars that have such planets; the data point to roughly one star in 200.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives orbital tilt, not planet size, as the reason planets go undetected, and giant planets are the easiest to see.
explanation.C: Correct. Because most such orbits are not tilted toward Earth, the 26 detections must be only a fraction of the planets actually present.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the fraction of detectable orbits is "far smaller" for wider orbits, not that such planets can never be detected.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians of trade often treat customs ledgers as rough measures of commerce, since officials recorded the cargoes that passed through a port. Akosua Mensah's study of one Mediterranean port complicates that practice. The port's ledgers list pepper and cloves in nearly every year from 1620 to 1649, record almost none from 1650 to 1671, and list them regularly again thereafter. Mensah also located a city charter that, hoping to lure merchants away from a rival port, exempted spice cargoes from customs duties between 1650 and 1671, and she observes that clerks entered a cargo in the ledgers only when duty was owed on it. Mensah's findings therefore suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the port's spice imports fell sharply between 1650 and 1671 before recovering to their earlier level.
choices.B: the exemption succeeded in drawing spice merchants away from the rival port to Mensah's port.
choices.C: customs ledgers cannot serve as reliable evidence for the trade of any port in any period.
choices.D: the ledgers' near silence about spices from 1650 to 1671 may reflect the exemption rather than the trade.

explanation.why: Combine the two facts Mensah found: clerks recorded only cargoes that owed duty, and spice cargoes owed no duty from 1650 to 1671. Spices would then vanish from the ledgers during exactly those years whether or not they kept arriving, so the gap cannot be read as a drop in trade.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This takes the ledgers at face value, which is exactly the reading Mensah's findings call into question.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The charter shows what the city hoped for, but because exempt cargoes went unrecorded, the ledgers cannot show whether more spice merchants actually came.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Mensah's point concerns one gap at one port caused by a specific exemption; it does not show that all ledgers everywhere are unreliable.
explanation.D: Correct. Since untaxed cargoes went unrecorded, the missing spice entries could result from the exemption rather than from fewer spices arriving.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Indus river dolphin, found mainly in Pakistan, has eyes so reduced that it is nearly blind; it finds prey in the river's muddy water by echolocation, interpreting the echoes of its own rapid clicks. Biologist Saima Qureshi recorded the dolphins along two stretches of the river that held similar numbers of fish. Along the stretch with heavy motorboat traffic, the dolphins clicked far more often than along a quiet stretch. Qureshi points out that animals relying on echolocation tend to repeat their signals when background noise drowns out the returning echoes. If her reasoning is correct, the higher click rate in the busy stretch most likely indicates that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the busy stretch offered the dolphins more prey to locate than the quiet stretch did.
choices.B: the dolphins there needed more clicks to perceive their surroundings, not that they had more to find.
choices.C: motorboat noise has left the dolphins in the busy stretch unable to catch enough food to survive.
choices.D: the dolphins there were clicking to keep in contact with one another over the noise of the boats.

explanation.why: Two pieces of the text must be combined. The stretches held similar numbers of fish, so the extra clicking was not caused by more prey. Qureshi's point about noise drowning out echoes then explains it: in the noisy stretch, the dolphins had to click more to get usable echoes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says both stretches held similar numbers of fish, which rules out more prey as the cause.
explanation.B: Correct. With prey similar in both places and noise masking echoes, extra clicks most likely reflect the extra effort needed to sense the surroundings.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text shows that the dolphins clicked more, not that they were failing to catch food or were in danger of starving.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes the clicks as a tool for echolocation; it never says the dolphins use them to communicate.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea turtle hatchlings usually leave their nests at night and must reach the ocean quickly. On a natural beach, the brightest direction is the open horizon over the water, where moonlight and starlight reflect off the waves, and hatchlings crawl toward that brightness. On beaches lined with hotels and streetlights, however, the brightest light often comes from the land behind the beach. As a result, hatchlings on brightly lit beaches are likely to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: stay in their nests until the lights are turned off.
choices.B: crawl away from the ocean instead of toward it.
choices.C: reach the water faster than hatchlings on natural beaches.
choices.D: use the sound of the waves to find the water.

explanation.why: The text says hatchlings crawl toward the brightest direction. On a lit beach, the brightest light comes from the land, not the sea, so the hatchlings will be drawn toward the land, away from the water.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says hatchlings wait in their nests; it describes them crawling toward light.
explanation.B: Correct. Hatchlings move toward the brightest light, and on lit beaches that light is on land, away from the ocean.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Lights on land pull hatchlings in the wrong direction, so they would reach the water more slowly, not faster.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text discusses only light as a guide; sound is never mentioned.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Jute, a plant fiber used to make rope and sacks, has long been one of Bangladesh's most important crops. After the tall stalks are harvested, they must be soaked in water for several weeks so that the fibers loosen and can be pulled away from the woody stem. Bangladesh lies on a low river delta, where ponds, canals, and slow-moving streams are found almost everywhere. This geography means that many Bangladeshi farmers ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: have water for soaking their jute close to their fields.
choices.B: can harvest their jute only once every several years.
choices.C: grow jute mainly for its woody stems rather than its fibers.
choices.D: rarely need to soak their jute before removing the fibers.

explanation.why: Jute stalks must be soaked in water for weeks, and the text says Bangladesh's delta has ponds, canals, and slow streams almost everywhere. Putting these facts together, farmers there usually have the water they need for soaking nearby.
explanation.A: Correct. Soaking needs standing or slow water, and the delta has such water almost everywhere.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how often jute can be harvested.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says jute is used for its fiber; the stems are what the fibers are pulled away from.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the stalks must be soaked; the delta's water makes soaking easy, not unnecessary.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: All week, Marisol hurried to her room after school and shut the door. When her mother knocked, Marisol called out that she was busy and slid something under her bed before opening the door. On Saturday morning, her mother's birthday, Marisol came to breakfast holding a small package wrapped in paper she had painted herself. Marisol's behavior during the week most likely suggests that she ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: had been secretly preparing a gift for her mother.
choices.B: was upset with her mother and wanted to be left alone.
choices.C: was studying for an important test at school.
choices.D: had forgotten that her mother's birthday was coming.

explanation.why: Marisol hid something whenever her mother came to the door, and on her mother's birthday she appeared with a package wrapped in paper she painted herself. Her secrecy during the week is best explained by her getting a birthday gift ready.
explanation.A: Correct. The hiding, the timing, and the handmade wrapping all point to a secret birthday gift.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing shows that Marisol was upset; the gift at the end suggests the opposite.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions a test, and studying would not explain hiding something under the bed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The prepared package shows that she remembered the birthday.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In true fresco, a method used by many Italian Renaissance painters, pigment is brushed onto fresh, wet plaster. As the plaster dries, the color becomes locked into the wall, but once the plaster has dried, it no longer absorbs new paint. For this reason, painters spread fresh plaster over only the section of wall they expected to finish in a single day. This practice suggests that a large fresco ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was usually painted on dry plaster prepared weeks earlier.
choices.B: was typically painted in sections on different days.
choices.C: could be completed by one painter in a single day.
choices.D: used fewer colors than paintings made on wood or canvas.

explanation.why: Painters plastered only as much wall as they could paint in one day, because dry plaster no longer takes paint. A large fresco covers more wall than one day's work, so it must have been built up section by section over many days.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says pigment goes onto fresh, wet plaster; dry plaster no longer absorbs paint.
explanation.B: Correct. Since each day's plaster covered only one section, a large work had to be made in many daily sections.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Each day covered only one section, so a large fresco would take more than one day.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares the number of colors in frescoes with other paintings.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pacific salmon hatch in freshwater streams, then swim out to the ocean, where they spend several years feeding and growing. When they are ready to reproduce, most return to the very stream where they hatched, sometimes traveling hundreds of kilometers. Each stream carries a distinctive mix of chemicals from its soil and plants, and young salmon appear to memorize this scent before leaving. These observations suggest that adult salmon ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: rely mainly on their eyesight to recognize familiar landmarks.
choices.B: probably use smell to help them find their home streams.
choices.C: can reproduce only in the ocean, far from where they hatched.
choices.D: choose a new stream each year based on how much food it holds.

explanation.why: Each stream has its own scent, young salmon seem to memorize it, and adults return to the stream where they hatched. The most logical link is that the remembered scent helps guide them home.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes scent, not sight; eyesight is never mentioned.
explanation.B: Correct. A memorized stream scent is the only guide the text describes, so smell probably helps them return.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says salmon return to freshwater streams to reproduce, not that they reproduce in the ocean.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says most salmon return to the same stream where they hatched, not a new one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, merchants carried goods across Asia along the routes now known as the Silk Road, often on camels that could carry only a limited load. A journey could take many months, and traders had to pay for food, animals, and protection along the way. Silk was especially popular with these merchants because a small, light bundle of it could be sold for a very high price. This suggests that merchants on these routes probably preferred goods that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: were worth a great deal compared with their weight.
choices.B: were heavy but cheap to produce, such as stone or timber.
choices.C: could already be bought in every town along the way.
choices.D: would spoil quickly if the journey took too long.

explanation.why: Loads were limited and long journeys were costly, and silk was popular because a light bundle sold for a high price. Merchants would therefore favor goods that packed high value into little weight.
explanation.A: Correct. Silk is the example: light to carry but sold for a high price.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Heavy, cheap goods would use up the limited loads without paying for the costly trip.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Goods available everywhere would be hard to sell at a high price after a long journey.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The long trips would make quickly spoiling goods a poor choice; nothing suggests merchants wanted them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The seawater around Antarctica stays close to −1.9°C, a temperature below the point at which the blood of most fish would freeze. Yet many fish thrive there. One group, the notothenioids, produces special proteins that attach to tiny ice crystals in the fishes' blood and body fluids and stop the crystals from growing larger. Without these proteins, ice would spread through the fishes' tissues. These proteins therefore most likely allow the fish to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: swim north to warmer water whenever ice begins to form.
choices.B: survive water colder than their blood could otherwise stand.
choices.C: warm the surrounding seawater to above its freezing point.
choices.D: grow larger ice crystals that help protect their tissues.

explanation.why: The water is colder than the freezing point of most fish blood, but the proteins stop ice crystals from growing in these fishes' bodies. That is what lets them live in such cold water.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the fish thrive in Antarctic water; nothing mentions moving north.
explanation.B: Correct. By keeping ice crystals small, the proteins let the fish live in water that would otherwise freeze their blood.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The proteins work inside the fish; the text never says they change the temperature of the seawater.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The proteins stop ice crystals from growing; they do not make them larger.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Yoruba, a language spoken by millions of people in Nigeria and neighboring countries, is a tonal language: whether a syllable is spoken at a high, middle, or low pitch can change the meaning of a word. Yoruba drummers play an hourglass-shaped instrument called the dùndún, whose pitch rises or falls as the player squeezes the cords along its sides. Because the drum can copy these rises and falls in pitch, skilled drummers can ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: imitate spoken phrases that listeners can recognize.
choices.B: replace the Yoruba language with a new system of sounds.
choices.C: play only a single note during an entire performance.
choices.D: be heard more clearly than any other instrument in Nigeria.

explanation.why: In Yoruba, pitch helps carry the meaning of words, and the dùndún can copy the rises and falls in pitch of speech. A drum that copies the pitch patterns of words can therefore imitate speech that listeners understand.
explanation.A: Correct. Because Yoruba meaning depends on pitch, a drum that copies those pitches can imitate recognizable phrases.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The drum copies the pitch patterns of Yoruba itself; it does not replace the language.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the drum's pitch rises and falls, so it is not limited to one note.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares how loudly or clearly different instruments can be heard.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Below about 1,000 meters, the deep ocean receives no sunlight at all, and food is scarce. Many female anglerfish living there have a long spine on the head that ends in a glowing tip, lit by bacteria living inside it. The fish holds this lure in front of its mouth and stays almost perfectly still. Small fish and shrimp in the deep sea are often drawn toward points of light. The lure most likely helps the anglerfish ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: avoid being noticed by other animals nearby.
choices.B: attract prey close to its mouth without chasing it.
choices.C: warm the cold water that surrounds its body.
choices.D: spot predators approaching from far away in the dark.

explanation.why: Small fish and shrimp swim toward points of light, and the anglerfish holds a glowing lure in front of its mouth while staying still. The lure therefore brings food to the anglerfish instead of the anglerfish going after its food.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A glowing light in total darkness draws attention; it does not help the fish hide.
explanation.B: Correct. Prey drawn to the light come right up to the mouth of the still anglerfish.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The lure gives off light; the text never suggests it gives off heat.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about using the light to watch for predators.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When the results of the 800-meter race were announced, Tobias had finished fourth, one place short of a medal. He shook hands with the winner, smiled for his teammates, and told his coach that he felt fine. But on the bus ride home, he sat alone in the back row, staring out the window, and did not answer when his best friend asked if he wanted to play cards. These details suggest that Tobias ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was pleased with his result but too tired to talk.
choices.B: did not care at all how he had done in the race.
choices.C: was more disappointed than he had shown others.
choices.D: was angry at the winner for beating him unfairly.

explanation.why: In public, Tobias shook hands, smiled, and said he felt fine. Later, alone on the bus, he stared out the window and ignored his friend. The contrast suggests that his calm behavior hid real disappointment about missing a medal.
explanation.A: Incorrect. His silence and isolation on the bus suggest unhappiness, not pleasure with his result.
explanation.B: Incorrect. His withdrawn behavior on the bus shows that the result did matter to him.
explanation.C: Correct. His cheerful public behavior contrasts with his silence later, showing hidden disappointment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. He shook hands with the winner, and nothing suggests he thought the race was unfair.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to travel all the way around the southern tip of South America, a voyage of more than 20,000 kilometers. That year, the Panama Canal opened across a narrow strip of land in Central America, connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Ships could now pass between the two oceans without going around the continent. As a result, the voyage from New York to San Francisco most likely became ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: longer, because ships now had to wait to enter the canal.
choices.B: possible by sea for the first time in history.
choices.C: much shorter than it had been before the canal opened.
choices.D: unnecessary, because the canal linked the two cities directly.

explanation.why: Before the canal, ships had to sail around South America. The canal let them cross between the oceans through Central America instead, which cut out that long detour and made the trip much shorter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about waiting times, and avoiding a 20,000-kilometer detour would shorten the trip.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says ships already made this voyage before 1914 by going around South America.
explanation.C: Correct. Skipping the trip around South America would greatly shorten the voyage.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The canal crosses Central America; it does not connect New York and San Francisco directly.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Water heats up and cools down much more slowly than land does. In summer, the ocean slowly stores heat, and in winter it slowly releases that heat into the air above it. Lisbon, Portugal, sits on the Atlantic coast, while Madrid, Spain, lies far inland at a similar distance from the equator. Based on these facts, winter temperatures in Lisbon are most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: determined mainly by Lisbon's distance from the equator.
choices.B: colder than Madrid's because the ocean absorbs heat from the air.
choices.C: nearly the same as summer temperatures in Lisbon.
choices.D: generally milder than those in inland Madrid.

explanation.why: In winter, the ocean releases heat it stored during summer, warming the air near the coast. Lisbon is on the coast and Madrid is inland at a similar latitude, so Lisbon should have the milder winters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The two cities are a similar distance from the equator, so that distance cannot explain a difference; the ocean can.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says that in winter the ocean releases heat into the air, which would make the coast warmer, not colder.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The ocean only softens the change between seasons; nothing suggests winter and summer would feel the same.
explanation.D: Correct. Heat released by the Atlantic in winter would keep coastal Lisbon milder than inland Madrid.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Biologists have long debated why zebras have stripes. One idea is that the stripes discourage biting flies such as horseflies, which spread disease among grazing animals. To test this idea, researchers observed horseflies around horses wearing either plain cloth coats or black-and-white striped ones. Flies approached both groups of horses at similar rates, but they landed far less often on the striped coats, frequently flying past or bumping into them. Because the animals beneath the coats were all horses, these results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: striped coats keep horses cooler than plain coats do.
choices.B: horseflies cannot detect striped animals from a distance.
choices.C: a striped pattern itself can make it harder for flies to land.
choices.D: stripes protect animals from every insect that spreads disease.

explanation.why: The only difference between the two groups was the pattern of the coat; the animals underneath were all horses. Since flies approached both groups equally but landed less on the striped coats, the stripes themselves seem to interfere with landing.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about temperature; the study measured fly behavior.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Flies approached both groups at similar rates, so they did detect the striped horses; the difference came only at landing.
explanation.C: Correct. With the same animal under every coat, the pattern is the factor that reduced landings.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The study observed only horseflies, so it cannot support a claim about every disease-carrying insect.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Under the Mughal Empire, which ruled much of South Asia from the 1500s to the 1700s, official messages were often carried by a relay system. Posts were set up at regular intervals along major roads, and each kept fresh horses or runners ready. A messenger hurried to the next post, where a rested rider or runner took the message and set off at once. Because no single messenger or horse had to cover the whole route, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: each messenger had to know the entire route from one end of the empire to the other.
choices.B: messages were delivered more slowly than if one rider had traveled the whole way.
choices.C: ordinary people across the empire came to depend on the system for their letters.
choices.D: messages could cross long distances faster than one rider could have carried them.
