items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: occurred because ships carrying barrels were less likely to sink.
choices.B: proves that Roman trade collapsed in the centuries after 100 CE.
choices.C: shows that seaborne trade in the Mediterranean actually grew after 100 CE.
choices.D: may overstate how much seaborne trade actually declined after that time.

explanation.why: Wrecks are found mainly by their heaps of amphorae, and after the second century some cargo moved in barrels that leave little trace. Ships carrying barrels would be undercounted, so part of the drop in known wrecks may reflect changing containers rather than less trade. The decline in trade may therefore be smaller than the wreck count suggests.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says barrels are hard to find, not that ships carrying them sank less often.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text's point is that the wreck count may be misleading, so it cannot prove a collapse.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text suggests the decline may be overstated, not that trade grew; it gives no evidence of growth.
explanation.D: Correct. Barrels leave few traces, so wrecks after the shift are harder to find, which could exaggerate the apparent decline.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Mughal India, the right to have coins struck in one's own name was among the clearest public claims to rule, and each coin recorded the name of the ruler and the city whose mint produced it. Numismatist Imran Qadri examined coins from a provincial mint during a period when a rebellious prince challenged the emperor. Coins from that mint dated to one year carry the prince's name; coins from the same mint dated to the years just before and after carry the emperor's name. Because a prince could strike coins at a mint only if he controlled the city where it operated, Qadri's findings suggest that the prince ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was accepted as the rightful ruler throughout Mughal India for that year.
choices.B: probably held that city for a time before the emperor's forces regained it.
choices.C: persuaded the emperor's own officials to strike coins in his name as an honor.
choices.D: never controlled that city, since its mint went on using the emperor's name.

explanation.why: Coins could be struck in a ruler's name only where he controlled the mint's city. Coins from one year carry the prince's name, so he held the city then; coins from the years before and after carry the emperor's name, so the emperor held it before and again afterward. Together, the coins point to a brief period of control by the prince.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Coins from one provincial mint cannot show that the prince was accepted everywhere.
explanation.B: Correct. The switch to the prince's name and back to the emperor's fits a short period of control before the city was lost.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text presents coins as a claim to rule, not as an honor granted by the emperor's officials.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The coins from that one year carry the prince's name, which shows he did control the city then.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Nineteenth-century theaters kept prompt books, working copies of plays in which the stage manager marked cuts, added lines, and recorded cues for performers. For one popular melodrama of the 1840s, two versions survive: the text the playwright published the year the play opened, and the prompt book from the theater that first staged it. The prompt book cuts nearly a third of the second act and adds a song for the heroine that appears nowhere in the published text. Several newspaper reviews of the play's opening week praise that song. These sources suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the playwright wrote the heroine's song after the published text had appeared.
choices.B: the published text may not reflect what audiences at the first performances saw.
choices.C: the playwright disapproved of the changes that the theater made to the second act.
choices.D: prompt books are more reliable guides than published texts for every play of the period.

explanation.why: The prompt book records a version of the play with a shortened second act and an added song. Reviews of the opening week praise the song, which is missing from the published text, so audiences saw the prompt-book version, at least in part. The published text therefore may not match what was performed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The reviews show the song was sung in the opening week, the same year the text was published; nothing indicates who wrote it or when.
explanation.B: Correct. The reviews confirm that a feature found only in the prompt book was performed, so the published text differs from what audiences saw.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text gives no information about the playwright's opinion of the changes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Evidence about one melodrama cannot establish a rule for every play of the period.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Merriam's kangaroo rats live in the deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where open water is rare. These small rodents eat mostly dry seeds. When their bodies break down the seeds for energy, the chemical reactions release water as a by-product, and the animals' kidneys are extremely efficient at holding on to that water. These facts suggest that kangaroo rats ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: must find a pond or stream to drink from every few days.
choices.B: can survive for long periods without drinking any water at all.
choices.C: choose seeds because seeds hold more water than other desert foods.
choices.D: lose more water through their kidneys than most other rodents do.

explanation.why: The text says open water is rare where kangaroo rats live, that digesting seeds releases water inside their bodies, and that their kidneys hold on to that water. An animal that makes and keeps its own water does not need to drink, so it can go a long time without drinking.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text stresses that open water is rare and explains how the rats get water without drinking, so it gives no reason to think they need ponds or streams.
explanation.B: Correct. Water released while digesting seeds, kept by very efficient kidneys, lets the rats go without drinking.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text calls the seeds "dry"; the water comes from breaking the seeds down, not from water stored in them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says their kidneys are extremely efficient at holding on to water.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Inca Empire, which stretched along the Andes Mountains of South America in the 1400s and 1500s, had no horses or wheeled vehicles for carrying messages. Instead, it relied on chasquis, runners stationed at posts along its roads. Each runner carried a message only a short distance before handing it to a fresh runner waiting at the next post. Because no single runner had to cover the whole route, messages could ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: be carried on horseback along the empire's flatter stretches of road.
choices.B: travel long distances much faster than one tired runner could carry them.
choices.C: reach distant cities only after long delays caused by exhausted runners.
choices.D: be written down so that runners would not have to remember them.

explanation.why: Each runner covered only a short stretch and then passed the message to a rested runner. Since nobody had to run the whole way and grow tired, the message could keep moving at a fast pace over long distances.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the empire had no horses for carrying messages.
explanation.B: Correct. Handing the message to a fresh runner at each post keeps it moving quickly, which one runner could not do over a long route.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The relay system avoided exhausted runners, so it would reduce delays rather than cause them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about writing messages down or about runners' memory.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The khejri tree grows across the Thar Desert of India and Pakistan, where nearly all the year's rain falls in just a few months. Its main root can grow many meters down to reach water stored deep underground, far below the dry upper layers of soil where most grasses and small shrubs have their roots. As a result, the khejri is likely to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: draw most of its water from the upper layers of the soil.
choices.B: stay green in the dry months, after many shallow-rooted plants have withered.
choices.C: lose its leaves earlier in the dry season than the grasses around it do.
choices.D: grow shorter than the grasses and small shrubs that grow near it.

explanation.why: Rain falls in only a few months, so the upper soil dries out for most of the year. The khejri's deep root reaches water far below that dry layer, so the tree can keep getting water when plants with shallow roots cannot.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the root reaches water "far below the dry upper layers," the opposite of this choice.
explanation.B: Correct. Reaching deep water lets the khejri keep growing when the upper soil, where shallow-rooted plants get water, is dry.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the logic: the khejri's deep root gives it water after the grasses' shallow roots have dried out, so it should keep its leaves longer, not lose them sooner.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the tree's height compared with nearby plants.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Japan during the Edo period (1603–1868), color woodblock prints were made by teams of artists and craftspeople. In the usual method, a carver cut a separate wooden block for each color in a design. A printer then pressed each block onto the same sheet of paper, one color at a time, lining up every block carefully. Under this method, a print that used ten colors would have required ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a carver who had also designed the picture being printed.
choices.B: one carved block holding all ten colors at the same time.
choices.C: more carved blocks than a print that used three colors.
choices.D: fewer carved blocks than a print that used three colors.

explanation.why: The text says each color had its own block. A ten-color print therefore needed ten blocks, which is more than the three blocks a three-color print needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes teams of workers but never says carvers designed the pictures.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says a separate block was cut for each color, not one block for all of them.
explanation.C: Correct. One block per color means ten blocks for ten colors, more than a three-color print needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the relationship: more colors means more blocks, not fewer.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most birds make a whooshing sound when they flap their wings, but many owls fly almost silently. The front edges of an owl's main flight feathers have stiff, comblike fringes, and the back edges are soft and frayed. Together, these features break up the rushing air that would otherwise make noise. Since owls often hunt mice and other small animals with sharp hearing, silent flight probably helps owls ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: catch mice that make no sound at all as they move.
choices.B: get close to their prey before the prey can hear them coming.
choices.C: fly faster than birds whose feathers lack comblike fringes.
choices.D: frighten their prey out of hiding before diving at it.

explanation.why: The text links two facts: owls fly almost silently, and their prey has sharp hearing. An owl that makes no noise can approach without warning the animal it is hunting.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text is about the owl's sound, not the sound the mice make.
explanation.B: Correct. Prey with sharp hearing would notice a noisy bird, so silence lets the owl approach unheard.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text discusses noise, not speed, so it gives no basis for this comparison.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Silent flight would keep prey from noticing the owl; frightening prey would require noise.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Amaka's grandmother had never flown a kite, but she held the spool of string while Amaka ran across the field. On the fourth try, the wind caught the kite and lifted it high above the trees. Amaka turned around, expecting to see her grandmother staring up at the sky. Instead, her grandmother was watching Amaka, smiling widely and clapping with the spool tucked under her arm. The grandmother's behavior suggests that she ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: did not notice that the kite had finally risen into the air.
choices.B: wanted to take a turn running across the field with the kite.
choices.C: took more pleasure in Amaka's success than in the kite itself.
choices.D: was disappointed that the kite had needed four tries to fly.

explanation.why: When the kite finally rises, the grandmother is not looking at the kite; she is looking at Amaka, smiling and clapping. Her attention and joy are focused on her granddaughter's achievement.
explanation.A: Incorrect. She is clapping as the kite flies, which shows she knows it has risen.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests she wanted to run with the kite herself.
explanation.C: Correct. She watches Amaka rather than the kite and claps happily, showing that Amaka's success is what delights her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Smiling widely and clapping show delight, not disappointment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Starting in April 1860, riders of the Pony Express carried mail on horseback between Missouri and California, a trip that took about ten days. In October 1861, workers completed a telegraph line across the United States, allowing messages to cross the country in a matter of minutes. The Pony Express shut down just days later. These events suggest that the Pony Express most likely closed because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the telegraph had made messages between the states slower to arrive.
choices.B: the telegraph could deliver messages far faster than riders could.
choices.C: its riders could no longer find horses that were fast enough.
choices.D: the new telegraph line had been built across the riders' route.

explanation.why: The Pony Express took about ten days, while the telegraph took minutes. The service closed right after the telegraph line was finished, which points to the much faster telegraph as the reason.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the text: the telegraph made messages arrive much faster, not slower.
explanation.B: Correct. A ten-day trip could not compete with minutes, and the timing of the closure fits this cause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions any shortage of horses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not say where the telegraph line ran or that it blocked anything.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the dry zone of northern and eastern Sri Lanka, most of the year's rain falls within a few months, and the land can be parched for the rest of the year. More than two thousand years ago, communities there began building tanks, large reservoirs enclosed by earthen banks, to catch and hold rainwater. Channels then carried water from the tanks to rice fields. These tanks most likely allowed farmers to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: move their rice fields to the wetter parts of the island.
choices.B: stop depending on rain as a source of water for their crops.
choices.C: grow rice only during the months of heaviest rain.
choices.D: water their crops even during months with little rain.

explanation.why: Rain falls in only a few months, but the tanks stored that rain and channels carried it to the fields. Stored water could therefore reach the crops during the dry part of the year.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about moving fields elsewhere on the island.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This goes too far: the tanks were filled by rainwater, so farmers still depended on rain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the purpose of the tanks; storing water frees farmers from the rainy months alone.
explanation.D: Correct. Water stored during the rainy months could be sent to fields when little rain was falling.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, at an average distance of about 58 million kilometers, and Venus is nearly twice as far away. Yet the surface of Venus, at about 465 degrees Celsius, is hotter than even the hottest parts of Mercury. Venus is wrapped in a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide that traps heat, while Mercury has almost no atmosphere. This comparison suggests that a planet's surface temperature ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: depends only on how far the planet is from the Sun.
choices.B: cannot be measured on planets with thick atmospheres.
choices.C: depends on its atmosphere as well as its distance from the Sun.
choices.D: rises whenever a planet is farther away from the Sun.

explanation.why: If distance were all that mattered, Mercury would be hotter than Venus. Venus is hotter even though it is farther away, and the text explains that its thick atmosphere traps heat, so the atmosphere must also affect temperature.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Venus is farther from the Sun but hotter, which shows distance is not the only factor.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives a temperature for Venus, which has a thick atmosphere, so this cannot be right.
explanation.C: Correct. Venus's heat-trapping atmosphere makes it hotter than Mercury despite its greater distance, so both factors matter.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This overgeneralizes from one comparison; the text explains Venus's heat by its atmosphere, not by its distance.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In medieval Europe, books were often written on parchment, a material made from animal skin that was costly and slow to produce. When a book was no longer wanted, a scribe would sometimes scrape the ink off its pages and write a new text on the same parchment. Faint traces of the older writing often remained, and modern scientists have used special imaging to read them. As a result, some old parchment books ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: show no trace of the writing that was scraped off their pages.
choices.B: contain hidden texts older than the ones that can be seen on their pages.
choices.C: were copied onto paper by scribes before their pages were scraped.
choices.D: were scraped clean because parchment was cheap and easy to replace.

explanation.why: Scribes wrote new texts over scraped-off older ones, and traces of the older writing remained. Scientists can now read those traces, so some books hold an earlier text underneath the one that is visible.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says faint traces of the older writing often remained.
explanation.B: Correct. The scraped-off writing came first and still leaves traces under the newer text, so these books contain older, hidden texts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions copying old texts onto paper.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says parchment was costly and slow to produce, which is why it was reused.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Changthangi goats are raised by herding families on the Changthang plateau of Ladakh, in northern India, where winter nights are bitterly cold. As winter approaches, each goat grows a thick layer of extremely fine wool, called pashm, beneath its coarse outer hair. When the weather warms in spring, the goats begin to shed this soft layer. It is therefore most likely that herders collect pashm ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: only from goats that live in warmer valleys below the plateau.
choices.B: from the coarse outer hair rather than the layer beneath it.
choices.C: in spring, around the time the goats begin to shed it.
choices.D: in early autumn, before the goats have grown their soft layer.

explanation.why: The pashm grows as winter approaches and is shed when spring comes. The sensible time to collect it is in spring, when the layer is full and starting to come loose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about goats in warmer valleys; it links the soft layer to cold weather.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says pashm is the fine layer beneath the coarse outer hair, not the outer hair itself.
explanation.C: Correct. In spring the layer is fully grown and already loosening, so herders can gather it then.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Before winter the goats have not yet grown the soft layer, so there would be little pashm to collect.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In ancient Mesopotamia, scribes wrote by pressing marks into tablets of soft clay. Many tablets were simply left to dry in the sun, and sun-dried clay can crumble or turn back into mud if it gets wet. Strong heat, however, hardens clay into a material much like pottery. When the city of Nineveh was burned by invading armies in 612 BCE, the fire may have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: led scribes to stop writing on clay and start writing on stone.
choices.B: softened the tablets so that their marks could no longer be read.
choices.C: destroyed every clay tablet that had been stored in the city.
choices.D: helped preserve some tablets by baking them hard.

explanation.why: Sun-dried tablets are fragile, but strong heat turns clay hard like pottery. A large fire would have supplied that heat, so it could have made some tablets more durable.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about scribes switching to stone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says heat hardens clay rather than softening it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says heat hardens clay, so a fire would not necessarily destroy the tablets.
explanation.D: Correct. Strong heat hardens clay, so the fire could have baked some tablets into a lasting form.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Rafael had played his audition piece for the city orchestra that morning, and the results would be posted at six o'clock. By five, he had tuned his violin twice, though he had no plans to play it, and had reread the same page of his book so many times that he could not have said what it was about. Every few minutes, he glanced at the clock on the wall. These details suggest that Rafael ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was confident that he had already won a place in the orchestra.
choices.B: was too anxious about the results to focus on anything else.
choices.C: was hoping to practice once more before the results appeared.
choices.D: had lost interest in music after a difficult audition.

explanation.why: Rafael keeps doing pointless tasks, cannot take in what he reads, and checks the clock again and again while waiting for the results. These are signs of nervous waiting.
explanation.A: Incorrect. His restless behavior shows worry, not calm confidence.
explanation.B: Correct. Retuning an instrument he will not play, rereading without understanding, and watching the clock all show anxiety.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says he had no plans to play the violin.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing suggests he has lost interest in music; he is eagerly waiting for the results.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On Earth, footprints in soil or sand are soon erased by wind and rain. The Moon, however, has almost no atmosphere, so it has no wind and no weather. Astronauts who walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972 left footprints in its fine, powdery dust. Given these conditions, many of those footprints are most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: deeper now than they were when the astronauts made them.
choices.B: preserved only because the dust froze solid after the astronauts left.
choices.C: still there today, since no wind or rain has worn them away.
choices.D: long gone, swept away by winds blowing across the lunar surface.

explanation.why: Wind and rain erase footprints on Earth, but the Moon has neither. Without those forces, the footprints have nothing to wear them away quickly, so they are probably still there.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests the footprints would grow deeper over time.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text explains the footprints' survival by the lack of wind and weather, not by freezing.
explanation.C: Correct. With no wind or weather to erase them, the footprints should remain.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the Moon has no wind.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Much of the Netherlands consists of polders, areas of low land surrounded by dikes, which are earthen walls that hold back rivers and the sea. Many polders lie below sea level, so rainwater and water seeping through the ground collect in them instead of draining away. Beginning in the 1400s, the Dutch built windmills that lifted this water over the dikes. Without some way to remove water, the polders would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: rise slowly above the level of the sea.
choices.B: need fewer dikes to keep out the sea.
choices.C: dry out and become too dusty to farm.
choices.D: gradually fill with water and flood.

explanation.why: Water collects in the polders because they are low and cannot drain on their own. The windmills removed that water, so without them it would keep building up.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests the land would rise.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text links removing water to the number of dikes needed; the dikes hold back rivers and the sea, which would still be there.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the problem: polders collect water rather than lose it.
explanation.D: Correct. Water collects in the polders and cannot drain away, so without pumping it would build up until the land flooded.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, which kill many other small fish. It has often been assumed that clownfish are simply born immune to the stings. To test this idea, marine biologist Lena Okoro raised young clownfish in tanks without anemones and then placed each fish beside one. At first, the fish only brushed briefly against the tentacles, sometimes darting away after being stung. Over several hours, their contact grew longer, and within a day they were nestling among the tentacles unharmed. Okoro's results suggest that a clownfish's protection from anemone stings ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: is permanently lost if the fish spends its early life in a tank without anemones.
choices.B: comes mainly from the fish's ability to dart away before the tentacles can sting it.
choices.C: develops through contact with an anemone rather than being fully present at birth.
choices.D: is present at birth, which is why the young fish settled among the tentacles at once.

explanation.why: The young fish were stung at first but, after hours of gradually longer contact, could nestle among the tentacles unharmed. Protection that appears only after contact must build up through that contact, which challenges the idea that clownfish are born fully immune.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Fish raised without anemones still became protected within a day, so the protection was not lost.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Darting away happened only at first; later the fish stayed among the tentacles unharmed, so escape cannot explain their protection.
explanation.C: Correct. The fish were stung at first and became unharmed only after repeated contact, so their protection developed over time.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The fish did not settle in at once; they were stung and darted away at first.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At Vindolanda, a Roman fort in northern England, archaeologists have recovered hundreds of thin wooden tablets on which soldiers and their families wrote letters, supply lists, and even party invitations nearly two thousand years ago. Wood normally rots quickly in the ground, but these tablets lay in waterlogged soil containing almost no oxygen, which slowed their decay. At most other Roman forts, the soil is dry and well drained, and no such tablets have been found there. The absence of tablets at those other forts therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: indicates that soldiers at those forts wrote on stone instead of on wood.
choices.B: proves that writing was rare among the soldiers stationed at them.
choices.C: shows that the Vindolanda tablets were carried there from other forts.
choices.D: may reflect conditions in the soil rather than how much people there wrote.

explanation.why: The tablets at Vindolanda survived only because unusual soil slowed the decay of the wood. In the dry soil of other forts, any tablets would probably have rotted away, so finding none there does not tell us whether people at those forts wrote less.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions writing on stone; it gives soil conditions, not a different writing material, as the likely explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This goes too far: tablets at the other forts may simply have rotted in dry soil, so their absence proves nothing about how often people wrote.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says nothing about tablets being moved from one fort to another.
explanation.D: Correct. Because wood rots quickly in dry soil, the missing tablets could be explained by poor preservation rather than by a lack of writing.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the Mithila region of Bihar, India, women have long painted bright scenes of gods, animals, and plants on the mud walls of their homes, often to mark a wedding or a festival. Mud walls must be replastered regularly, however, and each fresh coat covered the paintings beneath it. In the 1960s, artists from the region began painting the same kinds of images on paper, which could be sold and carried far away. Because of this history, scholars studying Mithila painting most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: believe the tradition began in the 1960s, when the first paintings on paper appeared.
choices.B: have many more surviving examples made after the 1960s than made before them.
choices.C: find that the paintings on paper show entirely different subjects from those on walls.
choices.D: rely mainly on wall paintings that have survived in homes for many centuries.

explanation.why: Wall paintings were regularly covered by new plaster, so few older ones would survive. Paintings on paper, made from the 1960s on, could be kept and spread widely. Scholars would therefore have far more examples from the later period.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says women had painted on walls long before the 1960s, so the tradition is older than the paintings on paper.
explanation.B: Correct. Older wall paintings were plastered over, while later paintings on paper could be kept, so later examples should greatly outnumber earlier ones.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says artists painted "the same kinds of images" on paper.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Because the walls were regularly replastered, wall paintings would rarely survive for centuries.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Common cuckoos lay their eggs in the nests of other bird species, leaving the hosts to raise the chicks. Some host species push out any egg that looks different from their own, and cuckoos that lay in those species' nests tend to produce eggs closely matching the hosts' eggs in color and pattern. Researchers found, however, that cuckoos laying in the nests of dunnocks, a species that rarely rejects odd-looking eggs, produce eggs that look little like dunnock eggs. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: dunnocks are unable to see the colors and patterns of the eggs in their nests.
choices.B: hosts' rejection of odd eggs is likely what favors cuckoo eggs that match theirs.
choices.C: cuckoos match host eggs by copying the eggs they see in each nest they visit.
choices.D: cuckoos avoid laying their eggs in the nests of species that reject odd eggs.

explanation.why: Cuckoo eggs closely match host eggs where hosts reject odd eggs, but not where the host (the dunnock) rarely rejects them. The match appears only when rejection is a threat, which suggests that rejection by hosts drives the matching.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says only that dunnocks rarely reject odd eggs; it never says they cannot see differences.
explanation.B: Correct. Matching eggs occur where hosts reject odd eggs and not where they rarely do, linking the match to rejection.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never explains how the match is produced, and copying eggs in each nest is not suggested.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says cuckoos do lay in the nests of rejecting species, producing matching eggs there.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For three weeks, old Mr. Castellano had said nothing about Divya's bread except "Again." She had kneaded, shaped, and baked loaf after loaf, and each time he had broken one open, studied the inside, and pushed the tray back toward her. On Friday, he broke open her loaf and looked at it for a long while. Then, without a word, he set the rest of her loaves in the front window beside his own, where every customer would see them. Mr. Castellano's action most likely indicates that he ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: now considered Divya's bread good enough to offer to his customers.
choices.B: regretted having been so harsh with Divya during her first weeks.
choices.C: had decided to stop teaching Divya because she was not improving.
choices.D: wanted his customers to see how much Divya's bread still needed work.

explanation.why: For weeks Mr. Castellano rejected every loaf. On Friday, instead of saying "Again," he placed her loaves in the front window beside his own, where customers would see them. Displaying the bread with his own shows he finally judged it good enough to sell.
explanation.A: Correct. Putting her loaves in the shop window next to his own, after weeks of rejecting them, signals approval.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text shows him approving her bread but gives no sign that he regrets how he treated her.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He did not push the tray back this time, and he displayed her bread, which suggests she had improved.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A baker would not display bread beside his own to show customers its flaws; the change from "Again" signals approval, not criticism.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Norway's medieval stave churches are built almost entirely of wood, and few written records say when they were constructed. Researchers can, however, use the growth rings in a church's timbers to find the year in which the trees were cut down. In one church in western Norway, the outermost rings of several beams show that the trees were felled in the winter of 1131–1132. Since medieval builders usually shaped and raised timber soon after felling it, while the wood was still easy to work, the church was most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: built from timber that had been stored for decades before being used.
choices.B: constructed in 1132 or within a few years afterward.
choices.C: built over many decades, as wood from later years was gradually added.
choices.D: the oldest wooden church still standing in Norway.

explanation.why: The trees were cut down in the winter of 1131–1132, and builders usually used timber soon after cutting it. So the church was probably built in 1132 or shortly after.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says builders usually used timber soon after felling it, not after storing it for decades.
explanation.B: Correct. Felling in 1131–1132 plus the habit of building soon afterward points to construction in or soon after 1132.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says only that several beams came from trees felled in one winter; it gives no evidence of wood added over many decades.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives a date for one church but compares it with no other churches, so it cannot show this church is the oldest.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mawsynram, a village in the Khasi Hills of northeastern India, is often listed among the wettest places on Earth. During the summer monsoon, moist winds blow north from the Bay of Bengal and meet the steep southern slopes of the hills. As the air is forced upward, it cools, and much of its moisture falls as rain on those slopes, where Mawsynram lies. By the time the air crosses the hills and descends on the northern side, it has lost much of its moisture. Places on the northern side of the hills therefore most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: receive their monsoon rain from winds blowing south rather than north.
choices.B: receive considerably less monsoon rain than Mawsynram does.
choices.C: receive more monsoon rain than Mawsynram, because the air there is cooler.
choices.D: receive no rain at all during the summer monsoon season.

explanation.why: The moist air drops much of its water on the southern slopes, where Mawsynram is. When the air reaches the northern side, it has "lost much of its moisture," so less rain can fall there.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes only winds blowing north and gives no information about winds from the north.
explanation.B: Correct. Air that has lost much of its moisture on the southern slopes has less left to drop on the northern side.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The air reaching the northern side has already lost much of its moisture, so those places should get less rain, not more.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This goes too far: the air has lost much of its moisture, not all of it, so some rain is still possible.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Mesoamerica, both before and after the Spanish arrived in the 1500s, cacao beans served as a form of money: people used them to pay for food, cloth, and other goods. Spanish observers described counterfeiters who carefully removed the insides of cacao beans and refilled the empty shells with earth so that they looked whole. Making such fakes took real effort, and a fake bean could not be eaten or made into a drink. That anyone bothered to make them suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: cacao beans were widely accepted as payment, so fakes could be worth making.
choices.B: Spanish observers invented the counterfeiters to discourage the use of cacao.
choices.C: most of the cacao beans in circulation were fakes filled with earth.
choices.D: cacao was valued mainly as a drink and only rarely used as payment.

explanation.why: A fake bean was useless as food or drink and took effort to make. The only reason to make one would be to spend it, which shows that cacao beans were trusted and accepted as money.
explanation.A: Correct. Since fakes had no use except as money, people made them only because real beans were readily accepted as payment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests the observers made up their reports.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text shows that fakes existed, not that they made up most of the beans in use.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Fakes that could not be drunk would be pointless if cacao were valued only as a drink; their existence points to its use as money.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Young sunflower plants turn their tops to follow the Sun across the sky each day, facing east in the morning and west by evening, then swinging back overnight. Once the flower heads open, however, they stop moving and stay facing east. Because they face the rising Sun, east-facing heads warm up quickly in the morning, and bees, which prefer warm flowers, visit them more often than they visit heads that face west. These facts suggest that the mature sunflower's fixed eastward position ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: results from the plant losing its ability to sense sunlight as it ages.
choices.B: lets the flower head collect more total sunlight than a moving head would.
choices.C: may increase the number of bee visits that the flower head receives.
choices.D: makes the flower head too warm for bees to visit during the morning.

explanation.why: East-facing heads warm quickly in the morning, and bees prefer warm flowers and visit east-facing heads more often. Facing east, then, probably helps the sunflower attract bees.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about why the heads stop moving or about any loss of the ability to sense light.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text discusses morning warmth, not total sunlight, and a head that follows the Sun might well collect more light.
explanation.C: Correct. East-facing heads warm up early, and bees visit warm heads more often, so the position may bring more bee visits.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says bees prefer warm flowers and visit east-facing heads more often.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the eighteenth century, opera audiences sat in auditoriums that stayed lit by candles throughout the performance, and many people bought printed copies of the libretto, the text of the opera, to read along as the singers performed. In 1876, however, the composer Richard Wagner had the auditorium darkened during performances at his new theater in Bayreuth, Germany, and over the following decades many opera houses adopted the practice. In darkened theaters, audience members who did not understand the singers' language most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: relied more heavily than before on reading printed libretti during the performance.
choices.B: found it harder to follow the words while the opera was being performed.
choices.C: asked theaters to keep their auditoriums lit during Wagner's operas.
choices.D: stopped attending operas that were sung in languages other than their own.

explanation.why: Audiences had used printed libretti to follow along, which required light. Once auditoriums were darkened, they could no longer easily read during the performance, so those who did not know the language would have more trouble following the words.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Reading a printed libretto requires light, so a darkened auditorium would make this harder, not more common.
explanation.B: Correct. Without light to read the libretto, listeners who did not know the language would lose their main way of following the words.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says nothing about audiences making requests to theaters.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This goes too far: the text shows that following the words became harder, not that people stopped attending.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Cities of the Indus civilization, which flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE in what is now Pakistan and northwestern India, were often hundreds of kilometers apart. Yet builders in many of them used bricks of the same proportions: in each brick, the width was twice the thickness, and the length was twice the width. Because the Indus script has not been deciphered, no written rules for brickmaking are known. Even so, the matching proportions suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: builders in widely separated cities followed common building practices.
choices.B: the Indus script was used mainly to record rules for making bricks.
choices.C: all bricks used in Indus cities were made in a single central workshop.
choices.D: the cities were built by unrelated groups with no contact with one another.

explanation.why: Builders in cities hundreds of kilometers apart made bricks with the same proportions. Even without written rules, this shared pattern points to shared practices across the civilization.
explanation.A: Correct. The same brick proportions in distant cities point to shared building practices, even though no written rules survive.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The script has not been deciphered, so nothing is known about what it mainly recorded.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This goes too far: matching proportions show a shared standard, not that every brick came from one workshop.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the evidence: identical proportions in distant cities suggest connection, not isolation.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In a European oak forest, a small songbird feeds its chicks mostly on caterpillars, which are plentiful for only a few weeks each spring. As spring temperatures in the forest have risen over recent decades, the caterpillars have emerged earlier and earlier. Ecologist Ingrid Solberg found, however, that the birds still begin laying their eggs on about the same dates as before, a timing that appears to depend largely on day length rather than on temperature. If this pattern continues, the birds' chicks may increasingly ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: hatch while the caterpillars are at their most plentiful.
choices.B: be raised on a food other than the caterpillars.
choices.C: hatch after the caterpillars' brief peak has passed.
choices.D: hatch earlier in the spring, just as the caterpillars have.

explanation.why: The caterpillars now emerge earlier because of warming, but the birds' egg laying follows day length, which warming does not change. The birds' timing stays fixed while their food arrives earlier, so the chicks may hatch after the caterpillars' peak.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Because the caterpillars now peak earlier while egg laying has not shifted, the chicks will hatch later relative to the caterpillars, not at their peak.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never suggests the birds switch to another food.
explanation.C: Correct. With the food supply peaking earlier and the birds' timing unchanged, chicks will tend to hatch after the brief peak.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the birds still lay eggs on about the same dates as before, so the chicks are not hatching earlier.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On the morning Kenji left for the university in the city, his father went out in the fishing boat as usual, before dawn. Kenji had packed the night before and waited on the dock with his bag, but the boat did not return in time, and the bus would not wait. At the station, he found, tucked into the side pocket of his bag, a small knife with a worn wooden handle: the one his father had used to mend nets for as long as Kenji could remember. The knife most likely suggests that Kenji's father ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: had found his own way to mark Kenji's departure, even without saying goodbye.
choices.B: had forgotten that Kenji was leaving for the city that morning.
choices.C: planned to join Kenji in the city once the fishing season had ended.
choices.D: wanted Kenji to give up the university and stay in the village as a fisherman.

explanation.why: The father was not there to say goodbye, but someone had slipped his own well-used knife into Kenji's bag. Leaving such a personal object shows that he knew Kenji was leaving and wanted to mark the moment in his own quiet way.
explanation.A: Correct. Placing his own treasured knife in Kenji's bag is a quiet farewell that takes the place of a spoken goodbye.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Hiding the knife in Kenji's packed bag shows the father knew he was leaving.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the father's plans to move to the city.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the father opposed Kenji's going; the gift travels with Kenji to the city.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In ancient Athens, citizens could vote to send a powerful person into exile for ten years by scratching that person's name on a piece of broken pottery called an ostrakon. In 1937, archaeologists found about 190 ostraka bearing the name of the politician Themistocles in a single pit near the Acropolis. Analysis of the handwriting showed that they had been inscribed by only about fourteen people, and they appear to have been thrown away unused. Whether these ostraka were meant to sway a vote or to help citizens who could not write is unclear. Either way, the find suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: ostracism votes were counted by a group of about fourteen officials.
choices.B: most citizens of Athens were unable to write names on their own.
choices.C: not every ostrakon was inscribed by the citizen who used it to vote.
choices.D: Themistocles was sent into exile because of these particular ostraka.

explanation.why: About 190 ballots were written by only about fourteen people, so they were prepared for others to use. Whatever the purpose, this shows that some voters could cast an ostrakon that someone else had written.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The fourteen people were the writers of the ostraka; the text says nothing about who counted votes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This goes too far: helping voters who could not write is only one possible purpose, and it would not show that most citizens were unable to write.
explanation.C: Correct. Ballots prepared in bulk by a few writers were meant to be used by other people, so voters did not always write their own.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says these ostraka appear to have been thrown away unused, so they could not have decided any vote.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ice cores drilled from glaciers and ice sheets contain tiny bubbles of ancient air, which scientists analyze to learn what Earth's atmosphere was like in the past. The bubbles do not form when snow first falls, however. Fresh snow is loose and porous, and air from the atmosphere keeps moving through it until the snow has been buried deeply enough to be squeezed into solid ice, a process that can take many years. As a result, the air in a bubble is most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: younger than the ice that surrounds it.
choices.B: older than the ice that surrounds it.
choices.C: useless for learning about the past atmosphere.
choices.D: unchanged from the air of the year the snow fell.

explanation.why: The snow that becomes the ice fell first, but newer air kept moving through it for many years until it was sealed into solid ice. The trapped air therefore comes from a later time than the snow around it.
explanation.A: Correct. Air kept circulating through the snow until it turned to ice, so the trapped air is from later than the snow itself.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the timing: the air is sealed in years after the snow fell, so it is younger, not older.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This goes too far: the text says scientists use the bubbles to study the past atmosphere; the age difference does not make them useless.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Air from the atmosphere kept moving through the snow for years, so the trapped air is not simply air from the year the snow fell.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many ant species distinguish nestmates from outsiders by smell: each worker carries a blend of waxy compounds on its body surface, and workers attack ants whose blend differs too much from their own. Some of these compounds are produced by the ants' own bodies, but others are absorbed from the food they eat. In one laboratory experiment, a single colony of Argentine ants was divided into two halves that were kept apart and fed different kinds of insect prey for several weeks. When workers from the two halves were brought back together, they frequently attacked one another. Because both halves came from the same colony, the experiment suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: diet has little effect on the blend of compounds that ants carry on their bodies.
choices.B: ants in the wild attack only those outsiders that have eaten different food from their own.
choices.C: the two halves of the colony became genetically different during the weeks they were kept apart.
choices.D: diet alone may make closely related ants treat one another as outsiders.

explanation.why: Combine two facts. Some of the compounds ants use to recognize nestmates come from food, and the two groups came from one colony, so they were related and started with the same smell. The only thing the experiment changed was diet, so diet alone was apparently enough to make former nestmates seem like strangers.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This contradicts the result: changing only the diet led to attacks, which suggests diet changed the ants' smell.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The experiment shows that diet can be enough to cause attacks; it does not show that diet is the only cause of attacks among ants in the wild.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests the ants' genes changed; the point of using one colony is that the two groups were related.
explanation.D: Correct. The halves differed only in what they ate, yet they attacked each other, so a diet difference alone may be enough to change how related ants treat one another.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each year, ornithologist Meera Vaghela counts nests at a flamingo breeding colony on the salt flats of Kutch, in western India. The birds nest there only when heavy monsoon rains flood the flats with shallow water that lasts long enough for chicks to be raised; in years of weak rain, the flats stay dry and the site is nearly empty. In one recent year, Vaghela counted thousands of nests, and the following year only a few dozen. Banding studies show that adult flamingos often travel hundreds of kilometers between seasons and commonly live for decades. Given this information, it can most reasonably be concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: heavy monsoon rains in the second year flooded the nests and drove the flamingos away.
choices.B: a low nest count in a given year need not mean that many adults have died.
choices.C: the flamingos left the site in the second year because the colony had grown too crowded.
choices.D: the region's population of adult flamingos fell sharply between the first year and the second.

explanation.why: The text gives two facts that work together. Nesting at the site depends on rain, so in a dry year few birds nest there even if they are alive; and adult flamingos are long-lived and range widely. A sudden drop in nests can therefore reflect conditions at the site rather than deaths among the adults.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the role of rain: heavy rain is what makes the site usable, and weak rain is what leaves it nearly empty.
explanation.B: Correct. Because nesting at the site depends on rain and adults live long and travel far, few nests in one year does not show that the adults died.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions crowding; it links the number of nests to rainfall.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reads the nest count as a population count, but the text shows that nesting depends on rain, so adults can be alive and simply not nesting there.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Members of the fish species Astyanax mexicanus that live in pitch-dark caves in Mexico have greatly reduced eyes or none at all, while members of the same species living in surface rivers have normal eyes. Because the eye and the brain tissue used for vision consume a great deal of energy, biologists have proposed that eyes become a costly burden in total darkness, where they provide no benefit. Biologist Rocío Altamirano compared cave fish from two caves that are equally dark: one receives regular floods that wash in plant debris and insects, while the other receives almost no food from outside. Fish from the food-poor cave had even smaller eyes. If the biologists' proposal is correct, this difference suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the fish in the two caves are descended from two different surface populations.
choices.B: fish in the flood-fed cave will eventually regain fully working eyes.
choices.C: fish in the flood-fed cave use their eyes to find the food that the floods bring in.
choices.D: the cost of maintaining eyes may weigh more heavily on fish where food is scarce.

explanation.why: The proposal says eyes are a burden in the dark because they use energy and give nothing back. Where food, and so energy, is scarcer, that cost should matter more. The fish in the food-poor cave have the smallest eyes, which fits the idea that the energy cost of eyes is felt most where food is scarce.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the ancestry of the two cave populations.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text compares eye size in two caves; it gives no basis for predicting that any cave fish will regain working eyes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Both caves are equally and completely dark, so eyes would give no benefit in either one, including for finding food.
explanation.D: Correct. If eyes are a burden because they use energy, that burden should be heaviest where energy from food is hardest to get, matching the smaller eyes in the food-poor cave.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When medieval scribes copied a text, they sometimes skipped from one line to a later line with the same ending, accidentally leaving out everything in between, an error called eye-skip. Because two scribes rarely make the identical omission independently, when two manuscripts share the same unusual gap, scholars generally conclude either that one was copied from the other or that both descend from a common earlier copy. Philologist Anselm Brandt found that manuscripts P and Q of a twelfth-century poem omit the same three lines at the same point. Analysis of the parchment and handwriting indicates that P was written several decades before Q. If these dates are correct, Brandt's findings indicate that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the scribe of P left out the three lines on purpose because he judged them to be weak.
choices.B: P was copied from Q, which explains why both lack the same three lines.
choices.C: P and Q were both copied from a lost manuscript that already lacked the three lines.
choices.D: P was not copied from Q, though Q may have been copied from P.

explanation.why: A shared gap means one manuscript copied the other or both share an ancestor. A manuscript cannot be copied from one written decades after it, so P cannot come from Q. That leaves two possibilities, Q copied from P or both from a common source, and the text gives no way to choose between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes the omission as the kind of accident scholars call eye-skip and gives no evidence that any scribe left lines out on purpose.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the possible direction of copying: P is decades older than Q, so P cannot have been copied from Q.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A common lost source is one possibility, but Q could just as well have been copied directly from P; the evidence does not decide between them.
explanation.D: Correct. Since P is older, it cannot have been copied from Q, while copying of Q from P remains one of the possibilities the shared gap allows.

items.subject: science
items.passage: At many wind farms in North America, most of the bats killed by turbine blades die on nights with light winds, when the flying insects the bats hunt are most active. A turbine's blades can spin even in such light winds, yet they generate little electricity then, because a turbine's power output rises steeply with wind speed: a modest increase in wind speed produces a large increase in output. Operators can program turbines to hold their blades still until the wind reaches a chosen speed. Taken together, these facts suggest that modestly raising that chosen speed would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: eliminate bat deaths at wind farms while leaving electricity output unchanged.
choices.B: lower electricity output so sharply that the turbines would no longer be worth running.
choices.C: reduce bat deaths while sacrificing a relatively small share of electricity output.
choices.D: increase the number of insects available to bats hunting near wind farms.

explanation.why: Two facts combine. Bats die mostly in light winds, and turbines produce little power in light winds. Keeping the blades still in those conditions should therefore protect many bats while giving up only the small amount of power produced at low wind speeds.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Some output would still be lost, and the text says most deaths, not all, happen in light winds, so this overstates the effect.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the text's point: output at light wind speeds is small, so holding the blades still then costs relatively little electricity.
explanation.C: Correct. Stopping the blades in light winds targets the conditions in which most bats die, and those are the conditions in which turbines produce little power.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about turbines affecting the number of insects.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians often estimate how many people in a past society could read by counting the share of brides and grooms who signed their names in marriage registers rather than making a mark. The method assumes that people who learned to read also learned to write. In eighteenth-century Sweden, however, the Lutheran church required its members to learn to read religious texts, and clergy regularly examined each household's reading ability; writing, by contrast, was neither required by the church nor commonly taught. Applied to Swedish marriage registers from that century, the signature method would therefore most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: show that most Swedes of that time could write as well as read.
choices.B: overstate the share of Swedes who were able to read.
choices.C: be equally unreliable for every European country of that time.
choices.D: understate the share of Swedes who were able to read.

explanation.why: The signature method counts only people who could write. In eighteenth-century Sweden, many people were taught to read but not to write, so many readers would have made a mark instead of signing. Counting signatures would therefore miss those readers.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says writing was not commonly taught, which gives no reason to think most Swedes could write.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the effect: the method misses readers who could not write; it does not add people who could not read.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes conditions in Sweden only; it does not show that the method fails in the same way everywhere.
explanation.D: Correct. Many Swedes learned to read without learning to write, so they would not appear among the signers, making the count too low.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mangrove forests grow where rivers meet the sea, but mangrove species differ in how much salt they can tolerate. In the Indus River delta in Pakistan, earlier surveys recorded several mangrove species growing in substantial numbers. Today a single species, Avicennia marina, makes up the great majority of the delta's mangroves, and it is known to tolerate saltier water than the species that have become scarce. Over the same period, dams and irrigation barrages upstream have sharply reduced the amount of fresh river water reaching the delta, allowing seawater to make its channels saltier. These observations suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the shift in the delta's mangrove species may be linked to its reduced fresh water.
choices.B: Avicennia marina arrived in the delta only after the river's flow had been reduced.
choices.C: the species that became scarce tolerate salt better than Avicennia marina does.
choices.D: restoring the river's flow would cause Avicennia marina to vanish from the delta.

explanation.why: The delta's water has grown saltier as fresh river water declined, and the one species that now dominates is the one best able to tolerate salt. Putting these together suggests, though does not prove, that the reduced fresh water helped shift the delta's mix of species.
explanation.A: Correct. Saltier water favors the salt-tolerant species that now dominates, so the reduced fresh water plausibly helps explain the change.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the delta once had several species but never says Avicennia marina was absent before.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says Avicennia marina tolerates saltier water than the species that have become scarce.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Even if reduced flow helped Avicennia marina dominate, nothing suggests that more fresh water would make it disappear entirely.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Musicologist Ilse Kaarna wanted to know the pitch at which music was performed in a north German town around 1700. The town's church organ, built in 1698, survives and today sounds close to modern standard pitch. Later organ builders who raised an instrument's pitch to keep up with changing fashions usually did so by trimming its pipes, since a shorter pipe sounds higher; lowering a pipe's pitch requires adding metal to lengthen it. Kaarna found that most of the organ's pipes bear trim marks made with tools first used in the mid-1800s, but she found no sign that metal had ever been added. Based on this evidence, Kaarna can most reasonably conclude that the organ ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was the only organ in the region to have its pitch changed after 1700.
choices.B: sounded higher around 1700 than it does today.
choices.C: can reveal nothing about the pitch that musicians used around 1700.
choices.D: probably sounded lower around 1700 than it does today.

explanation.why: Trimming a pipe raises its pitch, and the trim marks were made long after the organ was built. No metal was added, so nothing was done that would have lowered the pitch. The organ's pitch was therefore raised at some point, which means it was probably lower in 1700 than it is now.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text discusses only this one organ and says nothing about other organs in the region.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the evidence: the later trimming raised the pitch, so the organ was most likely lower in 1700, not higher.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The evidence does tell Kaarna something: the direction of the change suggests the pitch around 1700 was lower than today's.
explanation.D: Correct. Later trimming raised the pipes' pitch and nothing lowered it, so the organ most likely sounded lower when it was new.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Whenever the family asked Uncle Matthias to play at a wedding, he gave the same answer: he had sold his violin thirty years ago and had long since forgotten every note. Sofia had always believed him. But on the afternoon she helped him clear out his workshop, she noticed that the fingertips of his left hand were hard and ridged, as a violinist's become from pressing down strings, and that the sleeve of his good coat was dusted with a fine pale powder, like the rosin her own teacher rubbed onto his bow before every lesson. She said nothing, but she began to suspect that her uncle ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: had bought back the very violin he sold thirty years ago.
choices.B: hoped that Sofia would ask her teacher to give him lessons.
choices.C: had never actually learned to play the violin when he was young.
choices.D: still played the violin, despite what he told the family.

explanation.why: Two clues point the same way. Hardened fingertips on the left hand come from pressing violin strings, and the powder on his sleeve looks like rosin used on a bow. Both suggest recent playing, which contradicts his claim to have forgotten the violin.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The clues suggest he plays a violin, but not that it is the same one he sold; he could have any instrument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests that Matthias wants lessons from Sofia's teacher.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The clues suggest the opposite: his fingertips and sleeve show signs of a practiced player, not someone who never learned.
explanation.D: Correct. Fingertips hardened by strings and rosin dust on his sleeve both suggest that he still plays, though he tells the family otherwise.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Planetary scientists often estimate the relative ages of surfaces by counting impact craters: the longer a surface has been exposed, the more craters it accumulates. Lucía Ferreyra compared two plains on Mars. Plain 1 has far fewer small craters than Plain 2, which would ordinarily suggest that Plain 1 is younger. Ferreyra's images show, however, that Plain 1 is blanketed by drifting dust deep enough to fill and hide small craters, though not large ones, and when she counted only craters too large for the dust to conceal, the two plains had nearly identical totals. Ferreyra's findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the two plains may be similar in age.
choices.B: crater counts cannot be used to estimate the ages of planetary surfaces.
choices.C: Plain 2 was struck more often because of its location on Mars.
choices.D: Plain 1 is considerably younger than Plain 2.

explanation.why: Plain 1's shortage of small craters could come from dust hiding them rather than from youth. When Ferreyra counted only large craters, which dust cannot hide, the plains matched. So the evidence points toward similar ages, and the small-crater difference is explained by the dust.
explanation.A: Correct. Large craters, which the dust cannot hide, are about equally common on both plains, so the plains may well be about the same age.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Ferreyra still uses crater counts; she simply counts the craters the dust cannot hide.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never links the number of craters to a plain's location on Mars.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the conclusion the dust evidence undercuts: the missing small craters on Plain 1 can be explained by burial, not youth.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Sociologist Yoon Seo-yeon wanted to estimate how many adults in a large city feel chronically short of time. Her team telephoned randomly chosen households on weekday afternoons and asked whoever answered how often they felt rushed; about one in five respondents said they felt rushed on most days. Yoon notes, though, that the adults most likely to be at home and free to answer a phone on a weekday afternoon are those with fewer work and caregiving duties, and such duties are the most common sources of time pressure. Yoon's observation suggests that the true share of the city's adults who feel rushed on most days is likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: lower than one in five, since people tend to exaggerate how busy they are.
choices.B: impossible to estimate with any kind of survey.
choices.C: about one in five, since the households were chosen at random.
choices.D: higher than the roughly one in five found by the survey.

explanation.why: Choosing households at random does not make the people who answer typical. The adults who answered on weekday afternoons are the ones with fewer duties, and duties are the main cause of feeling rushed. The busiest adults were left out, so the true share is probably higher than the survey's figure.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never suggests that respondents exaggerated; it points to a bias in who answered, which would push the true figure up, not down.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Yoon identifies a problem with this survey's timing, not with every possible survey.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Random households do not guarantee typical respondents; Yoon's point is that the people who answered were less busy than average.
explanation.D: Correct. The survey mostly missed adults with heavy work and caregiving duties, who are the most likely to feel rushed, so the true share is likely higher.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Lahore's air is usually far more polluted in winter than in summer. According to an emissions inventory compiled by environmental scientist Asma Rauf, however, the city's traffic and factories release broadly similar amounts of pollution in every season. In winter, the ground cools rapidly on clear nights, often leaving a layer of cold air near the surface beneath warmer air above, an arrangement known as a temperature inversion. Because the cold air is denser, it does not rise and mix with the air above it, so pollutants released near the ground stay concentrated there. These facts suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: reducing traffic emissions would have no effect on the quality of Lahore's winter air.
choices.B: Lahore's vehicles and factories release more pollution in cold weather than in warm weather.
choices.C: winter weather can worsen Lahore's air even when emissions do not increase.
choices.D: temperature inversions are themselves a major source of the pollutants in Lahore's air.

explanation.why: Combine the two parts of the text. The city's traffic and factories release similar amounts in every season, yet winter air is dirtier; inversions explain the difference by trapping pollution near the ground. So weather alone can make the air worse without any rise in emissions.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Inversions concentrate whatever is released, so the text gives no reason to think lower emissions would make no difference.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This contradicts Rauf's inventory, which finds broadly similar emissions in every season.
explanation.C: Correct. With emissions steady, the inversions that trap pollutants near the ground can account for dirtier winter air.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says inversions trap pollutants; it never says they produce them.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The earliest photographic processes, introduced in the late 1830s, required exposures that could last several minutes. During that time, anything that moved through the scene, such as a walking person or a passing carriage, left too little light in any one spot to register, whereas anything that held still was recorded sharply. Several early views of city boulevards known to have been crowded during the day show almost no one, apart from the occasional figure who happened to stay in place, such as a man standing still while his boots were polished. Viewers who conclude from such images that the boulevards were nearly empty are therefore most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: mistaking a limitation of the process for a feature of the scene.
choices.B: overlooking crowds that the photographers later scraped off the plates.
choices.C: correct, since the photographs recorded everything within the frame.
choices.D: wrong to trust any image produced by the photographic processes of the 1830s.

explanation.why: The long exposure meant that moving people left no image, while still figures did. The boulevards were known to be crowded, so their emptiness in the photographs comes from the process, not from the streets themselves.
explanation.A: Correct. Moving crowds did not register during the long exposures, so the empty look of the boulevards reflects how the process worked rather than what was there.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives exposure time, not any retouching by photographers, as the reason crowds are missing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: moving people and carriages did not register, so the photographs did not record everything in the frame.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Still objects, such as buildings and the man having his boots polished, were recorded sharply, so the images are not worthless.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Historical dictionaries date each word by the earliest written use their editors can find. As huge collections of old newspapers, letters, and pamphlets have been digitized and made searchable, editors have repeatedly found uses of familiar words decades older than the dates previously given in their entries. Lexicographer Tendai Moyo points out that a word must already be in use before anyone writes it down, and that a newly discovered document can reveal a use older than a word's recorded date but can never show that the word first appeared later than a text already found. It follows that, as more archives are searched, the recorded first dates of words ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: will tend to move earlier or else remain unchanged.
choices.B: will be accurate for words found in newspapers but not for those in letters.
choices.C: will eventually match the dates on which the words were first spoken.
choices.D: will tend to move later as more documents come to light.

explanation.why: Moyo makes two points. A newly found document can push a word's first recorded date earlier, but it cannot push it later, since the older text already found still exists. Searching more archives can therefore only move dates earlier or leave them where they are.
explanation.A: Correct. New documents can only reveal earlier uses, never later ones, so recorded dates can only move earlier or stay the same.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text does not compare the accuracy of dates from newspapers with dates from letters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Since words are in use before anyone writes them down, written records may never reach the date a word was first spoken.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses Moyo's point that a new document can never show a word appeared later than a text already found.

items.subject: history_social
