items.passage: Before a canal linked an inland farming district to a coastal city in the 1820s, hauling grain overland was so expensive that wheat sold in the city for nearly twice its price in the district. Economic historian Bilal Okonkwo compiled wheat prices for both places over the decade after the canal opened. By the end of that decade, the gap between the two prices had nearly disappeared, yet the city's wheat price had fallen only slightly. Okonkwo's data therefore imply that, over the same decade, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: wheat prices rose in every farming district that was linked to a city by canal.
choices.B: the canal lowered the price of wheat in both the city and the district.
choices.C: farmers in the district sold less of their wheat to the city than before.
choices.D: the price of wheat in the farming district rose substantially.

explanation.why: Start with a gap: the city price was nearly double the district price. If the gap nearly closed while the city price fell only a little, the district price must have climbed most of the way up to meet it. That means wheat became much more expensive in the district.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Okonkwo's data cover one district and one city, so they cannot show what happened in every canal-linked district.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If the district price had fallen too, the gap could not have closed while the city price dropped only slightly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text gives no figures on how much wheat was sold, and cheaper transport would if anything make selling to the city easier.
explanation.D: Correct. Since the city's price barely fell, the nearly closed gap means the district's price must have risen a great deal.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Seawater absorbs red light far more strongly than blue light, so the faint sunlight that reaches depths of several hundred meters is almost entirely blue. Most of the light that deep-sea animals produce themselves is blue as well, and the eyes of most deep-sea species contain no pigments sensitive to red wavelengths. A few species of dragonfish are striking exceptions: in addition to the usual blue light, they emit red light from organs beneath their eyes, and their own eyes, unlike those of most of their neighbors, can detect it. For these dragonfish, the red light most likely provides a way to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: remain completely invisible to every predator in the deep ocean.
choices.B: signal to other dragonfish across long distances, since red light carries far in seawater.
choices.C: illuminate nearby animals without most of those animals perceiving the light.
choices.D: avoid competing with other species for the blue light produced at great depths.

explanation.why: Combine what the text says about the light and about eyes. The dragonfish produce red light and can see it, while most deep-sea animals cannot see red at all. The dragonfish can therefore light up their surroundings with a beam that most other animals do not notice.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The dragonfish also give off ordinary blue light, which other animals can see, so they are not invisible to everything.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says seawater absorbs red light strongly, so red light would not carry far; this reverses the text.
explanation.C: Correct. Because most deep-sea animals cannot detect red light but the dragonfish can, the red light lets them see nearby animals without being noticed by most of them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never suggests that animals compete for blue light or that the red light helps avoid such competition.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At Mehrgarh, a Neolithic site in Balochistan, Pakistan, archaeologists found small, neat holes in the molars of several adults buried between about 9,000 and 7,500 years ago. The holes are nearly perfect cones, matching the shape produced by the flint-tipped bow drills that the site's residents used to bore holes in beads. Many of the drilled teeth are back molars, which would have been difficult to reach inside a living person's mouth. On some of these teeth, though, the edges of the holes are smoothly worn, a kind of wear that forms only when a tooth continues to be used for chewing over a long period. Taken together, these observations suggest that at least some of the holes were most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: drilled while their owners were still alive and using their teeth.
choices.B: made after death, since back molars would have been hard to reach in a living mouth.
choices.C: drilled to cure tooth decay that affected most of the people living at Mehrgarh.
choices.D: made with metal tools that were later adapted for drilling holes in beads.

explanation.why: The difficulty of reaching back molars might suggest the holes were made after death, but the worn edges settle the question for some teeth: that wear forms only through continued chewing. A tooth that went on being used for chewing after it was drilled must have been drilled in a living person.
explanation.A: Correct. Smooth wear around the holes forms only through continued chewing, so those teeth must have been drilled while the people were alive.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the tempting conclusion the worn edges rule out: chewing continued after the drilling, which only a living person could do.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not say why the holes were drilled or how many residents had tooth decay.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the drills were flint-tipped and the same kind used for beads; it never mentions metal tools.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Neoclassical sculptors of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, hoping to revive the art of ancient Greece, carved gleaming white marble figures and praised the purity of unpainted stone, a quality they believed the ancient Greeks had prized. The ancient statues they studied had, for the most part, lain buried or stood exposed to the weather for many centuries. Using ultraviolet light and chemical analysis, researchers have since detected traces of paint on many such statues, sometimes in arrangements indicating patterned clothing, colored eyes, and tinted skin, and the binders and many of the pigments used in ancient paint are known to break down over long periods underground or outdoors. These findings suggest that the neoclassical sculptors ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: would have painted their own figures if suitable pigments had been available to them.
choices.B: were wrong to admire any feature of ancient Greek sculpture.
choices.C: knew that ancient statues had been painted but chose to leave their own works white.
choices.D: may have taken the effects of centuries of decay for the intentions of ancient artists.

explanation.why: Two pieces of information combine. The statues the sculptors studied had spent centuries buried or outdoors, and ancient paint is known to break down in those conditions. The whiteness the sculptors admired as an ancient ideal may therefore have been the result of paint wearing away.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never suggests that the sculptors lacked pigments or wanted to paint their figures.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The findings concern only the sculptors' belief about unpainted stone, not every feature they admired.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the sculptors believed the ancient Greeks prized unpainted stone, so they did not know the statues had been painted.
explanation.D: Correct. The paint on the statues had largely broken down over the centuries, so the white stone the sculptors admired probably reflected decay, not the original artists' choices.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Radiocarbon dating estimates age from the amount of carbon-14 remaining in once-living material. Because the deep ocean exchanges carbon with the atmosphere only slowly, the carbon in seawater is relatively poor in carbon-14; as a result, fish and shellfish yield radiocarbon dates centuries older than those of land plants that lived at the same time, and so do the bones of people who ate mostly seafood. At a coastal cemetery, archaeologist Noa Halevi obtained dates for skeletons roughly 400 years older than the dates of charcoal from a funeral hearth sealed in the same undisturbed layer as the graves. Chemical analysis of the bones indicates a diet dominated by fish. Halevi's results therefore suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: charcoal from land plants gives less dependable radiocarbon dates than bone does.
choices.B: the bones' older dates may not mean that the burials came before the hearth.
choices.C: radiocarbon dates obtained from any human bone are about 400 years too old.
choices.D: the hearth was first lit roughly four centuries after the people in the graves had died.

explanation.why: Taken at face value, the dates would put the burials four centuries before the hearth. But the people ate mostly fish, and a seafood diet makes bones date older than they are, while the hearth and graves lie in the same undisturbed layer. The age gap can therefore be explained by diet, so it does not show that the burials were earlier.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says charcoal gives unreliable dates; the problem it describes affects material from seafood eaters, such as these bones.
explanation.B: Correct. A seafood diet makes bones date older, so the 400-year gap could come from diet rather than from the burials preceding the hearth.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The effect applies to people who ate mostly seafood, not to all human bone, and its size need not always be 400 years.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This takes the bone dates at face value, ignoring that a fish-heavy diet makes bones appear centuries older than they are.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Penhallow had let it be known, at every tea table in Ashcombe, that she thought the new schoolmaster's methods absurd: he took the children into the fields to count wildflowers, and he permitted them to ask questions in the middle of a lesson. When the parish council proposed that his salary be reduced, the vicar received an unsigned letter arguing, at considerable length and with some heat, that the village had never been better served. The vicar, who had exchanged notes with Miss Penhallow about the church flowers every week for twenty years, recognized the handwriting at once, and he folded the letter away without mentioning it to anyone. These details suggest that Miss Penhallow's public criticisms of the schoolmaster ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: were shared by the vicar, who had long been her friend.
choices.B: did not fully reflect her view of his value to the village.
choices.C: had given way to approval of every one of his methods.
choices.D: expressed a sincere hope that he would soon leave Ashcombe.

explanation.why: The passage connects two details. The unsigned letter defends the schoolmaster warmly, and the vicar recognizes the handwriting from twenty years of Miss Penhallow's notes, so she wrote it. Her complaints at tea tables therefore did not tell the whole story of what she thought of him.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never reveals the vicar's own view of the schoolmaster's methods.
explanation.B: Correct. Her unsigned letter, recognized by the vicar, praises the schoolmaster's service, so her public complaints were not the whole of her opinion.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The letter defends his value to the village; it does not show that she had come to approve of all his methods.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Her secret letter argues against cutting his salary, which hardly fits a wish for him to leave.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In one sixteenth-century European kingdom, laborers were paid in silver coins, and merchants generally priced goods according to the amount of silver a coin actually contained rather than the value stamped on it. Between 1540 and 1560, the crown repeatedly reduced the silver content of its coins, so that by 1560 a coin held less than half the silver it had held in 1540, while the prices of bread and other basic goods, measured in silver, changed little. Historian Margit Lindqvist found that the daily wage recorded for building laborers in the kingdom's capital doubled over the same period. Lindqvist's findings suggest that, compared with laborers in 1540, laborers in 1560 most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: could buy about twice as much with a day's wages as before.
choices.B: were paid partly in gold to protect them from the loss of silver.
choices.C: earned more than workers in any other part of the kingdom.
choices.D: could buy less with a day's wages, even though they received more coins.

explanation.why: Work out the silver in a day's pay. Laborers got twice as many coins, but each coin held less than half as much silver, so a day's pay held less silver than before. Since goods were priced by silver and those prices barely changed, a day's wages bought less in 1560 than in 1540.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This takes the doubled wage at face value, ignoring that each coin contained less than half its former silver.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says laborers were paid in silver coins and never mentions payment in gold.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Lindqvist's data cover building laborers in the capital only, so they cannot show how their pay compared with that of all other workers.
explanation.D: Correct. Twice as many coins, each with less than half the silver, means less silver per day; with silver prices steady, that buys less.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the late 1800s, the railways of British India were built to two main track widths: broad-gauge trunk lines and cheaper meter-gauge lines serving many outlying districts. Trains built for one gauge could not run on the other, so freight passing between the two networks had to be unloaded from one train and reloaded onto another at junction stations, a process that added labor costs and days of delay and often damaged goods. Economic historian Aditya Venkataraman found that after a meter-gauge line connected one cotton-growing district to a broad-gauge junction, the district's shipments to a distant broad-gauge port rose far less than those of a comparable district that was connected directly by broad-gauge track. Venkataraman's findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the directly connected district grew far more cotton than the other district did.
choices.B: building meter-gauge lines instead of broad-gauge lines saved railway companies no money.
choices.C: transferring freight between gauges may have limited some districts' gains from rail links.
choices.D: meter-gauge lines were unable to carry cotton at all.

explanation.why: Two districts that were otherwise comparable both gained rail links, but only one had to send its cotton through a change of gauge, with the extra cost, delay, and damage that involved. That district's shipments grew much less, which suggests the transfer between gauges reduced the benefit of its rail connection.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text calls the districts comparable and gives no evidence that one grew far more cotton.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This contradicts the text, which calls the meter-gauge lines cheaper.
explanation.C: Correct. The district whose cotton had to be moved between gauges gained much less than a comparable district linked directly, pointing to the cost of the transfer.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The meter-gauge district's shipments did rise, just much less, so its line clearly carried some cotton.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before the late 1920s, record companies had not agreed on a standard turntable speed, and discs were recorded at anywhere from about 70 to 90 revolutions per minute; today such discs are usually played back at 78. Playing a disc faster than it was recorded raises the pitch of everything on it. Music historian Kwabena Asante studied a 1910 recording of an aria by a celebrated soprano. Played at 78, it sounds almost a half step higher than the key in which the aria is written, and several critics have cited it as evidence that she sang the piece above its written key to show off her range. Asante found company records showing that the studio's recording machines ran at about 74 revolutions per minute in 1910, a difference that would raise the pitch by nearly a half step. Asante's research suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the critics' conclusion may reflect playback speed rather than the soprano's singing.
choices.B: the soprano deliberately sang the aria about a half step above its written key.
choices.C: the studio's recording machines ran too slowly to capture the soprano's highest notes.
choices.D: every disc recorded before the late 1920s sounds too high when played at 78.

explanation.why: The disc was recorded at about 74 but is played at 78, which is faster, and playing faster raises the pitch by nearly a half step. That is almost exactly how far above the written key the recording sounds. So the high pitch can be explained by the playback speed, and the critics' claim about her singing is not supported by this recording.
explanation.A: Correct. Playing a disc recorded at 74 at a speed of 78 raises the pitch by nearly a half step, which explains the recording's high pitch without assuming the soprano sang above the key.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the critics' view, which Asante's evidence undercuts: the faster playback alone accounts for the higher pitch.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never suggests that the slower machines failed to record any notes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Discs were recorded at speeds from about 70 to 90, so those recorded faster than 78 would sound lower, not higher, when played at 78.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Earthquakes send two main kinds of waves through Earth's interior. Primary (P) waves compress and stretch the material they pass through and can travel through solids and liquids alike; secondary (S) waves shake material from side to side, a motion that only a rigid material can pass along, so S waves cannot travel through liquid. Early twentieth-century seismologists found that seismometers fairly close to an earthquake, reached by waves traveling only through the mantle, recorded both kinds of waves. Seismometers on the side of Earth roughly opposite the earthquake, reached only by paths that pass through the core, recorded P waves, though bent and delayed, but no direct S waves. These observations indicate that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: at least part of Earth's core is liquid rather than solid.
choices.B: P waves are unable to pass through Earth's core.
choices.C: Earth's mantle is liquid, since waves traveling through it are recorded.
choices.D: Earth's entire core, from its boundary to its center, is liquid.

explanation.why: S waves crossed the mantle but never arrived along paths through the core. Since S waves are stopped only by liquid, something along those core paths must be liquid. The observations show that at least part of the core is liquid, not that all of it is.
explanation.A: Correct. S waves travel through the mantle but are missing along every path through the core, and only liquid stops them, so some of the core must be liquid.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This contradicts the text, which says P waves did reach the far side, though bent and delayed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. S waves passed through the mantle, which shows that the mantle is rigid, not liquid.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Blocking S waves requires only a liquid layer somewhere along the path; the observations do not show that the whole core is liquid.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the streets of Pompeii, the Roman town buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, archaeologists have found well over a thousand painted notices urging residents to vote for particular candidates in local elections. Many of the notices were painted by professional sign writers, whom candidates or their supporters paid for the work. The notices appear not only near the grand houses of wealthy families but also along ordinary commercial streets, on the walls of bakeries, workshops, and taverns frequented by laborers and shopkeepers. Taken together, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: candidates probably expected many ordinary passersby to be able to read the notices.
choices.B: only wealthy citizens were allowed to vote in Pompeii's local elections.
choices.C: most residents of Pompeii could write as well as read.
choices.D: the sign writers chose where to paint the notices without consulting the candidates.

explanation.why: Candidates paid professionals to paint these notices, so they presumably wanted them read. Placing them on streets and shops used by laborers and shopkeepers would make sense only if candidates believed many ordinary people could read them.
explanation.A: Correct. Paying to place written appeals where laborers and shopkeepers passed suggests candidates expected many of those people to read them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Painting appeals on walls frequented by laborers and shopkeepers suggests candidates sought ordinary residents' votes, not only the wealthy's.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Painted notices say something about reading, not writing, and professionals did much of the painting.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says candidates or supporters paid for the notices but says nothing about who chose their locations.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In her first week at the conservatory, Celestine heard Madame Roux tell the assembled students that correctness was "the virtue of a metronome" and that she had no wish to train metronomes. For the rest of the term, Madame Roux spent much of each class urging the students to take risks with phrasing, and she praised a boy named Anton, whose performances were often untidy, for his "daring." When Celestine finished her own piece at the last class of the term, every note in place, Madame Roux nodded, said that it was "perfectly correct," and turned to the next student. Celestine walked home slowly, the phrase echoing in her ears. The details of the text suggest that Madame Roux's comment on Celestine's performance was most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: an expression of disappointment that Celestine had played several wrong notes.
choices.B: an admission that she had changed her mind about the importance of correctness.
choices.C: a sign that she considered Celestine the most gifted student she had ever taught.
choices.D: less approving than its words might seem on their own.

explanation.why: Connect the comment to Madame Roux's first-week remark. She called correctness "the virtue of a metronome" and said she had no wish to train metronomes, so calling Celestine's playing "perfectly correct" is faint praise at best. Celestine's slow walk home suggests she heard it that way too.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says every note was in place, so the comment cannot be about wrong notes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no sign that Madame Roux changed her view; her brief nod and quick move to the next student suggest she had not.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing suggests such high regard; Madame Roux's warmest praise that term went to Anton's daring, not to correctness.
explanation.D: Correct. Because Madame Roux had dismissed correctness as a metronome's virtue, calling the performance "perfectly correct" was likely faint praise.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: An ancient Greek medical treatise survives in a dozen Greek manuscripts, all of which scholars have traced to a single copy made in Constantinople in the tenth century. The treatise also survives in an Arabic translation that a ninth-century translator in Baghdad prepared from a different Greek manuscript, one older than the Constantinople copy and unrelated to it. The Arabic version contains a long passage on treating fevers that appears in none of the Greek manuscripts. Some editors have concluded that the translator must have composed the passage himself, citing its absence from every surviving Greek copy. Given the history of the manuscripts, this reasoning is questionable because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the Arabic translator is known to have added passages to other works that he translated.
choices.B: Greek manuscripts are generally less reliable than translations made from them.
choices.C: the passage on fevers is written in a style typical of Arabic medical writing of the ninth century.
choices.D: all the Greek copies could share a single omission inherited from their common source.

explanation.why: The editors treat twelve Greek manuscripts as twelve separate witnesses, but they all descend from one tenth-century copy. If that one copy lacked the passage, every later copy would lack it too. Meanwhile, the Arabic translation was made from an older, independent manuscript that may have preserved it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text says this about the translator, and such a fact would support the editors rather than weaken their reasoning.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text makes no general claim about the reliability of Greek manuscripts compared with translations.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A style typical of Arabic medicine would support the editors' conclusion, not cast doubt on their reasoning.
explanation.D: Correct. Because all the Greek copies come from one source, their shared silence counts as a single piece of evidence: one lost passage in that source would explain it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In continuously flooded rice paddies, the waterlogged soil contains almost no oxygen, conditions in which certain microbes thrive and release methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Under a practice called alternate wetting and drying, which agricultural agencies in Bangladesh have promoted, farmers let their fields dry out for several days at a time between floodings. Soil scientist Farhana Chowdhury measured emissions from paired plots and found that the practice cut methane emissions by nearly half. She also found, however, that the drying periods increased emissions of nitrous oxide, another greenhouse gas that soil microbes produce as wet soil begins to dry out. Chowdhury's findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the practice raises the total greenhouse gas emissions of rice fields rather than lowering them.
choices.B: farmers who use the practice harvest less rice than farmers who keep their fields flooded.
choices.C: the practice may benefit the climate less than its methane savings alone would suggest.
choices.D: nitrous oxide is released mainly while fields remain continuously flooded.

explanation.why: Chowdhury found a gain and a cost. Drying cut methane by nearly half but raised nitrous oxide, another greenhouse gas. Without knowing how large the nitrous oxide increase was, we can say only that the overall benefit is smaller than the methane figure suggests, not that it disappears.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no amounts for the nitrous oxide increase, so it cannot show that total emissions rose.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about rice harvests under either practice.
explanation.C: Correct. Lower methane is partly offset by higher nitrous oxide, so the overall climate benefit is likely smaller than the methane cut by itself implies.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says nitrous oxide rose during the drying periods, as wet soil dries out.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In a number of psychology experiments, two groups of students were given the same science passage and the same total amount of study time. One group spent the whole time rereading the passage, while the other read it once and then spent the remaining time writing down everything they could recall without looking back. Immediately afterward, the students who had reread predicted that they would remember more of the passage a week later than the students in the recall group predicted for themselves. A week later, however, it was the recall group that remembered substantially more. If these results hold generally, they suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: rereading a passage does not help students remember any of its content.
choices.B: the students in the recall group spent more time studying than the students who reread.
choices.C: students' own sense of which study method works better may be an unreliable guide.
choices.D: the recall group remembered more because they found the passage more interesting.

explanation.why: Compare the predictions with the results. The rereading group expected to remember more, but the recall group actually did. Students' confidence pointed to the weaker method, so how well students feel they have learned may not tell them which method works best.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The rereaders remembered less than the recall group, not nothing; the results do not show rereading is useless.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says both groups had the same total study time.
explanation.C: Correct. The rereaders felt more confident yet remembered less, so students' impressions of which method works may mislead them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions how interesting the students found the passage.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Scientists have long debated whether most of Earth's ocean water was delivered by comets or by asteroids that struck the young planet. One clue is the ratio of deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, to ordinary hydrogen in water: the ratio differs among bodies that formed in different parts of the early solar system and is thought to have changed little in Earth's oceans since they formed. Of the comets whose water has been measured, most have a ratio roughly two to three times that of Earth's oceans, although a few match the oceans closely. Water locked in a common type of carbon-rich meteorite, believed to come from asteroids, has a ratio close to that of the oceans. These measurements suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: comets contain far less water than carbon-rich meteorites do.
choices.B: asteroids delivered all of the water now found in Earth's oceans.
choices.C: comets like most of those measured probably did not supply most of Earth's ocean water.
choices.D: the deuterium ratio of Earth's ocean water has risen steadily since the oceans formed.

explanation.why: If most ocean water came from comets like the typical ones measured, the oceans would have a much higher deuterium ratio than they do. The ratio is thought to have stayed fairly constant, so the mismatch counts against such comets as the main source. The asteroid material matches, but a few comets do too, so the evidence does not rule out every other source.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text compares the deuterium ratios of the water, not how much water comets and meteorites contain.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The close match with asteroid material is suggestive, but a few comets also match, so the evidence cannot show that asteroids supplied all the water.
explanation.C: Correct. Most measured comets have a ratio two to three times the oceans', so water from comets like them would not match Earth's oceans.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This contradicts the text, which says the oceans' ratio is thought to have changed little since they formed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The frilled lizard of northern Australia and New Guinea has a wide flap of skin around its neck that usually lies folded flat. When a predator comes close, the lizard opens its mouth, hisses, and spreads the frill so that its head suddenly looks several times larger. The frill is made only of thin skin supported by slender rods of cartilage, and it cannot bite, cut, or sting. If the display fails, the lizard turns and runs for the nearest tree. This suggests that the frill protects the lizard by ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: startling predators rather than by causing them any physical harm.
choices.B: injuring any predator that tries to attack the lizard's neck.
choices.C: making the lizard appear smaller and harder for predators to notice.
choices.D: helping the lizard climb trees faster than its predators can.

explanation.why: The text says the frill cannot bite, cut, or sting, so it cannot hurt a predator. What it does is make the lizard's head look suddenly much larger. The frill must therefore work by frightening predators, not by harming them.
explanation.A: Correct. A sudden, harmless increase in apparent size can only protect the lizard by scaring the predator off.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text states that the frill is thin skin that cannot bite, cut, or sting, so it cannot injure anything.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says the frill makes the head look several times larger, not smaller.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The lizard runs to a tree only after the display fails; the text does not connect the frill to climbing.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Derawar Fort rises from the flat sands of the Cholistan Desert in Punjab, Pakistan. Its forty round bastions and walls some thirty meters high can be seen from many kilometers away. Today the land around the fort is sparsely settled and receives very little rain. Yet the fort stands beside the dry bed of the Hakra, a river that flowed through Cholistan thousands of years ago, and archaeologists have recorded the remains of hundreds of ancient settlements strung along that same riverbed. These remains suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the Hakra still carries water underground during the rainy season.
choices.B: the region once supported far more people than it does today.
choices.C: Derawar Fort was built by the people who lived in the ancient settlements.
choices.D: the ancient settlements were abandoned because the fort was built.

explanation.why: The land is nearly empty now, but hundreds of ancient settlements once lined the riverbed when the Hakra flowed. Many settlements mean many people, so the region must once have been much more heavily populated than it is today.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text calls the riverbed dry and says nothing about underground water or a rainy season.
explanation.B: Correct. Hundreds of settlements along a river that once flowed point to a large past population in an area that is now sparsely settled.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not say who built the fort, and the settlements date from thousands of years ago.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the text links the fort to the settlements' abandonment; the settlements are far older.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On the first rainy afternoon of October, Jonas lent his umbrella to the new boy at the bus stop, a quiet student named Emeka who had arrived with nothing but a thin jacket. The umbrella was an old one, with a cracked wooden handle wrapped in tape and one bent rib. A week later, Emeka handed it back. The handle was now smooth, freshly varnished wood, and the bent rib had been replaced. Emeka said only, "Thanks," and walked away. The condition of the returned umbrella suggests that Emeka ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was embarrassed that he had damaged the umbrella during the week.
choices.B: had taken the trouble to repair the umbrella before returning it.
choices.C: planned to ask Jonas to lend him the umbrella again soon.
choices.D: had lost the original umbrella and bought a new one to replace it.

explanation.why: The umbrella went out with a taped, cracked handle and a bent rib and came back with a varnished handle and a replaced rib. It is the same umbrella, now fixed, so Emeka must have repaired it before giving it back.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The damage was already there when Jonas lent the umbrella; Emeka repaired it rather than causing it.
explanation.B: Correct. The specific repairs to the handle and rib show that Emeka fixed the umbrella.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests Emeka wanted to borrow the umbrella again.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes the same umbrella with its handle refinished and one rib replaced, not a new umbrella.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the Namib Desert of southwestern Africa, rain may not fall for years at a time, but on many mornings a thick fog rolls in from the cold Atlantic coast. Several species of darkling beetle climb to the tops of sand dunes before dawn and tilt their bodies head-down into the fog. Droplets of water collect on the beetle's bumpy back, join together, and run down to its mouth. This behavior suggests that the beetles ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: climb the dunes mainly to warm themselves in the first sunlight.
choices.B: can obtain the water they need even where rain is very rare.
choices.C: can survive only in parts of the desert where rain falls each year.
choices.D: store water in their bodies for months between fogs.

explanation.why: Rain is almost absent, but fog arrives on many mornings, and the beetles collect droplets from that fog and drink them. So the beetles get water from the fog, which means they can meet their water needs in a place where rain hardly ever falls.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the beetles tilt into the fog to collect water, not that they seek warmth or sunlight.
explanation.B: Correct. Drinking fog droplets lets the beetles get water without rain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the point: the beetles live where rain may not fall for years and get water from fog instead.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about storing water; fog comes on many mornings, so long storage is not implied.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When a traditional Dutch windmill is not working, the miller can stop its four sails in any position. Over the centuries, millers in the Netherlands developed a code based on where the sails came to rest: an upright cross meant a short break, a diagonal cross a longer stop, sails stopped just before the top a celebration, and sails stopped just past the top mourning. Since a mill's sails can be seen from far across the flat countryside, this code allowed ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the sails to turn in strong winds without being damaged.
choices.B: people at a distance to learn the mill's news without visiting it.
choices.C: each miller to keep the events of the household private.
choices.D: millers to grind grain more quickly during busy seasons.

explanation.why: The code is read from the resting position of sails that can be seen from far away. A signal that is visible across the countryside is useful because people do not need to come to the mill to learn what it says.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text concerns stopped sails and messages, not protecting the sails from wind.
explanation.B: Correct. Visible sails plus an agreed code let distant people read the mill's messages.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the purpose: the code announces events such as celebrations and mourning rather than hiding them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The code applies when the mill is stopped; it has nothing to do with the speed of grinding.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, English officials recorded debts and payments on tally sticks. A clerk cut notches into a wooden stick to show the amount, then split the stick lengthwise so that the notches ran across both halves. The treasury kept one half, and the person who had paid or was owed the money kept the other. To check the debt later, the two halves were fitted together. Because wood splits along an irregular path and no two sticks have the same grain, this method meant that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: tally sticks had to be replaced whenever the wood began to dry out.
choices.B: a forged half would be easy to detect, since it would not fit the genuine one.
choices.C: clerks could record much larger sums than written documents allowed.
choices.D: either half of a tally could be read on its own without the other.

explanation.why: The halves are checked by fitting them together, and the text stresses that wood splits irregularly and every stick's grain is unique. A false half made separately could not match the split or the grain of the real one, so forgery would be obvious.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about wood drying out or sticks being replaced.
explanation.B: Correct. A unique split and grain mean only the original matching half will fit, exposing any fake.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text compares nothing about the size of sums that tallies or documents could record.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the halves were fitted together to check a debt, which implies both halves were needed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Chilika, a large lagoon on the east coast of India, is home to a small population of Irrawaddy dolphins. Tour boats take visitors out to see them, and most of the boats work in the channels nearest the tourist villages. Wildlife biologist Pratap Sahoo counted dolphins across the lagoon for a year and found that the fish the dolphins eat were about equally common in every channel he studied. Nevertheless, he recorded far fewer dolphins in the channels with the heaviest boat traffic. His findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: tour boats help visitors see dolphins that would otherwise stay hidden.
choices.B: the dolphins prefer channels where fish are most plentiful.
choices.C: the number of dolphins in the lagoon rose over the course of the year.
choices.D: boat traffic, rather than food supply, may explain where the dolphins gather.

explanation.why: Food was equally available everywhere, so food cannot explain why some channels had fewer dolphins. The channels that had fewer dolphins were exactly those with the most boats, so boat traffic is the likely explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The dolphins avoided the areas with the most boats; nothing suggests the boats help reveal them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Fish were about equally common in all the channels, so food supply cannot account for the differences.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not describe any change in dolphin numbers over the year.
explanation.D: Correct. With food held roughly equal, the only difference the text offers is boat traffic, which matches the pattern.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Helena had been standing under the arrivals board for an hour, her coat buttoned to the chin. Every few minutes she looked up at the board, though only one train from the north was due that evening, and its time had not changed. When the train was finally announced, she pressed forward to the barrier before the first passengers had even stepped down, searching each face. The last to come through was a young woman with a battered suitcase, and Helena's hands went to her mouth. The way Helena waited suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: she had come to the station to catch a train herself.
choices.B: she did not know which train the young woman would be on.
choices.C: she was anxious to meet someone whose arrival mattered greatly to her.
choices.D: she was worried that the train would be canceled because of the weather.

explanation.why: Helena watches the board constantly even though nothing changes, rushes to the barrier before anyone gets off, and studies every face. Her reaction when the young woman appears confirms that she was waiting for a particular person who was very important to her.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Helena waits at the arrivals board and the barrier, watching passengers come through, not departing herself.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says only one train from the north was due, so Helena knew which train to watch for.
explanation.C: Correct. Her constant checking, eager rush to the barrier, and emotional reaction show she was anxiously awaiting someone important.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text mentions neither weather nor any fear that the train would be canceled.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most animals use more energy the faster they move, but kangaroos are an exception over a wide range of hopping speeds. Long, springy tendons in a kangaroo's legs stretch when it lands and then snap back, returning much of the energy of each landing to the next hop. Researchers who measured the oxygen used by red kangaroos hopping on a treadmill found that the animals used almost no more oxygen at a fast hop than at a slow one. These measurements suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: hopping faster costs a kangaroo little extra energy.
choices.B: the tendons in a kangaroo's legs are longer than those of other animals.
choices.C: kangaroos cannot hop for long without becoming exhausted.
choices.D: red kangaroos use more energy at slow speeds than at fast ones.

explanation.why: The oxygen an animal uses is a measure of the energy it spends. The kangaroos used almost no more oxygen at a fast hop than at a slow one, so going faster must cost them almost no extra energy, which fits the explanation about the springy tendons.
explanation.A: Correct. Nearly equal oxygen use at slow and fast speeds means little added energy cost for speed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text does not compare kangaroo tendons with those of other animals.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes an energy-saving mechanism and says nothing about exhaustion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says oxygen use was almost the same at both speeds, not higher at slow speeds.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Visitors to medieval European cathedrals sometimes notice small symbols cut into the stones: an arrow, a star, a letter-like shape. Each stonemason who worked on a building chose a personal symbol and cut it into the blocks he had shaped. On many building sites, masons were paid not by the day but for each finished stone, and the site's overseer kept the accounts. The presence of these marks suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: masons carved the symbols to show visitors how the cathedral had been built.
choices.B: the marks let the overseer tell which mason had shaped each stone and pay him accordingly.
choices.C: masons were paid more for stones that carried their symbol than for stones without it.
choices.D: every stone in a cathedral was shaped by the same small group of masons.

explanation.why: Each mason had his own mark and was paid per finished stone, while an overseer kept the accounts. To pay the right mason for the right stones, the overseer had to know who shaped each one, and the personal marks provide exactly that information.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text links the marks to the masons' pay, not to any message for visitors.
explanation.B: Correct. Personal marks plus payment per stone point to the marks as a record of who shaped what.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not compare pay for marked and unmarked stones; the marks identify the mason, not a higher rate.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text implies many masons with different marks, not one small group shaping every stone.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The town of Uch Sharif in Punjab, Pakistan, is known for a group of tombs built in the fifteenth century and covered with patterns of blue and white glazed tiles. The most famous, the tomb of Bibi Jawindi, was built as an eight-sided structure with the same design repeated on every side. In 1817, floodwaters washed away roughly half of the building. Because the tomb's design was so regular, the half that still stands allows conservators to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: determine the exact date on which the tomb was finished.
choices.B: identify the names of the craftsmen who made the tiles.
choices.C: work out how the parts that were lost must have looked.
choices.D: replace the missing half using the original fifteenth-century tiles.

explanation.why: The tomb had eight identical sides, and half of it survives. Since the design was repeated on every side, the surviving sides show what the lost sides looked like, so conservators can reconstruct the missing half's appearance.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A repeated design tells conservators about the shape of the lost parts, not about the completion date.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no information about the craftsmen or their names.
explanation.C: Correct. A symmetrical design means the surviving half is a model for the half that was lost.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the tiles on the missing half were washed away, so the original tiles are not available.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A shark's skin feels rough because it is covered with millions of tiny tooth-shaped scales called denticles. Engineers who studied the scales wondered whether they affect how easily a shark moves through water. They built two model surfaces of the same size and shape, one perfectly smooth and the other covered with a pattern copied from the denticles, and pulled both through a tank of water at the same speed. The surface with the denticle pattern met less resistance from the water than the smooth one did. This result suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the shape of a shark's body matters more than the texture of its skin.
choices.B: sharks swim faster than any other kind of fish.
choices.C: a textured surface can move through water more easily than a smooth one.
choices.D: a rough surface always meets more resistance in water than a smooth one.

explanation.why: The two surfaces differed only in texture, and the one with the denticle pattern met less resistance. So the textured surface, not the smooth one, slipped through the water more easily.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Body shape was held the same in the experiment, so no comparison with texture was made.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The experiment compared two surfaces, not sharks with other fish.
explanation.C: Correct. With size and shape equal, the denticle texture reduced resistance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the result; the textured surface met less resistance, not more.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants respond to being touched. In a greenhouse experiment, botanist Anneli Virtanen grew two sets of young bean plants under identical light, water, and soil conditions. For a few seconds each day, she gently brushed the stems of one set by hand and left the other set untouched. After three weeks, the brushed plants were noticeably shorter and had thicker stems than the untouched ones. Wind pushes on a stem in much the same way that a hand does. Virtanen's results therefore suggest that, all else being equal, bean plants growing in a sheltered spot ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: would be more likely to be damaged by being touched than wind-exposed plants.
choices.B: would likely grow taller than bean plants exposed to frequent wind.
choices.C: would likely develop thicker stems than bean plants exposed to frequent wind.
choices.D: would need more light and water than bean plants exposed to frequent wind.

explanation.why: Brushing made the plants shorter and thicker, and the text says wind acts on stems the way brushing does. So wind-exposed plants should resemble the brushed plants, and sheltered plants should resemble the untouched ones, which were taller.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not describe touching as damaging; it describes a change in growth.
explanation.B: Correct. Sheltered plants match the untouched set, which grew taller than the brushed set.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Thicker stems went with brushing, so wind-exposed plants, not sheltered ones, should have thicker stems.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Light and water were kept the same in the experiment, so nothing suggests different needs.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In England before the nineteenth century, few villages had accurate maps, and the boundaries of a parish, the district served by a local church, were often marked by nothing more than a stream, a hedge, or a large stone. Once a year, in a custom called "beating the bounds," the people of a parish walked the entire boundary together. Children were brought along and, at each boundary marker, were gently bumped against the stone or made to recite where the line ran. The involvement of children suggests that one purpose of the custom was to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: teach children the religious duties they would take on as adults.
choices.B: replace the old stone markers with written records of the boundary.
choices.C: pass knowledge of the boundary on to a new generation so it would not be forgotten.
choices.D: allow the parish to extend its boundary a little further each year.

explanation.why: Without maps, the boundary existed mainly in people's memories. Bringing children to each marker and making them remember it would ensure that, when the adults were gone, someone would still know where the line ran.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes learning the location of a boundary, not religious duties.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The custom relied on memory and physical markers; the text mentions no written records being made.
explanation.C: Correct. Making children memorize the markers preserves boundary knowledge across generations in the absence of maps.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The walk followed the existing boundary; nothing suggests the line was moved.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When Mr. Oduya finally agreed to sell the bicycle, he spent an entire Saturday preparing it. He oiled the chain, trued the wheels, and polished the frame until the old green paint shone. The buyer, a student from the college, paid what was asked without arguing and wheeled it toward the gate. At the last moment Mr. Oduya called him back, unscrewed the small brass bell from the handlebar, and put it in his pocket. "You can buy another for a few coins," he said. "This one was a gift." Mr. Oduya's behavior suggests that he ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: suspected that the student would not take proper care of the bicycle.
choices.B: valued the bell for reasons that had nothing to do with its cost.
choices.C: had decided at the last moment not to sell the bicycle after all.
choices.D: regretted the price he had agreed to and wanted to keep something back.

explanation.why: Mr. Oduya says the bell is cheap to replace yet keeps it because it was a gift. He is attached to it for its personal meaning, not its price, which is why he hands over the carefully prepared bicycle but not the bell.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text shows distrust of the student, who pays without arguing and takes the bicycle.
explanation.B: Correct. Keeping an inexpensive bell because it was a gift shows that its value to him is sentimental.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sale goes through; he takes back only the bell.
explanation.D: Incorrect. He prepared the bicycle with care and sold it for the asked price; the bell, he says, is worth only a few coins.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Sundarbans, a vast mangrove forest where the Ganges delta meets the Bay of Bengal, is crossed by countless channels. Some, fed by river water, are nearly fresh; others, close to the sea, are about as salty as the ocean. The saltwater crocodile, the largest reptile in the forest, has special glands on its tongue that remove excess salt from its body. Herpetologist Farida Rahman surveyed crocodiles in both the freshest and the saltiest channels and found them in similar numbers in both. Rahman's findings suggest that, within the Sundarbans, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the saltiest channels offer crocodiles more food than the freshest ones do.
choices.B: crocodiles rely on river water to flush salt from their bodies.
choices.C: crocodiles are more abundant than in any other mangrove forest.
choices.D: the saltiness of the water is not what decides where the crocodiles live.

explanation.why: The crocodiles have glands that handle excess salt, and the survey found them equally common in the saltiest and the freshest channels. If salt levels were controlling their distribution, the numbers would differ; since they do not, something other than salinity must determine where the crocodiles are.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about food in either type of channel.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the crocodiles remove salt with glands on the tongue, and they live equally well in salty channels.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The survey compared channels within the Sundarbans, not different forests.
explanation.D: Correct. Equal numbers in fresh and salty water mean salinity is not the deciding factor.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A pipe organ contains two main kinds of pipes. In a flue pipe, sound is produced by air vibrating inside the pipe, and because sound travels faster through warm air than through cold air, a flue pipe's pitch rises as the air around it warms. In a reed pipe, sound comes from a vibrating strip of metal whose pitch barely changes with temperature. Many large churches are cold in winter and warm in summer. A tuner who brings an organ's flue pipes and reed pipes into perfect agreement on a cold January morning should therefore expect that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the reed pipes will need retuning more often than the flue pipes.
choices.B: by a warm summer afternoon, the flue pipes will sound higher than the reed pipes.
choices.C: the organ will stay in tune as long as the church is heated in winter.
choices.D: by a warm summer afternoon, the reed pipes will sound higher than the flue pipes.

explanation.why: Flue-pipe pitch rises with temperature while reed-pipe pitch hardly changes. If the two agree in the cold, then when the church warms in summer the flue pipes will have risen in pitch and the reed pipes will not, so the flue pipes will sound higher.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The reed pipes are the stable ones; it is the flue pipes that drift with temperature.
explanation.B: Correct. Warming raises flue-pipe pitch but not reed-pipe pitch, so the flues end up higher.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Heating in winter does not prevent the summer warmth that will push the flue pipes out of agreement.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the relationship; it is the flue pipes, not the reed pipes, whose pitch rises with warmth.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Transportation economist Marcus Ellefsen studied what happened after a city began charging a toll on the highway that carried most commuters into its center. In the year after the toll began, the number of cars on the highway during the morning rush fell by nearly a third. Over the same period, traffic on the older, slower streets running parallel to the highway rose sharply, and the total number of cars entering the center each morning was almost unchanged. Ellefsen's data suggest that most drivers who left the highway ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: began paying the toll after a few months once the novelty wore off.
choices.B: switched from driving to taking buses or trains into the center.
choices.C: changed their route rather than giving up driving into the center.
choices.D: stopped traveling into the city center during the morning rush.

explanation.why: Highway traffic fell, but traffic on the parallel streets rose and the total number of cars entering the center stayed about the same. The cars that left the highway therefore still arrived in the center, just by a different road.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes the full year after the toll began and gives no sign that highway traffic recovered.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The total number of cars entering the center was almost unchanged, so drivers did not abandon their cars.
explanation.C: Correct. Falling highway traffic, rising parallel-street traffic, and a steady total point to drivers rerouting.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This contradicts the nearly unchanged total number of cars entering the center each morning.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the mountain valleys of Chitral, in northern Pakistan, walnut trees are a valued source of food and timber. Farmers there traditionally plant walnuts along the edges of their fields or beside irrigation channels rather than among their crops, and some say that little will grow beneath a walnut's branches. Plant scientist Zarina Baig tested soil collected under walnut trees and found that it contained juglone, a chemical released by walnut roots and fallen leaves, and that seedlings of wheat and several vegetables grew poorly in that soil. Baig's findings suggest that the farmers' traditional practice ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: prevents walnut trees from growing as large as they otherwise would.
choices.B: may help protect their crops from a harmful effect of the trees.
choices.C: was adopted mainly to make the walnuts easier to harvest.
choices.D: has reduced the amount of juglone that walnut trees produce.

explanation.why: The soil under walnut trees contains juglone, and crop seedlings grow poorly in it. Keeping walnuts at the edges of fields rather than among the crops keeps the crops away from that soil, so the traditional placement may shield the crops from the trees' harmful effect.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about the size of the trees.
explanation.B: Correct. Planting walnuts away from crops keeps crops out of juglone-affected soil, where seedlings grow poorly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not mention harvesting as a reason; it connects the practice to the effect on crops.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says juglone was present in the soil; nothing suggests the practice changed how much the trees produce.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Kushan Empire, which flourished from the first to the third century CE, stretched from Central Asia across what is now Afghanistan and Pakistan into northern India. Its best-known ruler, Kanishka, issued gold coins whose inscriptions were written in the Greek alphabet, even though Greek rule in the region had ended long before. On the reverse of the coins appear deities drawn from Greek, Iranian, and Indian traditions, each named in the inscription. The coins circulated throughout the empire. Taken together, these features of the coinage suggest that Kushan rulers ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: required their subjects to worship the deities shown on the coins.
choices.B: expected their coins to be used by people of many different backgrounds.
choices.C: hoped to restore Greek rule over the lands they governed.
choices.D: minted gold coins only for trade with lands beyond the empire.

explanation.why: The empire covered a huge, diverse region, and its coins combined a familiar script with gods from three different traditions and circulated everywhere in it. Designing money that speaks to Greek, Iranian, and Indian traditions makes sense if the rulers expected a mixed population to handle it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says only that the coins showed deities; it says nothing about requiring worship.
explanation.B: Correct. Multiple religious traditions on coins that circulated across a diverse empire point to a varied intended audience.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Using the Greek alphabet is not evidence of wanting Greek rule back; the text says Greek rule had ended long before.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the coins circulated throughout the empire, not only beyond it.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Aunt Rosalind answered every letter the day it arrived, but never with her first attempt. Her niece Clara, who stayed with her one summer, watched the ritual: a first draft, written quickly and covering three pages; a second, slower and shorter; and a third, rarely more than half a page, which was the one she sealed and sent. The first two she folded and dropped into the stove. "The long ones are for me," she told Clara. "The short one is for them." Aunt Rosalind's remark suggests that she regarded the early drafts as ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: failures caused by her inability to write quickly.
choices.B: a way of working out her own feelings before deciding what to say.
choices.C: copies to be kept as a record of what she had sent.
choices.D: letters meant for friends rather than for strangers.

explanation.why: The long drafts are written first, are burned, and are described as being "for me." They serve Aunt Rosalind herself, not the reader; since the version that is sent is short and comes last, the earlier drafts must be where she sorts out her own thoughts before she settles on what to say.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The first draft is written quickly; the drafts are part of her regular method, not a failure.
explanation.B: Correct. Drafts that are "for me" and destroyed before a short final letter is sent are a private step toward deciding what to say.
explanation.C: Incorrect. She burns the early drafts, so they cannot serve as a record.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text makes no distinction between friends and strangers; "them" refers to whoever will read the letter.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Snowshoe hares of northern North America turn white each fall and brown again each spring. The timing of the change is set not by the weather but by the shortening and lengthening of the days, which is the same from year to year. In a long-term study in a mountain forest, ecologists tracked hares with radio collars and recorded when snow arrived. In years when snowfall came late, many hares turned white while the ground was still bare, and these mismatched hares were killed by predators at a higher rate than hares whose coats matched their surroundings. These findings suggest that if snow continues to arrive later in the fall, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: more hares are likely to be lost to predators each fall.
choices.B: predators will have difficulty finding hares against the bare ground.
choices.C: the hares will stop turning white altogether.
choices.D: the hares will begin to turn white later to match the snow.

explanation.why: The coat change is triggered by day length, which does not shift, so later snow means more hares turning white on bare ground. Mismatched hares were killed more often, so later snow should lead to more hares being lost to predators.
explanation.A: Correct. Fixed timing plus later snow means more mismatch, and mismatch means higher predation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the finding; white hares on bare ground were easier, not harder, for predators to find.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The change is driven by day length, which continues as before; nothing suggests it would stop.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the timing is set by day length, not weather, so the hares cannot adjust to later snow.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the 1930s, researchers traveled through the Balkans with recording equipment to study singers who performed long traditional epic poems from memory, without written texts. The singers insisted that they sang each poem exactly as they had learned it, word for word. Yet when the researchers recorded the same singer performing the same poem on two occasions months apart, the two versions differed in length, in the order of some episodes, and in many of their lines, although the overall story stayed the same. These recordings suggest that the singers ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: had forgotten large portions of the poems between the two performances.
choices.B: were deliberately misleading the researchers about how they learned the poems.
choices.C: recomposed much of a poem during each performance rather than reciting a fixed text.
choices.D: had learned different versions of the poems from different teachers.

explanation.why: The singers believed they repeated each poem word for word, but the recordings show that the same singer's two performances differed in length, order, and wording while keeping the story. A fixed memorized text would not vary that way, so the singers must have been shaping the lines anew each time they performed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The overall story stayed the same and the versions differed in order and wording, which is not the pattern of forgetting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the singers insisted on their accuracy; nothing suggests they were lying rather than sincerely mistaken.
explanation.C: Correct. Variation in wording and order from one performance to the next, with the story intact, points to composition during performance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The comparison was between two performances by the same singer, so different teachers cannot explain the differences.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Urban planner Devika Menon surveyed passengers waiting at two sets of bus stops in the same city. At the first set, electronic displays showed how many minutes remained until the next bus; at the second set, there were no displays. Buses on both sets of routes ran on the same schedule, and Menon timed each passenger's actual wait. When passengers were asked how long they thought they had waited, those at stops without displays gave estimates well above their actual waits, while those at stops with displays gave estimates close to the truth. Menon's findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: not knowing when a bus will come makes a wait feel longer than it really is.
choices.B: most passengers do not look at the displays while they are waiting.
choices.C: passengers at stops with displays waited less time than those at stops without them.
choices.D: buses arrive more promptly at stops that are fitted with electronic displays.

explanation.why: Actual waits were the same at both kinds of stops, so the displays did not change how long anyone waited. What changed was perception: without a display, passengers overestimated their waits. So uncertainty about the bus's arrival is what makes the wait feel longer.
explanation.A: Correct. Equal real waits but inflated estimates only where there was no display point to uncertainty as the cause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Passengers at stops with displays estimated their waits accurately, which suggests they did use the displays.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says Menon timed actual waits and that the schedules were the same; only the estimates differed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The buses ran on the same schedule at both sets of stops; the displays did not affect arrivals.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Deosai Plains, a high plateau in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan, lie under snow for most of the year and are free of it for only about four months. Himalayan brown bears that live there spend the snowy months in hibernation, during which they neither eat nor drink and live entirely on stored body fat. Wildlife biologist Imran Haider fitted several bears with tracking collars and found that during the brief snow-free season they spent nearly all their daylight hours feeding on roots, grasses, and marmots. Haider's observations suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: Himalayan brown bears eat more food in a day than bears in warmer regions do.
choices.B: the bears would stop hibernating if food were available on the plateau in winter.
choices.C: marmots make up the largest part of the bears' summer diet.
choices.D: the bears must build up in a few months the reserves that carry them through a much longer fast.

explanation.why: The bears live on body fat alone for about eight snowy months and can feed only during the four snow-free months. Spending nearly all daylight feeding is what you would expect if all the fat for the long fast must be stored in that short window.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not compare these bears' daily intake with that of bears elsewhere.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text does not say what triggers hibernation or whether winter food would change it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text lists roots, grasses, and marmots but does not say which is the largest part of the diet.
explanation.D: Correct. A long fast on stored fat and a short feeding season together explain the near-constant feeding.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A ship's navigator sailing at night along a coast with several lighthouses faces a problem: one steady light looks much like another, and mistaking one lighthouse for its neighbor can send a ship onto the rocks. By the nineteenth century, lighthouse authorities had begun giving each lighthouse its own pattern, or "character," of flashes, such as one flash every five seconds or two quick flashes every fifteen seconds, and printing these patterns in lists that ships carried. The adoption of distinctive flash patterns suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: navigators of the period relied on lighthouses to tell them when to drop anchor.
choices.B: lighthouses with steady lights were no longer needed to warn ships away from the coast.
choices.C: a navigator could identify a particular lighthouse by timing its flashes and consulting the list.
choices.D: ships of the period could not carry charts of the coast they were sailing along.

explanation.why: The problem was that lights looked alike. Giving each lighthouse a unique timed pattern, and giving ships a list of the patterns, solves exactly that problem: the navigator times the flashes, looks up the pattern, and knows which lighthouse it is.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text concerns identifying lighthouses, not anchoring.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about removing lighthouses or that warning ships off the coast was no longer necessary.
explanation.C: Correct. Unique patterns plus a printed list let the navigator match a flashing light to a specific lighthouse.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text mentions printed lists of patterns carried by ships; it says nothing about charts being unavailable.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The piano stood in the front room of Mrs. Vance's house for as long as her neighbors could remember, and in all those years nobody had heard it played. Each April the tuner came, worked for an hour, and left. The lid stayed closed and the stool was never moved. When her nephew finally asked why she paid to tune an instrument no one used, Mrs. Vance answered that her late husband had played every evening, and that the house should be ready in case anyone ever wished to play again. Mrs. Vance's answer suggests that she kept the piano tuned ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: because the tuner had advised her that an untuned piano would be ruined.
choices.B: as a way of keeping faith with a part of her life that had ended.
choices.C: so that she could resume the lessons she had once taken.
choices.D: because she expected her nephew to learn to play it.

explanation.why: Her husband played every evening and is now gone, and she keeps the piano ready "in case anyone ever wished to play again," though no one has for years. Tuning it each spring is a way of holding on to the time when the music was part of her home.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives her own reason, which concerns her husband; it mentions no advice from the tuner.
explanation.B: Correct. Maintaining the piano her late husband played, for an unlikely future player, honors the past rather than serving a practical need.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says Mrs. Vance herself played or took lessons.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The nephew merely asks a question; nothing suggests she expects him to play.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Common starlings feed on the ground in flocks that range from a handful of birds to hundreds. Each bird feeding with its head down must regularly pause and lift its head to scan for hawks. Ornithologist Teodora Ilić filmed starling flocks of different sizes and measured how often each bird looked up. She found that birds in large flocks raised their heads far less often than birds in small flocks, yet when a model hawk was flown over, the large flocks reacted at least as quickly as the small ones. Ilić's findings suggest that a starling in a large flock ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: relies on its own vigilance rather than on the other birds in the flock.
choices.B: is less likely to be noticed by a hawk than a starling in a small flock.
choices.C: can spend more time feeding without being slower to detect danger.
choices.D: spends more of its time watching for hawks than a starling in a small flock.

explanation.why: Birds in large flocks looked up less, which means more time with the head down feeding, yet the large flocks detected the model hawk just as fast. So an individual in a large flock gains feeding time without losing early warning.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A bird that looks up less yet is warned as early must be benefiting from the vigilance of others, not relying only on its own.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The study measured how quickly flocks detected the hawk, not whether hawks noticed individual birds.
explanation.C: Correct. Less time scanning plus equally fast reaction means more feeding at no cost in detection.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the finding; birds in large flocks looked up less often, not more.

items.subject: humanities
