items.passage: The tappa is the shortest form of Pashto folk poetry, spoken across much of Pakistan and Afghanistan: two lines, the first shorter than the second, sung or recited at gatherings. Tappas are anonymous and have been passed down by word of mouth for generations. A large share of them speak in a woman's voice, about longing for an absent husband, the labor of the household, or a daughter's reluctance to leave her village. The written Pashto literature of the same centuries, by contrast, was produced almost entirely by men. These facts suggest that the tappa ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was composed mainly by the same poets who wrote the formal literature.
choices.B: has been recorded in writing more carefully than longer forms of Pashto poetry.
choices.C: preserves perspectives that the written literature of the time largely leaves out.
choices.D: was originally sung only by women and later taken up by men.

explanation.why: Written Pashto literature came almost entirely from men, while a large share of anonymous tappas speak with a woman's voice about women's lives. So the oral tappa carries viewpoints that the written record of the period mostly lacks.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text contrasts anonymous oral tappas with the written literature of men; nothing links the two sets of authors.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Tappas were passed down by word of mouth, so nothing suggests careful written recording.
explanation.C: Correct. Women's voices common in tappas but nearly absent from male-authored written literature make the tappa a record of what the written works omit.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says many tappas speak in a woman's voice, not that only women sang them or that men took them up later.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Hoping to slow traffic near a school, a town painted a crosswalk so that, from a driver's seat, its white stripes appeared to be solid blocks rising from the road. Traffic engineer Lucía Ferreira measured vehicle speeds at the crosswalk before the painting and at intervals afterward. In the first month, average speeds dropped by about a fifth. By the third month the drop had shrunk by half, and by the sixth month speeds were almost back to what they had been before the painting. Ferreira's measurements suggest that the crosswalk's effect ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was limited because most drivers never noticed the painted blocks.
choices.B: would have lasted longer if the stripes had been painted a brighter color.
choices.C: was strongest among drivers who rarely used the road.
choices.D: depended on drivers being unfamiliar with the illusion and faded once they grew used to it.

explanation.why: Speeds fell sharply at first and then returned toward the original level over six months, while the painting itself stayed the same. The steady fading of the effect as time passed fits drivers getting used to the illusion and no longer reacting to it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The sharp initial drop in speed shows that drivers did notice the blocks at first.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no information about colors or any comparison of paints.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The measurements were averages at the crosswalk; the text does not separate regular drivers from occasional ones, though this would be a plausible next question.
explanation.D: Correct. A large initial drop that steadily disappears while the paint remains points to drivers growing accustomed to the illusion.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Flowers typically carry a weak negative electric charge, while a bumblebee picks up a positive charge as it flies, and bees can sense the faint electric field that forms between them. Biologist Tomás Ferreira presented bumblebees with two sets of artificial flowers that looked identical. One set carried a small electric charge and offered sugar water; the other was uncharged and offered only plain water. After a few visits, the bees chose the charged flowers far more often than chance would predict. When Ferreira then switched off the charge on every flower, the bees' choices fell back to random. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the bees could taste the difference between sugar water and plain water before landing on a flower.
choices.B: the bees had been relying on the electric charge to tell the rewarding flowers from the others.
choices.C: bumblebees are unable to locate real flowers unless those flowers carry an electric charge.
choices.D: the bees came to prefer the uncharged flowers once they discovered that these held only plain water.

explanation.why: The two sets of flowers looked identical, so the bees needed some other cue to tell them apart. They chose well while the charged flowers were charged, and their choices became random as soon as the charge was turned off. The charge, then, was the cue that had been guiding them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If the bees could detect the sugar water directly, they would have kept choosing well after the charge was switched off, but their choices became random.
explanation.B: Correct. The bees could find the sugar water only while the charge was on, so the charge was the cue they were using.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The experiment used identical artificial flowers; it shows nothing about how bees find real flowers, which differ in color and scent.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The bees preferred the charged flowers, which held the sugar water, and chose at random once the charge was removed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Certain crust-forming lichens grow outward across bare rock at a slow and fairly steady rate, so the largest lichen on a boulder offers a rough measure of how long the rock has been exposed. Geologists use this method to date moraines, the ridges of rubble that a glacier leaves at its edge, after first calibrating the growth rate on gravestones and old walls of known age in the same valley. The method assumes that lichens settled on the rock soon after it was exposed and have grown undisturbed ever since. A lichen that was buried under snow for years, scraped off by a rockfall, or killed by drought would, however, restart the clock. Geologist Hanna Lindqvist therefore notes that the largest lichen on a moraine ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: is likely to be younger than the moraine only in valleys where no gravestones are available for calibration.
choices.B: indicates the least time that can have passed since the moraine formed, not the exact time.
choices.C: would have grown faster than usual if it had spent several years buried under snow.
choices.D: shows exactly how many years ago the moraine formed, provided the growth rate was calibrated nearby.

explanation.why: The lichen's size shows how long it has been growing. If nothing has disturbed it, that is also how long the rock has been exposed; if something has, the lichen is younger than the rock. Either way, the moraine is at least as old as the lichen, and possibly older.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Whether a lichen was disturbed has nothing to do with whether dated gravestones exist nearby; calibration and disturbance are separate issues.
explanation.B: Correct. Disturbances can make a lichen younger than its rock but never older, so the lichen's age is a minimum for the moraine's age.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text lists burial under snow as something that restarts the clock, that is, sets growth back, not something that speeds it up.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Calibration fixes the growth rate, but it cannot rule out a disturbance that restarted the lichen's growth after the moraine formed.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the late Middle Ages, enormous shoals of herring gathered each autumn off the coast of Scania, at the southern tip of what is now Sweden, and fishermen from around the Baltic Sea came to catch them. Herring spoils within a day or two unless it is packed in salt, and the Scania shore had no salt of its own. The nearest large supply was the salt works at Lüneburg, in northern Germany, whose output reached the fishing grounds by way of the port of Lübeck. Lübeck's merchants owned few fishing boats, yet contemporary records show them setting the terms on which much of the Scania catch was sold. Historian Pieter de Vries argues that this influence is best explained by the fact that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the Scania fishery would have been far more profitable if salt had been produced on the Scania shore.
choices.B: merchants who controlled salt could dictate the price of every good traded around the Baltic Sea.
choices.C: Lübeck's merchants caught most of the Scania herring themselves and so could set their own prices.
choices.D: whoever controlled the supply of salt controlled whether the catch could be preserved at all.

explanation.why: Two facts must be combined: herring is worthless unless salted within a day or two, and the only large supply of salt reached Scania through Lübeck. Fishermen therefore depended on Lübeck's merchants for the one thing that made their catch worth having, which explains the merchants' power over its sale.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never discusses the profits of the fishery or what local salt would have changed; it asks why Lübeck's merchants had influence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text explains influence over one trade that depended on salt; it says nothing about other goods.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says Lübeck's merchants owned few fishing boats; their power came from something other than catching the fish.
explanation.D: Correct. Without salt the herring spoiled within days, and the salt came through Lübeck, so Lübeck's merchants held the key to the whole trade even without boats of their own.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, many European cities passed sumptuary laws, which restricted the fabrics, furs, and jewels that people of each social rank were permitted to wear. Historians have sometimes taken the sheer number of these laws as a sign of how firmly rank was policed. One city's council, however, issued a law limiting the wearing of silk in 1432 and then reissued it, in nearly the same words, in 1439, 1447, 1455, and 1468, each time complaining that the earlier version was being "daily disregarded." A law that is obeyed rarely needs to be proclaimed again. Historian Beatriz Almeida therefore suggests that the repeated reissues are better read as evidence that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: social rank mattered less in this city than in cities that passed fewer sumptuary laws.
choices.B: the restrictions on silk were widely ignored than as evidence that they were strictly enforced.
choices.C: the council itself had little interest in controlling what the city's residents wore.
choices.D: silk became cheaper and more widely available over the course of the fifteenth century.

explanation.why: The council reissued the same law five times and each time complained that it was being ignored. The text adds that obeyed laws rarely need repeating. Together these points turn the usual reading on its head: many laws suggest weak enforcement, not strong.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text compares nothing between cities and draws no conclusion about how much rank mattered; it concerns whether one law was obeyed.
explanation.B: Correct. A law that has to be proclaimed five times, each time with a complaint that it is disregarded, is one that people were not obeying.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A council that reissues the same law five times clearly cares about it; the question is whether residents obeyed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the price or supply of silk; it discusses only the law and its reissues.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A printed geography of 1550 contains woodcut views of more than a hundred European towns, each labeled with the town's name, and historians have occasionally used these views to reconstruct the appearance of towns that were later rebuilt. Art historian Noor El-Amin compared the views closely. Several, she found, were printed from the very same wooden block: a view labeled as a town in Flanders shows the same walls, towers, and river, down to a small nick in the block's edge, as a view labeled as a town in Hungary hundreds of kilometers away. A few other views, by contrast, show distinctive buildings that still stand in the towns they name. El-Amin concludes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a view can be trusted only where something in it can be matched to the town it names.
choices.B: the views of the Flemish and Hungarian towns are accurate because both towns had similar walls and towers.
choices.C: none of the views in the geography depicts the actual appearance of the town it names.
choices.D: the printer visited each of the hundred towns in order to record its appearance.

explanation.why: The same block cannot show two towns hundreds of kilometers apart, so at least some views were not drawn from the towns they name. Yet a few views match buildings that still stand, so not every view is a stock image. The only safe rule is to trust a view when it can be checked against the town.
explanation.A: Correct. Some views are stock images reused for different towns, while a few can be tied to real buildings, so each view must be judged on its own evidence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The views match down to a nick in the block because they were printed from one block, not because the towns resembled each other.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says a few views show distinctive buildings that still stand, so some views do depict their towns.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A block reused for towns in Flanders and Hungary shows that at least those views were not drawn from observation of each town.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a conifer's trunk is pushed off vertical, the tree does not straighten the part that already leans. Instead, it begins laying down a dense tissue called compression wood on the lower side of the lean, which gradually pushes the newer growth back toward upright. Compression wood is easy to recognize in a cross-section of the trunk: on the lower side of the lean, the annual rings are wider and darker than those on the upper side. Forest ecologist Jiro Hasegawa cut a cross-section from a pine on a hillside and found evenly spaced, uniform rings in the inner 40 years of growth, followed by 25 outer rings that were markedly wider and darker on the downhill side. Hasegawa's observations indicate that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the pine began to lean as a seedling and has been straightening itself ever since.
choices.B: the soil on the downhill side became richer about 25 years ago, allowing faster growth on that side.
choices.C: the pine will fall within a few decades because compression wood cannot support a leaning trunk.
choices.D: the pine grew upright for about 40 years and has been leaning downhill for roughly the past 25.

explanation.why: Compression wood forms only on the lower side of a lean, and it shows as wider, darker rings on that side. The inner 40 rings are uniform, so the tree was upright then. The outer 25 rings are wider and darker on the downhill side, so the trunk has leaned downhill during those years.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The inner 40 rings are uniform, which shows that the tree was not leaning in its early years.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text explains wider, darker rings on one side as compression wood caused by a lean; it does not connect them to soil.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes compression wood as pushing growth back toward upright; it says nothing about the tree failing.
explanation.D: Correct. Uniform inner rings mean no lean during the first 40 years; compression wood on the downhill side of the last 25 rings means the trunk has been tilted downhill since then.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before governments began registering deaths, parish burial registers are often the only surviving record of when people died, and historians use them to trace the seasonal rhythm of mortality in past communities. Demographer Ewa Kowalczyk compiled monthly burial counts from the registers of several upland villages in northern Europe for the years 1700 to 1750 and found that burials peaked sharply in April each year, with relatively few recorded in January and February. She also notes that the registers give the date of burial, not of death, and that in these villages the ground was usually frozen too hard for grave digging from midwinter until the thaw in early spring. Kowalczyk cautions that the April peak ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: shows that April was consistently the deadliest month in these villages throughout the period.
choices.B: indicates that villagers were less likely to die in winter than in spring.
choices.C: may partly reflect burials delayed from the winter months rather than a true rise in deaths in April.
choices.D: cannot be explained, since no burials at all could take place while the ground was frozen.

explanation.why: The registers record burials, not deaths, and burials were impossible while the ground was frozen. Winter deaths would therefore be recorded only after the thaw, piling up in the first month when digging was possible. The April peak may thus be an artifact of frozen ground rather than of April deaths.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This takes the burial counts as death counts, which is exactly the reading Kowalczyk's note about frozen ground calls into question.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The low winter counts may reflect the impossibility of burial, not fewer deaths, so no such conclusion follows.
explanation.C: Correct. If graves could not be dug until the thaw, people who died in winter were buried in spring, so April's burials include winter's deaths.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The frozen ground explains the peak rather than making it mysterious: delayed burials would naturally cluster at the thaw.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For thousands of years the forests of the northern United States and Canada had no earthworms: the glaciers of the last ice age had wiped them out, and native species never returned. The earthworms found there today descend from European species carried in with plants and fishing bait. In these forests, fallen leaves normally build up into a thick, spongy layer in which many native wildflowers germinate and salamanders hunt. Earthworms feed on fallen leaves and pull them underground. Ecologist Marta Soler surveyed forest plots across a region where earthworms had spread over the previous thirty years and found that the plots with the most earthworms had the thinnest leaf layer. If the earthworms are responsible for the thinning, then the wildflowers and salamanders in heavily invaded plots ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: will adapt quickly to forests with little leaf litter, as European species have done.
choices.B: may be harmed even though the earthworms do not feed on them directly.
choices.C: had already begun declining before the earthworms arrived, which is why the leaf layer thinned.
choices.D: are being eaten by the earthworms along with the fallen leaves.

explanation.why: Two facts combine. Native wildflowers germinate in the leaf layer and salamanders hunt in it, and earthworms consume that layer. Earthworms eat leaves, not flowers or salamanders, yet removing the layer removes something these species rely on, so they can suffer without ever being eaten.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how European species adapted or how quickly native species might; it notes only that these forests developed without earthworms.
explanation.B: Correct. The earthworms eat the leaf layer, and the wildflowers and salamanders depend on that layer, so the harm reaches them indirectly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text attributes the thinning to earthworms eating leaves, not to a decline in wildflowers or salamanders.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says earthworms feed on fallen leaves; the threat to wildflowers and salamanders is the loss of their habitat, not predation.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most fig species depend on a single species of tiny wasp for pollination, and the wasp in turn can breed only inside that fig's fruit. An adult female wasp lives for just a day or two after leaving the fig in which she developed, and in that time she must find a tree whose young figs are ready to receive her. Within a tropical forest, the trees of a given fig species do not all produce figs at the same time; different individuals come into fruit in different months, so that in a large population some tree is almost always receptive. Botanist Lucía Herrera points out that this arrangement has a serious consequence for a small, isolated stand of fig trees: ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: it will be pollinated more reliably than a large forest, because the wasps have fewer trees to search.
choices.B: its wasps will live longer than wasps in large forests in order to survive the gaps between fruiting.
choices.C: if ever none of its trees has young figs, its wasps will die out and the trees will lose their pollinator.
choices.D: its trees will tend to produce figs all at once, since there are too few of them to spread fruiting across the year.

explanation.why: Wasps live one or two days and must find a receptive tree in that time. A large population always has some receptive tree, but a small stand may not. In any gap, every wasp dies before it can breed, and since the wasps breed only in figs and the figs depend only on this wasp, both partners are then stranded.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Fewer trees means more gaps with no receptive figs, which makes pollination less reliable, not more.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives the wasp's lifespan as a fixed day or two and offers no reason it would lengthen.
explanation.C: Correct. With only a few trees, there may be weeks when no tree is receptive; wasps live only a day or two, so none survive the gap, and no new wasps can arrive.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says trees of a species fruit in different months; a small stand has fewer trees, but nothing suggests that they synchronize.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Stalagmites grow upward from cave floors as mineral-rich water drips from above, and many add a thin layer every year. In a dry year, less water seeps through the rock, the layer is thinner, and in a severe drought growth can stop altogether, leaving a gap in the sequence. A gap, however, has another possible cause: the crack feeding a particular drip can become blocked or shift, starving one stalagmite while its neighbors continue to grow. Geologist Anjali Rao examined six stalagmites from different chambers of a cave in Southeast Asia and found that all six stopped growing within a few years of one another about 1,100 years ago and resumed roughly a decade later. Rao argues that this pattern is best explained by ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a steady increase in rainfall that lasted for roughly a decade.
choices.B: a drought that affected the whole region rather than a change in the path of any single drip.
choices.C: the blocking of six separate cracks, one above each stalagmite, at about the same time.
choices.D: the collapse of part of the cave's roof around 1,100 years ago.

explanation.why: The text offers two causes for a gap: drought, which cuts water to the whole cave, and a blocked crack, which affects one drip. Six stalagmites in different chambers stopped together and restarted together. A shared cause fits that pattern; six separate blockages happening at once would be an unlikely coincidence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. More rain means more drip water and thicker layers, not a halt in growth.
explanation.B: Correct. A shifted or blocked crack starves one stalagmite, but six in different chambers stopping and restarting together point to a cause that reached them all, such as a drought.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A blocked crack affects a single drip; six blockages coinciding and then clearing together would be a remarkable coincidence, whereas a drought explains all six at once.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions a collapse; it offers drought and shifting drips as the two explanations for a gap.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Meteorites fall at roughly the same rate over the whole planet, yet most of those ever collected come from two kinds of places: the ice fields of Antarctica and hot deserts such as the Sahara, where dark stones stand out against pale ground and few ordinary rocks confuse searchers. In Antarctica, a fallen stone lies frozen in ice until wind strips the ice away; in a hot desert, it rests on the surface, where heat, occasional rain, and windblown sand slowly break it apart. Planetary scientist Tobias Keller compared the two collections and found that small, crumbly types of meteorite make up a much larger share of the Antarctic finds than of the desert finds. Since the same mix of meteorites should fall in both regions, Keller's comparison suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the Antarctic collection contains more meteorites of every type than the desert collection does.
choices.B: the desert collections underrepresent fragile meteorites, which tend to disintegrate before they are found.
choices.C: fragile meteorites fall more often over Antarctica than over the Sahara.
choices.D: searchers in hot deserts deliberately leave small meteorites where they lie.

explanation.why: Start from the premise that the same mix of meteorites falls everywhere. The Antarctic and desert collections nonetheless differ, with far fewer crumbly types in the desert. The text supplies the reason: desert stones lie exposed to heat, rain, and sand that break them up, while Antarctic stones stay frozen. Fragile stones are therefore lost from the desert before anyone finds them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Keller compared the share of fragile types within each collection, which says nothing about the total number of meteorites in either.
explanation.B: Correct. The same mix falls in both places, and desert conditions break stones apart, so fragile types are the ones most likely to vanish from the desert record.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text states that the same mix of meteorites should fall in both regions, which rules out a difference in what falls.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests that desert searchers ignore small stones; the difference is explained by weathering.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A windcatcher is a tall shaft rising above a house's roof, with openings near the top that capture breezes and channel them down into the rooms below. In the Iranian city of Yazd, most old windcatchers have openings on four or more sides, each of which must be closed with a shutter whenever the wind blows from a different quarter. In Hyderabad, in Sindh, Pakistan, travelers in the 1800s described a skyline crowded with thousands of windcatchers, nearly all with a single opening and nearly all facing the same way, toward the southwest. Architectural historian Faiza Siddiqui observes that a one-sided windcatcher is useless whenever the wind comes from any other direction. The contrast between the two cities therefore suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: Hyderabad's windcatchers had to be closed with shutters more often than those of Yazd.
choices.B: the windcatchers of Hyderabad cooled houses more effectively than those of Yazd.
choices.C: builders in Hyderabad could count on breezes from one steady direction, whereas builders in Yazd could not.
choices.D: the builders of Yazd did not realize that a single opening could capture a breeze.

explanation.why: A windcatcher with one opening works only when the wind blows from that direction. Thousands of them all facing southwest would be pointless unless Hyderabad's wind reliably came from the southwest. Yazd's many-sided designs, with shutters for shifting winds, suggest the opposite situation there.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes shutters on Yazd's many-sided windcatchers, not on Hyderabad's single-opening ones.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text compares the designs' orientation, not how well either city's windcatchers cooled rooms.
explanation.C: Correct. A one-sided windcatcher pays off only if the wind reliably comes from that side; many-sided ones with shutters make sense where the wind shifts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Yazd's many-sided towers answer shifting winds; the text gives no reason to think its builders lacked knowledge.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Handmade paper of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries carries a watermark, a faint design left by a wire figure sewn onto the mold on which each sheet was formed. Because the wires bent and broke with use, a mold usually lasted only a year or two before its watermark was replaced, and no two molds left exactly the same mark. If an undated manuscript's watermark matches, flaw for flaw, the watermark in a letter dated 1521, the two sheets were formed on the same mold at about the same time. Paper historian Luc Moreau cautions, however, that a stack of paper might sit in a stationer's shop or a scribe's chest for years before anyone wrote on it. A matching watermark therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: proves that the manuscript and the dated letter were written by the same person.
choices.B: dates the manuscript's paper but gives only the earliest time the manuscript could have been written.
choices.C: shows that the manuscript was written in 1521 and not in any other year.
choices.D: is of no use for dating, because paper could be stored for an unlimited time before use.

explanation.why: The watermark ties the manuscript's sheet to a mold used around 1521, so the paper is dated. But Moreau's caution adds a second step: paper could wait years before being used. The writing therefore happened at 1521 or later, never earlier, and the match fixes only that lower limit.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Two sheets from the same mold could be bought by anyone; the text says nothing about who wrote on them.
explanation.B: Correct. The mold dates the sheet to about 1521, but since paper could be stored for years, the writing may be later; it cannot be earlier than the paper.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The paper was made about then, but Moreau's point is that the writing could have come years later.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The match still fixes the earliest possible date of the writing and the date of the paper; Moreau qualifies the method rather than dismissing it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Cookbooks printed in the early 1800s commonly tell the reader to add "a handful of flour" or "butter the size of a walnut" and to bake "in a quick oven until done." By the end of the century, many cookbooks gave level cup and spoon measurements, oven temperatures, and cooking times to the minute. Historians of food have sometimes attributed the change to the arrival of new kitchen tools. Historian Grace Mbeki points out, however, that a vague instruction is perfectly usable by a cook who has learned by watching others, and that the new cookbooks were marketed explicitly to women setting up kitchens far from the families in which they had grown up. In her view, the shift toward precise measurement mainly reflects ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a readership that could no longer rely on having been taught in person.
choices.B: the invention of the measuring cup and the oven thermometer.
choices.C: a decline in the skill of professional cooks over the course of the 1800s.
choices.D: a preference among all cooks for exact recipes once such recipes became available.

explanation.why: Mbeki offers two linked observations: vague instructions suffice for a cook trained by watching others, and the precise new cookbooks were aimed at readers who had moved away from the families that would have trained them. Put together, the precision made up for missing in-person instruction, which is the explanation she prefers to the one about tools.
explanation.A: Correct. Vague recipes work for cooks trained by watching; the new books were sold to readers who had left such training behind, so precision replaced what those readers lacked.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the explanation other historians offer and the one Mbeki argues against.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text discusses home cooks and their readers, not professional cooks, and never mentions a decline in skill.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Mbeki ties the change to one particular group of readers; the text does not claim that every cook preferred precision.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In kabaddi, a team sport played across South Asia, a "raider" crosses into the opposing half of the court, tries to touch as many defenders as possible, and must return to his own half without taking a breath. Under the traditional rules, the raider must also chant the word "kabaddi" aloud without pause for the whole of the raid; a raider whose chant stops is ruled out. Sports historian Arjun Bhattacharya notes that an official standing at the edge of the court cannot see whether a player has inhaled, and that a person cannot keep chanting steadily while breathing in. Considered in this light, the chanting rule most likely exists to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: frighten the defenders by allowing the raider to make as much noise as possible.
choices.B: make the no-breath rule enforceable by turning an invisible act into an audible one.
choices.C: replace the no-breath rule, which officials had found impossible to enforce.
choices.D: give raiders a way to hold their breath for longer than they otherwise could.

explanation.why: The breath rule has a problem: an official cannot see whether a raider has inhaled. The text supplies the missing link, that steady chanting is impossible while breathing in. A raider who keeps chanting has therefore not inhaled, and a chant that stops gives the official something to hear. The chant lets the breath rule be enforced.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never connects the chant to intimidation; it connects it to breathing and to what officials can detect.
explanation.B: Correct. Officials cannot see a breath, but they can hear a chant stop, and chanting cannot continue through an inhalation, so the chant is the breath rule made audible.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The chant supports the breath rule rather than replacing it; both rules apply to the raider.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Chanting uses up air; the text presents it as a check on breathing, not as a way to extend a breath.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The temples of Khajuraho, in central India, were built between about 950 and 1050 CE from a pale sandstone that does not occur at the site; the nearest outcrops lie well to the east, beyond the Ken River, so every block had to be hauled overland and across the water. The temple walls are covered with sculpted figures, many of which run across the joints between neighboring blocks: a dancer's arm carved on one block continues without a break onto the next. A sculptor carving a block before it was set in place could not have aligned such details so exactly. Art historian Rekha Nair observes that this feature, taken together with the distance to the quarries, implies that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the sculptors traveled to the quarries to carve the blocks before they were shipped to the site.
choices.B: the builders chose the distant sandstone because it was easier to carve than any local stone.
choices.C: each sculpted figure was carved by a single artist working on a single block.
choices.D: the blocks were transported as plain stone and carved only after they had been fitted into the walls.

explanation.why: Two observations combine. Details that flow unbroken across joints could not have been aligned if the blocks were carved separately, so the carving was done after the blocks were set. And since the quarries lay far away across a river, the blocks made that journey before they were carved, as plain stone.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Carving before placement is precisely what the unbroken figures rule out.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text explains why the stone had to be hauled, not why that stone was chosen.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says figures spread across several blocks, so a figure was not confined to one block.
explanation.D: Correct. Figures that continue perfectly across joints must have been carved after the blocks were in place, and the long haul from the quarries means the stone arrived plain.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before mechanical refrigeration, wealthy households in cool climates stored ice in ice houses: brick-lined pits, roofed and shaded, that were packed each winter with blocks cut from a frozen pond and covered with straw. Even in the best-built ice house, the stored ice slowly melted from its outer surfaces inward. The amount lost in a given period depends mainly on the area of ice exposed to the air, whereas the amount stored depends on its volume, and doubling every dimension of a block of ice quadruples its surface but multiplies its volume by eight. Historian Olivia Brandt notes that the ice houses of great estates were often several times the size of those at ordinary farms, and that estate records mention ice in August while farm diaries rarely do. Brandt's observations suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: farms harvested their ice later in the winter than estates did and so stored less of it.
choices.B: a large store of ice lasted longer because a smaller share of it was exposed to melting.
choices.C: the ice in a large ice house melted more slowly because its straw covering was thicker.
choices.D: estates stored ice because they could afford the labor of cutting it, which farms could not.

explanation.why: The text gives a rule: melting depends on surface, storage on volume, and volume grows much faster than surface as a block gets bigger. A large store therefore loses a smaller fraction of itself each day than a small one. That explains why estates, with their far larger ice houses, still had ice in August when farms did not.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about when ice was cut; it contrasts the size of the stores.
explanation.B: Correct. Volume grows faster than surface, so a big store loses a smaller fraction each day and survives into late summer, as the estate records show.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text ties melting to the exposed surface of the ice, not to the thickness of the straw.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says farms did store ice; the difference is how long it lasted, and labor is never mentioned.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Animals in zoos sometimes develop repetitive behaviors such as pacing the same route for hours, and zoos try to reduce such behaviors through "enrichment": new objects, scents, or puzzles that give the animal something to investigate. Zoologist Ibrahim Haddad measured pacing in a group of bears before and after keepers began placing scented logs and food puzzles in their enclosure, and found that pacing fell by roughly half. A second group of bears received no enrichment but, so that the two groups could be compared fairly, had keepers enter and move about their enclosure for the same amount of time each day. Pacing in the second group fell by nearly as much. Haddad concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the enrichment objects were useless and the bears had paced only because keepers ignored them.
choices.B: bears in zoos pace because their enclosures are too small to allow natural movement.
choices.C: the drop in pacing in the first group cannot be confidently attributed to the enrichment objects themselves.
choices.D: the bears in the first group would have paced even less if keepers had also spent time in their enclosure.

explanation.why: The first group received two things at once: enrichment objects and keepers spending time in the enclosure. The second group received only the keepers' time and improved nearly as much. Whatever reduced the pacing was present in both groups, so the objects cannot be singled out as the cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The results leave the objects' effect uncertain; they do not show that the objects did nothing, nor that neglect was the cause of pacing.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never discusses enclosure size as a cause of pacing.
explanation.C: Correct. The bears that got only keeper visits improved almost as much, so the visits, not the objects, may account for most of the change.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The keepers did spend time in the first group's enclosure when placing the objects; the text offers no basis for predicting a further drop.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every winter, Khala Nasreen brought out the same gray shawl, its border darned in a dozen places with thread that never quite matched. When Saba's first salary came through, she bought her aunt a new shawl of fine Kashmiri wool and laid it, folded, on the old woman's lap. Nasreen stroked it, declared it far too good for someone like her, and set it on the shelf, where it stayed in its paper for the rest of the season. Months later, Saba came in one evening to find her aunt at the window with a needle, working the gray shawl's torn edge back together, the new one untouched above her head. Only then did Saba understand that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: her aunt had found the Kashmiri wool too coarse to wear against her skin.
choices.B: her aunt intended to give the new shawl away to someone who needed it more.
choices.C: her aunt had forgotten that the new shawl was still on the shelf.
choices.D: the old shawl held something for her aunt that no new one, however fine, could replace.

explanation.why: The aunt does not reject the gift; she praises it and keeps it. Yet months later she is still repairing the worn gray shawl while the fine new one sits unused. The choice to mend rather than replace shows that the old shawl matters to her for reasons a new one cannot supply.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The aunt calls the new shawl too good for her, which is the opposite of finding fault with it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests the aunt planned to pass the gift on; it stays on her shelf.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The aunt placed it there herself and sits directly beneath it; her mending reflects a choice, not forgetfulness.
explanation.D: Correct. The aunt accepts the gift politely but keeps mending the old shawl rather than wear the new one, so her attachment is to the old shawl itself.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For the three years the Okonkwos had lived on Larch Street, Mr. Halloran next door had refused every invitation to dinner, always with the same courteous excuse about his hours at the depot. Still, on most Sunday mornings a loaf of soda bread appeared on their back step, wrapped in a clean cloth and still warm, and when Mrs. Okonkwo's roses failed one spring, a row of cuttings from his own bushes was found planted along her fence before she had so much as mentioned the loss. Mrs. Okonkwo came to understand that her neighbor's refusals ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: were no measure of his regard for her family.
choices.B: concealed a resentment that he could not bring himself to voice.
choices.C: were the reason he had begun leaving the bread in secret.
choices.D: would end as soon as his working hours at the depot changed.

explanation.why: Mr. Halloran declines every invitation, yet he bakes for the family weekly and quietly replaces their lost roses before being asked. Actions this generous cannot come from dislike. The refusals, then, say something about him, perhaps shyness or habit, but nothing about how little he values the family.
explanation.A: Correct. The warm bread and the unasked-for rose cuttings show real goodwill, so the refusals must mean something other than coldness.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Weekly gifts of bread and rose cuttings are the acts of a well-wisher, not of someone nursing resentment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never presents the bread as an apology for the refusals; it presents both as parts of the same quiet character.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text treats the hours as an excuse and gives no reason to think the refusals depend on them.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Marine insurance premiums, the fees that merchants paid underwriters to cover a voyage against loss, survive in large numbers from the eighteenth century, and economic historians have used them as a gauge of how dangerous particular routes were: the higher the risk of shipwreck or capture, the reasoning goes, the higher the premium. Historian Daniel Achterberg examined premiums charged on a route through waters troubled by pirates. Between 1718 and 1730 the premiums fell by nearly half, even though the number of ships reported taken on the route each year hardly changed. Achterberg also found that a new insurance exchange opened in the port in 1721 and that the number of underwriters competing for business there roughly tripled over the following decade. His findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the pirates became less active after 1721, which allowed underwriters to lower their rates.
choices.B: premiums are a reliable gauge of risk only on routes where no pirates were active.
choices.C: the fall in premiums may reflect competition among underwriters rather than any decline in the dangers of the route.
choices.D: underwriters knew less about the route's dangers after the exchange opened than they had before.

explanation.why: If premiums tracked danger, they should have stayed level, since ships were being taken at the same rate throughout. Instead they fell, and the fall coincides with a tripling of underwriters competing for the same business. Competition offers a reason for lower prices that has nothing to do with risk, which is why the premiums cannot simply be read as a gauge of danger.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text states that the number of ships taken each year hardly changed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text questions the gauge because of competition, which could affect premiums on any route, pirates or not.
explanation.C: Correct. Captures held steady while the number of underwriters tripled, so cheaper premiums point to rivals undercutting one another, not to safer seas.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about what underwriters knew; it reports how many of them there were.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Shahnama, the Persian epic completed by the poet Ferdowsi around 1010, was copied and illustrated for patrons across the Persian-speaking world for centuries, yet no two illustrated copies contain the same set of paintings. The poem has far more episodes than any manuscript could depict, so each workshop had to choose. Art historian Parvin Rostami compared the choices made in two copies produced in the same city within a decade of each other. The copy made for a ruling prince illustrates nearly every scene in which a king sits in judgment or receives tribute, while passing over famous battles that the second copy, made for a wealthy merchant, depicts in full. Workshop painters are known to have reused standard compositions, so Rostami does not take the difference as evidence of artistic originality. She does take it as evidence that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the choice of episodes could depend on what a patron wished to see, not only on what the poem offered.
choices.B: the prince's copy omitted battle scenes because its painters lacked standard compositions for them.
choices.C: the prince's workshop employed more skilled painters than the merchant's workshop could afford.
choices.D: patrons across the Persian-speaking world dictated every detail of the paintings in their copies.

explanation.why: Rostami holds the poem, the city, and the period constant and finds that the choice of scenes still differs between the two copies. The difference lines up with the patrons: kingship for the prince, battles for the merchant. Since she sets aside the painters' originality, the remaining explanation is that patrons' preferences shaped the selection.
explanation.A: Correct. Same poem, same city, same decade, yet the prince's copy favors scenes of kingship and the merchant's favors battles; the patron is the variable that differs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says painters reused standard compositions, and the merchant's copy in the same city shows that battle compositions were available.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text compares which scenes were chosen, not how well they were painted.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Two copies from one city show that patrons could influence the choice of scenes; the text does not extend this to every detail or every patron.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Hospitals commonly measure how often staff clean their hands when entering a patient's room by stationing a trained observer on a ward for an hour at a time, and the rates these observers record, often 80 percent or higher, are reported to regulators. Epidemiologist Sunita Varghese installed electronic sensors that logged every entry to the rooms of one ward and every use of the dispensers beside the doors, around the clock, for three months. The sensors recorded hand cleaning at about 45 percent of entries overall, but at close to 80 percent during the hours when an observer was present on the ward. Varghese notes that observers wear identifying badges and that staff can see them. Taken together, these results indicate that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the sensors failed to register many of the hand cleanings that observers were able to see.
choices.B: the rates reported to regulators chiefly describe how staff behave when they know they are being watched.
choices.C: observers should be stationed on the ward around the clock so that compliance stays near 80 percent.
choices.D: staff on this ward cleaned their hands less often than staff at hospitals without sensors.

explanation.why: Two numbers from the same sensors must be reconciled: 80 percent with an observer present, 45 percent overall. Observers are visible to staff. The simplest account is that staff clean their hands more when watched, which means the figure regulators receive is the watched figure, not the everyday one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The sensors matched the observers' 80 percent during observed hours, so they were not missing events; the difference arises when no observer is present.
explanation.B: Correct. The sensors agree with the observers while an observer is visible and drop sharply when none is, so the reported figure captures observed behavior rather than typical behavior.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text draws a conclusion about what the reported rates mean; it makes no recommendation about staffing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text compares observed and unobserved hours on one ward; it says nothing about other hospitals.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Diatoms are single-celled algae whose glassy shells survive in lake mud for thousands of years, and each species tolerates only a certain range of acidity. By identifying the diatoms in successive layers of a sediment core, scientists can reconstruct how a lake's acidity has changed. A lake in a mountain valley became markedly acidic during the twentieth century, and local opinion blames a smelter that opened on the valley floor in 1924. Limnologist Rhona McAllister's core shows acid-tolerant diatom species gradually replacing acid-sensitive ones beginning in layers that date, with an uncertainty of about a decade, to the 1870s, with the pace of change quickening after about 1930. If the dating is sound, McAllister's results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the acid-sensitive diatoms were displaced by species better suited to colder water.
choices.B: the smelter may have hastened the lake's acidification but cannot have started it.
choices.C: the smelter bore no responsibility for any of the change in the lake's acidity.
choices.D: the lake's acidity began to change only after the smelter opened in 1924.

explanation.why: The acid-tolerant species began taking over in the 1870s, and even allowing a decade of dating error, that is decades before 1924. Whatever began the acidification therefore predates the smelter. The quickening after about 1930, however, fits the smelter adding to a process already under way.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text links the species to acidity, not temperature, and never mentions cooling.
explanation.B: Correct. The shift began some fifty years before the smelter existed, so the smelter cannot be the origin; the faster change after 1930 leaves room for it to have made things worse.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The change sped up soon after the smelter opened, so the results leave open a role for it; they rule out only that it began the process.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The core shows the change starting in the 1870s, well before the smelter.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Some orchids produce no nectar; instead, their flowers mimic the shape and scent of a female bee, and male bees that attempt to mate with the flowers carry pollen from one plant to the next. Deception of this kind works only until the males learn. Entomologist Gael Monnier tracked marked male bees at a site where the orchids grew in a dense patch and at a second site where plants of the same species stood dozens of meters apart. At the dense patch, most males visited one or two flowers, flew off, and were never seen at the orchids again, while plants at the scattered site were visited repeatedly and set roughly three times as much fruit. Monnier suggests that for an orchid relying on this strategy, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: growing far from others of its kind may be an advantage rather than a handicap.
choices.B: offering a small amount of nectar would persuade deceived males to keep returning.
choices.C: a dense patch attracts more males than a scattered population and is therefore pollinated more reliably.
choices.D: the males at the scattered site were unable to learn because they met the flowers too rarely.

explanation.why: Males learn to avoid the orchids after being fooled. In a dense patch, each male is fooled once or twice and then abandons the whole cluster, so the remaining flowers lose him. Scattered plants, each met by a male who has not yet encountered the species nearby, keep receiving visits and set more fruit. For a plant that most species would expect to suffer from isolation, isolation here helps.
explanation.A: Correct. A fooled male avoids the orchids afterward, so a dense patch quickly runs out of naive visitors, while scattered plants keep meeting males that have not yet been deceived.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text describes nectarless orchids and never considers what nectar would do.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The scattered plants set about three times as much fruit, so they were pollinated more reliably, not less.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text shows that scattered plants received repeated visits; it does not show that the males there could not learn, only that each had fewer chances to be fooled.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The great temple complexes of Tamil Nadu, in southern India, grew over centuries by accretion. A modest early shrine was enclosed by a wall with a gateway tower, or gopuram; when later rulers wished to leave their mark, they rarely altered the sanctum, which was too sacred to touch, and instead added a new, larger wall outside the existing one, with a taller gopuram of their own. The result is a series of nested enclosures whose towers generally grow taller toward the outside. At one temple, however, architectural historian Meenakshi Sundaram found the tower of the outermost wall to be markedly shorter than the one just inside it. Inscriptions show that the outermost tower was begun in 1620 by a ruler who died three years later. Taken together, these details suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the sanctum at the center of this temple was altered by the rulers who added the outer walls.
choices.B: the outermost tower's height reflects an interrupted project rather than an exception to the usual order of building.
choices.C: the outermost wall was built before the wall inside it, reversing the temple's usual pattern of growth.
choices.D: the ruler who began the outermost tower intended it to be shorter than the others as a sign of humility.

explanation.why: The pattern is that each new ruler builds outward and taller. The short outermost tower looks like a violation until the inscription is added: its builder died three years after beginning it. A tower begun and then abandoned would naturally stand lower than planned. The order of building holds; only the height was cut short.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says rulers rarely touched the sanctum and offers nothing about this temple's sanctum in particular.
explanation.B: Correct. The outermost tower is still the latest, as the pattern predicts; it is short because its builder died three years after starting it, not because the temple grew in a different order.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The inscription dates the outermost tower to 1620 and explains its height; nothing indicates the walls were built in reverse order.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives the ruler's death, not his intentions, as the relevant fact.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A canal that crosses a ridge must climb to a summit level and descend the other side by means of locks. Each time a boat passes through a lock, one lockful of water drains from the level above to the level below, so every boat that crosses the summit draws water from the summit level, and that water can be replaced only from the reservoirs and streams that feed it. Economic historian Johan Lindgren studied the toll records of a canal of this kind, which carried coal to a growing industrial town. In the dry summers of 1826 and 1834, tolls fell by a third, while the price of coal in the town, which rose whenever supplies ran short, climbed to its highest levels of the decade. Lindgren's findings suggest that in those summers ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the reservoirs feeding the summit were enlarged in response to the shortage of water.
choices.B: boat owners stopped using the canal because the tolls charged had become too expensive for them.
choices.C: the town's demand for coal fell, so fewer boats were needed to supply it.
choices.D: the canal carried fewer boats because the summit lacked water to pass them, not because fewer were wanted.

explanation.why: Two signals point in opposite directions: tolls fell, so fewer boats passed, yet coal prices rose, so the town wanted more coal than it got. Demand was not the problem. The text explains what was: each boat drains water from the summit, and in a dry summer the reservoirs and streams could not replace it, so boats could not be passed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about any works on the reservoirs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text reports that tolls collected fell, not that the rate charged rose, and never mentions boat owners' choices.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Coal prices reached their highest levels of the decade, which the text says happened when supplies ran short, not when demand fell.
explanation.D: Correct. High coal prices show that the town wanted more coal, so the fall in traffic must have come from the canal's side, and dry summers starve the summit level that every boat draws on.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A chromolithographic poster of the 1890s was printed one color at a time, each from its own slab of limestone on which an artist had drawn only the parts of the design that were to appear in that color. A poster using eight colors passed through the press eight times, and the sheet had to be positioned precisely each time so that the colors lined up. Printers routinely pulled proofs partway through to check the alignment before continuing. Curator Simone Laurent examined a poster in a museum collection, long displayed as a finished work, that shows a woman in a yellow dress against a pale sky. The sheet carries only three colors and bears small alignment marks in its corners, and the printer's archive lists eight stones for the design. Laurent concludes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the yellow dress and pale sky were the only colors the artist originally intended.
choices.B: the printer abandoned the design after three colors because the stones could not be aligned.
choices.C: the museum's sheet was printed from different stones than those listed in the printer's archive.
choices.D: the museum's sheet is probably a proof pulled partway through printing rather than a finished poster.

explanation.why: The design needed eight stones, one per color, yet the sheet shows only three colors. Printers pulled proofs partway through to check alignment, and the sheet carries alignment marks. A three-color sheet of an eight-color design is therefore most likely one of those proofs, and the finished poster would have looked different.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Eight stones were prepared for the design, so eight colors were intended, not three.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no sign that the design was abandoned; the archive lists all eight stones.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Fewer colors on the sheet are explained by printing having stopped partway, not by a different set of stones.
explanation.D: Correct. Three of eight colors, plus the alignment marks that printers used on proofs, point to a sheet pulled before the printing was complete.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The brick-and-timber temples of the Kathmandu Valley, in Nepal, often carry an inscription on a stone slab or metal plate naming a donor and giving a date, and these dates have been used to build a chronology of the valley's architecture. The region, however, has suffered a major earthquake roughly every century, and a temple whose upper stories collapsed was customarily rebuilt by a new donor, who recorded the gift in a fresh inscription. Architectural historian Sabina Shrestha studied a temple whose plate is dated 1835, two years after a severe earthquake. Its carved wooden roof struts, which could have been salvaged from a damaged building, show a style found elsewhere in the valley only on buildings documented before 1700. If the plate and the struts are both genuine, the most reasonable conclusion is that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the plate was inscribed by a donor who wished to claim credit for a temple built entirely by others.
choices.B: none of the dated inscriptions in the valley can be trusted to give the date of a temple's founding.
choices.C: the carvers of 1835 deliberately revived a style that had gone out of use more than a century earlier.
choices.D: the temple was first built before 1700 and the 1835 plate records its restoration after the earthquake.

explanation.why: The plate says 1835; the struts say before 1700. The text supplies a way to reconcile the two: temples were rebuilt after earthquakes, with new inscriptions, and struts could be reused. A temple built before 1700, damaged in 1833, and restored under a new donor in 1835 accounts for every detail.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes donors recording genuine rebuilding; it offers no reason to suspect a false claim.
explanation.B: Incorrect. One temple's plate recording a restoration does not show that every inscription in the valley is misleading.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text points to the reuse of salvaged struts; a revival would require evidence the text does not give.
explanation.D: Correct. The struts point to a building from before 1700; the plate, dated two years after an earthquake, fits the custom of a new donor recording a rebuilding.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A census counts each person at the place where they are found on a single reference night, and it is often the only source for how a district's population has changed. Demographer Luis Carvalho studied an upland farming district whose recorded population fell by 12 percent between two national censuses taken twenty years apart. The first census had been held in midwinter, the second in late spring. From other records, Carvalho established that each spring a large share of the district's young men left for several months to work the harvests of the lowland plains, and that enumerators were instructed to count people only where they were found on census night. Carvalho argues that, before the decline is accepted as real, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the district's records of seasonal migration should be checked to confirm that the young men ever returned.
choices.B: it should be assumed that the men who left for the harvest settled permanently in the lowlands.
choices.C: the first census should be set aside, since people counted in midwinter were likely visitors rather than residents.
choices.D: allowance must be made for residents who were present at the first census but away at the second.

explanation.why: The two censuses were taken in different seasons. In midwinter the young men were at home and were counted; in late spring many were working in the lowlands and were counted there, if at all. Part of the 12 percent fall could therefore be a matter of timing, so the absent workers must be accounted for before the decline is treated as genuine.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Whether the men returned matters, but Carvalho's point is that the second census was timed to miss them; the problem lies in the census, not in the migration records.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the men left for several months each spring; nothing suggests they settled elsewhere.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Midwinter is when the district's own young men were at home; the text gives no reason to think visitors were present.
explanation.D: Correct. A midwinter count would include the seasonal workers; a late-spring count would miss them, which could produce an apparent drop without anyone leaving for good.

items.subject: science
notes: Venus and Earth are similar in size: Venus's diameter is about 95 percent of Earth's.
Venus has a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
The average surface temperature on Venus is about 465 degrees Celsius.
The average surface temperature on Earth is about 15 degrees Celsius.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between Venus and Earth. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Venus and Earth are similar in size, as Venus's diameter is about 95 percent of Earth's.
choices.B: Venus has a thick atmosphere that is made mostly of carbon dioxide.
choices.C: The average surface temperature on Venus is about 465 degrees Celsius, while on Earth it is about 15 degrees Celsius.
choices.D: Venus, a planet about the size of Earth, has an average surface temperature of about 465 degrees Celsius.

explanation.why: To emphasize a difference, the sentence must mention both planets and show how they are unlike each other. Only one choice sets a fact about Venus directly against the matching fact about Earth.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This sentence emphasizes a similarity in size, the opposite of the goal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes Venus's atmosphere but says nothing about Earth, so no difference is shown.
explanation.C: Correct. It contrasts the two average surface temperatures, about 465 degrees Celsius on Venus and about 15 degrees Celsius on Earth.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It gives Venus's temperature but not Earth's, and it mentions how similar the planets are in size, so it does not emphasize a difference.

items.subject: humanities
notes: The kora is a stringed instrument from West Africa.
Its body is made from a large gourd covered with cowhide.
A traditional kora has 21 strings.
Griots, musicians who preserve history through song, often play the kora.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce the kora to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The kora, a stringed instrument from West Africa, has a body made from a large gourd covered with cowhide.
choices.B: A traditional kora has 21 strings and a body made from a large gourd.
choices.C: Griots are musicians who preserve history through song.
choices.D: Griots often play the kora, which has 21 strings.

explanation.why: Readers who have never heard of the kora first need to know what it is and where it comes from. The best choice names the kora, identifies it as a stringed instrument, gives its region, and adds a detail about how it is made.
explanation.A: Correct. It tells a new reader what the kora is (a stringed instrument), where it is from (West Africa), and what it is made of.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives details about the kora's strings and body but never says what the kora is or where it comes from, so it assumes the reader already knows.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This sentence introduces griots, not the kora.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It mentions the kora's strings but does not explain that the kora is an instrument from West Africa, so an unfamiliar reader is left guessing.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The Shalimar Gardens in Lahore were built in 1641–1642 under the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.
The gardens are laid out on three descending terraces.
They contain more than 400 fountains.
In 1981 they were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with Lahore Fort.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the age of the gardens to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Built in 1641–1642 under the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, the Shalimar Gardens in Lahore are nearly four centuries old.
choices.B: The Shalimar Gardens contain more than 400 fountains spread across three terraces.
choices.C: In 1981, the Shalimar Gardens and Lahore Fort were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
choices.D: The Shalimar Gardens in Lahore are laid out on three descending terraces.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: stress how old the gardens are, and introduce them to readers who do not know them. Only a choice that names the gardens, says where they are, and gives the building date does both.
explanation.A: Correct. It identifies the gardens and their location for a new audience and stresses their age with the 1641–1642 date.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The fountains and terraces describe the gardens' layout, not their age.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 1981 is when the gardens were recognized, not when they were built, so it does not show their age.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes the layout and says nothing about age.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The Suez Canal in Egypt opened in 1869.
It connects the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea, allowing ships to avoid sailing around Africa.
The Panama Canal opened in 1914.
It connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, allowing ships to avoid sailing around South America.
The Panama Canal uses locks to raise and lower ships; the Suez Canal has no locks.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two canals. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Suez Canal opened in 1869, while the Panama Canal opened 45 years later, in 1914.
choices.B: Unlike the Suez Canal, which has no locks, the Panama Canal uses locks to raise and lower ships.
choices.C: The Panama Canal connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, allowing ships to avoid sailing around South America.
choices.D: Both the Suez Canal and the Panama Canal spare ships a long voyage around a continent: Africa in one case and South America in the other.

explanation.why: A similarity needs both canals and something they have in common. The notes show that each canal lets ships avoid sailing around a continent, so the best choice states that shared purpose for both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It compares the opening dates, which highlights a difference of 45 years, not a similarity.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Unlike" signals a difference: one canal has locks and the other does not.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes only the Panama Canal, so it cannot show what the two canals share. This is tempting because the fact it gives is half of the similarity.
explanation.D: Correct. It uses "Both" and shows the shared purpose: each canal lets ships avoid going around a continent.

items.subject: science
notes: The Indus river dolphin lives in the Indus River in Pakistan.
It is nearly blind and relies on echolocation, a series of clicks, to find prey.
Irrigation barrages divide the river into separate sections, and the dolphins rarely move between them.
Ecologist Farah Siddiqui wanted to know whether boat engine noise affects how often the dolphins echolocate.
Her team placed underwater microphones in a stretch of the river near the city of Sukkur.
The dolphins produced fewer echolocation clicks when engine noise was loud.
items.stem: The student wants to present the aim and method of Siddiqui's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Siddiqui's team found that Indus river dolphins near Sukkur produced fewer echolocation clicks when boat engine noise was loud.
choices.B: To learn whether boat engine noise affects how often Indus river dolphins echolocate, Siddiqui's team placed underwater microphones in the river near Sukkur.
choices.C: Siddiqui's team placed underwater microphones near Sukkur, where the nearly blind Indus river dolphin relies on echolocation to find prey.
choices.D: Indus river dolphins, the subject of Siddiqui's study, rarely move between the river sections created by irrigation barrages.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: the aim (what Siddiqui wanted to find out) and the method (what her team did to find out). Only one choice states both the question about engine noise and the use of underwater microphones.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This presents the study's finding, not its aim or its method.
explanation.B: Correct. "To learn whether boat engine noise affects how often … dolphins echolocate" is the aim, and placing underwater microphones near Sukkur is the method.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It gives the method and background about echolocation, but it never states what Siddiqui wanted to learn. It covers only half the goal, which makes it the closest near miss.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is accurate background about the dolphins but says nothing about the study's aim or method.

items.subject: humanities
notes: In ancient Mesopotamia, scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into tablets of wet clay.
In ancient Egypt, scribes wrote with ink on sheets made from the papyrus plant, which grew along the Nile.
In China during the Shang dynasty, inscriptions were carved on turtle shells and the shoulder bones of oxen.
In parts of South and Southeast Asia, texts were written on dried palm leaves for many centuries.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about the materials on which early writing was recorded. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Early writing was recorded on a wide range of materials, including clay tablets, sheets of papyrus, turtle shells and ox bones, and dried palm leaves.
choices.B: Scribes in ancient Mesopotamia pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay, while scribes in ancient Egypt wrote with ink on papyrus.
choices.C: During China's Shang dynasty, inscriptions were carved on turtle shells and on the shoulder bones of oxen.
choices.D: Texts were written on dried palm leaves for many centuries in parts of South and Southeast Asia.

explanation.why: A generalization is a broad statement that covers many cases. The notes describe four different regions, so the best choice draws a general conclusion that all of them support: early writing appeared on many kinds of materials.
explanation.A: Correct. It makes a broad claim about early writing and supports it with materials from all four notes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It compares two specific cultures instead of drawing a general conclusion. It uses more than one note, which makes it tempting, but it stays at the level of particular cases.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It reports a single case from China and makes no general claim.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It reports a single case from South and Southeast Asia and makes no general claim.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened in 2008 on a Norwegian island in the Arctic.
It stores duplicate copies of seed samples held by genebanks around the world, as a backup in case the originals are lost.
The genebanks that deposit seeds keep ownership of them; the vault only stores them.
The vault can hold up to 4.5 million seed samples.
In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) made the first withdrawal, using the seeds to rebuild collections it could no longer reach.
items.stem: The student wants to explain the purpose of the vault and illustrate it with an example. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, which opened in 2008 on a Norwegian island in the Arctic, can hold up to 4.5 million seed samples.
