items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a measurement, questions its accuracy, and then explains why later surveyors rejected it.
choices.B: It compares two methods of measuring mountains and argues that one was more reliable.
choices.C: It focuses on why Peak XV was so difficult to observe from the plains of northern India.
choices.D: It describes an obstacle to a measurement, how it was overcome, and how accurate the result proved.

explanation.why: The text first explains the obstacle: the surveyors had to measure Peak XV from more than 160 kilometers away, where air and the mountains' mass distorted readings. It then describes the response (mathematicians "spent years correcting the observations") and ends by noting that the 1856 figure is within "about thirty feet" of today's. That is obstacle, solution, and outcome.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The final sentence shows the measurement was remarkably accurate; nothing says later surveyors rejected it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Only one approach to measuring is described, and no comparison of methods is made.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The difficulty of observation is only the first part of the text; the corrections and the accuracy of the result are left out.
explanation.D: Correct. The text moves from the difficulty of measuring from far away, to the years of corrections, to the closeness of the result to the modern figure.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Typographers have long repeated the claim that serifs, the small strokes at the ends of letters, guide the eye along a line of print and so make serif typefaces easier to read than sans serif ones. The explanation is appealing, and it fits the fact that most printed books are set in serif type. Yet studies comparing the two styles have generally found small and inconsistent differences in reading speed and comprehension, and the differences that do appear seem to depend more on a reader's familiarity with a typeface than on its serifs. The prevalence of serif type in books, then, may reflect habit and tradition at least as much as any advantage built into the letters.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To question whether a popular explanation accounts for a common practice
choices.B: To show that familiarity is the only factor that affects how fast people read
choices.C: To argue that sans serif typefaces are easier to read than serif typefaces
choices.D: To explain how serifs guide a reader's eye along a line of printed text

explanation.why: The text presents a familiar claim (serifs make type easier to read) that seems to explain why books use serif type. "Yet" introduces studies finding "small and inconsistent differences," and the conclusion suggests the practice "may reflect habit and tradition." The author is casting doubt on the explanation, not replacing it with a strong opposite claim.
explanation.A: Correct. The author doubts that the serif-readability claim explains why books are set in serif type, suggesting habit as an alternative.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says differences "seem to depend more" on familiarity, a hedged comparison; "the only factor" goes far beyond it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The studies found small, inconsistent differences, not an advantage for sans serif type; the author makes no such claim.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text reports this explanation only to question it; it never explains how serifs would guide the eye.

items.subject: science
items.passage: After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996, willows began growing back along some streams where elk had browsed them for decades. A widely told account credits the wolves with this recovery: fearing attack, elk supposedly began avoiding streamside areas where escape was difficult. <u>Some studies tracking elk movements, however, have found that elk often continue to use such areas, particularly when wolves are not actively hunting nearby.</u> Several ecologists therefore attribute the willows' return less to elk fear than to a decline in elk numbers, a decline that hunting by people, bears, and cougars also helped bring about.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It establishes that the wolves played no role at all in the recovery of the willows.
choices.B: It explains why the willows recovered along only some of the streams in the national park.
choices.C: It provides support for the claim that elk avoided streams out of fear of the wolves.
choices.D: It presents evidence that challenges the mechanism proposed in the widely told account.

explanation.why: The widely told account says elk avoided streams out of fear. The underlined sentence, signaled by "however," reports that elk "often continue to use such areas." That evidence undercuts the fear mechanism, and the last sentence ("therefore") offers another explanation in which wolves still contribute to the decline in elk numbers.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The final sentence still counts wolves among the predators that reduced elk numbers, so the text does not deny them any role.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions that willows returned along "some streams" but never explains why only some.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sentence reports that elk keep using streamside areas, which works against the claim that they avoided them.
explanation.D: Correct. The tracking studies cast doubt on the claim that fear kept elk away from streams, the mechanism in the popular account.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Pryce had been told, in the agency's letter, that Thornleigh was a cheerful house, and she had resolved to find it so. When the housekeeper showed her to a room at the very top of the stairs, she remarked upon the fine prospect of the moor; when supper was brought up on a tray rather than served below, she said that she preferred a quiet meal after so long a journey; and when the lamp was found to hold barely an inch of oil, she observed that she had always been an early sleeper. Only after the housekeeper's step had died away did she sit down upon the narrow bed and allow herself, for the space of a minute, to look at the room as it was.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To portray a character who meets small slights with resolute cheer she drops only in private
choices.B: To suggest that Miss Pryce has been deceived by the agency and secretly plans to leave the house
choices.C: To describe the house at Thornleigh and the moorland landscape that surrounds it
choices.D: To show that the housekeeper deliberately mistreats Miss Pryce out of personal dislike

explanation.why: Miss Pryce "resolved to find" the house cheerful, and each disappointment (a top-floor room, supper on a tray, almost no lamp oil) gets a polite, positive remark. Only when alone does she let herself "look at the room as it was." The passage portrays her determined good cheer and the brief private moment when she sets it aside.
explanation.A: Correct. The series of cheerful replies to poor treatment, followed by her private, honest look at the room, is the passage's focus.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The letter's description may be optimistic, but nothing suggests Miss Pryce plans to leave; she allows herself only "a minute" of honesty.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The room and the moor are mentioned only as part of Miss Pryce's responses; the passage centers on her character.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives no motive for how Miss Pryce is treated; the housekeeper's feelings are never described.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the late eighth century, scribes working in monasteries across Charlemagne's empire began to adopt a new script, now called Carolingian minuscule. Earlier regional hands had often crowded letters together and joined them in ways that readers from other regions struggled to decipher; the new script gave each letter a distinct, rounded form and left clearer spaces between words. It spread with the books copied in it, but by the twelfth century it was giving way to the denser Gothic hands. Yet the script had a second life. Fifteenth-century Italian scholars, mistaking Carolingian manuscripts for ancient Roman ones, imitated their lettering, and early printers adapted those imitations into the lowercase letters still used in most printed text today.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It traces a script from its origins to its decline and argues that its influence ended there.
choices.B: It describes a script's features and spread, notes its decline, and traces a later revival.
choices.C: It contrasts two medieval scripts and explains why readers came to prefer the denser one.
choices.D: It identifies a flaw in earlier scripts and argues that monasteries resisted the new script.

explanation.why: The text explains what made Carolingian minuscule distinctive and how "it spread," then says it was "giving way" to Gothic hands. "Yet the script had a second life" turns to its revival by fifteenth-century scholars and printers, whose versions became today's lowercase letters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The last two sentences describe the script's influence continuing long after its decline, the opposite of this claim.
explanation.B: Correct. The text moves from features and spread, to decline, to the script's unexpected revival in print.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Gothic hands are mentioned only as what replaced the script; the text gives no reasons readers preferred them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says scribes across the empire adopted the script; it never says monasteries resisted it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In many households in India and Pakistan, dried neem leaves have long been tucked among stored grain or folded clothes to keep insects away. Chemists studying the neem tree have isolated a compound, azadirachtin, that helps explain the practice: concentrated mainly in the seeds, it discourages many insects from feeding and disrupts the hormones that control their molting. <u>Unlike many synthetic insecticides, azadirachtin breaks down within days when exposed to sunlight.</u> That instability limits how long a single application protects a crop, but it also means the compound is unlikely to linger in soil and water, a trade-off that has made neem extracts attractive to farmers who wish to reduce lasting chemical residues.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It suggests that synthetic insecticides are more effective than azadirachtin.
choices.B: It offers further support for the explanation of the household practice described earlier.
choices.C: It explains why dried neem leaves work well when placed among stored grain.
choices.D: It introduces a property that the text then treats as both a drawback and a benefit.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence states that azadirachtin breaks down quickly in sunlight. The next sentence calls this "instability" a limit on how long it protects a crop "but" also a reason it will not "linger in soil and water." So the sentence sets up a property presented as a trade-off.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The sentence compares how long the compounds last, not how well they work, and the text never ranks their effectiveness.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The sentence shifts from the household practice to crop use; it adds nothing to the explanation of why leaves repel insects.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The household practice was explained in the previous sentence; breaking down in sunlight has nothing to do with leaves stored indoors.
explanation.D: Correct. The quick breakdown shortens protection but also limits residues, which is the "trade-off" named in the last sentence.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the early 1900s, reproducing pianos promised something no earlier technology could offer: a record not just of which notes a pianist played but of how hard and how long each key was struck. Several composers, among them Claude Debussy and Gustav Mahler, recorded their own music on these instruments' paper rolls, and the rolls are sometimes treated as direct evidence of how the composers wished their works to sound. Such confidence is hard to sustain. Technicians often edited the rolls after a session, correcting wrong notes and adjusting dynamics, and what a roll sounds like today depends heavily on how the particular piano replaying it has been adjusted. The rolls preserve a performance, but one filtered through hands other than the composer's.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To caution against treating a kind of early recording as an unaltered record of composers' wishes
choices.B: To explain how reproducing pianos recorded the force and length of each note a pianist played
choices.C: To describe the ways in which technicians improved the sound of early composers' piano rolls
choices.D: To argue that composers' piano roll recordings are less valuable to musicians than their written scores

explanation.why: The text reports that rolls are "sometimes treated as direct evidence" of composers' intentions, then says "Such confidence is hard to sustain." It gives two reasons (editing by technicians and dependence on the replaying piano) and concludes that the rolls are "filtered through hands other than the composer's." The aim is to warn against overtrusting them.
explanation.A: Correct. The text questions the view that rolls directly show how composers wanted their music to sound, because others shaped what we hear.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The first sentence mentions what the pianos recorded, but this is background for the author's warning, not the main purpose.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text presents the technicians' editing as a problem for using the rolls as evidence, not as an improvement to celebrate.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares rolls with written scores or says the rolls lack value; it says they preserve a real but filtered performance.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For three days the fog had lain on the pass so thickly that Tomás Achá could not see the far end of his own measuring chain. He worked anyway, because the railway company in Lima wanted its figures by the month's end, and he had come to distrust the instruments less than he distrusted the men who read his reports. On the fourth morning he woke to an unfamiliar silence and stepped out of the tent to find the whole valley laid open beneath him, the river a thread of tin, the far peaks so sharp they seemed cut from paper. He stood there until his coffee went cold. Then he took out his notebook and, for the first time in his career, wrote something in it that was not a number.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It explains why a character resents his employers and then describes his decision to leave his job.
choices.B: It details the stages of a survey and then lists the measurements that the character recorded.
choices.C: It shows a character's dogged work in hard conditions and then a moment of wonder that breaks his habit.
choices.D: It presents a character's doubts about his instruments and then shows those doubts proving fully justified.

explanation.why: The first half shows Tomás working "anyway" in thick fog to meet a deadline. When the fog lifts, the view holds him "until his coffee went cold," and he writes, "for the first time in his career," something "that was not a number." The structure moves from persistence to a moment of wonder that changes his usual practice.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Tomás distrusts the men who read his reports, but the text never says he decides to leave his job.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The ending stresses that he wrote something that was "not a number," the opposite of listing measurements.
explanation.C: Correct. His persistent work in the fog is followed by the sudden view that leads him to write something other than figures.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Tomás distrusts the instruments less than the men who read his reports, and nothing shows the instruments failing.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Between 1924 and 1927, researchers at the Hawthorne Works, a factory near Chicago, varied the lighting in workrooms to see how it affected productivity. According to the account that later entered textbooks, output rose almost no matter what was changed, even when the lights were dimmed, and the researchers concluded that workers were responding simply to the attention of being studied. The phenomenon became known as the Hawthorne effect. <u>Yet the original lighting data were long believed lost, so for decades the effect's most famous demonstration was known chiefly through secondhand summaries.</u> When economists eventually located and reanalyzed surviving records, they found the evidence for the effect considerably weaker than the textbook version suggested.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains why the researchers concluded that attention caused workers' output to rise.
choices.B: It suggests that the Hawthorne researchers deliberately concealed their original lighting data.
choices.C: It points out a weakness in how a famous result was known, setting up a later reexamination.
choices.D: It provides evidence that the Hawthorne effect was a genuine and powerful phenomenon.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence, introduced by "Yet," notes that the data were "long believed lost," so the result was known "chiefly through secondhand summaries." The next sentence describes economists finding and reanalyzing the records, with weaker results. The sentence therefore exposes a gap in the evidence that the reanalysis then addresses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The researchers' reasoning appears in the second sentence; the underlined sentence concerns how the data were later known.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The data were "believed lost"; nothing suggests anyone hid them on purpose.
explanation.C: Correct. Reliance on secondhand summaries is a weakness, and the final sentence reports what a reexamination of the records found.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sentence raises doubt about the evidence, and the reanalysis it sets up found the effect weaker than claimed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most animal lineages that give up sexual reproduction seem to die out relatively quickly, a pattern biologists usually explain by noting that sex shuffles genes, helping populations purge harmful mutations and adapt to new threats. Bdelloid rotifers, microscopic animals found in ponds and damp moss, are an apparent exception: no male has ever been observed, and the group appears to have reproduced without sex for tens of millions of years. Genetic studies have offered a partial explanation. Bdelloids can survive being completely dried out, and as their cells repair the DNA damage that drying causes, they seem to take up genes from bacteria, fungi, and plants, acquiring by another route some of the genetic novelty that sex would otherwise supply.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To present a case that seems to defy a general pattern and evidence that may explain it
choices.B: To show that bdelloid rotifers reproduce sexually far more often than biologists had believed
choices.C: To argue that sexual reproduction offers no real advantage to animal populations
choices.D: To explain how bdelloid rotifers are able to survive being completely dried out

explanation.why: The text states a general pattern (asexual lineages die out because they lack the gene shuffling of sex) and then presents bdelloids as "an apparent exception." It closes with a "partial explanation": bdelloids may gain new genes from other organisms, getting "by another route" what sex provides. So the purpose is to present an exception and a possible way to account for it.
explanation.A: Correct. Bdelloids seem to contradict the pattern, and gene uptake during DNA repair is offered as a partial explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says no male has ever been observed; it does not suggest bdelloids reproduce sexually at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text accepts that sex supplies useful genetic novelty; its explanation of bdelloids depends on that idea.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Surviving drying is one detail used in the explanation; the text's focus is how bdelloids have lasted without sex.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Most monumental temples are built up from the ground, stone laid upon stone. The Kailasa temple at Ellora, in the Indian state of Maharashtra, was made in the opposite way. Beginning in the eighth century, workers cut deep trenches into a basalt hillside and then carved downward, freeing an entire temple, with its towers, halls, and sculpted elephants, from a single mass of rock. Such a method allowed no correction: a misjudged cut could not be undone by replacing a stone. Historians have estimated that around 200,000 metric tons of rock were removed, and they continue to debate how the builders planned the work so precisely, since no detailed plans from the period survive.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It contrasts the usual way of making a building with one temple's method and considers its demands.
choices.B: It describes a temple's towers and sculptures and then explains how historians measured its size.
choices.C: It explains a building method and then argues that it was more efficient than building upward.
choices.D: It presents the builders' surviving plans and then describes how the workers departed from them in places.

explanation.why: The text opens with the usual method (building "up from the ground") and says Kailasa "was made in the opposite way." After describing the carving, it considers what this required: no room for correction, huge amounts of rock removed, and precise planning that historians still debate.
explanation.A: Correct. The text sets ordinary construction against carving downward and then discusses the precision and planning this method required.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The towers and sculptures are mentioned in passing, and the text does not explain how historians measured anything.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never claims the method was efficient; it stresses how unforgiving and demanding it was.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says "no detailed plans from the period survive," so it cannot present the builders' plans.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The stage left Clara Whitcomb at the crossroads with her trunk, a letter of appointment, and the driver's assurance that someone would be along directly. No one came. The prairie ran off on every side, so level and so wide that the sky seemed to begin at her very feet, and the only building in sight was a sod house with a stovepipe leaning from its roof. <u>She had pictured, on the long journey west, a white schoolhouse with a bell.</u> Now she smoothed her gloves, sat down upon the trunk, and opened the primer she meant to teach from, reading it through from the first page as carefully as if a roomful of children were waiting to hear her.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It reveals an expectation at odds with what Clara finds, setting up her calm response.
choices.B: It foreshadows the white schoolhouse with a bell that Clara will soon discover near the crossroads.
choices.C: It explains the reasons that led Clara to accept a teaching position in the West.
choices.D: It shows that Clara bitterly regrets having left her home to travel so far west.

explanation.why: Before the underlined sentence, Clara sees only empty prairie and "a sod house." The underlined sentence tells what she had imagined: "a white schoolhouse with a bell." The contrast highlights her disappointment, and the next sentence ("Now she smoothed her gloves...") shows her composed reaction as she begins studying her primer.
explanation.A: Correct. Her imagined schoolhouse contrasts with the sod house, and the following sentence shows her meeting the letdown calmly.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing suggests a schoolhouse is nearby; the sentence describes an expectation that the scene has not met.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sentence describes what Clara imagined during the trip, not why she took the job.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Clara's calm, careful reading of the primer shows composure, not bitter regret.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The mirror test, in which an animal is marked in a spot it can see only in a mirror, has long served as a measure of self-recognition; passing it, by touching or inspecting the mark, has been convincingly documented in only a handful of species, such as great apes. In a 2019 study, researchers reported that cleaner wrasses, small reef fish, scraped marks on their throats against the seafloor after viewing themselves in a mirror. The result divided scientists. Some saw evidence that self-recognition is more widespread than assumed; others argued that the test itself may be flawed, since a fish that spends its life removing parasites from other fish might respond to a parasite-like mark for reasons unrelated to any sense of self.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To report a finding that raised questions about animals' abilities and the method used to test them
choices.B: To explain why scientists have now abandoned the mirror test as a reliable measure of self-recognition
choices.C: To describe how cleaner wrasses remove parasites from the bodies of other fish on coral reefs
choices.D: To argue that cleaner wrasses recognize themselves in mirrors in the same way that great apes do

explanation.why: The text explains the mirror test, reports the 2019 wrasse result, and then says it "divided scientists." One side reads it as evidence about animal self-recognition; the other questions whether "the test itself may be flawed." The text's purpose is to present the finding and the two kinds of questions it raised.
explanation.A: Correct. The finding led some to rethink which animals recognize themselves and others to doubt the test itself.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Some scientists argued the test "may be flawed," but the text never says it has been abandoned.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The wrasses' cleaning behavior is mentioned only to explain one group's doubt about the test.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text presents this as only one side of a disagreement; it does not take that position itself.

items.subject: science
items.passage: If most of a spiral galaxy's mass resided where most of its light does, in the bright central bulge, then stars orbiting far from the center ought to move more slowly than those closer in, just as the outer planets of the solar system orbit the Sun more slowly than the inner ones. Measurements made in the 1970s showed otherwise: across many galaxies, orbital speeds remain nearly constant well beyond the visible disk. <u>The most widely accepted interpretation holds that each galaxy is embedded in a vast halo of matter that emits no light.</u> That interpretation, however, rests on the assumption that gravity behaves at galactic scales as it does within the solar system, an assumption that a minority of physicists, proposing modified laws of gravity, have chosen to abandon rather than posit an unseen substance.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It introduces an explanation whose underlying premise the following sentence presents as contestable.
choices.B: It presents the alternative account of the speeds that a minority of physicists have come to favor.
choices.C: It reports the measurements that first revealed the gap between predicted and observed speeds.
choices.D: It resolves the puzzle described earlier by confirming that gravity works the same way at every scale.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence gives the dark-halo explanation for the unexpectedly constant speeds. The next sentence says this explanation "rests on the assumption" that gravity works at galactic scales as it does nearby, an assumption some physicists "abandon." So the sentence introduces an explanation whose foundation is then shown to be disputed.
explanation.A: Correct. The final sentence identifies the assumption beneath the halo explanation and notes that some physicists reject it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The underlined sentence gives the "most widely accepted" view; the minority's modified-gravity account appears in the final sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The measurements are reported in the previous sentence; the underlined sentence interprets them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The halo explanation assumes, rather than confirms, that gravity is the same at all scales, and the next sentence notes that some physicists reject that assumption.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Dear Cousin, You will forgive the brevity of this letter, for my engagements in Town leave me scarcely an hour to myself. I dine abroad almost every evening, and have been twice to the theater, where the company was so brilliant that I quite forgot the play. Pray do not imagine that I miss the country; I assure you I think of it very seldom. I should be obliged, however, if you would tell me whether the old pear tree by the mill has borne this year, and whether my mare is properly exercised, and whether the Marsh family still sit in the third pew, and whether you yourself walk to the brook on Sunday afternoons as we used to do. Your affectionate cousin, Edmund
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To suggest that the writer has been too busy in Town to remember his former life very clearly
choices.B: To reveal, through the writer's own words, a longing for home that undercuts his denials
choices.C: To describe the social pleasures that a fashionable young man could enjoy while living in Town
choices.D: To show that the writer resents his cousin for having chosen to remain behind in the country

explanation.why: Edmund insists he is too busy to write at length and that he thinks of the country "very seldom." Then, with "however," he asks a long, loving string of questions about the pear tree, his mare, the neighbors' pew, and Sunday walks "as we used to do." His detailed questions betray the homesickness he denies, which is the point of the letter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Edmund remembers small details of home vividly, from the pear tree to the third pew, so the letter shows the reverse.
explanation.B: Correct. The many affectionate questions about home contradict Edmund's claim that he seldom thinks of the country.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The dinners and theater appear only in the opening lines, which the rest of the letter undercuts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Edmund signs himself "affectionate" and fondly recalls walks with his cousin; nothing suggests resentment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries the Arthashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, was known to scholars mainly through references in other works; the text itself was presumed lost until R. Shamasastry, a librarian in Mysore, identified a manuscript of it in 1905. Its recovery was greeted as a window onto the court of Chandragupta Maurya in the fourth century BCE, since tradition credited the work to Kautilya, the emperor's minister. Subsequent scholarship has complicated that picture. Analyses of the treatise's vocabulary and style suggest that it was assembled by several hands over a long period, reaching its present form perhaps several centuries after Chandragupta's reign. The text, on this view, remains invaluable, but as evidence of how political thought accumulated over generations rather than as a portrait of a single court.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It recounts a text's recovery, raises doubts about its authenticity, and then exposes the text as a forgery.
choices.B: It recounts a text's recovery and early reception, notes findings that revised it, and reframes its value.
choices.C: It contrasts two scholars' readings of a text and then argues that the earlier reading was correct.
choices.D: It summarizes a text's contents, explains how it shaped a court, and then describes its rediscovery.

explanation.why: The text first describes how the Arthashastra was found in 1905 and "greeted as a window" onto one court. "Subsequent scholarship has complicated that picture" introduces evidence that it was assembled over centuries. The last sentence reframes its worth: still "invaluable," but as a record of political thought accumulating "over generations."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text questions the date and single authorship, not whether the work is genuine, and calls it "invaluable."
explanation.B: Correct. Recovery and first reception, then revising evidence, then a new account of what the text can show.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text contrasts a traditional view with later scholarship and sides with the later view, not the earlier one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not summarize the treatise's contents or describe its influence on a court, and the rediscovery comes first, not last.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When folklorists began carrying wax-cylinder phonographs into the field in the 1890s, the machines seemed to promise an end to the distortions of transcription by ear: at last a song could be preserved exactly as it was sung. The recordings that resulted are now among the most valuable sources for the music of the period, and later performers have often treated them as authoritative versions. <u>A cylinder, however, could hold only about two to four minutes of sound.</u> Singers accustomed to performing a ballad for a quarter of an hour cut verses to fit, and collectors, conscious of the cost of each cylinder, tended to favor shorter pieces. The archive that was meant to capture a tradition thus also reshaped it, privileging whatever suited the medium.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It introduces a technical constraint that the text then uses to qualify the recordings' authority.
choices.B: It explains why folklorists came to prefer phonographs to the older method of transcription by ear.
choices.C: It offers evidence that the recordings are of little value as sources for the music of the period.
choices.D: It identifies the main reason that later performers treated the recordings as authoritative versions.

explanation.why: Before the underlined sentence, the recordings are described as valuable and "authoritative." The underlined sentence, marked by "however," states a limit: two to four minutes per cylinder. The rest of the text shows how that limit led singers to cut verses and collectors to favor short songs, so the archive "also reshaped" the tradition.
explanation.A: Correct. The short recording time is a technical limit, and the text uses it to show the recordings are not simply exact versions of the songs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The folklorists' preference is explained in the first sentence; the underlined sentence describes a drawback of the machines.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text still calls the recordings "among the most valuable sources"; it qualifies their authority rather than dismissing them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The recording limit undermines the recordings' authority; it is not why performers trusted them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The deforestation of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) has often been presented as a cautionary tale: islanders, the account goes, cut down their forests to clear fields and to move their giant stone statues, and the society that depended on those forests collapsed. Ecological evidence complicates the story without wholly overturning it. The Polynesian rats that arrived with the first settlers multiplied rapidly on an island with no predators to check them, and most of the ancient palm nuts recovered by archaeologists bear the marks of rats' teeth, suggesting that the palms may have failed to reproduce even where no one felled them. People still cleared land; but if rats were consuming the seeds that would have replaced the trees, human choices alone cannot account for the speed and completeness of the loss.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a familiar explanation, offers evidence of an additional cause, and concludes the explanation is incomplete.
choices.B: It presents a familiar explanation, refutes it with new evidence, and concludes people played no part in the loss.
choices.C: It contrasts two archaeological methods and then explains why one of them produced more reliable evidence.
choices.D: It describes the arrival of the first settlers and then traces the stages by which they cleared the forests.

explanation.why: The text begins with the familiar account blaming islanders for cutting down the forests. It then says ecological evidence "complicates the story without wholly overturning it" and describes rats eating palm nuts. The conclusion keeps a human role ("People still cleared land") but says "human choices alone" cannot explain the loss.
explanation.A: Correct. The rat evidence adds a second cause, and the conclusion says the human-only explanation is incomplete rather than wrong.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the evidence does not "wholly" overturn the story and states that "People still cleared land."
explanation.C: Incorrect. No archaeological methods are compared; the text discusses causes of the deforestation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The settlers' arrival is mentioned only to explain where the rats came from; the text does not trace stages of clearing.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: It was past midnight when the coach set me down at the inn of St. Aurel, and the landlord, a stooped man who carried his candle as though it were heavier than it looked, led me without a word to the only chamber that remained. Above the hearth hung the portrait of a lady in the dress of a former age, whose painted eyes, by some trick of the artist, appeared to follow the light as it moved about the room. <u>I confess I laughed at myself for remarking it, and I took some pains to turn my back upon her while I undressed.</u> Of the night that followed I shall say only this: I did not sleep, and when the gray light came through the shutters, I found that I had, at some hour I cannot recollect, turned the portrait to face the wall.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It exposes a gap between the narrator's professed amusement and his conduct, anticipating his unease.
choices.B: It establishes that the narrator dismisses the portrait as harmless and is untroubled by it all night.
choices.C: It suggests that the landlord deliberately placed the narrator in a room meant to frighten him.
choices.D: It explains the method by which the artist made the eyes of the portrait appear to move.

explanation.why: In the underlined sentence the narrator says he "laughed at" himself for noticing the portrait, yet he also "took some pains" not to face it. That mismatch between words and behavior hints at hidden unease, which the final sentence confirms: he did not sleep and turned the portrait to the wall.
explanation.A: Correct. He laughs off the portrait yet avoids facing it, a tension that prepares for his sleepless night.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The final sentence shows the narrator sleepless and turning the portrait around, so he was clearly troubled.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The landlord gives him "the only chamber that remained," and nothing suggests any intent to frighten him.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The previous sentence mentions "some trick of the artist," but no method is explained anywhere.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Today the word "Luddite" is applied to anyone who distrusts new technology, a usage implying that the original Luddites, English textile workers who smashed machinery between 1811 and 1816, were simply hostile to machines. The record of their actions suggests a narrower grievance. Many of the stocking frames they broke were not new inventions at all, having been in use for more than two centuries, and raiders often wrecked the frames of employers who paid below customary rates or produced cheap, poorly made goods while sparing those of employers who did not. What the Luddites opposed, in other words, was less machinery as such than the uses to which particular employers put it, a distinction their modern namesake has largely erased.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To show that the Luddites opposed only machines that had recently been invented
choices.B: To argue that the Luddites' resistance succeeded in raising textile workers' wages
choices.C: To contend that a familiar term misrepresents the motives of the group it is named for
choices.D: To explain how the Luddites organized and carried out their raids on textile employers

explanation.why: The text opens with the modern meaning of "Luddite," which implies the original Luddites "were simply hostile to machines." It then gives evidence (old machines, selective raids) of "a narrower grievance" and concludes that the modern usage has "largely erased" that distinction. The purpose is to correct what the term suggests about the group.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text stresses that many frames they broke had been in use for more than two centuries.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says whether the raids changed wages; it discusses only what the Luddites objected to.
explanation.C: Correct. The author argues that the modern word wrongly implies a general hostility to machines that the Luddites' actions do not show.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Details about which frames were broken serve as evidence about motives; the text does not explain how raids were organized.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1921, returning to India by ship from a scientific meeting in England, the physicist C. V. Raman spent hours studying the deep blue of the Mediterranean. The prevailing explanation, associated with the British physicist Lord Rayleigh, held that the sea's color was largely a reflection of the blue sky. Raman doubted it. Viewing the water through a polarizing prism, which suppressed the light reflected from its surface, he found that the blue remained, and he argued that the color arose instead from light scattered by the water's own molecules. Pursuing that question, Raman and his colleagues in Calcutta spent the next several years studying how liquids scatter light, research that culminated in 1928 in the discovery of the effect that now bears his name and that earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the instrument Raman used to observe the sea during his voyage
choices.B: To argue that the Raman effect could have been found only by studying the sea
choices.C: To trace how a challenge to an accepted explanation led to a major discovery
choices.D: To argue that Rayleigh's explanation of the blue color of the sky was mistaken

explanation.why: Raman questions the accepted view that the sea is blue because it reflects the sky, tests it with a polarizing prism, and proposes molecular scattering instead. "Pursuing that question" links this doubt to years of research that led to the 1928 discovery and a Nobel Prize. The text follows the path from one challenge to a major result.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The polarizing prism is one detail in Raman's test, not the focus of the whole text.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the sea question started Raman's research, not that it was the only possible route to the discovery.
explanation.C: Correct. Raman's doubt about the reflection explanation started the line of research that produced the Raman effect.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Rayleigh's explanation that Raman doubted concerned the color of the sea, not the sky.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The story is often told that in 1890 a thirteen-year-old Pablo Casals, browsing in a secondhand music shop in Barcelona, rediscovered Johann Sebastian Bach's six suites for unaccompanied cello, forgotten since the composer's death. The suites had not, in fact, been lost: printed editions had circulated since the 1820s, and cello students had long worked through them. What they lacked was standing. Regarded chiefly as exercises for building technique, they were rarely performed whole before an audience. Casals studied them for more than a decade before playing them publicly, and his recordings of the complete set in the late 1930s helped establish them as concert works. His achievement, then, was not to recover the music but to change what listeners believed it was for.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes how Bach composed the suites and then traces their influence on later music for the cello.
choices.B: It recounts a popular story and then dismisses Casals's role in the suites' later fame as exaggerated.
choices.C: It recounts a popular story, confirms it with new evidence, and then explains why the suites were forgotten.
choices.D: It recounts a popular story, corrects an assumption in it, and then redefines the central figure's achievement.

explanation.why: The text opens with the story that Casals "rediscovered" forgotten suites. It corrects this ("had not, in fact, been lost"), explains that they lacked "standing," and concludes that Casals's real achievement was "to change what listeners believed it was for." The structure is story, correction, and a redefined achievement.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how Bach composed the suites or about later music they influenced.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The author still credits Casals with helping establish the suites as concert works; only the idea of rediscovery is rejected.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text contradicts the popular story; it says the suites were never lost or forgotten.
explanation.D: Correct. The assumption that the suites were lost is corrected, and Casals's achievement is redefined as changing how the suites were seen.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In large stretches of the open ocean, the water holds plenty of nitrate and phosphate yet supports surprisingly little phytoplankton, a puzzle that oceanographers in the late 1980s traced to a scarcity of iron. Experiments since the 1990s have confirmed the diagnosis: when ships have spread dissolved iron across patches of such water, phytoplankton have bloomed within days. <u>From this result, some have drawn a proposal: fertilize the oceans with iron on a vast scale, and the resulting blooms will draw carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere.</u> The step from bloom to lasting carbon storage, however, is longer than the proposal implies. Carbon is kept out of the atmosphere for centuries only if the plankton sink into the deep ocean before being consumed, and in most experiments only a small fraction appears to have done so.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It provides evidence that adding iron to the ocean would remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for centuries.
choices.B: It presents a proposal drawn from an experimental result, which the text then says overlooks a necessary condition.
choices.C: It states the hypothesis that the iron experiments described in the previous sentence were designed to test.
choices.D: It explains why waters rich in nitrate and phosphate nonetheless support little phytoplankton.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence turns the experimental finding (iron causes blooms) into a proposal to fight climate change. The next sentence says the step to "lasting carbon storage" is "longer than the proposal implies": the plankton must sink to the deep ocean, and in most experiments few did. So the text presents the proposal and then identifies the condition it overlooks.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The underlined sentence states a proposal, not evidence, and the text goes on to doubt that the carbon would stay out of the atmosphere.
explanation.B: Correct. The proposal assumes blooms will remove carbon, but the text explains that lasting removal also requires the plankton to sink, which rarely happened.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The experiments tested whether iron scarcity limits phytoplankton; the proposal was drawn from their results afterward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The first sentence explains the puzzle by pointing to iron scarcity; the underlined sentence describes a proposal.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Crossing the square at four o'clock, with the pigeons lifting and settling and the clock on the post office striking a quarter late, as it always had, Agnes was thinking of nothing in particular (of the price of lemons, of whether the cleaner's would have her blue coat ready) when the smell of roasting chestnuts from a cart by the fountain brought back, entire and without warning, the winter she was nine: her father's hand closed over hers inside his coat pocket, the steam of their breath, the paper cone too hot to hold. She stopped so abruptly that a man behind her stepped around her, muttering. And then the clock finished striking, and she went on, a little more slowly, toward the cleaner's.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It traces a character's idle thoughts, a memory revived by a smell, and her slightly altered return to her errand.
choices.B: It contrasts a character's errands with her father's habits and concludes that she has grown to resemble him.
choices.C: It shows a character straining to recall a memory and then succeeding only after she has left the square.
choices.D: It describes a character's memory of her father and then explains why she has avoided the square ever since.

explanation.why: Agnes begins "thinking of nothing in particular" when the chestnut smell brings back a childhood memory "entire and without warning." She stops, then continues "a little more slowly" toward the cleaner's. The text moves from ordinary thoughts, to a sudden memory, to her return to the errand with a small change in her pace.
explanation.A: Correct. Idle thoughts give way to a vivid memory, and she goes on with her errand, "a little more slowly."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares her habits to her father's or says she resembles him; it presents one memory of him.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The memory arrives suddenly and "without warning" while she is in the square; she makes no effort to recall it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Agnes crosses the square as part of an ordinary errand; nothing suggests she has avoided it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: After vast natural gas reserves were found in the northern Netherlands in 1959, gas exports brought the country a flood of foreign revenue. Yet by the 1970s, observers noticed that Dutch manufacturing was struggling, and in 1977 a British magazine coined a term for the paradox: "Dutch disease." The mechanism is now well understood. As foreign buyers acquire a country's currency to pay for its resource exports, the currency's value rises, making the country's other exports more expensive abroad; at the same time, workers and investment are drawn toward the booming sector. A resource windfall can thus weaken the very industries that might have sustained an economy after the resource runs out.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain how an apparent benefit can cause economic harm, using the case that named it
choices.B: To describe the discovery of natural gas reserves in the northern Netherlands in 1959
choices.C: To show that the struggles of Dutch manufacturing had causes unrelated to natural gas
choices.D: To argue that countries should avoid selling their natural resources to foreign buyers

explanation.why: The text calls the Dutch experience a "paradox": gas revenue arrived, yet manufacturing struggled. It explains the mechanism (a stronger currency and resources shifting to the booming sector) and concludes that a windfall "can thus weaken" other industries. The Netherlands is the example that gave the problem its name.
explanation.A: Correct. The text explains how a resource windfall can harm other industries, using the Dutch case that the term is named after.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The 1959 discovery is background in the first sentence; most of the text explains the mechanism.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text links the manufacturing problems directly to the effects of gas exports.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text explains a risk of resource exports; it never recommends that countries stop them.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every winter afternoon, when the sun came low and thin through the arches of the Qissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar, Gul Rahim set out his books on a faded carpet and waited. He did not call to the passersby as the fruit sellers did; he held that a book which must be shouted for is not worth the reading. Students stopped, turned a page or two, and went on. A soldier once bought a volume of verse for its red binding and was gently advised to take a cheaper one with better poems. By evening Gul Rahim had generally sold nothing, and he would wrap the books again in their cloth, one by one, with the air of a man who has spent his day exactly as he wished.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To suggest that a bookseller's gentle manner hides a growing bitterness
choices.B: To portray a bookseller whose principles matter more to him than making sales
choices.C: To describe the ordinary trade of a bazaar's fruit sellers and its booksellers
choices.D: To show how a bookseller's refusal to advertise eventually brings him success

explanation.why: Gul Rahim refuses to shout for customers on principle, and he even talks a buyer into a cheaper book with "better poems." Though he "generally sold nothing," he packs up like "a man who has spent his day exactly as he wished." The passage portrays someone who values his ideas about books over making money.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The last sentence shows contentment, not hidden bitterness.
explanation.B: Correct. His refusal to advertise, his advice to the soldier, and his contentment despite poor sales all show principles valued above profit.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The fruit sellers appear only once, as a contrast that shows Gul Rahim's character.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says he "generally sold nothing," so his methods do not bring success.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Until about 2010, the colors of extinct feathered dinosaurs were left to the imagination of illustrators. Then paleontologists, examining fossil feathers under powerful microscopes, identified melanosomes, tiny structures that hold the pigment melanin, and noticed that in living birds their shapes correspond closely to color: long, narrow melanosomes tend to produce black or gray, round ones reddish brown. By measuring fossil melanosomes, researchers reconstructed the plumage of several species. <u>The method, however, captures only part of the story of a feather's color.</u> Yellows and reds in many birds come from carotenoid pigments, which are not stored in melanosomes, and experiments simulating fossilization have shown that heat and pressure can alter melanosome shapes. Reconstructions are therefore best read as partial outlines of an animal's appearance, not finished portraits.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It supports the claim that melanosome shape reliably predicts color in living birds.
choices.B: It explains how researchers worked out which melanosome shapes produce which colors.
choices.C: It introduces a limit that the text then develops to temper confidence in the results.
choices.D: It suggests that reconstructions produced by the method are almost entirely inaccurate.

explanation.why: Before the underlined sentence, the text describes the melanosome method and its successes. The underlined sentence, signaled by "however," says the method captures "only part" of the story. The next sentence gives reasons (carotenoids, changes during fossilization), and the last calls reconstructions "partial outlines," not "finished portraits."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The underlined sentence starts a discussion of the method's shortcomings rather than adding support for it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The link between shape and color is described in the second sentence; the underlined sentence turns to the method's limits.
explanation.C: Correct. The limit is explained in the following sentence, and the conclusion urges reading reconstructions as partial.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text calls the reconstructions "partial outlines," which means incomplete, not almost entirely wrong.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In April 1855, during the Crimean War, the British photographer Roger Fenton made two exposures of the same desolate stretch of road from the same position. In one, cannonballs lie scattered across the road; in the other, the road is nearly clear and the balls lie in the ditch beside it. Which came first matters a great deal: if the empty road was photographed first, someone apparently moved the balls onto it to heighten the scene's drama. Because the pictures carry no dates, investigators have compared minute details, such as small rocks that seem to have shifted between exposures, and many now conclude that the empty road came first. Even so, that conclusion rests on inference, and the photographs themselves cannot reveal who moved the balls, or why.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes two images, explains why their order matters, reports a likely order, and notes what is unknown.
choices.B: It explains a photographer's wartime methods and then compares his work with that of later photographers.
choices.C: It describes two images, argues that Fenton staged both, and then explains how he arranged each scene.
choices.D: It describes two images and then argues that the order in which they were made cannot be determined.

explanation.why: The text describes the two photographs, explains that their order matters because it would show whether the scene was arranged, and reports that "many now conclude" the empty road came first. It ends by noting that the conclusion "rests on inference" and that the photos cannot show "who moved the balls, or why."
explanation.A: Correct. The text moves from the two images, to why their order matters, to the likely order, to the questions that remain.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text discusses only these two photographs and makes no comparison with later photographers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says both images were staged, and it does not explain how any scene was arranged.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text reports that many investigators have reached a conclusion about the order; what remains unknown is who moved the balls and why.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The southern cassowary, a large flightless bird of the rainforests of northern Australia and New Guinea, eats mainly fruit that has fallen to the forest floor. It swallows the fruit whole, and the seeds pass through its body undamaged. Because the bird walks long distances each day, it drops those seeds far from the parent tree. For some rainforest plants with very large fruit, the cassowary is the only animal big enough to spread their seeds at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the diets of the flightless birds of Australia
choices.B: To describe how far the cassowary walks in a single day
choices.C: To argue that the cassowary is the most important animal in the rainforest
choices.D: To explain the role the cassowary plays in spreading rainforest seeds

explanation.why: Every sentence points in the same direction: the cassowary eats fruit, the seeds "pass through its body undamaged," it carries them "far from the parent tree," and for some plants it is "the only animal big enough to spread their seeds." The text explains the bird's role as a seed spreader.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only one bird is discussed; the text never describes other flightless birds or their diets.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The bird's long walks are mentioned only to explain why seeds end up far from the parent tree; they are a detail, not the main point.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the cassowary is the only seed spreader for some large-fruited plants, not that it is the most important animal overall.
explanation.D: Correct. The text explains how the cassowary's eating and walking habits carry seeds away from parent trees, and why that matters for some plants.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On his first afternoon as a volunteer at the town library, Tariq was given a cart of returned books and told to put each one back where it belonged. He had expected to be bored. Instead, he found himself pausing at every shelf: a guide to Antarctic birds, a history of bridges, a book of old maps. When the librarian came to find him an hour later, the cart was still half full, and Tariq was sitting on the floor, reading.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To list the subjects Tariq discovers on the library shelves
choices.B: To explain how books are organized in a public library
choices.C: To portray how Tariq's expectation of a dull task is overturned by curiosity
choices.D: To show that Tariq is careless about the work he was given

explanation.why: The text sets up an expectation, "He had expected to be bored," and then reverses it with "Instead": Tariq keeps stopping to look at books and ends up reading on the floor. The passage is built around that reversal, from expected boredom to absorbed curiosity.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The three subjects are named only as examples of what distracts him; listing them is not the point of the text.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never explains the library's system for arranging books; shelving is only the task Tariq was given.
explanation.C: Correct. Tariq expected boredom, but the books on the shelves capture his attention so completely that he forgets the task.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Tariq's slowness comes from fascination with the books, not carelessness; the text's tone toward him is warm, not critical.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When Chicago prepared to host a world's fair in 1893, its organizers wanted a structure that could rival the Eiffel Tower, which had amazed visitors to the Paris fair four years earlier. The engineer George Ferris proposed something no one had built on such a scale: a giant turning wheel more than 80 meters tall, carrying 36 enclosed cars. Many doubted that the wheel would even turn. Yet it ran safely all summer, lifting more than a million riders above the fairgrounds.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It explains how the Ferris wheel was built and then lists the many wheels that imitated it.
choices.B: It presents a challenge the fair's organizers faced and then describes the invention that met it.
choices.C: It argues that the Ferris wheel was more impressive than the Eiffel Tower.
choices.D: It describes a famous tower and then explains why a copy of it was built in Chicago.

explanation.why: The first sentence states what the organizers wanted: "a structure that could rival the Eiffel Tower." The rest describes Ferris's proposal, the doubts about it, and its success. The text moves from a challenge to the invention that answered it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never explains the construction process or mentions later wheels.
explanation.B: Correct. The organizers needed a rival to the Eiffel Tower; Ferris's wheel, despite doubts, met that need by running safely all summer.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the wheel was meant to rival the tower but never claims it was more impressive.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The organizers wanted something to rival the tower, not a copy of it, and the wheel is nothing like a tower.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Warli, a community living in the hills north of Mumbai, in western India, have long decorated the mud walls of their homes with paintings. The painters use only a white paste made from rice, applied with a chewed bamboo stick, on a background of reddish-brown earth. Their pictures are built from a few simple shapes: circles, triangles, and squares. A circle and two triangles joined at the tips become a dancing figure, and rows of such figures become a wedding or a harvest.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain how the rice paste used in Warli painting is prepared
choices.B: To compare Warli painting with other art traditions of India
choices.C: To describe the materials and basic shapes used in Warli painting
choices.D: To argue that simple shapes make better art than detailed ones

explanation.why: After introducing the Warli, the text describes what they paint with (rice paste, a bamboo stick, an earth background) and what they paint from (circles, triangles, squares) and shows how those shapes combine into figures and scenes. The purpose is to describe the materials and shapes of the art.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the paste is made from rice but never explains how it is prepared.
explanation.B: Incorrect. No other art tradition is mentioned, so there is no comparison.
explanation.C: Correct. The text describes the paste, the stick, the earth background, and the three shapes from which Warli pictures are built.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes the Warli's use of simple shapes without claiming that such art is better than any other kind.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sandgrouse are pigeon-sized birds that nest in deserts of Africa and Asia, often many kilometers from the nearest water. Their chicks cannot fly for weeks after hatching, yet they need to drink every day. <u>The male solves this problem in an unusual way: he wades into a pool at dawn, soaks his belly feathers, and flies home with the water trapped in them.</u> His belly feathers are specially shaped to hold water, and the chicks drink by pulling them through their beaks.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It suggests that sandgrouse chicks can survive without drinking.
choices.B: It explains how the problem described in the previous sentence is solved.
choices.C: It explains why sandgrouse nest so far from water.
choices.D: It introduces a problem that the rest of the text goes on to explain.

explanation.why: The sentence before the underlined one states a problem: the chicks "cannot fly" but "need to drink every day." The underlined sentence begins "The male solves this problem" and describes how. Its function is to give the solution to the problem just raised.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the chicks "need to drink every day," and the underlined sentence describes how they get water, not how they do without it.
explanation.B: Correct. The previous sentence raises the chicks' need for water; the underlined sentence explains how the male delivers it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text states that sandgrouse nest far from water but never explains why.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The problem is introduced in the previous sentence; the underlined sentence supplies the solution, not the problem.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Whenever Lucía asked her grandmother how much salt went into the stew, the answer was always the same: "Enough." There were no measuring spoons in the kitchen and no written recipe, only a pinch here and a handful there. So that winter Lucía stood beside her with a notebook, catching each pinch in a spoon and writing down the amount. By spring the notebook was full. Her grandmother laughed at it, but she did not say the stew tasted wrong.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To suggest that Lucía's grandmother is a careless cook
choices.B: To show how Lucía sets out to record a method her grandmother never wrote down
choices.C: To explain why a stew needs the right amount of salt
choices.D: To describe the notebook that Lucía kept

explanation.why: The text first establishes that the grandmother cooks without measurements or a recipe. The word "So" introduces Lucía's response: she measures each pinch and writes it down until "the notebook was full." The passage mainly shows Lucía's project of capturing her grandmother's unwritten method.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The grandmother cooks by instinct rather than measurement, and the final sentence suggests her stew tastes right; nothing calls her careless.
explanation.B: Correct. The text shows Lucía measuring and recording what her grandmother does by feel, turning an unwritten method into a written one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never explains the role of salt in cooking; salt is just the first thing Lucía asks about.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The notebook is the tool of Lucía's project, not the subject of the text; its contents are described in a single sentence.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Kuldhara, a village in the desert of Rajasthan, in northwestern India, has stood empty for about two hundred years. Its stone houses, lanes, and temple remain, but no one lives in them. A popular legend says that all of its residents left together in a single night. Historians, however, point to more ordinary causes: a drying water supply, heavy taxes, and the decline of the trade routes that once passed nearby. Whatever the reason, the empty village now draws curious visitors from across the country.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a legend and then provides evidence that proves the legend true.
choices.B: It explains the history of trade in Rajasthan and then describes one village.
choices.C: It describes an abandoned village and then contrasts a legend about it with historians' explanations.
choices.D: It describes a village and then explains how it was rebuilt.

explanation.why: The text opens by describing Kuldhara as empty, then gives "a popular legend" about why. The word "however" introduces the historians' different, "more ordinary" explanations. The structure is description, then legend set against historical explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The historians' explanations differ from the legend; the text does not prove the legend true.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Trade routes are mentioned only as one possible cause of the village's abandonment; the text does not cover the history of trade.
explanation.C: Correct. After describing the empty village, the text sets the single-night legend against historians' explanations of why people left.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The village is still empty; the text says nothing about rebuilding.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Vultures are often seen as unpleasant because they feed on dead animals, yet this habit makes them valuable. Their stomach acid is strong enough to destroy many of the bacteria that grow in rotting flesh, so a vulture can eat a carcass that would make most other animals sick. By clearing away dead animals quickly, a flock of vultures also removes a breeding ground for disease before it can spread to livestock or people.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the bacteria that grow in rotting flesh
choices.B: To explain why vultures' feeding habits are useful
choices.C: To argue that vultures should be kept away from livestock
choices.D: To describe how vultures locate food from the air

explanation.why: The first sentence admits that vultures seem unpleasant "yet" says their habit "makes them valuable." The next two sentences explain why: their stomach acid lets them eat what would sicken other animals, and they remove sources of disease. The text explains the value of their feeding habits.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Bacteria are mentioned only to show what vultures' stomach acid can destroy; the text does not describe them.
explanation.B: Correct. The text explains that vultures can safely eat rotting carcasses and that doing so removes a source of disease.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says vultures protect livestock from disease, the opposite of this claim.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions how vultures find food.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The light, finely woven straw hats known as Panama hats have never been made in Panama. They are woven in Ecuador from the leaves of the toquilla palm, a craft practiced there for centuries, especially in the towns of Montecristi and Cuenca. In the 1800s, however, the hats were shipped north to Panama, where travelers crossing between the Atlantic and Pacific bought them in large numbers. Those travelers named the hats for the place where they had bought them, and the name has stuck ever since.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes how a hat is woven and then compares it with hats made in other countries.
choices.B: It describes the travelers who crossed Panama in the 1800s.
choices.C: It corrects a mistaken idea about where a product comes from and then explains how the mistake arose.
choices.D: It argues that the hats should be renamed for the country that makes them.

explanation.why: The opening sentence corrects a common assumption: Panama hats "have never been made in Panama." The second sentence says where they really come from, and the last two explain how the misleading name came about. The text corrects an error and then accounts for it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text names the material and the towns but does not explain the weaving process or compare the hats with others.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The travelers are mentioned only to explain the name; the text does not describe them.
explanation.C: Correct. The text states that the hats come from Ecuador, not Panama, and then explains that travelers named them for the place they bought them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text explains the name but never suggests changing it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1885, Wilson Bentley, a young farmer in Vermont, attached a camera to a microscope and, working outdoors in the freezing cold, took the first clear photograph of a single snowflake. Over the next forty-six winters he photographed more than 5,000 of them. Each had to be caught on a black board, moved under the lens with a feather, and photographed before it melted. Bentley's pictures, which showed that snow crystals take an astonishing variety of six-sided forms, are still reproduced today.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the farm in Vermont where Bentley lived
choices.B: To explain why snowflakes always have six sides
choices.C: To describe how Bentley produced his photographs of snowflakes
choices.D: To argue that Bentley was the greatest photographer of his time

explanation.why: The text follows Bentley's work step by step: the camera on the microscope, the cold, the black board, the feather, the race against melting. Its focus is on how he made his snowflake photographs.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Bentley is identified as a farmer in Vermont, but the farm itself is never described.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions six-sided forms but never explains why snow crystals have that shape.
explanation.C: Correct. Most of the text describes Bentley's method: catching each flake, moving it with a feather, and photographing it before it melted.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text praises the variety his pictures revealed but makes no comparison with other photographers.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The gharial is a long-snouted, fish-eating crocodilian that once lived in rivers across the northern Indian subcontinent. Today most of the world's wild gharials live along a single stretch of the Chambal River in central India. <u>The Chambal is unusual among the region's large rivers in that its water is relatively clean and its banks are lined with wide, undisturbed sandbanks.</u> Those sandbanks matter: female gharials dig their nests in them, and young gharials bask on them in the sun.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains what makes the Chambal a suitable home for the gharial.
choices.B: It suggests that the Chambal's water is too polluted for gharials.
choices.C: It contrasts the gharial's past range with its present one.
choices.D: It argues that gharials should be moved to other rivers.

explanation.why: The sentence before the underlined one says most gharials now live on the Chambal. The underlined sentence tells us what is special about that river: clean water and wide sandbanks. The next sentence confirms why the sandbanks matter to gharials. So the underlined sentence explains why the Chambal suits them.
explanation.A: Correct. The sentence names the features, clean water and undisturbed sandbanks, that make the Chambal a good home for gharials, as the next sentence confirms.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The sentence says the Chambal's water is "relatively clean," the opposite of polluted.
explanation.C: Incorrect. That contrast is made by the first two sentences; the underlined sentence describes the river itself.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the text proposes moving gharials anywhere.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The suanpan, the traditional Chinese abacus, is a wooden frame with rods of sliding beads. Each rod stands for a place value: ones, tens, hundreds, and so on. Beads below a central bar count one each, and beads above it count five. To add or subtract, the user flicks the beads up or down with quick, practiced motions. A skilled user can carry out long calculations at remarkable speed, and the device needs no power, no paper, and no batteries.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain the history of counting devices in China
choices.B: To argue that the abacus is superior to electronic calculators
choices.C: To describe how the suanpan is arranged and used
