items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A contact sheet prints every frame on a roll of film, at small size, on a single page; photographers once used it to pick the frames worth enlarging. For historians of photography, such sheets are ______: the famous image a photographer chose to print appears alongside the frames taken moments before and after it, showing how the photographer circled the subject, adjusted the framing, and finally settled on one version.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: revealing
choices.B: redundant
choices.C: decorative
choices.D: misleading

explanation.why: The colon introduces what the sheets offer: the famous image "alongside" the other frames, "showing how the photographer" worked toward the final version. Something that shows a hidden process is "revealing."
explanation.A: Correct. The sheets show the frames before and after the famous image, exposing the process by which the photographer "settled on one version."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The other frames add information the famous print alone cannot give, so the sheet is useful, not an unnecessary repetition.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text values the sheets for what they show about the photographer's choices, not for their appearance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sheets give historians an accurate picture of how the final image was chosen; nothing suggests they deceive.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Niall had assumed that the whistles were a kind of language with fixed words, one note for "left" and another for "right." Watching his uncle work the dog along the ridge, he saw that it was less ______ than that. The same rising note sent the dog wide one minute and brought her in close the next, and what changed was not the sound but the dog's distance, the slope, and the way his uncle leaned on his stick.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: rigid
choices.B: musical
choices.C: subtle
choices.D: effective

explanation.why: Niall expected "fixed words," one note for each command, but "the same rising note" means different things depending on the situation. So the system is less fixed, or less "rigid," than he assumed.
explanation.A: Correct. Niall assumed each note had one fixed meaning; instead, the same note means different things, so the system is less rigid than he thought.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The passage contrasts fixed meanings with meanings that change by situation; it says nothing about how musical the whistles are.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The whistling turns out to be more subtle than a fixed code, not less, since the same note shifts meaning with distance, slope, and posture.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The dog responds correctly in every case; nothing suggests the whistles work less well than Niall assumed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The sundew captures insects with sticky droplets on hair-like tentacles, and when prey touches one tentacle, its neighbors bend inward over several minutes. Botanists once treated this bending as a purely mechanical response to pressure. Experiments complicate that picture. Tentacles bend far more strongly when touched by a nitrogen-rich object, such as a fragment of insect, than by an equally heavy grain of sand, suggesting that the plant ______ among stimuli: it responds to the chemical signature of food, not merely to contact.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: vacillates
choices.B: deliberates
choices.C: intervenes
choices.D: discriminates

explanation.why: The experiments show that equally heavy objects produce different responses depending on whether they are nitrogen-rich. The colon restates the idea: the plant "responds to the chemical signature of food, not merely to contact." So the plant tells stimuli apart, which is what "discriminates" means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. To vacillate is to waver between options. The plant's response is consistent, strong for food and weak for sand, not undecided.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Deliberating means thinking something over, which implies conscious reasoning the text never attributes to the plant. It responds to chemistry, not to thought.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The plant does not step in between stimuli; it reacts to them. The sentence is about telling food from non-food, not about interrupting anything.
explanation.D: Correct. The plant responds differently to an insect fragment and to a grain of sand of the same weight, so it distinguishes between kinds of stimuli.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Cyclones that form over the Bay of Bengal can push a wall of seawater, the storm surge, across the low-lying coast of Bangladesh. Forecasting the surge has improved markedly since the 1970s, yet meteorologists caution that an accurate forecast is ______ a successful warning. A prediction issued in the capital must still reach coastal villages, be believed by people who may have little reason to trust it, and arrive early enough for families to walk to a shelter. Programs that train local volunteers to carry warnings from door to door address precisely this gap.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: no guarantee of
choices.B: a consequence of
choices.C: an obstacle to
choices.D: indistinguishable from

explanation.why: "Yet" and "caution" signal a limit: even an accurate forecast "must still" reach villages, be believed, and arrive in time. A forecast is therefore a necessary start but does not by itself ensure a successful warning, so it is "no guarantee of" one.
explanation.A: Correct. The forecast "must still" be delivered, believed, and timely, so an accurate forecast alone does not ensure that the warning succeeds.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the order of events. The forecast comes first and the warning depends on it, not the other way around.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The forecast is the basis of the warning, not something that stands in its way; the obstacles the text names are distance, distrust, and time.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text separates the two: a forecast is made in the capital, while a successful warning requires delivery, trust, and time. They are not the same thing.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Lichens, partnerships between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, can lose most of their water during a dry spell and resume photosynthesis within minutes of being wetted. This ability was long described as a kind of suspended animation, as if the lichen were simply switched off and on. More recent measurements suggest the metaphor is ______: during drying, cells rearrange their membranes and accumulate protective sugars, and after rewetting they repair damage before full activity returns, so the dry lichen is less a stopped machine than one that has prepared, at some cost, for a pause.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: antiquated
choices.B: unfalsifiable
choices.C: inexact
choices.D: apt

explanation.why: The old description was a switch turned "off and on." The measurements show preparation before drying and repair after wetting, so the lichen is "less a stopped machine" than the metaphor suggests. The metaphor is not completely wrong, but it is not accurate either; "inexact" fits.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The problem with the metaphor is its accuracy, not its age; the text does not say it has gone out of fashion.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text does not claim the metaphor cannot be tested; it reports measurements that test it and find it wanting.
explanation.C: Correct. The cells actively prepare and repair, so the lichen is "less a stopped machine" than the switch metaphor implies; the metaphor is imprecise.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The colon introduces evidence that the lichen is not simply switched off, which argues against the metaphor rather than for it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The wings of the glasswing butterfly are nearly transparent, an unusual trait among butterflies, whose wings are usually covered in pigmented scales. Transparency alone, however, would not make the insect hard to see: a smooth, clear surface reflects light, producing a glare that would ______ the butterfly to predators. The glasswing avoids this through a layer of tiny, irregularly spaced pillars on the wing surface, which reduce reflection to a small fraction of what flat glass produces. Seen against leaves or bark, the butterfly all but disappears.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: endear
choices.B: conceal
choices.C: betray
choices.D: accustom

explanation.why: The sentence explains why transparency alone "would not make the insect hard to see": a clear surface produces glare. Glare would make the butterfly visible to predators, so the blank must mean "reveal" or "give away," which "betray" means here.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The glare makes the butterfly visible, not likable; the sentence concerns being seen by predators, not winning their affection.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The glare is the problem the glasswing must avoid; it would make the butterfly easier to see, not hide it.
explanation.C: Correct. Glare would give the butterfly's position away to predators, which is why the wing's pillars that reduce reflection matter.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about predators getting used to the butterfly.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The wood frog survives northern winters by freezing: as much as two-thirds of the water in its body turns to ice, its heart stops, and in spring it thaws apparently unharmed. The frog's strategy is not to ______ freezing but to control it. As ice begins to form in its skin, the liver releases large amounts of glucose into the blood, and the sugar, taken up by cells, lowers the freezing point of the fluid inside them, so that ice forms only in the spaces between cells, where it does less damage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: regulate
choices.B: avert
choices.C: survive
choices.D: hasten

explanation.why: The sentence contrasts the blank with "control": the frog does not do one thing but does the other. Since the frog actually freezes, it does not keep freezing from happening; it directs where ice forms. The blank must mean "prevent," which is what "avert" means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Regulate" means almost the same as "control," so the sentence would contrast a word with itself instead of setting prevention against control.
explanation.B: Correct. The frog freezes rather than keeping freezing from happening, so its strategy is not to avert the freezing but to control where ice forms.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The frog does survive freezing, so a sentence saying its strategy is "not to survive" freezing contradicts the opening sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the text says the frog speeds freezing up, and the contrast with "control" requires a word for stopping the process, not accelerating it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Jumping spiders of the genus Portia hunt other spiders, often approaching a web by a roundabout path that takes them out of sight of their prey for minutes at a time before they arrive at a spot from which to attack. Because the spider must keep moving toward a goal it can no longer see, some researchers describe its behavior as planning. Others are more ______: a detour, they note, might be produced by simple rules, such as moving toward whichever route last appeared to lead upward, without any internal representation of the goal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: indifferent
choices.B: circumspect
choices.C: dismissive
choices.D: credulous

explanation.why: The first group calls the behavior "planning." The second group offers a simpler explanation, "simple rules," and uses hedged language ("might be"). They are not rejecting the planning view outright, only being cautious about it, so "circumspect" fits.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The second group engages closely with the question, offering a specific alternative; they are not uninterested.
explanation.B: Correct. The second group is careful: it points out that a simpler explanation "might" account for the detours and does not commit to planning.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is too strong. The researchers propose an alternative that "might" explain the behavior; they do not brush the planning idea aside as unworthy of consideration.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A credulous person believes too readily. The second group is slower to accept the planning claim, not quicker.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The dry zone of Sri Lanka holds thousands of small reservoirs, known as tanks, many of them built more than a thousand years ago. Engineers once studied each tank as an independent structure. Recent surveys instead treat the tanks as ______ systems: those along a single valley are linked in a cascade, so that water spilling from one feeds the next, and the fields, forests, and silt-trapping ponds between them perform functions that no single reservoir could perform alone. Restoring one tank while ignoring its neighbors, on this view, can shift problems downstream rather than solve them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: equivalent
choices.B: obsolete
choices.C: self-contained
choices.D: interdependent

explanation.why: "Instead" contrasts the new approach with studying each tank "as an independent structure." The colon explains: the tanks are linked, water from one feeds the next, and restoring one in isolation affects others. The tanks depend on one another, so they are "interdependent."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text stresses that the tanks are connected, not that they are alike; a cascade in which one feeds the next is a relationship of dependence, not sameness.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The tanks are still being restored and used; nothing in the text says they are out of date.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This describes the older view, each tank "as an independent structure," which "instead" signals the new surveys reject.
explanation.D: Correct. The tanks are "linked in a cascade," each affecting the next, so they must be studied as parts of one connected system.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the main roads of nineteenth-century British India stood dak bungalows, plain government rest houses where travelers could spend a night between stages of a journey. Memoirs of the period describe them with a mixture of gratitude and complaint: the rooms were bare, the caretaker's cooking unvarying, the furniture scarred by generations of guests. Yet the same writers concede that the bungalows were ______ to long-distance travel. Before railways, a journey of several hundred miles depended on finding shelter at predictable intervals, and the dak bungalow, whatever its discomforts, was almost always where the map said it would be.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: detrimental
choices.B: agreeable
choices.C: incidental
choices.D: indispensable

explanation.why: "Yet" and "concede" show that, despite their complaints, the writers admit something in the bungalows' favor. The final sentence explains it: long journeys "depended on" shelter at predictable intervals, which the bungalows reliably provided. So they were "indispensable" to such travel.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The writers concede a point in the bungalows' favor; saying they harmed travel would be another complaint, not a concession.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The memoirs list the bungalows' discomforts, and the sentence allows for them ("whatever its discomforts"); the point conceded is their usefulness, not their pleasantness.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Something incidental is a minor side matter, but the text says long journeys "depended on" the shelter the bungalows provided.
explanation.D: Correct. Despite their discomforts, the bungalows provided the predictable shelter that long journeys "depended on," so travelers could not do without them.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The muslin woven around Dhaka in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was so fine that European observers compared it to woven air. Its quality depended on a chain of specialized skills: spinners, often working in humid morning air that kept the fibers from snapping, drew thread from a local variety of cotton, and weavers handled that thread with tools of great delicacy. Historians argue that the craft's decline in the nineteenth century cannot be ______ a single cause. Cheaper machine-made cloth, changing fashions, and the loss of the courtly patrons who had bought the finest grades all played a part, and the disappearance of the local cotton itself made revival harder still.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: attributed to
choices.B: confused with
choices.C: divorced from
choices.D: compared with

explanation.why: The sentence after the blank lists several causes of the decline, each of which "played a part." So the decline cannot be assigned to one cause alone, which is what "attributed to" means.
explanation.A: Correct. The text names several contributing causes, so the decline cannot be credited to any single one of them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests anyone has mistaken the decline for its cause; the issue is how many causes there were.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This would mean the decline cannot be separated from one cause, the opposite of the point that many causes contributed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sentence is about what caused the decline, not about measuring the decline against something else.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Ancient writers describe the harbor of Carthage as a marvel: a rectangular commercial basin leading to a circular military harbor with an island at its center, where warships rested in covered slips. Because these accounts were written by Carthage's enemies or long after the city's destruction in 146 BCE, some scholars once treated them as ______. Excavations in the 1970s changed the picture. Archaeologists found the circular basin, the island, and the foundations of the slips roughly where the sources placed them, although the structures proved to belong to the city's later centuries rather than to its early history.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: confirmations
choices.B: exaggerations
choices.C: translations
choices.D: forgeries

explanation.why: The accounts came from enemies or much later writers, which gave scholars reason to doubt them, and the excavations "changed the picture" by confirming the main features. So the earlier view was that the descriptions overstated the harbor; "exaggerations" fits, and the final clause shows the accounts were partly, not wholly, accurate.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Confirmation is what the excavations provided later; before them, scholars doubted the accounts rather than treating them as proof.
explanation.B: Correct. Given the writers' hostility and distance in time, scholars suspected the marvelous descriptions overstated the harbor, until excavations found the features largely as described.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing in the text concerns the language of the accounts or whether they were rendered from another tongue.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is too strong. The scholars doubted the accuracy of the descriptions, not whether the texts were genuinely ancient.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Among the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois, belts of woven shell beads called wampum recorded agreements, and a belt presented at a treaty council was kept afterward as the agreement's authoritative form. Colonial officials who negotiated with the Haudenosaunee often treated the belts as ______ the written treaty text, a ceremonial gift exchanged alongside the real document. For the Haudenosaunee, the relationship was closer to the reverse: the belt, read aloud by a keeper who had memorized its meaning, was the binding record, and the paper was a translation of it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: identical to
choices.B: derived from
choices.C: incompatible with
choices.D: subordinate to

explanation.why: The phrase after the comma restates the colonial view: the belt was "a ceremonial gift" and the paper was "the real document." So officials ranked the belt below the text. The Haudenosaunee view is "the reverse," ranking the belt above. "Subordinate to" captures the colonial ranking.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The officials distinguished the belt (a gift) from the text (the real document); they did not treat the two as the same.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The idea that one record is a version of the other belongs to the Haudenosaunee view, in which the paper is "a translation" of the belt, not the colonial view.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The belts were exchanged "alongside" the documents; nothing suggests the officials saw a conflict between them.
explanation.D: Correct. The officials saw the paper as "the real document" and the belt as a ceremonial extra, so they ranked the belt below the text.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The long carnelian beads of the Indus civilization, some more than ten centimeters in length, required drilling a narrow hole through extremely hard stone. Archaeologists who reproduced the process with drills made from a stone found at Indus sites estimated that a single long bead could take many days of skilled work. Such estimates ______ the beads' presence in distant Mesopotamian royal graves: an object that demanded so much labor was precisely the kind of thing worth carrying along a long trade route and burying with a ruler.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: help explain
choices.B: postdate
choices.C: cast doubt on
choices.D: exaggerate

explanation.why: The colon gives the reasoning: because each bead took so much labor, it was "worth" transporting far and placing in a royal grave. So the labor estimates make the beads' presence in those graves understandable; they "help explain" it.
explanation.A: Correct. Knowing how much skilled labor each bead required shows why such beads were worth carrying to Mesopotamia and burying with rulers.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text draws no comparison between when the estimates were made and when the beads were buried.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The estimates make the beads' presence in the graves more understandable, not less; the colon gives a reason, not a problem.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The estimates concern labor time, and the beads' presence in the graves is an archaeological fact; an estimate of effort cannot overstate a fact of location.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The ghazal, a poetic form cultivated in Persian and Urdu, consists of couplets that share a rhyme and refrain but need not share a subject; a single poem may move from love to loss to wry philosophical observation. Translators into English have often tried to ______ this discontinuity by arranging the couplets into a narrative or thematic sequence. Scholars of the form object that the result is a different kind of poem, since much of the ghazal's pleasure lies in the leap between one self-contained couplet and the next.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: accentuate
choices.B: smooth over
choices.C: interpret
choices.D: replicate

explanation.why: The translators respond to the "discontinuity" by rearranging couplets into a sequence that connects them, which removes the leaps between couplets. They are trying to hide or reduce the discontinuity, so "smooth over" fits; the scholars' objection confirms that something of the original is lost.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Arranging the couplets into a connected sequence reduces the jumps between them rather than drawing attention to them.
explanation.B: Correct. By putting the couplets into a narrative or thematic order, the translators make the discontinuity less noticeable, which is why scholars say the leaps are lost.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is too neutral. The translators do not merely explain the discontinuity; they alter the poem to remove it, as the scholars' objection makes clear.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A translator who reproduced the discontinuity would keep the leaps between couplets, but these translators remove them by imposing a sequence.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The couplets attributed to the fifteenth-century poet Kabir circulated orally for generations before they were written down, and the manuscripts that survive disagree with one another in wording, in order, and even in which verses they include. Editors seeking an authentic text have found the goal ______. Each singer who passed the verses on adapted them to a local dialect or a favored melody, so the earliest recoverable versions are already plural, and a single original, if one ever existed, lies beyond the reach of the evidence.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: contentious
choices.B: straightforward
choices.C: elusive
choices.D: trivial

explanation.why: The editors want one authentic text, but the earliest versions are "already plural" and the original "lies beyond the reach of the evidence." The goal keeps escaping them, so it is "elusive."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes a goal that cannot be achieved, not a dispute among editors about whether to pursue it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The surviving manuscripts disagree in wording, order, and content, so establishing one authentic text is anything but simple.
explanation.C: Correct. Because the earliest versions are "already plural" and the original is "beyond the reach of the evidence," the authentic text keeps slipping away from the editors.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not say the goal is unimportant; editors pursue it seriously. The problem is that it cannot be reached.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Alexander Calder's mobiles, sculptures of balanced metal shapes that turn in moving air, pose a distinctive problem for museums. A painting can be stabilized and left alone; a mobile must move, and movement wears the wires and joints on which its balance depends. Conservators therefore cannot treat intervention as ______. Replacing a worn wire with one of a slightly different weight shifts the whole sculpture's equilibrium, and even cleaning can change how the pieces respond to a draft, so every repair is a decision about what the work should look like in motion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: routine
choices.B: infrequent
choices.C: arbitrary
choices.D: harmful

explanation.why: The sentence after the blank explains that even a small repair "shifts the whole sculpture's equilibrium" and that "every repair is a decision" about the work. Repairs therefore cannot be treated as ordinary, standard tasks, so "routine" is the precise word.
explanation.A: Correct. Because even a small change in wire weight or a cleaning alters the sculpture's balance and motion, each repair is a considered decision rather than a standard procedure.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text does not discuss how often repairs are needed; its point is about the consequences of each one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not suggest repairs are made at random; it says each is a deliberate "decision," which is why they are not routine.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says a mobile "must move" and that wear makes repair necessary; intervention is required, not something conservators should avoid as damaging.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Students of jazz learn improvised solos by transcribing recordings note for note, and published transcriptions of celebrated performances fill the shelves of music schools. Some musicians regard the practice with ______: notation, they point out, captures pitches and approximate rhythms but not the slight delays, bent tones, and shifts in attack that give a solo its character, so a student who masters a transcription has learned the outline of a performance rather than the performance itself. Few, however, propose abandoning transcription; the objection is to mistaking the page for the music.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: contempt
choices.B: indifference
choices.C: reservations
choices.D: enthusiasm

explanation.why: The musicians raise a specific limitation of transcription, but the last sentence says few want to abandon it; they object only to "mistaking the page for the music." Their attitude is doubt with qualifications, which "reservations" expresses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is too strong. Musicians who do not propose "abandoning transcription" do not despise it; they have a limited objection.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The musicians care enough to make a detailed objection; they are not uninterested in the practice.
explanation.C: Correct. The musicians have doubts about what transcription can capture, yet they do not reject the practice, which is exactly what having reservations means.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The colon introduces a criticism of what notation leaves out, not praise for the practice.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A museum's record of a tapestry's ownership, its provenance, is rarely complete, and the gaps are not evenly distributed: a work's early history may be documented in a noble household's inventories, while the decades after it entered the art market are a blur of dealers and unnamed private collections. Provenance researchers therefore treat the absence of records as ______ rather than as proof of anything. A gap may conceal a theft, but it may equally reflect a sale that no one bothered to record, and only further evidence can decide between the two.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: fabricated
choices.B: negligible
choices.C: incriminating
choices.D: inconclusive

explanation.why: A gap "may conceal a theft" or "may equally" be an unrecorded sale, and "only further evidence can decide." So a gap by itself settles nothing, which is what "inconclusive" means; the phrase "rather than as proof of anything" restates the same idea.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not suggest that gaps in the records are invented; it treats them as real but uninformative.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The researchers take gaps seriously enough to look for further evidence; they do not dismiss them as unimportant.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Treating a gap as evidence of wrongdoing would be treating it "as proof," which the sentence explicitly contrasts with the researchers' approach.
explanation.D: Correct. Because a gap could reflect either a theft or an unrecorded sale, it decides nothing on its own; "only further evidence" can.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Daguerreotypes, the earliest widely sold photographs, were fragile images on silvered copper plates, and their owners kept them in small hinged cases lined with velvet. Conservators who open these cases sometimes find pencil notes, locks of hair, or newspaper clippings tucked behind the plate. Such additions were once removed as ______ to the image. Today they are documented and kept with it, since a name written on the back of a plate may be the only record of who the sitter was, and the choice of what to tuck inside tells its own story about how the portrait was used.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: integral
choices.B: superior
choices.C: detrimental
choices.D: extraneous

explanation.why: The additions were "once removed," but "today" they are kept because they carry information about the sitter and the portrait's use. So the old view was that the notes and clippings had nothing to do with the image; "extraneous" expresses that.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If the additions had been seen as an essential part of the image, they would not have been removed; this is closer to today's view.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing suggests anyone ranked the additions above the image.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not say the notes and clippings were thought to damage the plate, only that they were treated as unrelated to it.
explanation.D: Correct. The additions were removed because they were seen as unrelated to the image; today they are kept because they turn out to carry information about it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Composed chess problems, positions constructed to be solved rather than played, are judged by standards that have little to do with competitive chess. A composer may reject a position because the winning move is too obvious, because a second, unintended solution exists, or simply because the pieces are arranged without economy. For composers, such flaws are not ______; an extra solution ruins a problem as surely as a false note ruins a melody, even though a player at the board would happily take either route to victory.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: intentional
choices.B: fatal
choices.C: trivial
choices.D: inevitable

explanation.why: The semicolon introduces the reason: an extra solution "ruins" a problem, even though a player would not mind it. So for composers these flaws are serious, not minor; "trivial" is the word the sentence denies.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The second solution is described as "unintended"; whether flaws are deliberate is not the contrast the sentence draws.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says an extra solution ruins the problem, so for composers the flaw is fatal; the sentence needs a word for what the flaws are not.
explanation.C: Correct. The flaws "ruin" a problem for composers, so composers do not regard them as minor, even though a player would.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not discuss whether such flaws can be avoided, only how seriously composers take them.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When Oren finally visited Mrs. Adeyemi, thirty years after she had taught him, he had rehearsed what he wanted to say about her influence. She listened, poured tea, and then corrected him on two dates. He laughed, and the speech he had prepared seemed suddenly ______: it had been composed for a figure in his memory, patient and faintly saintly, while the woman across the table was sharp, impatient with sentiment, and far more interested in what he was reading now than in what he had read at fourteen.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: incomplete
choices.B: overdue
choices.C: insincere
choices.D: misdirected

explanation.why: The colon explains the feeling: the speech "had been composed for a figure in his memory," not for the sharp woman actually in front of him. A speech aimed at the wrong person is "misdirected."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The speech did not lack parts; it addressed the wrong version of the teacher. The two dates she corrects do not make the speech unfinished.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Thirty years have passed, but the sentence is about whom the speech was written for, not about its lateness.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing suggests Oren did not mean what he had planned to say; the problem is that it suited his memory of her rather than the real woman.
explanation.D: Correct. The speech was written for an imagined, saintly teacher, while the real Mrs. Adeyemi is sharp and impatient with sentiment, so it was aimed at the wrong person.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The houseboat had been their aunt's, and when Lila and Marguerite found it half sunk in the reeds, they agreed, without saying so, that they would not discuss whether restoring it made sense. Sense had nothing to do with it. Over the summer they learned to ______ their expectations to the boat rather than the other way around: a cabin that would never be watertight became a porch, a stove that could not be repaired became a shelf, and the thing they launched in September was not the boat they remembered but, Lila thought, a fair argument with it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: accommodate
choices.B: apply
choices.C: attribute
choices.D: surrender

explanation.why: The colon shows what the sisters learned: when the cabin could not be made watertight, it "became a porch," and so on. They adjusted their plans to fit what the boat allowed, "rather than" forcing the boat to fit their plans. To adjust one thing to fit another is to "accommodate" it.
explanation.A: Correct. The sisters changed what they expected (a porch instead of a cabin, a shelf instead of a stove) to fit what the boat could be, adapting plans to the boat rather than the reverse.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Applying their expectations to the boat would mean imposing their plans on it, which is "the other way around," the approach the sentence rejects.
explanation.C: Incorrect. To attribute expectations to the boat would be to say the boat held them, which makes no sense; the sentence is about adjusting expectations to fit the boat.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is too extreme. The sisters did not give up their expectations entirely; they reshaped them and still launched a boat in September.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The kit had promised a working radio in an afternoon. By the third evening the twins had instead a tangle of wire, a diagram neither of them trusted, and a disagreement that had hardened into method: Tomas tested every connection twice before moving on, while Ana wired whole sections at a stretch and listened for the hiss that meant something was alive. It was Ana's section that first produced a voice, faint and in a language they did not know. Tomas pretended to be ______, but he had already begun redrawing the diagram to match what she had done.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: delighted
choices.B: unimpressed
choices.C: confused
choices.D: vindicated

explanation.why: "Pretended" and "but" signal that Tomas's outward reaction differs from his real one. His real reaction is to copy Ana's approach, which shows he is impressed. So he pretended the opposite: he pretended to be "unimpressed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. If Tomas pretended to be pleased, "but" would need to introduce a sign that he was not; instead, his redrawing shows he genuinely admired what Ana did.
explanation.B: Correct. Tomas acts as if Ana's success does not impress him, "but" his redrawing the diagram to match her work shows that it does.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing suggests Tomas failed to understand Ana's wiring; he understands it well enough to redraw the diagram around it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It was Ana's method, not Tomas's careful one, that produced the voice, so Tomas has not been proved right, and pretending otherwise would not fit the sentence.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Before dawn the town belonged to Dev and to a few others who had reasons to be awake: the baker, whose window was the only lit square on the main street; the night nurse walking home; a dog that followed his bicycle to the bridge and no farther. He had taken the paper route for the money and kept it for this hour, which seemed to him not empty but ______: every sound, the thump of a paper on a porch, a door, a train on the far side of the river, arrived separately and was given its full weight before the next one came.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: lonely
choices.B: silent
choices.C: spacious
choices.D: hurried

explanation.why: The sentence contrasts the blank with "empty" and then explains: each sound "arrived separately" and had room to be noticed before the next. The hour is not vacant but roomy, which "spacious" captures.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Dev keeps the route because he values this hour, and the sentence opposes the blank to "empty"; "lonely" would carry the emptiness the sentence denies.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The hour is full of sounds, a thump, a door, a train; what makes it special is that they arrive one at a time, not that there are none.
explanation.C: Correct. The hour has room in it: each sound arrives on its own and is "given its full weight" before the next, so the hour feels roomy rather than empty.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Each sound is given "its full weight before the next one came," the opposite of a rushed hour.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: My grandfather's model railway filled the attic, and visitors assumed it was a toy he had never outgrown. He did not correct them, but over several summers I learned that the railway was in fact ______ work: the gradients were calculated so that a loaded train would just make the climb, the bridges were built to scale from his own drawings, and when something failed he did not simply replace it but kept a notebook of why it had failed. The trains were the least of it. What he had built was a place where every problem was small enough to be solved completely.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: tedious
choices.B: playful
choices.C: exacting
choices.D: unfinished

explanation.why: "In fact" contrasts the truth with the visitors' assumption that the railway was "a toy." The colon lists calculated gradients, scale drawings, and a notebook of failures, all signs of demanding, careful work. "Exacting" fits.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The details show precision, not dullness; the narrator presents the work as absorbing, a place where problems "could be solved completely."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Playful" belongs with the visitors' idea of "a toy," which "in fact" signals the narrator is correcting.
explanation.C: Correct. Calculated gradients, scale bridges, and a notebook of failures show work that demands precision and care, the opposite of a toy.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the text says the railway was incomplete; it describes how carefully it was built and maintained.

items.subject: science
items.passage: At hydrothermal vents on the deep-sea floor, the giant tubeworm Riftia pachyptila grows to more than a meter in length despite having, as an adult, neither a mouth nor a digestive tract. Its nourishment comes from bacteria housed in a specialized internal organ; they oxidize the hydrogen sulfide seeping from the vents and use the energy to build sugars from carbon dioxide. The worm, for its part, uses an unusual hemoglobin to collect sulfide and oxygen from the water and deliver both to its tenants. The partnership is so complete that the animal is able to ______ digestion altogether, drawing everything it needs from compounds the bacteria release.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: regulate
choices.B: forgo
choices.C: replicate
choices.D: accelerate

explanation.why: The worm has "neither a mouth nor a digestive tract," and the final clause says it draws "everything it needs" from its bacteria. The blank must therefore mean "do without": the animal gives up digestion entirely, which is what "forgo" means. The word "altogether" confirms that the process is absent, not changed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Regulate" means control or adjust, which likewise assumes the worm digests food; the text says it does not.
explanation.B: Correct. To forgo something is to do without it, which fits an animal that has no gut and gets all its nourishment from bacteria.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Replicate" means copy. Nothing in the text suggests the worm reproduces digestion in another form; it simply lacks it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. An animal with no digestive tract cannot speed up digestion; "accelerate" assumes the process exists.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Delian League was formed in 478 BCE, after the Persian invasions of Greece, as an alliance of Greek city-states under Athenian leadership; its treasury was kept on the sacred island of Delos, and each member contributed ships or money to a common fleet. From the outset, however, Athens commanded that fleet and assessed what each member owed. ______ a partnership of equals, the League functioned within a few decades as something closer to an Athenian empire. Members that tried to withdraw, such as Naxos and Thasos, were compelled by force to remain; the treasury was moved to Athens in 454 BCE; and the contributions, still described as shared expenses, were in fact tribute.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: Initially
choices.B: Reluctantly
choices.C: Admittedly
choices.D: Ostensibly

explanation.why: The sentence sets up a contrast between how the League was described ("a partnership of equals") and how it "functioned" ("closer to an Athenian empire"). The blank must mark the first description as a matter of appearance only, which is what "ostensibly" means. The earlier sentence, "From the outset, however, Athens commanded that fleet," shows that the equality was never more than a label.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Initially" would mean the League really was a partnership of equals at first, but the text says Athens controlled the fleet and the assessments "from the outset."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Reluctantly" describes an unwilling attitude. The text says nothing about anyone being unwilling to form the alliance.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Admittedly" would concede that the League truly was a partnership of equals, but the text's point is that the equality was only apparent.
explanation.D: Correct. "Ostensibly" means apparently or in name, which fits a League that was called a partnership of equals while working as an Athenian empire.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. Osei had taught chemistry for thirty-one years, and in retirement he kept bees with the same temperament he had brought to the laboratory. He inspected his four hives every ninth day, never the eighth or the tenth, and recorded in a ruled notebook the weight of each, the temper of the colony, and the number of frames filled. His neighbor, who kept bees too, lifted a lid now and then and otherwise let the insects manage their own affairs; he thought Osei's methods excessive, and Osei thought his negligent. Yet it was the ______ old schoolmaster, not the easygoing neighbor, whose hives came through the hard winter intact.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: lenient
choices.B: ostentatious
choices.C: fastidious
choices.D: garrulous

explanation.why: The passage describes Osei's exacting habits: inspections "every ninth day, never the eighth or the tenth" and detailed records in "a ruled notebook." The blank contrasts him with the "easygoing neighbor," so it must mean extremely careful and particular, which is what "fastidious" means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Lenient" means easygoing or permissive, which describes the neighbor, not Osei; the sentence contrasts the two.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Ostentatious" means showy or designed to impress. Osei's notebook and schedule are private habits, not a display.
explanation.C: Correct. "Fastidious" means very attentive to detail and hard to satisfy, which matches the strict schedule and careful records that set Osei apart from his neighbor.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Garrulous" means talkative. The text describes Osei's care, not his conversation.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Peshawari chappal, the open leather sandal associated with the city of Peshawar in northern Pakistan, is still made largely by hand in small workshops. A visitor who watches one being assembled, its pieces passed from a cutter to a stitcher to a finisher at benches crowded together, might take the process for an improvised one. In fact the order of operations is fixed: the sole is cut and shaped before the straps are attached, the straps are stitched before they are trimmed, and the finisher's polish comes last, because any earlier step would mark the leather. Far from being ______, the sequence encodes the accumulated judgment of several generations of craftsmen.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: traditional
choices.B: elaborate
choices.C: laborious
choices.D: haphazard

explanation.why: The text says a visitor "might take the process for an improvised one," then corrects that impression: "In fact the order of operations is fixed." The final sentence begins "Far from being," so the blank must name the mistaken impression, disorderly or random, which is what "haphazard" means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The sequence reflects "several generations of craftsmen," so it is traditional; "far from being traditional" would contradict the text.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A process with fixed stages and reasons for each is elaborate; the text denies that it is disorderly, not that it is complex.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never argues about how much effort the work takes; it argues that the process is ordered, not improvised.
explanation.D: Correct. "Haphazard" means lacking order or plan, exactly the improvised appearance the text says is misleading.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea cucumbers, soft-bodied relatives of starfish, spend their lives swallowing sand and mud from the seafloor and extracting the organic matter mixed into it; a single animal can process many kilograms of sediment in a year. The sand that passes through them comes out cleaner and better mixed, and their constant burrowing lets oxygen reach layers that would otherwise turn stagnant. Marine ecologists have found that reefs stripped of sea cucumbers by overharvesting accumulate organic waste and lose some of their resilience. These benefits are ______ to the animals themselves, which are simply feeding, but they are substantial enough that some fisheries managers now treat sea cucumbers as a kind of maintenance crew.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: indispensable
choices.B: attributable
choices.C: incidental
choices.D: imperceptible

explanation.why: The clause "which are simply feeding" explains the blank: the cleaning and mixing happen as a side effect of the animals' feeding, not as their purpose. The blank must therefore mean "occurring by the way, as a byproduct," which is what "incidental" means. The "but" that follows contrasts this accidental origin with the benefits' importance to the reef.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Indispensable" means essential. The benefits are essential to the reef, not to the sea cucumbers, which gain nothing from cleaning the sand.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The benefits are indeed caused by the animals, but "attributable" does not fit the contrast with "simply feeding": the point is that the animals do not intend the benefits, not that they cause them.
explanation.C: Correct. "Incidental" describes something that happens as a byproduct of another activity, which fits benefits produced by animals that are "simply feeding."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Imperceptible" means too small to notice, but the text calls the benefits "substantial" and says reefs suffer without them.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The cursus publicus, the courier and transport service of the Roman state, was organized under the emperor Augustus and maintained for centuries afterward. Along the principal roads stood relay stations where official travelers could exchange tired horses for fresh ones, and larger posts offering lodging for the night. Use of the system required a written permit, and the burden of supplying animals, fodder, and drivers fell on the towns through which the roads passed, a cost they frequently complained of. The emperors tolerated the complaints but never abolished the system, because it was ______ to the work of governing an empire: orders, tax reports, and news of revolts all traveled by it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: onerous
choices.B: marginal
choices.C: integral
choices.D: comparable

explanation.why: The emperors "never abolished the system" despite the complaints, and the colon explains why: "orders, tax reports, and news of revolts all traveled by it." The blank must describe something essential to governing, which is what "integral" means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The system was indeed a burden to the towns, but the sentence gives the emperors' reason for keeping it, and a burden to governing would be a reason to abolish it, not to keep it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Marginal" means of minor importance. A system that carried orders and news of revolts, and that emperors refused to abolish, was not minor.
explanation.C: Correct. "Integral" means necessary to make a whole complete, which fits a service on which the work of governing depended.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Comparable" means similar. The sentence is about the system's importance to governing, not about a likeness between the two.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Around 1025, the Italian monk and music teacher Guido of Arezzo faced a practical problem: choirboys took years to memorize the chants they sang, because no reliable way existed to teach them to read an unfamiliar melody. Guido noticed that the six opening phrases of a well-known hymn each began one step higher than the last, on the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, and la. By having singers associate each pitch with its syllable, he gave them a ______ that could be applied to any new tune: a singer who had the hymn by heart could locate every note of an unknown melody by recalling the corresponding phrase.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: mnemonic
choices.B: ornament
choices.C: transcription
choices.D: repertoire

explanation.why: The colon explains what Guido gave his singers: a way to find "every note of an unknown melody by recalling the corresponding phrase" of a hymn they already knew. A device that helps the memory in this way is a "mnemonic." The text stresses recall ("had the hymn by heart," "recalling"), not writing or decoration.
explanation.A: Correct. A mnemonic is a memory aid; associating each pitch with a syllable from a familiar hymn let singers recall the right note for any tune.
explanation.B: Incorrect. In music an ornament is a decorative added note. The syllables help singers find pitches; they do not decorate the melody.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A transcription is a written copy of music. The text says the problem was reading unfamiliar melodies, and the solution works by memory, not by writing anything down.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A repertoire is the collection of pieces a performer knows. Guido gave the singers a tool for learning new pieces, not the pieces themselves.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Basketball players and fans alike believe in the "hot hand": the sense that a player who has made several shots in a row is more likely to make the next. A widely cited statistical analysis published in the 1980s examined shooting records and found no such pattern, and for decades the belief was cited by psychologists as a textbook case of people seeing streaks in random data. More recently, however, statisticians have shown that the method used in that analysis was subtly biased against detecting a streak, and several reanalyses of the same kind of data have found a modest hot hand after all. Taken together, the evidence remains ______: neither the believers nor the skeptics can yet claim to have been proved right.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: contrived
choices.B: conclusive
choices.C: equivocal
choices.D: anecdotal

explanation.why: The colon defines the blank: "neither the believers nor the skeptics can yet claim to have been proved right." Evidence that points both ways and settles nothing is "equivocal." The passage has shown one analysis finding no streak and later reanalyses finding "a modest hot hand," so the picture is genuinely mixed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Contrived" means artificially arranged. The text says the original method was biased, not that anyone faked or arranged the evidence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Conclusive" means decisive. The text says neither side has been proved right, so the evidence is the opposite of decisive.
explanation.C: Correct. "Equivocal" means open to more than one interpretation or inconclusive, which fits evidence that lets neither side claim victory.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Anecdotal" describes evidence based on personal stories rather than data. The text describes statistical analyses of shooting records, which are data.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In the Karachi shipping office where he had worked for twenty-two years, Mr. Fernandes occupied a desk by the window and was, by common consent, the least remarkable man in the building. He arrived before anyone else and left after; he spoke when spoken to; and the ledgers passed through his hands so quietly that the junior clerks, who had been told to learn from him, could not afterward say what they had learned. It was only when a fever kept him home for a fortnight, and the cargo manifests began to go astray, that the manager understood how much had depended on a man so ______ that his absence was the first thing about him anyone had noticed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: irreplaceable
choices.B: conspicuous
choices.C: unobtrusive
choices.D: meticulous

explanation.why: Everything in the text points to a man no one noticed: "the least remarkable man in the building," who "spoke when spoken to" and handled the ledgers "so quietly" that the clerks learned nothing. The blank is defined by its result clause, "that his absence was the first thing about him anyone had noticed," so the word must mean not attracting attention, which is what "unobtrusive" means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The office did depend on him, but being hard to replace is not what caused his absence to be the first thing noticed; the result clause needs a word about not being noticed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Conspicuous" means attracting attention, the opposite of "the least remarkable man in the building."
explanation.C: Correct. "Unobtrusive" means not noticeable, which fits a man whose absence was the first thing anyone noticed about him.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Meticulous" means very careful. His care is implied, but the sentence says he was so ______ that his absence was the first thing noticed, which describes being overlooked, not being careful.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The rock fortress of Sigiriya, in central Sri Lanka, was built in the fifth century CE by King Kashyapa, who placed his palace on the summit of a granite outcrop nearly two hundred meters high. Visitors who climb to the ruins often treat the gardens spread across the plain below as a pleasant preliminary to the main attraction. The gardens, however, were laid out on the same axis as the palace, with symmetrical pools and fountains fed by underground conduits that still run in the rainy season, and their walls and moats formed the outer line of the fortress's defenses. Archaeologists now argue that the gardens were not ______ to the royal complex but a planned part of it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: essential
choices.B: ancillary
choices.C: subsequent
choices.D: comparable

explanation.why: The text contrasts the visitors' view of the gardens as "a pleasant preliminary" with the archaeologists' view that they were "a planned part" of the complex, sharing its axis and forming its outer defenses. The blank, introduced by "not ... but," must name the lesser role the archaeologists reject: something secondary or supporting, which is what "ancillary" means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Essential" means necessary. Saying the gardens were "not essential ... but a planned part" makes no contrast, since a planned part of a fortress's defenses is essential.
explanation.B: Correct. "Ancillary" means providing support in a secondary role, which captures the dismissive view of the gardens as a mere preliminary that the archaeologists reject.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Subsequent" means coming later in time. The text does not discuss when the gardens were built relative to the palace; it discusses their importance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Comparable" means similar. The sentence is about whether the gardens belonged to the design, not about whether they resembled the palace.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Brahminy blind snake, a burrowing species about the length of a pencil, has been carried around the world in the soil of potted plants, which has earned it the nickname "flowerpot snake." Spending nearly all of its life underground, where it feeds on the eggs and larvae of ants and termites, it has little use for sight, and its eyes have become ______: two dark spots beneath translucent scales, able to register light and darkness but incapable of forming an image. Its other senses have taken over; it finds its prey by following the chemical trails that ants leave along their tunnels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: rudimentary
choices.B: acute
choices.C: redundant
choices.D: protruding

explanation.why: The colon describes the eyes: "two dark spots beneath translucent scales, able to register light and darkness but incapable of forming an image." They are simple and undeveloped but not useless, so the blank must mean basic or undeveloped, which is what "rudimentary" means.
explanation.A: Correct. "Rudimentary" means basic and undeveloped, which fits eyes reduced to light-sensing spots.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Acute" means sharp or keen, but these eyes cannot even form an image.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Redundant" means no longer needed or useless. The text says the eyes still "register light and darkness," so they retain a function, however small.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Protruding" means sticking out. The text says the eyes lie "beneath translucent scales," and nothing suggests they project.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The sixth-century historian Procopius of Caesarea wrote an account of the wars of the emperor Justinian that is measured in tone and, in its treatment of campaigns he witnessed in person, generally reliable. He also wrote a treatise praising the emperor's buildings, and a third work, circulated only after his death, in which Justinian and the empress Theodora appear as monsters of greed and cruelty. Because the same writer produced both the praise and the denunciation, historians read neither at face value. The point is not that Procopius invented his material, much of which can be checked against other sources, but that each of these works is ______, shaped to flatter or to wound rather than to weigh.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: impartial
choices.B: tendentious
choices.C: apocryphal
choices.D: fragmentary

explanation.why: The final clause defines the blank: each work is "shaped to flatter or to wound rather than to weigh." Writing that is slanted toward a purpose rather than balanced is "tendentious." The text explicitly separates this from inventing material ("not that Procopius invented his material"), so the word must concern bias, not falsehood.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Impartial" means unbiased, the opposite of works written "to flatter or to wound."
explanation.B: Correct. "Tendentious" means written to promote a particular point of view, which fits works shaped to flatter or to wound rather than to weigh.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Apocryphal" means of doubtful authenticity. The text does not question who wrote the works or whether the material is genuine; it says much of it "can be checked against other sources."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Fragmentary" means surviving only in pieces. The text says nothing about the condition of the texts, only about their slant.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The scholar al-Biruni, who traveled into northwestern India in the early eleventh century in the train of the armies of Mahmud of Ghazni, spent years learning Sanskrit and questioning Indian astronomers, mathematicians, and priests before composing his great description of the country's learning and customs. He announced at the outset that he would report what Indians themselves believed, in their own terms, and leave readers to judge; where he disagreed, he said so separately. Modern historians, who must otherwise rely on the far more partisan chronicles of the conquerors, value the work precisely for this ______ quality, though they note that al-Biruni's patience with his sources did not extend to flattering them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: credulous
choices.B: dispassionate
choices.C: cursory
choices.D: disparaging

explanation.why: The quality historians value is the one just described: al-Biruni reported Indian views "in their own terms," left readers "to judge," and kept his own disagreements separate. The text contrasts this with "the far more partisan chronicles of the conquerors." A method that keeps feeling and bias out of the account is "dispassionate."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Credulous" means too ready to believe. Al-Biruni recorded disagreements and did not flatter his sources, so he was not believing uncritically.
explanation.B: Correct. "Dispassionate" means free from bias or strong feeling, which fits reporting others' beliefs in their own terms and keeping one's own judgments separate.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Cursory" means hasty and superficial, but al-Biruni "spent years" learning Sanskrit and questioning experts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Disparaging" means belittling. Although he did not flatter his sources, his stated aim was to report their views fairly and let readers judge, not to run them down.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When Mrs. Hallam informed her, with a good deal of circumlocution, that the children were to be sent away to school and that her services would therefore no longer be required after the end of September, Miss Prior listened without interruption, thanked her employer for the notice, and inquired only whether she might take the smaller of the two globes, which had been her own purchase. Mrs. Hallam, who had rehearsed the interview expecting tears or reproaches, found herself unaccountably put out by this ______; it is one thing to dismiss a governess and quite another to discover that she regards the event as no more than a change of lodgings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: equanimity
choices.B: condescension
choices.C: indignation
choices.D: alacrity

explanation.why: Miss Prior "listened without interruption," thanked her employer, and asked a practical question, where Mrs. Hallam had expected "tears or reproaches." The final clause says the governess treats her dismissal "as no more than a change of lodgings." The blank must name this calm composure, which is what "equanimity" means.
explanation.A: Correct. "Equanimity" means calmness and evenness of mind, which fits a governess who takes her dismissal as calmly as a change of lodgings.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Condescension" means a patronizing attitude. Miss Prior thanks her employer and asks a modest question; nothing in her manner is superior.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Indignation" means anger at unfair treatment, which is the reaction Mrs. Hallam expected and did not get.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Alacrity" means cheerful eagerness. Miss Prior is composed, not eager; nothing suggests she welcomes the dismissal.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most salamanders breathe, at least in part, with lungs. The largest family of salamanders, however, has none: the lungless salamanders of the Americas take up oxygen entirely through their moist skin and the lining of the mouth. One might expect so limiting an arrangement to confine them to a sluggish existence in damp hollows, yet the family includes climbers that forage in the canopy of tropical forests, stream dwellers that hunt in fast water, and species that live out their lives in caves. The loss of lungs, it seems, does not ______ an active life so much as dictate its conditions: the skin must stay wet, the body must stay small, and the climate must stay cool.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: sustain
choices.B: guarantee
choices.C: prolong
choices.D: preclude

explanation.why: The text sets up an expectation ("One might expect ... a sluggish existence") and then overturns it with examples of climbers, stream hunters, and cave dwellers. So the loss of lungs does not rule out an active life; it only sets conditions for it. "Preclude" means rule out or make impossible.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Sustain" means support. Losing lungs does not support activity; the text's point is that it fails to prevent activity.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Guarantee" means ensure. No one expected the loss of lungs to ensure an active life; the expectation it overturns is that the loss would prevent one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Prolong" means extend in time. The text says nothing about how long these salamanders live or stay active.
explanation.D: Correct. "Preclude" means make impossible; the examples show that lacking lungs does not make an active life impossible, though it imposes conditions on it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: An albatross may spend months over the open ocean without once approaching land, and the only water available to it for most of that time is seawater, which contains far more salt than its kidneys could ever excrete. Like many seabirds, it manages this by means of a pair of glands lying in shallow grooves above the eyes. The glands draw salt from the blood and secrete it as a brine several times more concentrated than the blood itself, which drips from the tip of the beak or is shaken off. The arrangement does not merely supplement the kidneys; it ______ the bird's need for fresh water altogether, allowing it to drink the ocean it flies over.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: postpones
choices.B: regulates
choices.C: obviates
choices.D: intensifies

explanation.why: The sentence escalates from "does not merely supplement the kidneys" to something stronger, and ends with "altogether, allowing it to drink the ocean." The glands remove the need for fresh water entirely. "Obviate" means to make unnecessary.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Postpones" means delays. The word "altogether" and the ability to drink seawater show that the need is removed, not put off.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Regulates" means adjusts or controls. Controlling a need is weaker than what the sentence describes: the need is eliminated "altogether."
explanation.C: Correct. To obviate a need is to remove it; with salt glands the albatross needs no fresh water at all, since it can drink seawater.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Intensifies" means makes stronger. The glands solve the salt problem; they do not make the bird need fresh water more.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a person is cold or frightened, tiny muscles at the base of the body's hairs contract, pulling each hair upright and raising the skin around it into the small bumps commonly called goosebumps. In a furred mammal the same reflex serves a purpose: fluffed fur traps a thicker layer of air against the skin in cold weather, and a cat or dog that bristles looks larger to a rival. Humans have kept the reflex while losing nearly all of the fur, so that the response is now ______, a remnant that still fires on cue but accomplishes nothing the body needs. That it persists at all is a reminder that evolution removes only what it is pressed to remove.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: vestigial
choices.B: involuntary
choices.C: atavistic
choices.D: adaptive

explanation.why: The appositive after the comma defines the blank: "a remnant that still fires on cue but accomplishes nothing the body needs." A trait that survives from an ancestor but has lost its function is "vestigial." The contrast with the furred mammal, in which "the same reflex serves a purpose," confirms that the human version is a functionless leftover.
explanation.A: Correct. "Vestigial" describes a structure or behavior retained from ancestors that no longer serves its original function, exactly what the appositive describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The reflex is involuntary, but that is true of the furred mammal's useful reflex too; the blank must capture what changed in humans, the loss of function.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Atavistic" describes an ancestral trait that reappears after having been lost. The text says humans "have kept the reflex"; it never disappeared.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Adaptive" means useful for survival. The text says the human reflex "accomplishes nothing the body needs."

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1856, the American amateur scientist Eunice Foote reported a simple experiment. She filled glass cylinders with different gases, set them in sunlight, and recorded their temperatures. The cylinder containing carbon dioxide, which she called carbonic acid gas, grew hottest and cooled most slowly, and she remarked that an atmosphere richer in that gas would give the Earth a higher temperature. Her two-page paper, read on her behalf by a male colleague at a scientific meeting, attracted little notice, and the more precise laboratory work of John Tyndall three years later became the standard reference. Historians of science have since come to regard her remark as ______, a conclusion that would take a century to be widely accepted.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: pedantic
choices.B: derivative
choices.C: conclusive
choices.D: prescient

explanation.why: The appositive defines the blank: her remark was "a conclusion that would take a century to be widely accepted." A statement that correctly foresees what is later established is "prescient." The text stresses that she made the remark in 1856, before Tyndall's work and long before the idea was accepted.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Pedantic" means overly concerned with minor rules or details. Her remark was a broad inference about the Earth's atmosphere, not a fussy point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Derivative" means copied from earlier work. Her paper came three years before Tyndall's, so it could not have derived from the work that became the standard reference.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Conclusive" means settling a question beyond doubt. The text calls her experiment "simple," says Tyndall's work was "more precise," and says acceptance took a century, so her remark did not settle anything.
explanation.D: Correct. "Prescient" means showing knowledge of events before they happen; her 1856 remark anticipated a conclusion accepted a century later.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The remark "Let them eat cake," supposedly made by the French queen Marie Antoinette on learning that the poor had no bread, is among the most famous things ever attributed to a monarch and among the least likely to have been said by her. The anecdote appears in the Confessions of the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who wrote the relevant passage around 1765 and ascribed the words to an unnamed "great princess"; Marie Antoinette was then a child of nine living in Austria, and no one who knew her recorded her saying anything of the kind. The connection between the queen and the phrase, in short, rests on evidence so ______ that most historians treat the story as a later invention.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: partisan
choices.B: circumstantial
choices.C: ample
choices.D: tenuous

explanation.why: The text shows that the only early source names no one, was written when the queen was a child in another country, and is backed by no testimony from anyone who knew her. The link rests on almost nothing, and the result clause ("that most historians treat the story as a later invention") requires a word meaning weak or flimsy. "Tenuous" means very slight or weak.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Partisan" means biased toward a side. The text does not say the evidence is slanted; it says there is hardly any.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Circumstantial" evidence is indirect but can still be strong. The text's point is not that the evidence is indirect but that it is almost nonexistent: an unnamed princess, a child abroad, no witnesses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Ample" means plentiful, the opposite of what the text describes; plentiful evidence would not lead historians to call the story an invention.
explanation.D: Correct. "Tenuous" means thin and weak, which fits a connection that most historians reject as a later invention.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In conversations recorded late in his life, the German poet Goethe spoke of the coming of what he called world literature. He did not mean a single global style, still less the disappearance of German, French, or English writing; he meant a condition in which writers read one another across borders and let what they found alter what they wrote. He had himself been reading Persian poetry, Chinese novels, and a Sanskrit play in translation, and he argued that a literature which drew only on its own past would become ______, mistaking the habits of one place for the laws of art. The remedy was not imitation but traffic: exchange that left each tradition recognizably itself and nonetheless changed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: parochial
choices.B: obsolete
choices.C: cosmopolitan
